Course map, part 1: The first group of lessons covers the big picture: the von Neumann and Harvard models, how to measure performance correctly, Amdahl's law and design principles, how numbers are stored inside the CPU, and how the ALU does arithmetic, including multiplication, division and floating point.

Course map, part 2: The next group covers the instruction set: instruction formats, addressing modes, kinds of instructions, procedure calls and the stack, the RISC versus CISC debate, and a walk-through of a MIPS-style instruction set. Then we go inside the CPU: register transfer language, the instruction cycle, the single-cycle datapath, the control unit (hardwired and microprogrammed) and the multi-cycle datapath.

Course map, part 3: After that comes speed: pipelining, pipeline hazards and instruction-level parallelism such as superscalar and out-of-order execution. Then the memory system: the memory hierarchy, cache design in two lessons, and main and virtual memory. The course ends with input/output (interrupts and DMA) and parallel processors like multicore chips and GPUs.

What is not in this course: Gate-level design of adders and flip-flops was covered in Digital Logic Design, so we only recap it. The detailed programming of one specific chip, the Intel 8086, with its registers and assembly programs, belongs to the Microprocessors and Assembly Language course. Here we stay general: ideas that apply to every processor.

Why a stable architecture is so valuable: Companies spend years and huge amounts of money on software. If every new processor needed all programs to be rewritten, nobody would upgrade. Keeping the architecture stable while improving the organization lets old programs run on new, faster chips. The IBM System/360 family in the 1960s is famous for this: IBM sold several models at very different prices and speeds, but they all shared one architecture, so customers could move to a bigger model without rewriting their programs. That was one of the first clear separations of architecture from organization, and the x86 family has followed the same idea for decades, adding new instructions while keeping old ones working.

Real life example 1, a restaurant kitchen: Think of a busy biriyani restaurant in Old Dhaka. The menu is like the architecture. It tells customers exactly what they can order: kacchi, tehari, borhani, and so on. Customers do not care how the kitchen works. The kitchen setup is the organization: how many cooks, how many stoves, whether onions are cut by hand or by machine, how the orders move from the counter to the cooks. Two branches of the same restaurant can have the same menu but different kitchens. One branch with three stoves and an assistant to cut onions serves faster, even though the menu is identical. Same architecture, different organization, different speed.

Real life example 2, your phone and an app: When you install bKash or a game on an Android phone, the app often contains code built for the ARM instruction set, because most phones use ARM-based chips. A Samsung phone and a Xiaomi phone may use processors from different companies, with different numbers of cores, different cache sizes and different clock speeds. But because both follow the ARM architecture, the same app runs on both. The organization changes from phone to phone, so one runs the game more smoothly, but the architecture keeps everything compatible.

Common mistakes: First, thinking architecture and organization are the same thing. Remember: what versus how. Second, thinking that whether a machine has a multiply instruction is organization. It is architecture, because the programmer can use it. But whether that multiply is done by a fast special circuit or a slow repeated-add circuit is organization. Third, thinking a higher clock speed always means a faster computer. Speed also depends on how much work each clock cycle does, which we will measure in lesson 3.

What exams ask: 'Differentiate between computer architecture and computer organization with an example.' 'What is the stored-program concept?' 'List the layers of abstraction in a computer system.' 'Name the main functional units of a computer and their roles.' A good answer for the first question uses a table: architecture on one side (instruction set, addressing modes, data types, number of registers), organization on the other (control signals, interfaces, memory technology, internal bus width), plus the Intel and AMD example.

Recap: Architecture is the programmer-visible design, with the ISA as the contract between software and hardware. Organization is how the hardware carries out that contract. Computers are built in layers of abstraction, from applications down to transistors. The stored-program concept keeps instructions in memory as numbers. The CPU contains a datapath and a control unit and repeats the fetch, decode, execute cycle. Next lesson, we meet the von Neumann and Harvard models in detail.
key_points: Computer architecture is what the programmer sees: the instruction set, registers, data types, addressing modes and I/O model.
Computer organization is how the hardware carries it out: control signals, bus widths, pipeline, cache, memory technology.
The ISA is the contract between software and hardware.
Same architecture can have different organizations, like Intel and AMD chips both running x86-64.
Computers are built in layers of abstraction, from applications down to transistors.
The stored-program concept keeps instructions in memory as numbers, next to data.
The CPU has a datapath (registers, ALU) and a control unit, and repeats fetch, decode, execute.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a new feature in this course, ask yourself one question: can the programmer see this, or is it hidden inside? That single question sorts it into architecture or organization.
lessons.task: Pick two phones or laptops at home and look up their processor names. Find out which instruction set each uses (x86-64 or ARM) and how many cores and how much cache they have. Write which facts are architecture and which are organization.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of computer architecture, not organization?
quiz.explain: The instruction set is visible to the programmer, so it is architecture.

quiz.q: Intel and AMD chips both run the same Windows programs because they share the same:
quiz.explain: Both implement x86-64, so the architecture is the same while organization differs.

quiz.q: What is the stored-program concept?
options: Programs are set with cables and switches
Instructions are kept in memory as numbers, like data
Programs are stored only in the ALU
quiz.explain: The stored-program idea keeps instructions in memory so the CPU can fetch them.

quiz.q: Which part of the CPU tells the datapath what to do each clock cycle?
quiz.explain: The control unit generates the control signals for the datapath.

quiz.q: Whether multiplication uses a fast special circuit or repeated addition is an example of:
quiz.explain: The programmer just uses the multiply instruction; how it is built is organization.

lessons.title: Von Neumann and Harvard Models
lessons.content:
Picture a single narrow road leading into a busy market in Gulistan. Every rickshaw bringing goods in and every rickshaw taking goods out must use that same road. No matter how fast the shopkeepers work inside, the market can only move as much as the road allows. Now imagine a second market that has two roads: one only for incoming goods and one only for outgoing goods. That simple picture is the heart of today's lesson: the von Neumann model with one shared road to memory, and the Harvard model with two.

Where these models come from: In the 1940s, people were building the first electronic computers. ENIAC, completed in the mid 1940s in the United States, was fast for its time but had to be rewired to change its program. While working on its successor, EDVAC, a group including John von Neumann, J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly worked out the stored-program design. Von Neumann wrote it up in 1945 in a report called the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. Because his name was on that report, the design became known as the von Neumann architecture, even though several people contributed to the ideas.

The von Neumann model in one sentence: A single memory holds both instructions and data, and the CPU fetches both over the same path, one after the other. That is it. Everything else follows from this choice.

The five parts: The classic description splits a von Neumann computer into five units. First, the arithmetic and logic unit, which does calculations like add, subtract, AND and OR. Second, the control unit, which fetches instructions and decides what each part should do. Together, the ALU, registers and control unit make the CPU. Third, the memory, which stores numbers in numbered cells called addresses. Fourth, input devices, which bring data in. Fifth, output devices, which send results out. Some books merge input and output into one unit called I/O, so you may also see four units.

Key properties: Instructions and data look the same in memory, both are just binary numbers. The only thing that decides whether a number is an instruction or data is how the CPU uses it. Memory is addressed by location, not by content: you ask for address 100, and you get whatever is stored there. And execution is sequential by default: after one instruction, the CPU goes to the next address, unless an instruction like a jump or branch tells it to go somewhere else.

The IAS machine: A famous early machine built on this plan was the IAS computer at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, finished in the early 1950s. Its memory had 1,000 locations, each a 40-bit word, and each word could hold either one number or two 20-bit instructions. It had named registers that you still find, under similar names, in textbooks today: the program counter (PC), which holds the address of the next instruction; the memory address register (MAR), which holds the address to read or write; the memory buffer register (MBR), which holds the word just read or about to be written; the instruction register (IR), which holds the current opcode; and the accumulator (AC) with a helper register MQ for arithmetic results. When we trace the instruction cycle later, you will see PC, MAR, MDR (another name for MBR) and IR again.

The system bus: In a modern von Neumann style computer, the CPU, memory and I/O are joined by a set of wires called the system bus. It has three groups. The address bus carries the address the CPU wants to use; it goes one way, from the CPU out. The data bus carries the actual data, in both directions. The control bus carries signals such as read, write, clock, interrupt request and bus grant. When the CPU wants to read address 2000, it puts 2000 on the address bus, raises the read signal on the control bus, and memory answers by putting the stored value on the data bus.

Bus width matters: The number of wires in the address bus decides how much memory can be addressed. With n address lines you can make 2 to the power n different addresses. A 16-bit address bus gives 65,536 addresses, which is 64 KB if each address holds one byte. A 20-bit address bus gives 1 MB, which is what the original 8086 could reach. A 32-bit address bus gives 4 GB. The width of the data bus decides how many bits move in one transfer: a 64-bit data bus moves 8 bytes at once, twice as much as a 32-bit one.

The von Neumann bottleneck: Here is the weakness. The CPU can compute very fast, but every instruction and every piece of data must travel over the same path to and from memory. Memory is much slower than the CPU, and the path can only carry one thing at a time. So the CPU often sits waiting. The computer scientist John Backus gave this problem its famous name, the von Neumann bottleneck, in his 1977 Turing Award lecture. A big part of this course, especially caches, pipelining and the memory hierarchy, is really about clever ways to reduce this bottleneck.

A tiny example of the bottleneck: Suppose an instruction says: add the number at address 500 to the accumulator. The CPU must first read the instruction itself from memory, and then read the number at address 500, again from memory. That is two memory trips over the same bus for one small addition. If the instruction also had to store a result, that would be a third trip. The ALU addition might take a tiny fraction of the time; the waiting for memory takes the rest.

Ways to fight the bottleneck: Engineers have many tricks. Put a small, fast cache memory next to the CPU so most accesses never go all the way to main memory. Make the bus wider so each trip carries more bits. Prefetch, meaning fetch instructions or data before they are needed. Keep more values in registers inside the CPU so fewer memory trips are needed. Overlap work with pipelining so the CPU does something useful while waiting. And use separate paths for instructions and data, which brings us to the Harvard model.

The Harvard model: The Harvard architecture uses two separate memories: one for instructions and one for data, each with its own bus. The name comes from the Harvard Mark I, an electromechanical computer from 1944 that read its instructions from punched paper tape while keeping data in separate storage. Because there are two paths, the CPU can fetch the next instruction and read or write data at the same time. That removes one big part of the bottleneck.

Harvard pros and cons: The good side is speed and simplicity of parallel access: one instruction fetch and one data access can happen in the same cycle. Instruction memory and data memory can even have different word sizes; for example, a microcontroller may use 14-bit or 16-bit instruction words but 8-bit data. The bad side is flexibility. You must decide in advance how much memory is for code and how much is for data, and it is harder for a program to treat code as data, for example to load a new program from a file and then run it. Two sets of buses also mean more wires and pins.

Where Harvard is used: Many small microcontrollers, like the AVR chips used on Arduino Uno boards and many PIC chips, use a Harvard design with separate flash memory for the program and RAM for data. Many digital signal processors (DSPs), which do lots of multiply and add work on audio or radio signals, also use Harvard-style memories to feed data quickly.

The modified Harvard architecture: Most laptop, desktop and phone processors today use a mix. Main memory (the RAM chips) is shared, von Neumann style, so programs and data live in one big space and the operating system can load any program. But inside the CPU, the closest and fastest level of cache is split into two: an L1 instruction cache and an L1 data cache. So at the level that matters most for speed, the CPU behaves like a Harvard machine and can fetch an instruction and access data in the same cycle. This combination is often called a modified Harvard architecture. When an exam asks which model modern computers use, the safest answer is: von Neumann at the main memory level, with split instruction and data caches inside the CPU.

Comparison in short: von Neumann has one memory and one bus for both code and data; it is simple, flexible and cheaper, but suffers from the bottleneck. Harvard has separate memories and buses; it allows simultaneous instruction fetch and data access and is faster for that reason, but it is less flexible and needs more hardware. Modified Harvard keeps a shared main memory but splits the caches.

Real life example 1, a school canteen: Think of a school canteen with only one counter. Students who come to buy food and the staff who bring new trays of shingara from the kitchen both use that one counter. While new trays are being placed, nobody can be served. That is von Neumann: one path for both. Now imagine the kitchen gets a back door straight to the shelves, so new trays come in from the back while students are served at the front. That is Harvard: two separate paths working at the same time. Many canteens use a mix: one big storeroom (shared main memory) but a separate small shelf for snacks and one for drinks right behind the counter (split L1 caches).

Real life example 2, an Arduino project: A student in Rajshahi builds a soil-moisture alarm with an Arduino Uno for her family's rooftop garden. Her program is stored in the chip's flash memory, which holds the code even when power is off. The moisture readings and counters live in a small separate RAM. Because the ATmega328P chip on that board uses a Harvard design, it can fetch the next instruction from flash while working with data in RAM. Her laptop, which she uses to write and upload the code, keeps code and data together in its main memory but has split L1 caches: a modified Harvard design.

Common mistakes: First, thinking Harvard means two CPUs. It means two memories and two paths, still one CPU. Second, saying modern PCs are pure Harvard because of split caches. Main memory is still shared. Third, thinking the von Neumann bottleneck is about the ALU being slow. It is about the single path between CPU and memory. Fourth, mixing up which bus is one-directional: the address bus normally goes out from the CPU, while the data bus goes both ways.

What exams ask: 'Draw and explain the von Neumann architecture.' 'What is the von Neumann bottleneck and how is it reduced?' 'Differentiate between von Neumann and Harvard architecture.' 'How much memory can a CPU address with a 24-bit address bus?' The answer to the last one is 2 to the power 24, which is 16,777,216 addresses, or 16 MB if memory is byte-addressable. For the bottleneck question, mention caches, split instruction and data caches, wider buses, prefetching and pipelining.

Recap: The von Neumann model keeps instructions and data in one memory and uses one path to reach it. It has an ALU, control unit, memory, input and output, connected by address, data and control buses. Its weakness is the von Neumann bottleneck. The Harvard model uses separate instruction and data memories and buses, allowing parallel access. Modern processors are modified Harvard: shared main memory with split L1 caches. Next lesson, we learn how to measure how fast a computer really is.
key_points: Von Neumann model: one memory for both instructions and data, reached over one shared path.
Five classic units: ALU, control unit, memory, input and output.
The system bus has an address bus (out from CPU), a data bus (both ways) and a control bus.
n address lines can address 2^n locations; 32 bits gives 4 GB of byte addresses.
The von Neumann bottleneck is the single slow path between a fast CPU and memory.
Harvard model: separate instruction and data memories and buses, so fetch and data access can overlap.
Modern CPUs are modified Harvard: shared main memory with split L1 instruction and data caches.
lessons.tip: Draw the von Neumann diagram from memory at least three times: CPU (ALU plus control plus registers), memory, I/O, and the three buses. Exams love this diagram, and once your hand knows it, the rest of the lesson sticks.
lessons.task: Work out how many bytes can be addressed with 8, 16, 20, 24 and 32 address lines (2 to the power n each). Write them in a table, then convert each to KB, MB or GB.

quiz.q: In the von Neumann model, instructions and data are stored:
quiz.explain: Von Neumann keeps both in one memory and uses one path.

quiz.q: Which bus normally carries signals in only one direction, out from the CPU?
quiz.explain: The CPU sends addresses out; data can flow both ways.

quiz.q: How many locations can a 20-bit address bus reach?
quiz.explain: 2 to the power 20 is 1,048,576, which is 1 MB of bytes.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of the Harvard architecture?
options: Instruction fetch and data access can happen at the same time
It is easier to load programs as data
It removes the need for an ALU
quiz.explain: Separate paths for code and data allow parallel access.

quiz.q: A typical modern laptop CPU is best described as:
options: Pure von Neumann with no caches
Modified Harvard: shared main memory, split L1 caches
quiz.explain: Main memory is shared, but L1 instruction and data caches are separate.

lessons.title: Measuring Performance
lessons.content:
Two friends are arguing in a tea stall in Mirpur. One says his laptop is faster because it runs at 3.5 GHz. The other says hers is faster because it has eight cores. A third friend, who just finished this lesson, laughs and asks: faster at what, and measured how? That question is the whole point of today. Speed sounds simple, but measuring it correctly is one of the first real skills of a computer architect, and many advertisements get it wrong on purpose.

What performance means: For one program, the most honest measure of performance is execution time, the time from start to finish. Shorter time means better performance. So we define performance as 1 divided by execution time. If computer A runs a program in 10 seconds and computer B runs the same program in 15 seconds, then A is 15 divided by 10, which is 1.5 times faster than B. Notice the trick: to compare speed, divide the slower time by the faster time.

Response time and throughput: There are two kinds of speed. Response time, also called latency, is how long one job takes. Throughput is how many jobs finish per unit of time, like web requests per second. A phone user cares about response time: how fast does the app open? A server at a bank cares a lot about throughput: how many transactions per second? Making one job faster usually improves both. Adding more processors may improve throughput without making any single job faster.

Clock basics: A processor is driven by a clock, a signal that ticks at a fixed rate. Each tick is one clock cycle. The clock rate is measured in hertz, ticks per second; 2 GHz means 2 billion cycles per second. The clock cycle time, also called clock period, is 1 divided by the clock rate. At 2 GHz, the cycle time is 0.5 nanoseconds. At 4 GHz, it is 0.25 nanoseconds. All the hardware work, like moving data between registers, is lined up with these ticks.

CPI, cycles per instruction: Different instructions take different numbers of clock cycles. A simple add may take 1 cycle in a simple design, a load from memory may take more, a divide may take many. CPI is the average number of clock cycles per instruction for a program. It depends on the hardware design and on the mix of instructions the program uses. Its upside-down version, IPC, instructions per cycle, is used for modern processors that can finish more than one instruction per cycle; an IPC of 2 means a CPI of 0.5.

The CPU time equation: This is the most important formula of the lesson. CPU time equals instruction count times CPI times clock cycle time. Since cycle time is 1 over clock rate, you can also write: CPU time equals instruction count times CPI divided by clock rate. In words: how many instructions, times how many cycles each takes on average, times how long each cycle is. Every speed trick in this course attacks one of these three factors.

Worked example 1: A program runs 1 billion instructions. The average CPI is 2. The clock rate is 2 GHz. CPU time equals 1,000,000,000 times 2 divided by 2,000,000,000, which is exactly 1 second. If an engineer reduces the CPI to 1.5 without changing anything else, the time becomes 0.75 seconds, so the new design is 1 divided by 0.75, about 1.33 times faster.

Worked example 2, why clock rate alone lies: Machine A runs at 2 GHz with CPI 2.0 for a program. Machine B runs at 3 GHz with CPI 3.6 for the same program, same instruction count. Time per instruction on A is 2.0 divided by 2 GHz, which is 1 nanosecond. Time per instruction on B is 3.6 divided by 3 GHz, which is 1.2 nanoseconds. So A is 1.2 divided by 1, which is 1.2 times faster, even though B has the higher clock. A higher clock that needs many more cycles per instruction can lose.

Weighted CPI: When a program uses different kinds of instructions, you compute the average CPI by weighting each kind by how often it appears. Suppose 50 percent of instructions are ALU operations with CPI 1, 30 percent are loads and stores with CPI 2, and 20 percent are branches with CPI 3. Average CPI equals 0.5 times 1 plus 0.3 times 2 plus 0.2 times 3, which is 0.5 plus 0.6 plus 0.6, giving 1.7. If this program runs 2 billion instructions at 1 GHz, time equals 2 billion times 1.7 divided by 1 billion, which is 3.4 seconds.

Who affects which factor: The algorithm affects instruction count (a better algorithm does fewer steps) and sometimes CPI. The programming language and compiler affect instruction count and CPI, because they choose which instructions to use. The instruction set architecture affects all three. The organization (pipeline, caches) affects CPI and clock rate. The transistor technology mainly affects clock rate. This table is a classic exam question, so learn it as a story: software decides how many, hardware decides how long.

Elapsed time versus CPU time: When you time a program with a stopwatch, you get the elapsed time, also called wall-clock time. It includes everything: waiting for the disk, waiting for the network, and time the operating system spends running other programs. CPU time counts only the time the processor actually spends on your program. The CPU time equation above gives CPU time. For comparing processor designs we use CPU time, but the user in the end feels elapsed time, so a fast CPU with a slow disk can still feel slow.

MIPS and why it misleads: MIPS means millions of instructions per second. It equals instruction count divided by execution time times one million, or equivalently clock rate divided by CPI times one million. It sounds like a nice single number, but it has three problems. It ignores what each instruction does, so you cannot compare machines with different instruction sets. It changes from program to program on the same machine. And it can even go up while real performance goes down.

MIPS trap, worked: A 1 GHz machine runs two compiled versions of the same program. Version X uses 2 billion simple instructions, all with CPI 1. Time is 2 seconds, and MIPS is 2,000 million divided by 2, which is 1,000 MIPS. Version Y uses only 1 billion instructions but with CPI 1.5. Time is 1 billion times 1.5 divided by 1 billion, which is 1.5 seconds, and MIPS is 1,000 million divided by 1.5, about 667 MIPS. Version Y is faster in real time but has a lower MIPS rating. If you trusted MIPS, you would pick the slower version. A similar warning applies to FLOPS, floating-point operations per second, when it is quoted as a peak number the machine almost never reaches on real programs.

Benchmarks: The honest way to compare computers is to run real programs. A benchmark is a set of programs chosen to represent real work. The best known for processors is SPEC CPU, from the Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation, with integer and floating-point suites made from real applications such as compilers, compression and scientific codes. For each program, you compute a SPEC ratio: the time on a fixed reference machine divided by the time on your machine. Bigger is better.

Why the geometric mean: To combine many ratios into one score, SPEC uses the geometric mean: multiply all n ratios together and take the nth root. For example, ratios 2 and 8 give a geometric mean of the square root of 16, which is 4. The geometric mean has a useful property: when comparing two machines, the result does not depend on which reference machine you chose. The arithmetic mean of ratios does not have this property. For averaging raw execution times of a workload, though, the arithmetic mean of times is fine, because total time is what the user feels.

Other benchmarks: There are benchmarks for many fields. Phone reviewers use apps like Geekbench and AnTuTu. Graphics cards are tested with game frame rates. Servers are tested with transaction benchmarks. The rule is always the same: the best benchmark is the program you will actually run. A computer that wins at video games may not win at running a database.

The power wall: For many years, chip makers made processors faster mostly by raising the clock rate. The power used by switching transistors, called dynamic power, is roughly proportional to the capacitive load times the square of the voltage times the switching frequency. So higher frequency means more power and more heat. Engineers kept lowering the voltage to compensate, but voltage could not keep dropping, because transistors start leaking current and become unreliable. Around 2004 and 2005, chips hit a wall: they could not be cooled cheaply if clocks kept rising. Desktop clock rates have stayed in the few gigahertz range since then, and the industry turned to putting multiple cores on one chip instead.

A quick power calculation: Suppose a new chip lowers voltage by 15 percent and frequency by 15 percent, with the same capacitive load. New power relative to old equals 0.85 squared times 0.85, which is 0.85 cubed, about 0.61. So the chip uses about 61 percent of the old power, a saving of almost 40 percent, while running 15 percent slower clocks. This is why phones lower their clock and voltage when the battery is low.

Real life example 1, buying a laptop in Elephant Road: A student is choosing between two laptops for programming and video editing. The seller praises the clock speed of one model. The smart student instead looks up benchmark results for the actual work: compile times, video export times, maybe a well-known benchmark score. She finds the laptop with the slightly lower clock exports her videos faster, because it has a newer design with lower CPI and more cores that the video software can use. She saves money and gets better real performance.

Real life example 2, a bKash style payment server: A payment company in Dhaka cares about two numbers on Eid day, when millions of people send money home. Response time: each payment should finish in about a second so users are happy. Throughput: the system must handle a huge number of transactions per second. Adding more servers raises throughput. Making the database code use fewer instructions or fewer memory trips lowers response time. The engineers test both with benchmarks that copy real Eid-day traffic, not with a single MIPS number.

Common mistakes: First, comparing speed by subtracting times instead of dividing. Second, believing that higher clock means faster, forgetting CPI and instruction count. Third, mixing up CPI and IPC. Fourth, using MIPS to compare machines with different instruction sets. Fifth, forgetting units: 1 ns is 10 to the power minus 9 seconds, and GHz means 10 to the power 9.

What exams ask: 'Write the CPU performance equation and explain each term.' 'Given CPI for each instruction class and their frequencies, find average CPI and execution time.' 'Machine A has clock X and CPI Y, machine B has ... which is faster and by how much?' 'Why is MIPS a misleading metric?' 'What is the power wall?' Always show the formula first, then plug in numbers with units.

Recap: Performance is 1 divided by execution time. CPU time equals instruction count times CPI times clock cycle time. Clock rate alone does not decide speed. Weighted CPI averages over the instruction mix. MIPS can mislead; real benchmarks like SPEC, combined with the geometric mean, are better. The power wall stopped endless clock increases and pushed the world toward multicore. Next lesson, Amdahl's law tells us how much any single improvement can really help.
key_points: Performance = 1 / execution time; A is (time B / time A) times faster than B.
CPU time = instruction count x CPI x clock cycle time = IC x CPI / clock rate.
Clock rate alone does not decide speed; CPI and instruction count matter too.
Average CPI is weighted by how often each instruction class appears.
MIPS ignores what instructions do and can rise while real speed falls.
SPEC benchmarks use ratios to a reference machine combined with the geometric mean.
Dynamic power grows with C x V^2 x f; the power wall pushed the industry to multicore.
lessons.tip: Write the CPU time equation at the top of every problem before doing anything else, and put units on every number. Most mistakes in this chapter are unit mistakes, not idea mistakes.
lessons.task: Make your own exam question: invent an instruction mix with three classes, give each a CPI and a percentage, pick a clock rate and an instruction count, then compute the average CPI and the execution time. Then change one number and see how much the time changes.

quiz.q: A program has 2 billion instructions, CPI 1.5 and a 3 GHz clock. What is the CPU time?
quiz.explain: 2e9 x 1.5 / 3e9 = 1 second.

quiz.q: Machine A: 2 GHz, CPI 2. Machine B: 3 GHz, CPI 3.6. Same program. Which is faster?
options: B, because of the higher clock
quiz.explain: A: 1 ns per instruction; B: 1.2 ns. A is 1.2 times faster.

quiz.q: Mix: 50% CPI 1, 30% CPI 2, 20% CPI 3. Average CPI?
Why is MIPS a poor way to compare computers?
options: It ignores how much work each instruction does
quiz.explain: Different instruction sets do different amounts of work per instruction.

quiz.q: What mainly caused the power wall around 2004-2005?
options: Power and heat rose with clock rate and voltage could not keep falling
quiz.explain: Dynamic power grows with V^2 x f, and cooling limits were reached.

lessons.title: Amdahl's Law and Design Principles
lessons.content:
Imagine your daily trip to school takes 60 minutes: 50 minutes stuck in a bus in Dhaka traffic and 10 minutes walking from the bus stop. Your uncle offers you a super-fast bicycle that makes the walking part four times faster. Great, but how much faster is the whole trip? The walk drops from 10 minutes to 2.5 minutes, so the total becomes 52.5 minutes instead of 60. Only about 14 percent faster overall, even though one part became four times faster. The traffic part did not change, so it limits everything. This simple idea has a famous name in computer architecture: Amdahl's law.

Who Amdahl was: Gene Amdahl was a computer architect who worked at IBM, including on the System/360 family. In 1967 he presented an argument about the limits of speeding up computers with parallel processors. His reasoning was turned into the simple formula we use today. It applies to any improvement, not only parallel processing: a faster ALU, a better cache, a new instruction, or more cores.

Speedup: First, the word speedup. Speedup is old execution time divided by new execution time. If a program took 10 seconds before an improvement and 4 seconds after, the speedup is 10 divided by 4, which is 2.5. A speedup of 1 means no change. A speedup below 1 means the change made things slower.

The formula: Suppose a fraction f of the original execution time can be improved, and that part gets s times faster. The rest, 1 minus f, stays the same. The new time, as a fraction of the old time, is (1 minus f) plus f divided by s. So the overall speedup equals 1 divided by ((1 minus f) plus f over s). Read it slowly: the unchanged part stays at full size, and only the improved part shrinks.

Worked example 1: In a program, 80 percent of the time is spent doing floating-point work. A new floating-point unit makes that part 4 times faster. So f is 0.8 and s is 4. New time fraction equals 0.2 plus 0.8 divided by 4, which is 0.2 plus 0.2, giving 0.4. Overall speedup equals 1 divided by 0.4, which is 2.5. Not 4, because 20 percent of the time was untouched.

The limit: What if we could make the improved part infinitely fast? Then f over s becomes zero, and the speedup becomes 1 divided by (1 minus f). In the example above, that is 1 divided by 0.2, which is 5. So no matter how much money we spend on floating point, this program can never run more than 5 times faster. This is the most important message of Amdahl's law: the part you do not improve sets a hard ceiling.

Worked example 2, the school trip: Using the opening story, f is 10 out of 60, about 0.167, and s is 4. New fraction equals 0.833 plus 0.167 divided by 4, which is 0.833 plus 0.042, about 0.875. Speedup is 1 divided by 0.875, about 1.14. That matches the 52.5 minutes we found directly. Even an infinitely fast bicycle would give at most 1 divided by 0.833, which is 1.2.

Amdahl's law for multiple processors: Now suppose a fraction f of a program can run in parallel on n processors, and the rest is serial, meaning it must run on one processor. Then speedup equals 1 divided by ((1 minus f) plus f over n). If 90 percent is parallel and we use 10 processors: 1 divided by (0.1 plus 0.09), which is 1 divided by 0.19, about 5.26. With 100 processors: 1 divided by (0.1 plus 0.009), about 9.17. With infinitely many: at most 10. Going from 10 to 100 processors, ten times the hardware, did not even double the speedup.

Working backwards: Exams often ask the reverse question: how much must one part improve to reach a target? Say 60 percent of the time can be improved, and we want an overall speedup of 2. We need (1 minus 0.6) plus 0.6 over s to equal 0.5. So 0.4 plus 0.6 over s equals 0.5, which gives 0.6 over s equals 0.1, so s equals 6. The improved part must become 6 times faster. Now try a case where only 40 percent can be improved and we want speedup 2: we need 0.6 plus 0.4 over s to equal 0.5, but 0.6 is already bigger than 0.5. Impossible, no matter what s is.

Several improvements at once: The same idea works when two separate parts are improved. Each improved part shrinks by its own factor, and the untouched part stays. Suppose 30 percent of the time is made 2 times faster and a different 20 percent is made 4 times faster. The new time fraction is 0.5 (untouched) plus 0.3 divided by 2 plus 0.2 divided by 4, which is 0.5 plus 0.15 plus 0.05, giving 0.7. Overall speedup is 1 divided by 0.7, about 1.43. The key rule: the fractions must not overlap, and together with the untouched part they must add up to 1.

Gustafson's view: Amdahl's law assumes the problem size stays fixed. In 1988, John Gustafson pointed out that when people get more processors, they often solve bigger problems in the same time, like a weather model with a finer grid. In that case the parallel part grows while the serial part stays small, and speedup can grow nearly in step with the number of processors. Both views are correct; they answer different questions. Amdahl: how much faster can I solve this fixed problem? Gustafson: how much bigger a problem can I solve in the same time?

Design principle 1, make the common case fast: Amdahl's law tells architects where to spend effort. Improve what takes most of the time. If loads and adds appear in almost every program, make them fast before worrying about a rarely used instruction. The common case is also often simpler, so making it fast is cheaper. This principle explains many choices you will meet: fast simple instructions in RISC designs, caches for frequently used data, and branch prediction for loops that repeat many times.

Design principle 2, the principle of locality: Programs do not use memory randomly. Temporal locality means that if a program uses an item now, it will probably use it again soon, like a loop counter used in every loop round. Spatial locality means that if a program uses an item, it will probably use nearby items soon, like the next elements of an array, or the next instructions in a straight line of code. Locality is the reason caches and the memory hierarchy work, and it gets its own lessons later.

Design principle 3, parallelism: Doing several things at the same time is one of the most powerful tools. It appears at many levels. Bit-level: a 64-bit adder adds 64 bits at once instead of one by one. Instruction-level: pipelining and superscalar processors overlap instructions. Data-level: one instruction works on many numbers at once, as in SIMD and GPUs. Thread-level and processor-level: several cores run different threads. Amdahl's law reminds us that parallelism helps only the part of the work that can be split.

Design principle 4, pipelining and prediction: Pipelining is a special form of parallelism where a task is split into stages, like an assembly line, so different items are in different stages at the same time. Prediction means guessing what will happen, for example whether a branch will be taken, and starting work early; if the guess is usually right and fixing a wrong guess is not too expensive, the machine gains speed. Both get their own lessons.

Design principle 5, hierarchy and redundancy: A hierarchy of memories puts the fastest, smallest, most expensive memory closest to the processor and slower, bigger, cheaper memory further away, so that most accesses are fast while total storage stays large. Redundancy means adding extra parts, like spare disks or error-correcting bits in memory, so the system keeps working when something fails. This matters for servers that must never stop.

Moore's law as a design driver: In 1965, Gordon Moore, later a co-founder of Intel, observed that the number of components on a chip was doubling regularly; in 1975 he revised the pace to about every two years. This became known as Moore's law. It is an observation about industry progress, not a law of nature, and it has slowed in recent years. For decades, it meant architects had to design for the chip that would exist when their project finished, not the chip of today, because a design takes years.

Real life example 1, a garment factory: A garment factory in Gazipur finds that sewing takes 70 percent of the time to make a shirt, cutting takes 20 percent and packing takes 10 percent. The owner buys new sewing machines that make sewing twice as fast. Speedup equals 1 divided by (0.3 plus 0.7 divided by 2), which is 1 divided by 0.65, about 1.54. A manager suggests buying a super packing machine instead. Even if packing became instant, speedup would be 1 divided by 0.9, about 1.11. Amdahl's law shows clearly that the sewing upgrade was the smarter choice: make the common case fast.

Real life example 2, many people cooking for a wedding: A family in Sylhet is cooking for a big wedding. Cutting onions, washing rice and marinating meat can be split among many relatives, so that part is parallel. But the biriyani must cook in one big pot for a fixed time, and only one experienced cook can manage the dum. If the shared work takes 2 hours and the dum takes 1 hour, then with one person the total is 3 hours. With 4 helpers sharing the preparation, it is 0.5 plus 1, so 1.5 hours, a speedup of 2. Even with 100 helpers, it can never be less than 1 hour, a maximum speedup of 3. The pot is the serial part.

Common mistakes: First, multiplying the improvement directly, saying a 4 times faster unit makes the program 4 times faster. Second, forgetting that f is a fraction of time, not a fraction of instructions; a part with few instructions can still take a lot of time. Third, using the wrong f after the improvement: f must be measured before the improvement. Fourth, forgetting the ceiling of 1 divided by (1 minus f).

What exams ask: 'State and derive Amdahl's law.' 'A program spends X percent of time in a part that is made Y times faster; find the overall speedup.' 'What is the maximum speedup possible?' 'How many times faster must a part become to achieve speedup Z?' 'Explain the principle of locality with examples.' 'List the great ideas of computer architecture.' Always write the formula, define f and s, and check that your answer is below the ceiling.

Recap: Speedup is old time divided by new time. Amdahl's law says overall speedup equals 1 divided by ((1 minus f) plus f over s), and the maximum possible is 1 divided by (1 minus f). The unimproved part limits everything, including parallel speedup on many processors. Gustafson reminds us that bigger problems can use more processors well. The key design principles are: make the common case fast, use locality, use parallelism, pipelining and prediction, build memory hierarchies, and add redundancy for dependability. Next lesson, we look at how numbers are actually stored inside the CPU.
key_points: Speedup = old execution time / new execution time.
Amdahl's law: speedup = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / s), where f is the improved fraction of time.
The maximum speedup is 1 / (1 - f); the unimproved part sets a hard ceiling.
With n processors and parallel fraction f: speedup = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / n).
Gustafson: if the problem grows with the processors, speedup can grow nearly with n.
Make the common case fast; spend effort where the time is spent.
Locality (temporal and spatial), parallelism, pipelining, prediction, memory hierarchy and redundancy are core design ideas.
lessons.tip: Before any Amdahl problem, write two numbers in a box: f (fraction of OLD time that improves) and s (how much faster it gets). Then also write the ceiling 1/(1-f). If your answer is ever above that ceiling, you made a mistake.
lessons.task: Time one of your daily routines, like getting ready for school, and split it into parts with minutes for each. Pick one part and imagine making it 3 times faster. Use Amdahl's law to compute the overall speedup, then check it by adding the new minutes directly.

quiz.q: 80% of a program's time is improved to run 4 times faster. Overall speedup?
If 75% of the time can be sped up without limit, what is the maximum overall speedup?
90% of a program is parallel. Speedup with 10 processors is about:
60% of time can be improved. How much faster must that part get for an overall speedup of 2?
A loop counter used again and again in every round is an example of:
quiz.explain: Reusing the same item soon is temporal locality.

lessons.title: Data Representation for the CPU
lessons.content:
Imagine the shopkeeper at your local mudi dokan writes prices in a notebook with exactly three boxes for each number. He can write any price from 0 to 999 taka. One day a customer buys goods worth 1,250 taka. There is no fourth box, so he writes 250, and the account is wrong. Computers have exactly this problem. Every number lives in a fixed number of boxes, called bits, and the way we use those bits decides which numbers fit, how negative numbers look, and how fractions are stored. That is today's lesson: how the CPU actually sees data.

Bits, bytes and words: A bit is a single 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits, and almost all modern computers give a separate address to each byte, which is called byte-addressable memory. A word is the natural unit of data the processor works with, usually the size of its registers. In MIPS and 32-bit ARM, a word is 32 bits, which is 4 bytes. Most modern laptops and phones use 64-bit processors, whose general registers hold 64 bits. Be careful: different families use the word word differently. In Intel x86 documentation, a word means 16 bits for historical reasons, a doubleword is 32 bits and a quadword is 64 bits.

How many values fit: With n bits you can make 2 to the power n different patterns. With 8 bits, 256 patterns. With 16 bits, 65,536. With 32 bits, about 4.29 billion. With 64 bits, about 18.4 billion billion. How we interpret those patterns depends on the data type.

Unsigned integers: If all patterns mean non-negative numbers, n bits hold 0 up to 2 to the power n minus 1. So 8 bits hold 0 to 255, 16 bits hold 0 to 65,535 and 32 bits hold 0 to 4,294,967,295. Unsigned numbers are used for things that can never be negative, like memory addresses, pixel colours or counts.

Signed integers with two's complement: You learned two's complement in Digital Logic Design, so here is just a quick recap. The leftmost bit has a negative weight. For 8 bits, the weights are minus 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. So 11111011 is minus 128 plus 64 plus 32 plus 16 plus 8 plus 2 plus 1, which is minus 5. To negate a number, flip all bits and add 1. The range for n bits is minus 2 to the power n minus 1, up to 2 to the power n minus 1, minus 1. For 8 bits that is minus 128 to 127; for 16 bits minus 32,768 to 32,767; for 32 bits minus 2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. Almost every modern processor uses two's complement because the same adder circuit works for signed and unsigned numbers.

Integer overflow: When a result does not fit, it wraps around. In 8-bit signed arithmetic, 127 plus 1 gives the pattern 10000000, which means minus 128. In 8-bit unsigned arithmetic, 255 plus 1 gives 0. The hardware usually sets a flag to warn about this, which we will meet in the arithmetic lesson, but many languages like C silently ignore it. A famous real case: in 2014, the view counter of a very popular music video on YouTube passed 2,147,483,647, the maximum of a 32-bit signed integer, and YouTube had to move to a 64-bit counter.

Sign extension: Often a small number must be placed into a bigger register, for example an 8-bit value loaded into a 32-bit register. For an unsigned value, we fill the new upper bits with 0; this is zero extension. For a signed value, we copy the sign bit into all the new upper bits; this is sign extension. Example: minus 5 in 8 bits is 11111011. Sign-extended to 16 bits, it becomes 1111111111111011, still minus 5. Plus 5 is 00000101, and becomes 0000000000000101. If you zero-extended minus 5 by mistake, you would get 0000000011111011, which is 251, a completely different number. Instruction sets often have two versions of load-byte instructions for exactly this reason, one that sign-extends and one that zero-extends.

Characters: Text is also stored as numbers. ASCII uses 7 bits for English letters, digits and symbols: capital A is 65, small a is 97, and the digit 0 is 48. Unicode gives a number, called a code point, to characters of almost all world scripts, including Bangla. The Bangla letter অ is code point U+0985, in a block reserved for Bengali script. A common way to store Unicode is UTF-8, which uses 1 byte for ASCII characters and more bytes for others; Bangla letters take 3 bytes each in UTF-8. That is why a Bangla message often uses more bytes than an English message of the same length.

Endianness: A 32-bit word takes 4 bytes, but in which order are they placed in memory? Take the hexadecimal number 12345678 stored at address 100. In big-endian order, the most significant byte goes first: address 100 holds 12, 101 holds 34, 102 holds 56 and 103 holds 78. In little-endian order, the least significant byte goes first: address 100 holds 78, 101 holds 56, 102 holds 34 and 103 holds 12. The names come from Gulliver's Travels, where two groups fought over which end of a boiled egg to break first.

Who uses which: Intel and AMD x86 processors are little-endian. Most ARM processors can run either way but are almost always used in little-endian mode. Network protocols like TCP/IP send multi-byte numbers in big-endian order, called network byte order. Some older processors like the Motorola 68000 and many IBM mainframes are big-endian. Endianness only matters when you look at the individual bytes of a bigger number: when you send data to another machine, read a binary file made elsewhere, or inspect memory in a debugger.

Alignment: Many processors read memory fastest, or only correctly, when a value starts at an address that is a multiple of its size. A 4-byte word should start at an address divisible by 4, like 0, 4, 8 or 100. An 8-byte value should start at a multiple of 8. A word at address 101 would be misaligned. Some architectures, like classic MIPS, raise an error on a misaligned load. Others, like x86, allow it but may need two memory accesses, which is slower.

Alignment and padding, worked: In C, a structure with a 1-byte char followed by a 4-byte int often takes 8 bytes, not 5. The compiler places the char at offset 0, then adds 3 bytes of unused padding so the int starts at offset 4, which is aligned. If you reorder fields from biggest to smallest, you can often reduce padding. This is a nice example of organization affecting how programmers write code.

Floating point, the idea: Integers cannot hold 3.75 or 0.000001 or 6 times 10 to the power 23. For these we use floating point, which is scientific notation in binary. Instead of writing 6.02 times 10 to the power 23, we write something like 1.0101 times 2 to the power 5. A floating-point number stores three things: a sign, an exponent and a fraction, also called the mantissa or significand. The standard format used by almost all computers today is IEEE 754, first published in 1985.

IEEE 754 single precision: A single-precision float uses 32 bits: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. For normal numbers, the value is minus 1 to the power sign, times 1.fraction, times 2 to the power (exponent minus 127). The 127 is called the bias; it lets the exponent field hold both negative and positive exponents as an unsigned number. Because normal numbers always start with 1 before the binary point, that 1 is not stored. It is called the hidden bit, and it gives 24 bits of precision for the price of 23.

Double precision: A double uses 64 bits: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits with a bias of 1023, and 52 fraction bits. Single precision gives roughly 7 decimal digits of precision and a largest value around 3.4 times 10 to the power 38. Double gives roughly 15 to 16 decimal digits and a largest value around 1.8 times 10 to the power 308. That is why scientific programs and most calculations in languages like Python use double by default.

Worked example, encoding minus 6.75: First, write 6.75 in binary. 6 is 110 and 0.75 is 0.11 (half plus a quarter), so 6.75 is 110.11. Normalise it: move the binary point two places left to get 1.1011 times 2 to the power 2. Sign bit: 1, because the number is negative. Exponent field: 2 plus 127 is 129, which is 10000001 in binary. Fraction: the bits after the leading 1, which are 1011, followed by 19 zeros. Putting it together: 1, then 10000001, then 10110000000000000000000. In hexadecimal, that is C0D80000.

Decoding, worked: Take the pattern 0 10000010 01000000000000000000000. Sign 0 means positive. Exponent field 10000010 is 130, so the real exponent is 130 minus 127, which is 3. The significand is 1.01 in binary, which is 1.25. Value equals 1.25 times 2 to the power 3, which is 10. A good check: 10 in binary is 1010, which is 1.010 times 2 to the power 3. It matches.

Not every number fits exactly: Just as one third cannot be written exactly in decimal, many decimal fractions cannot be written exactly in binary. 0.1 in binary is 0.000110011001100 and so on forever. So a float can only store a very close approximation. That is why in many languages 0.1 plus 0.2 does not print exactly 0.3. Exponent fields of all zeros and all ones are reserved for special values like zero, infinity and NaN, which we cover in the next arithmetic lesson.

Real life example 1, a bank balance: A bank in Bangladesh should never store account balances as floating-point taka, because tiny rounding errors in values like 0.1 could add up over millions of transactions. Instead, banking software usually stores money as an integer number of the smallest unit, poisha, or uses special decimal formats. A balance of 1,234 taka 50 poisha becomes the integer 123,450 poisha. A 64-bit signed integer can hold over 9 billion billion poisha, more than enough.

Real life example 2, sending a cricket score over the internet: A live score app in Dhaka sends the number of runs as a 32-bit integer from a server to your phone. The server converts it to network byte order, which is big-endian, before sending. Your phone, which is little-endian, converts it back. If either side forgot the conversion, a score of 250 runs, hexadecimal 000000FA, could arrive as hexadecimal FA000000, which is over 4 billion. Every networking programmer learns this lesson early.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting the minus 1 in the ranges: 8-bit signed goes up to 127, not 128. Second, zero-extending a signed value. Third, mixing up which end goes first in little-endian: the little end, the least significant byte, sits at the lowest address. Fourth, forgetting the bias or the hidden bit in IEEE 754. Fifth, thinking floats are exact.

What exams ask: 'Represent minus 6.75 or 0.15625 in IEEE 754 single precision.' 'Find the decimal value of this 32-bit float pattern.' 'Show how 0x12345678 is stored in big-endian and little-endian memory.' 'Sign-extend this 8-bit number to 16 bits.' 'What is the range of an n-bit two's complement number?' Practise at least five float conversions by hand.

Recap: Data lives in fixed-size boxes: bytes, words and double words. Unsigned n-bit numbers hold 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1; two's complement holds a range around zero. Overflow wraps around. Sign extension copies the sign bit; zero extension fills with zeros. Endianness decides byte order; x86 is little-endian, networks are big-endian. Aligned data is faster and sometimes required. IEEE 754 floats store sign, biased exponent and fraction with a hidden 1. Next lesson, we see how the ALU actually does arithmetic on these numbers.
key_points: A byte is 8 bits; a word is the processor's natural data size, often 32 or 64 bits.
Unsigned n bits: 0 to 2^n - 1. Two's complement n bits: -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1.
Overflow wraps around: 8-bit signed 127 + 1 becomes -128.
Sign extension copies the sign bit into the new upper bits; zero extension fills with 0.
Big-endian stores the most significant byte first; little-endian (x86) stores the least significant byte first.
Aligned data starts at an address that is a multiple of its size; misaligned access is slow or illegal.
IEEE 754 single: 1 sign, 8 exponent (bias 127), 23 fraction bits with a hidden leading 1; double: 1, 11 (bias 1023), 52.
lessons.tip: For IEEE 754, always follow the same four steps: write the number in binary, normalise to 1.something times 2 to the power e, add the bias to e, and drop the leading 1. Say the steps out loud while you work until they become automatic.
lessons.task: Convert your age and your roll number into 8-bit binary, then find their negatives in two's complement. Next, encode 5.5 and minus 0.75 in IEEE 754 single precision on paper, and write each result in hexadecimal.

quiz.q: What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?
Sign-extend the 8-bit value 11110000 to 16 bits.
quiz.explain: Copy the sign bit 1 into the 8 new upper bits.

quiz.q: The 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored little-endian at address 200. What byte is at address 200?
quiz.explain: Little-endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address.

quiz.q: In IEEE 754 single precision, the exponent bias is:
quiz.explain: Single precision uses an 8-bit exponent with bias 127.

quiz.q: Which pattern encodes -6.75 in single precision?
quiz.explain: -6.75 = -1.1011 x 2^2: sign 1, exponent 129, fraction 1011... gives C0D80000.

lessons.title: Computer Arithmetic I: ALU, Flags, Shifts and Multiplication
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy sweet shop in Old Dhaka on the evening before Eid. Customers shout orders, and in the middle of the counter sits one person with a calculator who adds up every bill, subtracts discounts, multiplies kilos by price and tells everyone whether they paid too little. Inside a CPU, that person is the ALU, the arithmetic logic unit. Every add, subtract, compare, AND, OR and shift that your phone does passes through it. In this lesson we open the ALU, see how it adds and subtracts, how it raises little warning flags, how it shifts bits around, and how it multiplies, including a clever trick called Booth's algorithm.

What the ALU is: The ALU is a combinational circuit. It takes two operands, say A and B, each n bits wide, plus a few control bits that say which operation to perform. It produces an n-bit result and a handful of status bits called flags. It has no memory of its own; whatever comes in on the inputs decides what comes out, after a short delay. The registers that hold A, B and the result sit outside it, and the control unit chooses the operation by setting the control lines.

Building it from 1-bit slices: The easiest way to design an n-bit ALU is to design a 1-bit ALU and copy it n times. One slice has inputs a, b and carry-in. Inside it there is an AND gate, an OR gate and a full adder, and a multiplexer picks which of their outputs becomes the result bit. The carry-out of slice 0 feeds the carry-in of slice 1, and so on, exactly like the ripple-carry adder you met in Digital Logic Design. With a 2-bit operation code we can choose 00 for AND, 01 for OR and 10 for ADD.

Subtraction for free: Computers store signed integers in two's complement. To compute A - B, the ALU computes A + (NOT B) + 1. So each slice gets one extra control line, often called Binvert, which passes b through an inverter, and the carry-in of the lowest slice is set to 1. The same adder now subtracts. Example with 4 bits: 6 - 2 is 0110 + 1101 + 1 = 0110 + 1110 = 1 0100. Drop the carry out of the top and the answer is 0100, which is 4. No separate subtractor is needed.

Speed of the adder: In a ripple-carry design, the top bit cannot be final until the carry has travelled through every slice. For 64 bits that is 64 slices of delay, which is too slow for a fast clock. Real ALUs use carry-lookahead or similar adders that compute carries in parallel groups, so the delay grows roughly with log n instead of n. You studied the lookahead equations in Digital Logic Design; here the point is simply that the adder is usually on the critical path of the CPU, so its speed limits the clock.

Comparison is subtraction: To check whether A equals B, the ALU subtracts and looks at whether every result bit is 0. To check A < B for signed numbers, it subtracts and looks at the sign of the result, corrected for overflow. MIPS has an instruction called slt, set on less than, which writes 1 into a register if A < B and 0 otherwise. So one adder gives us addition, subtraction, equality tests and less-than tests.

Status flags: Most processors keep four classic flags after an ALU operation. Z, the zero flag, is 1 when the result is all zeros. N, the negative or sign flag, is a copy of the top bit of the result. C, the carry flag, is the carry out of the top bit, which signals unsigned overflow on addition. V, the overflow flag, signals signed overflow: the true answer does not fit in the signed range. Branch instructions later read these flags to decide whether to jump.

Flags worked example 1: Add 0111 and 0001 in 4 bits. The result is 1000. Z = 0 because the result is not zero. N = 1 because the top bit is 1. C = 0 because nothing carried out of the top. V = 1, because 7 + 1 = 8 does not fit in the 4-bit signed range of -8 to 7, and the answer looks like -8. Two positive numbers gave a negative result, which is the classic sign of signed overflow.

Flags worked example 2: Add 1111 and 0001. The result is 0000 with a carry out of 1. Z = 1, N = 0, C = 1. For unsigned numbers this is 15 + 1 = 16, which does not fit, so C warns us. For signed numbers it is -1 + 1 = 0, which is perfectly correct, so V = 0. The same bits mean different things depending on whether the program treats them as signed or unsigned. The hardware sets both flags and lets the program choose.

The overflow rule: Signed overflow happens only when two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the other sign. Adding a positive and a negative number can never overflow. In hardware, V is computed as the carry into the top bit XOR the carry out of the top bit. In example 1, the carry into bit 3 was 1 and the carry out was 0, so V = 1. In example 2, both were 1, so V = 0.

Shift operations: A shifter moves bits left or right. A logical left shift moves every bit one place left and puts 0 in the lowest bit, which multiplies by 2 as long as nothing important falls off the top: 0011 (3) becomes 0110 (6). A logical right shift puts 0 in the top bit, which divides an unsigned number by 2: 1000 (8) becomes 0100 (4). An arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit instead, so a negative number stays negative: 1100 (-4) becomes 1110 (-2). A rotate moves the bit that falls off one end back into the other end.

A small trap with arithmetic shift: An arithmetic right shift of -3 (1101) gives 1110, which is -2, not -1. It rounds down towards minus infinity, while integer division in C rounds towards zero. So compilers cannot always replace x / 2 by an arithmetic shift for negative x without a small correction. Fast hardware shifters, called barrel shifters, can shift by any amount from 0 to n-1 in one step using layers of multiplexers.

Multiplication the school way: Binary long multiplication is easier than decimal, because each digit of the multiplier is 0 or 1. For every 1 bit in the multiplier, we add a copy of the multiplicand shifted to that position; for every 0 bit we add nothing. Multiply 1011 (11) by 1101 (13). Bit 0 is 1: add 1011. Bit 1 is 0: add nothing. Bit 2 is 1: add 101100 (44). Bit 3 is 1: add 1011000 (88). Total 11 + 44 + 88 = 143, which is 10001111. Two n-bit numbers give a product up to 2n bits long.

Shift-add hardware: A simple sequential multiplier uses a register A that starts at 0, a register Q holding the multiplier, and a register M holding the multiplicand. Each step looks at the lowest bit of Q. If it is 1, add M to A. Then shift the pair A,Q right by one, with the carry going into the top of A. After n steps, the 2n-bit product sits in A and Q together. It needs only one adder and n clock cycles. Faster CPUs use array or tree multipliers that add many partial products at once, trading chip area for speed.

Why signed multiply is tricky: Shift-add works for unsigned numbers. For two's complement numbers, one simple option is to multiply the absolute values and fix the sign at the end. Booth's algorithm, published by Andrew Donald Booth in 1951, handles two's complement numbers directly and can also skip over long runs of 1s in the multiplier.

The idea behind Booth: A run of 1s like 0111 equals 1000 - 0001, that is 8 - 1. So instead of three additions we can do one subtraction at the start of the run and one addition just past its end. Booth looks at pairs of bits: the current lowest bit Q0 and the bit that was just shifted out, called Q-1, which starts as 0. The rules are: 10 means a run of 1s starts, so A = A - M. 01 means a run has ended, so A = A + M. 00 or 11 means we are in the middle of a run of 0s or 1s, so do nothing. After that, do an arithmetic shift right of A, Q and Q-1 together.

Booth worked example, 7 times 3: M = 0111, Q = 0011, A = 0000, Q-1 = 0. Step 1: Q0,Q-1 = 1,0, so A = 0000 - 0111 = 1001. Shift right arithmetically: A = 1100, Q = 1001, Q-1 = 1. Step 2: pair is 1,1, do nothing. Shift: A = 1110, Q = 0100, Q-1 = 1. Step 3: pair is 0,1, so A = 1110 + 0111 = 0101, ignoring the carry. Shift: A = 0010, Q = 1010, Q-1 = 0. Step 4: pair is 0,0, do nothing. Shift: A = 0001, Q = 0101, Q-1 = 0. The answer A,Q is 00010101, which is 21. Correct.

When Booth helps and when it does not: For a multiplier like 00111100, Booth does one subtract and one add instead of four adds. For an alternating pattern like 01010101, every pair is a boundary, so Booth does more additions and subtractions than plain shift-add would. Its main gift is handling signed numbers neatly. Modified Booth, or radix-4 Booth, looks at three bits at a time and halves the number of partial products, and versions of it are widely used in real multipliers.

Real life example 1, a bKash wallet: A mobile wallet shows your balance in taka and poisha. Many money systems store amounts as whole numbers of the smallest unit, so 152.50 taka is stored as 15250 poisha. Adding a cash-in is an ALU add. Checking whether you have enough balance for a send-money is a subtraction followed by a look at the sign. If the programmers used a type that was too small, a very large balance could overflow and appear negative, which is exactly what the V flag warns about. That is why money software uses wide integer types and checks for overflow.

Real life example 2, photo filters on a phone: When you make a photo brighter in an app, every pixel's brightness, a number from 0 to 255, is multiplied or shifted. Doubling brightness can be a left shift. But 200 doubled is 400, which does not fit in 8 bits. Many phone chips use saturating arithmetic for images, which clips the answer at 255 instead of letting it wrap around to a small number. Without it, a bright sky would suddenly turn dark in patches. The same carry and overflow ideas decide how the picture looks.

Common mistakes: First, mixing up carry and overflow. Carry is about unsigned numbers; overflow is about signed numbers; one can be set without the other. Second, using a logical right shift on a negative number, which turns it into a big positive number. Third, in Booth's algorithm, forgetting to use an arithmetic shift, or forgetting that Q-1 starts at 0. Fourth, forgetting that an n-bit by n-bit multiply needs 2n bits for the answer.

What exams ask: 'Design a 1-bit ALU slice and show how subtraction is done.' 'Add these two 8-bit numbers and give the values of Z, N, C and V.' 'Multiply -5 by 3 using Booth's algorithm and show every step in a table with columns A, Q, Q-1 and the action.' 'Explain why carry-lookahead is faster than ripple-carry.' A neat step table is usually what the examiner wants for Booth questions.

Recap: The ALU is a combinational block that adds, subtracts, compares, does logic and shifts. Subtraction is addition of the inverted operand plus one. Flags Z, N, C and V summarise the result; C is for unsigned overflow and V for signed overflow. Logical, arithmetic and rotate shifts each have their uses. Multiplication is repeated shift and add, and Booth's algorithm handles two's complement directly by subtracting at the start of a run of 1s and adding after it. Next lesson: division and floating-point arithmetic.
key_points: The ALU is a combinational circuit: two operands and an operation code in, a result and flags out.
An n-bit ALU can be built from n copies of a 1-bit slice with AND, OR, a full adder and a multiplexer.
Subtraction is A + NOT B + 1, so one adder does both add and subtract.
Flags: Z for zero, N for sign, C for unsigned carry out, V for signed overflow.
Signed overflow happens only when two same-sign numbers give a result of the other sign.
Logical left shift multiplies by 2; arithmetic right shift keeps the sign bit.
Shift-add multiplication adds a shifted multiplicand for each 1 bit; n-bit times n-bit needs 2n bits.
Booth's algorithm: pair 10 means subtract M, 01 means add M, 00 or 11 do nothing, then arithmetic shift right.
lessons.tip: For every Booth or flags question, draw a table first with one column per register. Filling a table step by step catches almost every mistake before it reaches the answer.
lessons.task: On paper, add 0101 and 0100 in 4 bits and write the Z, N, C and V flags. Then multiply 6 by 2 with Booth's algorithm in 4 bits, showing A, Q and Q-1 after each step, and check that you get 12.

quiz.q: What does the V flag signal after an addition?
options: Unsigned carry out of the top bit
quiz.explain: V is the overflow flag for signed numbers; C is the one for unsigned carry.

quiz.q: How does an ALU usually compute A - B?
quiz.explain: Two's complement subtraction adds the inverted B with carry-in 1.

quiz.q: In 4 bits, 0111 + 0001 = 1000. Which flags are set?
quiz.explain: The top bit is 1 so N = 1, and 7 + 1 does not fit the signed range so V = 1.

quiz.q: In Booth's algorithm, what is done when Q0,Q-1 = 0,1?
quiz.explain: 01 marks the end of a run of 1s, so M is added.

quiz.q: An arithmetic right shift of 1100 (-4) gives:
quiz.explain: The sign bit 1 is copied in, giving 1110, which is -2.

lessons.title: Computer Arithmetic II: Division and Floating Point
lessons.content:
Imagine your aunt brings home 7 mangoes from Rajshahi and wants to share them among 3 cousins. You give one mango to each cousin, again and again, until you cannot give a full round any more. Each cousin gets 2, and 1 mango is left over. That is division by repeated subtraction, and it is almost exactly what a simple hardware divider does. In this lesson we see two ways computers divide integers, restoring and non-restoring division, and then we learn how the CPU adds and multiplies numbers with decimal points using floating point, including rounding and the strange values infinity and NaN.

Division words: In 7 / 3 = 2 remainder 1, 7 is the dividend, 3 is the divisor, 2 is the quotient and 1 is the remainder. They always obey dividend = divisor x quotient + remainder, with the remainder smaller than the divisor. Division is the slowest of the four basic integer operations in most CPUs, often taking many more cycles than an addition, which is one reason compilers replace division by a constant with multiplications and shifts when they can.

The registers: A sequential divider for n-bit unsigned numbers uses three registers. Q starts with the dividend and slowly turns into the quotient. M holds the divisor. A starts at 0 and slowly turns into the remainder. Real designs keep A one bit wider than n so its sign is always clear after a subtraction. Each step shifts the pair A,Q one place left, so one more bit of the dividend moves into A, and then the hardware tries to subtract M.

Restoring division, the rule: Repeat n times. Shift A,Q left by one. Compute A = A - M. If A is now negative, the subtraction was too much: set the lowest bit of Q to 0 and restore A by adding M back. Otherwise, set the lowest bit of Q to 1 and keep the new A. After n steps, Q is the quotient and A is the remainder. It is just long division in base 2: at each position, does the divisor go into what we have so far, yes or no.

Restoring division, worked: Divide 7 by 3 with n = 4. Q = 0111, M = 0011, A = 0000. Step 1: shift gives A = 0000, Q = 1110. A - M = -3, negative, so Q0 = 0 and A is restored to 0000. Step 2: shift gives A = 0001, Q = 1100. A - M = -2, negative, so Q0 = 0, A restored to 0001. Step 3: shift gives A = 0011, Q = 1000. A - M = 0, not negative, so Q0 = 1, Q = 1001, A = 0000. Step 4: shift gives A = 0001, Q = 0010. A - M = -2, negative, so Q0 = 0, A restored to 0001. Final: Q = 0010 = 2, A = 0001 = 1. Correct.

The cost of restoring: Every time the subtraction fails, we spend an extra addition to put A back. In the worst case that is two arithmetic operations per step. Non-restoring division removes that waste with a neat observation. If A went negative, restoring means computing A + M, and the next step would shift it left, which doubles it, and then subtract M. That is 2(A + M) - M = 2A + M. So we can skip the restore and simply add M in the next step instead of subtracting it.

Non-restoring division, the rule: Repeat n times. If A is negative, shift A,Q left and then A = A + M. If A is not negative, shift A,Q left and then A = A - M. After the add or subtract, set Q0 = 1 if A is not negative, otherwise Q0 = 0. At the very end, if A is negative, add M once more to get the correct remainder. Only one add or subtract happens per step, plus at most one correction at the end.

Non-restoring, worked: Divide 7 by 3 again. Step 1: A = 0 is not negative. Shift: A = 0, Q = 1110. A = 0 - 3 = -3, negative, Q0 = 0. Step 2: A is negative. Shift: A = -5 (the shifted -3 with a 1 moved in from Q), Q = 1100. A = -5 + 3 = -2, Q0 = 0. Step 3: A is negative. Shift: A = -3, Q = 1000. A = -3 + 3 = 0, not negative, Q0 = 1, Q = 1001. Step 4: A = 0 not negative. Shift: A = 1, Q = 0010. A = 1 - 3 = -2, Q0 = 0. End: A is negative, so add M: A = 1. Again Q = 2 and remainder 1, with fewer operations.

Division by zero: If the divisor is 0, no quotient makes sense. Integer division hardware usually signals an exception, and the operating system typically stops the program with an error. Floating point handles this differently, as we will see. Signed integer division can be done by dividing the absolute values and then fixing the signs of the quotient and remainder.

Floating point recap: Lesson 5 showed the IEEE 754 layout. A single-precision number has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits with a bias of 127, and 23 fraction bits, with a hidden leading 1 for normal numbers. Its value is (-1)^sign x 1.fraction x 2^(exponent - 127). Double precision uses 1, 11 and 52 bits with a bias of 1023. Here we focus on what the hardware does to add and multiply such numbers.

Floating-point addition, the steps: First, align: compare the exponents and shift the significand of the smaller number right until both exponents match. Second, add or subtract the significands, depending on the signs. Third, normalise: shift the result so there is exactly one 1 before the binary point, adjusting the exponent, and check for overflow or underflow. Fourth, round the significand to the number of bits available. Rounding can sometimes produce a result that needs normalising again.

Addition in decimal first: Suppose a toy format keeps 4 decimal digits. Add 9.999 x 10^1 and 1.610 x 10^-1. Align: shift the smaller one by 2 places, 0.01610 x 10^1, which keeps 4 digits as 0.016 x 10^1. Add: 9.999 + 0.016 = 10.015 x 10^1. Normalise: 1.0015 x 10^2. Round to 4 digits: 1.002 x 10^2. Notice that digits were lost in the alignment step. Adding a tiny number to a huge one can lose the tiny one completely.

Addition in binary: Add 0.5 and -0.4375. In binary these are 1.000 x 2^-1 and -1.110 x 2^-2. Align the second to exponent -1: -0.111 x 2^-1. Add: 1.000 - 0.111 = 0.001 x 2^-1. Normalise: 1.000 x 2^-4. That is 2^-4 = 0.0625, and indeed 0.5 - 0.4375 = 0.0625. The exponent dropped by 3 because three leading bits cancelled.

Floating-point multiplication, the steps: Multiplication is easier because no alignment is needed. First, add the exponents. With biased exponents, add the two biased values and subtract the bias once, otherwise it would be counted twice. Second, multiply the significands. Third, normalise and check for overflow or underflow. Fourth, round. Finally, the sign is the XOR of the two signs: same signs give positive, different signs give negative.

Multiplication worked: Multiply 0.5 by -0.4375, that is 1.000 x 2^-1 times -1.110 x 2^-2. Biased exponents in single precision are 126 and 125. Add and subtract the bias: 126 + 125 - 127 = 124, which means 2^-3. Significands: 1.000 x 1.110 = 1.110, already normalised. Sign: positive XOR negative is negative. Result: -1.110 x 2^-3 = -0.21875. Check: 0.5 x -0.4375 = -0.21875. Correct.

Rounding: The exact result of an operation often has more bits than the format can hold. During the calculation the hardware keeps a few extra bits beyond the last kept bit: a guard bit, a round bit, and a sticky bit that is 1 if any bit further right was 1. IEEE 754 defines several rounding modes: round to nearest with ties to even (the default), round towards zero, round towards plus infinity, and round towards minus infinity. Ties to even means that a value exactly halfway is rounded so the last kept bit is 0, which avoids a steady upward bias over many operations.

Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3: 0.1 has no exact binary form, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form. It becomes a repeating binary fraction that must be rounded. In double precision, 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, and a test like 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false in most languages. Programmers compare floating-point numbers with a small tolerance instead of exact equality.

Special values: IEEE 754 reserves the all-zeros and all-ones exponent patterns. Exponent all 0 with fraction 0 is zero, and because there is a sign bit there are both +0 and -0, which compare equal.
