Micro-operations come in four kinds: transfer, arithmetic, logic and shift, all done by one arithmetic logic shift unit. A simple accumulator machine runs each instruction as a sequence of timed micro-operations. Next, we look at the full instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute and interrupts.
key_points: RTL notation: R2 <- R1 copies R1 into R2; the arrow points to the destination and the source is unchanged.
P: R2 <- R1 happens only when control signal P is 1; a comma means transfers in the same clock edge.
A common bus for k registers of n bits uses n multiplexers of size k-to-1, or three-state buffers.
Memory transfers: read DR <- M[AR], write M[AR] <- R1.
Four kinds of micro-operations: transfer, arithmetic, logic and shift.
Subtraction is R1 + R2' + 1; masks with AND, OR and XOR clear, set and flip chosen bits.
Arithmetic shift right keeps the sign bit (divide by 2); circular shift rotates the lost bit back in.
An accumulator machine runs each instruction as timed micro-operations, e.g. T0: AR <- PC; T1: IR <- M[AR], PC <- PC + 1.
lessons.tip: When you meet any new instruction, try to write its RTL steps yourself before looking at the book. If you can write the micro-operations, you truly understand the instruction.
lessons.task: Take the 8-bit value 1011 0110. On paper apply AND, OR and XOR with mask 0000 1111, then shl, shr, cil and ashr. Write each result and say which one keeps the sign.

quiz.q: What does the RTL statement T1: R2 <- R1 mean?
options: R1 and R2 are added when T1 is 0
R2 is copied into R1 at every clock
When T1 is 1, R1 is copied into R2 at the clock edge
R1 is cleared after the transfer
quiz.explain: The control function T1 gates the transfer; the arrow points to the destination R2.

quiz.q: How many multiplexers, and of what size, make a common bus for 8 registers of 16 bits each?
quiz.explain: One multiplexer per bit (16), each choosing among the 8 registers (8-to-1).

quiz.q: Which micro-operation computes R1 - R2 in 2's complement?
quiz.explain: Subtraction adds the 2's complement: R2' + 1.

quiz.q: What is arithmetic shift right of 1111 0100 (-12)?
quiz.explain: The sign bit is copied in, giving 1111 1010, which is -6.

quiz.q: Which memory transfer writes register R1 into memory?
quiz.explain: M[AR] <- R1 stores R1 at the address held in AR.

lessons.title: The Instruction Cycle
lessons.content:
Think about a hard-working rickshaw puller on a busy day in Sylhet. His day is one loop repeated hundreds of times: find the next passenger, hear where they want to go, pedal there, collect the fare, and then look for the next passenger. He never stops to plan the whole day. A CPU lives exactly like this. From the moment you switch it on until you switch it off, it repeats one loop billions of times: fetch the next instruction, figure out what it means, do it, and move on. This loop is called the instruction cycle, and it is the heartbeat of every computer.

The stored-program idea again: In lesson 01 we met the stored-program idea: instructions sit in memory as numbers, right next to the data. The CPU needs a way to find which instruction comes next, a place to keep the instruction while it works on it, and a way to talk to memory. Four special registers do these jobs, and once you know them, the whole cycle becomes easy to follow.

The four key registers: The program counter, PC, holds the address of the next instruction to fetch. The instruction register, IR, holds the instruction currently being worked on. The memory address register, MAR, holds the address the CPU wants to read or write. The memory buffer or memory data register, MBR or MDR, holds the data just read from memory or about to be written. Besides these, there are the general registers or an accumulator, AC, for data, and a status or flags register that remembers things like zero, carry and overflow.

The basic two-step view: The simplest picture says the instruction cycle has two parts: the fetch cycle and the execute cycle. In the fetch cycle the CPU brings one instruction from memory into IR. In the execute cycle it carries out what that instruction says. Then it starts the next fetch. The cycle ends only when the machine is switched off, hits a halt instruction, or meets an error it cannot handle.

The fetch cycle step by step: Step 1: MAR <- PC. The address of the next instruction is sent toward memory. Step 2: MDR <- M[MAR], and at the same time PC <- PC + 1 (or PC + 4 on a byte-addressed machine with 4-byte instructions). Memory returns the instruction, and the PC already moves forward so it points to the following instruction. Step 3: IR <- MDR. The instruction is now in the instruction register, ready to be understood. This is the same in almost every computer ever built; only the register names change.

Why increment PC early: The PC is increased during the fetch, before we even know what the instruction is. Most instructions are not jumps, so the next instruction is usually the one right after. Doing the increment early, while memory is busy, saves time. If the instruction later turns out to be a branch or jump, the execute step simply overwrites PC with the new target address.

Decode: The control unit looks at the opcode bits in IR and works out what kind of instruction it is, which registers are involved and whether a memory operand is needed. In a hardwired control unit, a decoder turns the opcode into one active line per instruction type. In a microprogrammed unit, the opcode picks the starting address of a small microprogram. Either way, decode turns a pattern of bits into a plan of control signals.

The detailed view: Many textbooks, such as William Stallings', break the cycle into finer states: instruction address calculation (find the next PC), instruction fetch, instruction operation decoding, operand address calculation, operand fetch, data operation (the actual work in the ALU), and operand store (write the result). Some steps repeat when an instruction has several operands, and some are skipped: an instruction with only register operands needs no operand fetch from memory.

Operand address calculation: If an instruction uses memory, the CPU must find the effective address. With direct addressing the address is right in the instruction. With register indirect it is in a register. With displacement it is a register plus a constant. These are the addressing modes from lesson 09, and this is the step where they are actually computed, often using the ALU or a separate address adder.

The indirect cycle: With indirect addressing, the address inside the instruction points to a memory word that contains the real address. So an extra memory read is needed: MAR <- IR(address); MDR <- M[MAR]; then the address part of IR is replaced by MDR's value. Textbooks draw this as a separate indirect cycle between fetch and execute. It costs one more memory access, which is why indirect addressing is slower.

Execute and write back: In execute, the ALU does the real work: add, subtract, compare, shift, or the CPU computes a branch target. Then the result is written back, either to a register or to memory. For a store, the execute step is MAR <- address; MDR <- AC; M[MAR] <- MDR. For a branch, it is PC <- target if the condition holds. For an add with a memory operand, it is MAR <- address; MDR <- M[MAR]; AC <- AC + MDR.

Instruction cycle versus clock cycle: Do not confuse the two. A clock cycle is one tick of the CPU clock, for example 0.5 nanoseconds on a 2 GHz chip. An instruction cycle is the whole job of handling one instruction, and on a simple machine it can take several clock cycles: maybe one or two for fetch, one for decode, and one or more for execute, depending on how many memory trips are needed. This is exactly where CPI from lesson 03 comes from: CPI is the average number of clock cycles per instruction cycle. Later, in lesson 18, pipelining overlaps the steps of different instructions, so that a new instruction can start every clock cycle even though each one still passes through all the steps.

A worked trace: Imagine a tiny machine with 16-bit instructions: the first 4 bits are the opcode and the last 12 bits are an address. Opcode 1 means load AC from memory, opcode 2 means store AC to memory, opcode 5 means add a memory word to AC. Numbers are written in hexadecimal. The program sits at addresses 200, 201 and 202: 1500, 5501, 2502. The data sits at 500 = 0007 and 501 = 0005. PC starts at 200.

Trace, first instruction: Fetch: MAR <- 200, MDR <- 1500, PC <- 201, IR <- 1500. Decode: opcode 1, load; address 500. Execute: MAR <- 500, MDR <- 0007, AC <- 0007. One instruction done, and PC already points to 201.

Trace, second and third instructions: Fetch: MAR <- 201, MDR <- 5501, PC <- 202, IR <- 5501. Decode: opcode 5, add; address 501. Execute: MAR <- 501, MDR <- 0005, AC <- 0007 + 0005 = 000C (12 in decimal). Next fetch: MAR <- 202, MDR <- 2502, PC <- 203, IR <- 2502. Decode: opcode 2, store; address 502. Execute: MAR <- 502, MDR <- 000C, M[502] <- 000C. Three instructions, three trips around the cycle, and memory location 502 now holds 7 + 5 = 12. Notice that each instruction needed two memory accesses: one to fetch the instruction and one for data.

Interrupts, what they are: Sometimes something outside the program needs attention right now: a key is pressed, a disk finishes reading, a timer goes off, or the program does something illegal like dividing by zero. An interrupt is a signal that asks the CPU to pause the current program, handle the event, and then come back. Common classes are program interrupts (overflow, division by zero, illegal instruction, memory access violation), timer interrupts, I/O interrupts and hardware failure interrupts.

The interrupt cycle: Interrupts are checked at the end of each instruction cycle, never in the middle of an instruction. If interrupts are enabled and one is pending, the CPU enters the interrupt cycle: it saves the current PC (and usually the status register), often by pushing them onto the stack, loads the PC with the starting address of the interrupt service routine, and usually disables further interrupts for a moment. The next fetch then brings the first instruction of the service routine. When the routine finishes, a return-from-interrupt instruction restores the saved PC and status, and the old program continues as if nothing happened.

Why interrupts matter: Without interrupts the CPU would have to keep asking a slow device "are you done yet?" over and over, wasting millions of cycles. With interrupts, the CPU does useful work and the device rings the bell only when it is ready. Interrupts also let the operating system take control back from a program at regular timer ticks, which is how many programs seem to run at the same time.

Multiple interrupts: If a second interrupt arrives while one is being handled, there are two simple policies. One is to disable interrupts during a service routine, so new ones wait and are handled in order. The other is to give interrupts priorities, so a higher-priority interrupt, say from a network card, can interrupt a lower-priority routine, say for a printer. Saved PCs then stack up and unwind in reverse order. Details of real interrupt controllers come in the Microprocessors and I/O lessons.

Real life example 1, typing in a cyber cafe: At a cyber cafe in Rajshahi you type an email. The CPU is busy running the browser, going round its instruction cycle. When you press a key, the keyboard controller raises an interrupt. At the end of the current instruction the CPU saves its PC, jumps to the keyboard routine, reads the key code, puts it in a buffer, and returns. All this takes a tiny fraction of a millisecond, so the letter appears instantly and the browser never notices the break.

Real life example 2, a bank ATM: An ATM in Gulshan runs a program that waits for a card. Its CPU does not spin in a loop checking the card slot. Instead, it can do other work, like updating the screen, and when a card is inserted the card reader sends an interrupt. Meanwhile, every instruction it runs, from reading your PIN to counting notes, goes through the same fetch, decode, execute steps. The same simple loop powers a pocket calculator and a huge bank server.

Common mistakes: Thinking the PC is increased only after execution; in most designs it is increased during fetch. Forgetting that a branch changes the PC in the execute step. Saying interrupts are handled in the middle of an instruction; they are checked at the end. Forgetting to save the PC before jumping to the service routine. Mixing up MAR (holds an address) and MDR (holds data).

What exams ask: Draw the instruction cycle state diagram with and without interrupts. Write the fetch cycle in RTL. Trace a short program like the one above, showing PC, MAR, MDR, IR and AC after each step. Explain the indirect cycle. Explain what happens during the interrupt cycle and why interrupts improve efficiency. Compare disabling interrupts with priority-based nesting.

Recap: The CPU repeats the instruction cycle forever: fetch (MAR <- PC, MDR <- M[MAR], PC <- PC + 1, IR <- MDR), decode the opcode, compute operand addresses, fetch operands, execute in the ALU and write back the result. Indirect addressing adds an extra memory read. At the end of each instruction the CPU checks for interrupts, and if one is pending it saves the PC, jumps to a service routine and later returns. Next lesson we build the actual hardware, a single-cycle datapath, that performs this cycle for MIPS-style instructions.
key_points: The CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute (and write back) for every instruction until it halts.
PC holds the next instruction address, IR the current instruction, MAR an address, MDR the data to or from memory.
Fetch in RTL: MAR <- PC; MDR <- M[MAR], PC <- PC + 1; IR <- MDR.
PC is incremented during fetch; a branch or jump overwrites it during execute.
Indirect addressing adds an indirect cycle: one extra memory read to get the effective address.
Interrupts are checked at the end of each instruction; the CPU saves PC and status and jumps to a service routine.
Interrupts save CPU time compared with repeatedly polling slow devices.
lessons.tip: Practise traces with a small table: one column each for PC, MAR, MDR, IR and AC, and one row per micro-step. Exam traces become mechanical once the table habit sticks.
lessons.task: Using the tiny machine from the lesson (1 = load, 2 = store, 5 = add), write a 4-instruction program that computes A + B + C and stores the result. Trace it on paper with a PC, MAR, MDR, IR, AC table.

quiz.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
quiz.explain: The program counter always points to the next instruction.

quiz.q: What is the first micro-operation of the fetch cycle?
quiz.explain: The address in PC is first placed in MAR so memory can be read.

quiz.q: When does a CPU normally check for a pending interrupt?
options: In the middle of the decode step
At the end of the instruction cycle
quiz.explain: Interrupts are checked after an instruction completes, so no instruction is left half done.

quiz.q: In the lesson's trace, memory holds 500 = 0007 and 501 = 0005. After 1500, 5501, 2502 run, what is in 502?
quiz.explain: Load 7, add 5, store 12 (hex 000C) at 502.

quiz.q: Why does indirect addressing make an instruction slower?
options: It needs an extra memory read to fetch the real address
quiz.explain: The indirect cycle reads memory once more to get the effective address.

lessons.title: The Single-Cycle Datapath
lessons.content:
Imagine a single kitchen counter at a roadside tea stall in Cox's Bazar. On it sit a kettle, a milk pot, a sugar jar, a strainer and a row of cups. Every order, whether plain tea, milk tea or lemon tea, is made on this one counter in one go. The stall owner simply decides which items to use for each order: lemon tea skips the milk pot, milk tea skips the lemon. A single-cycle datapath is that counter. All the hardware pieces sit side by side, every instruction runs through them in exactly one clock cycle, and the control unit decides which pieces each instruction uses.

What a datapath is: The datapath is the part of the CPU that holds and moves data: the registers, the ALU, the memories, the adders and the multiplexers that steer data between them. The control unit is the other part; it decides which way each multiplexer points and which units read or write. In this lesson we build a datapath for a small subset of MIPS: the R-type instructions add, sub, and, or and slt; the memory instructions lw and sw; and the branch beq. Later we add jump.

Two kinds of building blocks: Combinational elements produce outputs only from their current inputs: the ALU, adders, multiplexers and the sign extender. State elements remember values and change only on a clock edge: the PC, the register file and the memories. In a single-cycle design, the clock edge writes new values into state elements, and during the cycle the combinational logic computes what to write next time.

Step 1, fetching: The PC holds the address of the current instruction. It feeds the instruction memory, which outputs the 32-bit instruction. At the same time a separate adder computes PC + 4. If nothing else happens, PC + 4 is written into the PC on the next clock edge, so the machine moves to the next instruction. That is three pieces: PC register, instruction memory and a plus-4 adder.

Step 2, the register file: The register file holds the 32 registers. It has two read ports and one write port. You give it two 5-bit register numbers, and it outputs both register values; reading is combinational, so the values appear during the cycle. For writing, you give a 5-bit register number, a 32-bit value and a RegWrite control signal; the write happens at the clock edge only if RegWrite is 1.

Datapath for R-type: For add $t0, $s1, $s2, the fields rs and rt (bits 25 to 21 and 20 to 16) go to the two read ports. The two values go into the ALU. The control tells the ALU to add. The ALU result goes back to the register file's write data input, and rd (bits 15 to 11) gives the write register number. With RegWrite = 1, the sum lands in $t0 at the clock edge. The ALU also outputs a Zero signal that says whether the result was 0.

Datapath for loads and stores: For lw $t0, 8($s1), we read $s1 from the register file. The 16-bit offset 8 goes through a sign-extend unit to become 32 bits. The ALU adds base and offset to get the memory address. Data memory reads that address with MemRead = 1, and the word goes back to the register file, written into rt, here $t0. For sw $t0, 8($s1), the address is computed the same way, but now the second register read port supplies $t0's value to the data memory's write data input, and MemWrite = 1 stores it. Nothing is written to registers.

Datapath for beq: For beq $s1, $s2, Label, both registers are read and the ALU subtracts them. If the Zero output is 1, the two values were equal and the branch is taken. Meanwhile, the offset is sign-extended, shifted left by 2 (to change words into bytes) and added to PC + 4 by a second adder, giving the branch target. A multiplexer then chooses the next PC: PC + 4 normally, or the branch target when the branch is taken.

Why multiplexers appear: Different instructions want different things in the same place. That is exactly what a multiplexer solves. Four multiplexers do the steering in this design. RegDst chooses the write register: rd for R-type, rt for lw. ALUSrc chooses the ALU's second input: a register for R-type and beq, the sign-extended immediate for lw and sw. MemtoReg chooses what is written to the register: the ALU result for R-type, memory data for lw. PCSrc chooses the next PC: PC + 4 or the branch target.

Why two memories: In a single cycle, we need to read an instruction and, for lw or sw, also read or write data. A simple memory can do only one access at a time, so the single-cycle design uses a separate instruction memory and data memory. This is the Harvard idea from lesson 02. In real chips, this split shows up as separate instruction and data caches.

The main control signals: Besides the four multiplexer selects, the main control unit produces RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, Branch and a 2-bit ALUOp. PCSrc is not set directly; it equals Branch AND Zero, so the branch is taken only if the instruction is beq and the registers were equal. The control unit looks only at the 6-bit opcode to set all of these.

The control table: R-type: RegDst = 1, ALUSrc = 0, MemtoReg = 0, RegWrite = 1, MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 0, Branch = 0, ALUOp = 10. lw: RegDst = 0, ALUSrc = 1, MemtoReg = 1, RegWrite = 1, MemRead = 1, MemWrite = 0, Branch = 0, ALUOp = 00. sw: RegDst = X, ALUSrc = 1, MemtoReg = X, RegWrite = 0, MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 1, Branch = 0, ALUOp = 00. beq: RegDst = X, ALUSrc = 0, MemtoReg = X, RegWrite = 0, MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 0, Branch = 1, ALUOp = 01. X means don't care: since sw and beq write no register, it does not matter what RegDst and MemtoReg choose.

ALU control: The ALU needs a 4-bit operation code. A small ALU control unit makes it from ALUOp and the funct field. ALUOp = 00 means add (for computing lw and sw addresses). ALUOp = 01 means subtract (for beq). ALUOp = 10 means look at the funct field: funct 32 gives add, 34 subtract, 36 AND, 37 OR, 42 set on less than. In the classic textbook, the ALU lines are 0000 for AND, 0001 for OR, 0010 for add, 0110 for subtract and 0111 for slt. Splitting control into a main unit and a small ALU control unit is called multiple levels of decoding; it keeps each unit small and fast.

Adding jump: For j, the target is made by taking the 26-bit field, shifting it left by 2, and joining it with the top 4 bits of PC + 4. One more multiplexer, controlled by a new Jump signal, chooses this jump address as the next PC. Jump writes no register and touches no data memory.

Following a lw through the whole path: Clock edge: PC = 1000. Instruction memory outputs lw $t0, 8($s1). Adder makes 1004. Register file reads $s1, say 2000. Sign-extend makes 8. ALUSrc = 1 sends 8 into the ALU, ALUOp = 00 adds: 2008. Data memory reads address 2008, say value 55. MemtoReg = 1 sends 55 to write data, RegDst = 0 picks rt = $t0. Next clock edge: $t0 becomes 55 and PC becomes 1004. One instruction, one cycle.

The critical path: Every instruction gets exactly one clock cycle, so the cycle must be long enough for the slowest instruction. Use example delays from the textbook: memory access 200 ps, ALU 200 ps, register file read or write 100 ps, and ignore multiplexer and wire delays. R-type: fetch 200 + register read 100 + ALU 200 + register write 100 = 600 ps. lw: 200 + 100 + 200 + data memory 200 + register write 100 = 800 ps. sw: 200 + 100 + 200 + 200 = 700 ps. beq: 200 + 100 + 200 = 500 ps. j: just the fetch, 200 ps. The load is the longest path, so the clock cycle must be 800 ps.

Why single-cycle is slow: With an instruction mix of 25 percent loads, 10 percent stores, 45 percent R-type, 15 percent branches and 5 percent jumps, a magic clock that matched each instruction would average 0.25 x 800 + 0.10 x 700 + 0.45 x 600 + 0.15 x 500 + 0.05 x 200 = 200 + 70 + 270 + 75 + 10 = 625 ps. The fixed clock wastes time: 800 / 625 = 1.28, so the single-cycle design is about 1.28 times slower than ideal in this example. Worse, if we added a slow instruction such as floating-point divide, every instruction would pay its long delay. CPI is 1, but the clock is long. That is why lesson 17 builds a multi-cycle datapath and lesson 18 adds pipelining.

Real life example 1, a one-counter bank branch: Picture a small bank branch in Narayanganj with one counter where every customer, whether depositing, withdrawing or just asking for a balance, must be served in exactly 10 minutes, because 10 minutes is what the slowest job, a cash withdrawal with counting, needs. Balance inquiries take 2 minutes but still hold the counter for 10. That is the single-cycle datapath: simple and predictable, but the slowest job sets the pace for all.

Real life example 2, designing a teaching CPU: Many CSE students in Bangladesh build a small single-cycle MIPS processor in a lab using Verilog or a logic simulator like Logisim. They place the PC, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory and multiplexers, then wire the control table above. When they run a few lw, add and beq instructions and watch the registers change, the whole datapath suddenly makes sense. It is a common, very rewarding lab project.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the sign-extend unit before the ALU for lw and sw. Forgetting the shift left by 2 before adding the branch offset. Mixing up RegDst: rd is the destination for R-type but rt for lw. Thinking PCSrc comes straight from the control unit; it is Branch AND Zero. Using one memory for both instruction and data in a single-cycle design. Thinking single-cycle means fast because CPI = 1.

What exams ask: Draw the single-cycle datapath for R-type, lw, sw and beq. Fill in the control signal table for given instructions. Say which units are active for a given instruction and trace its values. Compute the critical path and minimum clock period from given delays. Compare single-cycle performance with a variable clock for an instruction mix. Explain why a single-cycle design is inefficient. Add support for a new instruction, such as jump or addi, and say which signals change.

Recap: A single-cycle datapath runs each instruction in one long clock cycle. It needs the PC, an instruction memory, a register file with two read ports and one write port, a sign extender, an ALU, a data memory, adders for PC + 4 and the branch target, and multiplexers chosen by RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg and PCSrc. The main control reads the opcode; the ALU control combines ALUOp with funct. The clock must fit the slowest instruction, usually lw, which wastes time on the faster ones. Next we look at how the control unit itself is designed, hardwired or microprogrammed.
key_points: A datapath holds and moves data (registers, ALU, memories, adders, multiplexers); control decides how it is used.
State elements (PC, register file, memories) change on clock edges; combinational elements compute during the cycle.
Register file: two read ports (rs, rt) and one write port controlled by RegWrite.
Multiplexers RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg and PCSrc steer data; PCSrc = Branch AND Zero.
Separate instruction and data memories are needed because both are used in the same cycle.
Main control reads the opcode; ALU control combines ALUOp (00 add, 01 subtract, 10 use funct) with funct.
Clock period must fit the slowest instruction (lw: 800 ps in the textbook example), so faster instructions waste time.
lessons.tip: Draw the datapath from memory, piece by piece: fetch first, then R-type, then add lw, sw and beq. Building it in stages is much easier than memorising the full picture.
lessons.task: Draw the single-cycle datapath on one page. Then take the instruction sw $t1, 12($t2) and colour in only the units and wires it uses. Write the values of all control signals next to it.

quiz.q: Which instruction sets the length of the clock cycle in the single-cycle design?
quiz.explain: lw uses instruction memory, register read, ALU, data memory and register write, the longest path.

quiz.q: What does the ALUSrc multiplexer choose?
options: The ALU's second input: a register or the sign-extended immediate
quiz.explain: ALUSrc = 1 for lw and sw sends the immediate; 0 sends the second register.

quiz.q: For beq, how is PCSrc produced?
quiz.explain: The branch is taken only if the instruction is a branch and the ALU result was zero.

quiz.q: With delays memory 200 ps, ALU 200 ps and register file 100 ps, how long does an R-type instruction need?
quiz.explain: 200 fetch + 100 read + 200 ALU + 100 write = 600 ps.

quiz.q: Why does the single-cycle datapath have separate instruction and data memories?
options: Data is always larger than code
Each memory can do only one access per cycle, and lw/sw need both in one cycle
quiz.explain: Fetching an instruction and accessing data happen in the same cycle.

lessons.title: Control Unit Design: Hardwired and Microprogrammed
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy traffic junction in Dhaka, say Shahbag at 9 in the morning. Buses, rickshaws, CNGs and cars all want to move. On their own they would crash into each other. Then a traffic police officer stands in the middle, looks at the situation and raises an arm: this lane stops, that lane goes, rickshaws wait. The vehicles have all the power, but the officer decides who moves and when. Inside a CPU, the datapath is the road with all the vehicles: registers, the ALU, memory and the wires between them. The control unit is the officer. In this lesson we learn how that officer is built.

What the control unit does: The datapath can do many things, but it does nothing by itself. Somebody must tell the register file whether to write, tell the ALU whether to add or subtract, tell memory whether to read or write, and tell each multiplexer which input to pass. These instructions are called control signals. The control unit looks at the instruction (mostly its opcode, and sometimes other fields) and, for a multi-step design, at which step we are in. From that it produces the right control signals at the right time. In short: input is the instruction and the current step, output is a bundle of on/off wires.

Control signals in a simple MIPS-style datapath: In the single-cycle datapath from the last lesson, the main control unit produces these signals. RegDst picks which instruction field names the destination register (rd for R-type, rt for loads). ALUSrc picks the second ALU input: a register or the sign-extended immediate. MemtoReg picks what gets written back: the ALU result or the data read from memory. RegWrite says whether the register file is written at all. MemRead and MemWrite turn data memory reading and writing on. Branch says this is a branch, so the zero output of the ALU may change the PC. ALUOp is a 2-bit code that tells the ALU control what kind of operation is needed.

The control table: For the four classic instructions we can write the whole job of the control unit as a table. For an R-type instruction such as add: RegDst 1, ALUSrc 0, MemtoReg 0, RegWrite 1, MemRead 0, MemWrite 0, Branch 0, ALUOp 10. For lw: RegDst 0, ALUSrc 1, MemtoReg 1, RegWrite 1, MemRead 1, MemWrite 0, Branch 0, ALUOp 00. For sw: ALUSrc 1, RegWrite 0, MemRead 0, MemWrite 1, Branch 0, ALUOp 00, and RegDst and MemtoReg are "don't care" because nothing is written to a register. For beq: ALUSrc 0, RegWrite 0, MemRead 0, MemWrite 0, Branch 1, ALUOp 01. Read the table row by row and you can see the logic. A store never writes a register, so RegWrite is 0. Only a load reads memory, so MemRead is 1 only for lw.

Two levels of control: Notice ALUOp is only 2 bits. That is because the control is split into two levels. The main control looks at the 6-bit opcode and says roughly what the ALU must do: 00 means add (to compute an address for lw and sw), 01 means subtract (for beq, to compare two registers), and 10 means "look at the funct field". The small ALU control unit then combines ALUOp with the 6-bit funct field of R-type instructions and produces the real 4-bit ALU operation, for example 0010 for add, 0110 for subtract, 0000 for AND, 0001 for OR and 0111 for set-on-less-than. Splitting the job this way keeps each part small and fast, like a head teacher who decides "today is a test" and a class teacher who decides which subject.

Two ways to build a control unit: There are two big families. Hardwired control builds the control unit directly from logic gates, decoders and flip-flops. Microprogrammed control stores the control signals as words in a small special memory and reads them out step by step, a bit like reading a recipe. Both produce the same kind of signals. They differ in speed, cost and how easy they are to change.

Hardwired control: In a hardwired design, each control signal is a Boolean function of the opcode bits and, if the machine works in steps, of timing signals. For the single-cycle MIPS case, we just turn the control table into logic. For example, the opcode of lw is 100011 (35), sw is 101011 (43), beq is 000100 (4) and R-type is 000000. A gate that detects "opcode = 100011" gives a signal we can call isLoad. Then MemRead = isLoad and MemtoReg = isLoad. RegWrite = isRtype OR isLoad. ALUSrc = isLoad OR isStore. It is just the K-maps and gates you met in Digital Logic Design.

Hardwired control with timing: Many textbook machines (for example the basic computer in Morris Mano's book) do one instruction over several clock steps. They use a sequence counter that counts 0, 1, 2, 3 and a decoder that turns the count into timing signals T0, T1, T2 and so on, where only one is high at a time. A second decoder turns the opcode into signals D0 to D7. Every micro-operation is then triggered by a product of these. For instance, the fetch steps are T0: AR gets PC, and T1: IR gets M[AR] and PC gets PC plus 1. A load-to-accumulator instruction might do its work only when D2 and T4 and T5 are true. The control unit is a big pile of AND and OR gates on the D and T lines.

Pros and cons of hardwired control: It is fast, because signals come straight out of gates with no memory lookup. That is why RISC processors, whose instructions are simple and regular, mostly use hardwired control. The downside: it is hard to design for a big, complicated instruction set, and once the chip is made you cannot change it. A bug in the control logic is a bug forever, and adding an instruction means redesigning the circuit.

Microprogrammed control: In 1951 Maurice Wilkes at Cambridge suggested a cleaner idea. Treat each step of an instruction as a tiny instruction of its own, called a microinstruction. A microinstruction is a word whose bits are (or encode) the control signals for one clock step. The microinstructions that carry out one machine instruction form a microroutine, and all of them together form the microprogram. The microprogram is stored in a special fast memory called the control memory or control store, usually a ROM inside the CPU.

The parts of a microprogrammed control unit: A control address register (also called the microprogram counter) holds the address of the current microinstruction. The control memory outputs that microinstruction. Its control bits go to the datapath. Its other fields go to a sequencer that decides the next address. The next address can be the current one plus 1, a jump to an address written inside the microinstruction, a jump only if some condition holds (for example the zero flag), or a jump to the start of the microroutine for the new opcode. That last jump uses a mapping logic, often a small ROM or a simple rule, that turns the opcode into the starting address of its microroutine.

A worked microroutine: Suppose our machine has an instruction ADD that adds a memory word to the accumulator. Its microroutine might be: address 0 to 2 hold the fetch steps shared by all instructions, and the last fetch step says "map the opcode". The opcode for ADD maps to, say, address 16. Microinstruction 16 copies the address part of IR into AR. Microinstruction 17 reads memory into the data register. Microinstruction 18 does AC gets AC plus DR and jumps back to fetch at address 0. Three microinstructions, each one clock step. Writing a new instruction is now like writing a short program, not wiring new gates.

Horizontal microcode: In a horizontal format, every control signal has its own bit. If the datapath has 48 control signals, every microinstruction is at least 48 bits wide plus the next-address bits. No decoding is needed, so it is fast, and many signals can be on together, which means a lot of parallel work per step. The cost is a wide, expensive control memory where most bits are 0 most of the time.

Vertical microcode: In a vertical format, signals that can never be on at the same time are grouped into a field and encoded. Say 7 different ALU operations exist and only one is chosen per step. Instead of 7 bits we can use a 3-bit field (3 bits can name 8 things: 7 operations plus "none"). Each field goes through a decoder before reaching the datapath. Microinstructions get much narrower and the control store smaller, but there is extra decoding delay and fewer actions can happen together. Real designs often sit in the middle.

A tiny size calculation: Suppose a machine needs 30 control signals. Fully horizontal, that is 30 bits. Now suppose 8 of them are mutually exclusive memory and bus selections, and 16 are mutually exclusive ALU and shifter functions, and the other 6 are independent. Encode the 8 (plus a "none" code, so 9 cases) with 4 bits and the 16 (plus "none", 17 cases) with 5 bits. Total 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 bits. The microinstruction shrank from 30 to 15 bits, at the cost of two decoders.

Pros and cons of microprogrammed control: It is flexible. Fixing a bug or adding an instruction means changing the microprogram. Complex instructions are easy to support, because a long microroutine can do many steps. It is also systematic, which made designing big CISC processors manageable. The cost is speed: each step needs a control memory read. IBM's System/360 family, launched in 1964, used microprogramming so that cheap and expensive models could all run the same instruction set, each with its own microcode on its own hardware.

Where each is used today: Simple RISC cores, such as many ARM and RISC-V designs, use hardwired control. Modern x86 processors mostly decode common instructions in hardware into simple internal operations, and use a microcode ROM only for rare or complicated instructions. Intel and AMD also ship microcode updates through BIOS and operating system updates, which can fix some processor bugs after the chip is sold. So the two ideas live side by side.

Real life example 1, the recipe card in a home kitchen: Think of your mother making khichuri on a rainy day. She does not rebuild the kitchen for each dish. The stove, pots and spoons are the datapath. The recipe in her head, step 1 wash the rice and dal, step 2 heat oil, step 3 add onion and spices, step 4 add water, is a microroutine. When she wants to cook a new dish she does not buy a new stove, she learns a new recipe. That is microprogrammed control. A rice cooker with only one button that always does exactly the same thing is closer to hardwired control: fast and simple, but it cannot learn new tricks.

Real life example 2, a laptop BIOS update: Sometimes a laptop maker in Bangladesh's market, for example a Walton or a foreign brand, releases a BIOS update and the notes say it includes a processor microcode update. After installing, the same CPU hardware behaves slightly differently, for example a security problem is closed. This is possible only because part of the control in that CPU is microcode, which can be patched at start-up, while the fast paths stay hardwired.

Common mistakes: First, confusing the control unit with the ALU. The ALU calculates; the control unit only commands. Second, thinking microprogramming means "software in RAM" that the user writes. The microprogram sits inside the CPU and normal programmers never see it. Third, mixing up horizontal and vertical: horizontal means wide with one bit per signal and little decoding; vertical means narrow, encoded fields and more decoding. Fourth, forgetting that "don't care" entries in the control table (like RegDst for sw) are allowed to be 0 or 1, which helps simplify the logic.

What exams ask: "Compare hardwired and microprogrammed control." "Draw the block diagram of a microprogrammed control unit and explain each part." "Fill the control signal table for R-type, lw, sw and beq." "Explain horizontal versus vertical microinstruction formats with an example of field encoding." "How many bits are needed if 9 mutually exclusive signals are encoded?" (answer: 4 bits, since 3 bits give only 8 codes). "Why do RISC processors prefer hardwired control?"

Recap: The control unit turns the opcode, and the current step, into control signals that drive the datapath. Hardwired control builds this with gates, decoders and a step counter: fast but rigid. Microprogrammed control stores the signals as microinstructions in a control memory, with a sequencer choosing the next address: flexible but slower. Horizontal microcode is wide and parallel; vertical microcode is narrow and encoded. Next lesson we split the datapath into several cycles and use a finite state machine as the controller.
key_points: The control unit turns the opcode (and the current step) into control signals for the datapath.
Single-cycle MIPS signals: RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, Branch and ALUOp.
Two-level control: main control gives a 2-bit ALUOp; ALU control adds the funct field to pick the real operation.
Hardwired control is built from gates, decoders and a step counter: fast but hard to change.
Microprogrammed control stores microinstructions in a control memory; a sequencer picks the next address.
Horizontal microcode: one bit per signal, wide, parallel. Vertical microcode: encoded fields, narrow, needs decoders.
RISC cores mostly use hardwired control; modern x86 mixes hardware decoding with a microcode ROM that can be updated.
lessons.tip: Learn the control table row by row and ask 'why' for every 1 and 0. Once the reason is clear (stores never write registers, only loads read memory), you never need to memorise it.
lessons.task: On paper, list 10 control signals for an imaginary machine. Mark which ones can never be on together and group them. Count the bits needed for a fully horizontal format and for your encoded vertical format.

quiz.q: Which signal is 1 for lw but 0 for an R-type add?
quiz.explain: lw writes data read from memory into the register, so MemtoReg = 1; add writes the ALU result, so MemtoReg = 0.

quiz.q: Who first proposed microprogrammed control, in 1951?
quiz.explain: Maurice Wilkes at Cambridge proposed microprogramming in 1951.

quiz.q: A horizontal microinstruction format is best described as:
options: Narrow words with encoded fields and decoders
Stored in main memory by the user
Wide words with roughly one bit per control signal
quiz.explain: Horizontal means one bit per signal: wide, little decoding, many signals at once.

quiz.q: How many bits are needed to encode 9 mutually exclusive choices?
quiz.explain: 3 bits give only 8 codes; 4 bits give 16, enough for 9.

quiz.q: Why do RISC processors usually use hardwired control?
options: It is easier to change after manufacture
It needs a bigger control memory
Simple, regular instructions make fast hardwired logic practical
It removes the need for an ALU
quiz.explain: Simple instructions keep the control logic small, and hardwired logic avoids a control memory read each step.

lessons.title: The Multi-Cycle Datapath
lessons.content:
Imagine a school where every class period is 90 minutes long, because the longest subject, a science practical, needs 90 minutes. A quick spelling test that needs only 20 minutes still takes a full 90-minute period, and the children sit around for 70 minutes doing nothing. That is wasteful. A smarter school would use short 20-minute slots, and let the spelling test take one slot while the practical takes several. That is exactly the idea of the multi-cycle datapath. The single-cycle design gives every instruction one long clock cycle sized for the slowest instruction. The multi-cycle design uses a short clock and lets each instruction take only as many cycles as it really needs.

The problem with single-cycle: In a single-cycle design, the clock period must be long enough for the slowest instruction, which for MIPS is the load word, lw. A load must read instruction memory, read the register file, use the ALU to compute the address, read data memory, and write the register file, all in one cycle. Using textbook numbers of 200 picoseconds for a memory access, 200 ps for the ALU and 100 ps for a register file access, lw needs 200 + 100 + 200 + 200 + 100 = 800 ps. So every instruction, even a simple branch that needs much less, gets 800 ps. A second problem: each functional unit can be used only once per cycle, so the single-cycle design needs separate instruction and data memories and extra adders for PC + 4 and the branch target.

The big idea: Break each instruction into steps, where each step takes one short clock cycle and uses each major unit at most once. A natural set of steps is: instruction fetch, instruction decode and register fetch, execution or address calculation, memory access, and write back. The clock period now only has to fit the slowest step, not the slowest instruction. Simple instructions finish in fewer steps. And because different steps happen in different cycles, the same unit can be reused: one memory for both instructions and data, and one ALU that also computes PC + 4 and the branch target.

New internal registers: If a value is produced in one cycle and used in a later one, it must be saved somewhere between cycles. So the multi-cycle datapath adds a few internal registers that the programmer never sees. The Instruction Register (IR) holds the fetched instruction for the whole time it executes. The Memory Data Register (MDR) holds data just read from memory. Registers A and B hold the two values read from the register file. ALUOut holds the ALU result. Each of these is written at the end of a cycle and read in the next. IR needs a write-enable signal, because it must keep its value while the instruction runs.

Extra multiplexers: Because units are shared, they need more input choices. The memory address can come from the PC (for fetching instructions) or from ALUOut (for loads and stores), so a multiplexer controlled by a signal often called IorD chooses. The first ALU input can be the PC or register A, chosen by ALUSrcA. The second ALU input can be register B, the constant 4, the sign-extended immediate, or the immediate shifted left by 2, chosen by a 2-bit ALUSrcB. The new PC can come from the ALU result, from ALUOut, or from the jump address, chosen by PCSource. More multiplexers, but fewer big units like memories and adders.

Step 1, fetch: Every instruction starts the same way. Read memory at address PC and put the instruction into IR. At the same time, use the ALU to compute PC + 4 and write it into PC. In register-transfer style: IR gets Memory[PC], and PC gets PC + 4. The ALU is free in this cycle, so using it for PC + 4 removes the need for a separate adder.

Step 2, decode and register fetch: We still do not know what the instruction is, but reading registers is harmless, so we do it anyway. A gets Reg[rs], B gets Reg[rt]. Also, the ALU is free, so we compute the branch target just in case: ALUOut gets PC + (sign-extended immediate shifted left by 2). If the instruction turns out to be a branch, the target is ready. If not, we simply ignore it. Doing useful work "just in case" when hardware is idle is a common trick.

Step 3, depends on the instruction class: For a load or store, compute the memory address: ALUOut gets A + sign-extended immediate. For an R-type instruction, do the operation: ALUOut gets A op B. For a branch, compare and finish: if A equals B, the PC gets ALUOut (the target computed in step 2). For a jump, finish too: the PC gets the upper 4 bits of the PC joined with the 26-bit address field shifted left by 2. So branches and jumps are already done after 3 cycles.

Step 4, memory access or R-type completion: For a load, read memory: MDR gets Memory[ALUOut]. For a store, write memory: Memory[ALUOut] gets B, and the store is finished. For an R-type instruction, write the result: Reg[rd] gets ALUOut, and it is finished.

Step 5, load completion: Only the load needs this. Reg[rt] gets MDR. The load is the longest instruction, and it takes 5 cycles. Summing up the classic textbook design: lw takes 5 cycles, sw 4, R-type 4, beq 3 and j 3.

Control as a finite state machine: The single-cycle control was just combinational logic: opcode in, signals out. Now the signals must change from cycle to cycle, so the control unit needs memory of which step it is in. It becomes a finite state machine (FSM). Each state represents one cycle of work and says which control signals are on. The next state depends on the current state and, after decoding, on the opcode. You met FSMs, Moore and Mealy machines, in Digital Logic Design; here is a real use.

The states of the classic FSM: State 0 is fetch. State 1 is decode and register fetch. From state 1 the FSM branches on the opcode. For lw or sw it goes to state 2, the address calculation. From state 2, lw goes to state 3 (memory read) then state 4 (write back to register), while sw goes to state 5 (memory write). R-type goes to state 6 (execute) then state 7 (write ALUOut to rd). beq goes to state 8 (branch completion). j goes to state 9 (jump completion). Every final state returns to state 0. Ten states in total, and you can draw them as circles with arrows.

What each state turns on: In state 0, MemRead is on, IorD selects the PC, IRWrite is on, ALUSrcA selects the PC, ALUSrcB selects 4, the ALU adds, and PCWrite is on. In state 2, ALUSrcA selects A, ALUSrcB selects the immediate, and the ALU adds. In state 3, MemRead is on and IorD selects ALUOut. In state 8, ALUSrcA selects A, ALUSrcB selects B, the ALU subtracts, and PCWriteCond is on so the PC is written only if the zero output is 1. You do not need to memorise every signal of every state, but you should be able to reason them out from the register transfers.

Implementing the FSM: The FSM can be built in either of the ways from the last lesson. A hardwired version uses a state register (4 bits are enough for 10 states) plus combinational logic, often a ROM or PLA, that takes the current state and the opcode and outputs the control signals and the next state. A microprogrammed version treats each state as a microinstruction in a control memory, with a sequencer that either goes to the next address, dispatches on the opcode, or goes back to fetch. The two are equivalent; the choice is about speed and convenience.

Computing CPI for multi-cycle: Since instructions take different numbers of cycles, the average cycles per instruction (CPI) depends on the program's mix. Suppose a program has 25 percent loads, 10 percent stores, 52 percent R-type, 11 percent branches and 2 percent jumps. CPI = 0.25 x 5 + 0.10 x 4 + 0.52 x 4 + 0.11 x 3 + 0.02 x 3 = 1.25 + 0.40 + 2.08 + 0.33 + 0.06 = 4.12. Compare that with the single-cycle CPI of exactly 1. Multi-cycle has a much higher CPI, but a much shorter clock.

Is multi-cycle actually faster: With the numbers above, the slowest step is a memory access or an ALU operation, 200 ps, so the clock period is 200 ps (ignoring register overhead). Average time per instruction is 4.12 x 200 = 824 ps. The single-cycle design took 800 ps per instruction. So, surprise, with these simple numbers multi-cycle is about the same, even slightly slower. The real gain appears when instructions vary a lot in length, for example a machine with multiply, divide or floating-point instructions that take many steps. In a single-cycle design every instruction would wait as long as the slowest of those. In a multi-cycle design, each instruction pays only for its own steps. Multi-cycle also saves hardware: one memory and one ALU instead of several.

A quick worked comparison with a slow instruction: Suppose we add a multiply instruction that needs 2000 ps in one go, and it is 5 percent of the program. A single-cycle clock must now be 2000 ps for everything. In a multi-cycle design with a 200 ps clock, say multiply takes 14 cycles in total while the others keep their old counts. The new CPI is 0.95 x 4.12 + 0.05 x 14 = 3.91 + 0.70 = 4.61, so the average time is about 4.61 x 200, roughly 920 ps, while single-cycle is 2000 ps per instruction. Now multi-cycle is clearly the winner.

Real life example 1, a passport office in Agargaon: Think of the passport office where you go through steps: token, photo and fingerprint, document check, and payment verification. A person only renewing might skip one step, and a new applicant does every step. If the office forced everyone to spend the time of the longest possible process at one counter, the line would barely move. Instead, each step has its own short slot, and each person goes through only the steps they need. Notice, though, that in this picture only one person is inside at a time. When several people are at different steps at once, that is pipelining, our next lesson.

Real life example 2, a tailor in a local market: A tailor in Gausia market has one sewing machine and one cutting table. For a simple hem he measures, cuts a little and sews: 3 steps. For a full kameez he measures, cuts, sews, adds lining and finishes: 5 steps. He reuses the same machine for different steps instead of buying a separate machine for each step. That is resource sharing in the multi-cycle datapath: one memory and one ALU, used in different cycles for different jobs.

Common mistakes: First, thinking multi-cycle always beats single-cycle. As we calculated, it depends on the instruction mix and on how unequal the instructions are. Second, forgetting the internal registers (IR, MDR, A, B, ALUOut). Without them, values from one cycle would be lost by the next. Third, counting cycles wrongly: remember lw 5, sw 4, R-type 4, beq 3, j 3 for the classic design. Fourth, thinking two instructions overlap in multi-cycle. They do not. One instruction finishes all its steps before the next begins.

What exams ask: "Why does the multi-cycle datapath need IR, MDR, A, B and ALUOut?" "Write the register transfers for each step of lw." "Draw the FSM for multi-cycle control." "Given an instruction mix, compute the CPI and compare execution time with the single-cycle design." "How many cycles does beq take, and why can the branch target be computed in step 2?"

Recap: The multi-cycle datapath splits each instruction into short steps, with one unit used at most once per step. It reuses one memory and one ALU, adds internal registers to carry values between cycles, and adds multiplexers. Control becomes a finite state machine with states like fetch, decode, address calculation and write back. Instructions take 3 to 5 cycles, so CPI depends on the mix. Next lesson: instead of letting one instruction use the steps one at a time, we overlap many instructions in a pipeline.
key_points: Single-cycle wastes time: every instruction gets a clock as long as the slowest one (lw, about 800 ps in the textbook numbers).
Multi-cycle splits each instruction into short steps; the clock only has to fit the slowest step.
One memory and one ALU are reused in different cycles; extra multiplexers choose their inputs.
Internal registers IR, MDR, A, B and ALUOut carry values from one cycle to the next.
Classic cycle counts: lw 5, sw 4, R-type 4, beq 3, j 3.
Control becomes a finite state machine with about 10 states, built hardwired or microprogrammed.
CPI depends on the instruction mix; multi-cycle wins clearly when instructions differ a lot in length.
lessons.tip: Write the register transfers for lw step by step on one line each. If you can do lw, the other instructions are just shorter versions of it.
lessons.task: Take this mix: 30 percent loads, 10 percent stores, 40 percent R-type, 20 percent branches. Using lw 5, sw 4, R-type 4, beq 3, compute the CPI on paper, then the average time with a 200 ps clock, and compare with 800 ps single-cycle.

quiz.q: Why does the multi-cycle datapath need registers like A, B and ALUOut?
options: To hold values produced in one cycle for use in a later cycle
To speed up the main memory
quiz.explain: Values from one step must survive until the next step, so they are kept in internal registers.

quiz.q: In the classic multi-cycle design, how many cycles does beq take?
quiz.explain: Fetch, decode (target computed), then compare and update PC: 3 cycles.

quiz.q: A mix of 50% R-type (4 cycles) and 50% lw (5 cycles) gives what CPI?
Why can the branch target be computed during the decode step?
options: The opcode is already known to be a branch
The ALU is otherwise idle, so computing it just in case costs nothing
quiz.explain: The ALU has no other job in step 2; if the instruction is not a branch, the result is simply ignored.

quiz.q: Which statement about multi-cycle is true?
options: It needs separate instruction and data memories
Its control unit is a finite state machine
quiz.explain: Instructions do not overlap, one memory is shared, CPI is above 1, and the control is an FSM.

lessons.title: Pipelining Basics
lessons.content:
Imagine a fuchka stall near Dhanmondi Lake on a Friday evening. One person is doing everything: crack the puri, fill it with potato and chickpeas, pour the tok, and hand the plate to the customer. Each plate takes four minutes, and the line grows longer and longer. Now three cousins join. One cracks puris, one fills them, one pours tok and serves. While the third cousin serves plate 1, the second is filling plate 2 and the first is cracking puris for plate 3. Each plate still takes about the same time from start to finish, but a plate now comes out much more often. That overlap is pipelining, and it is the most important speed trick inside every modern processor.

What pipelining is: Pipelining is a technique where several instructions are overlapped in execution, each one in a different stage. The work of one instruction is split into stages, and each stage has its own hardware. In every clock cycle, each stage works on a different instruction, and instructions move one stage forward per cycle, like products moving along a factory conveyor belt. The multi-cycle datapath of the last lesson also split instructions into steps, but only one instruction was inside at a time. A pipeline keeps all stages busy at once.

The laundry analogy: The textbook example uses laundry. Each load needs four steps: wash (30 minutes), dry (30 minutes), fold (30 minutes), and put away (30 minutes). Doing four loads one after another takes 4 x 2 hours = 8 hours. With pipelining, as soon as load 1 moves from the washer to the dryer, load 2 goes into the washer. Load 1 finishes at 2 hours, and after that a new load finishes every 30 minutes. Four loads finish in 2 + 3 x 0.5 = 3.5 hours. With many loads, the speedup approaches 4, the number of stages.

The five MIPS stages: The classic RISC pipeline has five stages. IF, instruction fetch: read the instruction from instruction memory and compute PC + 4. ID, instruction decode and register read: decode the instruction and read its source registers. EX, execute: the ALU does the operation or computes a memory address. MEM, memory access: loads read data memory, stores write it; other instructions do nothing here. WB, write back: the result is written into the register file. These are the same steps you saw in the multi-cycle design, now with each stage given its own hardware so they can work together.

A pipeline diagram: Picture the instructions as rows and clock cycles as columns. Instruction 1 is in IF in cycle 1, ID in cycle 2, EX in cycle 3, MEM in cycle 4, WB in cycle 5. Instruction 2 starts one cycle later: IF in cycle 2, ID in cycle 3, and so on until WB in cycle 6. Instruction 3 runs from cycle 3 to cycle 7. In cycle 5 the pipeline is full: instruction 5 is in IF, 4 in ID, 3 in EX, 2 in MEM, and 1 in WB. From then on, one instruction completes every cycle.

Counting cycles: With k stages and n instructions, the first instruction needs k cycles to come out. After that, one instruction finishes per cycle, so the remaining n - 1 instructions need n - 1 more cycles. Total = k + n - 1 cycles. With 5 stages and 100 instructions: 5 + 99 = 104 cycles. Without pipelining, if each instruction needs 5 of those same short cycles, it is 5 x 100 = 500 cycles. Speedup = 500 / 104, about 4.8, close to the ideal 5. For very large n, the speedup approaches k.

Pipeline registers: Between every pair of stages sits a pipeline register that holds everything the next stage needs. They are named after the stages they separate: IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB. At the end of each cycle, every pipeline register captures the output of the stage before it. This keeps each instruction's data travelling with it. For example, the destination register number of a load is read from the instruction in ID, but it is only needed in WB, three cycles later. So it must be carried through ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB, otherwise a later instruction would overwrite it.

Control in a pipeline: The control signals are generated in ID, from the opcode, the same way as in the single-cycle design. But each signal is only needed in a later stage. So the signals are also carried along in the pipeline registers, and each stage uses its own group: EX uses ALUSrc, ALUOp and RegDst; MEM uses MemRead, MemWrite and Branch; WB uses RegWrite and MemtoReg. Signals for later stages are dropped off as they are used, so the pipeline registers carry fewer control bits as you move right.

The clock period: In a pipeline, all stages move together on the same clock, so the clock period must fit the slowest stage, plus a small overhead for the pipeline registers. Using the textbook numbers of 200 ps for memory and ALU and 100 ps for register access, the stages are IF 200, ID 100, EX 200, MEM 200, WB 100. The slowest is 200 ps, so the clock is 200 ps. The ID and WB stages finish early and wait. That is why designers try to balance the stages: an unbalanced pipeline is limited by its slowest stage.

A worked comparison: Take three lw instructions. In the single-cycle design each needs 800 ps, so three take 2400 ps. In the 5-stage pipeline with a 200 ps clock, the first lw takes 5 x 200 = 1000 ps, and each of the next two completes 200 ps later, so the total is 1000 + 2 x 200 = 1400 ps. For only three instructions the gain is modest. For a million instructions, the pipeline completes one every 200 ps, compared with 800 ps, a speedup of about 4, not 5, because the stages are not perfectly balanced against the 800 ps single-cycle time.

Latency versus throughput: These two words are the heart of pipelining. Latency is how long one instruction takes from start to finish. Throughput is how many instructions finish per unit of time. Pipelining improves throughput, not latency. In fact, latency usually gets a little worse: in our example a single lw takes 1000 ps in the pipeline but only 800 ps in single-cycle, because every stage is stretched to 200 ps and pipeline registers add delay. The fuchka plate takes just as long to make, but the stall serves many more customers per hour.

Ideal speedup and why we never reach it: If the stages are perfectly balanced, the time between instructions in a pipeline is the non-pipelined time divided by the number of stages. That is the ideal: k stages give speedup k. In practice we get less, for three reasons. First, stages are not perfectly balanced. Second, pipeline registers add overhead to every cycle. Third, and most important, hazards: situations where the next instruction cannot proceed in the next cycle. Hazards are the topic of the next lesson.

Pipelining and the CPU time equation: Recall that CPU time = instruction count x CPI x clock period. Pipelining does not change the instruction count; the program is the same. Compared with the single-cycle design, the CPI stays close to 1 (one instruction finishes per cycle once the pipeline is full), but the clock period becomes much shorter. Compared with the multi-cycle design, the clock period is about the same, but the CPI drops from around 4 to close to 1. So the pipeline takes the short clock of multi-cycle and the CPI of single-cycle, the best of both. Hazards push the CPI above 1, and the size of that increase is what designers fight to keep small.

Why MIPS was designed for pipelining: The MIPS instruction set makes pipelining easier in several ways. All instructions are the same length, 32 bits, so fetching is simple and the next instruction's address is always known. There are only a few instruction formats, and the source register fields are in the same position in each, so registers can be read in ID while the instruction is still being decoded. Memory operands appear only in loads and stores, so the address can be computed in EX and memory accessed in MEM. And data in memory must be aligned, so one access always fits in one stage. x86, with its variable-length instructions, is much harder to pipeline directly.

Deeper pipelines: If 5 stages are good, why not 30? More stages means less work per stage and a faster clock. Some processors have gone very deep: Intel's Pentium 4 in the early 2000s had pipelines of about 20 and later about 31 stages. But deeper pipelines make hazards more costly, waste more power, and add more pipeline register overhead. Later Intel designs went back to shorter pipelines. Most modern high-performance cores use somewhere around 10 to 20 stages. There is a sweet spot, and it is not "as deep as possible".

Real life example 1, a garment factory in Gazipur: In a garment factory, a shirt is not made by one worker from start to end. One line cuts the fabric, the next sews the body, the next attaches the sleeves, the next adds buttons, and the last checks and folds. A single shirt might take an hour to go through all stations, but a finished shirt comes off the end every minute or so. If the button station is slow, every station before it has to wait, and the whole line runs at the button station's speed. That is exactly the "slowest stage sets the clock" rule.

Real life example 2, a wedding biryani serving line: At a big wedding in Chattogram, guests pass along a table: one person gives the plate, the next adds biryani, the next adds a piece of roast, the next adds borhani and salad. Each guest still needs all four steps, but four guests are being served at the same time. If the roast server is sometimes waiting because the kitchen has not brought more roast, the whole line pauses. That pause is a hazard, a stall in pipeline language, and that is exactly what the next lesson is about.

Common mistakes: First, saying pipelining makes each instruction faster. It does not; it makes the processor finish more instructions per second. Second, using k x n instead of k + n - 1 for the cycle count of a pipeline. Third, forgetting that the clock is set by the slowest stage plus register overhead. Fourth, thinking a pipeline with k stages always gives exactly k times speedup; that is only the ideal, for balanced stages, no overhead, no hazards and very many instructions.

What exams ask: "Explain pipelining with the laundry analogy." "Name and describe the five stages of the MIPS pipeline." "Draw a pipeline diagram for four instructions and show which instruction is in which stage in each cycle." "How many cycles do 200 instructions take on a 5-stage pipeline?" (answer: 204). "Given stage delays, find the clock period and the speedup over a single-cycle design." "Why does pipelining improve throughput but not latency?" "What are pipeline registers and why are they needed?"

Recap: Pipelining overlaps instructions so that every stage works on a different instruction in the same cycle. The classic pipeline has five stages, IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB, separated by pipeline registers that carry both data and control signals forward. n instructions on a k-stage pipeline take k + n - 1 cycles. The clock is set by the slowest stage. Pipelining boosts throughput, not latency, and the ideal speedup of k is reduced by unbalanced stages, register overhead and hazards. Next: the three kinds of hazards and how processors deal with them.
key_points: Pipelining overlaps instructions: each stage works on a different instruction in the same cycle.
Classic 5 stages: IF (fetch), ID (decode, read registers), EX (ALU), MEM (data memory), WB (write back).
n instructions on a k-stage pipeline take k + n - 1 cycles; speedup approaches k for large n.
Pipeline registers IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB carry data and control signals with each instruction.
The clock is set by the slowest stage plus pipeline register overhead, so stages should be balanced.
Pipelining improves throughput, not latency; one instruction may even take a little longer.
Ideal speedup is reduced by unbalanced stages, register overhead and hazards.
lessons.tip: Always draw the pipeline diagram (instructions as rows, cycles as columns) before answering a pipelining question. Most mistakes disappear once you can see which instruction is where.
lessons.task: Do the laundry analogy with real numbers: pick 3 household jobs with different times (for example 10, 20 and 15 minutes) and 5 items. Draw a timeline on paper, find the total time with and without overlap, and notice that the slowest job sets the pace.

quiz.q: How many cycles do 100 instructions take on an ideal 5-stage pipeline?
What does pipelining improve?
options: Throughput: instructions completed per unit time
quiz.explain: Each instruction takes about as long or longer, but more instructions finish per second.

quiz.q: Stage delays are 200, 100, 200, 200 and 100 ps. Ignoring register overhead, what is the clock period?
quiz.explain: The clock must fit the slowest stage, 200 ps.

quiz.q: In which stage does a MIPS load read data memory?
quiz.explain: EX computes the address; MEM reads the data; WB writes it into the register.

quiz.q: Why are pipeline registers needed?
options: To keep each instruction's data and control with it as it moves between stages
quiz.explain: Without them, the next instruction entering a stage would overwrite values a previous instruction still needs.

lessons.title: Pipeline Hazards: Structural, Data and Control
lessons.content:
Imagine the fuchka stall from the last lesson, running smoothly with three cousins in a line. Then three things go wrong. First, there is only one spoon, and both the filler and the tok-pourer need it at the same moment. Second, the tok-pourer cannot pour until the filler finishes the plate, but the filler is still waiting for potatoes. Third, a customer at the front changes her order halfway, and the plates already started for her must be thrown away. These three troubles have names in a pipeline: structural hazards, data hazards and control hazards. A hazard is any situation that stops the next instruction from running in the next clock cycle.

Why hazards matter: In the last lesson we said a 5-stage pipeline can ideally finish one instruction per cycle, a CPI of 1. Hazards force the pipeline to wait, and each wasted cycle is called a stall or a bubble. If a program has many stalls, the CPI rises, and the speedup we hoped for melts away. Designers spend a huge amount of effort on making hazards rare and stalls short. The three solutions you will meet again and again are: add hardware, forward results early, and predict the future.

Structural hazards: A structural hazard happens when two instructions need the same hardware unit in the same cycle. The classic case is memory. If there were only one memory, then in a cycle where a load is in MEM reading data, a later instruction in IF also wants to read memory to fetch itself. One of them must wait. The standard fix is simply more hardware: separate instruction and data memories, which in real processors means separate level-1 instruction and data caches. MIPS was designed so that each unit is used in only one stage, which avoids most structural hazards.

The register file trick: The register file is used in two stages: read in ID and write in WB. In some cycle an older instruction is in WB writing while a newer one is in ID reading. To avoid a conflict, the register file is written in the first half of the clock cycle and read in the second half. So if the instruction in WB writes register $s0 and the instruction in ID reads $s0 in the same cycle, the reader gets the new value. Remember this rule; it matters for counting stalls.

Data hazards: A data hazard happens when an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not produced yet. Example: add $s0, $t0, $t1 followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3. The sub needs $s0, but add only writes $s0 into the register file in its WB stage. This is called a read-after-write (RAW) dependence: the later instruction reads what the earlier one writes. It is a true dependence, because the data really flows from one to the other.

Counting stalls without forwarding: Put add in cycles 1 to 5: IF 1, ID 2, EX 3, MEM 4, WB 5. Normally sub would be in IF in cycle 2 and ID in cycle 3, reading $s0 too early. Because of the write-first-read-second rule, sub can safely read $s0 in cycle 5, the same cycle add writes it. So sub's ID moves from cycle 3 to cycle 5: 2 stall cycles. If every instruction depended on the one before, the CPI would be 3, and the pipeline would be almost useless.

Forwarding, also called bypassing: Look again. The value of $s0 is actually computed by the ALU at the end of cycle 3, in add's EX stage. It sits in the EX/MEM pipeline register. sub needs it as an ALU input at the start of its EX stage, cycle 4. So we add extra wires and multiplexers that feed the ALU directly from the EX/MEM or MEM/WB pipeline registers, instead of waiting for the register file. With forwarding, this add and sub run back to back with zero stalls.

How the forwarding unit decides: A small forwarding unit compares register numbers. In words: if the instruction in MEM (one ahead) will write a register, and that register is not $zero, and it equals a source register of the instruction now in EX, forward from EX/MEM. Otherwise, if the instruction in WB (two ahead) will write that register, forward from MEM/WB. The nearer instruction gets priority, because it holds the newest value. For example, in add $1,$2,$3 ; add $1,$1,$4 ; add $5,$1,$6, the third instruction must take $1 from the second, not the first.

The load-use hazard: Forwarding cannot fix everything. Consider lw $s0, 20($t1) followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3. The loaded value only arrives from data memory at the end of the load's MEM stage, cycle 4. But sub wants it at the start of its EX stage, also cycle 4. You cannot send data back in time. So even with forwarding, a load followed immediately by an instruction that uses its result needs one stall cycle. After that bubble, the value is forwarded from MEM/WB into sub's EX in cycle 5.

The hazard detection unit: Who inserts that stall? A hazard detection unit in the ID stage checks: is the instruction in EX a load (MemRead is 1), and is its destination register the same as one of the source registers of the instruction in ID? If yes, stall: keep the PC and IF/ID register unchanged so the same instructions are tried again next cycle, and put zeros into the control signals in ID/EX so a "do nothing" bubble moves down the pipeline. This is how hardware creates a nop on the fly.

Compilers can help, code scheduling: A clever compiler can reorder instructions to hide load-use stalls. Take the C code a = b + e; c = b + f. A simple translation is: lw $t1, 0($t0); lw $t2, 4($t0); add $t3, $t1, $t2; sw $t3, 12($t0); lw $t4, 8($t0); add $t5, $t1, $t4; sw $t5, 16($t0). Both adds use a value loaded just before them, so there are two stalls, and the 7 instructions take 13 cycles. Move lw $t4 up to the third position, before the first add. Now no add follows its load directly, the stalls vanish, and it takes 11 cycles. Same work, fewer cycles, just by changing order.

Control hazards: A control hazard comes from branches. The pipeline fetches a new instruction every cycle, but after fetching a beq it does not yet know whether the branch is taken. Which instruction should it fetch next? In the basic design the branch decision is only made in MEM, which would cost 3 cycles per taken branch. By adding a comparator and a target adder in ID, the decision moves to ID and the penalty drops to 1 cycle. That still hurts, because branches are common, often 15 to 20 percent of instructions.

Option 1, stall: The simplest choice is to stall after every branch until the decision is made. If 20 percent of instructions are branches and each costs 1 stall, CPI = 1 + 0.20 x 1 = 1.2. Safe, but slow, and much worse with longer pipelines where the decision comes later.

Option 2, predict not taken: Just assume the branch is not taken and keep fetching the next instructions. If the guess is right, no time is lost. If the branch turns out to be taken, flush the wrongly fetched instruction (turn it into a bubble) and fetch from the target. Only taken branches pay the penalty.

Option 3, dynamic branch prediction: Real processors remember how each branch behaved before. A branch prediction buffer, indexed by the low bits of the branch address, stores a little history. A 1-bit predictor just remembers "taken last time or not". The trouble: a loop branch that is taken 9 times and then falls through once will be mispredicted twice every time the loop runs, once at the exit and once at the first iteration of the next run. A 2-bit saturating counter fixes this: it has four states (strongly taken, weakly taken, weakly not taken, strongly not taken) and must be wrong twice in a row before it changes its prediction. Now the loop branch is mispredicted only once per run. Modern predictors are far more advanced and are right well over 90 percent of the time on typical code.

Branch target buffer: Predicting taken is only useful if we also know where to jump. A branch target buffer is a small cache that stores, for recently seen branches, the target address. In the IF stage, the PC is looked up in it, and if there is a hit and the prediction says taken, the next fetch starts at the stored target with no delay.

Option 4, delayed branch: Early MIPS used another trick. The instruction right after a branch, called the branch delay slot, is always executed, whether the branch is taken or not. The compiler tries to move a useful instruction from before the branch into that slot. This hides a 1-cycle penalty for free. But it ties the instruction set to one particular pipeline, and it helps little in deep or superscalar pipelines, so newer designs such as RISC-V do not use delay slots.

A note on other dependences: Besides read-after-write, two other kinds exist. Write-after-read (WAR) is when a later instruction writes a register that an earlier one still needs to read, and write-after-write (WAW) is when two instructions write the same register. In our simple in-order 5-stage pipeline, all reads happen in ID and all writes in WB in program order, so WAR and WAW cannot cause problems. They become important in out-of-order processors, which is the topic of the next lesson.

Real life example 1, the bKash cash-out queue: You are at an agent shop to cash out money, and the person ahead of you is depositing. The agent cannot give you cash until the deposit is recorded in his balance. That is a data dependence. A smart agent writes the new balance on a slip and uses that slip straight away instead of waiting for the app to refresh. That is forwarding: use the result as soon as it exists, not when it is officially stored.

Real life example 2, the road fork on the Dhaka-Mawa expressway: A bus driver approaching a fork is not sure whether the passengers want to go towards Bhanga or turn off. If he stops at every fork to ask, the journey is slow, like stalling. A driver who usually takes the left road keeps going left and turns back only if someone shouts. Most days he saves time.
