That is branch prediction, and turning back after a wrong guess is the flush.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting the write-first-read-second rule, so counting 3 stalls instead of 2 without forwarding. Second, thinking forwarding removes the load-use stall. It reduces it to 1 cycle but cannot remove it. Third, mixing the hazard types: a shared memory conflict is structural, a needed result is data, a branch is control. Fourth, in timing diagrams, forgetting that a stall delays every later instruction too.

What exams ask: "Define the three types of hazards with an example of each." "Draw the timing diagram for this sequence with and without forwarding and count the stalls." "Why does a load-use hazard need a stall even with forwarding?" "Reorder this code to avoid stalls." "Explain the 2-bit branch predictor with a state diagram." "Compute the CPI if 20 percent of instructions are branches with a 1-cycle penalty."

Recap: Hazards stop the pipeline from finishing one instruction every cycle. Structural hazards are fixed with more hardware, such as separate instruction and data memories. Data hazards are mostly removed by forwarding; the load-use case still needs one stall, detected by the hazard detection unit and often hidden by compiler scheduling. Control hazards are reduced by deciding branches early, predicting them, using a branch target buffer, or in older designs a delay slot. Next lesson: going beyond one instruction per cycle with instruction-level parallelism.
key_points: A hazard stops the next instruction from running in the next cycle; each lost cycle is a stall or bubble.
Structural hazards (two instructions need one unit) are fixed with more hardware, like separate instruction and data memories.
The register file is written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second half.
Data hazards (read-after-write) need 2 stalls without forwarding; forwarding from EX/MEM and MEM/WB removes most of them.
A load followed immediately by a use of its result still needs 1 stall, inserted by the hazard detection unit.
Compilers reorder code to hide load-use stalls (13 cycles down to 11 in the classic example).
Control hazards are reduced by deciding branches in ID, predicting not taken, 2-bit dynamic predictors and branch target buffers.
WAR and WAW cannot cause trouble in a simple in-order 5-stage pipeline; they matter in out-of-order processors.
lessons.tip: For every pair of instructions, ask three questions: does the second read a register the first writes, is the first a load, and how far apart are they? That decides the stalls almost every time.
lessons.task: Write these on paper: lw $t1,0($t0); add $t2,$t1,$t1; sub $t3,$t0,$t0. Draw the 5-stage timing diagram with forwarding and count the stalls. Then swap the add and sub and draw it again.

quiz.q: Two instructions need the same memory in the same cycle. What kind of hazard is this?
quiz.explain: A conflict over a hardware resource is a structural hazard.

quiz.q: add $s0,$t0,$t1 is followed directly by sub $t2,$s0,$t3. With full forwarding, how many stalls?
quiz.explain: The ALU result is forwarded from EX/MEM straight into sub's EX stage.

quiz.q: lw $s0,0($t1) is followed directly by add $t2,$s0,$t3. With forwarding, how many stalls?
quiz.explain: The loaded value is only ready after MEM, one cycle too late for add's EX, so one stall is needed.

quiz.q: 20% of instructions are branches and each costs a 1-cycle stall. What is the CPI (otherwise ideal)?
Why is a 2-bit predictor better than a 1-bit predictor for loops?
options: It needs two mispredictions in a row before changing its prediction
It removes the need for a branch target
It decides branches in the WB stage
quiz.explain: A single loop exit does not flip a 2-bit counter, so the next run starts with a correct prediction.

lessons.title: Instruction-Level Parallelism
lessons.content:
Imagine a small restaurant in Old Dhaka with one cook. Orders come in on slips, and the cook does them strictly in order: first the tehari, then the tea, then the paratha. If the tehari needs ten minutes on the fire, the tea waits, even though the kettle is free and tea takes two minutes. Now imagine a bigger kitchen with three cooks and a smart manager. The manager looks at the slips, sees that tea does not depend on the tehari, and gives it to a free cook right away. Orders still go out to customers in the right order, but much less time is wasted. Modern processors do exactly this. The ideas behind it are called instruction-level parallelism.

What instruction-level parallelism is: Instruction-level parallelism, or ILP, means running several instructions of one program at the same time. Pipelining is already a form of ILP, because up to five instructions are in flight at once, each in a different stage. But a simple pipeline can at best finish one instruction per cycle, a CPI of 1. To go beyond that, the processor must start more than one instruction per cycle, and it must find instructions that are independent of each other. This lesson gives you the main ideas; the full details belong to advanced courses.

Measuring with IPC: When CPI goes below 1, people often flip it around and use IPC, instructions per cycle, which is 1 divided by CPI. A processor with an IPC of 2 finishes two instructions per cycle on average, which is a CPI of 0.5. A pipeline that can start up to 4 instructions per cycle is called 4-wide or 4-issue, and its best possible IPC is 4, though real programs reach much less.

Dependences decide everything: Two instructions can run in parallel only if neither needs the other. Look at this sequence: 1. add r1, r2, r3; 2. mul r4, r1, r5; 3. sub r6, r7, r8. Instruction 2 needs r1 from instruction 1, a true data dependence (read after write), so they must happen in order. Instruction 3 uses nothing from 1 or 2, so it can run at the same time as 1. A program's available ILP is limited by chains of true dependences like 1 to 2.

Name dependences: There are two more kinds of dependence that only come from reusing register names. A write-after-read (WAR), or anti-dependence, is when a later instruction writes a register an earlier one still has to read. A write-after-write (WAW), or output dependence, is when two instructions write the same register, so the final value must come from the later one. No data actually flows between the instructions in these cases. They exist only because there are a limited number of register names. That is why they can be removed, as we will see.

Static multiple issue and VLIW: One way to start several instructions per cycle is to let the compiler do the planning. In a Very Long Instruction Word (VLIW) design, each instruction word contains several operations, for example one integer operation, one memory operation and one floating-point operation, which the hardware runs together in one cycle. The compiler must find independent operations and pack them into these bundles; if it cannot find enough, it fills the empty slots with no-ops. The hardware is simpler, because it does not check dependences between operations in a bundle. Intel and HP's Itanium used a related approach called EPIC. VLIW is common in digital signal processors, where the code is regular and predictable.

Loop unrolling, a compiler trick: Compilers expose more ILP by unrolling loops. Suppose a loop adds a constant to every element of an array, one element per iteration. Unrolling it 4 times means each new iteration handles four elements, with four separate loads, four adds and four stores, using different registers. Now there are four independent chains instead of one, and the loop overhead (counter update and branch) is paid once instead of four times. The cost is bigger code and more registers.

Dynamic multiple issue, superscalar: The other way is to let the hardware decide at run time. A superscalar processor fetches and decodes several instructions per cycle and has several execution units, for example two integer ALUs, a load/store unit and a floating-point unit. Each cycle, its logic checks which of the fetched instructions are independent and issues as many as it can. The same program binary runs on narrower and wider superscalar chips without recompiling, which is a big practical advantage. Almost every processor in a modern laptop or phone is superscalar.

In-order versus out-of-order: A simple superscalar issues instructions in program order. If the next instruction is waiting for data, everything behind it waits too, just like the one-cook restaurant. An out-of-order processor lets later independent instructions go ahead. Think back to our example: if instruction 2, the mul, is waiting for r1, instruction 3, the sub, can execute first. The processor still makes the results look as if everything ran in order, as we will see.

Dynamic scheduling, the idea of Tomasulo's algorithm: In 1967 Robert Tomasulo designed a scheme for the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91 that is the ancestor of modern out-of-order cores. Decoded instructions are placed in waiting areas called reservation stations in front of each execution unit. Each waiting instruction watches for its missing operands. When a unit finishes, it broadcasts its result on a common data bus with a tag saying which instruction produced it. Every reservation station that was waiting for that tag grabs the value. As soon as an instruction has all its operands, it can execute, regardless of program order.

Register renaming: The trick that removes WAR and WAW dependences is renaming. The processor has many more physical registers than the instruction set has register names, and it maps each new write to a fresh physical register. Example: 1. r1 = r2 + r3; 2. r4 = r1 x 2; 3. r1 = r5 + r6; 4. r7 = r1 - 1. Instruction 3 writes r1 again (WAW with 1, and WAR with 2, which still reads the old r1). Rename: instruction 1 writes p10, instruction 2 reads p10, instruction 3 writes p11, instruction 4 reads p11. Now instructions 3 and 4 have nothing to do with 1 and 2, and the two pairs can run in parallel. Only the true dependences remain.

The whole journey in an out-of-order core: Putting the pieces together, an instruction goes through these steps. It is fetched (several per cycle) and decoded. Its registers are renamed. It gets a place in a reservation station and an entry in the reorder buffer. It waits until its operands are ready, then executes on a free unit. Its result is broadcast to everyone waiting for it. Finally, it commits when it reaches the head of the reorder buffer. Fetch, decode, rename and commit happen in program order; only the waiting and executing in the middle are out of order.

Keeping it correct, the reorder buffer: If instructions finish out of order, what happens when one of them causes an exception, or turns out to be on a wrongly predicted path? The answer is the reorder buffer (ROB). Instructions enter it in program order when decoded. They may execute and produce results out of order, but they commit, meaning their results become officially visible in the architectural registers and memory, strictly in program order, from the head of the buffer. So the outside world always sees a clean, in-order history. This is "out-of-order execution, in-order commit".

Speculation: Out-of-order cores rely on branch prediction from the last lesson, and they go further: they execute instructions after a predicted branch before knowing whether the prediction is right. This is speculative execution. The results wait in the reorder buffer. If the prediction was right, they commit and much time is saved. If it was wrong, everything after the branch is thrown away and fetching restarts at the correct address. Good prediction is therefore essential; with deep, wide pipelines, every misprediction can waste the work of dozens of instructions.

When speculation leaks: Speculation is supposed to be invisible, because wrong-path results are discarded. But in 2018 researchers revealed the Spectre and Meltdown attacks, which showed that speculative execution can leave traces in the cache that an attacker can measure, leaking secret data. Processor makers and operating systems responded with fixes, some in microcode and software. It is a good reminder that clever performance tricks can have security side effects.

Micro-operations in x86: Out-of-order scheduling works best with simple, uniform operations. That is why x86 processors since Intel's Pentium Pro in 1995 translate complex x86 instructions into simpler internal micro-operations, and then schedule those out of order, much like a RISC core inside. This is one reason the old RISC versus CISC fight matters less today.

Limits of ILP: Why not build a 32-wide processor? Real programs do not have that much ILP; true dependences, branches and waiting for memory limit how many instructions are independent at once. The logic to check dependences and rename registers grows quickly with width, costing area and power. Typical high-performance cores today can issue somewhere around 4 to 8 operations per cycle, and real programs often average an IPC of around 1 to 3. Since about the mid-2000s, designers have turned to multiple cores and thread-level parallelism as the main way to use more transistors.

Real life example 1, the Eid shopping list: Your family goes to New Market before Eid with a long list: shoes for you, a sari for Ammu, a panjabi for Abbu, and a gift box that must be bought after you know the sari's colour. Going strictly in list order wastes time. Instead the family splits: Abbu buys his panjabi, you buy shoes, Ammu chooses the sari, and the gift waits until the sari is done. That is out-of-order execution with a true dependence (gift after sari) respected. At home, everyone shows the shopping in list order: that is in-order commit.

Real life example 2, an exam hall in Bangladesh: In a board exam, a smart student reads all questions first. If question 3 is easy and question 2 needs an answer from question 1, she does 1, then 3 while still thinking about 2, then 2. She writes the answers in the right numbered boxes so the examiner sees them in order. Guessing that the next question will be on a chapter she studied and preparing her thoughts early is like speculation. If the guess is wrong, she drops that thought and starts again.

Common mistakes: First, thinking superscalar and pipelined mean the same thing. A pipeline overlaps stages; superscalar issues several instructions per cycle, usually on top of a pipeline. Second, thinking out-of-order means results become visible out of order. Commit is in order. Third, thinking renaming removes true dependences. It only removes WAR and WAW name dependences. Fourth, confusing VLIW and superscalar: VLIW relies on the compiler to bundle operations, superscalar decides in hardware at run time.

What exams ask: "Define instruction-level parallelism and IPC." "Identify RAW, WAR and WAW dependences in this code and show how renaming removes some of them." "Compare static (VLIW) and dynamic (superscalar) multiple issue." "Explain the role of reservation stations and the reorder buffer." "What is speculative execution and what happens on a misprediction?" "Why does ILP have limits?"

Recap: ILP is about running several instructions of one program at once. Pipelining overlaps stages; multiple issue starts several instructions per cycle, either with compiler-planned bundles (VLIW) or hardware decisions (superscalar). Out-of-order processors use dynamic scheduling, reservation stations, register renaming to remove name dependences, a reorder buffer for in-order commit, and speculation past predicted branches. True dependences, branches, memory delays and power limit how far this goes. Next lesson: the memory hierarchy, because a fast core is useless if it waits for memory.
key_points: ILP means running several instructions of one program at the same time; IPC = 1 / CPI.
Only true (read-after-write) dependences force order; WAR and WAW are name dependences caused by reusing register names.
VLIW (static multiple issue): the compiler packs independent operations into one long instruction word.
Superscalar (dynamic multiple issue): hardware fetches several instructions per cycle and issues the independent ones.
Out-of-order execution uses reservation stations (from Tomasulo's 1967 design) to run instructions when their operands are ready.
Register renaming maps names to extra physical registers and removes WAR and WAW dependences.
The reorder buffer commits results in program order; speculation runs past predicted branches and is undone on a misprediction.
Dependences, branches, memory delays and power limit ILP, which pushed designers towards multicore.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a block of code, first mark every dependence with arrows and label it RAW, WAR or WAW. Almost every ILP exam question starts from that picture.
lessons.task: Write 6 simple lines like r1 = r2 + r3 on paper, reusing a few register names on purpose. Mark all RAW, WAR and WAW pairs, then rename each new write to a fresh name (p1, p2, ...) and see how many instructions could now run at the same time.

quiz.q: A processor has a CPI of 0.5. What is its IPC?
Which dependence can register renaming NOT remove?
quiz.explain: Renaming removes name dependences only; real data flow (RAW) must still be respected.

quiz.q: In a VLIW processor, who decides which operations run together?
options: The reorder buffer at run time
quiz.explain: VLIW relies on the compiler to bundle independent operations.

quiz.q: What does the reorder buffer guarantee?
options: Results are committed in program order
quiz.explain: Execution may be out of order, but commit is in order, so the visible state stays correct.

quiz.q: What happens to speculatively executed instructions when the branch prediction was wrong?
options: They are discarded and fetching restarts at the correct address
quiz.explain: Wrong-path work is thrown away; only correctly predicted work commits.

lessons.title: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
lessons.content:
Imagine you are studying for an exam at your desk at home. The book you are reading right now is open in front of you. A few other books you will need tonight are stacked on the desk. The rest of your books are on the shelf across the room, and old books from past classes are packed in a trunk under the bed. You keep the things you use most right next to you, and the things you rarely touch far away. A computer does exactly the same thing with its data, and the name for this arrangement is the memory hierarchy.

The basic problem: A processor today can do several billion simple steps every second. To do any step, it needs data and instructions. If every piece of data had to come from the slowest storage, the processor would spend almost all of its time waiting. We would love one memory that is huge, very fast and very cheap all at once. Sadly, no such memory exists. Fast memory is expensive and small; big memory is cheap and slow. So designers combine several kinds of memory, each one bigger and slower than the one above it.

The levels from top to bottom: At the very top are the CPU registers, a few dozen small storage boxes inside the processor itself, read in a fraction of a nanosecond. Next comes cache memory, built from SRAM, usually in two or three levels named L1, L2 and L3. L1 is tiny (often tens of kilobytes per core) and answers in a few clock cycles. L2 and L3 are larger, a few hundred kilobytes up to tens of megabytes, and a bit slower. Below the caches sits main memory, built from DRAM, measured in gigabytes and taking roughly tens of nanoseconds to answer. Below that is secondary storage: SSDs and hard disks, holding hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes but taking microseconds (SSD) or milliseconds (hard disk). At the bottom you can add tape or cloud archives for backups.

The three trade-offs: As you go down the hierarchy, three things change together. Capacity grows: from bytes to terabytes. Access time grows: from under a nanosecond to milliseconds. Cost per byte falls: a gigabyte of disk is far cheaper than a gigabyte of DRAM, which is far cheaper than a gigabyte of SRAM. A hard disk can be about a million times slower than a register. That huge gap is why the hierarchy matters so much.

Volatile and non-volatile: Registers, caches and DRAM are volatile, which means they forget everything when power goes off. SSDs, hard disks and tapes are non-volatile, they keep data with no power. This is why you lose an unsaved document during load-shedding but the saved file is still on the disk when electricity comes back.

Why the trick works, locality: The hierarchy would be useless if programs used data in a completely random way. Luckily, real programs show locality of reference. There are two kinds. Temporal locality means that if you used something just now, you will probably use it again soon. A loop counter is touched on every round of the loop. Spatial locality means that if you used one address, you will probably soon use the addresses next to it. When a program walks through an array, it reads element 0, then 1, then 2, all sitting side by side in memory.

Locality in a tiny program: Look at this code: sum = 0; for i = 0 to 999: sum = sum + a[i]. The variable sum and the counter i are used a thousand times, that is temporal locality. The array elements a[0], a[1], a[2] and so on lie next to each other, that is spatial locality. The instructions of the loop body are also fetched again and again, so the code itself has temporal locality too. Caches are built to exploit both kinds.

Blocks: Data does not move between levels one byte at a time. It moves in fixed-size chunks. Between cache and main memory the chunk is called a block or a cache line, commonly 64 bytes on modern machines. Between main memory and disk the chunk is called a page, often 4 kilobytes. Bringing a whole block at once is how the hardware uses spatial locality: you ask for a[0], and a[1] to a[15] (if they are 4-byte integers) arrive in the same 64-byte block for free.

Inclusion idea: In a simple model, each level holds a copy of a subset of the level below it. The cache holds copies of some blocks of main memory, and main memory holds some pages of what is on disk. The processor always looks at the top first. If the data is not there, it goes one level down, and the data is copied upward so next time it is close by. Real processors sometimes break strict inclusion between cache levels, but the subset picture is the right starting point.

Hit and miss: When the processor looks for data in a level and finds it, that is a hit. When the data is not there, it is a miss. The hit rate is the fraction of accesses that hit, and the miss rate is 1 minus the hit rate. The hit time is how long it takes to get data on a hit. The miss penalty is the extra time to fetch the block from the next level down and deliver it. Good caches in normal programs often reach hit rates well above 90 percent.

Average memory access time: The key formula of this lesson is AMAT = hit time + miss rate times miss penalty. Every access pays the hit time because you always check the cache first. Only the misses pay the extra penalty. This formula lets you compare designs with simple arithmetic.

Worked example 1: Suppose the cache hit time is 1 nanosecond, the miss rate is 5 percent, and the miss penalty (going to DRAM) is 100 nanoseconds. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 times 100 = 1 + 5 = 6 nanoseconds. Without any cache, every access would take about 100 nanoseconds. With the cache, the average is 6. The memory feels more than 16 times faster even though the DRAM itself did not change at all.

Worked example 2, why miss rate matters: Keep the same numbers but let the miss rate rise to 10 percent. AMAT = 1 + 0.10 times 100 = 11 nanoseconds. The miss rate only went from 5 to 10 percent, yet the average time nearly doubled. Because the penalty is so large, even small changes in miss rate make big differences. This is why architects fight hard for every bit of hit rate.

Two levels of cache: The formula nests nicely. For L1 and L2: AMAT = hit time L1 + miss rate L1 times (hit time L2 + miss rate L2 times penalty of memory). Take L1 hit 1 ns, L1 miss rate 10 percent, L2 hit 5 ns, L2 local miss rate 20 percent, memory 100 ns. The inside part is 5 + 0.2 times 100 = 25 ns. Then AMAT = 1 + 0.1 times 25 = 3.5 ns. Here the L2 miss rate is a local miss rate: the fraction of accesses that reach L2 and miss there. Lesson 23 goes deeper into multilevel caches.

Who manages each level: Registers are managed by the compiler, which decides which variables live in registers. Caches are managed fully by hardware; the programmer usually does not even see them. Main memory and disk are managed together by the operating system and hardware through virtual memory, which lesson 24 explains. Files on disk are managed by the operating system and the user.

Speed gap over the years: For decades processor speed improved much faster than DRAM speed. This growing difference is called the memory wall or processor-memory gap. Caches grew bigger and deeper (two levels, then three) mainly to hide this gap. Today a large part of a processor chip's area is cache, not computing logic.

Working set: At any moment a program uses only a part of all its data and code, for example the loop it is running and the arrays it is touching. This part is called its working set. If the working set fits in the cache, almost every access hits. If it is bigger than the cache, the program keeps evicting blocks it will soon need again, and the miss rate shoots up. Programmers who keep their hot data small and close together get big speedups for free.

Real life example 1, a Dhaka grocery shop: Think of a small mudi dokan in your para. The shopkeeper keeps biscuits, chips and tea bags right at the counter, within arm's reach, because people ask for them all the time. That counter is like L1 cache. Rice bags and oil tins sit inside the shop, a few steps away, like main memory. Extra stock is kept in a godown in another lane, like the disk. When a customer asks for something not on the counter, that is a miss; the shopkeeper walks in, brings it, and if many people ask for it, he moves it to the counter. Popular items near, rare items far: locality in action.

Real life example 2, your phone gallery: When you open the Gallery app and scroll through yesterday's photos from a trip to Cox's Bazar, the first scroll can be slow while the images are read from flash storage. Scroll back up and it is instant, because the thumbnails are now held in RAM and the processor's caches. Photos you looked at a second ago are found quickly (temporal locality), and photos next to them in the list were loaded together (spatial locality).

Common mistakes: First, thinking cache is a separate place where you save files. Cache holds copies of memory blocks, managed by hardware, and its content changes constantly. Second, mixing up hit time and miss penalty; hit time is paid by every access, penalty only by misses. Third, using hit rate where the formula needs miss rate. Fourth, saying faster memory is always better; it is also costlier and smaller, which is the whole reason for a hierarchy. Fifth, confusing temporal locality (same item again) with spatial locality (nearby items).

What exams ask: 'Draw the memory hierarchy and explain the trade-off in speed, size and cost.' 'Define temporal and spatial locality with an example from a loop.' 'Given hit time, miss rate and miss penalty, find the average memory access time.' 'Why does a computer need a memory hierarchy instead of one large fast memory?' For numerical questions, always write the formula first, put in the numbers with units, and give the answer in nanoseconds or cycles.

Units warning: Be careful with units. A nanosecond is one billionth of a second, a microsecond is one millionth, a millisecond is one thousandth. A 3 GHz clock has a cycle of about 0.33 nanoseconds. If a question gives the miss penalty in cycles and the hit time in nanoseconds, convert both to the same unit before adding.

Recap: No single memory can be big, fast and cheap together, so computers stack several levels: registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, DRAM main memory, and SSD or disk. Going down, size grows, speed drops and cost per byte falls. The hierarchy works because programs have temporal and spatial locality, and data moves between levels in blocks or pages. Performance is measured by hit rate, miss rate and AMAT = hit time + miss rate times miss penalty. Next lesson we open the cache and see exactly how an address finds its block.
key_points: No memory is big, fast and cheap at once, so computers use a hierarchy of levels.
Order from top: registers, L1/L2/L3 cache (SRAM), main memory (DRAM), SSD/hard disk.
Going down: capacity rises, access time rises, cost per byte falls.
Temporal locality: recently used data is used again soon; spatial locality: nearby data is used soon.
Data moves between levels in blocks (cache lines, often 64 bytes) or pages (often 4 KB).
Hit, miss, hit rate, miss rate = 1 - hit rate, miss penalty.
AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty; small miss-rate changes matter a lot.
lessons.tip: For every AMAT problem, write the formula first, then convert all times to one unit before plugging in numbers. Most lost marks come from mixed units, not hard maths.
lessons.task: Look at your study desk and room. List what is within arm's reach, what is on the shelf, and what is packed away. Match each group to registers, cache, main memory and disk, and write one sentence on why each item is where it is.

quiz.q: Which memory is usually fastest?
quiz.explain: Registers are inside the processor and are read in a fraction of a nanosecond.

quiz.q: A loop adds a[0], a[1], a[2] in order. Which locality does this show most clearly?
quiz.explain: Neighbouring addresses are used one after another.

quiz.q: Hit time 2 ns, miss rate 10%, miss penalty 50 ns. What is AMAT?
Moving down the hierarchy towards disk, what happens to cost per byte?
quiz.explain: Bigger, slower memories are cheaper per byte.

quiz.q: Which of these is non-volatile?
quiz.explain: SSDs keep data without power; the others lose it.

lessons.title: Cache Memory I: Mapping and Address Split
lessons.content:
Picture the parking lot of a big shopping mall in Dhaka like Jamuna Future Park. Some lots give every car one fixed spot based on the last digit of its number plate. Some lots split into zones, and inside a zone you can park in any free spot. And some let you park anywhere at all. Each rule makes it easier or harder to find your car later, and decides how often you are forced to kick someone else out. A cache has exactly the same choice to make about where each memory block is allowed to sit. That choice is called mapping, and it is the heart of this lesson.

Quick recap: Last lesson showed why caches exist: they keep copies of recently used memory blocks in small, fast SRAM close to the processor, and locality makes most accesses hit. Now we ask the practical questions. When the processor gives an address, how does the cache know whether the data is inside? If it is not, where should the new block go? To answer, we need to know how a cache is organised.

Lines, blocks and the parts of one cache line: Main memory is thought of as a long row of blocks, each block being, say, 16 or 64 bytes. The cache has a fixed number of slots called lines, each able to hold one block. Every line stores three things: the data block itself, a tag that says which memory block is sitting there, and a valid bit that says whether the line holds real data at all. When the computer starts, all valid bits are 0, so every first access misses. That kind of miss is called a cold or compulsory miss.

Splitting the address: The cache does not search through all of memory. It cuts the address into fields. The lowest bits are the offset: which byte inside the block you want. The middle bits are the index: which line or set to look in. The highest bits are the tag: the rest of the address, used to check that the block in that line is really the one you asked for. If a block is 2 to the power b bytes, the offset has b bits. If there are 2 to the power s sets, the index has s bits. The tag gets whatever is left.

Direct mapped cache: In a direct mapped cache each memory block can go into exactly one line: line number = block number mod number of lines. This is like the parking lot where your number plate decides your spot. To check for a hit, the hardware uses the index to pick one line, compares the stored tag with the address tag, and checks the valid bit. If valid is 1 and the tags match, it is a hit. Only one comparator is needed, so direct mapped caches are simple, cheap and fast.

Worked example, address split: Take 16-bit byte addresses, a 256-byte cache and 16-byte blocks. Number of lines = 256 / 16 = 16. Offset bits = 4 because 16 = 2 to the power 4. Index bits = 4 because there are 16 lines. Tag bits = 16 - 4 - 4 = 8. Now the address 0x2F4C. In hex each digit is 4 bits, which makes this easy: offset = C (12), index = 4, tag = 2F (47). So the processor looks at line 4, checks whether its tag is 0x2F and the valid bit is 1, and if so reads byte 12 of that block.

The weakness of direct mapping: Two blocks that share the same index fight over one line, even if the rest of the cache is empty. Imagine a tiny direct mapped cache of 4 lines holding one word each, and the program reads word addresses 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 4. Both 0 and 4 have index 0 (0 mod 4 and 4 mod 4). Each access kicks the other block out, so every single access misses, while lines 1, 2 and 3 sit empty. These are conflict misses, and they are the main problem of direct mapping.

Fully associative cache: The opposite extreme lets a block sit in any line. There is no index field; the address is just tag and offset. To find a block, the cache must compare the address tag with the tags of all lines at the same time, so it needs one comparator per line. There are no conflict misses at all, which is great, but the hardware is large, slow and power hungry for big caches. Fully associative designs are used for small structures with few entries, such as a TLB (lesson 24).

Set associative cache, the middle road: Group the lines into sets. A block maps to exactly one set (set = block number mod number of sets), but inside that set it may use any line. If each set has 2 lines, it is 2-way set associative; with 4 lines, 4-way, and so on. The index now selects a set, and the hardware compares the tag with every line in that set at once, needing only as many comparators as the number of ways. This is the zoned parking lot: your zone is fixed, but you pick any free spot inside it. Most real L1, L2 and L3 caches are set associative.

The same trace in a 2-way cache: Use the same 4 lines but arrange them as 2 sets of 2 ways. Word 0 goes to set 0 mod 2 = 0, and word 4 also goes to set 4 mod 2 = 0. But set 0 has two ways, so both can live there together. The trace 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 4 now gives miss, miss, hit, hit, hit, hit. Two misses instead of six. A little associativity removed the conflict completely.

One family, three members: Notice that all three designs are really the same idea with a different number of ways. A direct mapped cache is 1-way set associative: every set has one line. A fully associative cache with N lines is N-way set associative with just one set. So for a fixed cache size, raising the ways halves the number of sets each time, which removes one index bit and adds one tag bit.

Worked example, real-sized cache: A 32-bit address machine has an 8 KB cache with 32-byte blocks. Lines = 8192 / 32 = 256. Offset = 5 bits. Direct mapped: 256 sets, index = 8 bits, tag = 32 - 8 - 5 = 19 bits. 2-way: 128 sets, index = 7 bits, tag = 20 bits. 4-way: 64 sets, index = 6, tag = 21. Fully associative: index = 0, tag = 27 bits. Exams love this table; practise filling it in quickly.

Counting the extra storage: The cache needs space for tags and valid bits, not only data. In the 8 KB direct mapped example, each of the 256 lines stores 19 tag bits and 1 valid bit, so 20 bits times 256 = 5120 bits, which is 640 bytes on top of the 8 KB of data. If the cache uses write-back (lesson 23), each line also needs a dirty bit. Questions sometimes ask for the total number of bits in a cache, so remember to add this overhead.

Decoding an address step by step: For the same direct mapped 8 KB cache, take the address 0x1234ABCD. Offset = lowest 5 bits = 13. Next 8 bits give index = 94. The remaining 19 bits give tag = 0x91A5. So the hardware goes to line 94, compares the stored tag with 0x91A5, checks valid, and on a hit picks byte 13 of the 32-byte block. Doing this by hand means writing the address in binary and drawing lines between the fields.

What happens on a miss: On a miss, the cache asks the next level for the whole block containing the address. The block is placed in the line chosen by the mapping (in a direct mapped cache there is no choice), the tag is written, valid is set to 1, and the requested word is sent to the processor. In a set associative cache, if every line in the set is already full, one must be thrown out. Choosing which one is the replacement policy, which is the first topic of the next lesson.

Block size trade-off: Bigger blocks bring more neighbours per miss, so they use spatial locality better and usually lower the miss rate at first. But for a fixed cache size, bigger blocks mean fewer lines, so more blocks compete for each line, and the miss penalty grows because more bytes must be moved. Beyond some point the miss rate rises again. Designers pick a middle value; 64 bytes is very common today.

Real life example 1, school lockers: In a school in Rajshahi, lockers are assigned by roll number: roll mod 50 gives your locker. That is direct mapping. If roll 7 and roll 57 both need lockers, they clash even if 40 lockers are empty. The school then changes the rule: lockers are grouped in pairs, and roll mod 25 picks your pair, with either locker in the pair free to use. Now roll 7 and 57 share pair 7 happily. That is 2-way set associative.

Real life example 2, contact search: When you search a name in a phone with thousands of contacts, the phone does not compare your text with every contact one by one if it can avoid it. It keeps an index, often by first letter, so it looks only in a smaller group. That is the same spirit as the cache index: use part of the key to jump straight to a small set, then compare only inside it. Fully comparing every entry is what a fully associative cache does, and it is only cheap when the list is short.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting that the offset counts bytes, so a 32-byte block needs 5 offset bits even if words are 4 bytes. Second, using the number of lines instead of the number of sets for the index in a set associative cache. Third, mixing up address bits and cache size; the tag size depends on the address width. Fourth, thinking associativity makes the cache bigger; with the same size it only changes how lines are grouped. Fifth, forgetting the valid bit, so a fresh cache seems to hit on garbage.

What exams ask: 'For a cache of size X, block size Y and a 32-bit address, find the tag, index and offset bits for direct mapped, 2-way and fully associative.' 'Given this sequence of addresses, show hits and misses in a direct mapped and a 2-way cache.' 'Compare the three mappings in hardware cost and miss rate.' 'Find the total bits needed including tags and valid bits.' Draw the address as three boxes with bit counts; examiners look for that.

Recap: A cache is a set of lines, each holding a block, a tag and a valid bit. An address is split into tag, index and offset. Direct mapped puts each block in exactly one line: simple and fast but prone to conflict misses. Fully associative lets a block go anywhere: no conflicts but costly comparisons. Set associative puts each block in one set and anywhere within it, the usual compromise. More ways means fewer index bits and more tag bits for the same size. Next: what to throw out, how to handle writes, and how to measure cache performance.
key_points: Each cache line holds a data block, a tag and a valid bit.
An address splits into tag | index | offset; offset bits = log2(block size), index bits = log2(number of sets).
Direct mapped: block goes to line (block number mod lines); one comparator, but conflict misses.
Fully associative: block can go anywhere; compares all tags, no conflict misses, costly for big caches.
N-way set associative: block goes to one set, any of N lines inside it; the common real choice.
For fixed size, doubling the ways halves the sets: one fewer index bit, one more tag bit.
Tag and valid bits are extra storage on top of the data.
lessons.tip: Learn to fill the 'tag/index/offset' table for direct mapped, 2-way, 4-way and fully associative in under two minutes. Write sizes as powers of two first, then just subtract exponents.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a 4-line cache twice: once direct mapped, once as 2 sets of 2 ways. Run the word addresses 0, 8, 0, 8, 2, 0 through both, marking each access as hit or miss. Count which design wins.

quiz.q: A cache has 64-byte blocks. How many offset bits are needed?
quiz.explain: 64 = 2^6, so 6 offset bits.

quiz.q: In a direct mapped cache with 16 lines, where does memory block 37 go?
Which mapping has no conflict misses?
quiz.explain: A block can go into any line, so blocks never fight over one line.

quiz.q: 8 KB cache, 32-byte blocks, 2-way set associative. How many sets?
For the same cache size, going from direct mapped to 2-way changes the tag by how much?
quiz.explain: Sets halve, so the index loses 1 bit and the tag gains 1 bit.

lessons.title: Cache Memory II: Replacement, Writes and Performance
lessons.content:
Your school bag can only hold five books. Today you need a sixth one, the new Bangla grammar book. Something has to come out. Do you remove the book you have not opened for the longest time? The one you packed first? Or just any book at random? And when you write notes in a book, do you also copy them into your main notebook at home right away, or only when the book goes back on the shelf? A cache faces these same two questions all day long: what to throw out, and when to send changes back to memory.

Where we are: Lesson 22 showed how an address is split into tag, index and offset, and how direct mapped, set associative and fully associative caches decide where a block may live. This lesson finishes the cache story: replacement policies, write policies, the types of misses, multilevel caches, and the numbers that show how much a cache helps.

Replacement, when is there a choice: In a direct mapped cache there is no choice; the new block goes into its one line and whatever was there leaves. In a set associative or fully associative cache, a full set has several candidates. The replacement policy picks the victim. A good policy throws out the block least likely to be needed soon, so future hits stay high.

LRU, least recently used: LRU throws out the block that has not been used for the longest time. It is based on temporal locality: if something has not been touched in a while, it probably will not be touched soon. For a 2-way set, LRU is cheap: one bit per set says which way was used last. For 4 or 8 ways, exact LRU needs more bookkeeping, so real chips often use pseudo-LRU, a cheaper approximation.

FIFO and random: FIFO, first in first out, throws out the block that entered the set earliest, no matter how often it has been used since. It needs only a pointer per set. Random picks a victim at random; it needs almost no hardware and, surprisingly, is often not much worse than LRU for large, highly associative caches. Some caches use random for exactly that reason.

Worked example, LRU vs FIFO: Take one set of a 2-way cache, initially empty, and the block sequence A, B, A, C, B. LRU: A miss, B miss, A hit (now B is least recently used), C miss and evicts B, then B miss and evicts A. Result: 4 misses, 1 hit. FIFO: A miss, B miss, A hit (A is still the oldest arrival), C miss and evicts A, then B hit. Result: 3 misses, 2 hits. So no simple policy wins every time; LRU tends to win on typical programs, but small traces can go either way. Exams like this kind of trace table.

Optimal replacement idea: The best possible policy would evict the block whose next use is furthest in the future. It cannot be built because hardware cannot see the future, but it is used on paper as a yardstick: no real policy can beat it. You will meet the same idea again in operating systems page replacement.

Writes, the problem: Reads are easy, because copying data into the cache never makes anything wrong. Writes are trickier: if the processor changes a value in the cache, the copy in main memory becomes stale. When and how memory gets updated is the write policy. There are two main answers.

Write-through: On every write, update both the cache and main memory. Memory is always up to date, which is simple and safe. The cost is speed: memory is slow, and a program that writes the same variable 1000 times would send 1000 writes to memory. To avoid waiting, processors add a write buffer: the processor drops the write into a small queue and continues working, while the buffer drains to memory in the background. If the buffer fills up, the processor must stall.

Write-back: On a write, update only the cache line and set its dirty bit to 1. Memory is updated only later, when that dirty line is evicted. In the 1000 writes example, memory sees just one write, when the line finally leaves. This saves a lot of memory traffic, which is why most modern L1, L2 and L3 caches are write-back. The cost is complexity: an eviction of a dirty line takes extra time, and memory can be out of date for a while, which matters when other processors or devices read memory.

Write miss policies: What if the processor writes to an address that is not in the cache? Write allocate fetches the block into the cache first and then writes it, betting that nearby data will be used soon. No-write-allocate writes straight to memory and leaves the cache alone. The usual pairs are write-back with write allocate, and write-through with no-write-allocate.

The three C's of misses: Every miss can be put into one of three groups. Compulsory (cold) misses happen on the very first access to a block; even an infinite cache would have them. Capacity misses happen because the cache is too small to hold everything the program is using, so blocks are thrown out and later needed again. Conflict misses happen in direct mapped or set associative caches when too many blocks map to the same set, even though other sets have space. In multiprocessors a fourth C, coherence misses, also appears (lesson 25).

Reducing each C: Bigger blocks and prefetching reduce compulsory misses by bringing data before it is first used. A bigger cache reduces capacity misses. Higher associativity reduces conflict misses. Each fix has a price: bigger blocks raise the miss penalty, bigger caches are slower and costlier, and more ways need more comparators and can lengthen the hit time.

Multilevel caches: Instead of one cache, modern chips use a small, very fast L1 (often split into an instruction cache and a data cache), a bigger L2, and often a large shared L3. L1 is designed for short hit time. L2 and L3 are designed to catch L1 misses so that few accesses reach slow DRAM. The split L1 is the modified Harvard idea from lesson 2: instructions and data can be fetched in the same cycle.

Local and global miss rate: The local miss rate of L2 is misses in L2 divided by accesses that reach L2. The global miss rate is misses in L2 divided by all memory accesses from the processor. If L1 misses 10 percent of the time and L2's local miss rate is 20 percent, then the global L2 miss rate is 0.10 times 0.20 = 2 percent. Only 2 out of every 100 accesses go all the way to main memory.

Worked example, two-level AMAT: L1 hit time 1 cycle, L1 miss rate 4 percent, L2 hit time 10 cycles, L2 local miss rate 25 percent, memory penalty 200 cycles. L1 miss penalty = 10 + 0.25 times 200 = 60 cycles. AMAT = 1 + 0.04 times 60 = 3.4 cycles. Without L2, AMAT would be 1 + 0.04 times 200 = 9 cycles. Adding L2 made average memory access almost three times faster.

Worked example, CPI with memory stalls: A processor has a base CPI of 1 with a perfect cache. Every instruction is fetched (1 access), and 30 percent of instructions are loads or stores (0.3 more accesses), so 1.3 memory accesses per instruction. Miss rate is 2 percent and the miss penalty is 100 cycles. Stall cycles per instruction = 1.3 times 0.02 times 100 = 2.6. Real CPI = 1 + 2.6 = 3.6. The machine runs 3.6 times slower than with a perfect cache. This shows why memory, not arithmetic, often decides real speed.

Inclusive and exclusive caches: In an inclusive design, every block in L1 is also kept in L2 (and L3), so the bigger level is a superset of the smaller one. This makes it easy to check whether a block is anywhere on the chip, because looking at the last level is enough. In an exclusive design, a block lives in only one level at a time, so the total useful capacity is the sum of all levels. Real processors have used both styles, and some use a mix.

Prefetching: A cache can also guess. When the hardware sees the program reading blocks 10, 11 and 12 one after another, it may fetch block 13 before anyone asks for it. If the guess is right, a miss turns into a hit; if it is wrong, some bandwidth and a cache line are wasted. Compilers can also insert prefetch instructions in loops. Prefetching mainly attacks compulsory misses.

Software matters too: Programmers can help the cache. Walking a 2D array row by row in C (which stores rows next to each other) uses spatial locality; walking column by column jumps around memory and can cause many more misses. Splitting a big loop into small tiles that fit in the cache, called blocking or tiling, is a famous trick used in matrix multiplication libraries.

Real life example 1, a tea stall ledger: A tea stall owner near Dhaka University writes credit (baki) entries in a small daily notebook. Write-through would be like copying each entry into the big master khata at once, after every cup. Write-back is writing only in the small notebook during the day and copying the changed pages to the master khata at night. The second saves a lot of time, but if the small notebook is lost before night, the master khata is out of date. That is the exact trade-off.

Real life example 2, your phone's recent apps: Phones keep a limited number of apps in memory. When you open a new app and memory is full, the system usually closes one you have not used for a long time, an LRU-like choice. The app you were using a minute ago stays ready, while the game you played last week gets cleared. Same idea as cache replacement, just at a different level.

Common mistakes: First, thinking write-through means no cache; reads still hit in the cache. Second, forgetting that only dirty lines are written back on eviction; clean lines are simply dropped. Third, using local L2 miss rate as if it were global. Fourth, forgetting instruction fetches when counting memory accesses per instruction. Fifth, saying more associativity always helps; it removes conflict misses but not compulsory or capacity misses, and may slow the hit time.

What exams ask: 'Show the contents of a set with LRU and FIFO for this sequence and count misses.' 'Compare write-through and write-back.' 'Explain the three C's with an example of each and how to reduce them.' 'Compute AMAT for a two-level cache.' 'Find the effective CPI given base CPI, miss rate, miss penalty and percentage of loads and stores.' Draw a clear table with one row per access.

Recap: When a set is full, a replacement policy such as LRU, FIFO or random chooses the victim. Write-through updates memory every time, usually with a write buffer; write-back updates only the cache and uses a dirty bit, writing memory on eviction. Write allocate fetches a block on a write miss; no-write-allocate does not. Misses are compulsory, capacity or conflict. Multilevel caches cut the average access time, measured with nested AMAT, and memory stalls can easily dominate CPI. Next: main memory itself and virtual memory.
key_points: Replacement chooses which block leaves a full set: LRU, FIFO, random; optimal is a paper yardstick.
Write-through updates cache and memory on every write, helped by a write buffer.
Write-back updates only the cache, marks the line dirty, and writes memory when the line is evicted.
Write allocate loads the block on a write miss; no-write-allocate writes directly to memory.
Three C's: compulsory, capacity and conflict misses (plus coherence in multiprocessors).
Global L2 miss rate = L1 miss rate x L2 local miss rate.
Memory stall cycles per instruction = accesses per instruction x miss rate x miss penalty.
lessons.tip: For every trace question, draw a table with columns: access, hit or miss, set contents after, and victim. Updating the LRU order on hits is the step students forget most.
lessons.task: Take a 2-way set and the sequence A, B, C, A, B, D, A. Trace it with LRU and with FIFO on paper and count misses for each. Then write two sentences on why the results differ.

quiz.q: Which write policy uses a dirty bit?
quiz.explain: Write-back marks changed lines dirty so they are written to memory on eviction.

quiz.q: L1 miss rate 10%, L2 local miss rate 30%. What is the global L2 miss rate?
A program touches more data than the cache can hold, so blocks are evicted and needed again. Which miss type is this?
quiz.explain: The cache is simply too small for the working set.

quiz.q: Base CPI 1, 1.5 accesses per instruction, miss rate 2%, penalty 100 cycles. Real CPI?
Higher associativity mainly reduces which misses?
quiz.explain: More ways let blocks that share a set live together.

lessons.title: Main Memory and Virtual Memory
lessons.content:
Think of a big apartment building in Mirpur with a security guard at the gate. Visitors do not know which flat number a family actually lives in today; they just say 'I am here to see the Rahman family'. The guard checks his register, says 'flat 7B', and sends them up. If the family has moved out to their village home for a while, the guard has to phone them and bring them back first. Virtual memory works like that guard: programs use made-up addresses, and the hardware plus operating system quietly translate them into real places in memory.

Two topics in one lesson: First we look at main memory itself: how DRAM and SRAM differ and how memory is organised to deliver data faster. Then we look at virtual memory: pages, page tables, address translation, the TLB and page faults. Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1) will go deeper into page replacement and memory management policies; here we focus on the hardware view.

SRAM: Static RAM stores each bit in a small circuit of cross-coupled transistors, usually six transistors per bit. As long as power is on, the bit stays without any help. SRAM is fast but takes a lot of chip area per bit, so it is expensive. That is why it is used for caches and registers, not for gigabytes of main memory.

DRAM: Dynamic RAM stores each bit as charge in a tiny capacitor, controlled by one transistor. One transistor and one capacitor per bit makes DRAM very dense and cheap. But the charge leaks away, so every row must be refreshed (read and rewritten) many times a second, typically every few tens of milliseconds. Reading is also slower than SRAM. Main memory in your laptop or phone is DRAM.

How DRAM is organised: A DRAM chip is a grid of rows and columns. To read, the controller first opens a row, copying the whole row into a row buffer, and then picks the column it needs. If the next access is in the same open row, it is much quicker, because the row is already in the buffer. This is one more place where spatial locality pays off. Modern DRAM types such as DDR4 and DDR5 transfer data on both edges of the clock to send more bits per cycle.

Memory interleaving: Main memory is divided into several banks that can work at the same time. In low-order interleaving, consecutive addresses go to different banks: with 4 banks, word 0 is in bank 0, word 1 in bank 1, word 2 in bank 2, word 3 in bank 3, word 4 back in bank 0. Bank number = address mod 4. When the cache fetches a 4-word block, all four banks can start their access together, so the block arrives much faster than if one bank had to deliver the words one by one.

Why virtual memory: Without it, every program would use real physical addresses. Two programs could accidentally write over each other's data. A program would have to know exactly where it was loaded. And a program bigger than physical memory could not run at all. Virtual memory solves all three: each program gets its own private address space, starting at 0, as large as the address width allows, and the hardware maps it onto whatever physical memory is free.

Pages and frames: The virtual address space is cut into fixed-size pieces called pages, and physical memory is cut into pieces of the same size called frames (or page frames). A common page size is 4 KB. Any page can be placed into any free frame, so memory does not need to be one continuous region. A page that is not in memory at the moment lives on disk, in the swap area.

Splitting a virtual address: A virtual address has two parts: the virtual page number (VPN) and the page offset. With 4 KB pages, the offset is 12 bits because 4096 = 2 to the power 12. On a 32-bit machine the VPN is the remaining 20 bits. Translation only changes the page number into a frame number; the offset is copied as it is, because a page and a frame have the same size.

The page table: The operating system keeps a page table for each process. Entry number VPN holds a page table entry (PTE) with the physical frame number and some control bits: a valid (present) bit saying whether the page is in memory, a dirty bit saying whether it was modified, a reference bit saying whether it was recently used, and protection bits such as read, write and execute. A special processor register holds the address of the current process's page table.

Worked example, translating an address: Take 16-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. Offset = 12 bits, VPN = 4 bits, so 16 pages. The virtual address is 0x3A7F. The top hex digit is the VPN, 3, and the lower three hex digits, A7F, are the offset. Suppose the page table entry for page 3 is valid with frame number 7. The physical address is frame 7 followed by offset A7F, which is 0x7A7F. Done: the processor reads physical address 0x7A7F.

Page faults: If the valid bit of the PTE is 0, the page is not in memory. The hardware raises an exception called a page fault, and the operating system takes over. It finds a free frame (or evicts a page, writing it to disk first if it is dirty), reads the needed page from disk into the frame, updates the page table, and restarts the instruction that faulted. A disk access takes milliseconds, which is millions of processor cycles, so the operating system usually runs another program while it waits.

Why pages are big and fully flexible: Because a page fault is so costly, virtual memory is designed like a cache with a huge miss penalty. Pages are large (kilobytes) to bring a lot of useful data per fault. Placement is fully associative: any page can go in any frame, to avoid conflict faults. Replacement is done in software by the operating system, which can afford smart policies such as approximations of LRU. And writes are always write-back, using the dirty bit, because writing to disk on every store would be impossibly slow.

Choosing the page size: Bigger pages mean a smaller page table and more data brought in per page fault, and one TLB entry covers more memory. But bigger pages also waste more space inside the last, partly used page of each region, which is called internal fragmentation, and moving a big page to and from disk takes longer. Small pages waste less but need bigger tables. 4 KB is the classic compromise, and many modern systems also support much larger huge pages, such as 2 MB, for programs that use lots of memory.

Page table size problem: With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages there are 2 to the power 20, about a million, pages. If each PTE is 4 bytes, one page table is 4 MB per process, mostly for pages that the program never uses. Real systems use multi-level (hierarchical) page tables: the VPN is split into parts, the first part indexes a small top-level table, which points to second-level tables that only exist for regions actually in use. 64-bit systems use four or more levels.

The TLB: Translation needs a page table read in memory, so every load would cost two memory accesses: one for the PTE and one for the data. To avoid this, the processor has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB), a small, fast cache of recent translations, often a few dozen to a few thousand entries and highly associative. On a TLB hit, translation is almost free. On a TLB miss, the hardware or the operating system walks the page table and loads the entry into the TLB.

Worked example, effective access time: TLB lookup takes 1 ns, a memory access 100 ns, and the TLB hit rate is 98 percent. On a hit: 1 + 100 = 101 ns. On a miss: 1 + 100 (read the PTE) + 100 (read the data) = 201 ns. Effective time = 0.98 times 101 + 0.02 times 201 = 98.98 + 4.02 = 103 ns. Without a TLB every access would need about 200 ns. This is why the TLB is essential.

Protection: Since every access goes through the page table, the hardware can check permission bits each time. Writing to a read-only page, or user code touching a kernel page, causes an exception. This is how one buggy app cannot crash another app or the operating system, and how code pages can be marked non-executable to block some attacks.

Real life example 1, a hall seat plan: In an exam at a big public university, every student has a roll number (a virtual address), but the actual seat (a physical frame) in a hall like the TSC auditorium is assigned from a seat plan on the notice board (the page table). Two departments can both have a roll 101, yet they sit in different seats. If a student's name is missing from the plan, the office must find a seat first (a page fault). A quick list copied at the door for the most common rolls works like a TLB.

Real life example 2, many apps on a phone: Your Android phone may have 6 GB of RAM, yet apps like Facebook, YouTube, bKash and a game all think they have a large private address space. The operating system keeps only the pages each app is actively using in RAM. When you switch back to an app you left long ago, it may take a moment to reload, because its pages were pushed out and must be brought back.

Common mistakes: First, translating the offset; the offset never changes, only the page number does. Second, confusing a TLB miss with a page fault; a TLB miss only means the translation is not cached, while a page fault means the page itself is not in memory. Third, forgetting that DRAM needs refresh while SRAM does not. Fourth, computing the page table size with the number of frames instead of the number of virtual pages. Fifth, thinking virtual memory just means 'using the disk as RAM'; its biggest jobs are isolation, protection and simple loading.

What exams ask: 'Compare SRAM and DRAM.' 'Explain low-order interleaving with 4 banks.' 'Given page size and a page table, translate this virtual address to a physical address.' 'How many entries does the page table have and what is its size?' 'Explain the steps of handling a page fault.' 'With TLB hit rate h, compute the effective memory access time.'

Recap: SRAM is fast, six transistors per bit, used for caches; DRAM is dense, one transistor and one capacitor per bit, needs refresh, used for main memory. Interleaving lets banks work in parallel. Virtual memory gives each process its own address space split into pages, mapped to physical frames by a page table with valid, dirty, reference and protection bits. A virtual address is VPN plus offset; only the VPN is translated. Page faults bring pages from disk, the TLB caches translations, and multi-level page tables keep table size reasonable. Next, the last lesson: I/O and parallel processors.
key_points: SRAM: about six transistors per bit, fast, no refresh, used for caches.
DRAM: one transistor plus one capacitor per bit, dense and cheap, needs refresh, used for main memory.
Low-order interleaving puts consecutive words in different banks so a block is fetched in parallel.
Virtual address = virtual page number + offset; only the page number is translated to a frame number.
A page table entry holds the frame number plus valid, dirty, reference and protection bits.
A page fault happens when the page is not in memory; the OS loads it from disk and restarts the instruction.
The TLB caches recent translations so most accesses avoid an extra page table read.
lessons.tip: In every translation question, first write how many bits are offset (log2 of page size). Then mark that many bits on the right of the address and never touch them; translate only what is left.
lessons.task: With 4 KB pages and the page table {0 -> 5, 1 -> 2, 2 -> invalid, 3 -> 9}, translate the 16-bit virtual addresses 0x1234, 0x3ABC and 0x2000 by hand. Say which one causes a page fault.

quiz.q: Which memory stores a bit as charge on a capacitor and needs refresh?
quiz.explain: DRAM uses one transistor and one capacitor; the charge leaks, so it is refreshed.

quiz.q: With 4 KB pages, how many bits is the page offset?
16-bit virtual address 0x3A7F, 4 KB pages, page 3 maps to frame 7. Physical address?
quiz.explain: Replace the page number 3 with frame 7; keep offset A7F.

quiz.q: What happens on a TLB miss when the page is in memory?
options: A page fault is always raised
The page is loaded from disk
The page table is read and the entry is put in the TLB
quiz.explain: A TLB miss only means the translation is not cached; the page table supplies it.

quiz.q: TLB 1 ns, memory 100 ns, TLB hit rate 98%. Effective access time?

lessons.title: I/O, Parallel Processors and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
Think about a busy restaurant in Old Dhaka. The head cook (the processor) is fast, but he cannot also take orders, carry plates and wash dishes. Waiters bring orders in, helpers carry big trays straight from the store room, and when the rush hour hits, the owner hires more cooks who share one kitchen and one fridge. This lesson is about exactly those two ideas: how the processor talks to the outside world (input and output), and how many processors work together (parallelism). Then we wrap up the whole course.

I/O devices and controllers: Keyboards, screens, disks, network cards, cameras and sensors are I/O devices. The processor does not talk to the device's motors or pixels directly. Each device has a controller with a few registers: a data register to hold bytes going in or out, a status register with bits such as 'ready' or 'busy', and a command register to tell the device what to do. The processor reads and writes these registers to control the device.

Two ways to address device registers: In memory-mapped I/O, device registers get addresses in the normal memory address space, so ordinary load and store instructions reach them; ARM and RISC-V systems use this. In isolated or port-mapped I/O, devices have a separate address space and special instructions such as IN and OUT; the x86 family supports this, and the Microprocessors course (deep-cse-3-3) shows it in assembly. Memory-mapped I/O is simpler for the instruction set; port-mapped keeps the memory space free.

Programmed I/O and polling: The simplest method: the processor runs a loop, reading the status register again and again until the device says ready, then moves one item of data. In pseudo-code: while (status.ready == 0) { } ; data = device.data. This is called polling or busy waiting. It is easy and fine for slow, simple devices, but the processor wastes time spinning in the loop.

The cost of polling, a worked example: Suppose one poll takes 400 cycles on a 1 GHz processor. Polling a mouse 30 times per second costs 30 times 400 = 12,000 cycles per second, a tiny 0.0012 percent of the processor. But a device that needs 1 million polls per second costs 400 million cycles per second, which is 40 percent of the processor doing nothing useful. For fast or unpredictable devices we need something better.

Interrupt-driven I/O: Instead of the processor asking again and again, the device raises an interrupt signal when it needs attention. The processor finishes its current instruction, saves the program counter and some state, and jumps to an interrupt service routine (ISR) for that device. The ISR moves the data, tells the device it is done, and returns; the interrupted program continues as if nothing happened. In lesson 14 we saw the processor checks for interrupts at the end of each instruction cycle; this is that check in action.

Interrupt details: With many devices, the processor must know who interrupted. In vectored interrupts, the device supplies a number that selects an entry in an interrupt vector table holding the ISR's address. Devices have priorities, so a disk or timer can interrupt a less urgent keyboard handler. Interrupts can also be masked (temporarily ignored) during critical work. Interrupts are much better than polling when events are rare, but each one still costs some cycles for saving and restoring state.

DMA, direct memory access: Moving a large block, say a 4 KB page from disk, byte by byte through the processor would waste a huge number of interrupts. A DMA controller fixes this. The processor tells it the memory address, the device, the number of bytes and the direction. The DMA controller then moves the data directly between the device and memory over the bus, and interrupts the processor only once, when the whole block is done. Meanwhile the processor keeps running other work.

DMA modes and a side effect: In burst mode the DMA controller holds the bus for the whole block. In cycle stealing mode it takes the bus for one word at a time between processor cycles, slowing the processor slightly but never stopping it for long. One important side effect: DMA writes memory behind the cache's back, so the system must keep caches consistent, either by hardware snooping or by the operating system flushing or invalidating the affected cache lines.

Buses: A bus is a shared set of wires connecting parts of the computer. It has data lines (the values), address lines (where), and control lines (read, write, interrupt request, acknowledge, clock). A synchronous bus uses a common clock, simple and fast but limited in length. An asynchronous bus uses a handshake: the sender says 'data ready', the receiver answers 'got it'. Only one device can drive a shared bus at a time, so a bus arbiter decides who gets it. Modern links such as PCI Express and USB are fast serial point-to-point connections rather than one wide shared bus.

Why parallel processors: For years, computers got faster mainly by raising the clock. Around the mid-2000s, the power wall from lesson 3 stopped that: higher clocks made chips too hot. Designers started putting more processor cores on one chip instead. Today phones and laptops have several cores, and servers have dozens. But a program only runs faster if its work can be split, and Amdahl's law from lesson 4 limits the gain by the serial part.

Amdahl on a multicore, worked example: Suppose 90 percent of a program can run in parallel and 10 percent must run on one core. On 8 cores, speedup = 1 / (0.1 + 0.9 / 8) = 1 / 0.2125, which is about 4.7, not 8. Even with infinitely many cores the speedup can never pass 1 / 0.1 = 10. That is why programmers work hard to shrink the serial part.

Flynn's taxonomy: Michael Flynn classified machines by how many instruction streams and data streams they handle. SISD, single instruction single data: a classic one-core processor. SIMD, single instruction multiple data: one instruction works on many data items at once, such as vector units (SSE, AVX, ARM NEON) and, broadly, GPUs. MISD, multiple instruction single data: rare, sometimes linked to fault-tolerant systems. MIMD, multiple instruction multiple data: several independent processors, such as multicore chips and clusters.

SIMD example: Adding two arrays of 8 numbers each: a scalar loop does 8 separate add instructions. A SIMD unit that holds 8 numbers in one wide register does all 8 additions with one instruction. This is why image filters, audio processing and machine learning run so much faster with vector instructions.

Shared memory and message passing: In a shared memory multiprocessor, all cores see one address space and communicate by reading and writing the same memory, using locks to avoid stepping on each other. Multicore laptops work this way. In a distributed memory system, each node has its own memory and they communicate by sending messages over a network; big clusters and supercomputers do this. Shared memory is easier to program; message passing scales to many more machines.

Cache coherence: In a multicore chip, each core has its own L1 cache. If core 1 and core 2 both cache variable x, and core 1 writes x = 5, core 2 may still read the old value from its cache. Keeping all copies consistent is the cache coherence problem. A common solution is snooping with a protocol such as MSI: each line is Modified, Shared or Invalid. When core 1 wants to write, it broadcasts on the bus and other copies are invalidated; the next time core 2 reads x it misses and gets the new value. Large systems use a directory that tracks which cores hold each block instead of broadcasting. MESI adds an Exclusive state to save bus traffic.

GPUs: A graphics processing unit has hundreds or thousands of simple cores that run the same program on many pieces of data, grouped into threads that run together. It was built for drawing pixels, where every pixel needs similar work. The same shape fits matrix maths, so GPUs now power machine learning. A CPU has a few powerful cores with big caches and clever prediction for fast single-thread work; a GPU has many simple cores for high throughput.

Real life example 1, a bKash payment flow: When you tap 'Send Money' on your phone, the touch controller raises an interrupt, the ISR reads the touch position, and the app runs. The app's message goes to the network card, which uses DMA to read the packet from memory and send it out. Meanwhile other cores on your phone keep playing music and updating notifications. Interrupts, DMA and multicore all work together in a single tap.

Real life example 2, board exam results: When board exam results are published, a results website must answer huge numbers of requests at once. Servers with many cores (MIMD) handle many requests in parallel, each core serving different students, while network cards use DMA and interrupts to move packets. If one part of the work is serial, such as a single locked database table, Amdahl's law says adding more cores helps less and less.

Common mistakes: First, saying DMA means the processor is not involved at all; the processor still sets up the transfer and handles the final interrupt. Second, mixing up polling and interrupts. Third, calling a multicore chip SIMD; it is MIMD, even though each core may also have SIMD units. Fourth, thinking cache coherence is only a software problem; it is mainly solved in hardware. Fifth, believing that doubling cores always doubles speed.

What exams ask: 'Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O and DMA.' 'Explain the steps the processor takes when an interrupt arrives.' 'What is memory-mapped I/O?' 'Explain Flynn's taxonomy with examples.' 'What is the cache coherence problem and how does a snooping protocol solve it?' 'Compare CPU and GPU.' Draw the DMA block diagram and an MSI state diagram if you can.

Whole-course recap, part 1: We began by separating architecture (what the programmer sees, the ISA) from organization (how the hardware does it), and met the von Neumann stored-program model with its bottleneck. We measured performance with the CPU time equation, CPI and clock rate, and learned Amdahl's law. We saw how data is represented, including IEEE 754, and how the ALU adds, multiplies with Booth's algorithm and divides. We studied instruction formats, addressing modes, instruction types and procedure calls, compared RISC and CISC, and walked through a MIPS-style ISA.

Whole-course recap, part 2: We wrote register transfers, traced the fetch-decode-execute cycle, built a single-cycle datapath, designed hardwired and microprogrammed control, and split work into a multi-cycle datapath. We pipelined it into five stages, handled structural, data and control hazards with forwarding, stalls and branch prediction, and glimpsed superscalar and out-of-order execution. Then we climbed the memory hierarchy: locality, cache mapping, replacement and write policies, AMAT, DRAM and virtual memory with page tables and the TLB. Finally we connected the processor to I/O and to other processors.

What to learn next: Microprocessors & Assembly (deep-cse-3-3) puts these ideas on a real chip and real assembly programs. Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1) builds on interrupts, virtual memory and multicore. Compiler Design uses the ISA, registers and pipelines. Embedded Systems and Computer Networks reuse I/O and DMA. Keep the core idea of this whole course with you: fast computers come from keeping the common case fast, exploiting locality and doing work in parallel.
key_points: Device controllers have data, status and command registers; memory-mapped I/O uses normal addresses, port-mapped uses special instructions.
Programmed I/O polls a status bit in a loop; simple but wastes processor time.
Interrupt-driven I/O lets the device signal; the processor saves state, runs an ISR and returns.
DMA moves whole blocks between device and memory, interrupting the processor once at the end.
Buses have data, address and control lines; synchronous use a clock, asynchronous use a handshake.
Flynn's taxonomy: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD; multicore chips are MIMD, vector units and GPUs are SIMD-like.
Cache coherence keeps copies consistent across cores, e.g. snooping with MSI/MESI or directories.
Course theme: make the common case fast, exploit locality, use parallelism.
lessons.tip: Make one comparison table with three rows (polling, interrupts, DMA) and columns for who moves the data, when the processor is busy, and best use. That single table answers most I/O exam questions.
lessons.task: Open your phone's settings or an app like CPU-Z and find how many cores your processor has. Then list three things your phone does at the same time (music, download, chat) and guess which ones use interrupts, which use DMA, and which run on different cores.

quiz.q: Which I/O method moves a whole block to memory and interrupts the processor only once at the end?
quiz.explain: The DMA controller transfers the block itself and signals completion with one interrupt.

quiz.q: A multicore laptop processor running different programs on each core is which Flynn class?
quiz.explain: Several independent instruction streams on different data.

quiz.q: One poll costs 400 cycles on a 1 GHz CPU. What fraction of the CPU do 1 million polls per second use?
quiz.explain: 400 x 1,000,000 = 400 million cycles out of 1 billion = 40%.
