quiz.q: In MSI, what happens to other cores' copies when one core writes a shared line?
quiz.explain: Invalidation forces other cores to miss and fetch the new value.

quiz.q: What does a processor do first when an interrupt arrives?
options: Finishes the current instruction and saves the program counter
quiz.explain: It completes the instruction, saves state, then jumps to the ISR.

lessons.title: What a Microprocessor Is
lessons.content:
Imagine a tiny factory worker who sits inside every phone, calculator, washing machine and laptop. This worker cannot think like you, cannot see, cannot hear. It can only do very small jobs: pick up a number, add two numbers, compare them, put the answer somewhere, and then look at the next instruction on its list. But it does these small jobs millions or billions of times every second, without ever getting tired or bored. That tiny worker is the microprocessor. In this course we are going to open the factory door, meet the worker, learn its language, and even write instructions for it ourselves.

What it is: A microprocessor is a complete central processing unit, a CPU, built on a single chip of silicon. Before the 1970s, a computer's CPU was made from many separate boards full of parts, and it could fill a cupboard or a whole room. Engineers then learned to squeeze all of those parts, the circuits that do arithmetic, the circuits that control everything and the small storage boxes called registers, onto one chip smaller than your fingernail. The word micro means very small, and processor means the thing that processes, or works on, data. So a microprocessor is simply a very small data worker.

The three main parts inside: Every microprocessor has three big pieces. The ALU, or arithmetic and logic unit, is the calculator part. It adds, subtracts, does AND, OR and NOT on bits, and compares numbers. The control unit is the manager. It reads each instruction, decides what it means, and sends signals to the other parts telling them what to do and when. The registers are tiny, super fast storage boxes right inside the chip. A register might hold one number, like 25, while the ALU works on it. Think of the ALU as the cook, the control unit as the person reading the recipe aloud, and the registers as the small bowls on the kitchen counter.

The heartbeat called the clock: A microprocessor does not work whenever it likes. It follows a clock, a signal that goes high and low again and again, like a drum beat. Each beat lets the chip take one small step. Clock speed is measured in hertz, which means beats per second. The Intel 8085, a chip we will study soon, usually ran at about 3 MHz, which is 3 million beats per second. A modern laptop processor runs at a few GHz, which is a few billion beats per second. More beats per second usually means more work done, but how much work happens per beat also matters a lot.

Fetch, decode, execute: The worker repeats one cycle forever. First it fetches: it goes to memory and brings the next instruction into the chip. Second it decodes: the control unit figures out what that instruction means, for example add the number in box B to the number in box A. Third it executes: the ALU or other parts actually do the job, and the result is stored. Then the cycle starts again with the next instruction. A special register called the program counter keeps track of where the next instruction is in memory, a bit like a bookmark in a storybook. After each fetch, the bookmark moves forward.

A tiny walk through: Suppose memory holds three instructions: load 5 into A, add 3 to A, store A in memory box 2000. The program counter starts at the first one. Fetch, decode, execute: now A holds 5. The program counter moves on. Fetch, decode, execute: the ALU adds 3, so A holds 8. Next: the chip sends 8 out to memory box 2000. That is all a program is: a long list of these tiny steps. Even a video game is, deep down, millions of instructions like these running one after another very fast.

Buses, the roads of the system: The microprocessor must talk to memory and to input and output devices. It uses groups of wires called buses. The address bus carries the location number, telling memory which box we want. It goes one way, out of the processor. The data bus carries the actual data, and it goes both ways, because the processor both reads and writes. The control bus carries signals such as read, write and reset, saying what kind of trip this is. Think of a rickshaw puller in Dhaka: the address is the house number you shout, the data is the parcel being carried, and the control signal says whether he is picking up or delivering.

Why the number of address lines matters: Each address line is one bit of the address. With n address lines the processor can name 2 to the power n different memory locations. The 8085 has 16 address lines, so it can reach 2^16 = 65,536 locations, which is 64 KB. The 8086 has 20 address lines, so it can reach 2^20 = 1,048,576 locations, which is 1 MB. You will see these two numbers, 64 KB and 1 MB, again and again in this course. A quick exam trick: 10 lines give 1 K, 20 lines give 1 M, and every extra line doubles the size.

Word size: The word size of a processor is how many bits it can handle in one go, usually equal to the width of its registers and its data bus. The 8085 is an 8-bit processor: it adds two 8-bit numbers in one step, so numbers from 0 to 255. The 8086 is a 16-bit processor: it can work on numbers from 0 to 65,535 in one step. Modern laptop chips are 64-bit. A bigger word size also means more data moved per trip, like a pickup van carrying more rice sacks than a bicycle.

Microprocessor, microcontroller, microcomputer: These three words confuse many students, so let us sort them out. A microprocessor is only the CPU on a chip. To make it useful, you must add memory chips and input/output chips outside it. A microcomputer is a whole small computer built around a microprocessor, with memory and input and output added, like an old IBM PC. A microcontroller is a whole small computer squeezed onto one chip: CPU, some RAM, some ROM, timers and input/output pins all together. The Intel 8051 is a classic microcontroller, and the ATmega328P chip on an Arduino Uno board is a popular one today.

Where each one is used: Microcontrollers are cheap, small and use little power, so they sit inside things that do one fixed job: a microwave oven, a TV remote, a digital rice cooker, a car's engine control, a traffic light controller. Microprocessors are used where we need lots of computing power and flexibility, like laptops, desktops and servers. Your smartphone has a system on chip, which mixes a powerful processor with graphics, memory controllers and radios on one chip. So the line between them is not always sharp, but the basic idea, CPU alone versus whole computer on a chip, is what exams ask.

A short history, the 4-bit and 8-bit days: In 1971 Intel released the 4004, often called the first commercial microprocessor. It was a 4-bit chip with about 2,300 transistors and was made for a calculator company. In 1972 came the 8008, an 8-bit chip. In 1974 the 8080 became popular and powered some of the first home computers. In 1976 Intel released the 8085, an improved 8-bit chip that needed only a single +5 volt power supply. Because the 8085 is simple and clear, many universities, including those in Bangladesh, still use it to teach the basics.

The 16-bit jump and beyond: In 1978 Intel released the 8086, a 16-bit processor with about 29,000 transistors and a 1 MB address space. A cheaper version, the 8088, had the same inside but only an 8-bit external data bus, and IBM chose it for the first IBM PC in 1981. That choice made this family, called x86, the standard for personal computers. Then came the 80286 in 1982, the 32-bit 80386 in 1985, the 80486 in 1989 and the Pentium in 1993. The amazing part: modern Intel and AMD chips can still run very old 8086 style instructions. Learning the 8086 is like learning the grandfather's language that the grandchildren still understand.

Machine language and assembly language: The processor only understands numbers, patterns of 0s and 1s called machine code. For example, on the 8085 the byte 3E followed by 05 means put 5 into register A. Humans find that hard to read, so we write assembly language instead: MVI A, 05H. Each assembly line usually turns into one machine instruction. A program called an assembler does this translation. High level languages like C or Python are one level further up: one line of C can turn into many machine instructions. Assembly sits right next to the hardware, so it shows exactly what the chip is doing.

Why learn assembly in the age of Python: Fair question. First, it shows how computers really work, so everything from C pointers to operating systems suddenly makes sense. Second, small devices with tiny memory, like sensors and controllers, are sometimes programmed close to the hardware. Third, security experts read assembly to study viruses and find bugs. Fourth, compiler writers and driver writers need it. You may not write assembly every day, but knowing it makes you a much stronger engineer.

Real life example 1, a rice cooker: A digital rice cooker sold in a Dhaka market has a microcontroller inside. Step 1: you press the cook button; that is an input pin changing from 0 to 1. Step 2: the program, stored in the chip's ROM, notices the change and turns on the heater through an output pin. Step 3: a temperature sensor sends a value, which the chip reads again and again. Step 4: when the water is gone, the temperature rises above a set point; the program compares the reading with that number, just like a CMP instruction. Step 5: it switches to keep warm mode and beeps. All of this is fetch, decode, execute running on a tiny chip.

Real life example 2, a bKash payment on your phone: When you send money with bKash, your phone's processor runs billions of instructions. It reads your touches, draws the screen, encrypts your PIN with maths, and sends data through the radio. Each of those big jobs is made of small steps: move a number, add, compare, jump. The phone's processor is far more advanced than the 8086, with many cores and smart tricks, but the core idea is the same. The address bus still picks memory locations, the data bus still carries numbers, and the program counter still points to the next instruction.

How this course is organised: First we study the 8085, a simple 8-bit chip, to learn registers, flags, instructions and timing in a gentle way. Then we move to the 8086, the 16-bit grandfather of today's PCs, and learn its registers, segments, addressing modes and machine code. Next we write real x86 assembly programs: data movement, arithmetic, logic, loops, input and output, arrays, strings, the stack and procedures. After that we learn interrupts and how chips connect to memory and input/output devices, with famous helper chips: the 8259 interrupt controller, the 8255 parallel port, the 8253/8254 timer, the 8237 DMA controller and the 8251 serial chip. Finally we peek at modern x86.

Common mistakes: First, calling a microcontroller a microprocessor or the other way round; remember, microcontroller means CPU plus memory plus input and output on one chip. Second, thinking the address bus is bidirectional; on these chips it goes out from the processor, while the data bus goes both ways. Third, mixing up 64 KB and 1 MB: 16 address lines give 64 KB, 20 lines give 1 MB. Fourth, believing clock speed alone decides performance; how much work is done per beat matters too. Fifth, forgetting that machine code and assembly are two forms of the same instructions.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: define a microprocessor and draw its basic block diagram; differentiate between microprocessor and microcontroller; explain the three buses and their direction; how much memory can a processor with 20 address lines access; explain the fetch, decode, execute cycle; write a short history of Intel microprocessors; and what is the difference between machine language, assembly language and high level language. If you can explain each with a small example, like the 2^16 and 2^20 calculations, you will score well.

Quick recap: A microprocessor is a CPU on one chip, with an ALU, a control unit and registers, driven by a clock. It repeats fetch, decode, execute, using the program counter as a bookmark. It talks to memory and devices through the address, data and control buses. The number of address lines decides how much memory it can reach, and the word size decides how many bits it handles at once. A microcontroller packs a whole small computer on one chip. In the next lesson we will sharpen our tools: binary, hex, signed numbers and how bytes are stored, the everyday language of assembly programmers.
key_points: A microprocessor is a complete CPU on a single chip: ALU, control unit and registers.
It repeats fetch, decode, execute forever; the program counter points to the next instruction.
The address bus goes out of the processor, the data bus goes both ways, the control bus carries signals like read and write.
n address lines reach 2^n locations: 16 lines give 64 KB (8085), 20 lines give 1 MB (8086).
Word size is how many bits the processor handles at once: 8085 is 8-bit, 8086 is 16-bit.
A microcontroller puts CPU, memory, timers and I/O on one chip; a microprocessor is the CPU only.
Assembly language is a human readable form of machine code, translated by an assembler.
lessons.tip: Draw the block diagram of a microprocessor with the three buses from memory every day this week. Once the picture lives in your head, every later chip in this course will feel like a small change to the same drawing.
lessons.task: Pick three gadgets at home, for example a TV remote, a rice cooker and a phone. For each, write on paper whether it most likely has a microcontroller or a full microprocessor inside and why. Then calculate how much memory a chip with 12, 16 and 20 address lines could reach.

quiz.q: Which part of the microprocessor actually adds and compares numbers?
quiz.explain: The arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) does arithmetic like add and subtract and logic like AND, OR and compare.

quiz.q: How many memory locations can a processor with 20 address lines access?
quiz.explain: 2^20 = 1,048,576, which is 1 M. This is why the 8086 can address 1 MB.

quiz.q: Which bus is bidirectional on the 8085 and 8086?
quiz.explain: The processor both reads and writes data, so the data bus carries data in both directions. The address bus goes out from the processor.

quiz.q: What makes a microcontroller different from a microprocessor?
options: It puts CPU, memory, timers and I/O on one chip
quiz.explain: A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip, while a microprocessor is only the CPU and needs external memory and I/O chips.

quiz.q: Which Intel chip, with an 8-bit external data bus, was used in the first IBM PC?
quiz.explain: The 8088 had the 8086's 16-bit inside but an 8-bit external data bus. IBM chose it for the IBM PC in 1981.

lessons.title: Data for Assembly Programmers: Binary, Hex, Signed Numbers and Bytes
lessons.content:
Imagine you move to a new country where shops only accept coins of one taka, two taka, four taka, eight taka and so on, each double the last. At first counting money feels strange. After a week, you do it without thinking. Assembly programming feels exactly like that. The processor sees everything as bits, and programmers write those bits in hexadecimal. You learned number systems in Digital Logic Design, so here we will not start from zero. Instead we will sharpen those skills into fast, everyday tools: reading hex at a glance, handling negative numbers, storing digits and letters, and knowing how bytes sit in memory.

Bits, nibbles, bytes, words: A bit is one 0 or 1. Four bits make a nibble. Eight bits make a byte. On Intel processors, 16 bits make a word, and 32 bits make a doubleword, often written dword. With n bits you can make 2^n different patterns. So a nibble has 16 patterns, a byte has 256, and a word has 65,536. Registers on the 8085 are bytes, while the main registers of the 8086 are words. When you see a register's size, you immediately know the range of values it can hold.

Why hexadecimal: Writing 16 binary digits like 1011 0010 0111 1100 is slow and easy to mess up. Hexadecimal uses 16 symbols, 0 to 9 and A to F, where A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15. The magic is that one hex digit equals exactly one nibble. So you just group bits by fours and swap each group for one symbol: 1011 is B, 0010 is 2, 0111 is 7, 1100 is C, giving B27C. Going back is just as easy. That is why every memory address and every byte in this course will be written in hex.

The H suffix and the leading zero: In Intel style assemblers like MASM and TASM, a hex number ends with the letter H, as in 2050H. If a hex number starts with a letter, you must put a 0 in front, so you write 0FFH, not FFH. Why? Because FFH looks like a name to the assembler, maybe a label you defined. Some tools such as NASM also accept 0xFF, the C style. A binary number ends with B, as in 1010B, and a plain number like 25 is decimal. Small details like this cause real errors, so learn them now.

Quick conversions you should do in your head: To turn hex into decimal, multiply each digit by its place value: 1, 16, 256, 4096. For example C8H = 12 x 16 + 8 = 200. And 3E8H = 3 x 256 + 14 x 16 + 8 = 768 + 224 + 8 = 1000. To go from decimal to hex, divide by 16 again and again and read the remainders from bottom to top. For 200: 200 / 16 = 12 remainder 8, and 12 is C, so C8H. A handy list to remember: 0FFH = 255, 100H = 256, 0FFFFH = 65,535, 400H = 1024, and 10000H = 65,536.

Unsigned numbers: When all bits count as value, the number is unsigned. An 8-bit unsigned number goes from 0 to 255, and a 16-bit one from 0 to 65,535. If you add 200 and 100 in an 8-bit register, the true answer, 300, does not fit. The register keeps only the low 8 bits: 300 - 256 = 44, which is 2CH, and the processor raises a carry flag to say a bit fell off the top. We will meet flags properly in later lessons. For now just remember: for unsigned numbers, a carry out of the top bit means the answer was too big.

Negative numbers with two's complement: Processors need negative numbers too, like a temperature of -5 or a bank balance in the red. Almost every processor, including the 8085 and 8086, uses two's complement. The rule to make a negative: write the positive number in binary, flip every bit, then add 1. For -5 in 8 bits: 5 is 0000 0101, flipped it is 1111 1010, adding 1 gives 1111 1011, which is FBH. Check it another way: FBH is 251, and 251 - 256 = -5. In two's complement, the top bit is the sign bit: 0 means positive or zero, 1 means negative.

The signed ranges: Because one pattern is used for zero, the signed range is slightly lopsided. An 8-bit signed number goes from -128 to +127. In hex, 00H to 7FH are 0 to 127, and 80H to 0FFH are -128 to -1. So 80H is -128 and 0FFH is -1. A 16-bit signed number goes from -32,768 to +32,767, where 8000H is -32,768 and 0FFFFH is -1. A useful fact: the same bit pattern can mean two different things. FBH is 251 if you treat it as unsigned, or -5 if you treat it as signed. The processor does not care; you, the programmer, decide.

Why two's complement is so clever: With two's complement, subtraction becomes addition. To do 7 - 5, the processor can do 7 + (-5). That is 07H + FBH = 102H. In 8 bits the extra 1 at the top falls off, leaving 02H, which is 2. Correct! The same adder circuit handles both signed and unsigned numbers, so the chip stays simple. Also, there is only one zero, unlike the older sign and magnitude method, which had both +0 and -0. This is why exam papers love asking why computers prefer two's complement.

Sign extension: Sometimes we must copy a small signed number into a bigger register, like putting an 8-bit -5 into a 16-bit register. If we just add zeros on the left, 0FBH becomes 00FBH, which is +251, wrong! Instead we copy the sign bit into all the new bits. -5 becomes 0FFFBH, and +5 stays 0005H. This is called sign extension. The 8086 has special instructions for it, CBW and CWD, which we will meet in the arithmetic lesson. For unsigned numbers, we use zero extension: just fill with zeros.

Signed overflow: Unsigned numbers have carry; signed numbers have overflow. In 8-bit signed maths, 100 + 50 should be 150, but 150 is bigger than 127. The bits give 64H + 32H = 96H, and 96H read as signed is -106. Two positive numbers added and the answer looks negative: that is overflow. A simple rule: overflow happens when you add two numbers of the same sign and the result has the opposite sign. Adding a positive and a negative number can never overflow. The processor has a separate overflow flag for this, which we will study with the 8086 flags.

BCD, binary coded decimal: Some devices think in decimal digits, like a digital clock or a fuel pump display. BCD stores each decimal digit in its own nibble. So 47 is stored as 0100 0111, which looks like 47H. Notice that 47 in normal binary is 2FH, so BCD and binary are different. In packed BCD, two digits share one byte. In unpacked BCD, each digit has a whole byte: 47 becomes 04H and 07H. Nibbles 1010 to 1111 are not allowed in BCD. Processors have special adjust instructions, like DAA, that fix the result after adding BCD numbers.

ASCII, letters as numbers: Text is also stored as numbers, using ASCII codes. The digit characters '0' to '9' are 30H to 39H. Capital 'A' to 'Z' are 41H to 5AH. Small 'a' to 'z' are 61H to 7AH. A space is 20H, a carriage return is 0DH and a line feed is 0AH. Two tricks you will use again and again: to turn a digit value like 7 into its character '7', add 30H; to go back, subtract 30H. And to change a small letter to a capital, subtract 20H, since 'a' is 61H and 'A' is 41H. You will use these in input and output programs.

Little endian byte order: Memory holds bytes, one per address. When a processor stores a 16-bit word, which byte goes first? Intel chips, both 8085 and 8086, use little endian: the low byte goes at the lower address. So if the 8086 stores 1234H at address 2000H, memory holds 34H at 2000H and 12H at 2001H. The same happens in machine code: the 8085 instruction LXI H, 2050H is stored as the bytes 21H, 50H, 20H. Some other processors use big endian, putting the high byte first. Mixing these up is a classic exam trap and a classic bug.

A worked memory example: Suppose memory from address 3000H holds the bytes 78H, 56H, 34H, 12H. If you read a word from 3000H on the 8086, you get 5678H. If you read a word from 3002H, you get 1234H. If you read a doubleword from 3000H, you get 12345678H. Read the bytes from the highest address down to the lowest and you get the number. Practise this until it is automatic, because memory dump questions appear in many exams.

Real life example 1, a cricket scoreboard: Imagine a small electronic scoreboard at a school cricket match in Rajshahi. The score 147 must appear on three seven segment digits. If the program stores the score as plain binary, 147 is 93H, and showing it needs division to get each digit. If it stores the score in BCD, it keeps 01H and 47H in packed form, and each nibble can be sent straight to a digit driver. When a four is hit, the program adds 4 and uses a decimal adjust to keep it valid BCD: 47H + 04H gives 4BH, then adjusting gives 51H, meaning 51. So the scoreboard shows 151 with almost no extra work.

Real life example 2, a temperature logger: A cold storage warehouse in Munshiganj keeps potatoes near 4 degrees Celsius, but sometimes the sensor reads below zero. The sensor sends a signed 8-bit value. A reading of 0FDH means -3, not 253. If the program treated it as unsigned, it would think the room was extremely hot and might turn the cooling up even more. By using signed comparison and two's complement, the controller understands -3 correctly. When it stores readings in a 16-bit log, it sign extends 0FDH to 0FFFDH so the value stays -3.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting the leading zero, writing FFH instead of 0FFH. Second, confusing BCD with binary, thinking 47H means forty-seven in binary; it is seventy-one. Third, putting the bytes of a word in the wrong order in memory. Fourth, mixing carry and overflow: carry is for unsigned, overflow is for signed. Fifth, zero extending a negative number instead of sign extending it. Sixth, forgetting that a range like -128 to 127 is not symmetric.

What exams ask: Convert 2AFH to decimal and binary. Find the 8-bit two's complement of -37. What range can a 16-bit signed number hold? Represent 59 in packed and unpacked BCD. Show how the word 0ABCDH is stored at address 4000H. Add 70H and 50H in 8 bits and say whether carry and overflow happen. For that last one: 70H + 50H = 0C0H, no carry, but two positives gave a negative pattern, so overflow is set.

Quick recap: Hex is shorthand for binary, one digit per nibble, written with an H and a leading zero when needed. Unsigned numbers use every bit as value; signed numbers use two's complement, with the top bit as the sign. The same bits can mean different values, so the programmer decides. BCD stores decimal digits in nibbles, ASCII stores characters as codes, and Intel chips store multi-byte numbers in little endian order. With these tools ready, in the next lesson we open the 8085 and meet its registers.
key_points: One hex digit is exactly one nibble (4 bits); Intel assemblers write hex with an H suffix and a leading 0 if it starts with a letter, like 0FFH.
8-bit unsigned is 0 to 255; 8-bit signed (two's complement) is -128 to +127.
Two's complement negative: flip all bits and add 1, so -5 is 0FBH.
The same bits can be unsigned or signed; carry signals unsigned overflow, the overflow flag signals signed overflow.
Sign extension copies the sign bit: -5 as 16 bits is 0FFFBH.
BCD stores one decimal digit per nibble: 47 is 0100 0111; ASCII '0' is 30H, 'A' is 41H, 'a' is 61H.
Intel chips are little endian: 1234H at 2000H is stored as 34H then 12H.
lessons.tip: Keep a small card with powers of 16 (1, 16, 256, 4096) and the ASCII codes for '0', 'A' and 'a'. Look at it until you no longer need it; this saves minutes in every exam.
lessons.task: On paper, write the 8-bit two's complement of -1, -10 and -100 in hex, then check each by subtracting 256 from its unsigned value. Next, write how the word 0BEEFH and the doubleword 12345678H would be stored in memory starting at address 5000H.

quiz.q: What is the 8-bit two's complement form of -5?
quiz.explain: 5 is 0000 0101, flipping gives 1111 1010, adding 1 gives 1111 1011, which is 0FBH.

quiz.q: On the 8086, the word 1234H is stored at address 2000H. Which byte is at address 2000H?
quiz.explain: Intel chips are little endian, so the low byte 34H goes at the lower address 2000H and 12H goes at 2001H.

quiz.q: What is the range of an 8-bit signed two's complement number?
quiz.explain: With 8 bits there are 256 patterns. Two's complement uses 80H to 0FFH for -128 to -1 and 00H to 7FH for 0 to 127.

quiz.q: How is the decimal number 47 stored in packed BCD?
quiz.explain: Packed BCD puts each decimal digit in a nibble: 4 is 0100 and 7 is 0111, giving 0100 0111, which looks like 47H. 2FH is plain binary, and 04H 07H is unpacked.

quiz.q: In 8-bit signed arithmetic, 70H + 50H = 0C0H. What happened?
options: Overflow, because two positives gave a negative result
quiz.explain: 70H (112) + 50H (80) = 192, which does not fit in -128 to 127. The result 0C0H has its sign bit set, so overflow occurs. There is no carry out of bit 7.

lessons.title: Inside the 8085: Architecture, Registers, Flags and Pins
lessons.content:
Imagine walking into a small but busy tea stall near your college. There is one main cup where the tea is mixed, a few small jars of sugar, milk and tea leaves on the shelf, a little notebook where the owner ticks what each customer ordered, and a window where orders come in and cups go out. Everything has its place, and the owner knows exactly where to reach. The Intel 8085 is like that tea stall. It is small, it has only a few storage places, but each one has a clear job. In this lesson we walk around the stall: the registers, the flags, the buses and the important pins.

The chip at a glance: The 8085 is an 8-bit microprocessor released by Intel in 1976. It comes in a 40-pin package and runs from a single +5 volt supply, which was a big improvement over the older 8080 that needed several voltages. It has a 16-bit address bus, so it can address 64 KB of memory, and an 8-bit data bus. A crystal is connected to two pins called X1 and X2, and the chip divides the crystal frequency by 2 inside, so a 6 MHz crystal gives a 3 MHz operating clock. The chip also sends this clock out on a pin called CLK OUT for other chips to use.

The block diagram: Inside the 8085 you can picture five main areas. First, the ALU with the accumulator, a temporary register and the flag register. Second, the register array with B, C, D, E, H, L, the stack pointer and the program counter. Third, the instruction register and decoder, which hold and understand the current instruction. Fourth, the timing and control unit, which produces all the control signals. Fifth, the interrupt control and serial I/O control blocks. All of these are joined by an internal 8-bit data bus. Exam questions very often ask you to draw this diagram, so learn it as a picture.

The accumulator: Register A, the accumulator, is the star of the 8085. Most arithmetic and logic instructions use A as one of the inputs and also put the result back into A. For example, ADD B means A = A + B. SUB C means A = A - C. ANA D means A = A AND D. Think of A as the main mixing cup in our tea stall: everything gets mixed there. Because of this, many 8085 programs keep moving data into A, working on it, then moving the answer out.

The general purpose registers: The 8085 has six 8-bit general purpose registers: B, C, D, E, H and L. They hold data while a program runs, like small jars on the shelf. They can also be used in pairs to hold 16-bit values: BC, DE and HL. In a pair, the first letter is the high byte and the second is the low byte. So if B = 20H and C = 50H, the pair BC holds 2050H. Pairs are used mostly to hold memory addresses, since addresses on the 8085 are 16 bits long.

HL, the memory pointer: The HL pair has a special role. Many instructions use the address in HL to reach memory. In assembly this memory location is written as M. So MOV A, M means: take the byte from the memory address held in HL and put it into A. If H = 30H and L = 00H, then M is the byte at address 3000H. This is how 8085 programs walk through tables and arrays: set HL to the start, read M, then increase HL with INX H to move to the next byte.

The program counter and stack pointer: Two registers are always 16 bits. The program counter, PC, holds the address of the next instruction to fetch, and it is increased automatically after each byte is fetched. When the chip is reset, PC becomes 0000H, so the first program must start there. The stack pointer, SP, holds the address of the top of the stack, an area of memory used to save return addresses and register values. On the 8085, the stack grows downward: each push first decreases SP. We will study the stack in detail with the 8086.

Hidden registers: There are also registers the programmer cannot use directly. W and Z are temporary registers that hold bytes during some instructions, for example the two address bytes of a CALL. The instruction register holds the opcode while it is being decoded. The temporary register in the ALU holds the second input for an operation. You do not write instructions for these, but knowing they exist helps you understand how the chip works step by step.

The flag register: After many arithmetic and logic operations, the 8085 records some facts about the result in a special register called the flag register. It has five flags, each one bit. The sign flag S is a copy of bit 7 of the result, so S = 1 means the result is negative if you read it as signed. The zero flag Z is 1 when the result is zero. The auxiliary carry flag AC is 1 when there is a carry from bit 3 to bit 4. The parity flag P is 1 when the result has an even number of 1 bits. The carry flag CY is 1 when there is a carry out of bit 7 in addition, or a borrow in subtraction.

Where the flags sit: The flag register is 8 bits, but only five are used. From bit 7 down to bit 0 the layout is S, Z, unused, AC, unused, P, unused, CY. The accumulator and the flag register together are called the program status word, or PSW. The instruction PUSH PSW saves both on the stack, which is useful when you need to protect them. Exams sometimes ask you to draw this byte, so remember the order: S Z, then AC in bit 4, P in bit 2 and CY in bit 0.

A worked flag example: Suppose A = 9AH and B = 8BH, and we run ADD B. In binary, 1001 1010 + 1000 1011 = 1 0010 0101. The answer is 125H, but A holds only 8 bits, so A = 25H and the extra 1 goes to the carry flag: CY = 1. Bit 7 of 25H is 0, so S = 0. The result is not zero, so Z = 0. 25H is 0010 0101, which has three 1 bits, an odd number, so P = 0. The low nibbles were AH + BH = 10 + 11 = 21, which is more than 15, so there was a carry from bit 3 to bit 4 and AC = 1.

What flags are used for: Flags let the program make decisions. JZ means jump if the zero flag is set, JNZ means jump if it is not set, JC means jump if carry is set, and so on. A counting loop often decreases a register and then uses JNZ to repeat until the register reaches zero. The AC flag is used by the DAA instruction to fix BCD additions. Not every instruction changes the flags: data movement instructions like MOV and MVI leave them alone, which is a common exam point.

The address and data buses: The 8085 has 16 address lines but only 40 pins, so Intel saved pins with a trick. The upper 8 address lines, A8 to A15, have their own pins. The lower 8 address lines share pins with the 8 data lines, called AD0 to AD7. This is called multiplexing: the same wires carry the low address byte first, and then carry data a moment later. It is like a single road that carries school buses in the morning and delivery trucks in the afternoon.

ALE and demultiplexing: How does the outside world know when AD0 to AD7 hold an address and when they hold data? The 8085 raises a signal called ALE, address latch enable, during the first clock state of each machine cycle. When ALE is high, AD0 to AD7 carry the low byte of the address. An external latch chip, commonly the 74LS373, catches and holds that byte when ALE falls. After that, the AD lines are free to carry data. This process is called demultiplexing the bus, and drawing it is a favourite exam question.

Control and status signals: The RD signal, active low, tells memory or a device that the processor wants to read. The WR signal, also active low, means the processor is writing. The IO/M signal says whether the operation is for memory or for an input/output device: low means memory, high means I/O. Two status signals, S0 and S1, together with IO/M, tell what kind of machine cycle is happening, such as opcode fetch, memory read or memory write. By combining IO/M with RD and WR, designers make four control signals: MEMR, MEMW, IOR and IOW.

Other important pins: RESET IN, when pulled low, resets the chip and sets PC to 0000H. RESET OUT tells other chips that a reset is happening. READY lets slow memory or devices ask the processor to wait. HOLD and HLDA are used for direct memory access: another device asks for the bus with HOLD, and the 8085 answers with HLDA. TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR are interrupt inputs, and INTA acknowledges an interrupt; we study these in a later lesson. SID and SOD are serial input and output data pins for sending bits one by one.

Real life example 1, a shop's price display: Imagine a small 8085 trainer kit in your university lab used to run a price display for a pretend shop. The prices of ten items are stored in memory from 2050H. The program puts 20H in H and 50H in L, so HL points to the first price. MOV A, M brings that price into the accumulator. ADD B adds a tax value kept in register B. If CY becomes 1, the price went over 255 and the program shows an error. Then INX H moves HL to the next price. Registers, the memory pointer and the carry flag all work together in a few lines.

Real life example 2, a water pump controller: In many Bangladeshi apartment buildings, a controller turns the water pump on when the roof tank is low. Suppose a tiny 8085 system reads the water level from an input port into A. It then compares A with a limit using CMP. If the result sets the carry flag, the level is below the limit, and the program sends 1 to an output port to start the pump. If the zero flag is set, the level is exactly at the limit, and the program keeps the current state. Flags turn raw numbers into decisions.

Common mistakes: First, thinking the 8085 has 16-bit general registers; B, C, D, E, H, L are 8-bit, only pairs make 16 bits. Second, writing the pair order wrong: in BC, B is the high byte. Third, forgetting that M means the memory byte pointed to by HL, not a register inside the chip. Fourth, thinking MOV changes the flags. Fifth, mixing up which bits are multiplexed: only the low address byte shares pins with data. Sixth, forgetting that IO/M low means memory.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the architecture of the 8085. List the registers and their sizes. Explain each flag with an example. Why is the bus multiplexed and how is it demultiplexed using ALE? Explain the functions of IO/M, RD, WR, READY, HOLD and HLDA. Find the flags after adding two given numbers. For the last type, always write the addition in binary, then check each flag one by one in the order S, Z, AC, P, CY.

Quick recap: The 8085 is an 8-bit chip with a 16-bit address bus, a single +5 volt supply and a 40-pin package. Its accumulator is the main working register, helped by B, C, D, E, H and L, which pair up as BC, DE and HL. HL is the memory pointer M. PC and SP are 16 bits. Five flags, S, Z, AC, P and CY, describe each result. The low address byte is multiplexed with data on AD0 to AD7 and separated with ALE and a latch. Next we will learn the 8085 instruction set and its addressing modes.
key_points: The 8085 is an 8-bit processor (1976) with a 16-bit address bus (64 KB), single +5 V supply and 40 pins.
The accumulator A is the main working register; most arithmetic and logic results go back into A.
B, C, D, E, H, L are 8-bit registers that pair as BC, DE, HL; the first letter is the high byte.
HL is the memory pointer: M means the memory byte at the address in HL.
PC and SP are 16-bit; reset sets PC to 0000H.
Five flags: S (bit 7), Z (bit 6), AC (bit 4), P (bit 2), CY (bit 0); MOV and MVI do not change them.
AD0-AD7 carry the low address byte then data; ALE plus a latch like the 74LS373 separates them.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet an 8085 instruction, ask two questions: which register changes, and which flags change. Writing those two answers beside every example will make the instruction set lesson much easier.
lessons.task: Add these pairs by hand in 8-bit binary and write all five 8085 flags for each: 45H + 3BH, 0F0H + 10H and 7FH + 01H. Then draw the 8085 block diagram from memory and label the accumulator, flags, register pairs, PC and SP.

quiz.q: In the 8085, what does the operand M refer to?
options: The memory byte at the address held in HL
The memory byte at the address held in BC
quiz.explain: M is the memory location whose address is in the HL pair. MOV A, M copies that byte into the accumulator.

quiz.q: After ADD B with A = 9AH and B = 8BH, what is the carry flag?
quiz.explain: 9AH + 8BH = 125H, which does not fit in 8 bits, so A = 25H and the carry out of bit 7 sets CY = 1.

quiz.q: Why does the 8085 need the ALE signal?
options: To tell external circuits that AD0-AD7 currently hold the low address byte
To select I/O instead of memory
quiz.explain: AD0-AD7 are multiplexed. ALE goes high in the first state of a machine cycle so a latch can capture the low address byte before the lines carry data.

quiz.q: When the parity flag P of the 8085 is 1, what does it mean?
options: There was a carry from bit 3
The result has an even number of 1 bits
quiz.explain: On the 8085, P = 1 means even parity: the result contains an even number of 1s.

quiz.q: If B = 20H and C = 50H, what 16-bit value does the BC pair hold?
quiz.explain: In a register pair the first register is the high byte, so BC = 20H followed by 50H = 2050H.

lessons.title: The 8085 Instruction Set and Addressing Modes
lessons.content:
Imagine you are giving directions to a delivery rider from Foodpanda. Sometimes you hand him the food directly: here, take this. Sometimes you say: the food is in the box on the counter. Sometimes you say: go to house number 25, the food is there. And sometimes you say: look at the note in your pocket, it has the house number. The food is the same, but the way you tell him where to find it changes. In the 8085, these different ways of saying where the data is are called addressing modes. In this lesson we learn them, and we meet the most important instructions of the 8085.

What an instruction looks like: Every 8085 instruction has an opcode, which says what to do, and sometimes operands, which say what to do it with. In assembly we write the mnemonic, a short memory aid, like MOV, ADD or JMP, followed by the operands. For example, in MVI A, 32H, the mnemonic is MVI, the destination is A and the data is 32H. In Intel style, the destination always comes first and the source second. So MOV A, B means copy B into A, not A into B. This order rule is one of the first things to get right.

Instruction sizes: 8085 instructions are 1, 2 or 3 bytes long. A one-byte instruction has only the opcode, such as MOV A, B, which is 78H, or HLT, which is 76H. A two-byte instruction has an opcode and one data byte, such as MVI A, 32H, stored as 3EH 32H. A three-byte instruction has an opcode and a 16-bit address or data, such as LDA 2050H, stored as 3AH 50H 20H. Notice that the 16-bit value is stored low byte first, the little endian rule from lesson 2. Knowing sizes lets you work out where each instruction sits in memory.

Immediate addressing: In immediate mode, the data itself is written inside the instruction. Like handing the rider the food directly. MVI B, 25H puts 25H into B. LXI H, 2050H loads the 16-bit value 2050H into the HL pair. ADI 05H adds 5 to A. The letter I in many mnemonics stands for immediate: MVI is move immediate, ADI is add immediate, SUI is subtract immediate, CPI is compare immediate. Immediate mode is fast and simple, but the value is fixed when the program is written.

Register addressing: In register mode, the data is in a register inside the chip. Like saying the food is on the counter. MOV A, B copies B into A. ADD C adds C to A. INR D increases D by 1. These are usually one-byte instructions, because the register names fit inside the opcode bits. They are the fastest instructions, because no trip to memory is needed after fetching the opcode.

Direct addressing: In direct mode, the instruction carries the full 16-bit address of the data in memory. Like saying go to house number 25. LDA 2050H loads A with the byte stored at address 2050H. STA 3000H stores A into address 3000H. LHLD 2500H loads L from 2500H and H from 2501H. The input and output instructions IN 01H and OUT 02H are also counted as direct, because the port number is written in the instruction. Direct mode is easy to read, but each such instruction is 3 bytes long, except IN and OUT, which are 2.

Register indirect addressing: In indirect mode, a register pair holds the address of the data. Like saying check the note in your pocket for the house number. MOV A, M reads the byte at the address in HL. MOV M, B writes B into that memory location. LDAX B loads A from the address in BC, and STAX D stores A at the address in DE. This mode is perfect for loops over arrays, because you only change the pointer, not the instruction.

Implied addressing: In implied, or implicit, mode the operand is not written because the instruction always works on a fixed place, usually the accumulator. CMA complements A. RAL rotates A left through carry. STC sets the carry flag. DAA adjusts A after BCD addition. You just write the mnemonic, and the chip already knows where the data is. These instructions are one byte.

Instruction groups: The 8085 has about 74 basic instructions, which textbooks put into five groups. Data transfer instructions move data: MOV, MVI, LDA, STA, LXI, LDAX, STAX, LHLD, SHLD, XCHG, IN, OUT. Arithmetic instructions: ADD, ADC, ADI, SUB, SBB, SUI, INR, DCR, INX, DCX, DAD, DAA. Logical instructions: ANA, ORA, XRA, CMP, their immediate forms ANI, ORI, XRI, CPI, plus CMA, CMC, STC and the rotates RLC, RRC, RAL, RAR. Branch instructions: JMP, conditional jumps, CALL, RET and RST. Machine control: NOP, HLT, EI, DI, SIM and RIM.

How arithmetic instructions affect flags: ADD, SUB and their friends change all five flags. INR and DCR change all flags except CY, which surprises many students. INX and DCX, the 16-bit increment and decrement, change no flags at all. That means a loop using DCX B cannot use JNZ directly to test the pair for zero; you must check it another way, for example by moving B to A and ORing it with C. DAD adds a register pair to HL and changes only CY.

Logical instructions and compare: ANA B does A = A AND B and clears CY. ORA B and XRA B clear CY too. A neat trick: XRA A makes A zero and clears the carry in a single byte. CMP B compares A with B by doing A - B inside, setting flags, but not changing A. If A < B, CY = 1. If A = B, Z = 1. If A > B, both are 0. CPI does the same with an immediate value. Compare plus a conditional jump is how 8085 programs make every decision.

Branch instructions: JMP 2050H always jumps to 2050H. Conditional jumps check one flag: JZ and JNZ test zero, JC and JNC test carry, JP and JM test sign (plus or minus), and JPE and JPO test parity (even or odd). CALL 3000H jumps to a subroutine at 3000H after saving the return address on the stack, and RET returns. Calls and returns also come in conditional forms, like CZ and RNC. RST n is a one-byte call to address 8 times n, so RST 1 calls 0008H.

Stack and register pair instructions: A few more data transfer instructions work on 16-bit pairs. PUSH B saves the BC pair on the stack, and POP B brings it back; PUSH D, PUSH H and PUSH PSW work the same way for DE, HL, and A with the flags. XCHG swaps the contents of HL and DE in one byte, which is handy when you need two pointers. SHLD 2600H stores L at 2600H and H at 2601H, the opposite of LHLD. SPHL copies HL into the stack pointer, and XTHL swaps HL with the two bytes on top of the stack. None of these change the flags, except POP PSW, which of course reloads the flags from memory. Remember that PUSH and POP always move a pair, never a single 8-bit register.

A first complete program: Let us add two numbers stored at 2050H and 2051H and store the sum at 2052H. The program is: LDA 2050H ; MOV B, A ; LDA 2051H ; ADD B ; STA 2052H ; HLT. Step by step: the first LDA brings the first number into A, MOV B, A saves it in B, the second LDA brings the second number into A, ADD B adds them, STA stores the answer, and HLT stops. If 2050H holds 15H and 2051H holds 27H, then 2052H gets 3CH.

Assembling it by hand: Starting at address 2000H, the bytes are: 3AH 50H 20H for LDA 2050H, then 47H for MOV B, A, then 3AH 51H 20H, then 80H for ADD B, then 32H 52H 20H for STA 2052H, and finally 76H for HLT. That is 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 12 bytes, so the program ends at 200BH. In a university lab, you type these bytes into a trainer kit's keypad, press execute, and then check memory 2052H.

An opcode pattern to notice: MOV instructions follow a neat pattern: the opcode is 01 DDD SSS in binary, where DDD is the destination and SSS the source. Registers are coded as B = 000, C = 001, D = 010, E = 011, H = 100, L = 101, M = 110 and A = 111. So MOV A, B is 01 111 000 = 78H, and MOV B, A is 01 000 111 = 47H. Following the pattern, MOV M, M would be 76H, but that code is used for HLT instead, so there is no MOV M, M. This fact is a favourite trick question.

Real life example 1, an attendance counter: Imagine a school in Sylhet using a simple 8085 board connected to a button at the gate. Each time a student presses the button, the program runs INR M with HL pointing at a counter in memory. INR M adds 1 to the memory byte directly, using register indirect addressing. When the teacher wants the total, the program does MOV A, M and OUT 01H to send it to a display port. Indirect, register and direct style instructions all appear in a tiny, useful program.

Real life example 2, a petrol pump price calculator: At a filling station, the price per litre and the number of litres must be combined. On the 8085 there is no multiply instruction, so the program adds the price again and again in a loop. MVI C, litres sets the counter, XRA A clears A, then a loop does ADD B with B holding the price, DCR C, and JNZ back to the ADD. When C reaches zero, the zero flag is set and the loop ends. This shows how immediate, register and branching instructions build bigger operations.

Common mistakes: First, reversing source and destination: MOV A, B copies B into A. Second, thinking INR changes the carry flag. Third, trying to test a register pair for zero after DCX using JNZ; DCX sets no flags. Fourth, writing the 16-bit address bytes in the wrong order when hand-assembling. Fifth, forgetting that CMP does not change A. Sixth, confusing LDA, which uses a direct address, with LDAX, which uses a register pair as pointer.

What exams ask: Define addressing mode and explain each 8085 mode with an example. Classify given instructions into groups and modes. Find the size in bytes of a list of instructions and the address of each in memory. Explain how a given instruction affects the flags. Write a program to add, subtract or compare two numbers. Show the machine code of a short program. Explain the difference between JMP and CALL, and between LDA and LDAX.

Quick recap: An 8085 instruction is an opcode plus 0, 1 or 2 bytes of operands, with destination first. Immediate mode carries the data, register mode uses a register, direct mode carries an address, register indirect mode uses a pair as a pointer, and implied mode uses a fixed register. The instructions fall into data transfer, arithmetic, logical, branch and machine control groups. Flags change in specific ways, and conditional jumps use them to make decisions. Next lesson we will write longer 8085 programs and learn how long each instruction takes in clock states.
key_points: Intel syntax puts the destination first: MOV A, B copies B into A.
8085 instructions are 1, 2 or 3 bytes; 16-bit operands are stored low byte first.
Addressing modes: immediate (MVI A, 32H), register (MOV A, B), direct (LDA 2050H), register indirect (MOV A, M; LDAX B) and implied (CMA).
Five groups: data transfer, arithmetic, logical, branch, machine control.
INR/DCR change all flags except CY; INX/DCX change no flags; MOV changes none.
CMP sets flags from A minus operand without changing A: CY = 1 if A is smaller, Z = 1 if equal.
MOV opcodes follow 01 DDD SSS; the slot for MOV M, M is used by HLT (76H).
lessons.tip: Make a small table with four columns for each new instruction: bytes, addressing mode, what changes, flags affected. Filling it yourself teaches much more than reading a printed list.
lessons.task: Hand assemble this program starting at 2000H and write each address and byte: MVI A, 05H ; MVI B, 03H ; ADD B ; STA 2100H ; HLT. Then predict the value in 2100H and which flags are set after ADD B.

quiz.q: Which addressing mode does LDAX B use?
quiz.explain: LDAX B loads A from the memory address held in the BC pair, so the pair acts as a pointer: register indirect.

quiz.q: How many bytes long is LDA 2050H and how is it stored?
quiz.explain: LDA carries a 16-bit address, so it is 3 bytes. The address is stored low byte first, giving 3AH 50H 20H.

quiz.q: Which flag is NOT affected by INR and DCR?
quiz.explain: INR and DCR update S, Z, AC and P but leave the carry flag unchanged.

quiz.q: After CMP B with A = 20H and B = 35H, what is true?
quiz.explain: CMP subtracts internally without changing A. Since A (20H) is less than B (35H), a borrow occurs and CY = 1.

quiz.q: Why is there no MOV M, M instruction on the 8085?
options: Its code 76H is used for HLT
quiz.explain: Following the 01 DDD SSS pattern, MOV M, M would be 01 110 110 = 76H, but that opcode is assigned to HLT.

lessons.title: 8085 Programming and Timing: Loops, T-states and Delays
lessons.content:
Imagine you are cooking rice for a family dinner. The recipe does not only say what to do, it also says how long: boil the water for five minutes, add rice, cook for fifteen minutes. If you get the timing wrong, the rice is either crunchy or mushy. Programs are similar. In the last lesson we learned what each 8085 instruction does. In this lesson we put instructions together into real programs with loops and decisions, and we also learn how long each instruction takes, measured in tiny clock steps. With that knowledge you can even make the processor wait for an exact amount of time, which is how a simple chip blinks an LED or beeps a buzzer.

Labels and comments: Before writing longer programs, two small tools. A label is a name written at the start of a line, followed by a colon, such as LOOP:. The assembler replaces the label with the address of that line, so you can write JNZ LOOP instead of JNZ 2007H. A comment starts with a semicolon and is ignored by the assembler, like ; this counts down. Good labels and comments make your program readable, both for you and for the examiner. On a trainer kit without an assembler, you work out label addresses by hand from instruction sizes.

Program 1, adding with carry: Suppose two 8-bit numbers at 2050H and 2051H may add up to more than 255. We want the 8-bit sum at 2052H and the carry, 0 or 1, at 2053H. The program: LDA 2050H ; MOV B, A ; LDA 2051H ; MVI C, 00H ; ADD B ; JNC SKIP ; INR C ; SKIP: STA 2052H ; MOV A, C ; STA 2053H ; HLT. Register C starts at 0. If ADD produces a carry, JNC does not jump, INR C makes C equal 1. If there is no carry, JNC jumps straight to SKIP. For 0F0H and 20H, the sum 110H gives 10H at 2052H and 01H at 2053H.

The counter loop pattern: Almost every 8085 loop follows the same shape: load a counter, do the work, decrease the counter, jump back if it is not zero. In code: MVI C, 0AH ; LOOP: work ; DCR C ; JNZ LOOP. DCR C sets the zero flag when C reaches zero, and JNZ stops jumping at that moment. The work part runs exactly 0AH = 10 times. Learn this pattern by heart; it is like the for loop of the 8085.

Program 2, moving a block of data: Let us copy 10 bytes from 2050H onward to 3050H onward. We use HL as the source pointer and DE as the destination pointer. LXI H, 2050H ; LXI D, 3050H ; MVI C, 0AH ; LOOP: MOV A, M ; STAX D ; INX H ; INX D ; DCR C ; JNZ LOOP ; HLT. Each round reads a byte through HL, writes it through DE, moves both pointers forward and counts down. Notice INX does not affect flags, so it does not disturb the zero flag test, which comes from DCR C just before JNZ.

Program 3, finding the largest number: Suppose 2050H holds how many numbers there are, at least 2, and the numbers follow from 2051H. We want the largest at 3000H. LXI H, 2050H ; MOV C, M ; INX H ; MOV A, M ; DCR C ; LOOP: INX H ; CMP M ; JNC SKIP ; MOV A, M ; SKIP: DCR C ; JNZ LOOP ; STA 3000H ; HLT. A holds the biggest so far. CMP M compares A with the next number. If A is smaller, the carry flag is set, JNC does not jump, and MOV A, M takes the new bigger value. To find the smallest instead, change JNC to JC.

Timing words, T-state: Now the timing part. A T-state is one period of the processor clock. If the 8085 runs at 3 MHz, one T-state lasts 1 divided by 3 million seconds, which is about 0.333 microseconds, or 333 nanoseconds. Everything the chip does is counted in whole T-states. Think of T-states as the ticks of a very fast clock on the kitchen wall.

Timing words, machine cycle: A machine cycle is the time to do one basic trip on the bus, like fetching an opcode, reading a byte from memory or writing a byte. On the 8085, an opcode fetch usually takes 4 T-states, though some instructions need 6. A memory read takes 3 T-states, a memory write 3, an I/O read 3 and an I/O write 3. An instruction is made of one or more machine cycles. The time for one complete instruction, from fetch to finish, is called the instruction cycle.

What happens in an opcode fetch: In T1, the program counter's address goes out, the high byte on A8 to A15 and the low byte on AD0 to AD7, and ALE goes high so the latch can catch the low byte. IO/M is low because this is memory, and the status lines S1 and S0 are both 1, meaning opcode fetch. In T2, RD goes low, and memory puts the opcode on the data bus. In T3, the opcode is read into the instruction register and RD goes high again. In T4, the chip decodes the opcode and decides what to do next. Drawing this timing diagram is one of the most common exam questions on the 8085.

Breaking instructions into machine cycles: MOV A, B needs only an opcode fetch, so 1 machine cycle and 4 T-states. MVI A, 32H needs an opcode fetch plus a memory read to get 32H: 4 + 3 = 7 T-states. LDA 2050H needs an opcode fetch, two memory reads for the address bytes, and one more memory read for the data: 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 13 T-states. STA 2050H is similar, but the last cycle is a memory write: also 13 T-states. MOV A, M is an opcode fetch plus a memory read: 7 T-states.

More timing numbers to know: ADD B, DCR C and INR A take 4 T-states each. INX H and DCX B take 6, because their opcode fetch is longer. LXI H takes 10: a fetch plus two reads. JMP takes 10. JNZ takes 10 T-states when it jumps but only 7 when it does not, because it does not need to finish loading the target into PC. CALL takes 18 and RET takes 10. These numbers come from Intel's instruction tables, and many exams print the table for you, but knowing the common ones makes calculations fast.

A simple delay loop: Often a program must wait, for example to keep an LED on long enough to see. The simplest delay is: MVI C, count ; LOOP: DCR C ; JNZ LOOP. MVI takes 7 T-states once. Each round of DCR plus a taken JNZ takes 4 + 10 = 14. In the last round JNZ does not jump, so it takes 7 instead of 10, saving 3. Total T-states = 7 + 14 x count - 3. With count = 0FFH, which is 255: 7 + 3570 - 3 = 3574 T-states.

Turning T-states into time: At 3 MHz, each T-state is about 0.333 microseconds, so 3574 T-states take about 3574 x 0.333 = 1,190 microseconds, roughly 1.19 milliseconds. That is far too short to see an LED blink. So we need a longer delay. You can make it longer by putting one loop inside another, or by using a 16-bit counter in a register pair.

A 16-bit delay loop: LXI B, count ; LOOP: DCX B ; MOV A, C ; ORA B ; JNZ LOOP. Because DCX does not set any flags, we copy C into A and OR it with B. The result is zero only when both B and C are zero, so the zero flag now tells us when the pair has run out. Each round costs 6 + 4 + 4 + 10 = 24 T-states. Total = 10 + 24 x count - 3. With count = 0FFFFH, which is 65,535, the total is about 1,572,847 T-states, which at 3 MHz is about 0.52 seconds. Run it twice and the LED blinks about once per second.

Calculating a count for a target delay: Suppose you want exactly 1 millisecond at 3 MHz with the 8-bit loop. 1 millisecond is 3,000 T-states. Solve 7 + 14 x count - 3 = 3000, so 14 x count = 2996 and count is about 214, which is D6H. Real crystals are never perfect, so a real board might be a little fast or slow. That is why engineers keep the count as a value they can adjust after measuring with an oscilloscope.

Real life example 1, a traffic light on a trainer kit: In many university labs in Bangladesh, students build a model traffic light using LEDs connected to an output port of an 8085 kit. The program sends a pattern with red on using OUT, calls a delay subroutine several times to wait, then sends the pattern for yellow, waits a shorter time, then green, and loops forever with JMP. The delay subroutine is exactly the 16-bit loop above with a RET at the end. Change the count and the lights change speed. The whole project is just loops, output and timing.

Real life example 2, a counter for a garment factory: Imagine a conveyor in a garment factory in Gazipur where each finished shirt passes a sensor. A small 8085 system reads the sensor with IN, and when it sees a shirt, it adds 1 to a counter in memory using INR M. After every shirt, it waits a short delay so the same shirt is not counted twice while it is still in front of the sensor. Engineers call this debouncing. When the counter reaches 100, the program uses CPI 64H and JZ to turn on a lamp so a worker knows a box is full.

Common mistakes: First, using DCX in a loop and testing JNZ right after it; DCX sets no flags. Second, forgetting that a JNZ which does not jump takes fewer T-states, so the delay formula has a minus 3. Third, using the wrong clock: the T-state comes from the processor clock, which is half the crystal frequency. Fourth, starting the largest-number loop without loading the first value into A. Fifth, putting the counter in a register that the loop body also changes.

What exams ask: Write a program to add two numbers with carry, find the largest or smallest in an array, move or exchange a block, or count even numbers. Draw the timing diagram of opcode fetch, memory read or of an instruction like MVI A, 32H. Define T-state, machine cycle and instruction cycle. Find the number of T-states and the delay of a given loop at a given clock. Find the count needed for a given delay.

Quick recap: 8085 programs are built from a few patterns: load, work, store; counter loops with DCR and JNZ; pointers in HL and DE; and compare plus conditional jump. Timing is counted in T-states, grouped into machine cycles: an opcode fetch is usually 4 T-states and a memory read or write is 3. Using these numbers you can calculate delays and choose counts. In the next lesson we leave the 8-bit world and meet the 16-bit 8086, the ancestor of today's PCs.
key_points: Labels name addresses (LOOP:) and comments start with a semicolon.
The counter loop pattern: MVI C, n; LOOP: work; DCR C; JNZ LOOP runs the work n times.
A T-state is one processor clock period: about 0.333 microseconds at 3 MHz.
Machine cycles: opcode fetch usually 4 T-states (some 6), memory read 3, memory write 3.
Opcode fetch: T1 address out with ALE, T2 RD low, T3 opcode read, T4 decode.
Common counts: MOV r,r 4; MVI 7; LDA/STA 13; INX/DCX 6; JMP 10; JNZ 10 taken or 7 not taken; CALL 18.
8-bit delay = 7 + 14 x count - 3 T-states; DCX sets no flags, so 16-bit loops test with MOV A, C and ORA B.
lessons.tip: When you write any loop, count its T-states right away on the side of your paper. Doing it every time turns delay questions into easy marks instead of scary ones.
lessons.task: Write an 8085 program on paper that counts how many numbers in a block of 10 bytes at 2050H are greater than 50H, storing the count at 3000H. Then count the T-states of the 8-bit delay loop with count = 64H and work out the time at 3 MHz.

quiz.q: How long is one T-state when the 8085 runs at 3 MHz?
quiz.explain: One T-state is one clock period: 1 / 3,000,000 seconds, about 0.333 microseconds.

quiz.q: How many T-states does LDA 2050H take?
quiz.explain: LDA needs an opcode fetch (4) and three memory reads (3 each): two for the address and one for the data, total 13.

quiz.q: Why does a 16-bit delay loop use MOV A, C and ORA B after DCX B?
options: Because DCX B does not affect any flags
Because JNZ only checks register A
quiz.explain: DCX sets no flags, so the zero flag must be produced another way. ORing B with C in A gives zero only when the whole pair is zero.

quiz.q: In the opcode fetch machine cycle, in which T-state is the opcode decoded?
quiz.explain: T1 sends the address and ALE, T2 activates RD, T3 reads the opcode into the instruction register, and T4 decodes it.

quiz.q: In the largest-number program, which jump keeps the current value of A when A is greater than or equal to M?
quiz.explain: After CMP M, CY = 0 means A is greater than or equal to M, so JNC SKIP jumps over MOV A, M and keeps the larger value.

lessons.title: 8086 Architecture: BIU, EU and the Prefetch Queue
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy biryani shop in Old Dhaka on a Friday. If the same person had to go to the bazar for rice and meat, come back, cook, serve, and then go to the bazar again, customers would wait forever. Smart shops split the job. One helper keeps running to the bazar and stacks ingredients near the kitchen. The cook never stops cooking, because the next ingredients are already waiting. The Intel 8086 works exactly like this shop. It has two units: one that fetches, and one that cooks, or in computer words, executes. In this lesson we open the 8086 and see how these two units cooperate.

Meet the 8086: Intel released the 8086 in 1978. It was a 16-bit microprocessor, which means its ALU and its main registers handle 16 bits at a time. It had about 29,000 transistors and came in a 40-pin package. Common versions ran at 5 MHz, 8 MHz (the 8086-2) and 10 MHz (the 8086-1). The 8085 from the earlier lessons is 8-bit, so the 8086 can add two 16-bit numbers in one instruction, where the 8085 would need several steps. The 8086 started the family called x86, and the laptop or desktop you use today still understands its instructions.

The address bus and 1 MB: The 8086 has a 20-bit address bus, lines A0 to A19. With 20 bits you can make 2^20 different patterns, which is 1,048,576 addresses, or 1 MB. Each address points to one byte. The 8085 had only 16 address lines, so it could reach 2^16 = 65,536 bytes, which is 64 KB. So the 8086 can see sixteen times more memory. Addresses are usually written in hex, from 00000h to FFFFFh. Five hex digits, because each hex digit is 4 bits and 5 x 4 = 20.

The data bus: The 8086 has a 16-bit data bus, D0 to D15, so in one bus cycle it can read or write a whole 16-bit word from memory, as long as the word sits at an even address. To save pins, the lower 16 address lines and the 16 data lines share the same pins, called AD0 to AD15. This is called a multiplexed bus. The top four address lines A16 to A19 also share pins with status signals S3 to S6. You saw the same pin-saving trick on the 8085 with AD0 to AD7.

The big picture, two units: Inside, the 8086 is divided into two parts that work at the same time. The Bus Interface Unit, or BIU, talks to the outside world: it sends addresses, reads instruction bytes and data from memory, and writes results back. The Execution Unit, or EU, does the actual work: it decodes instructions and runs them using the ALU and the registers. The EU never touches the bus directly. When it needs data from memory, it asks the BIU, the way the cook asks the helper.

Inside the BIU: The BIU contains the four segment registers CS, DS, SS and ES, the instruction pointer IP, an adder that builds 20-bit physical addresses, the bus control logic, and a 6-byte instruction queue. The adder is special: it takes a 16-bit segment value and a 16-bit offset and makes a 20-bit address. For example, the next instruction is fetched from CS x 16 + IP. Lesson 7 explains this segment trick in detail, so here just remember that the BIU is the one doing the address math.

Inside the EU: The EU contains the ALU, which adds, subtracts, ANDs, ORs and shifts. It contains the general purpose registers AX, BX, CX and DX, the pointer and index registers SP, BP, SI and DI, the flags register, and a control unit that decodes instructions. The EU takes instruction bytes from the front of the queue, decodes them, and executes them. If an instruction needs a memory operand, the EU calculates the offset and hands it to the BIU, which fetches the data.

The prefetch queue: Here is the clever part. While the EU is busy executing one instruction, the BIU does not sit idle. It keeps fetching the next instruction bytes from memory and stores them in the 6-byte queue, which works first in, first out, like a line of people at a bKash shop. On the 8086, the BIU fetches a new word whenever at least 2 bytes of the queue are empty. When the EU finishes an instruction, the next one is usually already waiting in the queue, so no time is lost going to memory. Fetching ahead like this is called prefetching.

A small timeline: Suppose the program is MOV AX, 5 then ADD AX, BX then MOV CX, AX. While the EU executes MOV AX, 5, the BIU is already fetching the bytes of ADD AX, BX and MOV CX, AX into the queue. When the EU is ready, it grabs ADD from the queue immediately. Fetching and executing overlap in time. This overlap is a simple form of pipelining, with two stages: fetch and execute. The Computer Architecture course goes much deeper into pipelines, so we only need the basic idea here.

When the queue is wasted: Prefetching assumes the program runs in a straight line. But what if the EU executes a jump, a call, or a return? Then the bytes sitting in the queue belong to the wrong place. The 8086 simply throws them away, which is called flushing the queue, and the BIU starts fetching from the new address. For a moment the EU must wait. That is why a jump costs more clock cycles than a simple MOV. Programs with many jumps inside tight loops lose some of the queue's benefit.

When the EU waits anyway: There are other moments when the EU must wait. If an instruction needs a memory operand, the BIU must pause prefetching and do that data read or write first. If the queue is empty because of a flush, the EU waits for the next instruction byte. And some instructions like MUL and DIV take many clock cycles inside the EU, during which the BIU fills the queue completely and then waits, because there is no space left.

The bus cycle: Every time the BIU reads or writes memory or I/O, it runs a bus cycle of at least four clock periods, called T1, T2, T3 and T4. In T1 the BIU puts the address on the AD lines, and a pulse on the ALE pin, Address Latch Enable, tells outside latch chips to grab and hold that address. In T2 the pins switch from address to data, and the read or write signal turns on. In T3 and T4 the data moves and the cycle ends. If memory is slow, the READY pin can ask the 8086 to insert extra wait states, called Tw, between T3 and T4. At 5 MHz one clock period is 200 nanoseconds, so a normal bus cycle takes 800 nanoseconds.

Some important pins: M/IO tells the outside world whether the address is for memory or for an I/O port. On the 8086, a high level means memory. RD is the read strobe and WR is the write strobe; both are active low. BHE, Bus High Enable, together with A0 tells which byte of the 16-bit data bus is used; we will meet it again in the memory interfacing lesson. INTR and NMI are interrupt inputs, RESET restarts the chip, CLK is the clock input, and READY is used for wait states. There are also VCC and GND pins for power.

Minimum mode: The 8086 has a pin called MN/MX. If you tie it high, the chip runs in minimum mode. This is meant for a small system with just one processor. In minimum mode the 8086 itself produces all the control signals: M/IO, RD, WR, ALE, DEN (data enable), DT/R (data transmit or receive), INTA (interrupt acknowledge) and HOLD/HLDA for DMA. A simple trainer board in a university lab usually works this way.

Maximum mode: If you tie MN/MX low, the chip runs in maximum mode, meant for bigger systems with more than one processor, for example an 8086 together with the 8087 math coprocessor. In this mode some pins change their meaning. The 8086 sends out status signals S0, S1 and S2, and a separate chip, the 8288 bus controller, decodes them and generates the memory and I/O control signals. Pins such as RQ/GT0, RQ/GT1 and LOCK help several processors share the bus. You only need this overview for now.

8086 versus 8088: Intel also made the 8088, which is the same inside: same registers, same instructions, same 20-bit address bus and 1 MB space. The difference is outside: the 8088 has an 8-bit external data bus, so a 16-bit word needs two bus cycles. Its queue is 4 bytes instead of 6, and it fetches when at least 1 byte is free. Why build a slower chip? Because 8-bit support chips and memory boards were cheap and common then. IBM chose the 8088 for the first IBM PC in 1981, which made the x86 family famous.

Real life example 1, a garments factory line: Think of a factory in Gazipur. One worker at the cutting table keeps cutting fabric pieces and puts them in a small tray, which can hold only six pieces. The sewing operator takes pieces from the tray and sews. If the tray has space, the cutter keeps cutting. If the supervisor suddenly says 'stop, we are switching to a different shirt design', all pieces in the tray are useless and thrown out. The cutter starts again with the new design while the sewing operator waits. Cutter = BIU, sewing operator = EU, tray = queue, design change = jump.

Real life example 2, a teacher and a class captain: In a school in Rajshahi, the teacher writes on the board while the class captain fetches the next set of copies from the office. The captain uses the office address the teacher gave, but must calculate which room is which: building number times a fixed amount plus room number. That calculation is like the BIU's address adder. The teacher never leaves the classroom, just like the EU never drives the bus. Splitting talk-to-outside and do-the-work into two people keeps the class moving.

Common mistakes: First, thinking the 8086 has a 16-bit address bus. Its data bus is 16 bits, but its address bus is 20 bits, giving 1 MB. Second, placing the segment registers in the EU. They are in the BIU, because they are used for address calculation. Third, saying the queue is 4 bytes for the 8086. That is the 8088; the 8086 queue is 6 bytes. Fourth, forgetting that a jump flushes the queue. Fifth, mixing up the modes: MN/MX high is minimum mode, low is maximum mode.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the internal block diagram of the 8086. Explain the functions of the BIU and EU. What is the instruction queue, and why does it speed up the processor? Why does a jump make the queue useless? Compare the 8086 and the 8088. Differentiate minimum and maximum mode. Explain what ALE does and why the bus is multiplexed. If you can draw the two boxes, list what lives in each, and explain the queue with a timeline, most of these questions are easy marks.

Recap: The 8086 is a 16-bit processor from 1978 with a 20-bit address bus, so it can address 1 MB. Inside it has a BIU that fetches instructions and data and builds addresses, and an EU that decodes and executes. The 6-byte prefetch queue lets fetching overlap with executing, but jumps flush it. Bus cycles take T1 to T4, with ALE latching the address. MN/MX chooses minimum or maximum mode. In the next lesson we look closely at the registers and the segment trick that turns 16-bit values into 20-bit addresses.
key_points: The 8086 (1978) is a 16-bit processor with a 16-bit data bus and a 20-bit address bus, so it can address 2^20 bytes = 1 MB.
The BIU fetches instructions and data, holds the segment registers and IP, and builds 20-bit addresses.
The EU decodes and executes instructions using the ALU, general registers, pointer/index registers and flags.
The 6-byte prefetch queue lets the BIU fetch ahead while the EU executes, a simple two-stage overlap.
A jump, call or return flushes the queue, so the EU must wait for new bytes.
A bus cycle has T-states T1 to T4; ALE latches the address from the multiplexed AD0-AD15 pins, and READY adds wait states.
MN/MX high gives minimum mode (8086 makes control signals); low gives maximum mode (8288 bus controller, coprocessors).
The 8088 is the same inside but has an 8-bit external data bus and a 4-byte queue; it powered the first IBM PC.
lessons.tip: Draw the 8086 block diagram from memory once a day for a week: two boxes, BIU on top with segment registers, IP, adder and queue, EU below with ALU, registers and flags. Exams love this diagram.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a timeline for the program MOV AX,5 / ADD AX,BX / JMP NEXT / MOV CX,AX. Mark what the BIU and EU do in each step and show where the queue gets flushed.

quiz.q: How much memory can the 8086 address directly?
quiz.explain: The 8086 has 20 address lines, and 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes, which is 1 MB.

quiz.q: Which unit of the 8086 contains the segment registers and the instruction queue?
quiz.explain: The BIU handles all bus activity and address calculation, so it holds CS, DS, SS, ES, IP, the address adder and the queue.

quiz.q: What happens to the prefetch queue when the 8086 executes a JMP instruction?
options: It is flushed and refilled from the new address
It is saved on the stack
Nothing, the bytes are still used
quiz.explain: The bytes in the queue came from the old straight-line path, so they are thrown away and the BIU fetches from the jump target.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between the 8086 and the 8088?
options: The 8088 has an 8-bit external data bus and a 4-byte queue
quiz.explain: Inside they are the same, but the 8088 talks to memory 8 bits at a time and has a 4-byte queue instead of 6.

quiz.q: If the MN/MX pin of the 8086 is tied low, which mode does it run in?
quiz.explain: MN/MX low selects maximum mode, where an 8288 bus controller generates control signals and coprocessors can share the bus.

lessons.title: 8086 Registers and Memory Segmentation
lessons.content:
Imagine you live in a big city like Dhaka and someone asks for your address. You would not say 'I live at house number 1,048,000 of Bangladesh'. You would say 'Road 7, house 12, Dhanmondi'. The area name gets you close, and the small house number finds the exact door. The 8086 finds bytes in memory exactly this way. It has 1 MB of memory but only 16-bit registers, and a 16-bit number can only count up to 65,535. So it uses two numbers: a segment, like the area, and an offset, like the house number. In this lesson we meet all the 8086 registers and then learn this segment trick properly.

Why registers matter: Registers are tiny storage boxes inside the processor. Working with them is much faster than going to memory, because no bus cycle is needed. The 8086 has fourteen 16-bit registers. We can sort them into four groups: four general purpose registers, four pointer and index registers, four segment registers, and two special ones, the instruction pointer and the flags register. Assembly programming is mostly the art of moving data into these boxes, working on it, and putting results back.

The general purpose registers: AX, BX, CX and DX are 16 bits each, and each one can also be used as two 8-bit halves. AX splits into AH (the high byte) and AL (the low byte). BX splits into BH and BL, CX into CH and CL, DX into DH and DL. If AX = 1234h, then AH = 12h and AL = 34h. If you then do MOV AL, 0FFh, AX becomes 12FFh, because you only changed the low half. This splitting is very handy when you work with characters, which are one byte each.

What each one is good at: Although they are called general purpose, each has a favourite job.
