AX is the accumulator: multiply and divide use it automatically, and many instructions are shorter when AX or AL is used. BX is the base register: it is the only one of the four that can hold a memory address inside brackets, as in MOV AL, [BX]. CX is the count register: the LOOP instruction and the REP prefix count down using CX, and shift instructions use CL as a count. DX is the data register: it holds the high half of the result in a 16-bit multiply or divide, and it holds the port number for IN and OUT when the port is above FFh.

The pointer and index registers: SP is the stack pointer. It always points to the top of the stack, and PUSH and POP change it automatically. BP is the base pointer. It is used to reach data inside the stack, especially function parameters, as we will see in the procedures lesson. SI is the source index and DI is the destination index. They are used to walk through arrays, and the string instructions use SI for the source and DI for the destination. These four registers cannot be split into 8-bit halves; there is no such thing as an 8-bit SIL or SIH.

The segment registers: CS is the code segment register; it tells where the program's instructions are. DS is the data segment register; it tells where the normal variables are. SS is the stack segment register; it tells where the stack is. ES is the extra segment register; it is a spare data segment, used as the destination by string instructions. Each segment register holds the starting point of a block of memory, called a segment, which can be up to 64 KB long.

The instruction pointer and flags: IP holds the offset of the next instruction to fetch inside the code segment. You cannot write MOV IP, AX; IP only changes through jumps, calls, returns and interrupts, and of course by moving forward after each instruction. The flags register holds status bits such as zero, carry and sign, plus control bits. It has a whole lesson of its own, the next one, so we just mention it here.

A tiny register tour: Look at this short piece of code. MOV AX, 1234h puts 1234h in AX, so AH = 12h and AL = 34h. MOV BL, AL copies 34h into BL. MOV BH, 0 clears BH, so BX = 0034h. ADD AX, BX gives AX = 1268h. MOV CX, 3 sets a counter for a loop that will run three times. MOV SI, 0100h points SI at offset 0100h, so MOV DL, [SI] reads the byte at DS:0100h into DL. Every register in this little program is doing the job it was designed for: AX calculates, BX helps, CX counts, SI points and DL receives a byte.

The segment problem: The address bus is 20 bits, but every register is 16 bits. How do you make a 20-bit address out of 16-bit numbers? Intel's answer: shift the segment value left by 4 bits, which is the same as multiplying by 16, and add the offset. The formula is: physical address = segment x 16 + offset. In hex, multiplying by 16 is easy: just put a 0 on the right. So segment 2000h becomes 20000h. Then add the offset.

Worked example 1: CS = 2000h and IP = 0150h. Shift the segment: 20000h. Add the offset: 20000h + 0150h = 20150h. So the next instruction is fetched from physical address 20150h. We write this pair as 2000:0150, which is called a logical address, segment first and offset second, with a colon in between.

Worked example 2: DS = 1234h and the offset is 0022h. Shift: 12340h. Add: 12340h + 0022h = 12362h. Another one: SS = 4A00h and SP = 0FFEh. Shift: 4A000h. Add: 4A000h + 0FFEh = 4AFFEh. Practice doing the addition digit by digit in hex, and remember that hex digits go 0 to 9 and then A to F, so 8 + 8 = 10h, and A + 6 = 10h.

Worked example 3, with a carry: DS = 3FF0h and the offset is 0123h. Shift: 3FF00h. Add: 3FF00h + 0123h. The last two digits: 00 + 23 = 23. The next digit: F + 1 = 10h, so write 0 and carry 1. Then F + 0 + 1 = 10h again, write 0 and carry 1. Then 3 + 1 = 4. The answer is 40023h. Careful hex addition is the most common place where students lose marks.

How big is a segment: The offset is 16 bits, so it can go from 0000h to FFFFh. That means one segment covers 65,536 bytes, which is 64 KB. If DS = 2000h, the data segment runs from 20000h to 2FFFFh. Because the segment value is multiplied by 16, a segment can only start at an address that is a multiple of 16, for example 20000h or 20010h, never 20003h. A block of 16 bytes is called a paragraph, so we say a segment starts on a paragraph boundary.

Segments can overlap: Different segment:offset pairs can point to the same byte. 1000:0020 gives 10000h + 0020h = 10020h. 1002:0000 gives 10020h + 0000h = 10020h. Same byte! Segments can also overlap each other or even be the same. In a tiny program, CS, DS, SS and ES might all hold the same value, and then code, data and stack share one 64 KB area. Or they can be spread apart so that each part has its own room.

Default segment pairs: The 8086 knows which segment to use for which job, so you usually do not have to say it. Instructions are always fetched from CS:IP. Stack operations use SS:SP. Any memory access that uses BP as a base also goes to SS by default, as in SS:BP. Normal data accesses using BX, SI, DI or a direct address go to DS. String instructions read from DS:SI and write to ES:DI. You can override the data segment with a prefix, for example MOV AX, ES:[BX], which takes the data from ES instead of DS.

Why segmentation was useful: Segments allowed a 16-bit processor to reach 1 MB. They also made it easy to keep code, data and stack separate, so a program could be loaded anywhere in memory just by changing the segment registers, without changing the offsets inside the program. This is called relocation. The downside was that big arrays over 64 KB were awkward, because one segment cannot hold them. Later chips like the 80386 solved this with 32-bit offsets.

What happens at reset: When the 8086 is reset, CS becomes FFFFh and IP becomes 0000h, while DS, SS and ES become 0000h. So the first instruction is fetched from FFFF0h, just 16 bytes before the top of memory. That is why system ROM, like the BIOS in the IBM PC, sits at the top of the 1 MB space. The instruction there is usually a jump to the real start-up code.

Loading segment registers: You cannot put a number directly into a segment register. MOV DS, 2000h is not allowed. You must go through a general register: MOV AX, 2000h then MOV DS, AX. In most programs you will see MOV AX, @DATA followed by MOV DS, AX at the start; this sets DS to the program's data segment. Also, you cannot use MOV to change CS; CS changes only with far jumps, far calls, returns and interrupts.

Real life example 1, an apartment building in Mirpur: Think of segment as the building and offset as the flat number counted from the ground floor. The building number tells where the building starts, and the flat number tells how far inside it you go. A courier from Pathao only needs the building and the flat to deliver. Two different buildings that share a wall can describe the same flat in two ways, just like 1000:0020 and 1002:0000.

Real life example 2, school roll numbers: In a big school, students are first sorted by section, and then by roll inside the section. Section A starts at seat 0, section B starts at seat 64, and so on. Seat number = section start + roll. The teacher only remembers the section start and the roll, which are small numbers, but together they give the exact seat out of hundreds. The 8086 does the same with segment and offset, using 16 as the step instead of 64.

Common mistakes: First, adding segment and offset without shifting the segment. 2000h + 0150h = 2150h is wrong; the right answer is 20150h. Second, thinking SI, DI, SP or BP have 8-bit halves. Third, trying MOV DS, 1234h directly. Fourth, forgetting that BP uses SS by default, not DS. Fifth, thinking that each physical address has only one logical address; actually many segment:offset pairs can name the same byte.

What exams ask: List the registers of the 8086 and their special uses. Explain segmentation and its advantages. Calculate the physical address for given segment and offset values. Find the range of a segment. Show two logical addresses for the same physical address. Explain default segments and segment override. Where does the 8086 start after reset? Practise five address calculations until you can do them in under a minute each.

Recap: The 8086 has general registers AX, BX, CX, DX that split into high and low bytes, pointer and index registers SP, BP, SI, DI, segment registers CS, DS, SS, ES, plus IP and the flags. A 20-bit physical address is segment x 16 + offset. Each segment is up to 64 KB and starts on a 16-byte boundary. CS:IP fetches code, SS:SP and SS:BP use the stack, DS holds data, and ES:DI is the string destination. Next, we zoom into the flags register.
key_points: AX, BX, CX and DX are 16-bit and split into 8-bit halves (AH/AL, BH/BL, CH/CL, DH/DL).
Special jobs: AX accumulator for MUL/DIV, BX base for addressing, CX counter for LOOP/REP, DX for MUL/DIV high half and I/O ports.
SP and BP work with the stack; SI and DI are index registers for arrays and string instructions; they have no 8-bit halves.
CS, DS, SS and ES mark the start of the code, data, stack and extra segments, each up to 64 KB.
Physical address = segment x 16 + offset, e.g. 2000:0150 = 20150h.
Segments start on 16-byte (paragraph) boundaries, can overlap, and one byte can have many segment:offset names.
Defaults: CS:IP for code, SS:SP and SS:BP for stack, DS for data, ES:DI for string destination; prefixes like ES: override.
After reset CS = FFFFh and IP = 0000h, so execution starts at FFFF0h.
lessons.tip: When computing a physical address, always write the shifted segment on one line and the offset right below it, lined up like school addition. Most mistakes come from rushing the hex carry.
lessons.task: Calculate the physical addresses for 3000:0456, 1A2B:0010, 0FFF:0010 and FFFF:0000 on paper. Then find two different segment:offset pairs that point to 12345h.

quiz.q: If DS = 2000h and the offset is 0150h, what is the physical address?
quiz.explain: Shift the segment left by one hex digit: 20000h, then add 0150h to get 20150h.

quiz.q: Which register is used as a counter by the LOOP instruction?
quiz.explain: LOOP decrements CX and jumps back while CX is not zero, so CX is the count register.

quiz.q: By default, which segment does an address using BP, like [BP+4], refer to?
quiz.explain: BP is meant for reaching data on the stack, so its default segment is SS.

quiz.q: What is the maximum size of one 8086 segment?
quiz.explain: The offset is 16 bits, from 0000h to FFFFh, which covers 65,536 bytes = 64 KB.

quiz.q: Which instruction sequence correctly loads 2000h into DS?
options: MOV AX, 2000h then MOV DS, AX
MOV CS, 2000h then MOV DS, CS
quiz.explain: A segment register cannot take an immediate value, so the value goes through a general register like AX first.

lessons.title: The 8086 Flags Register
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket scoreboard at Mirpur stadium. Besides the score, it has little lights: one for a wide, one for a no-ball, one that shows a review is going on. The umpire does not write a sentence each time; a light simply turns on or off, and everyone understands what just happened. The 8086 has its own scoreboard lights, called flags. After almost every calculation, some of these lights change to tell the program: the answer was zero, the answer was negative, there was a carry, the answer was too big. Programs look at these lights to make decisions. In this lesson we learn every flag and practise setting them by hand.

What the flags register is: The flags register is a 16-bit register in the Execution Unit, but only 9 of its 16 bits are used on the 8086. Six of them are status flags, which the ALU sets after arithmetic and logic operations: CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF and OF. Three are control flags, which the programmer sets to control how the processor behaves: TF, IF and DF. The other bits are unused. Each flag is a single bit, so it is either 1, which we call set, or 0, which we call cleared or reset.

Where each flag sits: From bit 0 upward: CF is bit 0, PF is bit 2, AF is bit 4, ZF is bit 6, SF is bit 7, TF is bit 8, IF is bit 9, DF is bit 10, and OF is bit 11. Bits 1, 3, 5 and 12 to 15 are not used. Exams sometimes ask you to draw this register, so it is worth learning the order. A handy way to remember the low byte is the pattern S Z _ A _ P _ C, reading from bit 7 down to bit 0.

Carry flag, CF: CF is set when an unsigned addition produces a carry out of the top bit, or when a subtraction needs a borrow into the top bit. For 8-bit work, the top bit is bit 7; for 16-bit work, it is bit 15. Example: MOV AL, 0FFh then ADD AL, 01h. FFh + 01h = 100h, which needs 9 bits. AL keeps only the low 8 bits, 00h, and the extra 1 goes into CF. So CF = 1. CF tells you that the unsigned answer did not fit.

Zero flag, ZF: ZF is set when the result is exactly zero, and cleared otherwise. In the example above, AL became 00h, so ZF = 1. Be careful: ZF = 1 means the result is zero, not that the flag is zero. This flag is used all the time with compare instructions: if two numbers are equal, their difference is zero, so ZF = 1. The instruction JZ, jump if zero, and its twin JE, jump if equal, both test ZF.

Sign flag, SF: SF is simply a copy of the top bit of the result, bit 7 for bytes or bit 15 for words. In two's complement, a top bit of 1 means a negative number, so SF = 1 means the result looks negative if you treat it as signed. Example: MOV AL, 05h then SUB AL, 07h gives AL = FEh. FEh is 11111110 in binary; the top bit is 1, so SF = 1. Read as a signed number, FEh is -2, and indeed 5 - 7 = -2.

Parity flag, PF: PF looks only at the low 8 bits of the result and counts the 1 bits. If the count is even, PF = 1; if it is odd, PF = 0. Example: the result 00h has zero 1 bits, and zero is even, so PF = 1. The result 80h is 10000000, with one 1 bit, which is odd, so PF = 0. The result FEh has seven 1 bits, odd, so PF = 0. Parity was useful for simple error checking in old communication links.

Auxiliary carry flag, AF: AF is set when there is a carry from bit 3 into bit 4, which means a carry from the low nibble to the high nibble, or a borrow into the low nibble in subtraction. Example: 0Fh + 01h: the low nibble F plus 1 makes 10h, so a carry leaves the low nibble and AF = 1. Programmers rarely test AF directly. It exists for BCD arithmetic, where each nibble holds one decimal digit, and instructions such as DAA use it to fix the answer.

Overflow flag, OF: OF is set when a signed result is too big or too small to fit. For 8 bits, signed numbers go from -128 to +127; for 16 bits, from -32,768 to +32,767. A simple rule: if you add two numbers with the same sign and the result has the opposite sign, OF = 1. If you add two numbers with different signs, overflow can never happen. Example: MOV AL, 7Fh then ADD AL, 01h. 127 + 1 = 128, which does not fit in a signed byte. AL becomes 80h, which as signed is -128. Positive plus positive gave negative, so OF = 1.

Worked example A, full flags: MOV AL, 7Fh then ADD AL, 01h. Result AL = 80h. CF: 7Fh + 01h = 80h, no carry out of bit 7, so CF = 0. ZF: result not zero, ZF = 0. SF: top bit of 80h is 1, SF = 1. PF: 80h has one 1 bit, odd, PF = 0. AF: low nibble F + 1 carries into bit 4, AF = 1. OF: positive + positive gave negative, OF = 1. Notice that CF = 0 but OF = 1: as unsigned, 127 + 1 = 128 is fine; as signed, it overflowed.

Worked example B, the opposite case: MOV AL, 0FFh then ADD AL, 01h. Result AL = 00h. CF = 1 because there is a carry out. ZF = 1 because the result is zero. SF = 0. PF = 1 because 00h has zero 1 bits. AF = 1 because F + 1 carries from the low nibble. OF = 0, because as signed this is -1 + 1 = 0, which fits perfectly. Here CF = 1 but OF = 0. Comparing examples A and B is the best way to understand that CF is for unsigned and OF is for signed.

Worked example C, both set: MOV AL, 9Ah then ADD AL, 0B4h. As unsigned, 154 + 180 = 334, more than 255. As signed, 9Ah is -102 and B4h is -76, and -102 + -76 = -178, less than -128. In binary, 9Ah + B4h = 14Eh, so AL = 4Eh and CF = 1. The two inputs were negative and the result 4Eh has top bit 0, which looks positive, so OF = 1. SF = 0, ZF = 0. 4Eh is 01001110, four 1 bits, so PF = 1. The low nibbles A + 4 = E, no carry, so AF = 0.

Worked example D, a 16-bit case: MOV AX, 7000h then ADD AX, 2000h. Result AX = 9000h. There is no carry out of bit 15, so CF = 0. The two inputs were positive and the result's top bit is 1, so SF = 1 and OF = 1. ZF = 0. PF looks only at the low byte 00h, so PF = 1. AF = 0. This shows that for word operations, CF, SF and OF use bit 15, but PF still checks only the low 8 bits.

How CMP uses the flags: CMP subtracts the second operand from the first, sets the flags, and throws the answer away. Both operands stay unchanged. Example: AL = 05h, CMP AL, 05h gives 0, so ZF = 1, CF = 0. CMP AL, 09h gives 5 - 9, which needs a borrow: CF = 1, ZF = 0, and the 8-bit result FCh makes SF = 1. For unsigned numbers, CF = 1 after CMP means the first was smaller. For signed numbers, the first is smaller when SF and OF are different. Conditional jumps such as JB and JL are built exactly on these rules, as you will see in the branching lesson.

Who changes which flags: Not every instruction touches every flag. ADD, SUB, CMP and NEG update all six status flags. INC and DEC update all of them except CF; this is on purpose, so a loop counter can be changed without disturbing a carry you are saving. AND, OR, XOR and TEST always clear CF and OF and set ZF, SF and PF from the result. MOV, PUSH, POP and jumps do not change any flags at all. MUL sets CF and OF when the upper half of the product is not zero.

The control flags: DF, the direction flag, decides which way string instructions walk through memory. If DF = 0, SI and DI go up after each step; if DF = 1, they go down. CLD clears DF and STD sets it. IF, the interrupt flag, decides whether the processor answers maskable interrupts on the INTR pin. STI sets IF, enabling them, and CLI clears IF, disabling them; the NMI pin cannot be blocked by IF. TF, the trap flag, puts the processor in single-step mode: after every instruction it raises a type 1 interrupt, which is how debuggers step through code.

Changing flags directly: CF has three instructions of its own: STC sets it, CLC clears it, and CMC complements it, meaning it flips it. There is no instruction to set TF directly. Instead you copy the whole flags register to the stack with PUSHF, change it, and load it back with POPF: PUSHF, POP AX, OR AX, 0100h, PUSH AX, POPF. The value 0100h has only bit 8 set, which is TF. LAHF copies the low byte of the flags into AH, and SAHF copies AH back.

Real life example 1, a bKash balance check: Suppose an app stores a balance as an unsigned 16-bit number in taka and you try to subtract a payment bigger than the balance. The subtraction needs a borrow, so CF = 1. A program can test CF right after SUB and show 'insufficient balance' instead of a strange huge number. Without CF, the program would see something like 65,000 taka and happily approve the payment.

Real life example 2, a thermometer in a cold storage: A cold storage in Munshiganj keeps potatoes and stores temperatures as signed bytes, from -128 to +127 degrees. If a faulty sensor adds 100 to a reading of 50, the answer 150 cannot fit, and the stored byte would look like -106. OF = 1 tells the software that the signed result overflowed, so it can raise an alarm instead of believing the storage is suddenly freezing.

Common mistakes: First, mixing up CF and OF. CF is about unsigned results, OF about signed results. Second, thinking ZF = 0 means zero; it is the opposite. Third, checking parity on all 16 bits; PF looks only at the low byte. Fourth, expecting INC to change CF. Fifth, forgetting that MOV never changes flags, so a MOV between a CMP and a jump is safe.

What exams ask: Draw the 8086 flags register and explain each flag. Find the status of all flags after a given addition or subtraction, for example ADD AL, BL with AL = 7Fh and BL = 01h. Explain the difference between carry and overflow with examples. Which instructions control DF, IF and TF? How do you set TF when there is no direct instruction for it? Practise filling a table with six columns, one per status flag, for five different additions.

Recap: The 8086 flags register uses 9 bits. Six status flags, CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF and OF, describe the last result: carry, even parity, nibble carry, zero, sign bit and signed overflow. Three control flags, DF, IF and TF, steer string direction, interrupts and single-stepping. CMP sets flags without keeping the result, and jumps read those flags. Next we learn the many ways an instruction can find its operands: the addressing modes.
key_points: The 8086 flags register is 16 bits wide but uses 9 bits: 6 status flags and 3 control flags.
Bit positions: CF 0, PF 2, AF 4, ZF 6, SF 7, TF 8, IF 9, DF 10, OF 11.
CF signals unsigned carry or borrow; OF signals signed overflow; they are independent of each other.
ZF = 1 when the result is zero; SF copies the top bit; PF = 1 when the low byte has an even number of 1s; AF marks a carry from bit 3 to bit 4.
Adding two same-sign numbers that gives the opposite sign sets OF; different signs can never overflow.
CMP subtracts and sets flags without storing the result; INC/DEC leave CF unchanged; logic instructions clear CF and OF; MOV changes no flags.
DF (CLD/STD) controls string direction, IF (STI/CLI) enables INTR interrupts, TF enables single-step mode.
lessons.tip: Always solve flag questions with a fixed checklist in the same order: write the binary sum, then CF, ZF, SF, PF, AF, OF. Doing it in order stops you from forgetting a flag.
lessons.task: On paper, find all six status flags after: ADD AL,BL with AL=7Fh, BL=01h; with AL=0FFh, BL=01h; with AL=80h, BL=80h; and SUB AL,BL with AL=05h, BL=07h. Check that CF and OF behave differently.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 0FFh and ADD AL, 01h, which flags are set?
quiz.explain: FFh + 01h = 100h, so AL = 00h with a carry out: CF = 1 and ZF = 1. As signed, -1 + 1 = 0 fits, so OF = 0.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 7Fh and ADD AL, 01h, what are CF and OF?
quiz.explain: 7Fh + 01h = 80h with no carry out of bit 7, but 127 + 1 does not fit in a signed byte, so OF = 1.

quiz.q: When is the parity flag PF set?
options: When the whole 16-bit result is even
When there is a carry from bit 3
When the low byte of the result has an even number of 1 bits
quiz.explain: PF counts the 1 bits only in the low 8 bits of the result and is set if that count is even.

quiz.q: Which flag is NOT changed by INC and DEC?
quiz.explain: INC and DEC update all status flags except CF, so a saved carry survives a counter update.

quiz.q: Which instruction makes string instructions move SI and DI upward through memory?
quiz.explain: CLD clears the direction flag; with DF = 0, SI and DI increase after each string step.

lessons.title: 8086 Addressing Modes
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother sends you to get sugar. She can do it in many ways. She can hand you the sugar packet directly. She can say 'it is in the blue jar on the shelf'. She can say 'look in the drawer, there is a note telling you which jar'. Or she can say 'it is the third jar from the left on the second shelf'. In every case you end up with sugar, but the way of finding it is different. An instruction needs data too, and the 8086 gives it many ways to find that data. These ways are called addressing modes. In this lesson we learn all of them and calculate the exact memory address each one reaches.

What an operand is: Most instructions work on operands. In MOV AX, BX, the destination operand is AX and the source operand is BX. An operand can be a number written inside the instruction, a register, or a location in memory. The addressing mode describes where the operand lives and how the processor finds it. Data-related modes are the main ones, but there are also modes for program jumps, for strings and for I/O ports.

Immediate addressing: The data is part of the instruction itself. MOV AX, 1234h puts the number 1234h into AX. MOV CL, 5 puts 5 into CL. No memory lookup is needed for the data, because the bytes of the number come along with the instruction, like your mother handing you the packet. An immediate value can only be a source, never a destination; MOV 5, AX makes no sense. Also, you cannot move an immediate value straight into a segment register.

Register addressing: The data is in a register. MOV AX, BX copies BX into AX. ADD AL, CL adds CL to AL. This is the fastest mode, because everything stays inside the processor. Both operands must be the same size: MOV AX, BL is an error, because AX is 16 bits and BL is 8 bits.

Direct addressing: The instruction contains the offset of the data in memory. MOV AX, [1234h] reads the word at offset 1234h in the data segment. If DS = 2000h, the physical address is 20000h + 1234h = 21234h. Since a word is two bytes, AL gets the byte at 21234h and AH gets the byte at 21235h. In real programs you usually write a variable name instead of a number, as in MOV AX, TOTAL, and the assembler puts the variable's offset into the instruction.

The effective address: From now on, memory modes calculate an offset from registers and numbers. This offset is called the effective address, or EA. The general formula is EA = base + index + displacement, where the base is BX or BP, the index is SI or DI, and the displacement is a constant written in the instruction, 8 or 16 bits. Any of these three parts can be missing, but at least one must be there. The physical address is then segment x 16 + EA, using DS by default, or SS when BP is the base.

Register indirect addressing: The offset is in a register. MOV AL, [BX] reads the byte whose offset is in BX. The allowed registers are BX, SI and DI, which use DS, and BP, which uses SS. Example: DS = 3000h and BX = 0050h. MOV AL, [BX] reads from 30000h + 0050h = 30050h. This is like your mother's note in the drawer: the register does not hold the sugar, it holds the location of the sugar. You cannot write [AX], [CX] or [DX]; those registers are not allowed inside brackets on the 8086.

Based addressing: The offset is a base register plus a displacement. MOV AX, [BX+4] or MOV AX, [BP+4]. Example: DS = 2000h, BX = 0100h. MOV AL, [BX+05h] gives EA = 0100h + 05h = 0105h, so the physical address is 20105h. With BP the segment is SS: if SS = 4000h and BP = 0200h, MOV AX, [BP+04h] gives EA = 0204h and the physical address 40204h. Based mode is great for records: BX points to the start of a student record, and the displacement picks a field, such as +4 for marks.

Indexed addressing: The offset is an index register plus a displacement. MOV AL, [SI+10h] or MOV AL, ARRAY[SI], which means the same thing as [ARRAY+SI]. Here the displacement is usually the start of an array and SI is the position inside it. Example: DS = 1000h, ARRAY starts at offset 0200h and SI = 0003h. MOV AL, ARRAY[SI] gives EA = 0200h + 0003h = 0203h, physical address 10203h, which is element number 3 of a byte array, counting from 0. Increase SI by 1 to move to the next byte, or by 2 for a word array.

Based indexed addressing: The offset is a base register plus an index register, with or without a displacement. The allowed pairs are [BX+SI], [BX+DI], [BP+SI] and [BP+DI]. Example: DS = 2000h, BX = 0100h, SI = 0020h. MOV AL, [BX+SI] gives EA = 0120h, physical address 20120h. With a displacement: MOV AL, [BX+SI+05h] gives EA = 0125h and physical address 20125h. This mode suits two-dimensional tables: BX picks the row and SI picks the column.

What is not allowed: You cannot use two base registers together, so [BX+BP] is illegal. You cannot use two index registers together, so [SI+DI] is illegal. You cannot use AX, CX, DX or SP inside brackets on the 8086. And no 8086 instruction like MOV can move data from one memory location directly to another: MOV [BX], [SI] is illegal. You must go through a register, as in MOV AL, [SI] then MOV [BX], AL. String instructions, which you will meet later, are the special exception.

A quick way to check legality: Any memory operand on the 8086 is built from at most one item from each of three boxes. Box one is a base: BX or BP, or nothing. Box two is an index: SI or DI, or nothing. Box three is a displacement: an 8-bit or 16-bit number, or nothing. Pick at most one from each box, and at least one item overall. If the form you see can be built like this, it is legal; if it needs two items from the same box, or a register that is not in any box, it is illegal. One small detail: [BP] alone is written by the assembler as [BP+0], with a zero displacement, but you can still write it as [BP] in your program.

Putting modes to work, summing an array: Suppose LIST has five bytes and we want their total in AL. MOV CX, 5 sets the count. MOV SI, 0 starts at the first element. MOV AL, 0 clears the total. Then a loop: NEXT: ADD AL, LIST[SI] adds the current element using indexed mode, INC SI moves to the next byte, and LOOP NEXT repeats until CX reaches zero. In this tiny program you can see three modes at once: immediate in MOV CX, 5, register in INC SI, and indexed in ADD AL, LIST[SI]. Real programs mix modes like this all the time, picking whichever one makes the data easiest to reach.

Segment override: Each memory mode has a default segment, but you can choose another by writing a prefix. MOV AX, ES:[BX] reads from ES x 16 + BX instead of DS x 16 + BX. MOV AL, CS:[SI] reads data stored inside the code segment, which is sometimes done for lookup tables. The override costs one extra byte in the machine code. The only things you cannot override are instruction fetches, which always use CS, and the destination of string instructions, which always uses ES.

Byte or word: Sometimes the assembler cannot tell the size. In MOV [BX], 5, is 5 a byte or a word? There is no register to give a hint. You must say it: MOV BYTE PTR [BX], 5 stores one byte, while MOV WORD PTR [BX], 5 stores two bytes, 05h at [BX] and 00h at [BX+1]. When a register is involved, like MOV [BX], AL, the size comes from the register and no PTR is needed.

Other kinds of addressing: String addressing is used by instructions such as MOVSB: the source is always DS:SI and the destination is always ES:DI, with no operands written. I/O port addressing comes in two forms: direct, as in IN AL, 60h, where the port number 00h to FFh is in the instruction, and indirect, as in IN AL, DX, where DX holds a port number up to FFFFh. Relative addressing is used by jumps: JMP and conditional jumps often store a displacement that is added to IP, so the code still works if it is moved. Implied addressing means the operand is understood: CLC needs no operand because it always works on CF.

A worked practice set: Let DS = 1000h, SS = 2000h, BX = 0300h, BP = 0400h, SI = 0010h, DI = 0020h. Then [BX] is 10300h. [BP] is 20400h, because BP uses SS. [BX+SI] is 10310h. [BP+DI+6] has EA 0426h, physical 20426h. [SI+100h] is EA 0110h, physical 10110h. ES:[DI] needs the value of ES, say 3000h, giving 30020h. Make your own table like this and fill it in before exams.

Real life example 1, a Daraz warehouse: Picture a warehouse in Dhaka where each shelf row starts at some point and boxes are numbered along it. To find an order, a worker uses the row start, like BX, plus the box number inside the row, like SI, plus a fixed offset for the item inside the box, like a displacement. Based indexed addressing with displacement is exactly this three-part search. A computer program for the warehouse could keep row starts in BX and walk boxes with SI.

Real life example 2, a class marks register: Your class teacher keeps marks in a table, one row per student, five subjects per row, one byte each. To get student 3's subject 2, you compute row start 3 x 5 = 15 and add 2, giving position 17. In assembly, BX could hold 15, SI could hold 2, and MOV AL, MARKS[BX+SI] would fetch the right byte. Change SI to walk across subjects, or add 5 to BX to jump to the next student.

Common mistakes: First, using DS with BP; BP defaults to SS. Second, writing [AX] or [CX]. Third, writing [BX+BP] or [SI+DI]. Fourth, trying memory to memory MOV. Fifth, forgetting BYTE PTR or WORD PTR when no register gives the size. Sixth, mixing up the effective address and the physical address: EA is the 16-bit offset, the physical address is the 20-bit result after adding segment x 16.

What exams ask: Name and explain the addressing modes of the 8086 with one example each. Identify the addressing mode of a given instruction, such as MOV AX, [BX+SI+8]. Given register values, calculate the effective and physical addresses. Which of these instructions are invalid and why? Explain segment override. A neat answer shows the mode name, the formula EA = base + index + displacement, and the final physical address in hex.

Recap: Immediate puts the data in the instruction, register uses a register, and direct gives a fixed offset. Register indirect, based, indexed and based indexed build an effective address from BX or BP, SI or DI, and a displacement. BP uses SS, the others use DS, and prefixes can override. There are also string, I/O port, relative and implied modes. Next lesson, we see how these modes are actually packed into the bytes of machine code.
key_points: Immediate: data inside the instruction (MOV AX, 1234h); register: data in a register (MOV AX, BX); direct: fixed offset (MOV AX, [1234h]).
Effective address EA = base (BX or BP) + index (SI or DI) + displacement; physical address = segment x 16 + EA.
Register indirect [BX], [SI], [DI] use DS; [BP] and any BP-based form use SS by default.
Based [BX+d], indexed [SI+d] or ARRAY[SI], and based indexed [BX+SI+d] suit records, arrays and tables.
Illegal on the 8086: [AX], [CX], [DX], [BX+BP], [SI+DI], and memory-to-memory MOV.
Segment override prefixes like ES:[BX] change the data segment; BYTE PTR / WORD PTR fix ambiguous sizes.
Other modes: string (DS:SI to ES:DI), I/O port (direct port 00h-FFh or indirect via DX), relative (jumps) and implied (CLC).
lessons.tip: For every addressing mode question, write three lines: the mode name, EA = ... with numbers filled in, and PA = segment x 16 + EA. Examiners give marks for each line.
lessons.task: Let DS = 1000h, SS = 2000h, BX = 0300h, BP = 0400h, SI = 0010h, DI = 0020h. On paper find the mode, EA and physical address of: MOV AL,[BX]; MOV AL,[BP+2]; MOV AX,[BX+DI+10h]; MOV AL,[SI+5]. Then mark which of MOV AX,[CX] and MOV [SI],[DI] are illegal.

quiz.q: What is the addressing mode of MOV AX, [BX+SI+08h]?
quiz.explain: It uses a base register BX, an index register SI and a displacement 08h together.

quiz.q: If DS = 2000h, BX = 0100h and SI = 0020h, what physical address does MOV AL, [BX+SI+05h] read?
Which segment does MOV AX, [BP+4] use by default?
quiz.explain: Any address that uses BP as its base defaults to the stack segment SS.

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid 8086 instruction?
quiz.explain: [BX+DI] is an allowed base-index pair. CX cannot be used inside brackets, SI+DI uses two index registers, and memory-to-memory MOV is not allowed.

quiz.q: Why is MOV [BX], 5 a problem for the assembler?
options: BX cannot be used in brackets
The size is unknown, so BYTE PTR or WORD PTR is needed
quiz.explain: With no register involved, the assembler cannot tell whether to store one byte or two, so you must write BYTE PTR or WORD PTR.

lessons.title: Instruction Format and Machine Code
lessons.content:
Imagine you are sending a message to a friend by SMS, and every character costs money. You would invent short codes: 'gm' for good morning, 'ok' for okay. Both of you know the code book, so a few letters carry a whole idea. The 8086 does the same thing. It does not understand words like MOV or ADD. It only understands bytes, and a clever code book tells it which bytes mean which instruction, which registers and which memory address. Turning assembly into these bytes is called encoding, and the bytes are called machine code. In this lesson we open the code book and encode some instructions by hand.

Why learn this at all: The assembler does the encoding for you, so why bother? First, exams ask for it. Second, when you look at memory in a debugger like the one in emu8086, you see bytes, and you need to read them back as instructions. Third, it shows why some instructions are shorter or faster than others, and why some forms are illegal: if the code book has no slot for [SI+DI], the processor simply cannot do it. Knowing the format turns a mysterious rule into something obvious.

The general shape: An 8086 instruction is between 1 and 6 bytes long, not counting prefixes. For the common register and memory instructions, the bytes come in this order: an opcode byte, then a byte called MOD REG R/M, then 0, 1 or 2 displacement bytes, then 0, 1 or 2 immediate data bytes. Before all of this there can be prefix bytes, such as a segment override. Not every instruction uses every part; some are a single byte.

The opcode byte: For many instructions, the first byte has six bits of opcode followed by two special bits called D and W. The opcode says what to do, for example the pattern 100010 means MOV between a register and a register or memory. W is the width bit: W = 0 means byte operands, W = 1 means word operands. D is the direction bit: D = 1 means the register named in the REG field is the destination, D = 0 means it is the source. So for MOV, 100010 followed by d and w gives the four opcodes 88h, 89h, 8Ah and 8Bh.

The MOD REG R/M byte: The second byte is split into three fields: MOD is 2 bits, REG is 3 bits, and R/M is 3 bits, written as MOD REG R/M from left to right. REG always names a register. MOD and R/M together name the other operand, which may be a register or a memory location. Think of REG as one hand of the instruction and R/M as the other hand, while MOD tells what kind of thing the second hand is holding.

The register codes: REG uses these 3-bit codes. When W = 1, for words: AX 000, CX 001, DX 010, BX 011, SP 100, BP 101, SI 110, DI 111. When W = 0, for bytes: AL 000, CL 001, DL 010, BL 011, AH 100, CH 101, DH 110, BH 111. Notice the odd order: A, C, D, B, not A, B, C, D. A trick to remember it: 'All Cats Drink Badly', then for words 'SP BP SI DI', and for bytes the high halves AH CH DH BH in the same A C D B order.

The MOD field: MOD = 11 means R/M is a register, using the same register codes as REG. MOD = 00 means R/M is memory with no displacement. MOD = 01 means memory with an 8-bit displacement, which the processor sign-extends to 16 bits. MOD = 10 means memory with a 16-bit displacement. There is one special case: MOD = 00 with R/M = 110 does not mean [BP]; it means direct addressing, followed by a 16-bit address.

The R/M codes for memory: When MOD is not 11, R/M chooses the addressing form: 000 is [BX+SI], 001 is [BX+DI], 010 is [BP+SI], 011 is [BP+DI], 100 is [SI], 101 is [DI], 110 is [BP], and 111 is [BX]. Now you can see why [SI+DI] or [BX+BP] are illegal: there is no code for them. There are only eight slots, and Intel picked these eight combinations. Because MOD = 00 with R/M = 110 was taken for direct addressing, plain [BP] has to be written as [BP+0] with an 8-bit displacement of zero.

Example 1, MOV AX, BX: Both operands are 16-bit registers, so W = 1 and MOD = 11. Choose D = 0, so REG is the source BX = 011 and R/M is the destination AX = 000. The opcode byte is 100010 0 1 = 89h. The second byte is 11 011 000 = D8h. So MOV AX, BX is 89 D8. We could also choose D = 1: then REG is the destination AX = 000 and R/M is BX = 011, giving 8B and 11 000 011 = C3h, so 8B C3. Both are correct machine code for the same instruction; different assemblers may pick different ones.

Example 2, MOV CL, [BX]: The destination is the byte register CL, so W = 0 and we use D = 1 to make CL the REG field. Opcode: 100010 1 0 = 8Ah. REG = CL = 001. The memory operand [BX] has no displacement, so MOD = 00 and R/M = 111. Second byte: 00 001 111 = 0Fh. The instruction is 8A 0F, two bytes.

Example 3, MOV [SI+05h], AX: The source is AX, so D = 0, W = 1, opcode 89h. REG = AX = 000. The memory operand [SI+05h] has an 8-bit displacement, so MOD = 01 and R/M = 100 for [SI]. Second byte: 01 000 100 = 44h. Then the displacement byte 05h. Result: 89 44 05, three bytes.

Example 4, MOV DX, [BX+SI+1234h]: Destination DX, so D = 1, W = 1, opcode 8Bh. REG = DX = 010. 1234h needs 16 bits, so MOD = 10, and [BX+SI] is R/M = 000. Second byte: 10 010 000 = 90h. The displacement is stored little-endian, low byte first: 34h then 12h. Result: 8B 90 34 12, four bytes. Little-endian order trips up many students, so always write the low byte first.

Example 5, MOV [BP], AL: Source AL, D = 0, W = 0, opcode 88h. REG = AL = 000. Since [BP] with MOD = 00 is not available, the assembler uses MOD = 01 and R/M = 110 with a displacement of 00h. Second byte: 01 000 110 = 46h. Result: 88 46 00. This shows that the special case costs one extra byte.

Short forms: Some very common instructions have shorter special encodings. MOV register, immediate uses the pattern 1011 w reg, followed by the data. MOV AL, 05h is 1011 0 000 = B0h then 05h, so B0 05. MOV AX, 1234h is 1011 1 000 = B8h then 34 12, so B8 34 12. MOV BX, 1234h is BB 34 12, and MOV CL, 7 is B1 07. There is also a short form for loading the accumulator from a direct address: MOV AX, [1234h] is usually A1 34 12, three bytes, instead of the general 8B 06 34 12, four bytes.

One-byte instructions: Some instructions are just one byte, often with the register built into it. INC AX is 40h and INC BX is 43h, because INC word register uses the pattern 01000 reg. PUSH AX is 50h. NOP is 90h, which is really XCHG AX, AX. HLT is F4h, RET is C3h, CLC is F8h and STC is F9h. INT 21h is two bytes: CD 21. These numbers are worth knowing because you will see them often in a debugger.

Other instructions follow the same pattern: ADD uses the opcode bits 000000dw, so ADD AX, BX is 01 D8, with exactly the same second byte as MOV AX, BX. SUB uses 001010dw, so SUB CX, DX is 29 D1: MOD 11, REG DX = 010, R/M CX = 001, giving 11 010 001 = D1h. Once you know the MOD REG R/M byte, you can encode dozens of instructions just by swapping the opcode.

Prefixes: A segment override is a one-byte prefix placed before the instruction: 26h for ES, 2Eh for CS, 36h for SS and 3Eh for DS. So MOV AL, ES:[BX] is 26 8A 07. Other prefixes you will meet later include REP (F3h) for string instructions and LOCK (F0h). The 8086 reads the prefix, remembers it, and applies it to the next instruction.

Decoding, going backwards: Let us decode 8B 4F 02. 8Bh = 100010 1 1, so it is MOV with D = 1 and W = 1: a word, and REG is the destination. 4Fh = 01 001 111: MOD = 01 means memory with an 8-bit displacement, REG = 001 = CX, R/M = 111 = [BX]. The next byte, 02h, is the displacement. So the instruction is MOV CX, [BX+02h]. Decoding is just the same steps in reverse.

Real life example 1, a bus ticket code: On a long-distance bus from Dhaka to Chattogram, the ticket might print a code like 'AC-B-07': AC class, coach B, seat 07. Each part is in a fixed position with a fixed meaning, so the conductor reads it instantly. The MOD REG R/M byte is the same: fixed fields, fixed meanings, and you read them left to right.

Real life example 2, a phone keypad shortcut: When you dial *247# for bKash, the operator's system reads the digits in order and each part tells it what service to open. A wrong digit means a different service or an error. In machine code, one wrong bit in the MOD REG R/M byte can turn MOV AX, BX into MOV AX, CX, so programmers who patch bytes by hand must be very careful.

Common mistakes: First, using the order A B C D for register codes instead of AX 000, CX 001, DX 010, BX 011. Second, writing the displacement high byte first; the 8086 is little-endian. Third, forgetting that MOD = 00, R/M = 110 is direct addressing, not [BP]. Fourth, mixing up D: D = 1 means REG is the destination. Fifth, thinking there is only one correct encoding; MOV AX, BX can be 89 D8 or 8B C3.

What exams ask: Draw the general 8086 instruction format and explain the D, W, MOD, REG and R/M fields. Encode instructions such as MOV CL, [BX], MOV AX, BX or MOV [SI+05h], AX. Decode a given byte sequence into assembly. Why is [SI+DI] not allowed? What is the maximum length of an 8086 instruction? Show each field in binary, then convert to hex, so the examiner can follow your work.

Recap: Most 8086 instructions are an opcode byte with D and W bits, a MOD REG R/M byte, optional displacement and optional immediate data, from 1 to 6 bytes plus prefixes. REG and R/M use the codes AX CX DX BX SP BP SI DI, or AL CL DL BL AH CH DH BH. MOD picks register, memory without displacement, or memory with an 8 or 16-bit displacement. Multi-byte numbers are stored low byte first. Next lesson, we let the assembler do this work and write our first full program.
key_points: An 8086 instruction is 1 to 6 bytes (plus prefixes): opcode, MOD REG R/M, displacement, immediate data.
In the opcode byte, W = 1 means word and W = 0 means byte; D = 1 means REG is the destination.
Register codes: AX/AL 000, CX/CL 001, DX/DL 010, BX/BL 011, SP/AH 100, BP/CH 101, SI/DH 110, DI/BH 111.
MOD 11 = register, 00 = memory without displacement, 01 = 8-bit displacement, 10 = 16-bit displacement; MOD 00 with R/M 110 = direct address.
R/M memory codes: 000 [BX+SI], 001 [BX+DI], 010 [BP+SI], 011 [BP+DI], 100 [SI], 101 [DI], 110 [BP], 111 [BX].
Worked encodings: MOV AX,BX = 89 D8 (or 8B C3), MOV CL,[BX] = 8A 0F, MOV [SI+05h],AX = 89 44 05, MOV AX,1234h = B8 34 12.
Displacements and immediates are little-endian; segment override prefixes are 26h ES, 2Eh CS, 36h SS, 3Eh DS.
lessons.tip: Make a small card with the two code tables, register codes and R/M codes, and keep it beside you while practising. After about twenty encodings you will not need the card any more.
lessons.task: Encode by hand: MOV BX, CX; MOV AL, [SI]; ADD AX, [BX+DI+10h]; MOV DL, 41h. Then decode 8A 47 03 and 89 C1 back into assembly. Write every field in binary first.

quiz.q: In the 8086 opcode byte, what does W = 1 mean?
options: The REG field is the destination
quiz.explain: W is the width bit: W = 0 for byte operations and W = 1 for word operations.

quiz.q: What is the machine code for MOV CL, [BX]?
quiz.explain: Opcode 100010 D=1 W=0 = 8Ah; MOD 00, REG CL 001, R/M [BX] 111 gives 00001111 = 0Fh.

quiz.q: Which register has the 3-bit code 011 when W = 1?
quiz.explain: The word register order is AX 000, CX 001, DX 010, BX 011, so 011 is BX.

quiz.q: How is the 16-bit displacement 1234h stored in an instruction?
quiz.explain: The 8086 is little-endian, so the low byte 34h comes first, then the high byte 12h.

quiz.q: Decode the bytes 8B 4F 02.
quiz.explain: 8Bh is MOV with D=1, W=1; 4Fh = 01 001 111 means MOD 01 (8-bit displacement), REG CX, R/M [BX]; the displacement is 02h.

lessons.title: The Assembler and Program Structure
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to send a letter to a pen friend in Japan who only reads Japanese. You write in Bangla or English, and a translator turns your words into Japanese. The processor is that pen friend. It only understands machine code, long rows of bytes like B8 34 12. In lesson 10 we encoded a few instructions by hand, and you probably noticed how slow and easy to get wrong that is. So people built a translator program called an assembler. You write MOV AX, 1234h, which a human can read, and the assembler writes the bytes B8 34 12 for you. This lesson is about that translator, the other tools around it, and the shape of a complete assembly program.

What assembly language is: Assembly language is a human readable form of machine code. Almost every line of it becomes one machine instruction. The instruction names are short memory helpers called mnemonics, like MOV for move, ADD for add and JMP for jump. Instead of remembering memory addresses, you give places names, called labels or symbols, and the assembler works out the numbers. Assembly is tied to one processor family. 8086 assembly will not run on an ARM chip in your phone, because ARM has different instructions. Compare this with C, where one line such as total = a + b * c may turn into four or five machine instructions, and the same C code can be compiled for many different processors.

From source file to running program: Writing a program goes through four steps. First, you type the program in a text editor and save it with a name like HELLO.ASM. This is the source file. Second, the assembler reads HELLO.ASM and produces an object file, HELLO.OBJ, which contains machine code but is not yet ready to run, because some addresses may still be unfinished. Third, the linker takes one or more object files, plus any library code, joins them, fixes the remaining addresses and writes an executable file, HELLO.EXE. Fourth, when you type HELLO at the DOS prompt, the loader, which is part of the operating system, copies the program into memory, sets up registers such as CS, IP, SS and SP, and lets the processor start running it. A debugger lets you run it one instruction at a time.

Why assemblers make two passes: Look at this small piece of code. JMP DONE comes first, then some lines, then the label DONE: at the bottom. When the assembler reaches JMP DONE, it does not yet know where DONE is. This is called a forward reference. The usual solution is a two pass assembler. In pass one, it reads the whole file and only counts bytes, using a counter called the location counter. Every time it sees a label, it writes the label and its current address into a symbol table. In pass two, it reads the file again and now generates the real machine code, looking up every label in the symbol table. So by the time it needs the address of DONE, it already knows it.

Popular tools: MASM, the Microsoft Macro Assembler, and TASM, the Turbo Assembler from Borland, were the classic assemblers for DOS, and most textbooks use their syntax. NASM, the Netwide Assembler, is free and still widely used on Linux and Windows, but its syntax is a little different; for example it has no ASSUME directive and memory operands always need square brackets. In many university labs in Bangladesh, students use emu8086, an emulator that accepts MASM style code and shows every register, flag and memory byte while you step through the program. To run old DOS tools like MASM, TASM and DEBUG on a modern laptop, people often use DOSBox, a free DOS emulator.

The four fields of a line: Every line of an assembly program can have up to four parts, written in this order: label, mnemonic, operands, comment. For example: AGAIN: ADD AL, BL ; add BL into AL. Here AGAIN is the label, ADD is the mnemonic, AL, BL are the operands, and everything after the semicolon is a comment. The assembler throws comments away, but they are the most important part for humans. Labels on code lines end with a colon. MASM does not care about upper or lower case by default, so mov ax, bx and MOV AX, BX mean the same thing.

Instructions versus directives: An instruction is something the processor will do at run time, like MOV, ADD or INT. The assembler turns it into machine code bytes. A directive, also called a pseudo-op, is an order for the assembler itself. It tells the assembler how to organise the program, where segments start, how much memory to reserve or what a name means. Directives do not become processor instructions. Lines such as .MODEL, .DATA, DB, EQU and END are all directives.

Memory models: Because 8086 segments are at most 64 KB each, the assembler needs to know how many code and data segments the program will use. The .MODEL directive says this. TINY puts code and data together in one 64 KB segment, and it is used for .COM programs. SMALL gives one code segment and one data segment, each up to 64 KB. MEDIUM allows many code segments but one data segment. COMPACT allows one code segment but many data segments. LARGE allows many of both. HUGE is like LARGE but lets a single array be bigger than 64 KB. Almost every lab program uses .MODEL SMALL, because 64 KB of code is a lot of assembly.

The segment directives: After the model, three simplified directives mark the parts of the program. .STACK 100h reserves 100h bytes, which is 256 bytes, for the stack. .DATA starts the data segment, where you declare your variables. .CODE starts the code segment, where your instructions go.

Defining data with DB, DW and DD: DB means define byte and reserves one byte per value. DW means define word, two bytes per value. DD means define doubleword, four bytes per value. For example, AGE DB 12 makes one byte holding 12. MARKS DB 80, 75, 92 makes three bytes in a row. YEAR DW 2024 makes a two byte word. Remember from lesson 2 that the 8086 is little-endian, so VAL DW 1234h is stored in memory as 34h first, then 12h. A string is just a row of bytes: MSG DB 'Shubho Shokal$' stores the ASCII code of every character. If you do not care about the starting value, write a question mark, as in X DB ?, which reserves a byte without choosing its content.

The DUP operator: To reserve many copies of the same value, use DUP, short for duplicate. ARR DB 10 DUP(0) reserves ten bytes, all zero. BUF DW 5 DUP(?) reserves five words with no chosen value, which is ten bytes in total. TABLE DB 3 DUP(1, 2) gives 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2. This is how you make arrays in assembly, and you will use it a lot in lesson 17.

Constants with EQU: Sometimes you just want a name for a number, without using any memory. COUNT EQU 10 tells the assembler that wherever it sees COUNT, it should use 10. So MOV CX, COUNT is assembled exactly like MOV CX, 10. A name defined with EQU cannot be given a new value later in the file. The equal sign directive, as in LIMIT = 5, does a similar job for numbers but can be redefined further down.

Writing numbers: The assembler decides the base from a suffix. A plain number or one ending in d is decimal, so 25 and 25d are the same. A number ending in h is hexadecimal, like 4Ch. A number ending in b is binary, like 1010b. One trap: a hex number must start with a digit. If you write FFh, the assembler thinks it is a name, because names start with letters. Write 0FFh instead. The extra zero does not change the value.

Procedures and the END directive: Code is usually placed inside a procedure. MAIN PROC starts a procedure called MAIN, and MAIN ENDP ends it. Lesson 19 covers procedures properly. The very last line of the file is END MAIN. It tells the assembler two things: there is nothing more to read, and the program should start running at the label MAIN. Forget it and the assembler will complain or the program will start in the wrong place.

Your first complete program: Here it is, line by line. .MODEL SMALL. .STACK 100h. .DATA. MSG DB 'Hello, Dhaka!$'. .CODE. MAIN PROC. MOV AX, @DATA. MOV DS, AX. LEA DX, MSG. MOV AH, 09h. INT 21h. MOV AH, 4Ch. INT 21h. MAIN ENDP. END MAIN. Each full stop here separates one line of the program. When it runs, it prints Hello, Dhaka! on the screen and returns to DOS.

What each line does: @DATA is the segment address of the data segment, which only the loader knows for sure. MOV AX, @DATA puts it in AX, and MOV DS, AX copies it into DS, so that DS points to our variables. Why two steps? The 8086 has no instruction that moves an immediate number straight into a segment register, so MOV DS, @DATA is illegal. LEA DX, MSG loads the offset of MSG into DX, and MOV DX, OFFSET MSG would do the same job. MOV AH, 09h selects DOS function 9, which prints the string at DS:DX until it meets a dollar sign. INT 21h calls DOS. Then MOV AH, 4Ch with INT 21h is the DOS function that ends the program and returns to the command prompt. Lesson 16 explains these DOS functions in detail.

What goes wrong without DS: When DOS loads an .EXE program, DS does not point to your data segment. It points to a small area that DOS uses to describe the program, called the PSP. If you forget the two lines that set DS, function 9 will print whatever bytes happen to be at that address, usually a screen full of strange symbols, until it finds some random dollar sign.

.COM versus .EXE programs: A .COM program is the old, simple format. Code, data and stack all live in one segment of at most 64 KB, and the program must start at offset 100h, which is why .COM sources begin with ORG 100h. When it is loaded, CS, DS, ES and SS all hold the same value, so you do not need to set DS. An .EXE program has a header that tells the loader about its segments, so it can be bigger and can use separate code, data and stack segments. emu8086 offers templates for both.

Real life example 1, a lab class in Rajshahi: Suppose your microprocessor lab teacher asks you to print your name. You open emu8086, choose a new .EXE template, and type the program above with your name in MSG. You press emulate. Before running, you press single step. After MOV AX, @DATA you see AX change to some segment number, say 0710h. After MOV DS, AX you see DS become the same. After LEA DX, MSG, DX shows 0000 if MSG is the first variable. After INT 21h with AH = 09h, the emulator screen shows your name. Watching registers change is the fastest way to learn.

Real life example 2, peeking under a C program: Assembly is not only for old DOS programs. If you have gcc on a computer, the command gcc -S hello.c writes a file hello.s with the assembly code the compiler produced from your C program. You will see labels, directives and mnemonics, the same ideas as today, although for a modern 64 bit processor. People who write bootloaders, startup code for small boards or very fast routines still use this same chain of assembler, linker and loader.

Common mistakes: Forgetting MOV AX, @DATA and MOV DS, AX in an .EXE program. Forgetting the dollar sign at the end of a string for function 9. Writing a hex number that starts with a letter without a leading zero. Trying MOV DS, @DATA in one step. Missing END MAIN. Declaring NUM DB 5 and then writing MOV AX, NUM, which MASM rejects because a byte variable cannot be moved into a 16 bit register.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: explain the roles of the assembler, linker, loader and debugger; differentiate an instruction from a directive with examples; explain the memory models; why does an assembler need two passes; explain DB, DW, DUP and EQU with examples; write an assembly program to display a message and explain every line.

Recap: An assembler turns readable mnemonics into machine code, usually in two passes with a symbol table. The linker builds an executable from object files and the loader puts it in memory. A program is organised with directives: .MODEL, .STACK, .DATA, .CODE, PROC, ENDP and END. Data is declared with DB, DW, DD and DUP, constants with EQU. With MOV DS set up and INT 21h, you can already print a message. Next lesson, we look closely at the instructions that move data around.
key_points: An assembler translates mnemonics and labels into machine code; the linker joins object files into an executable; the loader puts it in memory and starts it.
Two pass assemblers first build a symbol table with the location counter, then generate code, which solves forward references.
Instructions run on the processor; directives like .MODEL, DB, EQU and END only guide the assembler.
.MODEL SMALL means one code and one data segment of up to 64 KB each; .STACK, .DATA and .CODE mark the parts.
DB, DW and DD reserve 1, 2 and 4 bytes per value; DUP repeats values; EQU names a constant without using memory.
In an .EXE program you must load DS with MOV AX, @DATA then MOV DS, AX, because an immediate cannot go straight into a segment register.
Hex numbers starting with a letter need a leading zero, like 0FFh.
lessons.tip: Always keep one working hello program as a template. Start every new lab task by copying it, so the .MODEL, DS setup and exit lines are never forgotten.
lessons.task: On paper, write the full hello program with your own name in the message. Then add a second message on a new line and mark which lines are directives and which are instructions. If you have emu8086 or DOSBox, run it and watch DS and DX change.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the linker?
options: Joining object files and libraries into one executable
Copying the program into memory and starting it
Running the program one instruction at a time
quiz.explain: The assembler makes object files; the linker joins them, fixes addresses and writes the executable. The loader and debugger come later.

quiz.q: Which of these is a directive, not an instruction?
quiz.explain: DB tells the assembler to reserve bytes. MOV, ADD and INT are executed by the processor.

quiz.q: Why do we write MOV AX, @DATA and then MOV DS, AX instead of MOV DS, @DATA?
options: It makes the program run faster
DOS function 9 only works with AX
The 8086 cannot move an immediate value directly into a segment register
quiz.explain: There is no 8086 instruction that loads an immediate into a segment register, so the value goes through a general register first.

quiz.q: What does ARR DB 5 DUP(7) reserve?
quiz.explain: The number before DUP is the count and the value inside the brackets is repeated: five bytes of 7.

quiz.q: Why should you write 0FFh instead of FFh?
options: The assembler would read FFh as a name, because it starts with a letter
Hex numbers must always be four digits long
quiz.explain: Names start with letters, so a hex number must start with a digit. The leading zero does not change the value.

lessons.title: Data Transfer Instructions
lessons.content:
Think about a busy kitchen before a wedding dinner in Dhaka. Most of the work is not actually cooking. It is carrying things: rice from the store room to the pot, spices from the shelf to the counter, plates from the cupboard to the table. A processor is just like that. In a typical program, a big share of the instructions do nothing clever at all; they simply move data from one place to another, between registers, memory and input/output ports. These are the data transfer instructions. They are the first ones you must know well, because almost every other instruction needs its data to be in the right place first.

What counts as a data transfer: A data transfer instruction copies a value from a source to a destination. The family on the 8086 includes MOV, XCHG, LEA, LDS, LES, XLAT, IN, OUT, PUSH, POP, and a few flag movers like LAHF and SAHF. An important fact about almost all of them: they do not change the flags. MOV AX, 0 does not set the zero flag, even though AX becomes zero. Only POPF and SAHF, which are designed to load flags, change them. Remember this; it is a favourite exam trap.

MOV, the workhorse: MOV destination, source copies the source into the destination. The source is not changed, so the name move is a bit misleading; copy would be more honest. MOV AX, BX copies BX into AX. MOV AL, 25 puts the number 25 into AL. MOV CX, [SI] reads a word from memory at the address in SI. MOV [DI], DL writes the byte in DL into memory. The destination always comes first, which is the opposite of the way many people read, so say it aloud: move into AX, from BX.

The allowed combinations: MOV can go register to register, memory to register, register to memory, immediate to register, and immediate to memory. It can also copy a 16 bit register or memory word into a segment register, and copy a segment register out to a 16 bit register or memory word. That is the complete list. Anything else is illegal and the assembler will refuse it.

The forbidden combinations: First, no memory to memory. MOV [SI], [DI] does not exist, because one 8086 instruction can have at most one memory operand. To copy one variable to another, go through a register: MOV AX, X then MOV Y, AX. Second, no immediate into a segment register. MOV DS, 2000h is illegal; write MOV AX, 2000h then MOV DS, AX, exactly like the @DATA trick from lesson 11. Third, no segment register to segment register. MOV ES, DS is illegal. Fourth, CS can never be a MOV destination; to change CS you use a far jump or call. Fifth, the sizes must match. MOV AX, BL is wrong because AX is 16 bits and BL is 8 bits. And of course an immediate value can never be a destination, since 5 = AX makes no sense.

Telling the assembler the size: When one side is a register, the size is clear. MOV [BX], AL is a byte move because AL is a byte. But in MOV [BX], 5 there is no register, and the assembler cannot know whether to store a byte 05h or a word 0005h. You must say it with a PTR operator: MOV BYTE PTR [BX], 5 or MOV WORD PTR [BX], 5. The word version writes two bytes, 05h at address BX and 00h at BX + 1. Named variables carry their size, so if COUNT was declared with DB, MOV COUNT, 5 is automatically a byte move.

XCHG, the swap: XCHG exchanges the contents of its two operands. If AX = 1111h and BX = 2222h, then after XCHG AX, BX, AX = 2222h and BX = 1111h. It works between two registers or between a register and memory, as in XCHG AL, [SI]. It cannot use segment registers, immediates or two memory operands, and it does not change flags. Without XCHG, swapping needs a third, temporary place, just like swapping the water in two glasses needs a third glass. A fun fact: the one byte instruction 90h, NOP, which does nothing, is really XCHG AX, AX.

Swapping two variables: To swap memory variables A and B, which are bytes, write MOV AL, A then XCHG AL, B then MOV A, AL. Trace it with A = 3 and B = 8. After MOV AL, A, AL = 3. XCHG AL, B puts 8 in AL and 3 in B. MOV A, AL puts 8 in A. Now A = 8 and B = 3. Three instructions, one register, done.

LEA, load effective address: LEA puts the address of a memory operand, not its contents, into a 16 bit register. Suppose BX = 1000h and the word at offset 1004h in the data segment is 5678h. LEA SI, [BX + 4] gives SI = 1004h. MOV SI, [BX + 4] gives SI = 5678h. That is the whole difference: LEA calculates where, MOV fetches what. LEA never even touches memory. For a simple variable, LEA DX, MSG and MOV DX, OFFSET MSG do the same job, but LEA can also handle addresses that are only known at run time, such as LEA DI, [BX + SI + 2]. Programmers sometimes use LEA as a quick calculator, since it adds registers and a constant in one step without changing any flags.

LDS and LES, loading a far pointer: Sometimes a program stores a full address, a segment and an offset, in memory as a doubleword. This is called a far pointer. The 8086 stores it offset first, then segment. LDS SI, PTR1 copies the first word at PTR1 into SI and the second word into DS, in one instruction. LES DI, PTR2 does the same but loads ES. So after LDS SI, PTR1, DS:SI points exactly where the pointer said. For example, if PTR1 DD 20001000h, the memory holds 00h, 10h, 00h, 20h. After LDS SI, PTR1, SI = 1000h and DS = 2000h, so DS:SI points to physical address 21000h. These are handy for string instructions in lesson 17, which use DS:SI and ES:DI.

XLAT, the table look-up: XLAT, also written XLATB, replaces AL with a byte from a table. It reads the byte at DS:[BX + AL] and puts it in AL. Before using it, you load BX with the start of the table and AL with the position you want, counting from zero. Example: HEXTAB DB '0123456789ABCDEF'. Then LEA BX, HEXTAB, MOV AL, 0Ch, XLAT. Position 12 of the table is the character C, so AL becomes 43h, the ASCII code of C. This turns a number from 0 to 15 into the character that prints it. Because AL is only 8 bits, the table can be at most 256 bytes long.

IN and OUT, talking to ports: Devices like keyboards, timers and the 8255 chip in lesson 23 sit at I/O port addresses, which are separate from memory addresses on the 8086. IN reads from a port into the accumulator, and OUT writes the accumulator to a port. There are two forms. With a fixed 8 bit port number, from 00h to FFh, you write the number directly: IN AL, 60h or OUT 43h, AL. For any port from 0000h to FFFFh, put the port number in DX first: MOV DX, 03F8h then IN AL, DX. The data register must be AL for bytes or AX for words; IN BL, 60h is not allowed. On the original IBM PC, port 60h is where the keyboard controller hands over key codes, which is why it appears in so many old examples.

PUSH and POP, a preview: The stack, covered fully in lesson 18, is a special area of memory used like a pile of plates. PUSH AX copies AX onto the top of the stack, and POP AX takes the top value back into AX. On the 8086 these always move 16 bit words, and SP goes down by 2 on PUSH and up by 2 on POP. You can push and pop general registers, memory words and segment registers, but POP CS is not allowed. Pushing an immediate number like PUSH 5 was added later, with the 80186; the original 8086 cannot do it. A common use right now: PUSH AX at the start of a block and POP AX at the end, to keep a value safe while you borrow AX.

Moving the flags: LAHF copies the low byte of the flags register, which holds SF, ZF, AF, PF and CF, into AH. SAHF does the opposite, copying AH into those flags. PUSHF and POPF push and pop the whole 16 bit flags register. These let you save the flags, test them or change bits that have no direct instruction.

Real life example 1, a scoreboard at Mirpur: Imagine a small electronic scoreboard made of seven segment digits, like the ones you see at local cricket grounds. Each digit has seven LED segments, a to g. To show the number 5, segments a, f, g, c and d must light. If bit 0 of a byte controls segment a, bit 1 controls b, and so on up to bit 6 for g, then on a display where a 1 lights a segment, the patterns for 0 to 9 are 3Fh, 06h, 5Bh, 4Fh, 66h, 6Dh, 7Dh, 07h, 7Fh and 6Fh. Store them as SEG DB 3Fh, 06h, 5Bh, 4Fh, 66h, 6Dh, 7Dh, 07h, 7Fh, 6Fh. Now, to show the runs digit in AL: LEA BX, SEG, then XLAT, then OUT to the display port. Three data transfer instructions and the scoreboard shows the right digit, with no arithmetic at all. That is the power of a lookup table.

Real life example 2, rearranging marks: Your class teacher keeps two students' marks in variables RAHIM and KARIM, and finds she typed them the wrong way round. In assembly the fix is the swap from before: MOV AL, RAHIM, XCHG AL, KARIM, MOV RAHIM, AL. Notice she cannot write XCHG RAHIM, KARIM directly, because that would be two memory operands. Every data transfer rule you learned shows up even in a tiny task like this.

Common mistakes: Writing memory to memory moves. Loading a segment register with an immediate. Mixing sizes, such as MOV AX, BL. Forgetting BYTE PTR or WORD PTR when storing an immediate through a pointer. Expecting MOV to set flags, for example MOV AX, 0 followed by JZ and thinking the jump depends on that MOV; it actually depends on whatever last changed the flags. Mixing up LEA and MOV. Using a register other than DX to hold a 16 bit port number, or using BL instead of AL with IN and OUT.

What exams ask: State which of these instructions are invalid and why, such as MOV DS, 1000h, MOV [SI], [DI] or MOV AX, BL. Explain the difference between LEA and MOV with an example. Explain XLAT and write a program to convert a number into its seven segment or ASCII code. Write the effect of LDS SI, [BX]. Explain the direct and indirect forms of IN and OUT.

Recap: Data transfer instructions copy values between registers, memory, ports and the stack, and they do not change flags except POPF and SAHF. MOV has strict rules: no memory to memory, no immediate or segment register into a segment register, no MOV into CS, and matching sizes. XCHG swaps, LEA gives an address, LDS and LES load a far pointer, XLAT looks up a table using BX and AL, and IN and OUT use AL or AX with a fixed port or DX. Next lesson, we start doing real arithmetic with the data we have learned to move.
key_points: Data transfer instructions copy data; except POPF and SAHF they do not change any flags.
MOV cannot do memory to memory, immediate to segment register, segment to segment, or write into CS, and both sizes must match.
Use BYTE PTR or WORD PTR when storing an immediate into memory through a pointer like [BX].
XCHG swaps two operands, register with register or register with memory.
LEA loads the address of an operand, while MOV loads its contents.
LDS and LES load a far pointer into a register plus DS or ES; XLAT sets AL to the byte at DS:[BX + AL].
IN and OUT use AL or AX; port numbers up to FFh can be written directly, larger ones must be in DX.
lessons.tip: Make a small card titled MOV rules with the five forbidden cases. Before each lab, check every MOV in your program against the card; most assembler errors in early lab work come from these five.
lessons.task: On paper, with BX = 2000h, SI = 0010h and the word 1234h stored at offset 2010h, write the result of LEA AX, [BX + SI] and MOV AX, [BX + SI]. Then write the three instruction swap for two byte variables A = 4 and B = 9 and trace AL, A and B after each line.

quiz.q: Which of these 8086 instructions is illegal?
quiz.explain: An 8086 instruction can have at most one memory operand, so memory to memory moves must go through a register.

quiz.q: If BX = 1000h, what does LEA SI, [BX + 4] put in SI?
quiz.explain: LEA calculates the effective address, BX + 4 = 1004h, without reading memory.

quiz.q: What does XLAT do?
options: Converts AL from binary to BCD
Loads AL with the byte at DS:[BX + AL]
Translates a port number into a memory address
quiz.explain: XLAT is a table look-up: BX holds the table start and AL the position, and AL receives the table entry.

quiz.q: To read a byte from port 03F8h you must
options: put 03F8h in DX and use IN AL, DX
quiz.explain: Direct port numbers are only 8 bits (00h to FFh). Larger ports must be in DX, and the data register must be AL or AX.

quiz.q: Which flags does MOV AX, 0 change?
quiz.explain: MOV and most data transfer instructions leave the flags unchanged, even when the value moved is zero.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Instructions
lessons.content:
Imagine a shopkeeper in a bazar who has no calculator, only a small slate that holds two digits. Adding 45 and 30 is easy. But adding 75 and 60 gives 135, which does not fit, so he writes 35 on the slate and keeps the extra 1 in his head for the next column. That extra 1 in his head is exactly what the 8086 calls the carry flag. The arithmetic instructions of the 8086 add, subtract, multiply and divide numbers in registers and memory, and they report extra information like carry, zero and sign in the flags you met in lesson 8. In this lesson you will learn each instruction, where its result goes, which flags it changes, and the small traps that catch almost everyone the first time.

ADD and SUB: ADD destination, source adds the source to the destination and stores the answer in the destination. SUB destination, source subtracts the source from the destination. The operand rules are the same as MOV: register or memory as destination, register, memory or immediate as source, at most one memory operand, and matching sizes. Unlike MOV, these instructions update the flags: CF, ZF, SF, OF, PF and AF. For example, MOV AL, 25 then ADD AL, 17 gives AL = 42. SUB AL, 50 then gives AL = 42 - 50 = -8, which is stored as F8h in two's complement, and CF becomes 1 because a borrow was needed.

Flags after ADD, two worked examples: First, MOV AL, 7Fh then ADD AL, 1. AL becomes 80h. CF = 0, because 127 + 1 = 128 fits in an unsigned byte. But OF = 1, because as signed numbers 127 + 1 should be +128, and a signed byte can only reach +127, so the result 80h looks like -128. SF = 1, ZF = 0. Second, MOV AL, 0FFh then ADD AL, 1. AL becomes 00h. CF = 1, because 255 + 1 = 256 does not fit in 8 bits. ZF = 1 since the result is zero. OF = 0, because as signed numbers this is -1 + 1 = 0, which is correct. So CF warns about unsigned overflow and OF warns about signed overflow. Which one you look at depends on how you think about your numbers.

ADC and SBB, carrying across words: ADC means add with carry. It adds the source, the destination and the carry flag. SBB means subtract with borrow; it subtracts the source and the carry flag. These let you work with numbers bigger than 16 bits, just like the shopkeeper carries a 1 to the next column. Suppose a 32 bit number is kept in DX:AX, with DX holding the high word, and another in CX:BX. To add them, write ADD AX, BX then ADC DX, CX. The first ADD adds the low words and may set CF. The ADC adds the high words plus that carry.

A multiword example: Add 0001FFFFh and 00000001h. Put DX = 0001h, AX = FFFFh, CX = 0000h and BX = 0001h. ADD AX, BX gives AX = 0000h with CF = 1. ADC DX, CX gives DX = 0001h + 0000h + 1 = 0002h. The answer in DX:AX is 00020000h, which is correct. Without ADC you would get 00010000h, quietly wrong. Subtraction works the same way: SUB AX, BX then SBB DX, CX.

INC and DEC: INC adds 1 and DEC subtracts 1. They are short and fast, perfect for counters and pointers, such as INC SI to move to the next byte in an array. They change OF, SF, ZF, AF and PF, but they do not change CF. This is deliberate: you can count with INC or DEC inside a multiword loop without destroying a carry you are saving for ADC. It also means you cannot test for unsigned overflow after INC with JC. If AL = FFh and you do INC AL, AL becomes 00h and ZF = 1, but CF keeps whatever value it had before.

NEG, change the sign: NEG destination replaces the operand with its two's complement, which is the same as 0 minus the operand. If AL = 05h, NEG AL gives FBh, which is -5. If AL = FBh, NEG AL gives back 05h. CF becomes 1 for any non-zero operand and 0 when the operand is zero. One odd case: NEG of 80h in a byte gives 80h again, with OF = 1, because +128 cannot be written in a signed byte.

CMP, subtract without keeping the answer: CMP destination, source works out destination minus source and sets the flags exactly like SUB, but it throws the result away. Neither operand changes. It is used just before a conditional jump. For example, CMP AL, 10 sets ZF = 1 if AL is exactly 10, and CF = 1 if AL is below 10 as an unsigned number. Lesson 15 explains which jump to use after CMP for signed and unsigned comparisons.

MUL, unsigned multiplication: MUL has only one operand, the multiplier, which can be a register or memory but not an immediate on the 8086; MUL 5 is illegal. The other number is always the accumulator. For a byte operand, AX = AL times the operand. For a word operand, DX:AX = AX times the operand, with the high word in DX. The answer is twice as wide as the inputs, because multiplying two 8 bit numbers can give up to 16 bits, for example 255 times 255 = 65025. After MUL, CF and OF are both set to 1 if the upper half of the answer, AH or DX, is not zero, and both cleared to 0 if it is zero. Other flags are undefined after MUL.

MUL worked example: MOV AL, 20, MOV BL, 15, MUL BL. 20 times 15 = 300, which is 012Ch, so AX = 012Ch, AH = 01h and AL = 2Ch. Since AH is not zero, CF = OF = 1, telling you the answer did not fit in AL alone. If instead BL = 5, the answer is 100 = 0064h, AH = 0 and CF = OF = 0.

IMUL, signed multiplication: IMUL works the same way for signed numbers. MOV AL, -4 then MOV BL, 6 then IMUL BL gives AX = -24, which is FFE8h. With MUL, the same bit patterns would mean 252 times 6 = 1512 = 05E8h, a completely different answer. The bits are the same but the meaning is different, so you must choose MUL or IMUL according to whether your numbers are unsigned or signed. For IMUL, CF and OF are set when the upper half is not just a sign extension of the lower half.

DIV, unsigned division: DIV also takes one operand, the divisor. For a byte divisor, the dividend is the whole of AX; the quotient goes to AL and the remainder to AH.
