For a word divisor, the dividend is DX:AX; the quotient goes to AX and the remainder to DX. Example: MOV AX, 100, MOV BL, 7, DIV BL. 100 divided by 7 is 14 remainder 2, so AL = 0Eh and AH = 02h. Word example: DX = 0001h and AX = 0000h make DX:AX = 65536. MOV CX, 10 then DIV CX gives AX = 6553 and DX = 6, since 65536 = 10 times 6553 + 6. All flags are undefined after DIV.

The divide error: Two things make division fail: a divisor of zero, or a quotient too big for its register. For example, AX = 1000 and BL = 2 gives 500, which cannot fit in AL. In both cases the 8086 raises interrupt type 0, the divide error, which you will meet in lesson 20; under DOS this usually stops your program with a message. The classic bug is forgetting to clear the upper half. If you want to divide the byte in AL by BL, AH must be 0 first, because DIV BL divides all of AX. Likewise, before DIV CX, set DX to 0 with MOV DX, 0 or XOR DX, DX, otherwise leftover rubbish in DX becomes part of the dividend.

IDIV, CBW and CWD: IDIV is signed division with the same register layout. The quotient is rounded toward zero, and the remainder has the same sign as the dividend. To prepare a signed dividend, you cannot just clear AH; you must copy the sign bit into it. CBW, convert byte to word, fills AH with copies of the sign bit of AL. CWD, convert word to doubleword, fills DX with copies of the sign bit of AX. Example: MOV AL, -7, which is F9h. CBW makes AX = FFF9h. MOV BL, 2 then IDIV BL gives AL = -3, which is FDh, and AH = -1, which is FFh. Check: 2 times -3 + -1 = -7. Correct. Use zero for DIV and CBW or CWD for IDIV.

BCD adjust, DAA: In lesson 2 you saw packed BCD, where each hex digit holds one decimal digit, so 38h means thirty-eight. If you ADD two packed BCD bytes, the binary answer may not be valid BCD. DAA, decimal adjust after addition, fixes AL. MOV AL, 38h, ADD AL, 45h gives 7Dh. DAA sees that the low digit D is bigger than 9 and adds 6, giving 83h, and 38 + 45 = 83 in decimal. Another: 29h + 18h = 41h, but the low digit addition 9 + 8 overflowed, setting AF, so DAA again adds 6 to give 47h, and 29 + 18 = 47. DAS does the same job after subtraction. There are also AAA, AAS, AAM and AAD for unpacked BCD, one digit per byte, often used with ASCII digits; you just need to know they exist and what they are for.

Real life example 1, a mobile wallet balance: Suppose a bKash style wallet program on an 8086 stores balances in taka. A 16 bit register only goes up to 65,535, so a balance of 50,000 plus a deposit of 30,000 would overflow. The program stores amounts as 32 bit values in DX:AX. 50,000 is C350h and 30,000 is 7530h. With DX = 0, AX = C350h, CX = 0 and BX = 7530h, ADD AX, BX gives AX = 3880h with CF = 1, and ADC DX, CX gives DX = 0001h. DX:AX = 00013880h, which is exactly 80,000. Thanks to ADC, nobody loses money.

Real life example 2, average marks: A school wants the average of Mitu's marks in three subjects: 85, 90 and 78. The marks are bytes, but their sum, 253, is close to the byte limit and the sum of more subjects would not fit. So the program clears AX, adds each mark into AL and uses ADC AH, 0 after each addition to catch any carry, which gives AX = 253. Then MOV BL, 3 and DIV BL gives AL = 84 and AH = 1. The average is 84, with a remainder of 1, meaning the true average is 84 and one third.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to clear AH or DX before DIV, or using MOV AH, 0 instead of CBW before IDIV. Trying MUL 10 with an immediate on the 8086. Looking at CF after INC or DEC. Mixing up which register gets the quotient and which gets the remainder. Using ADD instead of ADC for the high word of a multiword addition. Looking at CF when your numbers are signed, where OF is the one that matters.

What exams ask: Give the contents of AX, DX and the flags after a short sequence like MOV AL, 0F0h, MOV BL, 20h, MUL BL. Explain the difference between MUL and IMUL with an example. Write a program to add two 32 bit numbers. Explain CBW and CWD and why they are needed. Explain DAA with an example. Write a program to find the average of an array of numbers.

Recap: ADD, SUB, ADC and SBB do addition and subtraction and set all six status flags; ADC and SBB carry results across words. INC and DEC leave CF alone. NEG changes sign and CMP subtracts only for the flags. MUL and IMUL use the accumulator and give a double width answer in AX or DX:AX. DIV and IDIV divide AX or DX:AX, putting the quotient in AL or AX and the remainder in AH or DX, and they raise a divide error on zero or overflow. Prepare the dividend with zero for unsigned division and CBW or CWD for signed. Next lesson, we play with individual bits using logic, shift and rotate instructions.
key_points: ADD, SUB, ADC, SBB, NEG and CMP update CF, ZF, SF, OF, PF and AF; CMP keeps no result.
CF signals unsigned overflow and OF signals signed overflow, for example 7Fh + 1 sets OF but not CF.
ADC and SBB include the carry flag, so ADD AX, BX then ADC DX, CX adds two 32 bit numbers.
INC and DEC do not change CF.
MUL and IMUL: byte gives AX = AL x operand, word gives DX:AX = AX x operand; no immediate operand on the 8086.
DIV and IDIV: byte divides AX (AL quotient, AH remainder), word divides DX:AX (AX quotient, DX remainder); zero divisor or big quotient causes a divide error.
Clear AH or DX before DIV; use CBW or CWD before IDIV. DAA corrects AL after packed BCD addition.
lessons.tip: For every MUL or DIV you write, say aloud where the inputs come from and where the outputs go, like DIV BL: AX in, AL quotient, AH remainder. Saying it catches almost all register mix-ups.
lessons.task: On paper, work out AX and DX after: (1) MOV AL, 12, MOV BL, 25, MUL BL; (2) MOV AX, 250, MOV BL, 9, DIV BL; (3) MOV AL, -9, CBW, MOV BL, 4, IDIV BL. Then check your answers in emu8086 or with a calculator in programmer mode.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 0FFh and ADD AL, 1, what is true?
quiz.explain: 255 + 1 = 256 does not fit in 8 bits, so AL wraps to 00h, CF = 1 for the carry out and ZF = 1 because the result is zero.

quiz.q: Where does MUL BL put its result?
quiz.explain: For a byte operand, MUL multiplies AL by the operand and puts the 16 bit result in AX.

quiz.q: After DIV BL, where are the quotient and remainder?
options: Quotient in AX, remainder in DX
Quotient in AH, remainder in AL
Quotient in BL, remainder in BH
Quotient in AL, remainder in AH
quiz.explain: A byte divisor divides AX; the quotient goes to AL and the remainder to AH.

quiz.q: Which instruction does NOT change the carry flag?
quiz.explain: INC and DEC change OF, SF, ZF, AF and PF but leave CF unchanged.

quiz.q: AL holds a signed number. Before IDIV BL you should
quiz.explain: CBW copies the sign bit of AL into all of AH, making a correct signed dividend in AX. CWD is for word division.

lessons.title: Logic, Shift and Rotate Instructions
lessons.content:
Picture the light switch board in a classroom in Sylhet: eight switches in a row, each controlling one fan or light. Sometimes you want to turn on one fan without touching the others. Sometimes you want to turn everything off. Sometimes you want to check whether switch number 3 is on. A byte in a register is just like that switch board, eight bits standing side by side. The logic instructions, AND, OR, XOR, NOT and TEST, let you set, clear, flip and check individual bits. The shift and rotate instructions slide all the bits left or right, which turns out to be a very fast way to multiply and divide by 2 and a neat way to look at bits one at a time.

AND, keeping and clearing bits: AND destination, source does a bitwise AND: each result bit is 1 only if both matching bits are 1. A bit ANDed with 0 becomes 0, and a bit ANDed with 1 stays the same. So AND is used to clear bits. The second operand is called a mask. Example: AL = 7Ch, which is 0111 1100. AND AL, 0Fh uses the mask 0000 1111, keeps the lower four bits and clears the upper four, giving 0000 1100, which is 0Ch. A very common use: the ASCII digit '7' is 37h. AND AL, 0Fh turns it into 07h, the real number 7.

OR, setting bits: OR destination, source makes each result bit 1 if either bit is 1. A bit ORed with 1 becomes 1, and ORed with 0 stays the same. So OR is used to set bits. To turn the number 7 back into the printable digit '7', write OR AL, 30h, which changes 07h into 37h. OR AL, 80h sets the top bit without touching the other seven.

XOR, flipping bits: XOR gives 1 when the two bits are different and 0 when they are the same. A bit XORed with 1 flips, and XORed with 0 stays. XOR AL, 01h toggles bit 0: if AL was 06h it becomes 07h, and doing it again gives 06h. A famous trick: XOR AX, AX makes AX zero, because every bit is the same as itself. It is shorter than MOV AX, 0, and unlike MOV it also clears CF and sets ZF, which can be useful.

NOT, flip everything: NOT destination flips every bit, giving the one's complement. If AL = 0F0h, NOT AL gives 0Fh. Do not confuse it with NEG from lesson 13: NEG gives the two's complement, which is NOT plus 1. NOT 05h is FAh, while NEG 05h is FBh.

Flags after logic instructions: AND, OR, XOR and TEST always clear CF and OF to 0, and set ZF, SF and PF according to the result. AF is undefined. NOT is the odd one out: it changes no flags at all. Exams love asking which logic instruction leaves the flags untouched.

TEST, AND without the answer: TEST destination, source does an AND only to set the flags, and throws the result away, the same way CMP is a SUB that keeps nothing. It is perfect for checking a bit. TEST AL, 01h sets ZF = 1 if bit 0 of AL is 0, which means AL is even. So TEST AL, 01h followed by JZ EVEN jumps when the number is even. TEST AL, 80h checks the top bit, which tells you whether a signed byte is negative.

Case conversion with masks: In ASCII, the capital letters A to Z are 41h to 5Ah and the small letters a to z are 61h to 7Ah. The only difference between 'A' and 'a' is bit 5, which has the value 20h. So OR AL, 20h turns a capital letter into a small one, AND AL, 0DFh turns a small letter into a capital, and XOR AL, 20h swaps the case either way. Example: 'd' is 64h. AND AL, 0DFh gives 44h, which is 'D'. Make sure the character really is a letter first, because these masks also change other characters.

The shift family: The shift instructions move every bit of a register or memory operand left or right. On the 8086, the count is either 1, written directly, or the number in CL. So SHL AL, 1 is fine, and for three places you write MOV CL, 3 then SHL AL, CL. Writing SHL AL, 3 directly became legal only with the 80186 and later processors. The bit that falls off the end always goes into CF, so you can catch it and test it with JC or JNC.

SHL and SAL, shift left: SHL, shift logical left, moves every bit one place to the left. The top bit goes into CF and a 0 comes in at the bottom. SAL, shift arithmetic left, is exactly the same instruction with another name. Each left shift multiplies an unsigned number by 2, as long as nothing important falls out. AL = 05h, which is 0000 0101, becomes 0000 1010 = 0Ah = 10 after SHL AL, 1. With CL = 3, SHL AL, CL multiplies by 8, giving 40.

SHR, shift right logically: SHR moves every bit one place right. The bottom bit goes into CF and a 0 enters at the top. This divides an unsigned number by 2 and the bit in CF is the remainder. AL = 0F0h, which is 240, becomes 78h, which is 120, after SHR AL, 1, with CF = 0. AL = 07h becomes 03h with CF = 1, since 7 divided by 2 is 3 remainder 1.

SAR, shift right arithmetically: SAR is like SHR, but instead of bringing in a 0 at the top, it copies the old top bit, which is the sign bit. That keeps negative numbers negative. AL = F8h, which is -8, becomes FCh, which is -4, after SAR AL, 1. If you used SHR you would get 7Ch, which is +124, completely wrong for a signed number. One subtle point: SAR rounds toward minus infinity. SAR on -7, F9h, gives FCh, which is -4, while IDIV by 2 gives -3, because IDIV rounds toward zero.

Multiplying by 10 with shifts: Shifts are fast, so old programs often multiplied by constants with shifts and adds instead of MUL. Since 10 x = 8 x + 2 x, you can write SHL AX, 1 to get 2x, MOV BX, AX to save it, SHL AX, 1 and SHL AX, 1 again to reach 8x, then ADD AX, BX to get 10x. Start with AX = 7: 14, save 14, then 28, then 56, then 56 + 14 = 70. Correct. This is exactly what you need when converting typed digits into a number, as in lesson 16.

The rotate family: Rotates are like shifts, except the bit that falls off one end comes back in at the other end, like children going round in a circle game. ROL, rotate left, sends the top bit to the bottom and also copies it into CF. ROR, rotate right, sends the bottom bit to the top and into CF. RCL and RCR rotate through the carry: the carry flag becomes part of the circle, so a byte rotates as 9 bits and a word as 17 bits. They use the same count rule as shifts: 1 or CL.

Rotate worked examples: Let AL = 96h, which is 1001 0110. ROL AL, 1 gives 0010 1101 = 2Dh, with CF = 1, the bit that went round. Starting again from 96h, ROR AL, 1 gives 0100 1011 = 4Bh, with CF = 0. Now RCL with CF = 0 at the start: the old CF, 0, enters at the bottom and the top bit 1 goes into CF, giving 0010 1100 = 2Ch with CF = 1. And RCR with CF = 1 at the start: the old CF, 1, enters at the top and the bottom bit 0 goes into CF, giving 1100 1011 = CBh with CF = 0. A handy trick: MOV CL, 4 then ROL AL, CL swaps the two nibbles, so 96h becomes 69h. That is useful when printing a byte as two hex digits.

Shifting a 32 bit number: Because RCL and RCR pass bits through CF, they join registers together. To shift DX:AX left by one, write SHL AX, 1 then RCL DX, 1. The top bit of AX goes into CF, and RCL brings it into the bottom of DX. To shift right, write SHR DX, 1 then RCR AX, 1.

Counting the ones in a word: Here is a short program that counts how many bits of AX are 1. XOR BL, BL, then MOV CX, 16, then the label AGAIN: SHL AX, 1, ADC BL, 0, LOOP AGAIN. Each SHL pushes one bit into CF, and ADC BL, 0 adds that carry to the counter. LOOP, from lesson 15, repeats 16 times. If AX = 00F3h, which has the bits 1111 0011 in its low byte and nothing in the high byte, BL ends up as 6.

Real life example 1, a traffic signal at Farmgate: Imagine an 8086 controlling a traffic light through an output port. Bit 0 is the red lamp, bit 1 is yellow and bit 2 is green. The program keeps the current pattern in AL. To switch on green without touching the others, OR AL, 04h. To switch off red, AND AL, 0FEh. To make yellow blink, XOR AL, 02h again and again with a delay between. Each time, OUT sends AL to the port. The program never needs to know the other bits; the masks protect them. Real controllers use exactly this style to control many lamps, motors and buzzers from one byte.

Real life example 2, cleaning up names: A school in Barishal stores student names typed by different people, some as rahim, some as RAHIM, some as Rahim. To compare them, a program converts every letter to capitals. It walks through the string, and for each character between 'a' and 'z' it does AND AL, 0DFh. One instruction per letter turns rahim into RAHIM, and now the search finds every spelling. Lesson 17 will show how to walk through a string efficiently.

Common mistakes: Writing SHL AX, 4 on an 8086, when the count must be 1 or CL. Using SHR on negative numbers instead of SAR. Mixing up NOT and NEG. Forgetting that AND, OR and XOR clear CF, so a carry you wanted to keep is lost. Expecting NOT to set ZF. Confusing ROL with RCL; only RCL and RCR include the carry flag in the circle. Using case masks on characters that are not letters.

What exams ask: Find AL and CF after a sequence of shifts and rotates starting from a given value. Explain the difference between SHR and SAR, and between ROL and RCL, with diagrams. Write a program to count the number of 1s in a byte or word. Write a program to convert lowercase to uppercase. Explain how to multiply by 10 without MUL. Explain TEST and how it differs from AND.

Recap: AND clears bits, OR sets bits, XOR flips bits, NOT flips everything, and TEST checks bits without changing the operand. Logic instructions clear CF and OF, except NOT, which changes no flags. Shifts move bits and put the last bit out into CF; SHL multiplies by 2, SHR divides unsigned numbers by 2 and SAR divides signed numbers by 2. Rotates send bits around a circle, and RCL and RCR include CF. On the 8086 the count is 1 or CL. Next lesson, we use the flags these instructions produce to make decisions with jumps and loops.
key_points: AND with a mask clears bits, OR sets bits, XOR flips bits, and NOT flips every bit.
AND, OR, XOR and TEST clear CF and OF and set ZF, SF and PF; NOT changes no flags.
TEST is an AND that only sets flags, ideal for checking a bit such as TEST AL, 01h for odd or even.
Bit 5 (20h) is the only difference between capital and small ASCII letters, so AND 0DFh, OR 20h and XOR 20h change case.
On the 8086 the shift or rotate count is 1 or CL; the bit pushed out goes into CF.
SHL multiplies by 2, SHR divides unsigned numbers by 2, SAR keeps the sign and divides signed numbers by 2.
ROL and ROR rotate within the operand; RCL and RCR rotate through CF and can join registers like DX:AX.
lessons.tip: Always write the byte in binary, with a space between the two nibbles, before working out a logic, shift or rotate question. Most mistakes come from trying to do it in hex in your head.
lessons.task: Start with AL = 0B4h. On paper write AL and CF after each of these, always starting again from 0B4h with CF = 0: AND AL, 0Fh; OR AL, 01h; XOR AL, 0FFh; SHL AL, 1; SHR AL, 1; SAR AL, 1; ROL AL, 1; RCR AL, 1. Then check them with the programmer mode of a phone calculator.

quiz.q: If AL = 7Ch, what is AL after AND AL, 0Fh?
quiz.explain: 7Ch is 0111 1100. The mask 0000 1111 keeps only the lower four bits, giving 0000 1100 = 0Ch.

quiz.q: Which instruction makes AX zero and also clears CF?
quiz.explain: XOR of a register with itself gives zero, and XOR always clears CF and OF. MOV does not change any flags.

quiz.q: If AL = F8h (which is -8), what is AL after SAR AL, 1?
quiz.explain: SAR copies the sign bit into the top, so -8 becomes -4, which is FCh. SHR would give 7Ch.

quiz.q: Which instruction rotates through the carry flag?
quiz.explain: RCL and RCR include CF in the rotation. ROL and ROR only copy the rotated bit into CF, and SHL is a shift.

quiz.q: After TEST AL, 01h, a JZ jumps when
quiz.explain: TEST checks bit 0. ZF = 1 means bit 0 is 0, which is true for every even number.

lessons.title: Branching and Loops
lessons.content:
Imagine you are riding a bus from Mirpur to Motijheel. Most of the time the bus just goes to the next stop, then the next, then the next. But sometimes the driver checks something: is the road blocked at Farmgate? If yes, take the side road. If no, keep going straight. And the helper keeps shouting the same route again and again, trip after trip, until the day ends. A program is the same. Most instructions run one after another, but real programs need to make decisions and repeat work. In assembly language there is no if, no while and no for. There are only jumps. In this lesson you will learn how a handful of jump instructions are enough to build every decision and every loop you have ever written in C.

How the CPU normally moves: The 8086 keeps the address of the next instruction in CS:IP. After each instruction is fetched, IP is increased by the length of that instruction, so the CPU walks forward through memory. A jump instruction simply puts a new value into IP, and for a far jump into CS as well. That is all a jump is: changing where the next instruction comes from. Once you understand that, branching stops feeling like magic.

The unconditional jump: JMP always jumps, no questions asked. In your source code you write JMP NEXT, where NEXT is a label, and the assembler works out the numbers for you. There are three kinds. A short jump uses a signed 8-bit displacement, so it can reach from 128 bytes backwards to 127 bytes forwards, counted from the instruction after the jump. Its machine code is just 2 bytes: EB followed by the displacement. A near jump uses a 16-bit displacement and can reach anywhere inside the same code segment, which is 64 KB. A far jump loads both a new CS and a new IP, so it can go to a different segment anywhere in the 1 MB memory. Short and near jumps are intra-segment; far jumps are inter-segment.

Relative versus absolute: Short and near jumps are relative. The machine code does not store the destination address; it stores the distance from the next instruction. So if a JMP SHORT sits at offset 0100h and is 2 bytes long, the next instruction is at 0102h. If the target is at 0110h, the displacement is 0110h minus 0102h, which is 0Eh, and the code is EB 0E. A nice result of being relative is that the code still works if the whole block is moved to a different place in memory. Jumps can also be indirect, such as JMP BX, which takes the new IP from the BX register. Indirect jumps are how jump tables and switch statements are built.

Conditional jumps: A conditional jump looks at the flags, which you met in lesson 8. If the condition is true, it jumps. If not, the CPU just falls through to the next instruction. On the original 8086, every conditional jump is short only, so the target must be within -128 to +127 bytes. Later processors from the 80386 onwards also allow near conditional jumps, but on an 8086 you must remember this limit.

The usual pattern is compare then jump: CMP AX, BX subtracts BX from AX, throws the answer away, and keeps only the flags. Then a jump checks the flags. So CMP AX, BX followed by JE EQUAL means: if AX equals BX, go to EQUAL. Many other instructions also set flags, such as SUB, ADD, DEC, AND and TEST, so sometimes you do not need a CMP at all.

Flag-based jumps: Some jumps test just one flag. JZ jumps if ZF = 1, and JNZ jumps if ZF = 0. JE and JNE are just other names for JZ and JNZ; the assembler produces the same machine code. JC and JNC test the carry flag, JS and JNS test the sign flag, JO and JNO test the overflow flag, and JP and JNP test the parity flag. JP is also called JPE, parity even, and JNP is also called JPO, parity odd.

Unsigned comparisons: When you treat numbers as unsigned, like ages, marks or memory addresses, use the words above and below. JA, jump if above, jumps when CF = 0 and ZF = 0. JAE, jump if above or equal, jumps when CF = 0, and it is the same as JNB and JNC. JB, jump if below, jumps when CF = 1, the same as JC and JNAE. JBE, jump if below or equal, jumps when CF = 1 or ZF = 1. The logic is simple: after CMP AX, BX, a borrow happens only when AX is smaller than BX as an unsigned number, and the borrow shows up in CF.

Signed comparisons: When numbers can be negative, like temperatures or bank balance changes, use the words greater and less. JG, jump if greater, jumps when ZF = 0 and SF = OF. JGE jumps when SF = OF. JL, jump if less, jumps when SF is not equal to OF. JLE jumps when ZF = 1 or SF is not equal to OF. Why SF and OF together? The sign of the answer tells you which is bigger, unless the subtraction overflowed, in which case the sign is flipped. Comparing SF with OF corrects for that.

A worked example of the difference: Put AL = 0FFh and BL = 01h, then CMP AL, BL. As unsigned numbers, AL is 255 and BL is 1, so AL is above BL, and JA would jump. As signed numbers, 0FFh is -1, so AL is less than BL, and JG would not jump while JL would. Same bits, same CMP, different answer, depending on which jump you choose. The CPU does not know whether your numbers are signed. You tell it by picking the jump. This is the number one thing exams test in this topic.

Building if/else: Take the C code if (AX == 5) BX = 1; else BX = 2. In assembly it becomes: CMP AX, 5 then JNE ELSE_PART then MOV BX, 1 then JMP DONE, then the label ELSE_PART: with MOV BX, 2, and finally the label DONE:. Notice the trick. We jump on the opposite condition. If AX is not 5, skip the then-part. The JMP DONE at the end of the then-part is needed so the CPU does not fall into the else-part. Forgetting that JMP is a very common bug.

Building while: The C code while (CX > 0) { work; CX--; } becomes a test at the top and a jump back at the bottom. TOP: CMP CX, 0, then JLE DONE if CX is signed or JE DONE if it can never be negative, then the work, then DEC CX, then JMP TOP, then DONE:. The loop body may run zero times, exactly like a C while loop. A do-while loop is shorter: put the work first and test at the bottom, so the body always runs at least once.

The LOOP instruction: Counting loops are so common that the 8086 has a special instruction. LOOP label does two things: it decreases CX by 1, and if CX is not zero after that, it jumps to the label. LOOP does not change any flags. So to repeat something 10 times you write MOV CX, 10, then a label AGAIN:, then the work, then LOOP AGAIN. The body runs exactly 10 times. Like conditional jumps, LOOP uses a short displacement, so the body must fit within the short range.

The CX = 0 trap: What happens if CX is 0 when you reach LOOP the first time? LOOP decrements CX first, so CX becomes 0FFFFh, which is not zero, and the loop runs 65,536 times. That is almost never what you want. The 8086 gives you JCXZ, jump if CX is zero, which tests CX directly without touching flags. Put JCXZ SKIP just before the loop to protect it when the count might be zero.

LOOPE and LOOPNE: These are LOOP with an extra condition. LOOPE, also called LOOPZ, decrements CX and jumps if CX is not zero and ZF = 1. LOOPNE, also called LOOPNZ, decrements CX and jumps if CX is not zero and ZF = 0. They are perfect for searching. For example, to find the first space in a string you can compare each character with ' ' and use LOOPNE: keep looping while the character is not a space and characters remain.

A complete example, sum of 1 to 10: MOV AX, 0 then MOV CX, 10 then the label ADDUP: with ADD AX, CX and LOOP ADDUP. Trace it. First pass AX = 10, CX becomes 9. Next AX = 19, CX = 8. Then 27, 34, 40, 45, 49, 52, 54, and finally 55, at which point CX becomes 0 and the loop ends. AX = 55, which is the right answer. Counting down from 10 to 1 adds the same numbers as counting up, so the order does not matter here.

A for loop that counts up: Sometimes you need the counter going up, for example to use it as an index. MOV SI, 0, then TOP: CMP SI, 10, then JAE DONE, then the work using SI, then INC SI, then JMP TOP, then DONE:. We use JAE because SI is an unsigned index. Notice that INC does not change CF, but CMP sets every flag we need, so that is fine.

Nested loops: A loop inside a loop needs two counters. If both use CX, the inner loop destroys the outer count. The usual fix is to save CX on the stack: the outer loop starts with PUSH CX, sets the inner count with MOV CX, 5, runs the inner LOOP, then does POP CX before its own LOOP. You will see PUSH and POP properly in lesson 18. Another fix is to keep the outer count in a different register like DX and use DEC DX with JNZ.

The out of range error: Because conditional jumps on the 8086 are short, a big if-block can cause the assembler error 'relative jump out of range'. The classic fix is to flip the condition and use a near JMP. Instead of JE FAR_LABEL, write JNE SKIP, then JMP FAR_LABEL, then SKIP:. The short jump only has to hop over the 3-byte near JMP, which is always in range.

Real life example 1, a ticket counter at Kamalapur station: Suppose a machine checks a passenger's age to decide the fare. Age is never negative, so treat it as unsigned. MOV AL, age then CMP AL, 12 then JB CHILD then CMP AL, 60 then JAE SENIOR then MOV BX, full fare then JMP PRINT, CHILD: MOV BX, half fare then JMP PRINT, SENIOR: MOV BX, senior fare, PRINT:. Each test is a CMP and a jump on the right condition, and each branch ends with JMP PRINT so the branches never run into each other.

Real life example 2, a water pump controller: A small controller in a building in Chattogram reads the tank level from a sensor port, waiting until the level is high enough. WAIT_FULL: IN AL, 60h, then CMP AL, 200, then JB WAIT_FULL, then switch the pump off. This is called a polling loop: the program keeps checking until the condition becomes true. The port number here is just an example; you will meet real port interfacing with the 8255 in lesson 23.

Common mistakes: First, using JG or JL on unsigned values, or JA and JB on signed values. Second, forgetting the JMP at the end of the then-part. Third, starting LOOP with CX = 0. Fourth, changing CX inside a LOOP body by accident, for example with a MUL or a REP string instruction. Fifth, expecting INC or DEC to set CF; they set ZF, SF, OF, PF and AF, but never CF. Sixth, forgetting that conditional jumps on the 8086 are short.

What exams ask: 'Write an assembly program to find the larger of two numbers', 'Explain the difference between JA and JG with an example', 'What does LOOP do and which flags does it affect?', 'Convert this C for loop into 8086 assembly', 'What is the range of a short jump?' and 'Calculate the displacement byte of this JMP SHORT'. Practise tracing loops register by register on paper; examiners love asking for the value of AX and CX after a loop ends.

Recap: Jumps change IP, and far jumps change CS too. JMP is unconditional and comes in short, near and far forms. Conditional jumps test flags, usually after CMP. Use above and below for unsigned numbers and greater and less for signed numbers. if/else, while and for are all built from compare plus jump on the opposite condition. LOOP decrements CX and jumps while CX is not zero, and JCXZ protects against a zero count. With these tools, you can now write any control flow in assembly. Next we use them to talk to the user with DOS input and output.
key_points: A jump changes IP (and CS for a far jump); that is all branching is.
JMP has short (-128 to +127 bytes), near (same segment) and far (any segment) forms; short and near are relative.
On the 8086, conditional jumps are short only, so long jumps need the flip-the-condition plus JMP trick.
Unsigned comparisons use JA, JAE, JB, JBE (carry flag); signed use JG, JGE, JL, JLE (SF, OF, ZF).
if/else is built by jumping on the opposite condition and ending the then-part with JMP.
LOOP decrements CX and jumps if CX is not zero; it changes no flags.
If CX is 0 before LOOP, it runs 65,536 times; guard it with JCXZ.
LOOPE/LOOPZ and LOOPNE/LOOPNZ add a ZF condition and are handy for searching.
lessons.tip: Before writing a jump, ask one question out loud: are these numbers signed or unsigned? Then choose greater/less or above/below. That single habit removes most branching bugs.
lessons.task: On paper, convert this to 8086 assembly: if (AL > BL) CL = AL else CL = BL, treating AL and BL as unsigned. Then trace it twice, once with AL = 0F0h, BL = 10h, and once more using JG instead of JA. Write down which value CL gets each time and why they differ.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 0FFh / MOV BL, 1 / CMP AL, BL, which jump will be taken?
quiz.explain: As signed numbers 0FFh is -1, which is less than 1, so JL jumps. JG would not, JB would not (255 is above 1 unsigned), and the numbers are not equal.

quiz.q: What does the LOOP instruction do?
options: Decrements CX and jumps if CX is not zero
Increments CX and jumps if CX equals zero
Jumps if ZF is set, without touching CX
Decrements CX and jumps if CX is zero
quiz.explain: LOOP decreases CX by 1 and jumps back to the label while CX is not zero. It does not change any flags.

quiz.q: What is the range of an 8086 short jump?
options: Anywhere in the same 64 KB segment
-128 to +127 bytes from the next instruction
quiz.explain: A short jump uses a signed 8-bit displacement added to the address of the next instruction, giving -128 to +127 bytes.

quiz.q: If CX = 0 when LOOP runs for the first time, how many times will the loop body execute in total?
quiz.explain: LOOP decrements first, so CX becomes 0FFFFh and the loop keeps going until CX reaches 0 again, which is 65,536 runs of the body. JCXZ prevents this.

quiz.q: Which jump should you use for 'jump if below' on unsigned numbers after CMP?
quiz.explain: JB (same as JC) jumps when CF = 1, meaning the first operand was below the second as an unsigned number. JL is for signed values.

lessons.title: Input and Output with DOS
lessons.content:
Imagine you walk into a big government office in Dhaka to get a form signed. You do not walk straight into the officer's room and start pulling files from the cupboard yourself. You go to the front desk, say what you want with a token number, and the desk does the job for you. Talking to the keyboard and the screen in assembly is the same. Your program could, in theory, poke the hardware directly, but that is hard and messy. Instead, the operating system offers a front desk called a software interrupt. You put a service number in a register, call the desk with one instruction, and DOS does the work. In this lesson you will use that front desk to read keys, print characters and messages, and even read and print full numbers like 2024.

Why we need help with I/O: The 8086 itself only knows registers, memory and ports. It has no idea what a letter on the screen is. A keyboard sends scan codes, and the screen shows what is stored in video memory. Writing code for all of that would take pages. DOS, the Disk Operating System that ran on early IBM PCs, already has this code, and so does the BIOS, the small program stored in ROM on the motherboard. We just call them. Today we run these programs in emu8086 or in DOSBox, because modern 64-bit Windows cannot run old 16-bit DOS programs directly.

The INT 21h front desk: The instruction INT 21h calls the main DOS service routine. How does DOS know what you want? You put a function number in AH before calling. Other registers carry the extra information, such as which character to print. INT works like a special procedure call: the CPU saves the flags, CS and IP, jumps to the routine, and comes back when the routine finishes. You will see exactly how this works in lesson 20; for now, treat INT 21h as 'please do function AH for me'.

Function 01h, read one key with echo: MOV AH, 01h then INT 21h. The program waits until the user presses a key. Then the ASCII code of that key is in AL, and DOS also shows the character on the screen, which is what echo means. If the user presses 7, AL becomes 37h, not 7. That small difference is the source of many bugs, as you will see. There is also function 08h, which reads a key the same way but does not show it, handy for passwords.

Function 02h, print one character: Put the ASCII code in DL, then MOV AH, 02h and INT 21h. So to print the letter A, write MOV DL, 'A' then MOV AH, 02h then INT 21h. The assembler turns 'A' into 41h for you. Printing a new line needs two characters: carriage return, 0Dh, which moves the cursor to the start of the line, and line feed, 0Ah, which moves it down one line. So a new line is two calls to function 02h, first with DL = 0Dh and then with DL = 0Ah.

Function 09h, print a string: Put the address of the string in DS:DX, then MOV AH, 09h and INT 21h. DOS prints characters one by one until it sees a dollar sign, '$'. The dollar sign itself is not printed. So in the data segment you write MSG DB 'Assalamu Alaikum$'. If you forget the $, DOS keeps printing whatever bytes follow in memory, and you get a screen full of strange symbols. You can also put the new line inside the string: MSG DB 'Hello', 0Dh, 0Ah, '$'.

Function 4Ch, end the program: MOV AH, 4Ch then INT 21h returns control to DOS. AL can hold a return code, where 0 usually means success, so many programmers write MOV AX, 4C00h then INT 21h. Never let your program just run off the end of the code. The CPU does not stop at your last line; it keeps executing whatever bytes happen to come next.

A complete first program: Here is a full program in MASM/TASM style. .MODEL SMALL, then .STACK 100h, then .DATA with MSG DB 'Hello, Dhaka!$', then .CODE, then MAIN PROC, then MOV AX, @DATA, then MOV DS, AX, then LEA DX, MSG, then MOV AH, 09h, then INT 21h, then MOV AH, 4Ch, then INT 21h, then MAIN ENDP and END MAIN. The two lines MOV AX, @DATA and MOV DS, AX point DS at our data segment. You cannot move an immediate value straight into DS, which is why AX is used as a helper. Without these two lines, DS:DX would point at the wrong place and function 09h would print rubbish.

Function 0Ah, read a whole line: Reading one key at a time is slow when you want a name. Function 0Ah reads a line into a buffer until the user presses Enter. The buffer has a special shape. Byte 0 is the maximum number of characters you allow, including the Enter. DOS fills byte 1 with how many characters were actually typed, not counting the Enter. The characters themselves start at byte 2, and the Enter key is stored after them as 0Dh. For a 20-character name you could declare BUF DB 21, ?, 21 DUP(?). Then LEA DX, BUF, MOV AH, 0Ah, INT 21h. If the user types Rafi and presses Enter, byte 1 becomes 4 and bytes 2 to 5 hold R, a, f, i.

ASCII digits versus numbers: The key 5 gives AL = 35h, which is 53 in decimal. The digits 0 to 9 have codes 30h to 39h. To turn a digit character into its value, subtract 30h, or the character '0'. To turn a value from 0 to 9 back into a character for printing, add 30h. Remember these two rules: input, subtract 30h; output, add 30h.

Adding two single digits: Read the first key with function 01h, then SUB AL, 30h and MOV BL, AL to save it. Read the second key, SUB AL, 30h, then ADD BL, AL. Now BL holds the sum. To print it, MOV DL, BL, ADD DL, 30h, MOV AH, 02h, INT 21h. If the user types 3 and 4, BL = 7 and the screen shows 7. But if the user types 8 and 5, the sum is 13, and adding 30h gives 3Dh, which is the '=' sign. One character can show only one digit, so bigger answers need the method below.

Reading a multi-digit number: The idea is the same as reading 2024 aloud: start with 0, and for each new digit, multiply what you have by 10 and add the digit. 0 becomes 2, then 20, then 202, then 2024. In assembly, keep the result in BX. Start with MOV BX, 0. At the label READ: do MOV AH, 01h and INT 21h. Then CMP AL, 0Dh and JE DONE to stop at Enter. Then SUB AL, 30h, MOV AH, 0, MOV CX, AX to keep the digit. Then MOV AX, BX, MOV DX, 10, MUL DX, which leaves AX times 10 in DX:AX. Then ADD AX, CX, MOV BX, AX and JMP READ. At DONE, BX holds the number. This works for values up to 65,535 and does not check for wrong keys, which a real program should.

Printing a multi-digit number: Now the reverse. If AX = 305, how do we print 3, 0, 5? Divide by 10 again and again. The remainder is the last digit each time. 305 divided by 10 is 30 remainder 5. 30 divided by 10 is 3 remainder 0. 3 divided by 10 is 0 remainder 3. We got the digits backwards, 5, 0, 3. The stack fixes that, since the last thing pushed is the first thing popped.

The print code: MOV CX, 0 and MOV BX, 10. At DIVIDE: MOV DX, 0, then DIV BX, which puts the quotient in AX and the remainder in DX. Then PUSH DX, INC CX, CMP AX, 0 and JNE DIVIDE. Then at PRINT: POP DX, ADD DL, 30h, MOV AH, 02h, INT 21h, and LOOP PRINT. The MOV DX, 0 before each DIV is essential, because DIV BX divides the 32-bit number DX:AX. If DX holds garbage, the answer is wrong or the CPU raises a divide error. CX counts how many digits we pushed, and LOOP pops exactly that many.

Case conversion: In ASCII, 'A' is 41h and 'a' is 61h. Every lowercase letter is exactly 20h more than its capital. So to turn a lowercase letter into a capital, SUB AL, 20h, or AND AL, 0DFh, which clears bit 5. To go the other way, ADD AL, 20h or OR AL, 20h. A safe program checks the range first: CMP AL, 'a', JB SKIP, CMP AL, 'z', JA SKIP, then SUB AL, 20h, then SKIP:. Without the check, a digit or a space would also be changed into a strange symbol.

The BIOS layer: DOS functions sit on top of BIOS services. You can call the BIOS directly too. INT 10h is the video service; with AH = 0Eh it prints the character in AL in teletype style. INT 16h is the keyboard service; with AH = 00h it waits for a key and returns the ASCII code in AL and the scan code in AH. BIOS calls work even without DOS, which is why boot loaders use them. In university labs, though, INT 21h is the usual choice.

Real life example 1, a bKash-style PIN screen: Imagine a tiny menu program on a shop's old PC that asks for a four-digit PIN. It prints 'Enter PIN:$' with function 09h. Then it reads four keys with function 08h, so the digits are not shown, and prints '*' with function 02h after each key. It converts each key by subtracting 30h and builds the number with the multiply-by-10 method. Finally it compares the result with the stored PIN using CMP and JE. Every piece of that program is in this lesson.

Real life example 2, a cricket score display: A club in Sylhet keeps the total runs of a match in AX, for example 287. To show 'Runs: 287', the program first prints the label with function 09h, then calls the printing routine above. 287 divided by 10 gives remainder 7, then 28 gives 8, then 2 gives 2, so the stack holds 7, 8, 2 and pops 2, 8, 7. The screen shows 287. When the score changes, the same routine works for 5 runs or 312 runs, because it does not care how many digits there are.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting MOV AX, @DATA and MOV DS, AX, so strings print as garbage. Second, forgetting the $ at the end of a string. Third, treating the ASCII code of a digit as its value. Fourth, not clearing DX before DIV. Fifth, forgetting that INT 21h overwrites AL with its result, so a value you kept in AL is lost; keep important values in other registers. Sixth, ending without function 4Ch.

What exams ask: 'Write a program to read a character and display it in uppercase', 'Write a program to input two digits and display their sum', 'Explain functions 01h, 02h, 09h and 4Ch of INT 21h', 'Write a procedure to display a 16-bit number in decimal' and 'Describe the buffer format of function 0Ah'. Tracing the multiply-by-10 and divide-by-10 loops on paper is the best preparation.

Recap: Programs talk to the keyboard and screen through INT 21h, with the function number in AH. 01h reads a key into AL, 02h prints DL, 09h prints a $-ended string at DS:DX, 0Ah reads a line into a buffer, and 4Ch ends the program. Digits arrive as ASCII, so subtract 30h on input and add 30h on output. Multi-digit numbers are built by multiplying by 10 and printed by dividing by 10 and using the stack. Next we use these tools on whole arrays and strings.
key_points: INT 21h is the DOS service call; the function number goes in AH.
01h reads a key into AL with echo, 02h prints the character in DL, 09h prints a $-terminated string at DS:DX, 4Ch ends the program.
Set DS with MOV AX, @DATA then MOV DS, AX before printing strings.
Function 0Ah buffer: byte 0 = max length, byte 1 = count typed, text from byte 2, ending in 0Dh.
Digits arrive as ASCII 30h-39h: subtract 30h on input, add 30h on output.
Read a number by result = result x 10 + digit; print it by dividing by 10, pushing remainders and popping them.
Always clear DX before DIV with a 16-bit divisor.
Lowercase and capital letters differ by 20h, so SUB 20h or AND 0DFh converts to capitals.
lessons.tip: Keep a small cheat card with the five INT 21h functions and the two ASCII rules (minus 30h in, plus 30h out). Almost every lab program uses only these, so learning them by heart frees your mind for the logic.
lessons.task: Using emu8086 or DOSBox, or just paper, write a program that reads a lowercase letter and prints it as a capital on a new line. Then extend it to read a three-digit number like 125 and print it back. On paper, trace the stack contents while printing 125.

quiz.q: Which INT 21h function prints a string that ends with '$'?
quiz.explain: Function 09h prints the string at DS:DX until it meets the $ character. 01h reads a key, 02h prints one character and 4Ch ends the program.

quiz.q: The user presses the key 6 after MOV AH, 01h / INT 21h. What is in AL?
quiz.explain: AL holds the ASCII code. Digits 0 to 9 are 30h to 39h, so 6 is 36h. Subtract 30h to get the value 6.

quiz.q: Why must DX be set to 0 before DIV BX in the number-printing routine?
options: Because DIV BX divides the 32-bit value DX:AX by BX
Because DIV puts the quotient in DX
Because DX holds the loop counter
quiz.explain: A 16-bit DIV divides DX:AX. Leftover data in DX would make the result wrong or cause a divide error.

quiz.q: How do you convert the lowercase letter in AL into a capital letter?
quiz.explain: Capitals are 20h less than lowercase letters. AND AL, 0DFh clears bit 5, which subtracts 20h from a lowercase letter. ADD and OR with 20h go the other way.

quiz.q: In a function 0Ah buffer, what does byte 1 contain after the call?
options: The number of characters actually typed, not counting Enter
quiz.explain: Byte 0 is the maximum you set, byte 1 is filled by DOS with the count of characters typed, and the text starts at byte 2.

lessons.title: Arrays and String Instructions
lessons.content:
Imagine a row of lockers in a school corridor, numbered 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. If the teacher says 'bring me what is in locker 4', you walk to the first locker and count four steps along. That is exactly what an array is in memory: a row of bytes or words sitting side by side, and you reach any one of them by starting at the first and adding a step count. Now imagine the teacher says 'copy everything from this row of lockers into that row'. Doing it one by one is boring, so the 8086 has special string instructions that do the walking and copying almost by themselves. In this lesson you will learn both: how to handle arrays by hand with registers, and how to let string instructions do the heavy work.

Declaring arrays: In the data segment you write MARKS DB 5, 12, 7, 20, 3. That reserves 5 bytes one after another, and the name MARKS stands for the address of the first one. For 16-bit values use DW: PRICES DW 1200, 850, 3000. Each element now takes 2 bytes. To reserve space without fixed values, use DUP: BUF DB 50 DUP(0) makes 50 bytes filled with 0, and TABLE DW 10 DUP(?) makes 10 words with no starting value. A string is just a byte array of ASCII codes: NAME1 DB 'Karim'.

The address of element i: If the array starts at address A and each element is s bytes, then element i, counting from 0, is at A + i x s. For a byte array, element 3 of MARKS is at MARKS + 3, holding 20. For a word array, element 2 of PRICES is at PRICES + 4, holding 3000, not PRICES + 2. Forgetting to multiply by 2 for word arrays is one of the most common mistakes in this topic.

Accessing elements with registers: Recall the addressing modes from lesson 9. You can write MOV BX, 3 and then MOV AL, MARKS[BX], which uses based or indexed addressing with a displacement and loads the byte at MARKS + 3. Or you can put the address itself in a register: LEA SI, MARKS, then MOV AL, [SI] reads element 0, INC SI moves to element 1, and so on. Only BX, SI, DI and BP can be used inside square brackets on the 8086. Writing MOV AL, [CX] is an error.

Sum of an array: Let us add up MARKS. LEA SI, MARKS, then MOV CX, 5, then MOV AL, 0. At the label SUMUP: ADD AL, [SI], then INC SI, then LOOP SUMUP. Trace it: AL becomes 5, then 17, 24, 44 and finally 47. AL = 47, which is 2Fh. The sum fits in one byte here, but if the total could go above 255, you should add into a 16-bit register. A neat way is to use MOV AH, 0 with AL, or to load each byte into DL with MOV DL, [SI] and MOV DH, 0, then ADD AX, DX.

Sum of a word array: For PRICES, the step is 2. LEA SI, PRICES, MOV CX, 3, MOV AX, 0. At ADDW: ADD AX, [SI], then ADD SI, 2, then LOOP ADDW. AX ends as 1200 + 850 + 3000 = 5050. Using INC SI once instead of ADD SI, 2 would read half of one number and half of the next, giving a silly answer with no error message. Assembly never warns you about this; it just does what you say.

Finding the largest element: The plan is to assume the first is the biggest, then compare it with every other one. LEA SI, MARKS, MOV AL, [SI], MOV CX, 4. At NEXT: INC SI, CMP AL, [SI], JAE SKIP, MOV AL, [SI], then SKIP: and LOOP NEXT. CX is 4, not 5, because the first element is already in AL. Trace it: AL = 5, then 12 is bigger so AL = 12, 7 is not, 20 is bigger so AL = 20, 3 is not. Answer 20. We used JAE because marks are unsigned. For signed numbers like temperatures, use JGE instead. To find the smallest, flip the jump to JBE.

Why string instructions exist: Loops like the ones above repeat the same three steps: read with a pointer, do something, move the pointer. The 8086 designers built these steps into single instructions called string instructions. They always use SI as the source pointer, with DS as its segment, and DI as the destination pointer, with ES as its segment. After each operation they automatically move SI and DI forward or backward. 'String' here just means a block of bytes or words, not only text.

The direction flag: Which way do SI and DI move? That depends on DF, the direction flag from lesson 8. CLD clears DF to 0, and then the pointers increase after each step: by 1 for byte versions, by 2 for word versions. STD sets DF to 1, and then the pointers decrease. Always write CLD before using string instructions unless you really need to go backwards, because you cannot be sure what DF was left as.

Setting up ES: Since the destination is ES:DI, ES must point to the right segment. In a small program where everything is in one data segment, the start of the program becomes MOV AX, @DATA, then MOV DS, AX, then MOV ES, AX. Students often set DS and forget ES, and then the copy lands in some random place in memory.

MOVSB and MOVSW: MOVSB copies one byte from DS:[SI] to ES:[DI], then moves both pointers. MOVSW does the same for a word. The 8086 has no ordinary memory-to-memory MOV, but MOVS is the special case that copies memory to memory directly.

The REP prefix: A prefix is written before an instruction and changes how it runs. REP means: while CX is not 0, do the instruction and decrease CX. So to copy a 10-byte string: LEA SI, SRC, then LEA DI, DST, then MOV CX, 10, then CLD, then REP MOVSB. That one line replaces a whole loop. After it finishes, CX = 0, and SI and DI point just past the end of each block.

STOSB and LODSB: STOSB stores AL into ES:[DI] and moves DI. With REP it fills memory: MOV AL, '*', LEA DI, BUF, MOV CX, 10, CLD, REP STOSB fills 10 bytes with stars. STOSW stores AX. LODSB loads the byte at DS:[SI] into AL and moves SI. LODSB is not used with REP, because each load would overwrite the last one; instead it is used inside a normal loop together with STOSB.

A LODSB and STOSB pair, uppercase a string: Put SI and DI both at the start of the string, set CX to its length and use CLD. At UP: LODSB, then CMP AL, 'a', JB KEEP, CMP AL, 'z', JA KEEP, SUB AL, 20h, then KEEP: STOSB and LOOP UP. Each byte is read, changed if it is a lowercase letter, and written back to the same place. 'dhaka 2024' becomes 'DHAKA 2024', and the digits and space stay unchanged.

CMPSB and SCASB: CMPSB compares the byte at DS:[SI] with the byte at ES:[DI] by subtracting the second from the first, sets flags, and moves both pointers. The memory is not changed. SCASB, scan string, compares AL with the byte at ES:[DI], sets flags and moves DI. The word versions are CMPSW and SCASW, which use AX.

REPE and REPNE: For compare and scan you usually want to stop early. REPE, also written REPZ, repeats while CX is not 0 and ZF = 1, that is, while things are still equal. REPNE, also written REPNZ, repeats while CX is not 0 and ZF = 0, that is, while things are still different. To check whether two 8-character passwords match: set SI and DI, MOV CX, 8, CLD, REPE CMPSB, then JE SAME. If every byte matched, the last compare left ZF = 1. If any byte differed, the repeat stopped there with ZF = 0.

Searching with REPNE SCASB: To find the letter 'r' in the string 'Barisal': LEA DI, CITY, MOV CX, 7, MOV AL, 'r', CLD, REPNE SCASB, then JE FOUND. The scan compares B, a, then r, where ZF becomes 1 and it stops. DI now points one byte past the match, so the position of 'r' is DI - 1. If no match is found, CX reaches 0 and ZF = 0, so JE does not jump.

Overlapping blocks: Suppose you want to shift a block 2 bytes higher in memory so the source and destination overlap. If you copy forwards, you overwrite source bytes before reading them. The fix is to copy backwards: point SI and DI at the last byte of each block, use STD, then REP MOVSB, and finish with CLD. When the destination is at a lower address than the source, a forward copy is safe.

Real life example 1, a class result sheet: A school in Rajshahi stores the marks of 40 students as a byte array. The program uses a LOOP with [SI] to find the total and the highest mark, and then divides the total by 40 with DIV to get the average. To make a backup copy of the marks before editing, it uses REP MOVSB with CX = 40. And to reset the array to zero for a new term, REP STOSB with AL = 0 does it in one instruction.

Real life example 2, searching a contact list: An old feature phone stores names as fixed 16-byte records. To find whether 'Nusrat' is in the list, the program points DI at each record in turn and uses REPE CMPSB with CX = 6 to compare. If ZF = 1 after the compare, the name is found. To find the end of a name padded with spaces, REPNE SCASB with AL = ' ' finds the first space. These tiny loops are the same ideas phone software was built on.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to set ES. Second, forgetting CLD and getting a backward copy. Third, using INC SI on a word array. Fourth, forgetting that after REPNE SCASB the pointer has gone one past the match. Fifth, mixing up REPE and REPNE: comparing two strings needs REPE, but searching for one character needs REPNE. Sixth, putting CX inside brackets.

What exams ask: 'Write a program to find the largest number in an array of 10 bytes', 'Explain MOVSB, CMPSB, SCASB, LODSB and STOSB', 'What is the role of DF?', 'Write a program to copy a string using string instructions', 'Difference between REP, REPE and REPNE' and 'Search a character in a string and print found or not found'. Remember the table: source DS:SI, destination ES:DI, count CX, direction DF.

Recap: An array is a row of elements, and element i is at the start plus i times the element size. You can walk it with BX, SI or DI and a LOOP. String instructions automate the pattern using DS:SI as source, ES:DI as destination, and DF for direction. MOVS copies, STOS fills, LODS loads, CMPS compares two blocks and SCAS searches for AL or AX. REP repeats CX times, and REPE and REPNE also stop on the zero flag. Next you will look closely at the stack that PUSH and POP have been quietly using.
key_points: Element i of an array is at start + i x element size; word arrays step by 2.
Only BX, SI, DI and BP can be used as pointers inside square brackets on the 8086.
String instructions use DS:SI as source, ES:DI as destination, and update the pointers automatically.
CLD makes pointers increase, STD makes them decrease; set DF before using string instructions.
MOVSB copies, STOSB fills from AL, LODSB loads into AL, CMPSB compares two blocks, SCASB compares AL with ES:[DI].
REP repeats CX times; REPE/REPZ repeats while equal; REPNE/REPNZ repeats while not equal.
After REPNE SCASB finds a match, DI points one byte past it.
Copy backwards with STD when blocks overlap and the destination is higher.
lessons.tip: Draw memory as a row of boxes and write SI, DI and CX under it in pencil. Move the arrows by hand as each instruction runs. String instructions feel magical until you trace them like this a few times.
lessons.task: On paper, declare A DB 9, 4, 15, 2, 11. Write a loop that finds the smallest value, then write REP MOVSB code to copy A into a new array B. Trace SI, DI and CX after each step and check that B ends up the same as A.

quiz.q: Which registers do string instructions use as source and destination pointers?
options: DS:SI for source and ES:DI for destination
ES:SI for source and DS:DI for destination
CS:IP for source and SS:SP for destination
DS:BX for source and DS:BP for destination
quiz.explain: The source is always DS:SI (the segment can be overridden) and the destination is always ES:DI.

quiz.q: What does CLD do before a string instruction?
options: Clears DF, so SI and DI increase after each step
Sets DF, so SI and DI decrease
quiz.explain: CLD clears the direction flag. With DF = 0, string instructions increment SI and DI. STD sets DF and makes them decrement.

quiz.q: PRICES DW 1200, 850, 3000 starts at offset 0100h. At which offset is the value 3000?
quiz.explain: Each word is 2 bytes, so element 2 is at 0100h + 2 x 2 = 0104h.

quiz.q: Which prefix is right for comparing two strings and stopping at the first difference?
quiz.explain: REPE (REPZ) keeps repeating CMPSB while CX is not zero and ZF = 1, so it stops at the first mismatch.

quiz.q: After REPNE SCASB finds the searched character, where does DI point?
options: At the first byte of the string
One byte past the matching byte
At the last byte of the string
quiz.explain: SCASB moves DI after every compare, including the one that matched, so the match is at DI - 1 when DF = 0.

lessons.title: The Stack
lessons.content:
Imagine a wedding in a community hall in Dhaka. The catering boys stack clean plates one on top of another on a big table. When a guest wants a plate, they take the one on top, which is the plate that was put down last. Nobody pulls a plate from the bottom of the pile, because the whole pile would crash. This rule, last in, first out, or LIFO, is exactly how the stack works inside the 8086. The stack is a part of memory where the CPU and your program can quickly park values and get them back later, always in reverse order. It looks simple, but procedures, interrupts, local variables and even recursion all depend on it. In this lesson you will see exactly how it works, byte by byte.

What the stack is: The stack is an area of ordinary RAM inside the stack segment. Two registers manage it. SS, the stack segment register, holds the segment where the stack lives. SP, the stack pointer, holds the offset of the top of the stack, which is the last word that was pushed. So the physical address of the top is SS x 16 + SP, using the same segment rule from lesson 7. BP, the base pointer, is a helper register that also uses SS by default, which makes it useful for reading values deep inside the stack.

The stack grows downward: This surprises many students. On the 8086, every time you push, SP gets smaller, and every time you pop, SP gets bigger. So the stack grows toward lower addresses. Think of the plate pile hanging upside down from the ceiling. The 'bottom' of the stack is at a high address and new items are added below it. One reason for this design is that the program's data can grow upward from low addresses while the stack grows down from the top, so the two meet only if memory truly runs out.

Setting up the stack: In a MASM or TASM program, the line .STACK 100h reserves 256 bytes for the stack. When DOS loads the program, it sets SS to the stack segment and sets SP to point just past the end of the reserved area, so the first push lands at the very top of that space. You normally never change SS and SP yourself in simple programs. If you ever do, change them one right after the other, because an interrupt arriving between the two changes would use a half-set stack. The 8086 helps by holding off interrupts for one instruction after a MOV to SS.

PUSH step by step: PUSH source works only with 16-bit values on the 8086: a 16-bit register, a segment register or a word in memory. It does two things. First, SP = SP - 2. Second, the word is copied to SS:SP, with the low byte at the lower address and the high byte at the next address, in little-endian order. You cannot write PUSH AL, because the stack works in words. On the original 8086 you also cannot write PUSH 5 with an immediate number; that was added from the 80186 onwards.

A worked PUSH example: Let SS = 2000h, SP = 0100h and AX = 1234h. Execute PUSH AX. SP becomes 00FEh. The physical address is 20000h + 00FEh = 200FEh. Memory at 200FEh gets 34h, the low byte, and 200FFh gets 12h, the high byte. Now let BX = 5678h and execute PUSH BX. SP becomes 00FCh, 200FCh gets 78h and 200FDh gets 56h. The top of the stack is now BX's value, sitting below AX's value in memory.

POP step by step: POP destination does the reverse. First, the word at SS:SP is copied into the destination. Second, SP = SP + 2. Continuing the example, POP CX copies the word at 200FCh, which is 5678h, into CX, and SP returns to 00FEh. Then POP DX gets 1234h and SP returns to 0100h. Notice that POP does not erase the memory; the old bytes are still sitting there. They are simply considered free, and the next push will overwrite them. You can POP into any 16-bit register, memory word or segment register except CS.

The golden rule of order: Because of LIFO, you pop in the reverse order of pushing. If you write PUSH AX, PUSH BX, PUSH CX, you must write POP CX, POP BX, POP AX to get each value back into its own register. If you pop in the same order you pushed, the values get swapped around. Sometimes that is exactly what you want: PUSH AX, PUSH BX, POP AX, POP BX swaps AX and BX. XCHG AX, BX does the same in one instruction, but the stack trick works for any pair, even segment registers like DS and ES.

PUSHF and POPF: PUSHF pushes the 16-bit flags register onto the stack, and POPF pops a word into the flags register. These are useful to protect the flags while you do something that changes them. They are also the standard way to change the trap flag, TF, which has no direct set or clear instruction: you PUSHF, POP into AX, change bit 8 with OR or AND, PUSH AX and POPF. Debuggers use this trick to run a program one instruction at a time. Later processors also added PUSHA and POPA to save all general registers at once, but the original 8086 does not have them.

Who else uses the stack: You are not the only user. When the CPU executes CALL, it pushes the return address so that RET knows where to come back to. When an interrupt happens, the CPU pushes the flags, CS and IP, and IRET pops them back. Lesson 19 covers procedures and lesson 20 covers interrupts in detail. The key idea for now is that your pushes and pops share the stack with these automatic ones, so you must keep things balanced.

Balance: Every PUSH inside a block of code must be matched by exactly one POP before the block ends. Suppose a procedure does PUSH AX at the start but forgets the POP before RET. RET will pop the saved AX value and treat it as the return address, and the program jumps into nonsense. This is the most common stack bug, and it usually crashes the program or freezes the emulator.

Reading inside the stack with BP: Sometimes you want to look at a value on the stack without popping it. Copy SP into BP with MOV BP, SP. Now [BP] is the top word, [BP+2] is the one pushed before it, [BP+4] the one before that, and so on. Because BP uses SS by default, MOV AX, [BP+2] reads from the stack segment automatically. On the 8086 you cannot write [SP+2] as an address, which is why BP exists. Lesson 19 builds stack frames on this idea.

Example, reversing a string: Here the LIFO rule does real work. Suppose the user types a word ending with Enter. At READ: MOV AH, 01h and INT 21h, then CMP AL, 0Dh and JE SHOW. Then MOV AH, 0, PUSH AX, INC CX and JMP READ. We set AH to 0 because PUSH needs a full word. At SHOW: JCXZ DONE in case nothing was typed, then at OUT1: POP DX, MOV AH, 02h, INT 21h and LOOP OUT1. The popped word has the character in DL, which is exactly what function 02h prints. Remember to MOV CX, 0 before reading. If the user types 'Dhaka', the screen shows 'akahD'.

Example, saving a register you need: Suppose CX holds an outer loop count, but you want to call a DOS routine and use CX for something else. PUSH CX before, use CX freely, then POP CX after. This is the same trick we used for nested loops in lesson 15. The stack is like a temporary pocket where you keep things while your hands are busy.

Stack overflow: If you push too many values, SP keeps going down past the bottom of the reserved stack area and starts overwriting other memory, such as your data or even code. This is called stack overflow. The 8086 does not check for it at all. Runaway recursion, where a procedure calls itself forever, is the classic cause. The famous error message on modern systems, and the name of the website programmers use, both come from this.

Stack underflow: Popping more values than you pushed is underflow. SP goes above where the stack started, and you read whatever happened to be there, which is garbage. Again the 8086 does not stop you. Careful counting is the only defence: count the PUSHes and POPs along every path through your code, including early exits by jumps.

How much stack is enough: Each PUSH, CALL and interrupt uses 2 to 6 bytes. A simple lab program rarely needs more than 100h bytes. A program with deep recursion needs more: if each call pushes 6 bytes and recursion goes 100 levels deep, that is 600 bytes. Interrupts from hardware such as the timer can arrive at any moment and use your stack too, so always keep some spare room.

Real life example 1, the back button on your phone: When you open Facebook, then a profile, then a photo, then the comments, each screen is pushed onto a stack. Pressing back pops the top screen and shows the one below it. You come back through the screens in the reverse order you opened them. Phone operating systems keep exactly this kind of stack, called a back stack, though in a high-level form.

Real life example 2, checking brackets in a formula: Suppose a calculator app in a school checks whether brackets are balanced in (2 + [3 x 4]). Each opening bracket is pushed. Each closing bracket pops the top and checks that it is the matching type. At the end the stack must be empty. If a ] arrives when the top is (, or the stack is empty when a closing bracket comes, the formula is wrong. Compilers check your C code the same way, using the same idea of last in, first out.

Common mistakes: First, thinking the stack grows upward and adding 2 on a push. Second, trying PUSH AL or PUSH 5 on an 8086. Third, popping in the same order as pushing when you meant to restore. Fourth, leaving an unbalanced PUSH before RET. Fifth, forgetting that POP does not clear memory. Sixth, writing [SP] as an address instead of using BP.

What exams ask: 'Explain the operation of PUSH and POP with a diagram', 'Given SS = 3000h, SP = 0200h and AX = ABCDh, show memory and SP after PUSH AX', 'What is the physical address of the top of the stack?', 'Write a program to reverse a string using the stack', 'What are stack overflow and underflow?' and 'Why does the stack grow downward?'. Draw the memory boxes with addresses every time; marks are given for the diagram.

Recap: The stack is a LIFO area of memory at SS:SP. PUSH subtracts 2 from SP and then stores a word; POP reads a word and then adds 2. Low bytes go to lower addresses. Pop in reverse order to restore, and keep every path balanced. PUSHF and POPF save the flags, BP lets you read inside the stack, and CALL and interrupts use the same stack automatically. Next, you will see how procedures use the stack to return home and to pass parameters.
key_points: The stack is LIFO memory at SS:SP; its top is at physical address SS x 16 + SP.
On the 8086 the stack grows downward: PUSH makes SP smaller, POP makes it bigger.
PUSH: SP = SP - 2, then store the word (low byte at the lower address). POP: read the word, then SP = SP + 2.
Only 16-bit values can be pushed; the 8086 has no PUSH AL or PUSH immediate, and POP CS is not allowed.
Pop in reverse order to restore registers; same order swaps them.
PUSHF and POPF save and restore the flags; BP with SS reads values inside the stack.
CALL and interrupts use the same stack, so every PUSH must be balanced by a POP.
The 8086 never checks for stack overflow or underflow; careful counting is your job.
lessons.tip: For every stack question, draw a column of memory boxes with addresses going down, and an arrow labelled SP. Move the arrow by 2 for every PUSH or POP. If your drawing ends with SP back where it started, your code is balanced.
lessons.task: On paper, start with SS = 3000h, SP = 0200h, AX = 1111h, BX = 2222h, CX = 3333h. Run PUSH AX, PUSH BX, PUSH CX, POP AX, POP BX, POP CX. Write SP and the memory bytes after each step, then write the final values of AX, BX and CX.

quiz.q: SS = 2000h and SP = 0100h. After PUSH AX, what is SP?
quiz.explain: PUSH first subtracts 2 from SP, so 0100h becomes 00FEh, then stores the word there.

quiz.q: With SS = 2000h and SP = 00FEh, what is the physical address of the top of the stack?
quiz.explain: Physical address = SS x 16 + SP = 20000h + 00FEh = 200FEh.

quiz.q: Which instruction is NOT allowed on the original 8086?
quiz.explain: The 8086 stack works only with 16-bit words, so PUSH AL is invalid. PUSH BX, PUSH DS and PUSHF all push 16-bit values.

quiz.q: After PUSH AX, PUSH BX, which sequence restores both registers to their original values?
quiz.explain: The last value pushed, BX, is on top, so it must be popped first. Popping AX first would swap the two registers.

quiz.q: A procedure pushes AX at the start but forgets to pop it before RET. What happens?
options: RET pops the saved AX value as the return address and the program jumps to a wrong place
Nothing, the extra word is ignored
quiz.explain: RET simply pops the top word into IP. If AX is still on top, its value becomes the return address, and the program goes off into nonsense.

lessons.title: Procedures and Macros
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother sends you to the corner shop many times a day: once for eggs, once for salt, once for a packet of tea. Every time, the steps are the same: put on sandals, walk down the lane, buy the thing, walk back, and come home to exactly where you were before. Nobody writes these steps again for every trip. She just says "go to the shop" and you know the routine. In assembly language, a routine you can send the processor to, again and again, is called a procedure. In this lesson you will learn how the 8086 jumps into a procedure, how it finds its way back home, how to hand it values, how a procedure can even call itself, and how a macro is a different trick that looks similar but works in a completely different way.

What a procedure is: A procedure (also called a subroutine or function) is a group of instructions with a name, written once and used from many places. In MASM or TASM style you write it between two directives: PRINTNUM PROC NEAR at the top and PRINTNUM ENDP at the bottom, with a RET instruction inside to come back. PROC and ENDP are not instructions for the processor; they are notes for the assembler that mark where the procedure starts and ends. The real work of going and coming back is done by two instructions: CALL and RET.

Why bother: Procedures make programs shorter, because the same code is stored once. They make programs easier to read, because a name like READNUM tells you what a block does. They make bugs easier to fix, because you fix one place instead of ten. This is the same idea as functions in C, which you met in the structured programming course; here you see what happens underneath.

How CALL works: CALL has two jobs. First it saves the return address, which is the address of the instruction right after the CALL, by pushing it on the stack. Then it jumps to the procedure. For a near call, which stays inside the same code segment, only IP is pushed: SP goes down by 2 and the 16-bit IP is stored at SS:SP. Then IP is loaded with the procedure's address. CS does not change because we never leave the segment.

How RET works: RET does the opposite. A near RET pops the top word of the stack into IP, and SP goes up by 2. Since that word is the return address CALL saved, the processor continues with the instruction right after the CALL. This is why the stack must be tidy when RET runs. If your procedure pushed something and forgot to pop it, RET would pop that value into IP and the processor would jump to a random place. Most crashing beginner programs crash exactly here.

A tiny trace: Suppose SP = 0100h and a CALL at offset 0020h is 3 bytes long, so the next instruction is at 0023h. The procedure starts at offset 0050h. CALL pushes 0023h: SP becomes 00FEh and the word at SS:00FEh is 0023h. IP becomes 0050h. The procedure runs. Its RET pops 0023h into IP, and SP is back to 0100h. The program continues at 0023h as if nothing happened, except the work the procedure did.

Near and far: A near procedure is in the same code segment as the caller, which is called an intrasegment call. A far procedure may be in a different code segment, an intersegment call. A far CALL pushes two words: first the current CS, then IP, so SP goes down by 4. Then it loads both CS and IP with the new address. The matching far return, which MASM produces from RET inside a PROC FAR (or which you can write as RETF), pops IP first and then CS. If a near RET is used for a far call, only IP comes back and CS is wrong, which is a nasty bug. So the type of CALL and the type of RET must match.

Direct and indirect calls: CALL PRINTNUM is a direct call, the address is written inside the instruction. You can also call through a register or memory: CALL BX jumps to the near address held in BX. Jump tables use this: a list of procedure addresses in memory, and you call the one you need.

Passing parameters in registers: The simplest way to give a procedure its inputs is to put them in registers before the CALL. For example, a rule could be "put the number in AX, CALL PRINTNUM, and it prints AX". Results also come back in registers, often AX. This is fast and easy, but there are only a few registers, and you must write down clearly which register means what. DOS services work this way too, with a function number in AH.

Passing parameters in memory: Another way is to store the inputs in named variables in the data segment, or to pass the address of a block of data in a register such as SI or BX. To sum an array, you can put the array's offset in SI and its length in CX, then call SUMARR. The procedure walks through memory using SI. This is handy when there is a lot of data, because you pass only one address instead of copying everything.

Passing parameters on the stack: The most general way, and the one C compilers use, is to push the inputs on the stack before the CALL. Example for a near procedure that adds two numbers: (1) PUSH AX with the first number, (2) PUSH BX with the second, (3) CALL ADDTWO. Inside ADDTWO you write (1) PUSH BP, (2) MOV BP, SP. Now BP is a fixed bookmark into the stack. At [BP+0] is the old BP, at [BP+2] is the return address, at [BP+4] is the second parameter (the last one pushed), and at [BP+6] is the first parameter. So MOV AX, [BP+6] then ADD AX, [BP+4] gives the sum in AX. At the end you write POP BP and then RET 4.

Why BP and not SP: The 8086 cannot use SP inside square brackets as an address register, so MOV AX, [SP+4] is not allowed. BP can, and when you use BP in an address, the default segment is SS, which is exactly where the stack lives. Also, SP keeps moving every time you push or pop, while BP stays still, so the offsets +4 and +6 stay correct for the whole procedure. This BP setup is called a stack frame.

What RET 4 means: After the procedure returns, the two parameters are still sitting on the stack, wasting 4 bytes. Someone must remove them. RET n pops the return address and then adds n to SP, throwing away n bytes of parameters. RET 4 throws away two words. Alternatively the caller can clean up with ADD SP, 4 right after the CALL. Either is fine, but exactly one side must do it; if both do, or neither does, the stack goes wrong.

Saving registers: A good procedure leaves the caller's registers as it found them, except the ones used for results. So at the top it pushes the registers it will change, and at the bottom pops them in reverse order: PUSH BX, PUSH CX at the start, then POP CX, POP BX before RET. Reverse order matters because the stack is last in, first out. Popping in the same order would swap the values of BX and CX.

Recursion with factorial: A procedure can call itself, because each CALL saves its own return address on the stack. Here is a factorial procedure. Input: AX = n. Output: AX = n!. FACT PROC NEAR, then: (1) CMP AX, 1, (2) JA RECURSE, (3) MOV AX, 1, (4) RET. Then the label RECURSE: (5) PUSH AX to save n, (6) DEC AX so AX = n - 1, (7) CALL FACT so AX = (n - 1)!, (8) POP BX so BX = n, (9) MUL BX so DX:AX = AX times BX, (10) RET. Then FACT ENDP. For n = 3: the first call saves 3 and calls with 2; that call saves 2 and calls with 1; with 1, AX becomes 1 and it returns. Then 1 times 2 = 2, return, then 2 times 3 = 6. Done.

The limit of recursion: Each level of recursion uses stack space: here 2 bytes for the saved n and 2 bytes for the return address. A very deep recursion can run out of stack and overwrite other data, which is a stack overflow. Also notice the size limit of the answer: 8! = 40320 fits in 16 bits, but 9! = 362880 does not fit in AX, so this simple version is only correct up to n = 8 (higher bits would go to DX and later steps would ignore them).

What a macro is: A macro is a named piece of text that the assembler copies into your program wherever you use the name. Example: PRINT MACRO MSG, then (1) LEA DX, MSG, (2) MOV AH, 09h, (3) INT 21h, then ENDM. When you write PRINT HELLO in your code, the assembler replaces it with those three instructions, with HELLO in place of MSG. This happens at assembly time, before the program ever runs. The processor never sees the word PRINT.

Macro versus procedure: A procedure's code exists once, and each use is a CALL plus RET, so the program stays small but every use pays a little time for the jump and the stack work. A macro's code is copied at every use, so there is no CALL or RET, which is slightly faster, but the program grows bigger with each use. Macros can take text parameters easily; procedures take values in registers or on the stack. Rule of thumb: short, often-used pieces like printing a message are good macros, while long pieces like sorting an array should be procedures. One more catch: if a macro contains a label and you use the macro twice, the label appears twice and the assembler complains. The LOCAL directive inside the macro solves this by making a fresh label name for each copy.

Real life example 1, a bKash style menu: Think of a mobile wallet menu: 1 for Send Money, 2 for Cash Out, 3 for Check Balance. In an assembly program you could write three procedures, SENDMONEY, CASHOUT and BALANCE, plus one procedure READCHOICE that reads a key with INT 21h function 01h. The main program becomes a short loop: call READCHOICE, compare AL with '1', '2', '3', and call the right procedure. Each procedure saves the registers it uses, does its job, and returns. If the Cash Out rules change, you edit only CASHOUT. That is the power of procedures in a real system.

Real life example 2, a result sheet at school: Suppose a teacher in Rajshahi writes a small program to print marks of 40 students. Printing a number needs about fifteen instructions: divide by 10 again and again, push the digits, then pop and print them. Writing those fifteen lines 40 times is silly.
