Instead, PRINTNUM is written once as a procedure taking the number in AX. Meanwhile, printing a new line is just two or three instructions, so the teacher makes it a macro called NEWLINE. The program mixes both: CALL PRINTNUM for the long job, NEWLINE for the tiny job.

Common mistakes: First, unequal PUSH and POP inside a procedure, so RET pops the wrong value. Second, using a near RET with a far CALL, or the opposite. Third, forgetting that MUL BX changes DX too, so a value you kept in DX is lost. Fourth, getting stack offsets wrong: in a near procedure with the BP frame, the last pushed parameter is at [BP+4], not [BP+2]; in a far procedure it moves to [BP+6] because the return address is 4 bytes. Fifth, cleaning parameters twice, with both RET 4 and ADD SP, 4.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: "Explain what happens to the stack during near and far CALL and RET", "Differentiate between a macro and a procedure", "Write a procedure that finds the largest of an array passed by address", "Show how parameters are passed through the stack using BP", and "Write a recursive procedure for factorial and trace it for n = 3". Draw the stack as boxes with SP marked.

Recap: A procedure is reusable code entered with CALL and left with RET. CALL pushes the return address (IP for near, CS and IP for far) and RET pops it back. Parameters go in registers, in memory, or on the stack, where BP makes a stable frame and RET n cleans up. Save and restore registers in reverse order. Recursion works because each call has its own return address on the stack. A macro is text copied by the assembler, faster but bigger. Next, we look at interrupts, which are like procedure calls triggered by events.
key_points: A procedure is named, reusable code between PROC and ENDP, entered with CALL and left with RET.
A near CALL pushes IP (SP goes down by 2); a far CALL pushes CS then IP (SP goes down by 4); RET must match the CALL type.
Parameters can be passed in registers, in memory (often by address in SI or BX), or on the stack.
With PUSH BP and MOV BP, SP in a near procedure, the last pushed parameter is at [BP+4] and the one before it at [BP+6].
RET n pops the return address and then adds n to SP to discard parameters.
Save registers with PUSH at the start and POP them in reverse order before RET.
Recursion works because every CALL stores its own return address; deep recursion can overflow the stack.
A macro is expanded by the assembler at every use: no CALL/RET overhead but bigger code; use LOCAL for labels inside it.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write a procedure, draw the stack as a column of boxes on paper and mark SP after every PUSH, CALL, POP and RET. If SP is not back where it started after RET, you have found your bug.
lessons.task: On paper, trace the recursive FACT procedure for n = 4. Draw the stack after every CALL and every RET, writing the saved n values and return addresses. Check that the final AX is 24 (18h).

quiz.q: What does a near CALL push on the stack?
quiz.explain: A near (intrasegment) CALL stays in the same code segment, so it pushes only the 16-bit IP of the next instruction.

quiz.q: In a near procedure that begins with PUSH BP and MOV BP, SP, where is the last parameter the caller pushed?
quiz.explain: [BP+0] holds the old BP, [BP+2] the return address, so the last pushed parameter is at [BP+4].

quiz.q: What does RET 4 do?
options: Pops the return address, then adds 4 to SP
quiz.explain: RET n returns normally and then discards n bytes of parameters by adding n to SP.

quiz.q: Which statement about macros is true?
options: A macro is entered with CALL
A macro makes the program smaller every time it is used
The processor looks up macros while running
The assembler copies the macro's code at every place it is used
quiz.explain: A macro is expanded at assembly time; each use inserts a copy of its code, so there is no CALL/RET but the program grows.

quiz.q: A procedure does PUSH BX then PUSH CX at the start. What is the correct ending?
quiz.explain: The stack is last in, first out, so pop in reverse order (CX first, then BX) and only then RET.

lessons.title: 8086 Interrupts
lessons.content:
Imagine you are doing homework at the dining table. Suddenly the doorbell rings. You do not ignore it, and you also do not throw away your homework. You put a finger on the line you were writing, go to the door, take the parcel from the delivery man, come back, and continue from exactly that line. A processor lives the same life. It is busy running a program, and suddenly the keyboard has a key, or the timer ticks, or a calculation goes wrong. The processor pauses, handles the event, and comes back to where it was. This is an interrupt. In this lesson you will learn what kinds of interrupts the 8086 has, where it finds the code to handle each one, exactly what it does step by step, and how to write your own handler.

What an interrupt is: An interrupt is a signal or an instruction that makes the processor stop its current program for a while and run a special procedure called an interrupt service routine, or ISR. When the ISR finishes, the processor returns to the interrupted program and continues as if nothing happened. In the last lesson you saw that a procedure is entered with CALL. An ISR is similar, but it is entered because of an event, and it is left with a special return instruction, IRET.

Why not just keep checking: The other way to notice a key press is polling: the program asks the keyboard again and again, "Do you have a key? Do you have a key?" That wastes huge amounts of time, because most of the time the answer is no. With interrupts, the processor does useful work and the device taps it on the shoulder only when something actually happens. This is why every real computer, from the old IBM PC to your phone, uses interrupts for keyboards, timers, disks and network cards.

Three sources of interrupts: The 8086 can be interrupted in three ways. First, hardware interrupts come from outside the chip through two pins: NMI and INTR. Second, software interrupts come from the INT n instruction inside a program. Third, some interrupts are produced by the processor itself when something special happens, like dividing by zero. These are sometimes called exceptions or internal interrupts. All three kinds end up using the same table and the same steps.

The NMI pin: NMI means non-maskable interrupt. It is pin 17 of the 8086 and it is triggered by a rising edge, a change from low to high. The important word is non-maskable: the program cannot switch it off. NMI is kept for emergencies such as a power failure warning or a memory error, where the processor must react no matter what. NMI always uses interrupt type 2.

The INTR pin: INTR is pin 18 and is the normal, maskable hardware interrupt. It is level triggered, which means the device holds it high until the processor answers. The processor only listens to INTR when the interrupt flag IF is 1. The instruction STI sets IF to 1, allowing interrupts, and CLI clears it to 0, blocking them. When the 8086 accepts INTR, it sends two pulses on its INTA pin, the interrupt acknowledge. During the second pulse, the device, usually an 8259 interrupt controller which we meet in the next lesson, puts an 8-bit type number on the data bus. That number tells the processor which ISR to run.

Software interrupts: The instruction INT n, where n is a number from 0 to 255, makes an interrupt of type n happen right now. It is 2 bytes long: the opcode CDh followed by n. You have already used INT 21h, which is the MS-DOS service interrupt, and you may see INT 10h, the BIOS video service, in PC programs. INT 3 is special: it has its own one-byte opcode, CCh, so a debugger can put it over any instruction to make a breakpoint. INTO is another one: it causes a type 4 interrupt, but only if the overflow flag OF is 1.

The interrupt vector table: How does the processor find the ISR for type n? The 8086 keeps a table at the very bottom of memory, from address 00000h to 003FFh. That is 1024 bytes, or 1 KB. There are 256 possible types, and each entry, called an interrupt vector, takes 4 bytes: 256 times 4 = 1024. Each vector holds the address of one ISR as two words: first the new IP (offset), then the new CS (segment). So for type n, IP is at address 4 times n and CS is at 4 times n plus 2.

Worked example with the table: Where is the vector for INT 21h? 21h times 4 = 84h, so the vector is at 00084h to 00087h. If memory there holds the bytes 10h, 02h, 00h, 70h, then the new IP is 0210h and the new CS is 7000h, because words are stored little-endian, low byte first. The ISR starts at physical address 7000h times 16 plus 0210h = 70000h + 0210h = 70210h. Another quick one: the NMI vector, type 2, is at 2 times 4 = 8, so at 00008h to 0000Bh.

What the processor does, step by step: When an interrupt of type n is accepted, the 8086 does this sequence. One, it pushes the flags register on the stack. Two, it clears IF and TF, so no maskable interrupt or single step disturbs the start of the ISR. Three, it pushes CS. Four, it pushes IP, which points to the next instruction of the interrupted program. Five, it loads IP from address 4n and CS from address 4n + 2. Now the ISR runs. In total 6 bytes go on the stack: flags, CS and IP, each 2 bytes, so SP goes down by 6.

IRET: The ISR ends with IRET, interrupt return. IRET pops IP, then CS, then the flags, in exactly the opposite order of the pushes. Because the flags come back, IF returns to the value it had before, usually 1, so interrupts are enabled again. A normal RET is wrong at the end of an ISR: it would pop only IP, and the flags and CS would be left on the stack, which breaks everything.

When the 8086 checks: A hardware interrupt is not accepted in the middle of an instruction. The processor finishes the current instruction and then checks for pending interrupts. So the interrupted program always stops at a clean boundary between two instructions, which is why it can safely continue later.

The dedicated types 0 to 4: Intel fixed the first five types. Type 0 is divide error: it happens when DIV or IDIV divides by zero, or when the quotient is too big for the destination, for example dividing 1000h by 1 with an 8-bit divisor, since the quotient 1000h does not fit in AL. Type 1 is single step: if the trap flag TF is 1, the processor runs one instruction and then interrupts, so a debugger can show registers after every instruction. Type 2 is NMI. Type 3 is breakpoint, from the one-byte INT 3. Type 4 is overflow, from INTO when OF = 1. Intel reserved types 5 to 31 for future use, and types 32 to 255 are free for users and system software.

Priority: What if two interrupts arrive at once? The 8086 handles them in a fixed priority order. Internal interrupts such as divide error, INT n and INTO come first, then NMI, then INTR, and single step is lowest. In practice, many devices share INTR through an 8259 controller, which decides among them, as you will see next.

Writing an ISR: An ISR looks like a procedure, with a few extra rules. It must save every register it changes, because the interrupted program had no warning and expects all registers untouched. It should be short, so other interrupts are not delayed. It must end with IRET. Example skeleton: MYISR PROC FAR, then (1) PUSH AX, (2) PUSH DX, then the work, then (3) POP DX, (4) POP AX, (5) IRET, and MYISR ENDP. If a hardware ISR is triggered through the PC's 8259, it must also tell the 8259 it is finished, by sending an end of interrupt command, MOV AL, 20h then OUT 20h, AL, just before IRET.

Installing an ISR under DOS: You should not write the vector table directly while DOS runs; ask DOS to do it. INT 21h function 25h sets a vector: put the type number in AL, the handler address in DS:DX, AH = 25h, and do INT 21h. Function 35h reads a vector: AH = 35h, AL = type, and after INT 21h the old handler is in ES:BX. Good programs save the old vector with 35h first and put it back with 25h before they exit, so the system is left as it was.

Real life example 1, the keyboard on an IBM PC: On the classic IBM PC, the keyboard is wired to the 8259 and arrives as hardware interrupt type 09h. When you press a key, the keyboard controller raises its line, the 8259 raises INTR, the 8086 finishes its instruction, acknowledges, gets type 09h, looks up the vector at 9 times 4 = 24h, and runs the BIOS keyboard ISR. That ISR reads the key code from the keyboard port, stores it in a small buffer, sends EOI and does IRET. Later, when your program calls a DOS input function, it simply takes the key from that buffer. Your program was never stuck waiting.

Real life example 2, a timer in a factory: Think of a garment factory in Gazipur where a small 8086 based controller counts finished shirts on a conveyor belt. A sensor triggers a hardware interrupt each time a shirt passes, and the ISR just adds 1 to a counter in memory and returns. A timer interrupt arrives every second, and its ISR updates a display. The main program sits in a loop doing slow jobs, like printing reports. Because each ISR is short and saves its registers, the counting is never missed and the main loop never notices the interruptions. Now imagine a power cut warning: that goes to NMI, which cannot be masked, so the controller always gets a chance to save the count before the power dies.

Common mistakes: First, ending an ISR with RET instead of IRET. Second, forgetting to save registers in the ISR, which corrupts the interrupted program at random moments, one of the hardest bugs to find. Third, mixing up the vector layout: IP is at 4n and CS at 4n + 2, not the other way. Fourth, thinking CLI blocks NMI; it does not, it only blocks INTR. Fifth, forgetting that the 8086 clears IF on entry, so if you want other interrupts to be allowed inside a long ISR, you must use STI yourself.

What exams ask: Expect questions like: "Explain the interrupt vector table of the 8086", "Find the physical address of the ISR for INT 13h given the table contents", "Describe the sequence of actions when the 8086 responds to an interrupt", "Differentiate between NMI and INTR", "Explain the dedicated interrupt types 0 to 4", and "What is the difference between RET and IRET?" For the address calculation, write: vector address = type times 4, then IP from the first word, CS from the second, then physical = CS times 16 + IP.

Recap: An interrupt pauses the program to run an ISR and then returns. The 8086 gets interrupts from the NMI pin (non-maskable, type 2), the INTR pin (maskable with IF), INT n instructions, and internal events like divide error. The vector table at 00000h to 003FFh holds 256 four-byte vectors, IP first then CS. On entry the processor pushes flags, clears IF and TF, pushes CS and IP, and loads the vector. IRET undoes it. Next lesson: how the 8085 handles interrupts and how the 8259A lets many devices share one INTR pin.
key_points: An interrupt pauses the running program, runs an interrupt service routine (ISR), then returns to the next instruction.
Interrupts come from hardware pins (NMI, INTR), from INT n instructions, and from internal events such as divide error.
NMI (type 2) cannot be masked; INTR is maskable and only accepted when IF = 1 (STI sets it, CLI clears it).
The vector table is at 00000h-003FFh: 256 vectors of 4 bytes, with IP at 4n and CS at 4n + 2.
On an interrupt the 8086 pushes flags, clears IF and TF, pushes CS and IP, and loads the new CS:IP from the table.
IRET pops IP, CS and flags; an ISR must end with IRET, not RET.
Types 0-4 are divide error, single step, NMI, breakpoint (INT 3) and overflow (INTO).
Under DOS, INT 21h AH = 25h sets a vector and AH = 35h reads one.
lessons.tip: Learn the response sequence as a short chant: push flags, clear IF and TF, push CS, push IP, load from 4n. Then IRET is the same chant backwards. Half of the interrupt questions in exams are just this chant written neatly.
lessons.task: On paper, find the vector table address for INT 10h, INT 1Ch and INT 4. Then suppose the four bytes at the INT 1Ch vector are 53h, FFh, 00h, F0h. Work out the ISR's CS, IP and physical address (answer: CS = F000h, IP = FF53h, physical FFF53h).

quiz.q: Where is the interrupt vector for type 21h stored?
quiz.explain: Each vector is 4 bytes, so type 21h starts at 21h x 4 = 84h and occupies 00084h to 00087h.

quiz.q: Which interrupt can NOT be blocked by CLI?
options: The keyboard interrupt on a PC
quiz.explain: CLI clears IF, which only masks INTR. NMI is non-maskable.

quiz.q: What does the 8086 push on the stack when it accepts an interrupt?
quiz.explain: It pushes the flags, then CS, then IP, 6 bytes in total, after which it loads the new CS:IP.

quiz.q: Which interrupt type does a division by zero cause?
quiz.explain: Type 0 is the divide error, raised when the divisor is zero or the quotient does not fit.

quiz.q: Why must an ISR end with IRET and not RET?
options: IRET also pops CS and the flags that the interrupt pushed
RET is not allowed in far procedures
quiz.explain: The interrupt pushed flags, CS and IP; IRET pops all three so the program and IF are restored, while RET would pop only IP.

lessons.title: 8085 Interrupts and the 8259A PIC
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy doctor's chamber in Dhaka. Many patients arrive, but the doctor can see only one at a time. At the front desk sits an assistant who keeps a list of who is waiting, knows that an emergency patient must go before a routine check-up, can tell some patients "not today", and calls the next one in when the doctor is free. The processor is the doctor, the patients are devices asking for attention, and the assistant is a chip called the 8259A programmable interrupt controller. In this lesson you first see how the older 8085 handles interrupts with its five interrupt pins, and then how the 8259A lets many devices share one interrupt line, with priorities and masks, for both the 8085 and the 8086.

The 8085 interrupt pins: The 8085 has five hardware interrupt inputs: TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR. Their priority is fixed in exactly that order, with TRAP highest and INTR lowest. If two arrive together, the higher one is served first. Four of them are vectored, which means the processor itself knows the address of their service routine. Only INTR is non-vectored: the device must tell the processor where to go.

The vector addresses: The vectored interrupts jump to fixed addresses in low memory. TRAP goes to 0024h, RST 7.5 to 003Ch, RST 6.5 to 0034h and RST 5.5 to 002Ch. There is a neat trick to remember them: multiply the number by 8 and convert to hex. 5.5 times 8 = 44 = 2Ch. 6.5 times 8 = 52 = 34h. 7.5 times 8 = 60 = 3Ch. TRAP behaves like RST 4.5: 4.5 times 8 = 36 = 24h. Only 4 bytes separate some of these addresses, so the code there is usually just a JMP to the real routine somewhere else.

TRAP: TRAP is the non-maskable interrupt of the 8085. No instruction can disable it. It is both edge and level sensitive: the signal must go high and stay high for a while to be accepted, which protects it from tiny electrical noise spikes. Like NMI on the 8086, it is kept for emergencies such as a power failure.

RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5: These three are maskable. RST 7.5 is rising edge triggered, and the 8085 has a small internal flip-flop that remembers the edge even if the signal goes away quickly. RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are level triggered: the device must hold the line high until the processor responds. Each of the three can be masked separately with the SIM instruction, and all of them are also controlled by the overall interrupt enable.

INTR: INTR is the general purpose maskable interrupt. When the 8085 accepts it, it sends a low pulse on its INTA output. The device, or an 8259A, must then place an instruction on the data bus. Usually that is one of the one-byte RST instructions, or a 3-byte CALL. The processor executes whatever it receives, and that decides where the service routine is.

The RST instructions: The 8085 has eight one-byte restart instructions, RST 0 to RST 7. Each is like a tiny CALL to address 8 times n: RST 0 goes to 0000h, RST 1 to 0008h, RST 2 to 0010h, up to RST 7 at 0038h. They can be used as software interrupts inside a program, or a device can put one on the bus in response to INTA. The opcode of RST n is C7h + 8n, so RST 7 is FFh. Be careful not to confuse the software RST 5 (address 0028h) with the hardware pin RST 5.5 (address 002Ch).

EI and DI: EI, enable interrupts, sets the interrupt enable flip-flop, and DI, disable interrupts, clears it. This flip-flop affects all maskable interrupts, meaning RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5 and INTR, but never TRAP. When the 8085 accepts a maskable interrupt, it automatically disables interrupts so the routine is not interrupted again by accident. So an 8085 interrupt routine usually does EI just before its RET if it wants interrupts back on. Note that the 8085 has no special IRET instruction; the routine ends with a normal RET, and it should save A and the flags with PUSH PSW and restore them with POP PSW.

SIM, set interrupt mask: SIM takes its settings from the accumulator. Bit 0 masks RST 5.5, bit 1 masks RST 6.5, bit 2 masks RST 7.5, where 1 means masked and 0 means allowed. Bit 3 is mask set enable: it must be 1 for bits 0 to 2 to take effect. Bit 4, when 1, resets the RST 7.5 flip-flop, clearing a remembered edge. Bits 6 and 7 are for serial output, which we skip here. Example: to allow only RST 7.5, mask 5.5 and 6.5, keep 7.5 open and set mask set enable: 0000 1011 = 0Bh. The code is MVI A, 0Bh then SIM then EI.

RIM, read interrupt mask: RIM loads the accumulator with status. Bits 0 to 2 show the current masks of 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5. Bit 3 shows whether interrupts are enabled. Bits 4 to 6 show which of RST 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5 are pending, meaning they have arrived but are not yet served. Bit 7 is serial input data. A program can use RIM to check, for example, whether RST 7.5 is waiting, without actually enabling it.

Why the 8259A is needed: The 8086 has only one maskable interrupt pin, INTR, and the 8085's INTR is also just one line. A real system has a timer, a keyboard, a serial port, a disk and more. The 8259A programmable interrupt controller takes up to eight interrupt requests on pins IR0 to IR7, decides which is most important, and passes one at a time to the processor's INTR pin. It also supplies the type number (for the 8086) or the CALL instruction (for the 8085) so each device gets its own service routine.

Inside the 8259A: Three registers and a judge do the work. The interrupt request register, IRR, has one bit per IR pin and records every request that has arrived. The interrupt mask register, IMR, has one bit per pin; a 1 blocks that pin. The in-service register, ISR, has a bit set for each interrupt currently being served. The priority resolver looks at requests in IRR that are not masked in IMR, compares them with what is in ISR, and lets a request through only if it is more important than anything being served now.

The sequence with an 8086: One, a device raises its IR line and the matching IRR bit is set. Two, if it is not masked and has high enough priority, the 8259A raises INT, which is wired to the 8086 INTR pin. Three, if IF = 1, the 8086 finishes its instruction and sends two INTA pulses. Four, on the first pulse, the 8259A sets the ISR bit and clears the IRR bit for that request. Five, on the second pulse, it puts an 8-bit type number on the data bus. Six, the 8086 uses that type exactly as you learned in the last lesson: push flags, CS, IP, and load the vector at 4 times the type. With an 8085 instead, the 8259A answers three INTA cycles with a CALL opcode, CDh, and a 16-bit address.

End of interrupt: The ISR bit stays set while the routine runs, which blocks lower priority requests. At the end, the routine must tell the 8259A that it is done by sending an end of interrupt command, EOI. The common one is the non-specific EOI, the byte 20h written to the 8259A's command port. On the IBM PC the master 8259A sits at ports 20h and 21h, so the code is MOV AL, 20h then OUT 20h, AL, right before IRET. Forget this, and the 8259A thinks the device is still being served, so that device and all lower ones never interrupt again. There is also an automatic EOI mode that clears the bit by itself, but it is less common.

Programming the 8259A: Before use, the 8259A is set up with initialization command words, ICW1 to ICW4, sent in order. ICW1 and ICW2 are always needed. ICW3 is only needed when several 8259As are cascaded, and ICW4 is needed when ICW1 says so, which is always the case for the 8086. After that, operation command words OCW1 to OCW3 can be sent at any time. OCW1 simply writes the IMR. OCW2 sends EOI and priority rotation commands. OCW3 chooses whether the next read gives IRR or ISR: 0Ah selects IRR and 0Bh selects ISR.

A worked initialization: Suppose one 8259A with an 8086, edge triggered, and we want IR0 to IR7 to become types 40h to 47h. ICW1 = 13h: binary 0001 0011, where bit 4 = 1 marks it as ICW1, bit 3 = 0 means edge triggered, bit 1 = 1 means single (no cascade), and bit 0 = 1 means ICW4 will follow. ICW2 = 40h: the upper five bits of the type, and the 8259A fills the lower three bits with the IR number, so IR3 gives type 43h, whose vector is at 43h times 4 = 10Ch. No ICW3 because it is single. ICW4 = 01h: bit 0 = 1 selects 8086 mode with normal EOI. Then OCW1 = 0FCh, binary 1111 1100, allows only IR0 and IR1 and masks the rest.

Priority modes: By default the 8259A uses fully nested mode: IR0 has the highest priority and IR7 the lowest. A request can interrupt a running routine only if it has higher priority. For devices that are equally important, rotating priority can be chosen with OCW2: after a device is served it moves to the lowest priority, so everyone gets a fair turn, like a queue where whoever was just served goes to the back.

Cascading: One 8259A handles 8 inputs. For more, a master 8259A can have up to eight slave 8259As connected to its IR pins. Each slave's INT output goes to one IR pin of the master, and the master tells the slaves which one should respond using three cascade lines, CAS0 to CAS2. With one master and eight slaves you get 8 times 8 = 64 interrupt inputs. ICW3 tells the master which IR pins have slaves, and tells each slave its own ID. The IBM PC AT used one master and one slave, giving 15 usable inputs, since one master input carries the slave.

Real life example 1, the PC timer and keyboard: On the original IBM PC, the BIOS programs the master 8259A with ICW2 = 08h, so IR0 becomes type 08h and IR1 becomes type 09h. IR0 is connected to the timer, which ticks about 18.2 times a second, and IR1 to the keyboard. When both fire together, the timer, on IR0, wins because of fully nested priority. Each routine sends EOI to port 20h before IRET. This exact setup is why many old DOS programs that hook INT 08h or INT 09h must remember to send that EOI.

Real life example 2, a traffic signal controller: Imagine an 8085 based signal controller at a busy Chattogram crossing. A power failure sensor goes to TRAP, so the controller can always save its state. A pedestrian button goes to RST 7.5, because a quick press is a short pulse and the edge flip-flop remembers it. A slow vehicle counter goes to RST 5.5. During a fixed green phase, the program uses SIM with a mask to ignore the pedestrian button, and later unmasks it. The priority order means the power failure is handled before anything else.

Common mistakes: First, mixing up software RST 5 (0028h) with hardware RST 5.5 (002Ch). Second, forgetting EI at the end of an 8085 routine, so no interrupt ever comes again. Third, forgetting mask set enable, bit 3, in the SIM byte, so the masks are not changed. Fourth, forgetting EOI to the 8259A. Fifth, thinking ICW3 is always needed; it is only for cascade mode.

What exams ask: "List the 8085 interrupts with priority, vector address and triggering", "Write the SIM byte to enable only RST 6.5", "Draw the block diagram of the 8259A and explain IRR, ISR and IMR", "Explain the interrupt sequence of the 8259A with the 8086", "Write the ICWs for a given setup", and "How many interrupts can be handled with cascading?" (64).

Recap: The 8085 has TRAP, RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5 and INTR in falling priority. TRAP is non-maskable; the RST pins are vectored at 8 times their number; INTR needs an instruction from the device. EI, DI, SIM and RIM control and read the masks. The 8259A collects up to eight requests, masks and prioritises them with IMR, IRR, ISR and the priority resolver, gives the processor a type number, waits for EOI, and can be cascaded to 64 inputs. Next we connect memory chips to the processor.
key_points: 8085 interrupts in priority order: TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, INTR; only TRAP is non-maskable.
Vector addresses are 8 times the number: TRAP 0024h, RST 7.5 003Ch, RST 6.5 0034h, RST 5.5 002Ch; INTR is non-vectored.
RST 7.5 is edge triggered with a latch; RST 6.5 and 5.5 are level triggered; TRAP is edge and level sensitive.
SIM sets masks from A (bit 0-2 masks, bit 3 mask set enable, bit 4 resets 7.5); RIM reads masks and pending interrupts.
The 8259A has IRR (requests), IMR (masks), ISR (in service) and a priority resolver; it gives the 8086 a type number.
An ISR must send EOI (20h to the command port, port 20h on a PC) or that IR level stays blocked.
ICW1 and ICW2 are always sent, ICW3 only for cascade, ICW4 when requested (always for the 8086); OCW1 writes the mask.
One master and eight slaves give 64 interrupt inputs.
lessons.tip: Remember the 8085 vectors with the times-8 trick (5.5 x 8 = 44 = 2Ch, and TRAP acts like 4.5). For the 8259A, always write the control bytes in binary first and label each bit; examiners give marks for the labelled bits even if one value is wrong.
lessons.task: On paper, write the SIM byte that allows only RST 6.5 (answer: 0000 1101 = 0Dh). Then, for an 8259A with ICW2 = 60h, find the type number and the vector address for IR5 (answer: type 65h, vector at 194h).

quiz.q: Which is the highest priority interrupt of the 8085?
quiz.explain: The fixed order is TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, INTR, so TRAP is highest and also non-maskable.

quiz.q: What is the vector address of RST 6.5?
quiz.explain: 6.5 x 8 = 52 decimal = 34h.

quiz.q: Which 8259A register blocks requests from chosen IR pins?
quiz.explain: The interrupt mask register (IMR), written with OCW1, has a bit per pin; a 1 masks that pin.

quiz.q: What happens if an ISR forgets to send EOI to the 8259A?
options: That level and all lower levels stay blocked
Nothing, EOI is optional in all modes
quiz.explain: The ISR bit stays set, so the 8259A thinks the device is still being served and blocks equal and lower priority requests (unless automatic EOI mode is used).

quiz.q: With one master and eight slave 8259As, how many interrupt inputs are available?
quiz.explain: Each of the master's 8 inputs gets a slave with 8 inputs: 8 x 8 = 64.

lessons.title: Memory Interfacing
lessons.content:
Imagine a big apartment building in Mirpur with many flats. A courier arrives with a parcel addressed to "Building 3, Floor 5, Flat B". The guard at the gate looks at the building number and floor and sends the courier up the right lift; then the flat letter picks the exact door. The courier never knocks on every door. A microprocessor talking to memory works the same way. It sends out an address, and some small logic circuits look at the top part of the address to pick the right memory chip, while the bottom part picks the exact byte inside that chip. Connecting memory chips to a processor so that each byte gets a unique address is called memory interfacing. In this lesson you will learn how to read memory chip sizes, how to decode addresses, how to draw a memory map, and how the 8086 handles its two memory banks.

Why interfacing is needed: A processor has address lines, data lines and control lines. The 8085 has 16 address lines, so it can reach 2 to the power 16 = 65,536 bytes, which is 64 KB. The 8086 has 20 address lines, reaching 2 to the power 20 = 1,048,576 bytes, which is 1 MB. But a single memory chip is usually much smaller, like 2 KB or 8 KB or 32 KB. So a system uses several chips, and we need a circuit that turns on exactly one chip for each address. Otherwise two chips could fight on the data bus.

Memory chip types: ROM keeps its data without power and holds the startup program. Common old chips are EPROMs, which are erased with ultraviolet light: the 2716 is 2K x 8, the 2732 is 4K x 8, the 2764 is 8K x 8, the 27128 is 16K x 8 and the 27256 is 32K x 8. RAM loses its data when power goes, and holds variables and the stack. Common static RAM chips are the 6116 (2K x 8), the 6264 (8K x 8) and the 62256 (32K x 8). In a chip size like 8K x 8, the first number is how many locations and the second is how many bits each location holds.

How many address lines a chip needs: A chip with N locations needs log base 2 of N address lines. 2K = 2048 = 2 to the 11, so a 2K chip needs 11 lines, A0 to A10. 4K needs 12 lines, 8K needs 13 lines (A0 to A12), 16K needs 14 and 32K needs 15. These low lines connect straight from the processor's address bus to every memory chip in parallel. The remaining high address lines are not connected to the chip at all; they are used to choose which chip is active.

The chip's control pins: A typical memory chip has a chip select pin, often written CS with a bar on top, meaning it is active low: the chip works only when this pin is 0. ROM has an output enable pin, OE, also active low, which lets the chip drive the data bus during a read. RAM also has a write enable pin, WE, active low, used during a write. The processor's control signals feed these pins. On the 8085, IO/M is low for memory, and combined with RD and WR it makes the memory read signal MEMR and the memory write signal MEMW. So a chip is only active when its address range is selected and the operation is really a memory operation, not an I/O operation.

Address decoding: The job of the address decoder is to look at the high address lines and produce the chip select signal for the right chip. A popular choice is the 74LS138, a 3-to-8 line decoder. It has three select inputs, usually called A, B and C, and eight outputs Y0 to Y7, which are active low. It also has three enable inputs: G1 must be 1, and G2A and G2B must be 0. When it is enabled, exactly one output goes low, the one whose number matches the 3-bit input. Each output can drive the chip select of one memory chip.

Worked example, an 8085 system: We want an 8K ROM at the bottom and an 8K RAM right after it. 8K needs 13 lines, A0 to A12. The 8085 has 16 lines, so the top three, A13, A14 and A15, are left for decoding. Connect A15 to input C, A14 to B and A13 to A of a 74LS138. Now each output covers one 8K block of the 64K space. Y0 is active when A15 A14 A13 = 000, for addresses 0000h to 1FFFh: connect the ROM here. Y1 is active for 001, addresses 2000h to 3FFFh: connect the RAM here. Y2 to Y7 cover the other six 8K blocks, free for future chips. The decoder's enable G1 can be tied to 1 and G2A to IO/M, so it only works for memory cycles.

Why the ROM sits at the bottom on the 8085: After reset, the 8085 starts executing from address 0000h. So the startup program must be at 0000h, which means the ROM must be mapped there. If RAM were at the bottom, after power on the processor would run whatever random bits the RAM happened to contain.

Calculating a memory map: The rule is simple: end address = start address + size - 1. A 2K chip is 800h bytes, so a 2K chip starting at 8000h ends at 8000h + 7FFh = 87FFh. A 4K chip (1000h bytes) starting at 0000h ends at 0FFFh. To check an address belongs to a chip, write it in binary and look at the decoding lines. For example 2ABCh is 0010 1010 1011 1100. The top three bits are 001, so it falls in Y1, which is our RAM, at offset 0ABCh inside that RAM.

Full decoding: In full or absolute decoding, every address line that is not connected to the chip is used by the decoder. Then each byte in each chip has exactly one address, and no address is wasted or repeated. Our 74LS138 example is fully decoded: A0 to A12 go to the chip, and A13 to A15 all go to the decoder. Full decoding uses more logic but leaves the whole address space clean for adding chips later.

Partial decoding: In partial decoding, some upper address lines are simply ignored. This needs less hardware, which is cheaper for a small system, but each location then answers at several addresses. These extra copies are called mirror, alias or foldback addresses. Example: an 8085 with a single 2K RAM, A0 to A10 to the chip, and chip select made only from A15 = 0. Lines A11 to A14, four lines, are ignored, so they can be anything. Each RAM byte appears 2 to the 4 = 16 times, and the chip fills all of 0000h to 7FFFh: 0000h to 07FFh, 0800h to 0FFFh, and so on. Writing to 0005h or to 0805h changes the same byte.

The 8086 and two memory banks: The 8086 has a 16-bit data bus, so it can move a whole word in one bus cycle. But memory is addressed in bytes. The solution is to split the 1 MB space into two banks of 512 KB each. The even bank holds all even addresses and connects to the low data lines D0 to D7. The odd bank holds all odd addresses and connects to the high data lines D8 to D15. Address lines A1 to A19 go to both banks, and two signals choose the banks: A0 selects the even bank when it is 0, and a pin called BHE, bus high enable, which is active low, selects the odd bank when it is 0.

The four BHE and A0 cases: When BHE = 0 and A0 = 0, both banks are active, and a whole word at an even address moves in one cycle, low byte on D0 to D7 and high byte on D8 to D15. When BHE = 0 and A0 = 1, only the odd bank is active, moving one byte on D8 to D15. When BHE = 1 and A0 = 0, only the even bank is active, moving one byte on D0 to D7. When both are 1, no bank is selected. A word at an odd address, like MOV AX, [0101h], is misaligned: its low byte is in the odd bank and its high byte in the even bank at the next address, so the 8086 needs two bus cycles. This is why aligned words, at even addresses, are faster.

Worked example, 8086 with 64 KB RAM: Suppose we want 64 KB of RAM at 00000h to 0FFFFh using two 62256 chips of 32K x 8. One chip is the even bank and one is the odd bank, each holding 32K bytes, which needs 15 address lines: A1 to A15 go to both chips. The even chip's chip select is active when A0 = 0 and A16 to A19 are all 0. The odd chip's chip select is active when BHE = 0 and A16 to A19 are all 0. Byte 00000h is the first byte of the even chip, 00001h is the first byte of the odd chip, 00002h is the second byte of the even chip, and so on.

Where the 8086 needs ROM and RAM: After reset, the 8086 sets CS = FFFFh and IP = 0000h, so it starts at physical address FFFF0h, just 16 bytes below the top of memory. So the 8086 system needs ROM at the top of the address space. Meanwhile the interrupt vector table lives at 00000h to 003FFh and must be writable to install handlers, so RAM is placed at the bottom. This is the opposite arrangement from the 8085.

Speed and wait states: A memory chip needs some time after it gets an address before the data is ready, called its access time. If the chip is slower than the processor's bus cycle, the processor would read garbage. To handle this, the processor has a READY input. A small circuit pulls READY low for slow chips, and the processor adds extra clock periods, called wait states, until the data is ready. It makes the system slower but correct.

Real life example 1, a training kit in a university lab: Many CSE labs in Bangladesh use 8085 or 8086 trainer kits. Open the manual and you will find a memory map like "Monitor ROM at 0000h to 1FFFh, user RAM from 2000h" on an 8085 kit. Now you know what it means: the kit's designer used a decoder, mapped the ROM at the bottom because the 8085 starts at 0000h, and gave you RAM in the next block. When your lab teacher says "store your program at 2000h", that is the start of the RAM chip.

Real life example 2, a digital prepaid electricity meter: A prepaid meter, like the ones many homes in Dhaka now use, contains a small microprocessor or microcontroller with a ROM holding its program and some RAM holding the remaining balance and readings. The designer decides an address range for each chip, picks partial decoding if the system is tiny to save a chip, or full decoding if more memory might be added later.

Common mistakes: First, using the wrong number of address lines for a chip; always compute log base 2 of the number of locations. Second, getting the end address wrong by forgetting the minus 1. Third, forgetting that partial decoding creates mirrors and then putting another chip on a mirror. Fourth, connecting A0 to the 8086 memory chips as an address line; in the bank design A0 is a bank select, and A1 is the lowest address line of each chip. Fifth, placing ROM at the bottom in an 8086 system, where it must be at the top.

What exams ask: "Interface 16 KB EPROM and 8 KB RAM with the 8085 at given addresses, draw the circuit and the memory map", "Differentiate full and partial decoding", "Explain the role of BHE and A0 in the 8086", "Why does a misaligned word need two bus cycles?" and "How many chips of 2K x 8 are needed for 16 KB, and how many address lines go to each chip?" (8 chips, 11 lines).

Recap: Memory interfacing connects chips so each byte has one address. Low address lines go to every chip; high lines feed a decoder like the 74LS138 that makes chip selects. End address = start + size - 1. Full decoding gives unique addresses; partial decoding is cheaper but makes mirrors. The 8086 splits memory into even and odd banks chosen by A0 and BHE, places ROM at the top because it starts at FFFF0h, and puts RAM at the bottom for the vector table. Next we connect input and output devices, starting with the 8255.
key_points: A chip with N locations needs log2(N) address lines: 2K needs 11, 8K needs 13, 32K needs 15.
Low address lines go to every chip; the remaining high lines feed a decoder that makes active-low chip selects.
The 74LS138 is a 3-to-8 decoder (enables G1 = 1, G2A = G2B = 0) with active-low outputs Y0-Y7.
End address = start address + size - 1; for example a 2K chip at 8000h ends at 87FFh.
Full decoding uses all unused lines and gives unique addresses; partial decoding ignores some lines and creates mirror addresses.
The 8086 has an even bank (D0-D7, selected by A0 = 0) and an odd bank (D8-D15, selected by BHE = 0); A1-A19 go to both.
A misaligned word at an odd address needs two bus cycles on the 8086.
The 8085 starts at 0000h (ROM at the bottom); the 8086 starts at FFFF0h (ROM at the top, RAM at the bottom for the vector table).
lessons.tip: For every interfacing problem, first make a table with one row per chip: size, number of address lines, start address, end address, and the bits of the decoding lines. Draw the circuit only after the table is right; the table is where marks are won.
lessons.task: On paper, design an 8085 system with a 4K ROM at 0000h and two 4K RAMs right after it, using a 74LS138 driven by A12, A13 and A14 (with A15 used on an enable). Write the address range of each chip (answer: 0000h-0FFFh, 1000h-1FFFh, 2000h-2FFFh).

quiz.q: How many address lines does an 8K x 8 memory chip need?
quiz.explain: 8K = 8192 = 2 to the 13, so 13 lines, A0 to A12.

quiz.q: A 2K chip starts at 4000h. What is its last address?
quiz.explain: 2K = 800h bytes, so end = 4000h + 800h - 1 = 47FFh.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of partial decoding?
options: Each location appears at several (mirror) addresses
It cannot be used with ROM
quiz.explain: Ignored address lines mean the chip answers at many addresses, which wastes address space.

quiz.q: In the 8086, BHE = 1 and A0 = 0. What is transferred?
options: A byte on D8-D15 from the odd bank
A byte on D0-D7 from the even bank
quiz.explain: A0 = 0 enables the even bank (D0-D7) and BHE = 1 disables the odd bank, so only a low byte moves.

quiz.q: Why must an 8086 system have ROM at the top of memory?
options: The 8086 starts executing at FFFF0h after reset
RAM cannot be placed at high addresses
The vector table is at the top
BHE only works at high addresses
quiz.explain: Reset sets CS = FFFFh and IP = 0000h, so the first instruction is fetched from FFFF0h, which must be ROM.

lessons.title: I/O Interfacing and the 8255 PPI
lessons.content:
Imagine a very clever person locked in a room with no windows and no doors. They can do maths faster than anyone, but they cannot see the street, hear the rickshaw bells or press a light switch. Useless, right? A microprocessor alone is exactly like that. It can add, compare and jump all day, but to read a keyboard, light an LED, run a motor or print a page, it needs doors to the outside world. Those doors are called I/O ports, and connecting devices to them is called I/O interfacing. In this lesson we learn the two ways a processor can talk to devices, and then we meet the most famous door-opening chip of the 8085/8086 era: the Intel 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface.

What an I/O port is: An I/O port is simply an address where the processor can read or write data that belongs to a device instead of to memory. When the CPU writes a byte to an output port, a latch holds that byte and its bits appear as voltages on wires, maybe turning LEDs on and off. When the CPU reads an input port, a buffer lets the voltages from switches or sensors onto the data bus for a moment, and the CPU copies them into a register. A latch remembers, a buffer only passes through when enabled. That one difference is why output ports need latches and input ports need tri-state buffers.

Two ways to give devices addresses: There are two styles. In I/O-mapped I/O, also called isolated I/O, devices live in a separate address space from memory. The CPU uses special instructions, IN and OUT, and a control signal tells the outside world whether this bus cycle is for memory or for I/O. On the 8085 that signal is IO/M, and on the 8086 it is M/IO. In memory-mapped I/O, devices sit inside the normal memory address space. A port looks just like a memory location, so any instruction that can touch memory, like MOV, ADD or AND, can touch the device.

Comparing the two styles: I/O-mapped I/O keeps the full memory space free for real memory, and the decoding hardware can be smaller because port addresses are short. But you can only use IN and OUT, and data must pass through the accumulator. Memory-mapped I/O lets you use every powerful memory instruction directly on a device, for example AND [port], mask to clear some bits in one step. The price is that the device steals some memory addresses, and you need full-width address decoding. Many microcontrollers and ARM chips use memory-mapped I/O only. The x86 family supports both.

Port space on the 8085 and 8086: The 8085 has 8-bit port addresses, so it can have 256 input ports and 256 output ports, 00h to FFh. Its instructions are IN port and OUT port, and the data always goes through register A. The 8086 has a 16-bit I/O address space, so up to 65,536 byte-wide ports, 0000h to FFFFh. It has two forms. Fixed port: IN AL, 60h or OUT 43h, AL, where the port number is an 8-bit constant, 00h to FFh. Variable port: put the port address in DX, then IN AL, DX or OUT DX, AL. Ports above FFh can only be reached through DX. Using AX instead of AL moves 16 bits at once.

A tiny example: Suppose an output latch sits at port 80h with eight LEDs on it. MOV AL, 0F0h then OUT 80h, AL turns on the four LEDs connected to the high bits and turns off the low four. If the port were at 3F8h, you would write MOV DX, 3F8h, then OUT DX, AL. That is the whole idea of programmed output. Building every port from separate latch and buffer chips gets messy though, so Intel made one chip that does it all.

Meet the 8255: The 8255A Programmable Peripheral Interface is a 40-pin chip with 24 I/O lines grouped into three 8-bit ports: Port A, Port B and Port C. Port C can be split into two 4-bit halves, upper PC7 to PC4 and lower PC3 to PC0. The ports are arranged into two groups. Group A is Port A plus upper Port C. Group B is Port B plus lower Port C. The word programmable means you decide, by software, which ports are inputs and which are outputs, and in which mode they work. You do that by writing a control word into a fourth internal register.

How the CPU selects inside the 8255: The chip has a chip select pin CS, active low, plus read RD and write WR pins, a RESET pin and two address inputs A1 and A0. When CS is low, A1 A0 pick the internal register: 00 is Port A, 01 is Port B, 10 is Port C and 11 is the control register. So one 8255 uses four consecutive port addresses. In our example board the address decoder puts the 8255 at 80h to 83h: Port A 80h, Port B 81h, Port C 82h, control 83h. On 8086 boards the 8255 is often wired to the low data byte with CPU address lines A2 A1 going to the chip's A1 A0, which gives even addresses such as 80h, 82h, 84h and 86h instead. Always read your board's manual. After RESET, all three ports become inputs, which is a safe default.

The three modes: Mode 0 is basic input/output. Each port, and each half of Port C, is simply an input or an output with no handshaking. Outputs are latched, inputs are not. This is what you use for LEDs, switches and simple displays. Mode 1 is strobed input/output with handshake. Ports A and B can each work in Mode 1, and some Port C lines become handshake signals. For input there is STB, a strobe from the device saying data is ready, IBF saying the input buffer is full, and INTR to interrupt the CPU. For output there is OBF saying the output buffer has new data, ACK from the device saying it took the data, and INTR again. Mode 2 is bidirectional, and only Port A can do it: the same eight lines send and receive, with five Port C lines used for handshake.

The I/O mode control word: When bit D7 of the control word is 1, the 8255 treats it as an I/O mode definition. D6 and D5 set the Group A mode: 00 for Mode 0, 01 for Mode 1, 10 or 11 for Mode 2. D4 sets Port A direction: 1 means input, 0 means output. D3 sets upper Port C: 1 input, 0 output. D2 sets the Group B mode: 0 for Mode 0, 1 for Mode 1. D1 sets Port B: 1 input, 0 output. D0 sets lower Port C: 1 input, 0 output. A handy memory trick: 1 looks like I, for Input; 0 looks like O, for Output.

Worked control words: All ports output, Mode 0: 1 00 0 0 0 0 0 is 80h. All ports input, Mode 0: 1 00 1 1 0 1 1 is 9Bh. Port A input, Port B output, Port C output, Mode 0: 1 00 1 0 0 0 0 is 90h. Port A output, Port B input, Port C output, Mode 0: 1 00 0 0 0 1 0 is 82h. Port A input, upper C input, Port B output, lower C output: 1 00 1 1 0 0 0 is 98h. In exams, always write the eight bits with a label under each one before converting to hex. That way the examiner can give marks even if you slip on the final hex digit.

Bit Set/Reset mode: If D7 of the control word is 0, the 8255 does something completely different. It treats the byte as a command to set or clear just one bit of Port C, leaving the other seven untouched. D3, D2 and D1 choose the bit, 000 for PC0 up to 111 for PC7. D0 says what to do: 1 sets the bit, 0 resets it. D6 to D4 are not used and are usually written as 0. So setting PC7 is 0 000 111 1, which is 0Fh, and resetting PC7 is 0Eh. Setting PC3 is 07h. Resetting PC0 is 00h. Important: BSR commands are written to the control register address, not to Port C, and they only work on Port C. They are perfect for turning one relay or one buzzer on without disturbing the others.

A full program, switches to LEDs: Our board has eight switches on Port B and eight LEDs on Port A, with the 8255 at 80h to 83h. We want each LED to copy its switch. First configure: Port A output, Port B input, Port C output, all Mode 0, which is 82h. The program is: MOV AL, 82h then OUT 83h, AL to write the control word. Then the loop: AGAIN: IN AL, 81h reads the switches from Port B, OUT 80h, AL sends that byte to the LEDs on Port A, and JMP AGAIN repeats forever. Five instructions, and you have built a real hardware mirror. Flip switch 3 and LED 3 lights up almost instantly.

Driving a seven-segment display: A seven-segment display has segments named a to g. If a common-cathode display is wired with a on bit 0 up to g on bit 6 of Port A, then lighting a pattern is just an OUT. The digit 0 needs segments a, b, c, d, e and f, which is 0011 1111, or 3Fh. The digit 1 needs only b and c, which is 06h. The digit 2 needs a, b, d, e and g, which is 5Bh. Programs usually keep these patterns in a table and use XLAT or indexed addressing to turn a number into its pattern before sending it out.

Real life example 1, a traffic light model: Many Bangladeshi university microprocessor labs ask students to build a four-way traffic light, like the junction at Farmgate or Shahbag, with red, yellow and green LEDs. With the 8255 in Mode 0 and Port A as output, each direction gets three bits. You write a pattern such as green for north-south and red for east-west, call a delay of a few seconds, write the yellow pattern, delay again, then swap. If the lab later adds a pedestrian button, you connect it to a Port B input line and check it in the loop. If you want only the buzzer bit to change, you use a BSR command on a Port C bit so the light pattern on Port A is not disturbed.

Real life example 2, a printer handshake: Old parallel printers, the kind once found in every computer shop in Nilkhet printing assignments, did not take data at the CPU's speed. The computer had to put a byte on the lines, give a strobe pulse, and wait until the printer said it was ready for the next one. That is exactly Mode 1 output handshaking. The 8255 raises OBF to say new data is waiting, the printer takes it and pulses ACK, and the 8255 can then raise INTR so the CPU sends the next character. The CPU does not have to sit and stare at the printer; the handshake tells it when to act.

Common mistakes: First, writing the control word to Port C's address instead of the control register. Second, mixing up the direction bits, using 1 for output. Remember 1 is Input. Third, forgetting that BSR mode needs D7 equal to 0, and then wondering why the ports changed direction. Fourth, using OUT 3F8h, AL, which is not allowed because a fixed port number must fit in 8 bits; use DX instead. Fifth, forgetting that IN and OUT on the 8086 only work with AL or AX, not with BX or CX.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: compare memory-mapped and I/O-mapped I/O; draw the 8255 block diagram and explain the groups; write the control word format; find the control word for a given port setup; write BSR words to set or reset a given Port C bit; explain Mode 1 handshake signals; and write a small program that reads switches and drives LEDs or a seven-segment display. Practise converting between bits and hex until it feels boring; that is when it is fast enough for an exam hall.

Recap: A microprocessor talks to the world through ports. In I/O-mapped I/O, ports have their own space and use IN and OUT. In memory-mapped I/O, ports look like memory. The 8255 gives you three 8-bit ports in two groups, three modes, a control word with D7 equal to 1 for setting modes, and a BSR word with D7 equal to 0 for flipping single Port C bits. With just a control word and a loop, you can read switches, light LEDs, show digits and handshake with a printer. Next we meet another very useful helper chip: the 8253/8254 timer.
key_points: An I/O port is an address used to read or write a device; output ports need latches, input ports need tri-state buffers.
I/O-mapped I/O uses a separate address space and IN/OUT; memory-mapped I/O puts devices in memory space so any memory instruction works.
8086 fixed ports use an 8-bit number (IN AL, 60h); ports above FFh need DX (OUT DX, AL); data goes through AL or AX.
The 8255 has Ports A, B and C; Group A is Port A plus upper C, Group B is Port B plus lower C; A1 A0 = 11 selects the control register.
Modes: 0 simple I/O, 1 strobed I/O with handshake (A and B), 2 bidirectional (Port A only).
I/O control word has D7 = 1; a direction bit of 1 means input. Examples: 80h all output, 9Bh all input, 82h A out B in.
BSR mode has D7 = 0, bits D3-D1 pick the Port C bit and D0 sets or resets it; e.g. 0Fh sets PC7, 0Eh resets it.
lessons.tip: Draw the eight control word boxes from memory every day for a week: 1, mode A (two bits), A, C upper, mode B, B, C lower. Once the boxes are automatic, every 8255 question becomes a fill-in-the-blanks game.
lessons.task: On paper, find the 8255 control word for: Port A input, Port B output, upper C output, lower C input, all Mode 0. Then write the BSR words to set PC4 and to reset PC4. Check: 91h, 09h and 08h.

quiz.q: Which 8255 control word sets all three ports as outputs in Mode 0?
quiz.explain: 1 00 0 0 0 0 0 = 80h: D7 = 1 for I/O mode, both groups Mode 0, every direction bit 0 for output.

quiz.q: In the 8255, what do A1 A0 = 11 select?
quiz.explain: 00 is Port A, 01 is Port B, 10 is Port C and 11 is the control register.

quiz.q: Which 8255 port can work in Mode 2 (bidirectional)?
quiz.explain: Only Port A supports Mode 2, using five Port C lines for its handshake signals.

quiz.q: Which BSR command word sets bit PC7 of the 8255?
quiz.explain: BSR: D7 = 0, D3 D2 D1 = 111 for PC7, D0 = 1 to set: 0000 1111 = 0Fh. 0Eh would reset PC7.

quiz.q: Why is OUT 3F8h, AL not a valid 8086 instruction?
options: Port 3F8h does not exist on any computer
A fixed port number must fit in 8 bits, so ports above FFh need DX
OUT can only write to memory
quiz.explain: The fixed form only holds an 8-bit port number (00h-FFh). For 3F8h you write MOV DX, 3F8h then OUT DX, AL.

lessons.title: The 8253/8254 Programmable Interval Timer
lessons.content:
Think about the school bell at your school. Nobody wants the head teacher to stand next to the bell all day, staring at a watch, ringing it every 40 minutes. Instead, a simple timer does it, and the teacher is free to teach. A microprocessor has the same problem. You can make delays in software with a loop, as we did in the 8085 lessons, but while the CPU counts loops it cannot do anything else, and the delay changes if the clock speed changes. The clean solution is a separate chip that counts clock pulses by itself and tells the CPU when time is up. In the 8085/8086 world, that chip is the Intel 8253 Programmable Interval Timer, and its improved version, the 8254.

What a timer chip really does: A timer is just a counter that counts pulses. If the pulses come from a steady clock, counting them measures time. If you load a counter with 1000 and a 1 MHz clock decrements it once per microsecond, it reaches zero after 1000 microseconds, which is 1 millisecond. If the pulses come from a sensor instead, like a slot that a wheel blocks once per turn, the same counter now counts events. That is why such chips are often called counter/timers.

The big picture of the 8253/8254: Both chips are 24-pin devices with three independent 16-bit down counters, called Counter 0, Counter 1 and Counter 2. Each counter has its own three pins: CLK, the pulses to count; GATE, an enable or trigger input; and OUT, the output that the counter changes when it reaches certain counts. The CPU talks to the chip through an 8-bit data bus, with chip select CS, read RD, write WR and two address lines A1 and A0. A1 A0 = 00 selects Counter 0, 01 selects Counter 1, 10 selects Counter 2 and 11 selects the control word register. So, like the 8255, one timer chip takes four port addresses.

The IBM PC example: The original IBM PC used an 8253 at I/O ports 40h, 41h, 42h and 43h, and later PCs kept an 8254-compatible timer at the same ports. The input clock was 1.193182 MHz. Counter 0 created the system timer interrupt about 18.2 times per second, Counter 1 was used for memory refresh, and Counter 2 drove the little speaker that went beep. We will use these real ports in our examples, because many emulators still copy them.

The control word: Before using a counter you send one control byte to the control register. Bits D7 and D6, called SC1 and SC0, select the counter: 00 for Counter 0, 01 for Counter 1, 10 for Counter 2. On the 8254, 11 means the special read-back command; on the 8253 it is illegal. Bits D5 and D4, called RW1 and RW0, say how the count is read or written: 00 is the counter latch command, 01 means low byte only, 10 means high byte only, 11 means low byte first and then high byte. Bits D3, D2 and D1, called M2 M1 M0, choose the mode from 0 to 5. Bit D0 chooses the number format: 0 for a 16-bit binary count, 1 for a four-digit BCD count.

Mode bits in detail: Mode 0 is 000, Mode 1 is 001, Mode 2 is 010, Mode 3 is 011, Mode 4 is 100 and Mode 5 is 101. For Modes 2 and 3 the top bit M2 is a don't care, so 110 also means Mode 2 and 111 also means Mode 3, but you will normally write 010 and 011. With 16-bit binary counting the largest count is 65,536, which you load by writing 0, because the counter decrements first and reaches 0 only after a full cycle. In BCD mode the largest is 10,000, also loaded as 0.

The six modes, explained simply: Mode 0 is interrupt on terminal count: after you write the count, OUT goes low, the counter counts down, and when it reaches zero OUT goes high and stays high. Connect OUT to an interrupt line and you have a one-time alarm clock. Mode 1 is a hardware retriggerable one-shot: OUT goes low on a rising edge at GATE and returns high when the count expires, giving a single pulse of a chosen width; another trigger restarts it. Mode 2 is a rate generator, a divide-by-N counter: OUT stays high and goes low for one clock pulse every N clocks, then the count reloads automatically. Mode 3 is a square wave generator: like Mode 2, but OUT is high for half the count and low for the other half. Mode 4 is a software triggered strobe: after the count is written, OUT stays high, then gives one low pulse of one clock when the count expires. Mode 5 is a hardware triggered strobe: the same single pulse, but the counting starts on a GATE rising edge.

The gate input: In Modes 0, 2, 3 and 4, GATE works like an enable switch: when GATE is high, counting happens; when GATE is low, counting pauses. In Modes 1 and 5, GATE is a trigger: a rising edge starts or restarts the count. In Modes 2 and 3, GATE going low also forces OUT high, and a rising edge reloads the count. If you do not need gate control, simply tie GATE high.

The golden formula: For a rate generator or square wave, the count N equals the input clock frequency divided by the output frequency you want. Example: the clock is 2 MHz and you want a 1 kHz square wave. N = 2,000,000 / 1,000 = 2000. In hex, 2000 is 07D0h. You load low byte D0h first and then high byte 07h. Another example: with the PC clock of 1,193,182 Hz, a 440 Hz musical note A needs N = 1,193,182 / 440, which is about 2712.

Building the control word for that 1 kHz wave: Counter 0 is SC = 00. We want low byte then high byte, RW = 11. Mode 3 is 011. Binary counting, BCD = 0. Putting it together: 00 11 011 0, which is 0011 0110, or 36h. This 36h is exactly the value PC programmers write to port 43h to set the system timer, so you may see it in many old programs.

The program: MOV AL, 36h then OUT 43h, AL selects Counter 0, low then high byte, Mode 3, binary. Then MOV AX, 2000 puts the count in AX. OUT 40h, AL sends the low byte to Counter 0. MOV AL, AH copies the high byte into AL, because OUT can only send from AL for a byte. OUT 40h, AL sends the high byte. That is it. From now on, Counter 0's OUT pin produces a 1 kHz square wave by itself, while the CPU goes off to do other jobs.

Playing a beep on the PC speaker: Counter 2 drives the speaker. Its control word for low then high byte, Mode 3, binary is 10 11 011 0, which is 1011 0110, or B6h. So: MOV AL, 0B6h and OUT 43h, AL; then load the count 2712 into Counter 2 at port 42h, low byte first, high byte second. On a PC, bits 0 and 1 of port 61h connect Counter 2's gate and the speaker, so you also set those two bits: IN AL, 61h, OR AL, 03h, OUT 61h, AL. Clearing them stops the sound. On a real old PC or in a DOS emulator this plays the note A.

Odd counts in Mode 3: If N is even, OUT is high for N/2 clocks and low for N/2 clocks, a perfect square wave. If N is odd, the output is high for (N + 1)/2 clocks and low for (N - 1)/2 clocks. For N = 5, high is 3 clocks and low is 2. This small detail comes in exams, so remember: odd counts make the high part one clock longer.

When one counter is not enough: A 16-bit counter can only divide by up to 65,536. Suppose the clock is 2 MHz and you want a pulse once per second. You need to divide by 2,000,000, which is too big. The trick is cascading: feed Counter 0's OUT into Counter 1's CLK. Set Counter 0 as a divide-by-2000 to produce 1 kHz, then set Counter 1 as divide-by-1000 to turn that 1 kHz into 1 Hz. 2000 times 1000 is 2,000,000. Chaining counters multiplies their divisions.

Reading the count on the fly: Sometimes you want to know how far a counter has reached without stopping it, for example to measure how long a key was pressed. If you read the count directly while it is changing, you might read the low byte, then the count changes, then you read the high byte of a different value. The counter latch command fixes this: write a control word with RW = 00 for that counter, such as 00h for Counter 0, and the chip freezes a copy of the current count in an output latch. You then read the low and high bytes calmly while the real counter keeps running.

How the 8254 improves on the 8253: The 8254 is pin compatible with the 8253 and does everything the 8253 does. The 8253 works with clock inputs up to about 2.6 MHz, while the 8254 handles up to 8 MHz, and the 8254-2 up to 10 MHz. The 8254 adds the read-back command, using SC1 SC0 = 11, which can latch the counts of several counters at once and also read a status byte for each counter. The status byte tells you the counter's mode settings, the current level of its OUT pin, and whether a newly written count has been loaded yet.

Real life example 1, a cricket scoreboard clock: Imagine your school's inter-house cricket match in Rajshahi, and the computer club builds a small scoreboard that shows the innings time. A software delay would drift whenever the CPU got busy updating the score. Instead, they use an 8254 with Counter 0 in Mode 2 dividing a 2 MHz clock by 20,000 to give 100 pulses per second, and connect OUT to an interrupt line. Every interrupt adds one hundredth of a second to the clock. The CPU only wakes up for a tiny moment each time, and the display stays accurate even while the score is being updated.

Real life example 2, counting products on a factory belt: In a biscuit factory near Gazipur, every packet on the conveyor belt passes a light sensor that sends one pulse. Connect that sensor to the CLK input of Counter 1 instead of a clock. Load the counter with 24 in Mode 0, so OUT goes high when 24 packets have passed. That signal interrupts the CPU, which tells a robot arm to close the carton and then reloads the counter for the next carton. Here the chip is not timing anything; it is counting events, which shows why it is called a counter/timer.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to send the control word before the count. Second, writing only one byte when the control word said low byte then high byte, which leaves the counter waiting. Third, sending the high byte first. Fourth, writing the count to the control register address instead of the counter's own address. Fifth, mixing up decimal and hex, for example writing 2000h when you meant decimal 2000, which is 07D0h. Sixth, forgetting that a count of 0 means the maximum, not zero.

What exams ask: Draw the block diagram of the 8253/8254 and explain each pin. Write the control word format. Explain any two modes with timing diagrams, Mode 3 and Mode 0 being the favourites. Find the count and control word to produce a given frequency from a given clock, and write the program. Explain cascading counters for long delays. Compare the 8253 and the 8254. Practise drawing the Mode 3 waveform for both even and odd counts.

Recap: The 8253/8254 has three independent 16-bit down counters, each with CLK, GATE and OUT. One control word per counter sets the counter number, how the count is written, the mode from 0 to 5 and binary or BCD. The count is input frequency divided by output frequency, loaded low byte then high byte. Mode 3 makes square waves, Mode 2 makes regular pulses, Mode 0 makes a one-time alarm, and Modes 1, 4 and 5 make single pulses. The 8254 runs faster and adds read-back. With this chip, the CPU never has to babysit a clock again.
key_points: The 8253/8254 has three independent 16-bit down counters, each with CLK, GATE and OUT pins; A1 A0 = 11 selects the control register.
Control word: SC1 SC0 pick the counter, RW1 RW0 pick latch/LSB/MSB/LSB-then-MSB, M2 M1 M0 pick mode 0-5, D0 picks binary or BCD.
Count N = input clock frequency / desired output frequency; e.g. 2 MHz to 1 kHz needs 2000 (07D0h), low byte first.
Mode 0 interrupt on terminal count, 1 one-shot, 2 rate generator, 3 square wave, 4 software strobe, 5 hardware strobe.
36h sets Counter 0 to LSB-then-MSB, Mode 3, binary; B6h does the same for Counter 2 (the PC speaker).
Counters can be cascaded (OUT of one into CLK of the next) to divide by more than 65,536.
The 8254 is faster (8 MHz, 10 MHz for 8254-2, versus about 2.6 MHz) and adds the read-back command and status byte.
lessons.tip: For every timer question, write three lines before any code: which counter, what count (in decimal and hex), and the control word in binary with labels. Then the program almost writes itself.
lessons.task: On paper, design a 500 Hz square wave on Counter 1 from a 1.5 MHz clock: find the count (3000 = 0BB8h), build the control word (01 11 011 0 = 76h) and write the six MOV/OUT instructions using ports 40h-43h.

quiz.q: How many counters does an 8254 contain, and how wide is each?
quiz.explain: Both 8253 and 8254 have three independent 16-bit down counters: Counter 0, 1 and 2.

quiz.q: Which 8254 mode produces a square wave?
quiz.explain: Mode 3 is the square wave generator: OUT is high for about half the count and low for the other half.

quiz.q: A 2 MHz clock must produce a 1 kHz output. What count do you load?
quiz.explain: N = 2,000,000 / 1,000 = 2000, which is 07D0h, written low byte first.

quiz.q: What does control word 36h set up?
options: Counter 0, LSB then MSB, Mode 3, binary
quiz.explain: 36h = 00 11 011 0: Counter 0, read/write LSB then MSB, Mode 3, binary counting.

quiz.q: What feature does the 8254 add that the 8253 does not have?
options: The read-back command with a status byte
quiz.explain: The 8254 adds the read-back command (SC1 SC0 = 11) that can latch several counts at once and read each counter's status.

lessons.title: Data Transfer Schemes, 8237 DMA and 8251 USART
lessons.content:
Imagine you are waiting for a parcel from Daraz. There are three ways to handle it. One: you walk to the gate every five minutes to check if the delivery man has arrived. Two: you go about your day, and the delivery man rings your phone when he is at the gate. Three: you tell the building guard to collect the parcel and put it inside your room without disturbing you at all. A microprocessor faces exactly these three choices when it moves data between devices and memory. They are called programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O and direct memory access, or DMA. In this lesson we compare them, then meet two helper chips: the 8237 DMA controller and the 8251 USART for serial communication.

Programmed I/O, also called polling: In programmed I/O the CPU controls every step. It reads a status register again and again in a loop, waiting for a ready bit, then reads or writes one data byte, then goes back to waiting. A tiny polling loop on the 8086 looks like this: WAIT1: IN AL, STATUS, then TEST AL, 01h to check bit 0, then JZ WAIT1 to loop while the device is not ready, and finally IN AL, DATA to take the byte. It is simple and needs no extra hardware. But it wastes CPU time: while the CPU checks the gate, it cannot do anything else. If the device is slow, like a keyboard where a person types maybe five keys per second, the CPU spends almost all its time asking the same question.

Interrupt-driven I/O: Here the device itself signals the CPU when it is ready, using an interrupt line such as INTR, often through the 8259 controller you met earlier. The CPU runs its normal program. When the interrupt arrives, it finishes the current instruction, saves its place, jumps to the interrupt service routine, moves the byte, and returns with IRET. No time is wasted on checking. The cost is a little overhead for every interrupt: pushing flags and return address, jumping, saving registers, and returning. For a few bytes per second that is nothing. For a disk sending hundreds of thousands of bytes per second, the overhead of one interrupt per byte would eat the CPU alive.

Direct memory access: In DMA, the CPU steps aside completely while a special controller moves data directly between the device and memory. The CPU only sets up the job: the memory start address, the number of bytes and the direction. Then the DMA controller borrows the system buses and does the transfer at bus speed. When it finishes, it usually tells the CPU with an interrupt. This is the building guard in our story. It is the right choice for big blocks of fast data, such as disk sectors, sound samples or network packets.

How the CPU gives up the bus, HOLD and HLDA: Only one master can drive the address and data buses at a time. On the 8085, and on the 8086 in minimum mode, there are two pins for this: HOLD, an input, and HLDA, hold acknowledge, an output. When the DMA controller wants the buses, it raises HOLD. The CPU finishes its current bus cycle, then puts its address, data and control pins into the high-impedance state, which is like letting go of the steering wheel, and raises HLDA to say the buses are yours. When the DMA controller is done, it lowers HOLD and the CPU lowers HLDA and takes the buses back. In maximum mode the 8086 uses request/grant pins called RQ/GT instead.

The 8237 DMA controller: The Intel 8237A is a programmable DMA controller with four independent channels, numbered 0 to 3. Each channel has a 16-bit address register and a 16-bit count register, so one channel can move up to 64 KB in one job. Each channel has its own request input DREQ, from the device, and acknowledge output DACK, to the device. Channel priorities can be fixed, with channel 0 highest, or rotating, so that no channel gets starved. The chip also supports a memory-to-memory transfer using channels 0 and 1 together. In the original IBM PC, the 8237 handled the floppy disk transfers on channel 2, and extra page registers supplied the upper address bits, because the 8237 itself only produces 16 address bits.

A DMA transfer step by step: Suppose a disk controller wants to send 512 bytes to memory starting at address 2000h. Step 1, the CPU programs the 8237: channel number, start address 2000h, count, and mode. Because the 8237 transfers one byte more than the count it is given, the CPU loads 511 for 512 bytes. Step 2, when the disk has data, it raises DREQ on that channel. Step 3, the 8237 raises its HRQ output, which is connected to the CPU's HOLD. Step 4, the CPU finishes its bus cycle, floats the buses and answers with HLDA. Step 5, the 8237 sends DACK to the disk, puts the memory address on the bus, and activates the I/O read and memory write signals together, so the byte flows straight from the disk into memory without passing through any CPU register. Step 6, the address goes up by one and the count goes down by one. Step 7, when the count rolls past zero, the 8237 signals terminal count, called TC or EOP, releases the bus, and the disk controller usually interrupts the CPU to say the job is done.

The 8237's transfer modes: In single transfer mode, the 8237 moves one byte, then gives the bus back to the CPU for at least one cycle, so the CPU keeps running slowly. In block transfer mode, it keeps the bus until the whole block is done, which is fastest but freezes the CPU's bus access meanwhile. In demand transfer mode, it keeps transferring as long as the device keeps DREQ active, and pauses when the device runs out of data. Cascade mode lets you connect more 8237s for more channels. Each transfer can also be a read, write or verify transfer; verify goes through the motions without moving data, and is used for testing.

Serial versus parallel communication: Parallel transfer sends all eight bits at once on eight wires. It is fast over short distances, like inside a computer or the old printer cable. But many wires are expensive, and over long cables the bits can arrive at slightly different times, a problem called skew. Serial transfer sends one bit at a time on a single wire, plus ground. It needs very few wires and goes long distances, which is why USB, Ethernet, the old RS-232 COM port and most modern links are serial. To go serial, someone must turn a parallel byte into a stream of bits and back again. That is the job of a UART or USART.

Asynchronous serial frames: In asynchronous communication there is no shared clock wire. Both sides just agree on a speed, such as 9600 bits per second. The line rests at logic 1, called mark. To send a character, the sender first sends a start bit of 0, then the data bits with the least significant bit first, then an optional parity bit, then one or more stop bits of 1. The common format 8N1 means 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, which is 10 bits per character. So at 9600 baud you can send about 960 characters per second. Example: the letter A is 41h, which is 0100 0001. Sent LSB first, the data bits on the wire are 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, framed by a 0 start bit and a 1 stop bit.

Synchronous serial: In synchronous mode, characters are sent back to back without start and stop bits, and the receiver stays in step using special sync characters or a separate clock. This wastes less time on framing, so it is more efficient for large blocks, but both sides must stay perfectly in step. The S in USART means the chip can do synchronous as well as asynchronous communication.

The 8251 USART: The Intel 8251A is a Universal Synchronous Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter, a 28-pin chip that connects to the CPU's 8-bit data bus on one side and to a serial line on the other. Its pin C/D tells it whether the CPU is writing a control byte or a data byte. Inside it has a transmit buffer that turns parallel bytes into serial bits on TxD, a receive buffer that turns serial bits from RxD into bytes, a modem control block with signals like DTR, DSR, RTS and CTS, and a status register. Status bits such as TxRDY and RxRDY tell the CPU when it can send the next byte or when a received byte is waiting, so the CPU can poll them or use them as interrupts.

Programming the 8251, the mode word: After reset, the first control byte is the mode word. For asynchronous mode, bits D1 D0 give the baud rate factor: 01 means the clock is 1 times the baud rate, 10 means 16 times, 11 means 64 times, and 00 means synchronous mode. Bits D3 D2 give the character length: 00 for 5 bits, 01 for 6, 10 for 7 and 11 for 8. D4 enables parity, D5 chooses even parity when 1, and D7 D6 give the stop bits: 01 for 1, 10 for 1.5 and 11 for 2. So asynchronous, 16 times clock, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit is 01 0 0 11 10, which is 0100 1110, or 4Eh, the most famous 8251 mode word.
