Iteration 2: m = 2.25, g = 1.890625, interval [2, 2.25]. Iteration 3: m = 2.125, g = 0.345703, interval [2, 2.125]. Iteration 4: m = 2.0625, g = -0.351318, interval [2.0625, 2.125]. Iteration 5: m = 2.09375, g = -0.008942, interval [2.09375, 2.125]. Iteration 6: m = 2.109375, g = 0.166836. Iteration 7: m = 2.101562, g = 0.078562. Iteration 8: m = 2.097656, g = 0.034714. The true root is about 2.094551, and the bracket after 8 steps is [2.09375, 2.097656], width 0.003906.

Sub-heading: How many iterations do we need: Because the bracket halves each time, after n steps its width is (b - a) / 2^n. If we answer with the midpoint, the error is at most half the current bracket. A common, simple rule is: choose n so that (b - a) / 2^n is at most the tolerance. That gives n >= log2((b - a) / tol), and we round n up to a whole number. For [1, 2] and tol = 0.01, n = 7, since 2^7 = 128. For tol = 0.001, n = 10, since 2^10 = 1024. For tol = 0.000001, n = 20, since 2^20 = 1048576. The amazing part is that we know this number before we start, and it does not even depend on what f is.

Sub-heading: Linear convergence: Every step of bisection gains the same amount of accuracy: one binary digit, which means about one decimal digit every 3.3 steps, since 2^3.3 is about 10. When the error shrinks by a constant factor each step, here a factor of about one half, we call it linear convergence. It is reliable but slow. In our example, bisection needed 19 steps before the midpoint was within 0.000001 of the root. In the coming lessons you will see Newton-Raphson reach the same accuracy in about 5 steps from x0 = 1. Bisection is the tortoise in the race: never fast, never lost.

Sub-heading: Stopping criteria: A real program needs a clear rule for when to stop. Common choices are: stop when the half width (b - a) / 2 is below a tolerance, stop when |f(m)| is below a small number, or stop when the approximate relative error |m_new - m_old| / |m_new| is small enough, the idea from the error lessons. Always add a maximum iteration count too, as a safety net, so that a bug never makes your program loop forever. Be careful with |f(m)| alone: a very flat function can have a tiny f(m) far from the root, and a very steep one can have a big f(m) even when m is very close.

Sub-heading: Strengths and weaknesses: Bisection always converges if you start with a valid bracket and f is continuous. It needs only values of f, no derivative. It is easy to code and easy to explain in an exam. On the bad side, it is slow. It cannot find a root where the curve touches the axis without crossing it, like f(x) = (x - 1)^2, because there is no sign change. It finds only one root per bracket, and if the bracket holds three roots you cannot choose which one you get. Because of all this, real software often starts with a bracketing step for safety and then switches to a faster method.

Sub-heading: Real life example, splitting the bazar bill: Imagine you and your cousin share a fixed bazar budget and you want to find the price of a kilo of fish that makes the total exactly 1000 taka (example numbers). You guess 400 taka, total too big. You guess 200 taka, total too small. So the answer is between 200 and 400. Try 300, still too big, so it is between 200 and 300. Each try halves the range. A shopkeeper doing this in his head is doing bisection. Any time you can only check "too much or too little", halving is the safe strategy.

Sub-heading: Real life example, finding the bad commit: Programmers use bisection all the time without equations. Say an app worked fine in version 1 and is broken in version 100. Instead of testing all 100 versions, you test version 50. If it is broken, the bug came between 1 and 50, otherwise between 50 and 100. After about 7 tests you have the exact version, since 2^7 = 128 is more than 100. The git tool even has a command for this called git bisect. It is the same sign change idea: "works" and "broken" play the role of negative and positive.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget to check f(a) * f(b) < 0 before starting. Others update the wrong end: the rule is to keep the half where the signs still differ. Some round too early in the table and get lost, so keep at least two more decimals than you need. A typical exam question says: "Find the root of x^3 - x - 2 = 0 in [1, 2] correct to 2 decimal places by bisection", or "How many iterations are needed for an error less than 0.001 on [1, 2]?" For the second question, show the formula n >= log2((b - a) / tol) and the answer n = 10. Presenting a neat table with columns a, b, m and f(m) and the sign gets you full marks.

Sub-heading: Recap: A root is where f(x) = 0. If f is continuous and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, a root hides between them. Bisection keeps halving the bracket, keeping the half with the sign change. The number of steps is known ahead: n >= log2((b - a) / tol). It converges linearly, one binary digit per step, slow but guaranteed. Next lesson, false position keeps the safety of a bracket but uses a smarter point than the middle, by drawing a straight line between the two ends.
key_points: A root of f(x) = 0 is where the graph of f crosses or touches the x-axis.
Intermediate value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a) * f(b) < 0, there is at least one root in (a, b).
Bracketing methods (bisection, false position) never lose the root; open methods (Newton, secant, fixed point) are faster but can fail.
Find a starting bracket by tabulating f at a few points and looking for a sign change.
Bisection: m = (a + b) / 2, keep the half where the sign changes, repeat.
After n steps the bracket width is (b - a) / 2^n, so n >= log2((b - a) / tol) steps are enough.
Bisection converges linearly, about one binary digit per step; for x^3 - x - 2 on [1, 2] it reached 1.521240 after 12 steps.
Use a tolerance plus a maximum iteration count as stopping rules; bisection cannot find roots that touch without crossing.
lessons.tip: In exams, always draw the table with columns n, a, b, m, f(m) and write the sign of f(m) in a separate column. The sign column alone tells you which end to move, and the examiner can follow your work at a glance.
lessons.task: With a phone calculator, run 6 steps of bisection for x^2 - 3 = 0 on [1, 2] and write the table. Then use n >= log2((b - a) / tol) to predict how many steps would give an error below 0.0001, and compare your last midpoint with sqrt(3) from the calculator.

quiz.q: Bisection needs f(a) and f(b) to have what property before it starts?
quiz.explain: Opposite signs plus continuity guarantee, by the intermediate value theorem, that a root lies between a and b.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 on [1, 2], the first midpoint is 1.5 and f(1.5) = -0.125. What is the new interval?
quiz.explain: f(1.5) is negative like f(1) = -2, so the sign change, and the root, is in the right half [1.5, 2].

quiz.q: How many bisection steps guarantee a bracket width of at most 0.001 starting from [1, 2]?
What kind of convergence does bisection have?
options: Linear, the error bound halves each step
quiz.explain: The bracket width is multiplied by 1/2 every step, a constant factor, which is linear convergence.

quiz.q: Why can bisection not find the root of f(x) = (x - 1)^2?
options: f never changes sign, so there is no bracket
quiz.explain: (x - 1)^2 is never negative. It touches zero at x = 1 without crossing, so no interval has a sign change.

lessons.title: False Position (Regula Falsi)
lessons.content:
Imagine you are guessing where a cricket ball landed on a long, straight boundary rope. One friend stands at the left end and shouts "it is 2 metres away from me". Another friend at the right end shouts "it is 4 metres away from me". Would you walk to the exact middle? Of course not. The ball is closer to the first friend, so you would walk closer to him. Bisection always walks to the middle and ignores how big the values are. False position, also called regula falsi, uses those sizes to make a smarter guess. That is today's lesson.

Sub-heading: Quick reminder: In the last lesson we learned that if f is continuous and f(a) * f(b) < 0, a root of f(x) = 0 is trapped in [a, b]. Bisection kept halving that bracket. It was safe but slow: for f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 on [1, 2] it needed 19 steps to get within 0.000001 of the root 1.521380. False position keeps the same safety, the root stays trapped, but tries to reach it faster.

Sub-heading: The chord idea: Plot the two points (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)). One is below the x-axis and one is above. Join them with a straight line, called a chord. The chord must cross the x-axis somewhere between a and b. False position takes that crossing point as the new guess. If the curve is nearly straight near the root, the chord crossing lands very close to the true root. It is like assuming the function is a straight line between the two ends, and then correcting that assumption step by step.

Sub-heading: Deriving the formula: The line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) has slope (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a). Start at point b and go down the line until the height becomes zero. We need to move left by f(b) divided by the slope. So the new point is c = b - f(b) * (b - a) / (f(b) - f(a)). If you tidy up the algebra you get the same thing in a symmetric form: c = (a * f(b) - b * f(a)) / (f(b) - f(a)). Both forms are correct. The first one is nicer on a computer, the second is easy to remember for exams.

Sub-heading: The old name: Regula falsi is Latin for "rule of false position". The name comes from very old arithmetic, where people solved problems by trying a false answer, seeing how wrong it was, and then correcting it in proportion. Our chord formula does exactly that: it uses two wrong guesses, a and b, and their errors f(a) and f(b), to calculate a better one.

Sub-heading: The algorithm: Start with a, b where f(a) * f(b) < 0. Step 1: compute c = b - f(b) * (b - a) / (f(b) - f(a)). Step 2: compute f(c). Step 3: if f(c) = 0, stop. If f(a) * f(c) < 0, the root is between a and c, so set b = c. Otherwise set a = c. Step 4: check the stopping rule and repeat. Notice that it is exactly bisection with one line changed: the midpoint (a + b) / 2 is replaced by the chord point c. The bracket rule, keep the side where the sign changes, is the same.

Sub-heading: Worked example, step 1 by hand: Use f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 on [1, 2], with f(1) = -2 and f(2) = 4. Values are rounded to 6 decimal places. With the symmetric formula: c = (1 * 4 - 2 * (-2)) / (4 - (-2)) = (4 + 4) / 6 = 8 / 6 = 1.333333. Then f(1.333333) = -0.962963. That is negative, like f(1), so the root is between 1.333333 and 2, and we set a = 1.333333. Compare: bisection would have guessed 1.5, which happens to be closer this time. False position is not better at every single step, but it usually wins over several steps.

Sub-heading: Worked example, step 2 by hand: Now a = 1.333333 with f(a) = -0.962963, and b = 2 with f(b) = 4. The top part is a * f(b) - b * f(a) = 5.333333 + 1.925926 = 7.259259. The bottom part is f(b) - f(a) = 4 + 0.962963 = 4.962963. So c = 7.259259 / 4.962963 = 1.462687, and f(1.462687) = -0.333339. Still negative, so again a moves: a = 1.462687, and b stays at 2.

Sub-heading: The full table: Continuing the same way, the new points are: iteration 1, c = 1.333333, f(c) = -0.962963. Iteration 2, c = 1.462687, f(c) = -0.333339. Iteration 3, c = 1.504019, f(c) = -0.101818. Iteration 4, c = 1.516331, f(c) = -0.029895. Iteration 5, c = 1.519919, f(c) = -0.008675. Iteration 6, c = 1.520957, f(c) = -0.002509. Iteration 7, c = 1.521258, f(c) = -0.000725. Iteration 8, c = 1.521344, f(c) = -0.000209. The true root is 1.521380, so after 8 steps the error is about 0.000035. Bisection after 8 steps was at 1.519531, with an error of about 0.001848.

Sub-heading: Did you spot the pattern: Every single f(c) in that table is negative. That means a moved every time and b stayed stuck at 2 for all 8 iterations. This is the famous one-sided behaviour of false position. Because of it, the bracket width b - a does not shrink to zero. It shrinks towards 2 - 1.521380, about 0.478620. So with false position you cannot use "bracket width is small" as a stopping rule. Use the change between successive guesses, |c_new - c_old|, or |f(c)|, instead.

Sub-heading: Why one end gets stuck: Our function x^3 - x - 2 is convex on [1, 2], which means it curves upward like a smile, because its second derivative 6x is positive there. For a curve that bends like this, the chord always lies above the curve between the two points. So the chord hits the x-axis a little before the true root, on the same side as a, every time. The far end b never gets replaced. Whenever f keeps the same bending direction across the bracket, one endpoint tends to stay fixed.

Sub-heading: Convergence of false position: If you divide each error in our table by the one before it, the ratio settles near 0.289. So the error shrinks by a constant factor at each step, which is linear convergence, just like bisection. The difference is the factor: about 0.289 here, against 0.5 for bisection. That is why false position needed 11 steps to get within 0.000001 of the root, while bisection needed 19. But the factor depends on the function. For some functions the stuck end makes false position much slower than bisection, and the ratio creeps very close to 1.

Sub-heading: The second example: Take g(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 on [2, 3], with g(2) = -1 and g(3) = 16. Step 1: c = (2 * 16 - 3 * (-1)) / (16 - (-1)) = 35 / 17 = 2.058824, and g(c) = -0.390800. Step 2: c = 2.081264, g = -0.147204. Step 3: c = 2.089639, g = -0.054677. Step 4: c = 2.092740, g = -0.020203. Step 5: c = 2.093884, g = -0.007451. Step 6: c = 2.094305, g = -0.002746. The true root is 2.094551. Again every g(c) is negative and b = 3 never moves. Same story, same cause: g is convex on [2, 3].

Sub-heading: Bisection versus false position: Both are bracketing methods and both always keep the root trapped. Both need only function values. Bisection ignores the values of f and uses only their signs, so its speed is fixed and predictable, and you can count the needed steps in advance with n >= log2((b - a) / tol). False position uses the actual values, so it usually gets close faster, but you cannot predict the step count in advance, and a stuck endpoint can make it crawl. Each step of both methods costs one new function evaluation.

Sub-heading: The Illinois modification: There is a clever fix for the stuck end. If the same endpoint has stayed in place for two steps in a row, we pretend its function value is only half as big: we replace f(b) by f(b) / 2 before computing the next chord. This tilts the chord, so the next point lands on the other side of the root and the stuck end finally moves. For our example on [1, 2], b stayed for steps 1 and 2, so step 3 used f(b) = 2 instead of 4. The new point was 1.539447, with f = 0.108882, positive, so b moved at last. The next points were 1.520547, 1.521368 and 1.521391, closing in from both sides.

Sub-heading: How much Illinois helps: With the Illinois trick, our example got within 0.000001 of the root in 7 steps, compared with 11 for plain false position and 19 for bisection. It is still a bracketing method, so it stays safe. Numerical analysts have shown that its convergence is faster than linear. There are similar variants with other scaling factors, and the general idea of mixing safety with speed leads to the methods that real libraries use, which combine bisection with faster steps. For your exam, knowing the idea of halving the stuck value is enough.

Sub-heading: Real life example, guessing a rickshaw fare: Say a rickshaw ride of 2 km costs 40 taka and a ride of 6 km costs 100 taka (example numbers). Your friend paid 70 taka. How far did he go? You draw a straight line between the two known rides: 60 extra taka for 4 extra km, so 15 taka per km. 70 taka is 30 more than 40, so about 2 more km, about 4 km in total. That is a single false position step: assume a straight line between two known points and read off where the target lands.

Sub-heading: Real life example, tuning a water heater: An engineer wants a water heater setting that gives exactly 40 degrees Celsius. Setting 3 gives 32 degrees and setting 7 gives 52 degrees (example numbers). Instead of trying 5, the middle, she draws the line and tries 3 + (40 - 32) / (52 - 32) * 4 = 3 + 1.6 = 4.6. If the heater behaves almost like a straight line, she is very close in one try. If the temperature curve bends, she repeats with the new pair of settings, just like false position.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common error is a sign slip in the formula. Write c = (a * f(b) - b * f(a)) / (f(b) - f(a)) and double check the minus signs, because f(a) is negative. Another is keeping the wrong side; the rule is the same as bisection. Some students stop when b - a is small, but with a stuck end that never happens. Typical exam questions: "Find the root of x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0 by regula falsi correct to 3 decimals", "Derive the false position formula from similar triangles", and "Compare bisection and false position". Mention the stuck endpoint and the Illinois fix for extra marks.

Sub-heading: Recap: False position draws a chord between (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) and uses its x-axis crossing c = b - f(b) * (b - a) / (f(b) - f(a)) as the new guess. It keeps the root bracketed, needs no derivative, and is usually faster than bisection, as in our example with 11 steps against 19. But if f curves the same way across the bracket, one end gets stuck, and convergence stays linear. The Illinois modification halves the stuck value to unstick it. Next lesson, Newton-Raphson drops the bracket entirely and uses the tangent line, which is much faster when it works.
key_points: False position (regula falsi) replaces the midpoint with the x-intercept of the chord through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)).
Formula: c = b - f(b) * (b - a) / (f(b) - f(a)) = (a * f(b) - b * f(a)) / (f(b) - f(a)).
It is a bracketing method: keep the side where the sign changes, exactly as in bisection.
For x^3 - x - 2 on [1, 2], the guesses were 1.333333, 1.462687, 1.504019 ... and b stayed stuck at 2.
When f curves the same way across the bracket, one endpoint stays fixed and the bracket width does not go to zero.
Convergence is linear; the error ratio was about 0.289 in our example, versus 0.5 for bisection.
The Illinois modification halves the function value of an endpoint that stays fixed twice in a row, which unsticks it.
Stop false position using |c_new - c_old| or |f(c)|, not the bracket width.
lessons.tip: When you finish a false position table, scan the sign column. If all signs are the same, write one line saying "b stayed fixed because f is convex here". It shows the examiner you understand the method, not only the formula.
lessons.task: On paper or with a phone calculator, run 4 steps of false position for x^2 - 3 = 0 on [1, 2]. Check whether one endpoint stays stuck, and then try the Illinois trick (halve the stuck end's f value) for 2 more steps. Compare both answers with sqrt(3).

quiz.q: Which point does false position choose as the next guess?
options: The point where the tangent at b meets the x-axis
Where the chord joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) crosses the x-axis
quiz.explain: The chord through the two bracket points crosses the x-axis between a and b, and that crossing is the new guess.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 on [1, 2], with f(1) = -2 and f(2) = 4, what is the first false position point?
In our example b stayed at 2 for every step. Why?
options: f is convex on [1, 2], so each chord crosses the axis on the same side of the root
quiz.explain: With f'' = 6x > 0, the chord lies above the curve, so every new point lands left of the root and only a moves.

quiz.q: What does the Illinois modification do?
options: Uses the derivative instead of a chord
Halves the function value of an endpoint that stays fixed, to tilt the chord
quiz.explain: Halving the stuck end's f value tilts the chord so the next point lands on the other side and the stuck end moves.

quiz.q: Which stopping rule is unsafe for plain false position?
options: The bracket width b - a small
quiz.explain: With a stuck endpoint the width tends to a nonzero value (about 0.478620 in our example), so it may never become small.

lessons.title: The Newton-Raphson Method
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing on a hillside on a foggy morning, trying to walk down to a river at the very bottom. You cannot see the river, but you can feel the slope under your feet. If the ground tilts steeply, the river is probably close. If it tilts gently, the river may be far away. So you use the slope to decide how far to walk. Newton-Raphson does exactly this with a function: it looks at the value and the slope at your current guess, and jumps straight to where the slope says the zero should be. When it works, it is the fastest method in this part of the course.

Sub-heading: Where we are: In the last two lessons we used bracketing methods, bisection and false position, to solve f(x) = 0 for our running example f(x) = x^3 - x - 2, whose root is about 1.521380. They were safe but slow: 19 and 11 steps to get within 0.000001. Newton-Raphson is an open method. It starts from one guess x0, needs no bracket, and uses the derivative f'(x). In exchange for losing the safety of a bracket, it gains huge speed.

Sub-heading: The tangent idea: At the point (x0, f(x0)) on the curve, draw the tangent line, the straight line that just touches the curve with the same slope f'(x0). Near x0 the tangent is a good copy of the curve. A straight line is easy to solve: just find where it crosses the x-axis. That crossing is our next guess x1. Then draw a new tangent at x1, find where it crosses, and so on. Each tangent slides us down towards the root.

Sub-heading: Deriving the formula from the tangent: The tangent at x0 is y = f(x0) + f'(x0) * (x - x0). Set y = 0 and solve for x. We get x = x0 - f(x0) / f'(x0). So the Newton-Raphson formula is x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n). It is short enough to remember forever: new guess equals old guess minus the value divided by the slope. You can also see it as "rise over run": if the height is f(x0) and the slope is f'(x0), you must run f(x0) / f'(x0) to reach height zero.

Sub-heading: Deriving it from Taylor series: The same formula comes out of Taylor series, which you met in Calculus and in the error lessons. If the root is at x0 + h, then 0 = f(x0 + h) = f(x0) + h * f'(x0) + (h^2 / 2) * f''(x0) + ... When h is small we drop the h^2 term and everything after it. That leaves 0 = f(x0) + h * f'(x0), so h = -f(x0) / f'(x0). The dropped h^2 term is exactly why Newton is not exact in one step, and also, as we will see, why its error behaves like the square of the previous error.

Sub-heading: The algorithm: Choose a starting guess x0, a tolerance and a maximum number of steps. Repeat: compute f(x_n) and f'(x_n); if f'(x_n) is zero or nearly zero, stop and report a problem; otherwise compute x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n). Stop when |x_(n+1) - x_n| is below the tolerance, or the relative change is small, or the step limit is reached. Each step needs two evaluations: one of f and one of f'. For our running example, f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1.

Sub-heading: Worked example, step by step: Take f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 and x0 = 1.5. Here we keep 10 decimal places, because Newton gets accurate so fast that 6 decimals would hide what happens. Step 1: f(1.5) = -0.125 and f'(1.5) = 3 * 2.25 - 1 = 5.75. So x1 = 1.5 - (-0.125) / 5.75 = 1.5 + 0.0217391304 = 1.5217391304. Step 2: f(x1) = 0.0021369278 and f'(x1) = 5.9470699433, so x2 = 1.5213798060. Step 3: f(x2) = 0.0000005894 and f'(x2) = 5.9437895420, so x3 = 1.5213797068. Step 4 gives 1.5213797068 again. The root to 10 decimals is 1.5213797068.

Sub-heading: Watch the errors collapse: The distance from the true root was about 0.0214 at x0, then about 0.000359 after one step, then about 0.0000000992 after two steps, and after the third step it was about 0.00000000000001, right at the limit of ordinary double precision. Look at the number of correct decimals: roughly 1, then 3, then 7, then about 14. The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. That is the magic of Newton-Raphson.

Sub-heading: Starting further away: Now try x0 = 1 with 6 decimals. f(1) = -2 and f'(1) = 2, so x1 = 1 + 1 = 2. That jump overshoots the root quite a lot. Then x2 = 1.636364, x3 = 1.530392, x4 = 1.521441 and x5 = 1.521380. Five steps were enough to get within 0.000001, compared with 19 for bisection and 11 for false position. Notice that the first steps were clumsy. Newton is fast once it is close, but far away it can wander.

Sub-heading: Second example: Solve g(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0 with g'(x) = 3x^2 - 2, starting at x0 = 2, with 10 decimals. Step 1: g(2) = -1 and g'(2) = 10, so x1 = 2 + 0.1 = 2.1. Step 2: g(2.1) = 0.061 and g'(2.1) = 11.23, so x2 = 2.1 - 0.061 / 11.23 = 2.0945681211. Step 3: x3 = 2.0945514817. Step 4: x4 = 2.0945514815. In three or four steps we have ten correct decimals. Bisection on the same equation was still at 2.097656 after 8 steps.

Sub-heading: Square roots by Newton: To find sqrt(a), solve f(x) = x^2 - a = 0. Then f'(x) = 2x and the formula becomes x_(n+1) = x_n - (x_n^2 - a) / (2 x_n) = (x_n + a / x_n) / 2. In words: average your guess and a divided by your guess. This rule is much older than Newton; it is often called the Babylonian method. For a = 2 and x0 = 1, with 10 decimals: x1 = 1.5, x2 = 1.4166666667, x3 = 1.4142156863, x4 = 1.4142135624, which is sqrt(2) to 10 decimals. The errors were about 0.0858, 0.00245, 0.00000212 and 0.0000000000016, again doubling the correct digits.

Sub-heading: Reciprocals without dividing: Here is a cool trick. To compute 1/a without any division, solve f(x) = 1/x - a = 0. Then f'(x) = -1/x^2, and after simplifying, Newton's formula becomes x_(n+1) = x_n * (2 - a * x_n). Only multiplications and a subtraction! For a = 7 and x0 = 0.1, with 10 decimals: x1 = 0.13, x2 = 0.1417, x3 = 0.1428477700, x4 = 0.1428571422, x5 = 0.1428571429, which is 1/7. Some computer hardware has used this idea to do division with multipliers. It converges when the start satisfies 0 < x0 < 2/a.

Sub-heading: Quadratic convergence: If e_n is the error at step n, Newton satisfies, close to a simple root r, e_(n+1) is approximately C * e_n^2, with C = f''(r) / (2 f'(r)). When the error is squared each step, we call it quadratic convergence, or order 2. For our running example, C = 6r / (2 * (3r^2 - 1)), which is about 0.768. Using the unrounded errors, e1 / e0^2 is about 0.786 and e2 / e1^2 is about 0.768, matching nicely. Compare that to bisection, where the error is only multiplied by about 1/2 each step.

Sub-heading: Failure case one, zero or tiny derivative: The formula divides by f'(x_n). If the slope is zero, the tangent is flat and never meets the x-axis, so the method crashes. For f(x) = x^3 - x - 2, f'(x) = 0 at x = 1/sqrt(3), about 0.577350. Starting there is impossible. Starting near a flat spot is also bad: a tiny slope sends the next guess very far away. Starting at x0 = 0 gives x1 = -2, x2 = -1.272727, x3 = -0.550127, and then a giant jump to x4 = -18.103573, after which it slowly crawls back. After 12 steps it is only at 0.296722, still far from the root.

Sub-heading: Failure case two, cycling: Sometimes Newton goes round in circles forever. A classic example is h(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2 with x0 = 0. Then h(0) = 2 and h'(0) = -2, so x1 = 1. Then h(1) = 1 and h'(1) = 1, so x2 = 0 again. The guesses go 0, 1, 0, 1, ... and never settle, even though h does have a real root near -1.77. This is why every Newton program needs a maximum iteration count.

Sub-heading: Failure case three, bad start and the wrong root: When a function has several roots, the root you get depends on where you start, and the answer can be surprising. A start near a flat region may jump over the root you wanted and land near a different one. A practical cure is to first trap the root with a few bisection steps and then switch to Newton. Many real solvers mix the two exactly like this: the bracket gives safety, Newton gives speed.

Sub-heading: Multiple roots: A root is called multiple if the curve touches the axis there, like x = 1 for f(x) = (x - 1)^2, where both f and f' are zero. Newton still converges, but only linearly. For (x - 1)^2 from x0 = 2, the guesses are 1.5, 1.25, 1.125, 1.0625, 1.03125, the error just halves each step, no faster than bisection. If you know the multiplicity m, the modified formula x_(n+1) = x_n - m * f(x_n) / f'(x_n) restores fast convergence. For (x - 1)^2, m = 2, and it reaches 1 in one step.

Sub-heading: Real life example, your calculator: When you press the square root key, the calculator does not look up an answer in a giant table. Software that computes square roots often uses Newton-style steps, because each step roughly doubles the correct digits, so a good first guess plus a few steps is plenty. Our sqrt(2) example reached 10 correct decimals in 4 steps. You can repeat it on paper with just averaging: (x + 2 / x) / 2.

Sub-heading: Real life example, a bKash savings plan: Suppose you put 1000 taka per month in a savings plan, and after 12 months you have 12,500 taka (example numbers). What monthly interest rate i does that mean? The formula for the total is 1000 * ((1 + i)^12 - 1) / i = 12500, and there is no simple algebra trick to get i. Finance apps solve such equations with Newton-type iterations: guess i, compute the total and its slope, correct the guess, and repeat. A few steps give the rate to many decimals.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget the minus sign, or write f'(x) wrongly; always write f'(x) separately first. Some round too early, which hides the quadratic convergence. Others never check whether f'(x_n) is near zero. Typical exam questions: "Derive the Newton-Raphson formula geometrically", "Find sqrt(N) or 1/N by Newton and show the iteration formula", "Find the root of x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0 correct to 4 decimals", "Show that Newton converges quadratically", and "Give an example where Newton fails". Remember examples like the 0, 1, 0, 1 cycle and the halving error for (x - 1)^2.

Sub-heading: Recap: Newton-Raphson follows the tangent: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n). It comes from the tangent line or from the first two Taylor terms. Near a simple root it converges quadratically, roughly doubling the correct digits each step. It gives fast rules for square roots and reciprocals. But it needs the derivative, it can fail with a flat slope, a bad start or a cycle, and it slows to linear at a multiple root. Next lesson, the secant method keeps most of Newton's speed without needing the derivative at all.
key_points: Newton-Raphson: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n), the x-intercept of the tangent at x_n.
The formula comes from the tangent line, or from keeping the first two terms of the Taylor series.
It is an open method: one starting guess, no bracket, but it needs the derivative.
Square root: x_(n+1) = (x_n + a / x_n) / 2; reciprocal: x_(n+1) = x_n * (2 - a * x_n).
Near a simple root the convergence is quadratic: e_(n+1) is about C * e_n^2, correct digits roughly double.
It can fail with a zero or tiny derivative, a bad start, or cycling (x^3 - 2x + 2 from 0 gives 0, 1, 0, 1, ...).
At a multiple root Newton slows to linear; x_(n+1) = x_n - m * f / f' fixes it when the multiplicity m is known.
lessons.tip: Before starting the iteration in an exam, write f(x) and f'(x) on separate lines and check f'(x0) is not near zero. Then keep a column for |x_(n+1) - x_n| so you can show the quadratic shrinking and justify when you stopped.
lessons.task: Use your phone calculator and x_(n+1) = (x_n + 10 / x_n) / 2 starting from x0 = 3 to compute sqrt(10). Write down how many correct decimals you have after each step and check that they roughly double. Then try x_(n+1) = x_n * (2 - 3 * x_n) from x0 = 0.3 to get 1/3.

quiz.q: What is the Newton-Raphson iteration formula?
quiz.explain: The next guess is where the tangent at x_n meets the x-axis: x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n).

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 and x0 = 1.5, with f(1.5) = -0.125 and f'(1.5) = 5.75, what is x1?
Which iteration finds sqrt(a) by Newton's method?
quiz.explain: Applying Newton to x^2 - a gives x_n - (x_n^2 - a) / (2 x_n), which simplifies to the average of x_n and a / x_n.

quiz.q: What does quadratic convergence mean in practice?
options: The method needs exactly two steps
It only works on quadratic equations
The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step
quiz.explain: The new error is about a constant times the old error squared, so correct digits roughly double.

quiz.q: Newton on h(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2 from x0 = 0 gives 0, 1, 0, 1, ... What kind of failure is this?
quiz.explain: The guesses repeat forever without settling, so a maximum iteration count is always needed.

lessons.title: The Secant Method
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to know how steep a hill is, but you have no special tool to measure the slope at one exact spot. What can you do? Easy: stand at two places a little apart, note the height at each, and divide the height difference by the distance. That gives you an average slope, and if the two places are close, it is almost the true slope. The secant method uses this same trick. It takes Newton-Raphson, which needs the derivative f'(x), and replaces that derivative with a slope measured from two points. No calculus needed at each step, and it is still very fast.

Sub-heading: Why we need it: Newton-Raphson, from the last lesson, is wonderful: near a simple root it roughly doubles the correct digits each step. But it needs f'(x). Sometimes the derivative is hard to work out by hand. Sometimes the function is not even a formula: it may be the output of a long computer simulation, or a measurement from a machine, and there is no formula to differentiate. And sometimes computing f'(x) costs as much time as computing f(x) itself. The secant method avoids all of this.

Sub-heading: What a secant is: A tangent touches a curve at one point. A secant is a straight line that cuts the curve at two points. If the two points are (x_(n-1), f(x_(n-1))) and (x_n, f(x_n)), the slope of the secant is (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))) / (x_n - x_(n-1)). When the two points are close together, this slope is very close to the derivative f'(x_n). In fact, this is just the difference quotient from the definition of the derivative, before taking the limit.

Sub-heading: The formula: Start from Newton, x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n), and replace f'(x_n) with the secant slope. We get x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) * (x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))). Geometrically, x_(n+1) is the point where the secant line through the last two points crosses the x-axis. You need two starting values, x0 and x1, but they do not have to bracket the root. After that, each step needs only one new function value, f(x_(n+1)), because the previous value is reused.

Sub-heading: Looks familiar: Compare it with the false position formula from lesson 06: c = b - f(b) * (b - a) / (f(b) - f(a)). It is the same chord formula! The big difference is which two points we keep. False position keeps the two points that bracket the root, so the root stays trapped. The secant method simply keeps the two most recent points, whatever their signs. That one change removes the safety of the bracket, but it also removes the stuck endpoint problem, and the method becomes much faster.

Sub-heading: The algorithm: Choose x0 and x1, a tolerance and a maximum number of steps. Compute f0 = f(x0) and f1 = f(x1). Repeat: if f1 - f0 is zero, stop with a warning; otherwise x2 = x1 - f1 * (x1 - x0) / (f1 - f0); compute f2 = f(x2); then shift: x0 = x1, f0 = f1, x1 = x2, f1 = f2. Stop when |x1 - x0| is below the tolerance. Notice how the old values slide along, like a window that moves forward. Each loop calls the function only once.

Sub-heading: Worked example, the first steps: Take our running example f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 with x0 = 1 and x1 = 2. All values are rounded to 6 decimal places. f(1) = -2 and f(2) = 4. Step 1: x2 = 2 - 4 * (2 - 1) / (4 - (-2)) = 2 - 4 / 6 = 1.333333, and f(x2) = -0.962963. Step 2 uses x1 = 2 and x2 = 1.333333: x3 = 1.462687, with f(x3) = -0.333339. So far this is exactly what false position gave, because so far the last two points happened to be the bracket points too.

Sub-heading: Where secant and false position split: In step 3, false position would keep b = 2, because f(1.462687) is negative. The secant method instead uses the two newest points, 1.333333 and 1.462687, both with negative f values. The difference of x values is 0.129353, the difference of f values is 0.629624, and the correction f(x3) * 0.129353 / 0.629624 is -0.068483. So x4 = 1.462687 - (-0.068483) = 1.531169, and f(x4) = 0.058626. Notice that x4 is outside the interval between the two points used. The secant line was extended, which is allowed in this method.

Sub-heading: The full table: Continuing: x5 = 1.520926 with f = -0.002693, x6 = 1.521376 with f = -0.000020, and x7 = 1.521380 with f = 0.000000 to 6 decimals. The errors from the true root were about 0.188, 0.0587, 0.00979, 0.000453, 0.00000339 and 0.00000000118 for x2 to x7. Look how the number of correct decimals jumps: roughly 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. That is faster than linear, but a little slower than Newton's doubling.

Sub-heading: The second example: Solve g(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0 with x0 = 2 and x1 = 3, so g(2) = -1 and g(3) = 16. Step 1: x2 = 3 - 16 * 1 / 17 = 2.058824, with g = -0.390800. Step 2: x3 = 2.081264, with g = -0.147204. Step 3: x4 = 2.094824, with g = 0.003044. Step 4: x5 = 2.094549, with g = -0.000023. Step 5: x6 = 2.094551. The true root is 2.094551 to 6 decimals. Compare: false position from the same start was only at 2.094305 after 6 steps, because its endpoint 3 stayed stuck.

Sub-heading: Order of convergence, about 1.618: Close to a simple root, the secant error behaves like e_(n+1) is approximately C * e_n * e_(n-1), with the same constant C = f''(r) / (2 f'(r)) that appeared for Newton. The new error is the product of the last two errors, not the square of one. Working this out shows the order is p = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2, about 1.618, the golden ratio. This is called superlinear convergence: faster than linear, slower than quadratic.

Sub-heading: Checking the order from our table: If the order is p, then log(e_(n+1) / e_n) divided by log(e_n / e_(n-1)) should approach p. Using the unrounded errors from our running example, these ratios come out about 1.59, 1.63 and 1.62 for the last steps, very close to 1.618. And the values of e_(n+1) / (e_n * e_(n-1)) settle near 0.768, which matches C = f''(r) / (2 f'(r)) for our function, the very same 0.768 we found for Newton. It is satisfying when the theory and the numbers agree like this.

Sub-heading: Secant versus Newton, the real race: Newton has order 2, secant about 1.618, so per step Newton wins. But per step Newton needs two evaluations, f and f', while secant needs only one new f. A fair way to compare is speed per function evaluation. Two secant steps cost the same as one Newton step and give order about 1.618^2, which is about 2.618, better than 2. In our running example, secant got within 0.000001 after 6 steps, using 8 function values including the two starts, while Newton from x0 = 1 needed 5 steps, which means 5 values of f and 5 of f'. When f' is expensive, secant is often the smarter choice.

Sub-heading: Secant versus false position: Both use the chord formula. False position always keeps a bracket, so it can never lose the root, but its convergence is only linear and an endpoint can get stuck. Secant always uses the newest two points, so it is superlinear, but it can wander away. In our running example, false position needed 11 steps to get within 0.000001 and secant needed 6. Think of false position as a careful walker holding a rope on both sides, and secant as a runner who sometimes takes a risky shortcut.

Sub-heading: How the secant method can fail: The formula divides by f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1)). If the two function values are equal, the secant line is flat and never meets the axis, just like Newton's zero derivative problem. If they are nearly equal, the next guess shoots far away. Also, because there is no bracket, the iteration can move away from the root you wanted, or even diverge, if the starting values are poor or the function curves strongly. And at a multiple root, like (x - 1)^2, the secant method also slows down to linear convergence.

Sub-heading: Keeping it safe in practice: The usual cure is the same as for Newton: start close to the root, for example after a few bisection steps, and always use a maximum iteration count. Good library routines combine bracketing with secant-like steps, taking the fast step when it stays inside the bracket and falling back to bisection when it does not. Brent's method is a well known example. You do not need its details for this course, only the idea of mixing safety and speed.

Sub-heading: Real life example, a phone's battery estimate: Suppose a phone app knows the battery was at 80 percent at 2 pm and at 70 percent at 3 pm (example numbers), and it wants to guess when the battery reaches 20 percent. It has no formula for the battery curve and no derivative, only two recent readings. It draws a line through them: 10 percent per hour, so 50 more percent needs 5 more hours, about 8 pm. As new readings arrive, it drops the oldest and redraws the line with the two newest ones. That is the secant idea: always use the latest two points.

Sub-heading: Real life example, a simulation in an engineering lab: Imagine engineers in Dhaka running a computer simulation that tells how much a bridge bends under a load (example scenario). One run takes an hour, and there is no formula, so no derivative. They want the load that gives exactly a certain bend. With the secant method, they run two loads, draw the line, run the predicted load, and keep using the newest two runs. Because each step needs just one new run and converges superlinearly, they reach a good answer in only a handful of hours.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes and exam questions: A common slip is mixing up the order of points: in x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) * (x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))), both differences must use the same order. Another is checking signs and keeping a bracket, which turns secant into false position by mistake. Typical exam questions: "Derive the secant formula from Newton's method", "Use the secant method to find the root of x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0 starting with 2 and 3", "What is the order of convergence of the secant method?", and "Compare Newton, secant and false position". For the last one, write a small table: derivative needed, bracket kept, order, cost per step.

Sub-heading: Recap: The secant method is Newton without the derivative: it replaces f'(x_n) with the slope through the last two points, giving x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) * (x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))). It needs two starting values but only one new function value per step. Its order is about 1.618, the golden ratio, so it is superlinear, and per function evaluation it often beats Newton. It shares the chord formula with false position, but it drops the bracket, so it is faster and less safe. Next lesson, fixed-point iteration gives us a general way to look at all these methods and to talk about their order of convergence.
key_points: Secant method: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) * (x_n - x_(n-1)) / (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))).
It is Newton's method with f'(x_n) replaced by the slope of the line through the last two points.
It needs two starting values, which do not have to bracket the root, and one new function value per step.
Same chord formula as false position, but secant keeps the newest two points instead of a bracket.
Order of convergence is (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2, about 1.618: superlinear, between linear and quadratic.
Per function evaluation it often beats Newton, especially when f' is expensive or unknown.
It fails when f(x_n) = f(x_(n-1)), can wander without a bracket, and slows to linear at multiple roots.
lessons.tip: Learn Newton, secant and false position as one family of three line-based methods: tangent, newest chord, bracketing chord. In exams, a small comparison table of these three, with derivative needed, bracket kept, and order, wins easy marks.
lessons.task: With a phone calculator, run the secant method on x^2 - 3 = 0 starting from x0 = 1 and x1 = 2 for 5 steps. Write the table, then compare how many steps you needed with what Newton (x_(n+1) = (x_n + 3 / x_n) / 2 from x0 = 2) needs to reach sqrt(3) to 6 decimals.

quiz.q: What does the secant method replace in Newton's formula?
options: The derivative f'(x_n), by the slope through the last two points
quiz.explain: Secant uses (f(x_n) - f(x_(n-1))) / (x_n - x_(n-1)) instead of f'(x_n), so no derivative is needed.

quiz.q: What is the order of convergence of the secant method near a simple root?
quiz.explain: The error behaves like C * e_n * e_(n-1), which gives order (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2, about 1.618.

quiz.q: How is the secant method different from false position?
options: It keeps the two most recent points instead of a bracket
quiz.explain: Both use the chord formula, but secant always uses the newest two points, whatever their signs, so it does not keep a bracket.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 with x0 = 1 and x1 = 2, what is x2?
When does the secant step break down completely?
options: When f(x_n) = f(x_(n-1)), so the denominator is zero
When the tolerance is too small
quiz.explain: Equal function values make the secant line flat, so it never crosses the x-axis and the formula divides by zero.

lessons.title: Fixed-Point Iteration and Comparing Root Methods
lessons.content:
Imagine you have a magic photocopier that slightly shrinks every picture you feed it. You copy a photo, then copy the copy, then copy that copy, again and again. Every picture gets smaller, but one tiny dot in the very middle never moves. That dot is special: when you copy it, you get the same dot back. Mathematicians call such a point a fixed point. In this lesson we turn root finding into a hunt for a fixed point, and we learn when the copying machine pulls us toward the answer and when it throws us far away.

Where we are: In the last few lessons we found roots of f(x) = 0 with bisection, false position, Newton-Raphson and the secant method. All of them used the same running example, f(x) = x^3 - x - 2, whose root is about 1.5214. Fixed-point iteration is the simplest open method of all. It needs no derivative and no bracket. You only need to rewrite the equation in a clever shape and then repeat one formula. It is also the idea behind many other methods.

Sub-heading: The idea in one line. Take f(x) = 0 and move things around until it looks like x = g(x). Then pick a starting guess x0 and keep computing x1 = g(x0), x2 = g(x1), x3 = g(x2), and so on. In short, x(n+1) = g(x(n)). If the numbers settle down to some value r, then r = g(r), which means r is a fixed point of g. And because x = g(x) is just f(x) = 0 rearranged, r is also a root of f. That is the whole method.

Sub-heading: Many ways to rearrange. Here is the surprising part. One equation can be rewritten as x = g(x) in many different ways, and they behave very differently. Take x^3 - x - 2 = 0. Way A: move x to one side, x^3 = x + 2, then take the cube root, so x = (x + 2)^(1/3). Way B: move x to the other side, x = x^3 - 2. Way C: factor the left part, x(x^2 - 1) = 2, so x = 2/(x^2 - 1). All three are correct algebra. All three have the true root 1.5214 as a fixed point. But only one of them will actually walk you there.

Sub-heading: Worked example with a good g. Use Way A, g(x) = (x + 2)^(1/3), and start at x0 = 1.5. Values are rounded to 6 decimal places, and the last number in each line is the change |x(n) - x(n-1)|. Step 1: x1 = 1.518294, change 0.018294. Step 2: x2 = 1.520935, change 0.002641. Step 3: x3 = 1.521316, change 0.000380. Step 4: x4 = 1.521370, change 0.000055. Step 5: x5 = 1.521378, change 0.000008. Step 6: x6 = 1.521380, change 0.000001. Look how calm it is. Each step the change shrinks to roughly one seventh of the previous change. After 6 steps we already have 1.521380, which matches the true root 1.5213797 to 6 decimals.

Sub-heading: Worked example with a bad g. Now try Way B, g(x) = x^3 - 2, from the same start x0 = 1.5, rounded to 4 decimals. x1 = 1.3750. x2 = 0.5996. x3 = -1.7844. x4 = -7.6819. The numbers run away and get bigger and bigger in size. We started very close to the root and still got thrown out. Way C, g(x) = 2/(x^2 - 1), is not better: from 1.5 it gives 1.6000, 1.2821, 3.1073, 0.2311, -2.1128, jumping around wildly. Same equation, same root, same start, totally different fate. So the real question is: how do we tell a good g from a bad one before we waste our time?

Sub-heading: The convergence condition. The answer is the slope of g near the root. If |g'(x)| < 1 near the root r, and you start close enough, the iteration converges. If |g'(r)| > 1, it moves away. Why? Write the error as e(n) = x(n) - r. Since x(n+1) = g(x(n)) and r = g(r), the mean value theorem says x(n+1) - r = g'(c) times (x(n) - r) for some c between x(n) and r. So each new error is the old error multiplied by about g'(r). Multiply by a number smaller than 1 in size again and again, and the error shrinks toward zero. Multiply by a number bigger than 1, and it grows.

Sub-heading: Checking our three ways. For Way A, g'(x) = (1/3)(x + 2)^(-2/3). At the root this is about 0.1440. That is well below 1, so it converges, and the error shrinks to about 0.144 of itself each step, which is the "one seventh" we saw. In fact, the error ratios computed from our table are 0.1443, 0.1441, 0.1440, 0.1440, 0.1440, matching g'(r) beautifully. For Way B, g'(x) = 3x^2, which is about 6.9438 at the root. Far bigger than 1, so it diverges. For Way C, g'(x) = -4x/(x^2 - 1)^2, which is about -3.5214 at the root. Its size is bigger than 1, so it diverges too, and the minus sign explains why it jumps from side to side.

Sub-heading: A second example, x = cos(x). Type any number into a calculator in radian mode and keep pressing the cos button. You will land near 0.739085. That is fixed-point iteration with g(x) = cos(x). From x0 = 1, rounded to 6 decimals: 0.540302, 0.857553, 0.654290, 0.793480, 0.701369, 0.763960, 0.722102, 0.750418, 0.731404, 0.744237. It does converge, but slowly, and notice the values go below, above, below, above the answer 0.739085. Here g'(x) = -sin(x), and at the root that is about -0.6736. The size 0.6736 is less than 1, so it converges, but it is not tiny, so each step only removes about a third of the error. The negative sign makes it zigzag around the root.

Sub-heading: The cobweb picture. Draw two graphs on the same axes: the straight line y = x and the curve y = g(x). A fixed point is where they cross. Now start at x0 on the horizontal axis. Go straight up to the curve; that height is g(x0) = x1. Go sideways to the line y = x; now you are above x1. Go up or down to the curve again, then sideways to the line, and repeat. The path you draw is the iteration. When 0 < g'(r) < 1, the path looks like a staircase walking into the crossing point, which is what Way A does. When -1 < g'(r) < 0, the path spirals around the crossing like a cobweb, which is what cos(x) does. When the curve is steeper than the line, the staircase or spiral walks outward and you never arrive.

Sub-heading: How to make a good g. A useful trick is to solve for the x that appears in the "strongest" term. In x^3 - x - 2 = 0 the x^3 term dominates near 1.5, so keep x^3 and isolate x from it, giving the cube root form with a small slope. Another trick is x = x - c f(x) for a constant c chosen so that 1 - c f'(r) is small. With f'(1.5214) about 5.94, choosing c around 1/6 makes the slope close to zero. If you let c change every step as 1/f'(x(n)), you get g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x), which is exactly Newton-Raphson. So Newton is a fixed-point iteration whose g has slope zero at the root.

Sub-heading: Order of convergence. We now define precisely how fast a method is. Suppose the errors satisfy |e(n+1)| is about C times |e(n)|^p for large n, where C is a positive constant. The number p is the order of convergence and C is the asymptotic error constant. If p = 1 and 0 < C < 1, we call it linear convergence; the number of correct digits grows by about the same amount each step. If p = 2, it is quadratic; the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. Fixed-point iteration is normally linear, with C = |g'(r)|. If g'(r) = 0 and g''(r) is not zero, the order jumps to 2, which is why Newton is quadratic for simple roots.

Sub-heading: Linear in practice. With C = 0.144, each step gives roughly 0.84 more correct decimal digits, because log10(1/0.144) is about 0.84. With C = 0.674 from the cos example, each step gives only about 0.17 extra digits, so you need around six steps to gain one more decimal place. This is why a small |g'(r)| matters so much. The number C, not just "less than 1", decides whether you wait 7 steps or 70.

Sub-heading: Stopping the loop. Like the other methods, we stop when the change |x(n+1) - x(n)| drops below a tolerance, or when the relative change is small, or when we hit a maximum number of iterations. That last rule is important for fixed-point iteration, because a bad g will never settle, and your program should give up instead of running forever. A simple loop: x = x0; repeat up to N times: xnew = g(x); if |xnew - x| < tol then stop; x = xnew. If the loop ends without stopping, report "did not converge" and try a different g.

Sub-heading: Comparison table of root methods. Let us race all five methods on f(x) = x^3 - x - 2, using the same rule as lessons 05 to 08: count the steps until the estimate is within 0.000001 of the true root 1.5213797. Bisection on [1, 2]: 19 iterations (the formula guarantees 20), always safe but slow, linear with C = 1/2. False position on [1, 2]: 11 iterations, bracketed and safe, but linear because one endpoint gets stuck; the Illinois fix cuts it to 7. Newton from x0 = 1: 5 iterations, quadratic, but needs f'(x) and a good start. Secant from 1 and 2: 6 iterations, order about 1.618, no derivative needed, but not bracketed. Fixed-point with g(x) = (x + 2)^(1/3) from 1.5: 6 iterations (7 if you start at 1), linear with C about 0.144, easy to code, but only works if you pick a good g.

Sub-heading: Reading the table. Bracketing methods (bisection, false position) are guaranteed to converge once you have a sign change, which makes them the safe choice. Open methods (Newton, secant, fixed-point) are faster when they work, but they can fail with a poor start or a bad formula. A common real-world plan is a hybrid: use a few bisection steps to get close safely, then switch to Newton or secant to finish fast. These counts are for this one function and these starts only.

Real life example 1, the bKash savings guess: Suppose you want a monthly interest rate that grows your savings in a certain way, and the formula ends up as an equation you cannot solve by hand. A banking app can rearrange it into rate = g(rate) and repeat. It starts with a guess like 1 percent, plugs it in, gets a new guess, and repeats until two guesses agree to many decimals. The convergence ideas from today decide whether such a loop is safe.

Real life example 2, the rickshaw that adjusts its fare: Imagine an example rickshaw puller in Mirpur who decides his fare based on how many passengers he expects, while the number of passengers depends on the fare. He guesses a fare, sees the crowd, adjusts, sees the crowd again, and adjusts again. If each adjustment is gentle, like multiplying the gap by 0.3, the fare settles to a steady value. If he overreacts, doubling or tripling his change each time, the fare swings wildly from cheap to expensive and never settles. That is |g'| < 1 versus |g'| > 1 in everyday life. Economists study exactly these settle-or-explode loops.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistake one, thinking any rearrangement works. Always check |g'(x)| < 1 near the root first. Mistake two, checking g' at the starting point only and forgetting it must stay below 1 in the whole region the iterates visit. Mistake three, mixing up the order p and the constant C. Mistake four, using degrees instead of radians for cos(x). Typical exam questions: "Find a root of x^3 - x - 2 = 0 by fixed-point iteration correct to 4 decimals, choosing a suitable g(x) and justifying it", "State and prove the condition for convergence", "Show that Newton's method is a special case of fixed-point iteration", and "Define the order of convergence and find it for a given method".

Recap: Fixed-point iteration rewrites f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and repeats x(n+1) = g(x(n)). It converges near a root r when |g'(r)| < 1, and the error shrinks by about |g'(r)| each step, so it is linear in general. A positive slope gives a staircase in the cobweb picture, a negative slope gives a spiral. The choice of g is everything: (x + 2)^(1/3) works for our cubic, x^3 - 2 does not. Newton's method is the fixed-point iteration with the best possible g. In the next lesson we move to polynomials and to systems of nonlinear equations, where Newton's idea grows into its matrix version.
key_points: Fixed-point iteration rewrites f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and repeats x(n+1) = g(x(n)).
One equation has many rearrangements; for x^3 - x - 2 = 0, g(x) = (x + 2)^(1/3) converges but g(x) = x^3 - 2 diverges.
Convergence condition: |g'(x)| < 1 near the root and a start close enough; |g'(r)| > 1 means divergence.
The error is multiplied by about g'(r) each step, so fixed-point iteration is usually linear with C = |g'(r)|.
Cobweb picture: staircase when 0 < g'(r) < 1, spiral when -1 < g'(r) < 0.
Order p: |e(n+1)| is about C |e(n)|^p; p = 1 linear, p = 2 quadratic.
Newton is fixed-point iteration with g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x), whose slope is zero at a simple root.
Bracketing methods are safe but slower; open methods are faster but can fail.
lessons.tip: Before iterating, always compute g'(x) near your guess. Ten seconds of checking |g'| < 1 saves you ten minutes of pressing a calculator that is running away from the answer.
lessons.task: Put your phone calculator in radian mode, type 1, and press cos ten times, writing each value. Then draw y = x and y = cos(x) on paper and sketch the cobweb path for your first four values.

quiz.q: For which rearrangement of x^3 - x - 2 = 0 does fixed-point iteration converge from x0 = 1.5?
quiz.explain: g(x) = (x + 2)^(1/3) has |g'| about 0.144 at the root, which is less than 1, so it converges.

quiz.q: What is the usual condition for fixed-point iteration to converge near a root r?
quiz.explain: The error is multiplied by about g'(r) each step, so its size must be below 1.

quiz.q: Pressing cos repeatedly gives values that go below and above 0.739085. Why?
options: Because the start was too far
quiz.explain: A negative slope flips the error sign each step, giving a zigzag or spiral cobweb.

quiz.q: If |e(n+1)| is about C |e(n)|^2, the method has order
quiz.explain: The power p on |e(n)| is the order of convergence; p = 2 is quadratic.

quiz.q: Newton-Raphson can be seen as fixed-point iteration with which g?
quiz.explain: Newton's update x - f(x)/f'(x) is a g whose derivative is zero at a simple root.

lessons.title: Polynomials and Nonlinear Systems: Horner, Deflation and Newton in 2D
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother is making pitha for the whole neighbourhood. She could mix a fresh bowl of batter for every single pitha, or she could make one big bowl and reuse it again and again. The second way is faster and wastes less. Evaluating polynomials on a computer is the same story. A clumsy method recomputes powers of x over and over, while a smart method reuses each step. In this lesson we learn that smart method, called Horner's method, use it to speed up Newton's method on polynomials, peel off roots one by one, and finally solve two nonlinear equations at the same time.

Why polynomials get special treatment: Polynomials like p(x) = a0 x^n + a1 x^(n-1) + ... + an show up everywhere: in curve fitting, in physics formulas, in computer graphics and in control systems. They are smooth and easy to differentiate, so Newton's method from lesson 07 works very well on them. But we usually need to evaluate p(x) and p'(x) many, many times, so even a small saving in each evaluation adds up. And a polynomial of degree n has n roots (counting repeats and complex ones), so we often want all of them, not just one.

Sub-heading: The clumsy way. Take p(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 and x = 3. The direct way computes 3^3 = 27, times 2 is 54; 3^2 = 9, times 6 is 54; 2 times 3 is 6; then 54 - 54 + 6 - 1 = 5. If you compute each power from scratch, a degree n polynomial needs 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 multiplications. For degree 10 that is 55 multiplications. Not terrible by hand, but a computer might do this millions of times inside a loop.

Sub-heading: Horner's nested form. Here is the trick. Rewrite the polynomial by pulling x out again and again: 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 = ((2x - 6)x + 2)x - 1. Now evaluate from the inside out. Start with 2. Multiply by 3 and add -6: 0. Multiply by 3 and add 2: 2. Multiply by 3 and add -1: 5. Same answer, 5, but only 3 multiplications and 3 additions. In general Horner needs only n multiplications and n additions for degree n. For degree 10 that is 10 multiplications instead of 55. This is also called nested multiplication.

Sub-heading: Horner as a recipe. Write the coefficients a0, a1, ..., an. Set b0 = a0. Then for k = 1 to n, compute bk = b(k-1) times x + ak. The last number bn is p(x). In pseudo-code: b = a[0]; for k in 1..n: b = b*x + a[k]. Two lines. It is also numerically nicer than adding up big separate powers, because it avoids building huge intermediate numbers when x is large.

Sub-heading: Synthetic division, the bonus. The middle numbers b0, b1, ..., b(n-1) are not garbage. They are the coefficients of the quotient when you divide p(x) by (x - c), where c is the point you used. And bn is the remainder. In our example with c = 3, the row was 2, 0, 2, 5. So 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 = (x - 3)(2x^2 + 0x + 2) + 5. You can check: (x - 3)(2x^2 + 2) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 6, and adding 5 gives the original. This also proves the remainder theorem in action: the remainder when dividing by (x - c) equals p(c). If the remainder is 0, then c is a root.

Sub-heading: Getting p'(x) for free. Newton's method needs both p(x) and p'(x). Write p(x) = (x - c) q(x) + bn. Differentiate: p'(x) = q(x) + (x - c) q'(x). Put x = c and the second part vanishes, so p'(c) = q(c). And q has coefficients b0, ..., b(n-1), which we already have. So we run Horner a second time on the b row to get p'(c). This is called double Horner or the Birge-Vieta idea: one synthetic division gives p(c), the second one gives p'(c).

Sub-heading: Worked example, Newton with Horner. Find the positive root of p(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5, a classic polynomial that Newton himself used as an example. Coefficients: 1, 0, -2, -5. Start x0 = 2. First Horner row at 2: 1, 2, 2, -1, so p(2) = -1. Second Horner on 1, 2, 2 at 2: 1, 4, 10, so p'(2) = 10. Newton step: x1 = 2 - (-1)/10 = 2.1. At 2.1, values rounded to 6 decimals: the first row is 1, 2.1, 2.41, 0.061, so p(2.1) = 0.061, and the second row gives p'(2.1) = 11.23. Then x2 = 2.1 - 0.061/11.23 = 2.094568. One more round: p(2.094568) is about 0.000186 and p'(2.094568) is about 11.161647, giving x3 = 2.094551. That matches the true root 2.0945515 to 6 decimals in just three steps.

Sub-heading: Deflation, peeling off roots. Once you find a root r, divide it out. The quotient from synthetic division is a polynomial of degree one less, and its roots are the remaining roots of p. This is called deflation. Example: p(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6. Newton with Horner from x0 = 0.5 gives, rounded to 6 decimals, 0.826087, 0.967693, 0.998544, 0.999997, 1.000000. So r = 1. Synthetic division by (x - 1): coefficients 1, -6, 11, -6 become 1, -5, 6 with remainder 0. The deflated polynomial is x^2 - 5x + 6, which factors as (x - 2)(x - 3). So all three roots are 1, 2 and 3.

Sub-heading: The danger of deflation. In real problems the root you find is only approximate, say 0.999997 instead of 1. When you divide by (x - 0.999997), the small error leaks into every coefficient of the quotient. Find the next root from that slightly wrong quotient, deflate again, and the errors pile up. Two good habits help. First, find the roots with the smallest size first, since dividing them out usually spoils the rest less. Second, after you get an approximate root from the deflated polynomial, polish it by running one or two Newton steps on the original p(x).

Sub-heading: A note on complex roots. Polynomials with real coefficients can have complex roots that come in pairs like a + bi and a - bi. Plain Newton with a real start stays on the real line, so it cannot find them. Methods such as Bairstow's method, which divides out quadratic factors x^2 + px + q, or Muller's method, which can step into complex numbers, are designed for this. You only need to know they exist at this stage.

Sub-heading: Now, two equations at once. Many real problems give several nonlinear equations with several unknowns. Take f1(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 4 = 0 and f2(x, y) = xy - 1 = 0. The first is a circle of radius 2, the second is a curve called a hyperbola. We want a point where they cross. There is no single f(x) to plug into the old Newton formula, so we need its bigger brother.

Sub-heading: The Jacobian. In one variable, Newton uses the slope f'(x). In two variables, the slope becomes a 2 by 2 table of partial derivatives called the Jacobian matrix J. Row one holds df1/dx and df1/dy, row two holds df2/dx and df2/dy. For our system: df1/dx = 2x, df1/dy = 2y, df2/dx = y, df2/dy = x. So J = [[2x, 2y], [y, x]]. It tells you how each equation changes when you nudge x or y a little.

Sub-heading: Newton's method for systems. The one-variable rule x(new) = x - f(x)/f'(x) becomes: solve J times d = -F for the correction d = (dx, dy), then set x(new) = x + dx and y(new) = y + dy. Here F is the column of values (f1, f2). We never compute the inverse of J; we just solve the small linear system, which is exactly what the next two lessons on Gauss elimination teach. Each Newton step for systems is really "make a linear approximation, then solve a linear system".

Sub-heading: Worked example, the circle and the curve. Start at (x, y) = (1.9, 0.5). Values are rounded to 6 decimals. F = (1.9^2 + 0.5^2 - 4, 1.9 times 0.5 - 1) = (-0.140000, -0.050000). J = [[3.8, 1.0], [0.5, 1.9]], with determinant 6.72. Solving 3.8 dx + 1.0 dy = 0.14 and 0.5 dx + 1.9 dy = 0.05 gives dx = 0.032143 and dy = 0.017857. New point: (1.932143, 0.517857). Step 2: F = (0.001352, 0.000574), the new J has determinant 6.930000, and the correction is dx = -0.000291, dy = -0.000219, giving (1.931852, 0.517638). Step 3 changes nothing at 6 decimals. The exact answer is x = sqrt(2 + sqrt(3)) and y = sqrt(2 - sqrt(3)), which are 1.931852 and 0.517638. Two steps were enough, the same quadratic speed we love from Newton.

Sub-heading: When systems Newton struggles. Everything that can go wrong in one variable can go wrong here too. A bad start can lead to a different crossing point or to nowhere. If the determinant of J becomes zero, the linear system cannot be solved, just like dividing by f'(x) = 0. And for large systems, building J and solving with it each step is costly. A practical trick is to draw a quick sketch or scan a grid of values to find a good starting point, exactly like tabulation for single roots.

Real life example 1, a GPS-style position: Your phone figures out where you are from distances to satellites. Each distance gives an equation like (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 + (z - c)^2 = d^2, which is nonlinear. With several such equations, the phone solves a nonlinear system, and Newton-type methods (often in a least squares form) are a standard tool for this. While you ride a CNG through Dhaka traffic, a small version of today's Jacobian idea may be running in your pocket.

Real life example 2, a sweet shop's price curve: Suppose, as example numbers, a mishti shop in Old Dhaka models its daily profit as a cubic polynomial in the price of roshogolla. To find break-even prices, the owner needs the roots of that polynomial. A small spreadsheet can evaluate the cubic at many prices with Horner's nested form, use Newton with double Horner to find one root, deflate to a quadratic, and solve that with the usual formula. Fast, tidy, and no repeated powers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistake one, forgetting zero coefficients. For x^3 - 2x - 5 the coefficient list is 1, 0, -2, -5; skip the 0 and everything is wrong. Mistake two, using the last Horner row value bn as part of the quotient; it is the remainder. Mistake three, in systems Newton, writing J d = F instead of J d = -F, which sends you the wrong way. Mistake four, computing J at the new point but F at the old point. Exams love: "Evaluate p(c) by Horner's method and find the quotient", "Use Birge-Vieta (Newton with synthetic division) to find a root correct to 4 decimals", "Explain deflation and its danger", and "Do two iterations of Newton's method for a given 2 by 2 nonlinear system".

Recap: Horner's method evaluates a degree n polynomial with n multiplications by nesting. The same table gives synthetic division: the quotient by (x - c) and the remainder p(c). A second Horner pass gives p'(c), which makes Newton on polynomials quick. Deflation removes a found root and leaves a smaller polynomial, but errors can grow, so polish roots on the original. For two or more nonlinear equations, Newton's method uses the Jacobian matrix and solves J d = -F at each step. Since that needs solving linear systems, the next lesson starts Gauss elimination.
key_points: Horner's nested form ((a0 x + a1) x + a2) x + ... evaluates degree n with only n multiplications and n additions.
The Horner row is synthetic division: middle numbers are the quotient by (x - c), the last number is the remainder p(c).
A second Horner pass on the quotient gives p'(c), so Newton on polynomials needs only two quick passes per step.
Newton with Horner on x^3 - 2x - 5 from 2 gives 2.1, 2.094568, 2.094551.
Deflation divides out a found root; x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 divided by (x - 1) gives x^2 - 5x + 6.
Deflation spreads round-off, so polish each root with Newton on the original polynomial.
Newton for systems solves J d = -F with the Jacobian J of partial derivatives, then updates x + d.
For x^2 + y^2 = 4 and xy = 1 from (1.9, 0.5), two steps give (1.931852, 0.517638).
lessons.tip: Draw the Horner table as a neat grid with the coefficients on top, and always write a 0 for every missing power. Most exam mistakes in this topic are a forgotten zero, not hard math.
lessons.task: On paper, use Horner's method to evaluate p(x) = x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 7 at x = 2, then write the quotient and remainder of dividing p(x) by (x - 2). Check the remainder by direct substitution on your phone calculator.

quiz.q: How many multiplications does Horner's method need for a polynomial of degree n?
quiz.explain: Each of the n steps does one multiply and one add, so n multiplications in total.

quiz.q: Horner's row for p(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 1 at x = 3 is 2, 0, 2, 5. What is the quotient of p(x) divided by (x - 3)?
quiz.explain: The middle numbers 2, 0, 2 are the quotient coefficients: 2x^2 + 0x + 2; the last number 5 is the remainder.

quiz.q: In Newton with synthetic division, how is p'(c) found?
options: By a second Horner pass on the quotient coefficients
It cannot be found without calculus
quiz.explain: Since p(x) = (x - c)q(x) + p(c), we get p'(c) = q(c), and Horner on the quotient gives q(c).

quiz.q: Why should deflated roots be polished on the original polynomial?
options: Because deflation changes the degree upward
Because Newton cannot run on quotients
Because errors in found roots leak into the quotient coefficients
quiz.explain: Dividing by an approximate root spoils the quotient a little, and those errors pile up.

quiz.q: In Newton's method for a nonlinear system, what linear system is solved each step?
quiz.explain: The correction d solves J d = -F, then the new point is the old point plus d.

lessons.title: Gauss Elimination: Forward Elimination and Back Substitution
lessons.content:
Imagine three friends go to the bazar on the same day. Each buys a different mix of potatoes, onions and eggs, and each tells you only the total bill. Can you figure out the price of one kilogram of potatoes, one kilogram of onions and one egg? You can, if the three bills give you three independent clues. Puzzles like this are called systems of linear equations, and computers solve millions of them every day, from weather forecasts to the graphics in games. The most famous, most basic way to solve them is Gauss elimination, and that is our topic today.

Recap, Ax = b: You met this in Linear Algebra. A system like 2x + y - z = 8, -3x - y + 2z = -11, -2x + y + 2z = -3 can be written as A x = b. Here A is the 3 by 3 matrix of coefficients [[2, 1, -1], [-3, -1, 2], [-2, 1, 2]], x is the column of unknowns (x, y, z), and b is the right-hand side column (8, -11, -3). The system has exactly one solution when det(A) is not zero. We usually write A and b together as the augmented matrix [A | b], so every row is one equation.

Why not just use Cramer's rule or the inverse? Cramer's rule writes each unknown as a ratio of determinants. That is lovely for 2 by 2 and fine for 3 by 3 by hand, but computing many big determinants by cofactor expansion is hopelessly slow for large systems. Computing the inverse of A and then multiplying by b also does more work than needed and loses a bit more accuracy. Gauss elimination goes straight to the answer. It is the method inside most "solve" buttons, usually in its LU form, which we meet in lesson 13.

Sub-heading: The big idea. Gauss elimination has two phases. Phase one, forward elimination: use row operations to make every number below the main diagonal zero, so the matrix becomes upper triangular. Phase two, back substitution: the last equation now has only one unknown, so solve it, plug it into the equation above, and climb up to the top. Row operations are safe because they do not change the solution: swapping two equations, multiplying one by a non-zero number, or subtracting a multiple of one equation from another.

Sub-heading: A warm-up with two unknowns. Example numbers from a bazar: 2 kg potatoes and 1 kg onions cost 130 taka, so 2x + y = 130. 1 kg potatoes and 3 kg onions cost 240 taka, so x + 3y = 240. To kill x in equation two, use the multiplier m = 1/2, which is (coefficient to remove) divided by (pivot). Equation two minus 1/2 times equation one: 3 - 1/2 = 5/2 for y, and 240 - 65 = 175 on the right. So (5/2) y = 175, y = 70. Back to equation one: 2x + 70 = 130, x = 30. Potatoes 30 taka per kg, onions 70 taka per kg. Check: 30 + 3 times 70 = 240. That is the whole method in miniature.

Sub-heading: Pivots and multipliers. In each column, the diagonal number we use to clear the entries below is called the pivot. For row i below the pivot row k, the multiplier is m(ik) = a(ik) / a(kk). Then we replace row i by row i minus m(ik) times row k, including the right-hand side. After that, the entry in column k of row i becomes exactly zero. We repeat for every row below, then move to the next column and the next pivot.

Sub-heading: Full 3 by 3 example, step 1. Augmented matrix rows: R1 = [2, 1, -1 | 8], R2 = [-3, -1, 2 | -11], R3 = [-2, 1, 2 | -3]. The first pivot is a11 = 2. Multipliers: m21 = -3/2 = -1.5 and m31 = -2/2 = -1. New R2 = R2 - (-1.5) R1 = R2 + 1.5 R1. Work it: -3 + 3 = 0, -1 + 1.5 = 0.5, 2 - 1.5 = 0.5, -11 + 12 = 1. So R2 = [0, 0.5, 0.5 | 1]. New R3 = R3 - (-1) R1 = R3 + R1: -2 + 2 = 0, 1 + 1 = 2, 2 - 1 = 1, -3 + 8 = 5. So R3 = [0, 2, 1 | 5]. Column one is now clean below the pivot. All numbers here are exact fractions, so no rounding was needed.

Sub-heading: Full 3 by 3 example, step 2. Now the pivot is the new a22 = 0.5. The multiplier for row three is m32 = 2 / 0.5 = 4. New R3 = R3 - 4 R2: 0 - 0 = 0, 2 - 2 = 0, 1 - 2 = -1, 5 - 4 = 1. So R3 = [0, 0, -1 | 1]. The system is now upper triangular: 2x + y - z = 8, 0.5y + 0.5z = 1, -z = 1. Notice how the staircase of zeros appeared under the diagonal. That shape is the goal of forward elimination.

Sub-heading: Back substitution. Start at the bottom. From -z = 1, we get z = -1. Move up: 0.5y + 0.5(-1) = 1, so 0.5y = 1.5 and y = 3. Move up again: 2x + 3 - (-1) = 8, so 2x + 4 = 8 and x = 2. The solution is x = 2, y = 3, z = -1. Always check in the original equations: -3(2) - 3 + 2(-1) = -11, correct. -2(2) + 3 + 2(-1) = -3, correct. The general formula for back substitution is x(i) = (b(i) - sum of a(ij) x(j) for j > i) / a(ii), working from i = n down to 1.

Sub-heading: The algorithm in pseudo-code. Forward elimination: for k = 1 to n-1: for i = k+1 to n: m = a[i][k] / a[k][k]; for j = k to n: a[i][j] = a[i][j] - m * a[k][j]; b[i] = b[i] - m * b[k]. Back substitution: for i = n down to 1: s = b[i]; for j = i+1 to n: s = s - a[i][j] * x[j]; x[i] = s / a[i][i]. Three nested loops for elimination, two for back substitution. That nesting is exactly why the cost grows like n cubed.

Sub-heading: A free determinant. Row operations of the type "subtract a multiple of another row" do not change the determinant. And the determinant of a triangular matrix is just the product of its diagonal. So after elimination without row swaps, det(A) = product of the pivots. In our example: 2 times 0.5 times (-1) = -1. You can confirm det(A) = -1 by cofactor expansion. If you swapped rows along the way, flip the sign once for every swap. This is a much faster way to get determinants of big matrices than cofactor expansion.

Sub-heading: Operation count. How much work is Gauss elimination? Counting carefully, forward elimination needs about n^3/3 multiplications and about the same number of additions, so about 2n^3/3 floating point operations in total. Back substitution needs only about n^2/2 multiplications, which is tiny in comparison. For n = 10, n^3/3 is about 333. For n = 100, about 333,333. For n = 1000, about 333 million. Doubling the size of the system makes the work about 8 times bigger. This "cubic growth" is why engineers try hard to exploit special structure, such as matrices that are mostly zeros.

Sub-heading: When it breaks, a zero pivot. Look at this system: y + z = 3, x + y + z = 4, 2x + y + 3z = 9. The first pivot a11 is 0, so the multiplier a21/a11 means dividing by zero. Plain Gauss elimination crashes. But the system itself is perfectly fine. The cure is simple: swap R1 and R2 so the first pivot is 1. Now eliminate: R3 - 2 R1 gives -y + z = 1, and adding R2 gives 2z = 4. Back substitution: z = 2, y = 1, x = 1. Check: 1 + 2 = 3, 1 + 1 + 2 = 4, 2 + 1 + 6 = 9. A zero pivot can also pop up in the middle of elimination, not only at the start, so a program must check every pivot.

Sub-heading: When the system truly has no unique answer. Sometimes no row swap helps, because a whole column below and including the pivot position is zero. That happens when det(A) = 0, meaning the matrix is singular.
