Then the system has either no solution (the equations contradict each other, like x + y = 2 and x + y = 3) or infinitely many solutions (one equation is just a copy of another in disguise). Elimination reveals this: you end up with a row like [0, 0, 0 | 5], which says 0 = 5, impossible, or [0, 0, 0 | 0], which says nothing new.

Sub-heading: A tiny pivot is also trouble. Even a pivot that is not exactly zero but very small causes big multipliers, which magnify rounding errors in a computer. The fix is called pivoting: before each step, swap in the row with the biggest pivot in that column. That is the main topic of the next lesson, together with Gauss-Jordan and the condition number, so here we only flag the danger.

Real life example 1, the electric circuit: When engineers analyse a circuit with several loops, Kirchhoff's laws give one linear equation per loop or per junction. The unknowns are the currents. A small household circuit might give a 3 by 3 system, while a circuit-simulation program for a chip may build a system with thousands of unknowns. Under the hood, an elimination method like today's solves it. The IPS that keeps your fan running during a load-shedding evening in Dhaka was designed with circuit tools that solve such systems.

Real life example 2, the poultry feed mix: A poultry farm in Gazipur wants to mix three ingredients, say maize, soybean meal and rice bran, so that each sack has exactly the right amount of protein, energy and fibre. Each nutrient gives one equation: (protein per kg of maize) times (kg of maize) plus the same for the other two equals the protein target. Three nutrients, three ingredients, three unknowns: a 3 by 3 system. Write each condition as a row, form [A | b], eliminate, and back substitute. The same steps work whether there are 3 unknowns or 300; only the computer does the boring part. Sports statistics and chemistry equation balancing lead to the same kind of systems.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistake one, forgetting to apply the row operation to the right-hand side b. Mistake two, getting the multiplier sign wrong; always use m = (entry to kill) / (pivot) and then subtract m times the pivot row. Mistake three, rounding too early in hand calculations; keep fractions or at least 4 to 6 digits until the end. Mistake four, not checking the answer in the original equations. Typical exam questions: "Solve this 3 by 3 system by Gauss elimination, showing multipliers", "Write the algorithm or pseudo-code for Gauss elimination with back substitution", "Derive the operation count", and "What happens if a pivot is zero, and how do you fix it?".

Recap: Gauss elimination solves Ax = b in two phases. Forward elimination uses multipliers m(ik) = a(ik)/a(kk) to create zeros below each pivot, turning A into an upper triangular matrix. Back substitution then solves from the last equation upward. Our example 2x + y - z = 8, -3x - y + 2z = -11, -2x + y + 2z = -3 gave multipliers -1.5, -1 and 4, and the solution x = 2, y = 3, z = -1. The pivots also give the determinant, here -1. The cost grows like n^3/3 multiplications. A zero pivot stops the plain method, and a row swap fixes it; next lesson shows how to swap rows wisely.
key_points: Ax = b is written as an augmented matrix [A | b]; each row is one equation.
Forward elimination makes zeros below the diagonal using multipliers m(ik) = a(ik) / a(kk).
Back substitution solves the last equation first and climbs upward: x(i) = (b(i) - sum a(ij) x(j)) / a(ii).
Worked example: multipliers -1.5, -1, 4 give the triangular system and the solution x = 2, y = 3, z = -1.
Without row swaps, det(A) equals the product of the pivots: 2 times 0.5 times -1 = -1.
Elimination costs about n^3/3 multiplications; back substitution only about n^2/2.
A zero pivot crashes the plain method; swapping rows fixes it if the matrix is not singular.
A row like [0, 0, 0 | 5] means no solution; [0, 0, 0 | 0] means infinitely many.
lessons.tip: Write the multiplier next to each row before you subtract, and keep fractions instead of decimals. Examiners give marks for the steps, and neat multipliers make your steps easy to follow.
lessons.task: Make your own bazar puzzle: pick secret prices for potatoes, onions and eggs, write three shopping lists with their totals, then give the three equations to a friend or solve them yourself by Gauss elimination and see if you recover the secret prices.

quiz.q: In Gauss elimination, what is the multiplier used to clear a(ik) below the pivot a(kk)?
quiz.explain: m(ik) = a(ik) / a(kk); subtracting m(ik) times the pivot row makes a(ik) zero.

quiz.q: After forward elimination, the matrix is
quiz.explain: Forward elimination puts zeros below the diagonal, giving an upper triangular matrix.

quiz.q: Roughly how many multiplications does forward elimination need for an n by n system?
quiz.explain: The three nested loops give about n^3/3 multiplications.

quiz.q: The pivots in an elimination without row swaps are 2, 0.5 and -1. What is det(A)?
quiz.explain: Row subtractions do not change the determinant, and a triangular determinant is the product of the diagonal: 2 x 0.5 x -1 = -1.

quiz.q: The first pivot is 0 but the system has a unique solution. What should you do?
options: Give up, the system is singular
Swap that row with a lower row that has a non-zero entry in the column
Divide by a very small number instead
quiz.explain: A row swap does not change the solution and gives a usable pivot.

lessons.title: Pivoting, Gauss-Jordan and Conditioning
lessons.content:
Imagine balancing a cricket bat on your fingertip. Hold it near the middle and it stays steady. Try to balance it on the thin tip of the handle and the tiniest wobble sends it crashing down. Solving linear systems on a computer has the same feeling. With a good pivot, small rounding errors stay small. With a tiny pivot, they explode. And some systems are wobbly by nature, no matter how you hold them. In this lesson we learn how to choose pivots wisely, how Gauss-Jordan elimination works and how it gives the inverse, and how to tell when a system is so sensitive that no method can save it.

Where we are: In lesson 11 we solved Ax = b with Gauss elimination: forward elimination with multipliers, then back substitution. We saw that a zero pivot crashes the method and a row swap fixes it. Today we go further. A computer does not work with exact fractions; it keeps only a fixed number of significant digits, as we saw in the floating point lesson. That limited precision is where small pivots become dangerous.

Sub-heading: The tiny pivot disaster. Take the system 0.0001x + y = 1 and x + y = 2. The exact solution is x = 10000/9999 and y = 9998/9999, which are about 1.0001 and 0.9999 to 4 decimals. Now pretend our computer keeps only 3 significant digits after every operation. Without any row swap, the pivot is 0.0001 and the multiplier is m = 1 / 0.0001 = 10000. New coefficient of y in row two: 1 - 10000 = -9999, which rounds to -10000 with 3 significant digits. New right side: 2 - 10000 = -9998, which also rounds to -10000. So y = (-10000)/(-10000) = 1.00, which is fine. But back substitution gives x = (1 - 1.00) / 0.0001 = 0. The true x is about 1, and we got 0. A 100 percent error from one bad pivot!

Sub-heading: What went wrong. The huge multiplier 10000 made the second equation's original numbers (1 and 2) look like dust next to 10000, and rounding wiped them out. Then, in back substitution, we divided a tiny difference by the tiny pivot 0.0001, which blows up any error. The lesson: small pivots create big multipliers, and big multipliers magnify round-off.

Sub-heading: Partial pivoting to the rescue. Before eliminating in column k, look at all entries in that column from the pivot row downward, and swap in the row whose entry has the largest absolute value. For our system, compare |0.0001| and |1|, so we swap. Now the system is x + y = 2 and 0.0001x + y = 1. The multiplier is m = 0.0001. New y coefficient: 1 - 0.0001 = 0.9999, which rounds to 1.00. New right side: 1 - 0.0002 = 0.9998, which rounds to 1.00. So y = 1.00 and x = 2 - 1.00 = 1.00. With the same 3-digit computer, the answer is now correct to the digits we keep. One swap made all the difference.

Sub-heading: Why it works. With partial pivoting, every multiplier satisfies |m| <= 1, because we always divide by the biggest number in the column. Small multipliers mean rounding errors are not magnified as they flow down the rows. Partial pivoting is cheap, since it only compares numbers and swaps rows, and it is the default in practically every serious linear solver. If every candidate in the column is zero, the matrix is singular, so the search also detects that case.

Sub-heading: Partial pivoting on last lesson's system. Take 2x + y - z = 8, -3x - y + 2z = -11, -2x + y + 2z = -3 again. In column one the biggest size is |-3|, so swap R1 and R2. Multipliers become -2/3 for the old first row and 2/3 for the third row. After elimination the lower rows are [0, 1/3, 1/3 | 2/3] and [0, 5/3, 2/3 | 13/3]. In column two, 5/3 is bigger than 1/3, so swap those two rows. The multiplier is (1/3)/(5/3) = 1/5, and the last row becomes [0, 0, 1/5 | -1/5]. Back substitution: z = -1, then (5/3)y + (2/3)(-1) = 13/3 gives y = 3, then -3x - 3 - 2 = -11 gives x = 2. Same answer, and every multiplier had size at most 1.

Sub-heading: Scaled partial pivoting idea. Partial pivoting can be fooled when rows have very different sizes. Take 2x + 100000y = 100000 and x + y = 2, whose true answer is about x = 1.00002, y = 0.99998. Plain partial pivoting picks 2 over 1 as the pivot. With 3-digit arithmetic, the multiplier is 0.5, the new y coefficient 1 - 50000 = -49999 rounds to -50000, the right side 2 - 50000 = -49998 rounds to -50000, so y = 1.00 and x = (100000 - 100000)/2 = 0. Wrong again. Scaled partial pivoting first finds each row's largest coefficient size, its scale: 100000 for row one, 1 for row two. Then it compares the candidate pivots relative to their scale: 2/100000 = 0.00002 versus 1/1 = 1. Row two wins. With that pivot, the 3-digit computation gives y = 1.00 and x = 1.00, correct to the digits kept. There is also complete pivoting, which searches the whole remaining matrix and swaps columns too, but it costs more and is rarely needed.

Sub-heading: Gauss-Jordan elimination. Gauss elimination stops at an upper triangular matrix. Gauss-Jordan keeps going: at each step it divides the pivot row so the pivot becomes 1, and it clears the entries both below and above the pivot. At the end the coefficient part is the identity matrix, and the right-hand column is the answer itself. No back substitution needed.

Sub-heading: Gauss-Jordan worked example. Same system, rows [2, 1, -1 | 8], [-3, -1, 2 | -11], [-2, 1, 2 | -3]. Step 1: divide R1 by 2 to get [1, 1/2, -1/2 | 4], then clear column one: R2 becomes [0, 1/2, 1/2 | 1] and R3 becomes [0, 2, 1 | 5]. Step 2: divide R2 by 1/2 to get [0, 1, 1 | 2], then clear column two above and below: R1 becomes [1, 0, -1 | 3] and R3 becomes [0, 0, -1 | 1]. Step 3: divide R3 by -1 to get [0, 0, 1 | -1], then clear column three: R1 becomes [1, 0, 0 | 2] and R2 becomes [0, 1, 0 | 3]. The answer reads straight off: x = 2, y = 3, z = -1. All values are exact fractions.

Sub-heading: Cost of Gauss-Jordan. Because it also clears above the diagonal, Gauss-Jordan needs about n^3/2 multiplications instead of about n^3/3. That is roughly 50 percent more work. So for solving one system, Gauss elimination with back substitution is preferred. Gauss-Jordan shines in one special job: finding the inverse of a matrix.

Sub-heading: Matrix inverse by Gauss-Jordan. Write [A | I], the matrix next to the identity, and run Gauss-Jordan until the left side is I. The right side is then A^(-1). Example: A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]]. Start with [2, 1 | 1, 0] and [5, 3 | 0, 1]. Divide R1 by 2: [1, 1/2 | 1/2, 0]. R2 minus 5 R1: [0, 1/2 | -5/2, 1]. Multiply R2 by 2: [0, 1 | -5, 2]. R1 minus 1/2 R2: [1, 0 | 3, -1]. So A^(-1) = [[3, -1], [-5, 2]]. Check: 2 times 3 plus 1 times (-5) = 1, and 2 times (-1) plus 1 times 2 = 0, so the first row of A times A^(-1) gives [1, 0], as it should. In practice, you rarely need the inverse itself; solving Ax = b directly is cheaper and more accurate.

Sub-heading: Ill-conditioned systems. Some systems are sensitive no matter how cleverly you pivot. Look at x + y = 2 and x + 1.0001y = 2.0001. The solution is x = 1, y = 1. Now change the second right side by just 0.0001, to 2.0002. The new solution is x = 0, y = 2. A change in the fourth decimal of the data moved the answer by a whole unit. Geometrically, the two equations are two lines that are almost parallel, so their crossing point slides a long way when one line shifts a hair. Such a system is called ill-conditioned. A well-conditioned system is one where small changes in the data cause only small changes in the answer.

Sub-heading: The condition number. We measure sensitivity with the condition number cond(A) = ||A|| times ||A^(-1)||, using a matrix norm. A simple choice is the infinity norm: the largest row sum of absolute values. For A = [[1, 1], [1, 1.0001]], ||A|| = 2.0001. The inverse is [[10001, -10000], [-10000, 10000]], with ||A^(-1)|| = 20001. So cond(A) is about 40004. The rule that matters: the relative error in x can be up to cond(A) times the relative error in b. Here the relative change in b was 0.0001/2.0001, and the bound says the relative change in x can be up to about 2.0001; the actual change was 1 relative to a size of 1, inside the bound. A rough rule of thumb: you may lose about log10(cond(A)) decimal digits, here about 4.6 digits. The best possible condition number is 1, for example for the identity matrix.

Sub-heading: Is the determinant a good test? Not really. A small determinant does not by itself mean ill-conditioning, because you can scale a perfectly nice matrix, like 0.001 times the identity, and its determinant becomes tiny while its condition number stays 1. The condition number is the right measure, not the determinant.

Sub-heading: The residual check. After solving, compute the residual r = b - A x~, where x~ is your computed answer. If r is large, something went wrong. But a small residual is not a guarantee for ill-conditioned systems. Try the wrong answer x~ = (0, 2) in our original system x + y = 2, x + 1.0001y = 2.0001. The residual is (2 - 2, 2.0001 - 2.0002) = (0, -0.0001). Tiny, yet the answer is completely wrong. For well-conditioned systems, a small residual does mean a good answer. So always check the residual and also think about the condition number.

Real life example 1, the bridge model: Engineers model a bridge as a big linear system linking forces and small movements of its joints. If the model is ill-conditioned, a tiny mistake in measuring a beam's stiffness could produce a wildly wrong deflection on the computer screen. Good structural software uses pivoting and monitors conditioning before anyone trusts the numbers for something like a river crossing in Bangladesh.

Real life example 2, mixing two nearly identical spices: Example numbers. A shop sells two garam masala blends that are almost the same recipe. You know the total weight and total cost of a bag mixing both, and you want to know how much of each blend is inside. Because the two blends are so similar, the two equations are nearly parallel lines, just like our ill-conditioned example. A one-taka error on the bill could change your answer from "half and half" to "all of one kind". The math is not broken; the question itself is sensitive.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistake one, choosing the pivot by its signed value instead of its absolute value; -3 beats 2 because |-3| = 3. Mistake two, forgetting to swap the right-hand side together with the row. Mistake three, thinking a small residual always means an accurate answer. Mistake four, using a small determinant as proof of ill-conditioning. Typical exam questions: "Solve this system with and without partial pivoting using 3 or 4 significant digits and compare", "Find the inverse of a matrix by Gauss-Jordan", "Define the condition number and explain ill-conditioning with an example", and "Compare the cost of Gauss and Gauss-Jordan".

Recap: Tiny pivots create huge multipliers that magnify round-off; with 3 digits, 0.0001x + y = 1, x + y = 2 gave x = 0 without pivoting and x = 1.00 with it. Partial pivoting swaps in the largest absolute entry so every |m| <= 1; scaled pivoting compares entries relative to each row's size. Gauss-Jordan clears above and below to reach the identity, costs about n^3/2, and is the classic way to compute an inverse, such as [[3, -1], [-5, 2]] for [[2, 1], [5, 3]]. Ill-conditioned systems, measured by a large cond(A) = ||A|| ||A^(-1)||, are sensitive by nature, and a small residual cannot prove accuracy there. Next lesson we package elimination into the LU decomposition.
key_points: A tiny pivot creates a huge multiplier that magnifies rounding error.
With 3 significant digits, 0.0001x + y = 1, x + y = 2 gives x = 0 without pivoting but x = 1.00 with partial pivoting.
Partial pivoting swaps in the row with the largest absolute entry in the column, so every |multiplier| <= 1.
Scaled partial pivoting compares each candidate pivot to its row's largest coefficient.
Gauss-Jordan makes each pivot 1 and clears above and below, giving the answer directly; it costs about n^3/2 versus n^3/3.
Running Gauss-Jordan on [A | I] gives [I | A^(-1)]; for [[2, 1], [5, 3]] the inverse is [[3, -1], [-5, 2]].
cond(A) = ||A|| ||A^(-1)||; large values mean ill-conditioning, and you may lose about log10(cond) digits.
A small residual b - Ax~ does not guarantee accuracy when the system is ill-conditioned.
lessons.tip: Whenever you start a new column in elimination, circle the entry with the biggest absolute value before doing anything else. That one habit gives you partial pivoting for free and protects you from silly round-off disasters.
lessons.task: On paper, solve x + y = 2 and x + 1.0001y = 2.0001, then change 2.0001 to 2.0002 and solve again. Sketch the two lines roughly and explain in two sentences why the crossing point moved so much.

The row with the smallest value
The row with the largest right-hand side

lessons.title: LU Decomposition
lessons.content:
Imagine your school canteen makes the same three kinds of sandwich every day. Each morning the cook cuts the bread, spreads the butter and slices the vegetables. Only the filling changes from day to day. A smart cook does the slow cutting and slicing once, stores the pieces, and then just adds the new filling each day. LU decomposition is that smart cook for systems of equations. We do the slow, heavy part of Gauss elimination once, save it, and then every new right-hand side is quick and cheap.

In lesson 11 we solved Ax = b with Gauss elimination: forward elimination to make a triangle, then back substitution. In lesson 12 we added pivoting so small pivots do not wreck the answer. Today we take the same elimination and keep its pieces instead of throwing them away. The pieces are two triangular matrices, L and U, and together they rebuild A. This idea is used inside almost every serious linear algebra library on computers.

Sub-heading: What A = LU means. We write the square matrix A as a product of two simpler matrices. L is lower triangular, which means every number above its main diagonal is zero. U is upper triangular, which means every number below its main diagonal is zero. So L looks like a staircase going down on the left, and U looks like a staircase going down on the right. When you multiply L times U you get back A exactly.

Why triangles? Because a triangular system is super easy to solve. If the matrix is lower triangular, the first equation has only one unknown, so you get it at once. Put that into the second equation and it now has only one new unknown. Keep going down. This is called forward substitution. For an upper triangular matrix you do the same thing but start from the last equation and go up. That is back substitution, which you already know from Gauss elimination.

Sub-heading: How LU solves Ax = b. Since A = LU, the equation Ax = b becomes L(Ux) = b. Give the bracket a name: let y = Ux. Now solve in two easy steps. Step one: solve Ly = b for y using forward substitution. Step two: solve Ux = y for x using back substitution. Two triangle solves, and we are done. No more elimination is needed once L and U are known.

Sub-heading: Doolittle and Crout. One matrix A can be split into L and U in more than one way, because you could move numbers between the two. To make the split unique we fix the diagonal of one of them. In the Doolittle method, L has 1s on its diagonal. In the Crout method, U has 1s on its diagonal. Both are correct; they just put the diagonal numbers in a different matrix. Doolittle is the one that matches Gauss elimination most directly, so we start there.

Sub-heading: Worked example with Doolittle. Take A with rows (2, 1, 1), (4, 3, 3) and (8, 7, 9). Do Gauss elimination and watch the multipliers. To kill the 4 under the first pivot 2, the multiplier is 4 / 2 = 2. To kill the 8, the multiplier is 8 / 2 = 4. Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2: (4, 3, 3) minus (4, 2, 2) gives (0, 1, 1). Subtract 4 times row 1 from row 3: (8, 7, 9) minus (8, 4, 4) gives (0, 3, 5).

Now the second pivot is 1. To kill the 3 below it, the multiplier is 3 / 1 = 3. Subtract 3 times the new row 2 from the new row 3: (0, 3, 5) minus (0, 3, 3) gives (0, 0, 2). The triangle we end with is U, with rows (2, 1, 1), (0, 1, 1) and (0, 0, 2). And here is the magic: L is just the multipliers we used, placed below a diagonal of 1s. So L has rows (1, 0, 0), (2, 1, 0) and (4, 3, 1). The 2 and 4 went in column one, the 3 went in column two.

Check it, because checking is a great habit. Multiply row 2 of L, which is (2, 1, 0), by the columns of U. First column: 2 times 2 = 4. Second column: 2 times 1 plus 1 times 1 = 3. Third column: 2 times 1 plus 1 times 1 = 3. That gives (4, 3, 3), which is row 2 of A. Row 3 of L is (4, 3, 1). First column: 4 times 2 = 8. Second: 4 times 1 plus 3 times 1 = 7. Third: 4 times 1 plus 3 times 1 plus 1 times 2 = 9. That is (8, 7, 9). It works.

Sub-heading: Solving with the factors. Let b = (4, 10, 24). Forward substitution on Ly = b: the first row says y1 = 4. The second row says 2 y1 + y2 = 10, so y2 = 10 minus 8 = 2. The third row says 4 y1 + 3 y2 + y3 = 24, so y3 = 24 minus 16 minus 6 = 2. So y = (4, 2, 2). Now back substitution on Ux = y: the last row says 2 x3 = 2, so x3 = 1. The middle row says x2 + x3 = 2, so x2 = 1. The top row says 2 x1 + x2 + x3 = 4, so x1 = 1. The answer is x = (1, 1, 1).

Sub-heading: A second right-hand side for almost free. Now say tomorrow we need b = (1, 2, 5). We do NOT factor A again. Forward: y1 = 1, y2 = 2 minus 2 = 0, y3 = 5 minus 4 minus 0 = 1, so y = (1, 0, 1). Back: 2 x3 = 1 gives x3 = 0.5, x2 + 0.5 = 0 gives x2 = -0.5, and 2 x1 - 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 gives x1 = 0.5. So x = (0.5, -0.5, 0.5). Plug it into the first equation of A to check: 2 times 0.5 plus (-0.5) plus 0.5 = 1. Correct. All numbers in this example are exact, no rounding was needed.

Sub-heading: Why LU pays off. For an n by n matrix, the elimination part costs about n^3 / 3 multiplications. The two triangle solves together cost only about n^2. Take n = 1000. Factoring costs about 333 million multiplications, but each new right-hand side costs only about 1 million. So if an engineer must solve the same A with 50 different b vectors, LU does the big job once and then 50 small jobs. Redoing full Gauss elimination 50 times would waste a huge amount of work.

Sub-heading: Crout version of the same matrix. In Crout, U gets the 1s on its diagonal and L keeps the pivots. For our A, Crout gives L with rows (2, 0, 0), (4, 1, 0), (8, 3, 2) and U with rows (1, 0.5, 0.5), (0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 1). You can see it is the same information moved around: the pivots 2, 1, 2 now sit on the diagonal of L, and the first row of U was divided by 2. Multiply them and you get A back again. Exams often ask you to do one method by name, so learn which matrix holds the 1s.

Sub-heading: The determinant comes free. The determinant of a triangular matrix is just the product of its diagonal. Also det(A) = det(L) times det(U). In Doolittle, det(L) = 1 because its diagonal is all 1s. So det(A) is the product of the diagonal of U: 2 times 1 times 2 = 4. Computing a determinant by cofactor expansion is very slow for big matrices, so this is the way computers actually do it. If you used row swaps for pivoting, each swap flips the sign.

Sub-heading: Pivoting and PA = LU. If a zero or tiny pivot shows up, plain LU breaks just like plain Gauss elimination. The fix from lesson 12 still works: swap rows. We record the swaps in a permutation matrix P, and the factorization becomes PA = LU. To solve, first reorder b the same way, then do forward and back substitution as usual. Libraries do this automatically, so LU with partial pivoting is the standard tool.

Sub-heading: Cholesky for special matrices. Some matrices are symmetric, meaning A equals its transpose, and positive definite, meaning x^T A x is positive for every nonzero x. These show up a lot in physics, statistics and engineering. For them we can write A = L L^T, where L is lower triangular and L^T is its transpose. This is Cholesky decomposition. It needs about half the work of LU and only stores one triangle. Example: A with rows (4, 2) and (2, 5). Then l11 = sqrt(4) = 2, l21 = 2 / 2 = 1, and l22 = sqrt(5 minus 1^2) = sqrt(4) = 2. So L has rows (2, 0) and (1, 2). Check: L L^T gives rows (4, 2) and (2, 5). If you ever need the square root of a negative number during Cholesky, the matrix was not positive definite.

Real-life example 1: a bridge in Bangladesh. Engineers model a bridge as a big grid of beams. The matrix A describes how stiff the beams are, and b describes the loads, like the weight of buses, trucks and rickshaws. The bridge does not change, but the loads do: morning rush hour, an empty night, a heavy truck parked in the middle. Each load pattern is a new b. With LU, the stiffness matrix is factored once, and each new traffic case is solved in a blink. (These cases are just an example; real bridge software has many more details.)

Real-life example 2: a circuit on your desk. Think of a small electric circuit with resistors. Kirchhoff's laws give a system Ax = b, where x is the currents and b holds the battery voltages. If you want to test the circuit with 6 V, then 9 V, then 12 V batteries, only b changes. Circuit simulator programs factor A once and reuse L and U. It is the same canteen trick: cut the bread once, change the filling.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes. First, students put the multipliers in the wrong place in L. Remember: the multiplier used to clear row i, column j goes into L at row i, column j. Second, students mix Doolittle and Crout and end with 1s on both diagonals, which is wrong. Third, students forget that LU without pivoting can fail on a zero pivot even when A is perfectly solvable, for example rows (0, 1) and (1, 1). Fourth, in forward substitution with Doolittle there is no division, because the diagonal of L is 1; in back substitution you must divide by the diagonal of U.

Sub-heading: What exams ask. A classic question: factor a given 3x3 matrix by Doolittle or Crout, then use it to solve Ax = b. Another: find det(A) from the LU factors. Another: explain why LU is better than Gauss elimination when there are many right-hand sides, with the n^3 versus n^2 argument. Sometimes they ask for Cholesky of a small symmetric matrix, or ask whether a matrix is positive definite. Always show the multipliers, always check one row of L times U, and write your answers neatly as matrices.

Recap: LU decomposition writes A as L times U, two triangles. It is Gauss elimination where we keep the multipliers in L and the final triangle in U. To solve Ax = b, solve Ly = b forward, then Ux = y backward. Doolittle puts 1s on the diagonal of L, Crout puts them on U. The determinant is the product of the pivots. Cholesky is the fast version for symmetric positive definite matrices. In the next lesson we try a completely different idea: instead of factoring, we guess and improve, again and again, with Jacobi iteration.
key_points: LU decomposition writes a square matrix as A = LU, with L lower triangular and U upper triangular.
L stores the elimination multipliers and U is the final triangle from Gauss elimination.
To solve Ax = b: forward substitution on Ly = b, then back substitution on Ux = y.
Doolittle puts 1s on the diagonal of L; Crout puts 1s on the diagonal of U.
Factoring costs about n^3/3 operations once; each new right-hand side costs only about n^2.
det(A) equals the product of the diagonal of U in Doolittle (flip the sign for each row swap).
With pivoting the factorization is PA = LU.
Cholesky, A = L L^T, works for symmetric positive definite matrices with about half the work.
lessons.tip: After every factorization, multiply one row of L by U and check you get the matching row of A. It takes a minute and catches almost every mistake.
lessons.task: On paper, factor the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (3, 8) by Doolittle. Then use your L and U to solve Ax = b for b = (5, 19) and again for b = (1, 3). Check both answers by putting them back into A.

quiz.q: In the Doolittle method, which matrix has 1s on its diagonal?
quiz.explain: Doolittle fixes the diagonal of L to 1. Crout fixes the diagonal of U instead.

quiz.q: For A = LU, how do we solve Ax = b?
options: Solve Ux = b first, then Ly = x
Solve Ly = b by forward substitution, then Ux = y by back substitution
quiz.explain: Ax = L(Ux) = b. Call Ux = y, solve Ly = b going down, then Ux = y going up.

quiz.q: For A with rows (2,1,1), (4,3,3), (8,7,9), Doolittle gives U with diagonal 2, 1, 2. What is det(A)?
quiz.explain: det(L) = 1, so det(A) = 2 x 1 x 2 = 4.

quiz.q: Why is LU useful when the same A is used with many right-hand sides b?
options: The expensive factoring (about n^3/3) is done once and each new b costs only about n^2
LU needs no arithmetic at all
quiz.explain: Factor once, then each b needs only two cheap triangle solves.

quiz.q: Cholesky decomposition A = L L^T can be used when A is:
options: a matrix with a zero on the diagonal
quiz.explain: Cholesky needs A symmetric and positive definite; then all square roots are of positive numbers.

lessons.title: Jacobi Iteration
lessons.content:
Have you ever played the game where a friend hides a number and you guess? You say 50, they say too high. You say 30, they say too low. Each guess uses what you learned from the last one, and soon you are right on it. Jacobi iteration solves systems of equations in a similar way. Instead of doing exact elimination like Gauss or LU, it starts with a guess for every unknown and keeps improving all the guesses together until they stop changing.

In lessons 11 to 13 we used direct methods. A direct method does a fixed amount of work and, apart from round-off, gives the exact answer at the end. Today we meet our first iterative method. An iterative method makes a sequence of better and better approximations. It never claims to be perfect, but we stop when it is good enough. This is the same spirit as bisection and Newton from the root finding lessons, now used for many unknowns at once.

Sub-heading: The idea of iterative solving. Suppose a system has n equations and n unknowns. In equation 1 we solve for x1, in equation 2 we solve for x2, and so on, so each unknown sits alone on the left side. The right side still contains the other unknowns. We plug our current guesses into the right side and get new values on the left. Then we repeat with the new values. If things go well, the values settle down to the true solution.

Sub-heading: Our example system. We will use this system all through this lesson and the next one, so we can compare. Equation 1: 10x + y + z = 12. Equation 2: 2x + 10y + z = 13. Equation 3: 2x + 2y + 10z = 14. Check that x = y = z = 1 works: 10 + 1 + 1 = 12, 2 + 10 + 1 = 13, and 2 + 2 + 10 = 14. Yes. So we know the true answer, which lets us watch how fast Jacobi gets there.

Sub-heading: Rearranging the equations. From equation 1, x = (12 - y - z) / 10. From equation 2, y = (13 - 2x - z) / 10. From equation 3, z = (14 - 2x - 2y) / 10. Notice we divide by the diagonal number each time, here always 10. In matrix words, the diagonal of A is used to solve for each unknown, and everything off the diagonal moves to the right side.

Sub-heading: The Jacobi rule. In Jacobi, every new value is computed only from the OLD values of the previous round. Write the round number as k. Then x(k+1) = (12 - y(k) - z(k)) / 10, y(k+1) = (13 - 2 x(k) - z(k)) / 10, and z(k+1) = (14 - 2 x(k) - 2 y(k)) / 10. Since all three formulas use only round k values, you could even compute them at the same time on three different computers. That is why Jacobi is sometimes called the method of simultaneous displacements.

Sub-heading: Worked example, round 1. Start with the simplest guess, x = y = z = 0. Then x = (12 - 0 - 0) / 10 = 1.2, y = (13 - 0 - 0) / 10 = 1.3, and z = (14 - 0 - 0) / 10 = 1.4. After round 1 our guess is (1.2000, 1.3000, 1.4000). All values in this lesson were computed with a small Python program and are rounded to 4 decimal places for display; the program kept full precision inside.

Sub-heading: Round 2. Now use the round 1 values. x = (12 - 1.3 - 1.4) / 10 = 0.93. y = (13 - 2 times 1.2 - 1.4) / 10 = (13 - 2.4 - 1.4) / 10 = 0.92. z = (14 - 2 times 1.2 - 2 times 1.3) / 10 = (14 - 2.4 - 2.6) / 10 = 0.9. So round 2 gives (0.9300, 0.9200, 0.9000). Round 1 went too high, round 2 went a bit too low. The guesses are swinging around 1, and each swing is smaller.

Sub-heading: The full table. Here are the rounds, written as (x, y, z). Round 3: (1.0180, 1.0240, 1.0300). Round 4: (0.9946, 0.9934, 0.9916). Round 5: (1.0015, 1.0019, 1.0024). Round 6: (0.9996, 0.9995, 0.9993). Round 7: (1.0001, 1.0002, 1.0002). Round 8: (1.0000, 1.0000, 0.9999). Round 9: (1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000). The error shrinks by roughly a factor of 3 or 4 each round. It is like a swing slowing down after you stop pushing.

Sub-heading: When to stop. We cannot compare with the true answer in real problems, because we do not know it. So we compare each round with the one before. A common rule: stop when the largest change in any unknown is smaller than a tolerance, say 0.0001. In our table the largest change was 1.4000 in round 1, then 0.5000, 0.1300, 0.0384, 0.0108, 0.0031, 0.0009, 0.0002, and in round 9 it dropped below 0.0001. So Jacobi stops after 9 rounds. Other rules use the relative change, or the residual, which means putting the guess into the equations and seeing how far b is missed. Always also set a maximum number of rounds, so a non-converging run cannot loop forever.

Sub-heading: Diagonal dominance. Will Jacobi always work? No. A simple test is diagonal dominance. A matrix is strictly diagonally dominant by rows if, in every row, the absolute value of the diagonal number is bigger than the sum of the absolute values of the other numbers in that row. In our system: row 1 has 10 versus 1 + 1 = 2, row 2 has 10 versus 2 + 1 = 3, row 3 has 10 versus 2 + 2 = 4. All pass easily. If the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant, Jacobi converges from any starting guess.

Why does dominance help? Each new value is the right side divided by the big diagonal number. Errors in the other unknowns are multiplied by small fractions like 1/10 or 2/10. So a mistake in the guess gets shrunk each round instead of growing. When the diagonal is weak, errors get multiplied by numbers bigger than 1 and they blow up.

Sub-heading: A bad example. Take x + 2y = 3 and 3x + y = 4. The answer is x = 1, y = 1. Row 1 has diagonal 1 but the other number is 2, so it is not dominant. Jacobi gives x = 3 - 2y and y = 4 - 3x. Starting at (0, 0): round 1 gives (3, 4), round 2 gives (-5, -5), round 3 gives (13, 19), round 4 gives (-35, -35). The guesses run away from the answer. These numbers are exact.

Sub-heading: Fixing it by reordering. Just swap the two equations: 3x + y = 4 first, then x + 2y = 3. Now row 1 has 3 versus 1, row 2 has 2 versus 1, so it is diagonally dominant. Jacobi becomes x = (4 - y) / 3 and y = (3 - x) / 2. From (0, 0): round 1 gives (1.3333, 1.5000), round 2 gives (0.8333, 0.8333), round 3 gives (1.0556, 1.0833), rounded to 4 decimals. Now it is heading to (1, 1). Same equations, better order, totally different result.

One honest note: diagonal dominance is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. Some systems that are not dominant still converge. The exact condition involves the spectral radius of the iteration matrix, which must be less than 1, meaning all its eigenvalues have size less than 1. You will meet that in advanced courses. For exams and everyday use, checking dominance is the quick test.

Sub-heading: Why iterative methods matter for sparse systems. In real problems, like heat flowing through a metal plate or water pressure in a city pipe network, each unknown is linked only to a few neighbours. The matrix is mostly zeros. We call it sparse. For example, a 1000 by 1000 tridiagonal matrix has 1,000,000 entries but only 2,998 of them are nonzero. Gauss elimination tends to fill those zeros with new numbers, which wastes memory. Jacobi only multiplies by the nonzero entries and never changes A, so each round is cheap and the memory stays small.

Real-life example 1: temperature in a tin roof. Imagine a tin roof in a village in Rajshahi on a hot afternoon. Split the roof into a grid of small squares. A simple model says the temperature of each square is roughly the average of its four neighbours, with the edges fixed. That gives one equation per square, with 4 on the diagonal and at most four -1s for the neighbours. The diagonal is never smaller than the rest of its row, and for grids like this Jacobi is known to converge. Start by guessing every square is 30 degrees, then keep replacing each square by the average of its neighbours. Watching the numbers settle is exactly Jacobi. (The temperatures here are example numbers, not real measurements.)

Real-life example 2: a cricket ranking puzzle. Suppose three friends rate each other's batting, and each person's score depends mostly on their own runs plus a little from the scores of the others. That kind of rule gives equations with a big diagonal and small off-diagonal parts. A simple way to compute everyone's score is to start with a guess, update all three from the old scores at once, and repeat. Web page ranking systems use iterative methods of this flavour on huge sparse matrices, which is why iteration is so important in computing.

Sub-heading: Jacobi as an algorithm. In pseudo-code: set x_old to the starting guess. Repeat: for each i, compute x_new[i] = (b[i] - sum of A[i][j] times x_old[j] for j not equal to i) / A[i][i]. Then find the largest |x_new[i] - x_old[i]|. If it is below the tolerance, stop. Otherwise copy x_new into x_old and repeat. Notice you need two arrays, old and new, because Jacobi must not mix them.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes. The biggest one is using a new value too early. In Jacobi, when you compute y in round 2, you must use x from round 1, not the x you just got in round 2. Using the new x is a different method, Gauss-Seidel, which is the next lesson. Other mistakes: forgetting to check or arrange diagonal dominance, dividing by the wrong coefficient, and stopping after a fixed number of rounds without checking the change. Exams often ask you to do 3 to 5 rounds in a neat table, to test dominance, or to explain why a given ordering diverges.

Recap: Jacobi iteration rewrites each equation to solve for its own diagonal unknown. Each round uses only the old values, so all updates are independent. For our system, starting from zero, Jacobi reached (1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000) to 4 decimals in 9 rounds. Strict diagonal dominance guarantees convergence, and reordering the equations can create it. Iterative methods shine for large sparse systems. Next lesson, we make one small change, using new values the moment we get them, and see Gauss-Seidel finish the same system faster.
key_points: Iterative methods start with a guess and improve it round by round, unlike direct methods such as Gauss and LU.
Jacobi solves equation i for unknown i: x_i = (b_i - sum of other terms) / a_ii.
Each Jacobi round uses only the values from the previous round, so updates are independent.
For 10x+y+z=12, 2x+10y+z=13, 2x+2y+10z=14 from zero, Jacobi reaches 1.0000 for all three (4 decimals) in 9 rounds.
Stop when the largest change between rounds is below a tolerance, and always cap the number of rounds.
Strict diagonal dominance (|a_ii| bigger than the sum of the other |a_ij| in its row) guarantees Jacobi converges.
Reordering equations can turn a diverging system into a dominant, converging one.
Iterative methods are ideal for large sparse matrices because they never fill in the zeros.
lessons.tip: Draw your iteration table with one column per unknown and one extra column for the largest change. Fill it row by row and circle the round where the change goes below your tolerance.
lessons.task: On paper or a phone calculator, run 4 Jacobi rounds from (0, 0) on 4x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 4 (answer x = 1, y = 1). Write each round to 4 decimals and the largest change. Then swap the equations and see if Jacobi still behaves.

quiz.q: In Jacobi iteration, which values are used to compute round k+1?
options: The newest values as soon as they are computed
quiz.explain: Jacobi uses only the old round k values for every unknown. Using new values immediately is Gauss-Seidel.

quiz.q: For 10x + y + z = 12, 2x + 10y + z = 13, 2x + 2y + 10z = 14, starting at (0,0,0), what is round 1 of Jacobi?
A matrix is strictly diagonally dominant by rows when:
options: the diagonal entries are all equal
in each row, |diagonal| is bigger than the sum of |other entries|
quiz.explain: That row test is the quick sufficient condition for Jacobi to converge.

quiz.q: Jacobi on x + 2y = 3, 3x + y = 4 from (0,0) gives (3,4), (-5,-5), (13,19). What should you do?
options: Swap the two equations to make it diagonally dominant
Run more rounds, it will settle
quiz.explain: Swapping gives 3x + y = 4 and x + 2y = 3, which is diagonally dominant, and Jacobi then converges to (1, 1).

quiz.q: Why are iterative methods good for large sparse systems?
options: They give the exact answer in one step
They only multiply by nonzero entries and do not fill in zeros, saving memory
quiz.explain: Elimination tends to fill zeros with new numbers; iteration keeps A unchanged and only uses its nonzeros.

lessons.title: Gauss-Seidel and SOR
lessons.content:
Picture a group chat with three friends planning a picnic. In one style, everyone writes their plan at the same time, then they all read each other's plans and rewrite at the same time again. In another style, the first friend posts, the second friend reads it right away and posts an updated plan, and the third friend reads both new posts before writing. The second style usually agrees faster, because news spreads during the round, not only between rounds. That second style is Gauss-Seidel.

In lesson 14 we met Jacobi iteration, where each round uses only the values from the previous round. Gauss-Seidel makes one small change: the moment a new value is computed, it is used in the very next formula of the same round. That tiny change usually makes it converge faster. Then we will see SOR, successive over-relaxation, which pushes each update a little further to speed things up even more. We finish by comparing iterative methods with the direct methods of lessons 11 to 13.

Sub-heading: The same system as last lesson. We use 10x + y + z = 12, 2x + 10y + z = 13, and 2x + 2y + 10z = 14, whose exact answer is x = y = z = 1. Rearranged, x = (12 - y - z) / 10, y = (13 - 2x - z) / 10, and z = (14 - 2x - 2y) / 10. These formulas are exactly the same as in Jacobi. Only the order in which we plug in values is different.

Sub-heading: The Gauss-Seidel rule. In round k+1, compute x using the old y and z. Then compute y using the NEW x and the old z. Then compute z using the NEW x and the NEW y. In symbols: x(k+1) = (12 - y(k) - z(k)) / 10, y(k+1) = (13 - 2 x(k+1) - z(k)) / 10, z(k+1) = (14 - 2 x(k+1) - 2 y(k+1)) / 10. Because each value overwrites the old one right away, you only need one array in a program, not two.

Sub-heading: Round 1. Start from (0, 0, 0). x = (12 - 0 - 0) / 10 = 1.2. Now y uses the new x: y = (13 - 2 times 1.2 - 0) / 10 = (13 - 2.4) / 10 = 1.06. Now z uses the new x and new y: z = (14 - 2 times 1.2 - 2 times 1.06) / 10 = (14 - 2.4 - 2.12) / 10 = 0.948. So round 1 gives (1.2000, 1.0600, 0.9480). Compare with Jacobi round 1, which was (1.2000, 1.3000, 1.4000). Already y and z are much closer to 1. All numbers here came from a Python program and are shown rounded to 4 decimal places.

Sub-heading: Round 2. x = (12 - 1.06 - 0.948) / 10 = 0.9992. Then y = (13 - 2 times 0.9992 - 0.948) / 10 = 1.00536, which rounds to 1.0054. Then z = (14 - 2 times 0.9992 - 2 times 1.00536) / 10 = 0.999088, which rounds to 0.9991. So round 2 gives (0.9992, 1.0054, 0.9991). The worst error is now about 0.0054. In Jacobi, round 2 was (0.9300, 0.9200, 0.9000), with a worst error of 0.1. That is a big difference for the same amount of arithmetic.

Sub-heading: The full Gauss-Seidel table. Round 3: (0.9996, 1.0002, 1.0001). Round 4: (1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000). The largest change between rounds went 1.2000, 0.2008, 0.0052, 0.0004, and in round 5 it fell below 0.0001. So with the tolerance 0.0001, Gauss-Seidel stops after 5 rounds, while Jacobi needed 9 rounds on the same system with the same start and the same rule. Roughly half the work. For many diagonally dominant systems Gauss-Seidel is about twice as fast as Jacobi, but that is a rule of thumb, not a law.

Sub-heading: Why using new values helps. When you compute y, the new x is already a better guess than the old x. Using a better input gives a better output. It is like correcting your homework using the answer your friend just checked, instead of the one from yesterday. The improvement travels down through the equations inside one round.

Sub-heading: The matrix view. Textbooks often split A into three parts: D, the diagonal; L, the part below the diagonal; and U, the part above it, so A = L + D + U. (This L and U are just pieces of A, not the LU factors of lesson 13.) Jacobi can be written as D x(k+1) = b - (L + U) x(k). Gauss-Seidel moves the lower part to the left: (D + L) x(k+1) = b - U x(k). Since D + L is lower triangular, each round is just one forward substitution, which is exactly the top to bottom sweep we did by hand.

Sub-heading: Convergence condition. The good news from Jacobi carries over. If the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant by rows, Gauss-Seidel converges from any starting guess. There is a second famous case: if the matrix is symmetric and positive definite, Gauss-Seidel also converges, even without dominance. Like Jacobi, dominance is a sufficient test, not a necessary one. And the order of equations still matters.

Sub-heading: The bad example again. Take x + 2y = 3 and 3x + y = 4, with answer (1, 1). Gauss-Seidel uses x = 3 - 2y and y = 4 - 3x. From (0, 0), round 1 gives x = 3, then y = 4 - 9 = -5. Round 2 gives x = 13, y = -35. Round 3 gives x = 73, y = -215. It blows up even faster than Jacobi did. Now swap the equations: x = (4 - y) / 3 and y = (3 - x) / 2. From (0, 0): round 1 gives (1.3333, 0.8333), round 2 gives (1.0556, 0.9722), round 3 gives (1.0093, 0.9954). It heads quickly to (1, 1). Using new values speeds up good behaviour and bad behaviour alike, so arrange for dominance first.

Sub-heading: Jacobi versus Gauss-Seidel at a glance. Jacobi uses only old values, needs two arrays, and every unknown in a round can be computed in parallel. Gauss-Seidel uses new values immediately, needs one array, and is usually faster, but each step waits for the one before it, so it is harder to run in parallel. On modern computers with many cores, that parallel advantage is one reason Jacobi style methods are still used.

Sub-heading: SOR, successive over-relaxation. Gauss-Seidel moves each unknown from its old value to a new value. What if we notice it always moves in the right direction but not quite far enough? Then we could step a bit further. SOR does exactly that. First compute the Gauss-Seidel value, call it x_gs. Then set x_new = (1 - w) times x_old + w times x_gs. The number w is called the relaxation factor.

If w = 1, the formula gives x_new = x_gs, which is plain Gauss-Seidel. If w is between 1 and 2, we overshoot on purpose, which is over-relaxation. If w is between 0 and 1, we take a smaller step, which is under-relaxation and can help a system that is jumpy. A known theorem says SOR can only converge if 0 < w < 2, and for symmetric positive definite matrices any w in that range does converge.

Sub-heading: SOR round 1 with w = 1.1. Start from (0, 0, 0). The Gauss-Seidel value of x is 1.2, so x = (1 - 1.1) times 0 + 1.1 times 1.2 = 1.32. For y, the Gauss-Seidel value using the new x is (13 - 2 times 1.32 - 0) / 10 = 1.036, so y = 1.1 times 1.036 = 1.1396. For z, the Gauss-Seidel value is (14 - 2 times 1.32 - 2 times 1.1396) / 10 = 0.90808, so z = 1.1 times 0.90808, about 0.9989. Round 1 is (1.3200, 1.1396, 0.9989).

Sub-heading: An honest result. Continuing with w = 1.1, the largest changes were 1.3200, 0.3672, 0.0511, 0.0039, 0.0004, and the change fell below 0.0001 in round 6. That is one round slower than Gauss-Seidel on this system. With w = 1.05 it took 5 rounds, the same as Gauss-Seidel. Why no win? Our system is so strongly dominant that Gauss-Seidel is already very fast. SOR shines on large systems where Gauss-Seidel crawls, like big grid problems, where a well chosen w can cut the number of rounds many times over. Choosing the best w is a science of its own; in practice people often find a good w by experiment.

Sub-heading: Direct versus iterative methods. Direct methods like Gauss elimination and LU finish in a known number of steps, give the exact answer apart from round-off, and work for any nonsingular matrix with pivoting. But they cost about n^3 / 3 operations and fill in the zeros of sparse matrices. Iterative methods like Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel and SOR cost little per round, keep the matrix untouched, and can stop early when a rough answer is enough. But they need a convergence condition, a good ordering, and a stopping rule. Small or dense systems: use direct. Huge sparse systems: iterative is usually the way.

Real-life example 1: a water pipe network in Dhaka. Imagine a city water company modelling pressure at hundreds of pipe junctions. Each junction connects to only a few pipes, so the matrix is huge and sparse. Engineers start with a guess, for example equal pressure everywhere, and update each junction using its neighbours' latest values. That is Gauss-Seidel style. Each round spreads news through the network, like a rumour passing from house to house in a para. (This is an illustration, not a description of any real company's software.)

Real-life example 2: adjusting a family budget. Suppose your family splits money between bazar, rickshaw fare and electricity, and each part depends a little on the others. Ammu decides bazar first. Abbu immediately uses Ammu's new number to adjust the rickshaw budget. Then you set electricity using both new numbers. Next month you go around again. Because each person uses the latest decision, the family settles on a plan faster. That is the Gauss-Seidel habit in daily life.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes. Students often mix up the methods: using old values in Gauss-Seidel by accident turns it into Jacobi, and using new values in Jacobi turns it into Gauss-Seidel. In SOR, people forget the (1 - w) times x_old part, or apply w to the whole equation instead of to the step. Another mistake is forgetting to check diagonal dominance and then being surprised when the numbers explode. Exams often ask: do 3 rounds of Gauss-Seidel in a table, compare with Jacobi, state the convergence condition, write the SOR formula, or list advantages of direct versus iterative methods.

Recap: Gauss-Seidel is Jacobi with fresh news, using each new value as soon as it appears. On our system it reached 1.0000 for all three unknowns (4 decimals) in 5 rounds, compared with 9 for Jacobi. Strict diagonal dominance or a symmetric positive definite matrix guarantees convergence. SOR blends old and Gauss-Seidel values with a factor w between 0 and 2, and can speed up large slow problems a lot. Next lesson we leave linear systems behind and start working with tables of data, using finite differences.
key_points: Gauss-Seidel uses each new value immediately inside the same round; Jacobi waits for the next round.
On 10x+y+z=12, 2x+10y+z=13, 2x+2y+10z=14 from zero with tolerance 0.0001, Gauss-Seidel stops after 5 rounds versus 9 for Jacobi.
Gauss-Seidel round 1 here is (1.2000, 1.0600, 0.9480) and round 2 is (0.9992, 1.0054, 0.9991).
Strict diagonal dominance, or a symmetric positive definite matrix, guarantees Gauss-Seidel converges.
Jacobi parallelises easily; Gauss-Seidel needs only one array and is usually faster.
SOR: x_new = (1 - w) x_old + w x_gs; w = 1 is Gauss-Seidel, 1 < w < 2 is over-relaxation, and convergence needs 0 < w < 2.
SOR helps most on large slow systems; on an already fast system it may give no gain.
Direct methods suit small or dense systems; iterative methods suit huge sparse systems.
lessons.tip: When doing Gauss-Seidel by hand, cross out each old value the moment you write its new one. Then you can never accidentally use a stale number.
lessons.task: Run 3 rounds of Gauss-Seidel from (0, 0) on 4x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 4 (answer (1, 1)), keeping 4 decimals. Then do the same with Jacobi and count how many rounds each needs before the largest change is below 0.001.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Gauss-Seidel and Jacobi?
options: Gauss-Seidel uses each new value immediately in the same round
quiz.explain: The formulas are the same; Gauss-Seidel just plugs in the newest values straight away.

quiz.q: For 10x + y + z = 12, 2x + 10y + z = 13, 2x + 2y + 10z = 14 from (0,0,0), what is y after Gauss-Seidel round 1?
In SOR, x_new = (1 - w) x_old + w x_gs. What does w = 1 give?
options: The exact answer in one step
quiz.explain: With w = 1 the old value drops out and x_new = x_gs.

quiz.q: Which statement about SOR is correct?
options: SOR can only converge if 0 < w < 2
quiz.explain: A known theorem: SOR needs 0 < w < 2 to converge; for symmetric positive definite matrices every such w works.

quiz.q: For a huge sparse system with millions of unknowns, which choice is usually best?
options: An iterative method like Gauss-Seidel or SOR
quiz.explain: Iterative methods keep memory small and cost little per round on sparse matrices.

lessons.title: Finite Differences
lessons.content:
Imagine you climb the stairs of a tall building and write down how high you are after every step. If every step is the same size, the gaps between your numbers are all equal. If the stairs get steeper as you go up, the gaps grow. And if they grow in a regular way, the gaps between the gaps are equal. Finite differences are exactly this game of subtracting neighbours in a table, again and again, to discover the hidden pattern behind the numbers.

So far in this course we solved equations, first single equations and then systems. Now we start a new part: working with tables of data. Very often we do not have a formula for a function, only values measured at some points, like temperature every hour or a sensor reading every second. Finite differences are the basic tool for these tables. They lead straight into interpolation in lessons 17 to 19, and later into numerical differentiation and integration.

Sub-heading: Equally spaced tables. Suppose we know y = f(x) at points x0, x1, x2 and so on, with a fixed gap h between them. So x1 = x0 + h, x2 = x0 + 2h, and in general xi = x0 + i h. We write yi = f(xi). The number h is called the step size or interval. All the formulas in this lesson need equal spacing. Unequal spacing needs divided differences, which come in lesson 18.

Sub-heading: Forward differences. The first forward difference at y0 is Delta y0 = y1 - y0. In general, Delta yi = y(i+1) - yi. It looks forward to the next value. The second forward difference is the difference of the first differences: Delta^2 yi = Delta y(i+1) - Delta yi. The third is the difference of the second differences, and so on. The Greek capital letter Delta, written as a triangle, is the name of the forward difference operator.

Sub-heading: Worked example with f(x) = x^3. Take x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, so h = 1. The values are 0, 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216. First differences: 1 - 0 = 1, 8 - 1 = 7, then 19, 37, 61, 91. Second differences: 7 - 1 = 6, then 12, 18, 24, 30. Third differences: 12 - 6 = 6, then 6, 6, 6. Fourth differences: all 0. All numbers in this lesson are exact integers, checked with a small Python program.

Sub-heading: Reading a difference table. We usually write the table sideways, like a staircase. The first column is x, the second is y, then each new column holds the differences of the column before, written between the two numbers it came from. So each new column is one entry shorter. The entries along the top slanted line, y0, Delta y0, Delta^2 y0, Delta^3 y0, are called the leading differences. For our cube table they are 0, 1, 6, 6. These leading differences are exactly what Newton's forward interpolation formula uses in lesson 17.

Sub-heading: Differences of polynomials. Look at what happened: for x^3, the third differences are constant and the fourth differences are zero. This is a general rule. If f is a polynomial of degree n and the spacing is h, then the n-th differences are constant and equal to a times n! times h^n, where a is the leading coefficient. All higher differences are zero. For x^3 with h = 1, that is 1 times 3! times 1 = 6. It matches our table.

Let us test the rule with a different step. Take x^3 at x = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, so h = 2. The values are 0, 8, 64, 216, 512. First differences: 8, 56, 152, 296. Second: 48, 96, 144. Third: 48, 48. The rule says 1 times 3! times 2^3 = 6 times 8 = 48. Correct again. One more: f(x) = x^2 + x at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 gives 0, 2, 6, 12, 20. First differences 2, 4, 6, 8, second differences 2, 2, 2, and third differences 0. Degree 2, leading coefficient 1, so 1 times 2! times 1 = 2.

Why does this matter? It works backwards too. If some table has constant third differences, the data comes from a cubic polynomial, at least on that range. So looking at a difference table tells you what degree of polynomial will describe the data well. If the k-th differences are nearly constant, a degree k polynomial is a good model. This is how we choose how many terms to use in interpolation.

Sub-heading: Backward differences. The backward difference looks back to the previous value: nabla yi = yi - y(i-1). The symbol nabla is an upside-down triangle. Higher ones work the same way: nabla^2 yi = nabla yi - nabla y(i-1). In our cube table at x = 6: nabla y6 = 216 - 125 = 91, nabla^2 y6 = 91 - 61 = 30, and nabla^3 y6 = 30 - 24 = 6. Here is the surprise: these are the very same numbers as in the forward table, just named from the other end. The bottom slanted line of the table holds the backward differences of the last value. Newton's backward formula uses them to work near the end of a table.

Sub-heading: Central differences. The central difference is centred on a point, looking half a step each way. It is written with a small Greek delta, while the forward one uses a capital Delta: small delta yi = y(i + 1/2) - y(i - 1/2). Half-step values do not exist in the table, but even powers land on real points. The second central difference is small delta^2 yi = y(i+1) - 2 yi + y(i-1). For x^3 at x = 3: 64 - 2 times 27 + 8 = 18. That is the same 18 sitting in the second difference column, right in the row of x = 3. Central differences give the most balanced, usually most accurate, formulas when you work in the middle of a table.

Sub-heading: The shift operator E. Now a neat idea: treat these as operators, like machines that act on a function. The shift operator E moves forward one step: E f(x) = f(x + h). So E^2 f(x) = f(x + 2h), and E^(-1) f(x) = f(x - h). Example: for f(x) = x^3 with h = 1, E^2 f(2) = f(4) = 64.

Sub-heading: Operator relations. Since Delta f(x) = f(x + h) - f(x) = E f(x) - f(x), we can write Delta = E - 1, or E = 1 + Delta. Similarly nabla f(x) = f(x) - f(x - h), so nabla = 1 - E^(-1). The central operator is small delta = E^(1/2) - E^(-1/2). Another useful one: Delta = E nabla = nabla E, because the forward difference at x equals the backward difference at x + h. Check with our table: Delta y5 = 216 - 125 = 91, and nabla y6 = 91. These relations let you prove formulas by plain algebra, as if E were a number.

Sub-heading: Using the relations. Here is a powerful example. Since Delta = E - 1, we get Delta^3 = (E - 1)^3 = E^3 - 3E^2 + 3E - 1. Apply it to f at x0: Delta^3 y0 = y3 - 3 y2 + 3 y1 - y0. For x^3: 27 - 3 times 8 + 3 times 1 - 0 = 27 - 24 + 3 = 6. Matches the table. Notice the numbers 1, 3, 3, 1 are binomial coefficients with alternating signs. That pattern is the key to the next trick. Also, E = 1 + Delta gives E^n = (1 + Delta)^n, which is the seed of Newton's forward formula.

Sub-heading: Spotting an error in a table. Suppose a value was typed wrong. Take x^3 at x = 0 to 8, but write 65 instead of 64 at x = 4. The values are 0, 1, 8, 27, 65, 125, 216, 343, 512. The fourth differences should all be 0, but now they are 1, -4, 6, -4, 1. Those are the binomial coefficients of (a - b)^4 times the error e = 1. The error spreads through the table in this fan shape, and the biggest entry, 6e, sits in the row of the bad value, x = 4. So the fix is 65 - 1 = 64.

In real tables the true high differences are not exactly zero, just small and smooth. But a mistake still shows up as this zig-zag pattern, e, -4e, 6e, -4e, e in the fourth column, or e, -3e, 3e, -e in the third column. Look for the zig-zag, find its centre, and you have found the wrong number and its size. Teachers love this question.

Real-life example 1: cricket scoreboard. Here are example numbers, not a real match. A team's total runs after overs 0 to 5 are 0, 6, 14, 25, 33, 45. The first differences, 6, 8, 11, 8, 12, are the runs scored in each over. The second differences, 2, 3, -3, 4, show whether the scoring is speeding up or slowing down. Here they jump around, so there is no simple polynomial pattern. That is normal for real cricket. Differences turn a running total into a rate, and a rate into a change of rate.

Real-life example 2: checking a printed table. Long ago, engineers used printed tables of logarithms and sines, and finding typing mistakes was a real job. Even today, if you copy readings from a temperature sensor in a factory in Gazipur into a spreadsheet, one wrong digit can sneak in. Making a difference table and looking for the binomial zig-zag in a high column is a quick way to catch it, without knowing the true formula.

Sub-heading: Common mistakes. First, subtracting in the wrong order: always later minus earlier, y(i+1) - yi, or the signs flip. Second, mixing up the index names: Delta y0 and nabla y1 are the same number, so always say which point you mean. Third, using these formulas on unequally spaced data, which is wrong. Fourth, expecting higher differences to be exactly zero for real data. Exams ask you to build a difference table, find the degree of the polynomial, prove relations like E = 1 + Delta or Delta = E nabla, compute Delta^n of a polynomial, or locate and fix an error in a table.

Recap: A finite difference is a subtraction of neighbouring table values. Forward differences look ahead, backward differences look back, central differences sit in the middle, and all live in one difference table. For a polynomial of degree n, the n-th differences are constant, equal to a n! h^n, and higher ones are zero. The shift operator E links them: Delta = E - 1, nabla = 1 - E^(-1), Delta = E nabla. A wrong entry shows up as a binomial zig-zag. Next lesson, we turn these differences into Newton's forward and backward interpolation formulas.
key_points: Finite differences work on tables with equal spacing h: xi = x0 + i h.
Forward difference: Delta yi = y(i+1) - yi; higher orders are differences of differences.
Backward difference: nabla yi = yi - y(i-1); central: small delta^2 yi = y(i+1) - 2 yi + y(i-1).
For a degree n polynomial the n-th differences are constant (a n! h^n) and higher differences are zero; for x^3 with h = 1 that constant is 6.
Shift operator E f(x) = f(x + h); Delta = E - 1, nabla = 1 - E^(-1), Delta = E nabla.
Delta^3 y0 = y3 - 3y2 + 3y1 - y0, using binomial coefficients from (E - 1)^3.
A wrong table entry shows as a binomial zig-zag (e, -4e, 6e, -4e, e in fourth differences) centred on the bad value.
lessons.tip: Draw difference tables as a staircase with each difference written between its two parent numbers. Then reading forward differences on the top line and backward differences on the bottom line becomes automatic.
lessons.task: Make a difference table for f(x) = 2x^2 + 1 at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Check that the second differences equal 2 times 2! = 4. Then change one value by 1 and watch the error pattern in the third differences.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 with h = 1, what are the third differences?
quiz.explain: a n! h^n = 1 x 3! x 1 = 6, and the table 0, 1, 8, 27, 64 shows third differences of 6.

quiz.q: Which relation between operators is correct?
quiz.explain: Delta f(x) = f(x + h) - f(x) = (E - 1) f(x), so E = 1 + Delta.

quiz.q: In the table 0, 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216 (x = 0..6), what is nabla y6?
In a cubic table, fourth differences come out as 1, -4, 6, -4, 1. What does this suggest?
options: The data is a quartic polynomial
One entry is wrong by 1, at the row of the 6
The step size is not equal
quiz.explain: This binomial zig-zag is the fingerprint of a single error e = 1, centred on the bad value.

quiz.q: Second central difference small delta^2 y at x = 3 for x^3 (h = 1) is:

lessons.title: Newton Forward and Backward Interpolation
lessons.content:
Imagine your school notes the temperature only at 8 am, 9 am, 10 am and 11 am. Your little brother asks, what was the temperature at 9:30? Nobody measured it. But you can make a very smart guess by looking at the numbers around 9:30 and how they change. That smart guessing, done with a clear formula, is called interpolation. In this lesson we learn the two most famous formulas for it when the table points are equally spaced: Newton's forward formula and Newton's backward formula.

What interpolation means: We have a table of values, x0, x1, x2 and so on, with matching y values. We do not know the real function, or it is too hard to use. We want the value of y at some x that sits between the table points. Interpolation builds a polynomial that passes exactly through the table points, and then we read off its value at our new x. A polynomial is just a formula made of powers of x, like 3 + 2x + x^2. Polynomials are easy to add, multiply and calculate, which is why we love them here.

Why it matters: Before calculators, people used printed tables of logarithms, sines and square roots. If you needed sin of a value between two table rows, you interpolated. Today the same idea lives inside computer graphics, weather data, sensor readings, animation, and many science programs. Whenever data comes in steps, interpolation fills the gaps. It is also the base for later lessons: numerical differentiation and numerical integration are both built from interpolating polynomials.

What we already know: In lesson 16 we built difference tables. We learned the forward difference delta y0 = y1 - y0, the backward difference nabla, and the shift operator E. We also learned that for a polynomial of degree n, the n-th differences are constant and the next ones are zero. Here we only use those tables. If the words delta and nabla feel rusty, flip back to lesson 16 for a minute.

The step size h: Our table must have equally spaced x values. The gap between neighbours is called h. So x1 = x0 + h, x2 = x0 + 2h, and so on. If x goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then h = 1. If x goes 10, 20, 30, then h = 10. Newton's forward and backward formulas only work when h is the same everywhere. For uneven gaps we need divided differences, which come in lesson 18.

The p variable: Instead of working with x directly, we measure how many steps x is away from a starting point. We write p = (x - x0)/h. If x0 = 1, h = 1 and x = 1.5, then p = 0.5, which means half a step after x0. If x = 3, p = 2, which is exactly two steps. This small trick makes the formula clean, because every table point now sits at p = 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on.

Newton's forward formula: Here it is, written in plain text. y(x) = y0 + p delta y0 + p(p - 1)/2! delta^2 y0 + p(p - 1)(p - 2)/3! delta^3 y0 + and so on. The pattern is simple. Each new term uses the next difference from the top row of the table, multiplied by p, then p times (p - 1), then p times (p - 1) times (p - 2), divided by the factorials 1, 2, 6, 24 and so on. It looks like a Taylor series, but with steps instead of derivatives. We use the top line of the difference table: y0, delta y0, delta^2 y0, delta^3 y0.

Where it comes from, in one breath: Using the shift operator, y at p steps is E^p y0, and E = 1 + delta. So y(x) = (1 + delta)^p y0. Expanding (1 + delta)^p with the binomial series gives exactly 1 + p delta + p(p - 1)/2! delta^2 + and so on. That is the whole proof idea. If the data comes from a polynomial of degree n, the series stops after the delta^n term because higher differences are zero.

Worked example 1, cubes: Take x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = x^3, so y = 1, 8, 27, 64, 125. The first differences are 7, 19, 37, 61. The second differences are 12, 18, 24. The third differences are 6, 6. The fourth difference is 0. The top row is y0 = 1, delta y0 = 7, delta^2 y0 = 12, delta^3 y0 = 6. Let us find y at x = 1.5. Here h = 1, so p = (1.5 - 1)/1 = 0.5.

Now the terms: First term is 1. Second term is p times 7 = 0.5 times 7 = 3.5. Third term is p(p - 1)/2 times 12 = (0.5)(-0.5)/2 times 12 = -1.5. Fourth term is p(p - 1)(p - 2)/6 times 6 = (0.5)(-0.5)(-1.5) = 0.375. Add them: 1 + 3.5 - 1.5 + 0.375 = 3.375. And 1.5^3 is exactly 3.375. Perfect! Since the data came from a cubic, the formula gives the exact answer, no error at all.

Newton's backward formula: Now suppose we want a value near the end of the table, like x = 4.5. The forward formula starts at the top, far away. It is better to start from the bottom. We put xn as the last x and define p = (x - xn)/h, which is now negative for points before the end. The formula is y(x) = yn + p nabla yn + p(p + 1)/2! nabla^2 yn + p(p + 1)(p + 2)/3! nabla^3 yn + and so on. Notice the plus signs inside: p + 1, p + 2. And we use the bottom diagonal of the table.

Worked example 2, backward on cubes: Same table. The bottom diagonal is yn = 125, nabla yn = 61, nabla^2 yn = 24, nabla^3 yn = 6. For x = 4.5, p = (4.5 - 5)/1 = -0.5. Terms: 125. Then -0.5 times 61 = -30.5. Then (-0.5)(0.5)/2 times 24 = -3. Then (-0.5)(0.5)(1.5)/6 times 6 = -0.375. Total: 125 - 30.5 - 3 - 0.375 = 91.125. And 4.5^3 = 91.125. Exact again, as it should be for a cubic.

Worked example 3, square roots: Real data is usually not a nice polynomial. Take x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = sqrt(x) rounded to 4 decimals: 1.0000, 1.4142, 1.7321, 2.0000. First differences: 0.4142, 0.3179, 0.2679. Second differences: -0.0963, -0.0500. Third difference: 0.0463. All numbers here are rounded to 4 decimals. Find sqrt(1.5) with the forward formula, p = 0.5. Terms: 1.0000, then 0.5 times 0.4142 = 0.2071, then (0.5)(-0.5)/2 times -0.0963 = 0.0120, then (0.5)(-0.5)(-1.5)/6 times 0.0463 = 0.0029. Sum: 1.2220. The true value is 1.2247. Close, but not exact, because sqrt(x) is not a cubic.

Same table, backward: Find sqrt(3.5). Now p = (3.5 - 4)/1 = -0.5, and the bottom diagonal is 2.0000, 0.2679, -0.0500, 0.0463. Terms: 2.0000, then -0.1340, then 0.0063, then -0.0029. Sum: 1.8694, rounded to 4 decimals. The true value is 1.8708. Again close. Notice the answer near the end of the table is quite good, because we started from the end points that are nearest.

Which formula to choose: The simple rule is: use forward when x is near the beginning of the table, and backward when x is near the end. Why? The early terms of each formula use points close to its starting point. If you stop after a few terms, you want those few terms to be about nearby points. For a point right in the middle, both work, and there are central difference formulas like Gauss, Stirling and Bessel that are made for the middle. Many syllabuses only mention them by name, so just know they exist.

How many terms to use: Look at the difference table. If some difference column is almost constant, the next column is almost zero, and you can stop there. For the cubes, the third differences were all 6, so three difference terms were enough. For the square roots, the differences were shrinking but not zero, so each extra term gave a small correction. A practical rule: stop when the next term is smaller than the accuracy you need, for example smaller than 0.0001 if you want 4 decimals.

Extrapolation warning: Extrapolation means using the formula outside the table, like asking for x = 10 when the table only goes from 1 to 4. The polynomial fits the table points, but outside them it can run away. With our square root table, the forward formula at x = 10 gives p = 9 and the result 5.1502, rounded to 4 decimals. The true sqrt(10) is about 3.1623. That is a huge mistake! Inside the table the formula was great. Outside, it guessed badly. So use extrapolation only a little way past the ends, and always with care.

Real life example 1, a cricket chase: Example numbers. Bangladesh's total after overs 10, 20, 30, 40 is noted in a scorebook, but a friend asks what the score was after 25 overs. The overs are equally spaced with h = 10. Since 25 is in the middle, either formula works, with p = (25 - 10)/10 = 1.5 for forward. You build the difference table of runs, plug in, and get a sensible estimate. It will not be the exact real score, because batting does not follow a polynomial, but it is a fair guess from the data you have.

Real life example 2, a phone battery: Example numbers. Your phone's battery percentage is shown each hour: 100 at 8 am, 86 at 9 am, 74 at 10 am, 64 at 11 am. You want to know the charge at 10:30 am. Since 10:30 is near the end, use the backward formula with xn = 11 am, h = 1 hour, and p = -0.5. Apps that draw smooth battery graphs, or games that move a character smoothly between saved positions, use the same kind of idea, filling the gaps between known points.

In code: A computer does this very simply. Store the y values in a list. Build the difference table with a loop: for each level, each new entry is the next entry minus the current one. Then keep a running product term = 1, and for k = 1, 2, 3 multiply term by (p - k + 1)/k and add term times delta^k y0. That one loop computes the whole forward formula. For the backward formula, multiply by (p + k - 1)/k and use the bottom diagonal instead.

Common mistakes: The biggest one is forgetting to compute p and using x directly. Another is using the top row for the backward formula or the bottom row for the forward formula. Students also mix up p - 1 in forward with p + 1 in backward. Some forget the factorials 2!, 3!, 4!. And some apply Newton's formulas when the x values are not equally spaced, which is wrong. Always check the spacing first, then write the table neatly, then underline the row or diagonal you will use.

What exams ask: Typical questions give a table of 4 to 6 equally spaced points, such as years and population or x and sin x, and ask you to estimate a value near the start or near the end. You must build the difference table, pick the right formula, compute p, and add terms to a stated number of decimals. Sometimes they ask you to derive the forward formula using E = 1 + delta. Sometimes they ask for the polynomial itself, which you get by expanding the formula in powers of x.

Recap: Interpolation estimates values between known table points by fitting a polynomial through them. With equal spacing h we use p = (x - x0)/h. Newton's forward formula uses the top row of differences and is best near the beginning. Newton's backward formula uses p = (x - xn)/h and the bottom diagonal, and is best near the end. For polynomial data the answer is exact. Outside the table, be careful. Next lesson, we drop the equal spacing rule with divided differences and Lagrange's formula.
key_points: Interpolation estimates y at an x between table points by passing a polynomial through the points.
Newton's forward and backward formulas need equally spaced x values with step h.
Forward: p = (x - x0)/h, y = y0 + p delta y0 + p(p - 1)/2! delta^2 y0 + ..., using the top row of the difference table.
Backward: p = (x - xn)/h, y = yn + p nabla yn + p(p + 1)/2! nabla^2 yn + ..., using the bottom diagonal.
Use forward near the start of the table and backward near the end; central formulas suit the middle.
For data from a degree n polynomial the formula is exact (cubes example gave 1.5^3 = 3.375 exactly).
Stop adding terms when the next difference term is below the accuracy you need.
Extrapolation far outside the table can be badly wrong (sqrt table gave 5.1502 for sqrt(10), true 3.1623).
lessons.tip: Before using any formula, draw the difference table and circle the top row in one colour and the bottom diagonal in another. Most mistakes in this topic come from reading the wrong numbers, not from the formula itself.
lessons.task: Make a table of y = x^2 + 1 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 on paper. Build the difference table, then use the forward formula to find y at x = 0.5 and the backward formula to find y at x = 3.5. Check both answers by putting the x values straight into x^2 + 1.

quiz.q: In Newton's forward formula, what is p when x0 = 10, h = 5 and x = 12?
Which values does Newton's backward formula use from the difference table?
options: The bottom diagonal: yn, nabla yn, nabla^2 yn, ...
The top row: y0, delta y0, delta^2 y0, ...
The largest values in each column
quiz.explain: The backward formula starts from the last point and uses the differences on the bottom diagonal.

quiz.q: For the table of y = x^3 at x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, what does Newton's forward formula give at x = 1.5?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3.5 - 1.5 + 0.375 = 3.375, which equals 1.5^3 exactly because the data is a cubic.

quiz.q: When can you NOT use Newton's forward or backward formula directly?
options: When the x values are unequally spaced
When the y values are decimals
When x is near the start of the table
quiz.explain: Both formulas assume a constant step h. For unequal spacing use divided differences or Lagrange.

quiz.q: Why is extrapolation risky?
options: The formula cannot be computed outside the table
The polynomial fits only the table points and can move far from the true function outside them
quiz.explain: Inside the table the polynomial is pinned down by the data; outside it can run away, like 5.1502 instead of 3.1623 for sqrt(10).

lessons.title: Divided Differences and Lagrange Interpolation
lessons.content:
