Imagine you are tracking how tall a mango sapling grows. You measure it on day 1, then you forget, measure again on day 2, then on day 4, and then on day 7. The gaps are 1 day, 2 days and 3 days. Now you want to guess its height on day 3. Newton's forward and backward formulas from the last lesson cannot help, because they need equal gaps. In this lesson we learn two tools that do not care about the gaps at all: Newton's divided difference formula and Lagrange's formula.

The problem with unequal spacing: In real life, data is often messy. A sensor may miss a reading. A doctor may check a patient's fever at 8 am, 11 am and 6 pm. A shop may record sales only on days it opens. The step h is not constant, so the variable p = (x - x0)/h makes no sense. We need differences that take the size of each gap into account. That is exactly what a divided difference does: it divides a change in y by the change in x.

First divided difference: For two points (x0, y0) and (x1, y1), the first divided difference is f[x0, x1] = (y1 - y0)/(x1 - x0). You already know this from school: it is the slope of the straight line joining the two points. If y goes from 3 to 7 while x goes from 1 to 2, the slope is 4/1 = 4. It tells us how fast y is changing between those two points.

Higher divided differences: The second divided difference uses three points: f[x0, x1, x2] = (f[x1, x2] - f[x0, x1])/(x2 - x0). Notice the bottom is the gap between the first and last x, not the gap between neighbours. The third divided difference uses four points in the same way: f[x0, x1, x2, x3] = (f[x1, x2, x3] - f[x0, x1, x2])/(x3 - x0). Each level is the change of the level below, divided by the full width it covers.

A nice property: The order of the points does not matter. f[x0, x1] equals f[x1, x0], and the same is true for every level. This is called symmetry. Another nice fact: if the data comes from a polynomial of degree n, then the n-th divided differences are all the same and the next level is zero. This is just like ordinary differences in lesson 16, which makes divided differences a good tool for spotting the degree of the data too.

Building the table, worked example: Take four unequally spaced points: x = 1, 2, 4, 7 and y = 3, 7, 21, 57. First divided differences: (7 - 3)/(2 - 1) = 4, then (21 - 7)/(4 - 2) = 7, then (57 - 21)/(7 - 4) = 12. Second divided differences: (7 - 4)/(4 - 1) = 1, then (12 - 7)/(7 - 2) = 1. Third divided difference: (1 - 1)/(7 - 1) = 0. All numbers here are exact, no rounding needed. The second differences are both 1 and the third is 0, so the data is a quadratic.

Newton's divided difference formula: Now we build the polynomial. P(x) = f[x0] + f[x0, x1](x - x0) + f[x0, x1, x2](x - x0)(x - x1) + f[x0, x1, x2, x3](x - x0)(x - x1)(x - x2) + and so on. We take the top entry of each column of the table. Each term adds one more bracket (x - xk). It is the same shape as Newton's forward formula, but with divided differences and real x gaps instead of p and factorials. In fact, when the spacing happens to be equal, it turns into the forward formula.

Using it: From our table, the top entries are 3, 4, 1 and 0. So P(x) = 3 + 4(x - 1) + 1(x - 1)(x - 2) + 0. Let us find the height on day 3. P(3) = 3 + 4 times 2 + 1 times 2 times 1 = 3 + 8 + 2 = 13. And on day 5: P(5) = 3 + 4 times 4 + 4 times 3 = 3 + 16 + 12 = 31. If you expand P(x), you get 3 + 4x - 4 + x^2 - 3x + 2 = x^2 + x + 1. Check: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. It fits every point.

Why Newton's form is handy: Suppose you get one more reading later. With Newton's form you do not throw away your work. You just add one new row to the table, compute one new diagonal of divided differences, and add one more term to the polynomial. The old terms stay the same. This is a big advantage when data keeps arriving, and it also lets you see how much each new term changes the answer.

Lagrange's idea: Lagrange took a totally different road. He asked: can I build a little polynomial that equals 1 at one table point and 0 at all the others? Call it L0 for the first point, L1 for the second, and so on. These are called Lagrange basis polynomials. Then the interpolating polynomial is simply P(x) = y0 L0(x) + y1 L1(x) + y2 L2(x) + and so on. At x0, L0 is 1 and the others are 0, so P(x0) = y0. The same happens at every point. Very clever.

Building a basis polynomial: For three points x0, x1, x2, the first one is L0(x) = (x - x1)(x - x2) / ((x0 - x1)(x0 - x2)). The top makes it zero at x1 and x2. The bottom is the top with x replaced by x0, so at x0 the fraction is exactly 1. In the same way L1(x) = (x - x0)(x - x2) / ((x1 - x0)(x1 - x2)) and L2(x) = (x - x0)(x - x1) / ((x2 - x0)(x2 - x1)). The rule: for Lk, leave out the bracket with xk on top, and put xk in place of x on the bottom.

Lagrange worked example: Use the first three points of our sapling: (1, 3), (2, 7), (4, 21). Find P(3). L0(3) = (3 - 2)(3 - 4) / ((1 - 2)(1 - 4)) = (1)(-1)/3 = -1/3. L1(3) = (3 - 1)(3 - 4) / ((2 - 1)(2 - 4)) = (2)(-1)/(-2) = 1. L2(3) = (3 - 1)(3 - 2) / ((4 - 1)(4 - 2)) = 2/6 = 1/3. Now P(3) = 3 times (-1/3) + 7 times 1 + 21 times (1/3) = -1 + 7 + 7 = 13. The same answer as Newton's formula. A neat check: the weights -1/3, 1 and 1/3 add up to 1, which always happens.

The same polynomial: Newton's formula and Lagrange's formula always give the same polynomial for the same points. They are two ways of writing one answer, like 0.5 and 1/2. This is because there is only one polynomial of degree at most n through n + 1 points with different x values. Lesson 19 talks more about this uniqueness. So pick whichever form is easier for the job in front of you.

Inverse interpolation: Sometimes the question flips. You know y and want x. For example: on which day was the sapling 12 cm tall? Since Lagrange does not care which variable is which, we can swap roles: treat y as the input and x as the output. Using the points (y, x) = (3, 1), (7, 2), (21, 4) and y = 12, the weights come out as -0.6250, 1.4464 and 0.1786, rounded to 4 decimals. So x = -0.6250 times 1 + 1.4464 times 2 + 0.1786 times 4, which is about 2.9821.

How good was that guess? Our data really follows y = x^2 + x + 1. Solving x^2 + x + 1 = 12 gives x = (-1 + sqrt(45))/2, which is about 2.8541. So the inverse guess of 2.9821 is close but not exact. Why? Because x as a function of y is not a polynomial here, it has a square root in it. Inverse interpolation works best when the y values change steadily, always going up or always going down, and when the target is well inside the table.

Comparing the two methods: Lagrange is easy to write straight away and is nice for theory and for proofs. But if you add a new point, you must redo every basis polynomial. Newton's divided difference form takes a little table first, but adding a point is cheap, and the size of the last terms shows you how accurate you are. For hand calculation with 3 or 4 points, both are fine. For a computer with many points, Newton's form, or a special form called barycentric Lagrange, is usually preferred.

Real life example 1, Dhaka traffic: Example numbers. You check a maps app at odd times and note how long the drive from Mirpur to Motijheel takes: at 7:00 am, 7:45 am, 9:00 am and 10:30 am. The gaps are uneven, so Newton's forward formula is out. With a divided difference table, or with Lagrange, you can estimate the travel time at 8:15 am. It is only an estimate, traffic can jump suddenly, but it is much better than a wild guess.

Real life example 2, mayer ranna: Example numbers. Your mother puts a thermometer in the biryani pot and checks it at 2, 5, 6 and 10 minutes. You want to know when it reached 80 degrees. That is inverse interpolation: you know the y value, 80, and you want the time x. Swap the columns, use Lagrange with temperature as input and time as output, and get a sensible time. Food scientists and engineers use the same trick to read tables backwards.

In code: Lagrange is two nested loops. For each i, start L = 1, then for each j not equal to i, multiply L by (x - xj)/(xi - xj). Add yi times L to the total. That is all. The divided difference table is also a short loop: column k entry i is (previous column entry i + 1 minus entry i) divided by (x[i + k] - x[i]). Then evaluate Newton's form with nested multiplication, much like Horner's method from lesson 10.

Common mistakes: In divided differences, many students divide by the gap between neighbours instead of the full width x[i + k] - x[i]. In Lagrange, they forget to leave out the matching bracket, which makes the bottom zero. Sign mistakes are very common when x values are bigger than the target. Another mistake is using points that share the same x value, which is impossible because you would divide by zero. A quick check: in Lagrange, the weights at any x should add up to 1.

What exams ask: Expect a table with unequal spacing and a request like: build the divided difference table and find f at some x, or find the polynomial and simplify it. Also common: use Lagrange's formula to find a value, show that Lagrange and Newton give the same answer, or find x for a given y by inverse interpolation. Sometimes they ask you to prove that divided differences are symmetric, or to show that they become ordinary differences divided by h^k times k! when spacing is equal.

Recap: When gaps are unequal, divided differences divide each change in y by the matching span of x. Newton's divided difference formula builds the polynomial term by term and is easy to extend. Lagrange's formula adds up y values times basis polynomials that are 1 at their own point and 0 at the others. Both give the same unique polynomial. Inverse interpolation swaps x and y to find x from a known y. Next lesson: how big the error is, and why splines are often better than one big polynomial.
key_points: Divided differences handle unequally spaced data: f[x0, x1] = (y1 - y0)/(x1 - x0), and higher levels divide by the full span x[i + k] - x[i].
Newton's divided difference formula: P(x) = f[x0] + f[x0, x1](x - x0) + f[x0, x1, x2](x - x0)(x - x1) + ...
Divided differences are symmetric, and for degree n data the n-th level is constant.
Lagrange: P(x) = sum of yk Lk(x), where Lk is 1 at xk and 0 at the other points.
Worked example: points (1, 3), (2, 7), (4, 21), (7, 57) give P(x) = x^2 + x + 1 and P(3) = 13 by both methods.
Newton and Lagrange give the same unique polynomial; Newton is easier to extend with a new point.
Inverse interpolation swaps x and y to find x for a known y; it is approximate unless x(y) is itself a polynomial.
lessons.tip: After every Lagrange calculation, add up your weights L0 + L1 + L2 + ... at that x. If the sum is not 1, you made a slip somewhere. It takes ten seconds and saves many marks.
lessons.task: Take the points (0, 1), (1, 3), (3, 13). Build a divided difference table and write Newton's polynomial. Then use Lagrange's formula to find P(2). Check that both methods agree and that the Lagrange weights add up to 1.

quiz.q: For points x = 1, 2, 4 with y = 3, 7, 21, what is the second divided difference f[x0, x1, x2]?
quiz.explain: First differences are 4 and 7. Then (7 - 4)/(4 - 1) = 1.

quiz.q: What is special about the Lagrange basis polynomial L1(x)?
options: It is always a straight line
It equals 1 at x1 and 0 at all the other table points
quiz.explain: Each Lk is built to be 1 at its own point and 0 at the others, so P(xk) = yk.

quiz.q: What advantage does Newton's divided difference form have over Lagrange's form?
options: Adding a new data point only needs one new term
It gives a different, more accurate polynomial
quiz.explain: Old terms stay the same; you add one new diagonal of differences and one more term.

quiz.q: What is inverse interpolation?
options: Finding x for a known y by treating y as the input
quiz.explain: You swap the roles of x and y, for example with Lagrange, and estimate the x that gives the target y.

quiz.q: Why must all x values in an interpolation table be different?
options: Because the denominators would become zero otherwise
quiz.explain: Divided differences and Lagrange both divide by (xi - xj); equal x values would mean dividing by zero.

lessons.title: Interpolation Error and Splines
lessons.content:
Imagine joining dots in a colouring book. With a few dots, you can draw a smooth curve through them easily. But suppose someone tells you: draw ONE single smooth curve through 20 dots, using one formula only. Your pencil might start swinging wildly between the dots near the edges. In the last two lessons we learned how to pass one polynomial through all the points. In this lesson we ask two honest questions. How wrong can that polynomial be between the points? And is there a better way when there are many points? The answer to the second question is splines.

Why care about error: An interpolated value is a guess. A good engineer never gives a guess without saying how good it is. If a bridge designer reads a value from a table, she wants to know if the answer is good to 2 decimals or only to 1. The error formula tells us how the error depends on the function, on the number of points, and on where x sits among the points. It also explains why adding more points does not always help.

Uniqueness first: Through n + 1 points with different x values, there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n. Here is the reason, in kid language. Suppose two different polynomials P and Q, each of degree at most n, both pass through all n + 1 points. Then P - Q is also a polynomial of degree at most n, and it is zero at all n + 1 points. But a nonzero polynomial of degree n can have at most n roots. So P - Q must be zero everywhere, and P = Q. That is why Newton's forward, backward, divided difference and Lagrange forms always agree.

The interpolation error term: If f has enough smooth derivatives, then for any x in the range, f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(c)/(n + 1)! times (x - x0)(x - x1)...(x - xn). Here c is some unknown point in the interval holding x and all the table points. Do not worry that c is unknown. We usually replace f^(n+1)(c) by its largest possible size on the interval, and that gives an upper bound for the error.

Reading the formula: There are three parts. The derivative part says: if f is very curvy, with big high derivatives, the error can be big. The factorial part, (n + 1)!, grows fast and helps make the error small. The product part, (x - x0)(x - x1)...(x - xn), is small when x is close to the table points and big when x is far away, which is why extrapolation is so dangerous. Near the middle of the table the product is usually smallest.

Worked example 1, a square root: Estimate sqrt(5) by a straight line through (4, 2) and (9, 3). The slope is (3 - 2)/(9 - 4) = 0.2, so P(5) = 2 + 0.2 times 1 = 2.2. The true value is 2.2361, rounded to 4 decimals, so the actual error is about 0.0361. Now the bound: here n = 1, so we need the second derivative. For f(x) = sqrt(x), f''(x) = -1/(4 x^(3/2)). Its largest size on [4, 9] is at x = 4: 1/(4 times 8) = 1/32 = 0.03125. The bound is 0.03125/2 times |(5 - 4)(5 - 9)| = 0.015625 times 4 = 0.0625. The real error, 0.0361, is indeed below the bound.

Worked example 2, polynomial data: In lesson 17, the cubes table gave exact answers. The error formula explains why. The data was f(x) = x^3, and we used 4 or more points, so n is at least 3 and the error needs f'''' or a higher derivative. For a cubic, the fourth derivative is zero everywhere. So the error is exactly zero. In general, interpolation through n + 1 points is exact for every polynomial of degree n or less.

Error from a difference table: When you only have a table and not the formula for f, you cannot take derivatives. A practical trick is to look at the first term you did not use. In Newton's forward formula, the next term, with the next difference, is a good estimate of the error. If that term is tiny, your answer is good. This links back to lessons 16 and 17: shrinking differences mean a small error.

More points is not always better: You might think: if 4 points are good, 11 points must be great. Surprisingly, not always! In 1901, the German mathematician Carl Runge found a simple, smooth function where using more equally spaced points makes things worse. The function is f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2) on the interval from -1 to 1. It looks like a gentle hill. Nothing scary.

The Runge phenomenon in numbers: Using 6 equally spaced points, so a degree 5 polynomial, the largest error on the interval is about 0.4327, at x = 0. Using 11 equally spaced points, a degree 10 polynomial, the largest error grows to about 1.9157, near x = 0.94 and x = -0.94. For example at x = 0.95 the degree 10 polynomial gives about 1.9236, while the true value is about 0.0424. All these numbers are rounded to 4 decimals. The middle part of the curve gets better, but near the ends the polynomial swings up and down like a wild jump rope. That wobbling near the edges is called the Runge phenomenon.

Why it happens and the cures: With equally spaced points, the product (x - x0)(x - x1)...(x - xn) becomes huge near the ends of the interval, and the high derivatives of Runge's function grow very fast too. One cure is to put more points near the ends, using special points called Chebyshev nodes. The other cure, used everywhere in practice, is to stop using one big polynomial. Instead, use many small, low degree pieces. That is piecewise interpolation.

Piecewise linear interpolation: The simplest piecewise method is connect the dots with straight lines. Between each pair of neighbours, use the line through them. Take the points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 5), which come from y = x^2 + 1. At x = 0.5 the line gives (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5, and at x = 1.5 it gives (2 + 5)/2 = 3.5. The true values are 1.25 and 3.25. It never wobbles wildly, and a far away point cannot spoil it. But the joined line has sharp corners: the slope is 1 on the left of x = 1 and 3 on the right. For a car path or a font curve, corners look ugly and feel bumpy.

Cubic splines, the idea: A spline was originally a thin flexible strip of wood that ship designers bent through fixed points, held by weights, to draw smooth curves. A cubic spline copies that. Between each pair of neighbouring points, use a cubic polynomial. Then glue the pieces so that, at each inside point, the value, the slope and the curvature, meaning the first and second derivatives, all match. The result is one smooth curve with no corners and no sudden bends, made of small friendly pieces.

Counting the conditions: With n intervals, we have n cubics, and each cubic has 4 coefficients, so 4n unknowns. Each piece must hit its two end points: that is 2n conditions. At each of the n - 1 inside points, the first and second derivatives must match: that is 2(n - 1) more. Total: 4n - 2. We are 2 short. A natural spline adds the two missing conditions by saying the second derivative is zero at both ends, so the curve goes straight at its ends, just like a free wooden strip. Other choices, such as fixing the end slopes, give a clamped spline.

Worked example 3, a natural spline: Use the same points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 5) with h = 1. Let M be the second derivative at each point. Natural means M0 = 0 and M2 = 0. The standard spline equation for equal spacing is M0 + 4 M1 + M2 = 6/h^2 times (y0 - 2y1 + y2). That gives 4 M1 = 6 times (1 - 4 + 5) = 12, so M1 = 3. Building the pieces from M gives S(x) = 0.5x^3 + 0.5x + 1 on [0, 1], and S(x) = 0.5(2 - x)^3 + 1.5(2 - x) + 5(x - 1) on [1, 2].

Checking the spline: At x = 0.5, S = 0.0625 + 0.25 + 1 = 1.3125. At x = 1.5, S = 0.0625 + 0.75 + 2.5 = 3.3125. The true values are 1.25 and 3.25, so the spline errors are 0.0625 each, better than the 0.25 errors of the straight lines. At the join x = 1, both pieces have slope 2 and second derivative 3, so the curve is perfectly smooth there. At the ends the second derivative is 0, as a natural spline demands. For many points, the M equations form a tridiagonal system, which a computer solves very fast.

Real life example 1, fonts and drawing apps: Example. When you type Bangla or English on your phone, each letter's outline is stored as a set of points joined by smooth curves, and drawing apps let you drag points and see a smooth path follow. These smooth paths are built from piecewise polynomial pieces, the same family as splines. One huge polynomial through every point of the letter would wobble, just like Runge's example.

Real life example 2, a smooth road or rail: Example. Engineers designing a curved section of an expressway in Dhaka cannot let the road bend suddenly, or vehicles would jerk. They use smooth curves where the direction and the bending change gradually, which is the same goal as matching first and second derivatives in a cubic spline. Animations in cartoons and games move characters smoothly between key poses with splines too.

Common mistakes: Students often think that more points always means better accuracy. With one big polynomial on equally spaced points, that can be false, as Runge showed. Another mistake is forgetting that the error formula's point c is unknown, so we can only give a bound, not the exact error. In splines, people forget the end conditions, or mix up natural, where the second derivative is zero at the ends, with clamped, where the slope at the ends is given. Also, a spline passes through the points, so it is still interpolation, not curve fitting.

What exams ask: State and use the interpolation error formula, for example bound the error of linear interpolation for sqrt(x), sin x or e^x on a given interval. Prove the uniqueness of the interpolating polynomial. Explain the Runge phenomenon and how to avoid it. Write the conditions for a cubic spline and count them. Find a natural cubic spline through three or four points and use it to estimate a value. Short notes on piecewise linear interpolation versus cubic splines are also common.

Recap: The interpolating polynomial through n + 1 points is unique. Its error is f^(n+1)(c)/(n + 1)! times the product of (x - xi), so it depends on curviness, number of points and distance from the points. One high degree polynomial on equally spaced points can wobble badly near the ends, the Runge phenomenon. Piecewise methods fix this: straight line pieces are simple but have corners, while cubic splines join cubic pieces with matching slope and curvature. Next lesson we leave exact interpolation and learn to fit a best line through noisy data.
key_points: Through n + 1 points with different x values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n.
Error term: f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(c)/(n + 1)! times (x - x0)(x - x1)...(x - xn), for some unknown c.
Linear interpolation of sqrt(5) from 4 and 9 gives 2.2; actual error about 0.0361, bound 0.0625.
Interpolation is exact for data from polynomials of degree n or less.
Runge phenomenon: for 1/(1 + 25x^2) with equal spacing, max error grows from about 0.4327 (degree 5) to about 1.9157 (degree 10).
Piecewise linear interpolation never wobbles but has corners at the joins.
A cubic spline uses cubic pieces with matching value, slope and second derivative; a natural spline has zero second derivative at both ends.
lessons.tip: When you meet the error formula, say the three parts out loud: how curvy the function is, how many points you used, and how far x is from the points. If you can explain each part with one example, you understand the formula.
lessons.task: On graph paper, plot the points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 5). Draw straight line pieces between them in one colour. Then plot S(x) = 0.5x^3 + 0.5x + 1 on [0, 1] and S(x) = 0.5(2 - x)^3 + 1.5(2 - x) + 5(x - 1) on [1, 2] at x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, ... 2 in another colour, and compare both with y = x^2 + 1.

quiz.q: How many polynomials of degree at most 3 pass through 4 points with different x values?
quiz.explain: The interpolating polynomial is unique: if two existed, their difference would have 4 roots but degree at most 3, so it must be zero.

quiz.q: In the error formula f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(c)/(n + 1)! times (x - x0)...(x - xn), why does the error grow when x is far outside the table?
options: Because the product (x - x0)...(x - xn) becomes large
Because f has no derivatives there
quiz.explain: Far from the table points every bracket (x - xi) is large, so their product is large.

quiz.q: What is the Runge phenomenon?
options: Newton's formula failing for unequal spacing
Wild wobbling near the ends when one high degree polynomial interpolates equally spaced points
quiz.explain: For f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2), more equally spaced points made the polynomial swing more near the ends.

quiz.q: Which conditions does a natural cubic spline add at the two end points?
quiz.explain: Natural means S'' = 0 at both ends, giving the 2 extra conditions needed.

quiz.q: For a natural cubic spline through (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 5), what is M1, the second derivative at x = 1?
quiz.explain: M0 + 4M1 + M2 = 6(y0 - 2y1 + y2) with M0 = M2 = 0 gives 4M1 = 6 times 2 = 12, so M1 = 3.

lessons.title: Least Squares Line Fitting
lessons.content:
Imagine you throw a handful of rice grains onto a table, and they land in a rough slanting stripe. Now someone hands you a ruler and says: lay the ruler down so it follows the stripe as well as possible. The ruler cannot touch every grain. Some grains are a bit above it, some a bit below. But there is one best position. Finding that best line through scattered, noisy points is what the least squares method does. It is one of the most used ideas in all of science and engineering.

Interpolation versus fitting: In lessons 17 to 19 we passed a curve exactly through every point. That makes sense when the data is exact, like a table of sqrt(x). But real measurements are noisy. A weighing scale wobbles, a student reads a stopwatch late, a sensor jitters. If we force a curve through every noisy point, we get a wiggly curve that copies the noise. With 5 points, interpolation would give a degree 4 polynomial that bends up and down. Fitting instead chooses a simple shape, like a straight line, and places it as close to all the points as possible, without touching each one.

The model: We assume y is roughly a + bx, where a is the intercept, the value when x = 0, and b is the slope, how much y grows when x grows by 1. Our job is to find the best a and b from the data. We have n data points (x1, y1), (x2, y2) up to (xn, yn). For any choice of a and b, the line predicts a + b xi at each xi.

Residuals: The residual at a point is the actual value minus the predicted value: ei = yi - (a + b xi). A positive residual means the point is above the line. A negative residual means it is below. A good line has small residuals. But how do we combine them into one score? If we just add them up, positives and negatives cancel, so a terrible line could still score zero. We need something better.

Sum of squared errors: The least squares idea is to square each residual and add them: S = e1^2 + e2^2 + ... + en^2. Squaring makes every term positive, so nothing cancels. It also punishes big misses much more than small ones: a miss of 2 counts as 4, but a miss of 0.5 counts as only 0.25. The best line is the one that makes S as small as possible. That is why it is called least squares: the least sum of squares.

Why squares and not absolute values: You could add |ei| instead. That is a real method too, but it is harder to solve, because |e| has a sharp corner at zero and calculus does not like corners. Squares give a smooth bowl shaped function of a and b, and the bottom of a smooth bowl can be found by setting derivatives to zero. That gives simple linear equations. Squares also connect nicely with statistics, but we do not need that here.

Deriving the normal equations: S(a, b) = sum of (yi - a - b xi)^2. At the minimum, the partial derivative with respect to a is zero and so is the one with respect to b. Taking them and dividing by -2 gives sum of (yi - a - b xi) = 0 and sum of xi(yi - a - b xi) = 0. Rearranging gives the two normal equations: n a + b (sum x) = sum y, and a (sum x) + b (sum x^2) = sum xy. Two equations, two unknowns. Easy.

The ready formulas: Solving those two equations gives b = (n sum xy - sum x sum y) / (n sum x^2 - (sum x)^2), and then a = (sum y - b sum x)/n. Another way to say the second one: a = ybar - b xbar, where xbar and ybar are the averages. This means the best line always passes through the point (xbar, ybar), the centre of the data. That is a handy fact to check your answer.

Worked example 1, the table: Take x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1. These are example numbers. Make columns for x, y, x^2 and xy. The sums are: sum x = 15, sum y = 30.1, sum x^2 = 55, sum xy = 110.2, and n = 5. Always build this table neatly. Most mistakes happen when adding these columns.

Worked example 1, solving: The normal equations are 5a + 15b = 30.1 and 15a + 55b = 110.2. Using the formula, b = (5 times 110.2 - 15 times 30.1) / (5 times 55 - 15^2) = (551 - 451.5)/(275 - 225) = 99.5/50 = 1.99. Then a = (30.1 - 1.99 times 15)/5 = (30.1 - 29.85)/5 = 0.05. So the best line is y = 0.05 + 1.99x. Check: xbar = 3 and ybar = 6.02, and 0.05 + 1.99 times 3 = 6.02. The line passes through the centre, as promised.

Worked example 1, residuals: The line predicts 2.04, 4.03, 6.02, 8.01, 10.00 at x = 1 to 5. The residuals are 0.06, -0.13, 0.18, -0.21, 0.10. Notice they add up to exactly 0, which always happens for a least squares line with an intercept. Squaring and adding: S = 0.107, rounded to 3 decimals. For comparison, the simple guess y = 2x gives S = 0.11. Close, but the least squares line is a tiny bit better, and no other straight line can beat 0.107.

Predicting with the line: Once we have the line, we can predict. At x = 6 the line says y = 0.05 + 1.99 times 6 = 11.99. This is a fitted prediction, not an exact value. The same extrapolation warning from lesson 17 applies: predicting a little beyond the data is fine if the straight line pattern really continues, but far beyond it, the pattern might change.

Goodness of fit: How do we know if a line fits well? The sum of squared errors S tells us how much is left unexplained. To judge its size, compare it with the total spread of y around its average: SST = sum of (yi - ybar)^2. For our data SST = 39.708, while S = 0.107. A common score is R^2 = 1 - S/SST, which here is about 0.9973, rounded to 4 decimals. R^2 near 1 means the line explains almost all the up and down of y. Near 0 means a line is a poor model. Also look at the residuals: if they show a curved pattern instead of random scatter, a straight line is the wrong shape.

Worked example 2, rickshaw fares: Example numbers, not real survey data. Suppose you note rickshaw fares for trips of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km as 30, 40, 55, 60, 75 taka. The sums are sum x = 15, sum y = 260, sum x^2 = 55, sum xy = 890. Then b = (5 times 890 - 15 times 260)/50 = (4450 - 3900)/50 = 11, and a = (260 - 11 times 15)/5 = 19. So fare is about 19 + 11 times distance: a base of 19 taka plus 11 taka per km. For a 2.5 km trip, the line predicts 46.5 taka.

Rickshaw residuals: The line predicts 30, 41, 52, 63, 74. The residuals are 0, -1, 3, -3, 1, which again add to 0. The sum of squared errors is 20, and SST is 1230, so R^2 is about 0.9837, rounded to 4 decimals. Bargaining makes fares noisy, but a straight line still captures the main pattern very well. This is exactly why fitting beats interpolation here: no one wants a fare formula that wiggles to match every single bargain.

Real life example, cricket practice: Example. A coach records how many minutes each player practised batting in a week and their runs in the next match. The points are scattered: practice helps, but luck and bowling also matter. A least squares line through the points shows the average trend, like roughly how many extra runs per extra hour of practice. The line does not promise any one player's score. It summarises the overall pattern.

Link to linear algebra: In matrix language, we want A c close to y, where each row of A is [1, xi], c is the column [a, b], and y is the data column. There are more equations than unknowns, so usually no exact solution exists. The least squares solution satisfies A^T A c = A^T y. If you multiply this out, you get exactly the two normal equations above. Geometrically, A c is the projection of y onto the space spanned by the columns of A, so the residual vector is perpendicular to that space. This is the same least squares you may have met in linear algebra.

In code: Loop over the data once, adding up n, sum x, sum y, sum x^2 and sum xy. Then compute b and a with the two formulas. That is about five lines in any language. Spreadsheet programs have a built in trend line that does the same computation. For very large or badly scaled data, libraries solve the A^T A c = A^T y problem with more careful methods, like QR factorisation, to avoid round-off trouble, but the idea is the same.

Common mistakes: Confusing sum x^2 with (sum x)^2 is the classic one: here 55 versus 225. Another is mixing up a and b, so the slope ends up as the intercept. Some students try to make the line pass through every point, which is interpolation, not fitting. Others minimise vertical distances and then wonder why swapping x and y gives a different line: least squares in y measures vertical gaps only, so y on x and x on y are different lines. And do not forget to state the units and how many decimals you rounded to.

What exams ask: The classic question gives 5 to 7 data points and says: fit a straight line y = a + bx by the method of least squares. You must build the table of x, y, x^2 and xy, write the normal equations, solve for a and b, and often predict y at a new x. Other questions ask you to derive the normal equations by minimising S, compute the residuals or the sum of squared errors, or explain the difference between interpolation and curve fitting.

Recap: Least squares fits a simple model through noisy data instead of passing through every point. A residual is actual minus predicted. We minimise the sum of squared residuals. For a straight line, setting derivatives to zero gives the normal equations n a + b sum x = sum y and a sum x + b sum x^2 = sum xy. The best line passes through (xbar, ybar), its residuals add to zero, and S and R^2 tell us how good the fit is. Next lesson we fit parabolas and curves like y = a e^(bx) using the same idea.
key_points: Interpolation passes through every point; least squares fitting finds the line closest to noisy points overall.
Residual ei = yi - (a + b xi); least squares minimises S = sum of ei^2.
Normal equations for y = a + bx: n a + b sum x = sum y, and a sum x + b sum x^2 = sum xy.
Formulas: b = (n sum xy - sum x sum y)/(n sum x^2 - (sum x)^2), a = ybar - b xbar.
The best line passes through (xbar, ybar) and its residuals add up to zero.
R^2 = 1 - S/SST measures goodness of fit; values near 1 mean a good straight line fit.
In matrix form the normal equations are A^T A c = A^T y.
lessons.tip: Always make the four column table of x, y, x^2 and xy, and add each column twice. After solving, check that your line passes through (xbar, ybar). These two habits catch almost every arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: Write down the time your phone shows for 5 different short tasks and how many steps or taps each took, or invent 5 example points such as x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 3, 5, 6, 9, 10. Build the x, y, x^2, xy table, find a and b by least squares, compute the residuals and check that they add to zero.

quiz.q: What does least squares make as small as possible?
quiz.explain: It minimises S = e1^2 + e2^2 + ... + en^2. Plain sums of residuals can cancel out.

quiz.q: Which pair is the correct normal equations for y = a + bx?
options: a + b = sum y and a - b = sum x
n a = sum y and b = sum x
n a + b sum x = sum y and a sum x + b sum x^2 = sum xy
a sum x^2 + b = sum y and a + b sum x = n
quiz.explain: Setting the partial derivatives of S with respect to a and b to zero gives exactly these two equations.

quiz.q: For x = 1..5 with sum x = 15, sum y = 30.1, sum x^2 = 55, sum xy = 110.2, what is the slope b?
Which statement about a least squares line with an intercept is always true?
options: It passes through every data point
It passes through the point (xbar, ybar)
quiz.explain: From the first normal equation, a = ybar - b xbar, so the line goes through the centre of the data.

quiz.q: Why do we usually fit a line instead of interpolating noisy data?
options: Interpolating would copy the noise and give a wiggly curve
Fitting always passes through every point
quiz.explain: With noisy data an exact curve chases the noise; a simple fitted line shows the real trend.

lessons.title: Curve Fitting Beyond Lines: Parabolas, Exponentials and Power Laws
lessons.content:
Imagine you throw a ball to your friend in the school field. If you mark where the ball is every split second, the dots do not sit on a straight line. They go up, slow down, and come back down in a curve. Now imagine someone gives you those dots and asks for a formula. A straight ruler line would be a bad answer, because the dots clearly bend. In the last lesson we fitted straight lines with least squares. In this lesson we learn to fit curves: parabolas, exponential growth curves and power curves. The big secret is that we reuse the same least squares idea, with only small changes.

Quick recap of least squares: We have data points (x, y). Our model gives a predicted value for each x. The residual is the gap: actual y minus predicted y. We square every residual, add them up, and call that the sum of squared errors, or SSE. The best model is the one with the smallest SSE. For a straight line y = a + bx, setting the derivatives of SSE to zero gave us two normal equations. That was lesson 20. Today the shape changes, but the rule stays the same: make SSE as small as possible.

Why a straight line is not always enough: Many things in nature and in daily life do not grow at a steady rate. A ball's height follows a parabola. Money with compound profit, or bacteria in leftover rice, grows faster and faster, which is an exponential curve. The area of a square plot grows like the side squared, a power curve. If you force a straight line through curved data, the residuals show a pattern: positive at the ends and negative in the middle, or the other way round. A pattern in the residuals is a loud signal that your model has the wrong shape.

Fitting a parabola: The model is y = a + bx + cx^2. Now there are three unknowns, a, b and c. SSE is the sum of (y - a - bx - cx^2)^2 over all points. We take the derivative of SSE with respect to a, b and c, and set each one to zero. That gives three normal equations. You do not need to memorise the calculus. Just remember the pattern below, which is easy to rebuild.

The three normal equations: First, n a + (sum x) b + (sum x^2) c = sum y. Second, (sum x) a + (sum x^2) b + (sum x^3) c = sum xy. Third, (sum x^2) a + (sum x^3) b + (sum x^4) c = sum x^2 y. See the trick? Start from the model y = a + bx + cx^2 and sum it over all points. Then multiply the model by x and sum again. Then multiply by x^2 and sum again. Each multiplication gives one equation. The powers of x march up by one each time, from x^0 to x^4.

Worked example, building the table: Here are five example data points, made up for practice: x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 1.1, 1.9, 4.2, 8.1, 12.8. First we make a table with columns x, x^2, x^3, x^4, y, xy and x^2 y. Adding the columns gives: n = 5, sum x = 10, sum x^2 = 30, sum x^3 = 100, sum x^4 = 354, sum y = 28.1, sum xy = 85.8 and sum x^2 y = 296.4. Always double check these sums, because one wrong sum ruins everything that follows.

Worked example, solving: The normal equations become 5a + 10b + 30c = 28.1, then 10a + 30b + 100c = 85.8, then 30a + 100b + 354c = 296.4. This is a 3 by 3 linear system, so we solve it with Gauss elimination from lesson 11. The answer, rounded to 4 decimals, is a = 1.0429, b = 0.2743 and c = 0.6714. So our fitted parabola is y = 1.0429 + 0.2743x + 0.6714x^2. Plug in x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and you get predictions 1.0429, 1.9886, 4.2771, 7.9086 and 12.8829, which sit very close to the real y values.

How good is the fit? The SSE of the parabola is about 0.0606, rounded to 4 decimals. If we fit the best straight line to the same five points, we get y = -0.3 + 2.96x, and its SSE is about 6.372. That is roughly a hundred times bigger. The straight line misses badly at the ends and in the middle. The parabola follows the bend. This is exactly how you compare models: same data, compute SSE for each, and smaller wins, as long as the models have a fair number of parameters.

The same idea for higher degree: For a cubic y = a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3 you get four normal equations, using sums of x up to x^6. In general, a polynomial of degree m needs m + 1 normal equations. In linear algebra language, this is the least squares solution of an overdetermined system, solved by the normal equations A^T A c = A^T y. For high degrees these equations can become ill conditioned, which links back to lesson 12, so in practice programmers keep the degree small or use more stable methods.

Linearising: Some curves are not polynomials. For example y = a e^(bx) has the unknown b inside the exponent, so the normal equations would not be linear. The clever trick is to change the variables so the curve turns into a straight line. Then we can use the line fitting from lesson 20 directly. This trick is called linearisation, and logarithms are the main tool. Remember the rules: ln(pq) = ln p + ln q, and ln(p^r) = r ln p, and ln(e^t) = t.

Exponential model y = a e^(bx): Take the natural log of both sides. We get ln y = ln a + bx. Now call Y = ln y and A = ln a. The equation is Y = A + bx, a straight line in x and Y. So the recipe is: convert every y to ln y, fit a straight line to the points (x, Y), read off A and b, and finally get a back with a = e^A. Note that this only works when all y values are positive, because the log of zero or a negative number is not defined.

Worked exponential example: Suppose a science club counts bacteria in a dish, in thousands, every hour. Example numbers: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 hours and y = 2.0, 3.1, 5.0, 7.9. Taking natural logs, rounded to 4 decimals, Y = 0.6931, 1.1314, 1.6094, 2.0669. The sums are sum x = 6, sum x^2 = 14, sum Y = 5.5008 and sum xY = 10.5509. The line normal equations are 4A + 6b = 5.5008 and 6A + 14b = 10.5509. Solving gives A = 0.6853 and b = 0.4599, rounded to 4 decimals. Then a = e^0.6853 = 1.9844.

Checking the exponential fit: The fitted curve is y = 1.9844 e^(0.4599x). Its predictions at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, rounded to 3 decimals, are 1.984, 3.143, 4.979 and 7.886. Compare with 2.0, 3.1, 5.0 and 7.9. Very close. The value b = 0.4599 tells us the growth speed: every hour the count is multiplied by about e^0.4599, which is roughly 1.58. One small honest note: this method makes the squared errors of ln y small, not the squared errors of y itself. The answer is usually very good, but it is not exactly the same as a direct least squares fit on y.

Power model y = a x^b: Again take logs. ln y = ln a + b ln x. Now set X = ln x, Y = ln y and A = ln a. We get Y = A + bX, a straight line in X and Y. So this time we take the log of both x and y. Both must be positive. Many people use log base 10 instead of natural log. That is fine too, as long as you use the same base everywhere and convert back with the same base, a = 10^A instead of e^A.

Worked power example: Example numbers: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 2.0, 5.7, 10.4, 16.0. With natural logs, rounded to 4 decimals, X = 0, 0.6931, 1.0986, 1.3863 and Y = 0.6931, 1.7405, 2.3418, 2.7726. Fitting a line to (X, Y) gives b = 1.4995 and A = 0.6956, so a = e^0.6956 = 2.0050. The fitted model is y = 2.0050 x^1.4995, which is almost y = 2 x^1.5. The predictions at x = 1, 2, 3, 4, to 3 decimals, are 2.005, 5.669, 10.412 and 16.029. Lovely.

Other handy linearisations: y = a b^x becomes log y = log a + x log b, a line in x. The model y = a + b/x becomes a line if you use 1/x as the new variable. The model y = x / (a + bx) can be turned into 1/y = b + a(1/x). In exams, the question usually gives the model and asks you to linearise it, build the table and find the constants. So practise writing the new X and Y clearly before you start adding columns.

Choosing a model: How do you know which shape to pick? First, think about the science. Falling objects suggest a parabola. Growth that keeps multiplying suggests an exponential. Second, plot the data. If plotting ln y against x looks straight, try the exponential. If ln y against ln x looks straight, try the power law. Third, fit the candidates and compare the SSE and the residual pattern. A good model leaves residuals that look random, small and with no clear pattern.

Overfitting warning: You might think, why not use a very high degree polynomial and get SSE equal to zero? With five points, a degree 4 polynomial can pass through all five exactly. But that curve often wiggles wildly between and beyond the points, just like the Runge phenomenon from lesson 19. It has memorised the noise instead of learning the trend. This is called overfitting. A good rule: use the simplest model that explains the data well, and always keep the number of parameters much smaller than the number of data points.

Real life example 1, a cricket ball's path: Your cousin films a cricket ball after a high catch and measures its height at a few moments. The heights go up then down. A parabola h = a + bt + ct^2 fits well, because gravity pulls with a steady force. Once you fit it, the value of c is linked to gravity, and you can predict when the ball lands by solving h = 0. Sports analysis tools use the same kind of curve fitting, often with many more points and more complex models.

Real life example 2, a mobile shop's growth: Imagine a small phone shop in Dhaka whose monthly bKash payments seem to grow faster each month. Example numbers only, of course. The owner takes logs of the monthly totals and fits a line, so he gets an exponential model. He can now say roughly how fast the business is multiplying. But he should be careful with extrapolation. Our bacteria model predicts about 12.491 thousand at x = 4 hours, but real growth always slows down when food or customers run out. A fit tells you about the range of your data, not the far future.

Common mistakes and exam tips: Students often forget that a comes back as e^A, and report A as if it were a. Some mix log base 10 and natural log in the same problem. Others make an arithmetic slip in sum x^4 or sum x^2 y, so always recheck the table. Remember too that you cannot take logs of zero or negative values. Typical exam questions are: fit a parabola to five points, fit y = a e^(bx) or y = a x^b by linearisation, and explain why a model was chosen.

Recap: Least squares works for curves too. For a parabola, you build three normal equations by summing the model multiplied by 1, x and x^2. For exponential and power models, you take logs to turn the curve into a straight line, fit the line, and convert back. Choose the model by thinking, plotting and comparing SSE, and keep it simple to avoid overfitting. Next lesson, we change direction completely: instead of fitting a formula, we estimate derivatives straight from numbers.
key_points: Least squares for curves still means: choose the constants that make the sum of squared residuals (SSE) smallest.
A parabola y = a + bx + cx^2 needs three normal equations, built by summing the model times 1, x and x^2.
The parabola normal equations use sums of x up to x^4, plus sum y, sum xy and sum x^2 y.
y = a e^(bx) is linearised as ln y = ln a + bx: fit a line to (x, ln y), then a = e^A.
y = a x^b is linearised as ln y = ln a + b ln x: take logs of both x and y; all values must be positive.
Compare models on the same data with SSE and look for a random, patternless residual plot.
Overfitting: too many parameters can hit every point but memorise noise; keep models simple and avoid far extrapolation.
lessons.tip: Before any curve fit, write the model, the substitution (X = ?, Y = ?) and the empty table headings on one line. Most lost marks come from a wrong column sum or forgetting to convert A back into a, not from the method itself.
lessons.task: Take the points x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3, 6, 12, 24 (made-up numbers that double each step). Take ln y for each, fit a straight line to (x, ln y) with a phone calculator, and find a and b in y = a e^(bx). Check that e^b comes out close to 2.

quiz.q: To fit y = a + bx + cx^2 by least squares, how many normal equations do you solve?
quiz.explain: There are three unknowns, a, b and c, so setting the three partial derivatives of SSE to zero gives three normal equations.

quiz.q: Which substitution turns y = a e^(bx) into a straight line?
options: Y = ln y, giving Y = ln a + bx
X = ln x, giving y = a + bX
quiz.explain: Taking the natural log gives ln y = ln a + bx, which is a line in x and ln y.

quiz.q: After fitting the line Y = A + bX for the power model y = a x^b (natural logs), how do you get a?
quiz.explain: A was defined as ln a, so a = e^A. If you used log base 10, then a = 10^A instead.

quiz.q: In the lesson's example, the parabola had SSE about 0.0606 and the best line had SSE about 6.372. What does this tell you?
options: The line is better because its SSE is bigger
The parabola fits these points much better
quiz.explain: On the same data, smaller SSE means a closer fit. The parabola's SSE is roughly a hundred times smaller.

quiz.q: Why is fitting a degree 4 polynomial through 5 noisy points usually a bad idea?
options: It always gives a straight line
It overfits: SSE is zero but the curve wiggles and memorises noise
Least squares only works for lines
quiz.explain: With as many parameters as points the curve passes through every point, but it learns the noise, not the trend, and behaves badly between and beyond the data.

lessons.title: Numerical Differentiation: Slopes from Numbers
lessons.content:
Imagine you are sitting in a rickshaw on a Dhaka road, and you want to know how fast it is going. There is no speedometer. But you have a phone that writes down your position every two seconds. Speed is just how quickly position changes, which is a derivative. In calculus class you found derivatives with rules, like the derivative of x^2 is 2x. But here you have no formula at all, only a list of numbers. Numerical differentiation is the art of estimating derivatives straight from numbers. That is today's topic.

What a derivative really is: The derivative f'(x) is the slope of the curve at the point x. The calculus definition says f'(x) is the limit of (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h as h goes to zero. A computer cannot take a true limit. So we do the next best thing: we pick a small but real h and compute the fraction. That gives an approximation. The whole lesson is about doing this cleverly, so the answer is as close as possible to the true slope.

Our test function: To see how good each formula is, we need a case where we know the true answer. We use f(x) = e^x at x = 1. The derivative of e^x is e^x itself, so the true answer is e = 2.718282, rounded to 6 decimals. We will need f(1) = 2.718282, f(1.1) = 3.004166 and f(0.9) = 2.459603, all to 6 decimals. In every example below we compute in Python with full precision and then round to 6 decimals.

Forward difference: The simplest formula looks ahead. f'(x) is approximately (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h. With h = 0.1: (3.004166 - 2.718282) / 0.1 = 2.858842. The error is about +0.140560. Not very accurate. Why? A Taylor series tells us f(x + h) = f(x) + h f'(x) + (h^2/2) f''(x) + more. Rearranging, the forward formula equals f'(x) + (h/2) f''(x) + smaller terms. So the error is about (h/2) f''(x), which is first order in h. We write it O(h).

Backward difference: The mirror version looks behind. f'(x) is approximately (f(x) - f(x - h)) / h. With h = 0.1: (2.718282 - 2.459603) / 0.1 = 2.586787. The error is about -0.131495. Again O(h), but with the opposite sign. Notice something interesting: forward is too big and backward is too small, by similar amounts. That is a hint that averaging them could cancel the error.

Central difference: Average the two and you get the central difference. f'(x) is approximately (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2h). With h = 0.1: (3.004166 - 2.459603) / 0.2 = 2.722815. The error is only about +0.004533. That is roughly 30 times better than forward, using the same h. Taylor series explains why. When you subtract f(x - h) from f(x + h), the f''(x) terms cancel. The error becomes about (h^2/6) f'''(x), so central difference is O(h^2), second order.

Watching the order in action: Halve the step to h = 0.05. Forward gives 2.787386 with error about 0.069104. Backward gives 2.651443 with error about -0.066838. Central gives 2.719415 with error about 0.001133. Look at the errors. Forward went from 0.1406 to 0.0691, roughly halved, as O(h) predicts. Central went from 0.004533 to 0.001133, roughly divided by 4, as O(h^2) predicts. This is a great way to check your understanding: halve h and watch how the error shrinks.

Second derivative formula: Sometimes we need f''(x), for example acceleration from position. Add the Taylor series for f(x + h) and f(x - h) and the odd terms cancel. We get f''(x) approximately equal to (f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)) / h^2. This is also O(h^2). For e^x at x = 1 with h = 0.1, it gives 2.720548. The true value is again e = 2.718282, so the error is about 0.002266. The pattern 1, -2, 1 is worth remembering: it shows up again when we solve differential equations on a grid.

Why not make h tiny? You may think: if the error shrinks with h, let us take h = 0.000000000001. But computers store numbers with limited digits, as we saw in lesson 4. When h is tiny, f(x + h) and f(x) are almost equal, and subtracting them causes catastrophic cancellation. Then we divide that noisy small number by a tiny h, which blows the noise up. So there are two errors fighting: truncation error, which gets smaller as h shrinks, and round-off error, which gets bigger as h shrinks.

The step size experiment: Here is forward difference for e^x at x = 1 in Python double precision. With h = 0.1 the error is about 0.14. With h = 0.0001 it is about 0.000136. With h = 0.00000001, which is 10^-8, it is about 0.0000000066, the best in our run. With h = 10^-12 the error grows back to about 0.00043. So smaller is not always better. For forward difference in double precision, the best h is usually near the square root of machine epsilon, about 10^-8. For central difference, the best h is somewhat larger.

Derivatives from a table: Often you do not have f at all, only a table of equally spaced values. Then we can differentiate the interpolation polynomial from lesson 17. Using Newton's forward formula at the first point x0, we get f'(x0) approximately (1/h) times (delta y0 - delta^2 y0 / 2 + delta^3 y0 / 3 - delta^4 y0 / 4 and so on). For the end of the table, Newton's backward formula gives f'(xn) approximately (1/h) times (nabla yn + nabla^2 yn / 2 + nabla^3 yn / 3 and so on). Inside the table, central differences are the natural choice.

Worked table example: Take e^x rounded to 4 decimals at x = 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3: the values are 2.7183, 3.0042, 3.3201 and 3.6693. The first differences are 0.2859, 0.3159 and 0.3492. The second differences are 0.0300 and 0.0333. The third difference is 0.0033. Then f'(1.0) is approximately (1/0.1)(0.2859 - 0.0300/2 + 0.0033/3) = 2.7200. The true value is 2.718282, so the error is about 0.0017. If we used only the first term, we would get 2.859, much worse. The extra difference terms really help.

Second derivative from a table: In the same way, Newton's forward formula gives f''(x0) approximately (1/h^2) times (delta^2 y0 - delta^3 y0 + (11/12) delta^4 y0 and so on). You will meet this formula in exam questions that ask for both velocity and acceleration from a table. Remember the warning, though. Each difference column amplifies rounding errors in the table, so higher differences of noisy data can be mostly noise.

Richardson extrapolation: Here is a beautiful trick. We know the central difference error is roughly C h^2 for some constant C. Let D(h) be the central estimate with step h. Then D(h) is about f' + C h^2 and D(h/2) is about f' + C h^2 / 4. Multiply the second by 4, subtract the first, and divide by 3. The C h^2 terms cancel. So f' is approximately (4 D(h/2) - D(h)) / 3. We combine two rough answers into one much better answer.

Richardson worked example: For e^x at x = 1, D(0.2) = (e^1.2 - e^0.8) / 0.4 = 2.736440, with error about 0.018158. D(0.1) = 2.722815, with error about 0.004533. Now combine: (4 times 2.722815 - 2.736440) / 3 = 2.718273. The error is about -0.000009. We went from an error in the third decimal to an error in the sixth decimal, with no new function evaluations beyond the two estimates. The same idea, applied to the trapezoidal rule, gives Romberg integration, which we meet in lesson 24.

Differentiation is harder than integration: Here is a surprising fact. Numerically, differentiation is the touchy one. Integration adds things up, so small random errors tend to average out. Differentiation subtracts nearby values, so small errors get magnified. If your data comes from a real sensor with noise, a raw difference formula can give wild slopes. A common fix is to smooth or fit the data first, for example with least squares from lessons 20 and 21, and then differentiate the fitted curve.

Real life example 1, rickshaw speed: Back to the rickshaw. Your phone records position 0 m at t = 0 s, 9 m at t = 2 s and 20 m at t = 4 s. These are example numbers. The central difference speed at t = 2 is (20 - 0) / 4 = 5.0 m/s. The forward estimate at t = 0 would be (9 - 0) / 2 = 4.5 m/s. The acceleration at t = 2, using the 1, -2, 1 formula, is (20 - 2 times 9 + 0) / 2^2 = 0.5 m/s^2. So the rickshaw is speeding up gently. Phone apps estimate speed from GPS readings in a similar spirit, often with extra smoothing.

Real life example 2, cooling dal: Your mother takes a pot of dal off the stove, and you measure its temperature every minute: 90, 84, 79 degrees Celsius, example readings. How fast is it cooling at minute 1? Central difference: (79 - 90) / 2 = -5.5 degrees per minute. The forward estimate at minute 0 is (84 - 90) / 1 = -6.0 degrees per minute. The negative sign means the temperature is falling. Scientists use rates like this to test cooling models, such as Newton's law of cooling, against real measurements.

Where it is used in computing: Numerical derivatives appear everywhere. Image processing finds edges by taking differences of neighbouring pixel brightness. Physics engines in games estimate velocity from positions. Optimisation programs sometimes estimate gradients with finite differences when no formula is available, and programmers use the same trick to test that a hand written gradient is correct. Solving differential equations on a grid, which we touch on in lessons 25 and 26, is built on these same difference formulas.

Common mistakes and exam tips: Students mix up the denominators. Forward and backward divide by h, central divides by 2h, and the second derivative divides by h^2. Another slip is forgetting the signs in the Newton table formula: minus, plus, minus for forward differences, but all plus for backward differences. Some think a smaller h is always better, which ignores round-off. Typical exam questions: derive the central difference and its error order with Taylor series, compute f' and f'' from a table, and use Richardson extrapolation to improve an estimate.

Quick memory card: Forward is (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h, error O(h). Backward is (f(x) - f(x-h)) / h, error O(h). Central is (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / (2h), error O(h^2). Second derivative is (f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)) / h^2, error O(h^2). Richardson for an O(h^2) method is (4D(h/2) - D(h)) / 3. Write these five lines on a card and test yourself until you can derive each one from Taylor series.

Recap: When there is no formula, we estimate derivatives from nearby values. Forward and backward differences are first order. The central difference is second order and usually much better for the same h. The second derivative uses the 1, -2, 1 pattern. Tables can be differentiated through Newton's interpolation formulas. Choosing h is a balance between truncation and round-off. Richardson extrapolation combines two estimates to cancel the main error. Next lesson we go the other way, from slopes to areas, with the trapezoidal rule.
key_points: Numerical differentiation estimates f'(x) from nearby values using a small but finite step h.
Forward (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h and backward (f(x) - f(x-h)) / h differences have error O(h).
Central difference (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / (2h) has error O(h^2): halving h cuts the error by about 4.
Second derivative: (f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)) / h^2, also O(h^2).
Tables can be differentiated with Newton's forward or backward formulas, e.g. f'(x0) about (1/h)(delta y0 - delta^2 y0/2 + delta^3 y0/3 - ...).
Too small an h makes round-off error explode; for forward differences in double precision the best h is near 10^-8.
Richardson extrapolation (4D(h/2) - D(h)) / 3 cancels the h^2 error of the central difference.
Differentiation amplifies noise, so smooth or fit noisy data before differentiating.
lessons.tip: Do not memorise the formulas as pictures. Practise deriving forward, central and second derivative formulas from the Taylor series of f(x+h) and f(x-h). Once you can derive them, you also get the error order for free, and exams love asking for both.
lessons.task: On a phone calculator, estimate the derivative of sin x at x = 0.5 (radians) with forward and central differences using h = 0.1 and h = 0.05. Compare with the true value cos 0.5, and check that the central error drops by about 4 times when h is halved.

quiz.q: What is the central difference formula for f'(x)?
quiz.explain: The central difference uses one point on each side and divides by the distance between them, 2h.

quiz.q: If you halve h, roughly what happens to the error of the central difference?
quiz.explain: Central difference is O(h^2), so halving h divides the error by about 4. In the lesson it went from 0.004533 to 0.001133.

quiz.q: Why can a very tiny h, like 10^-12, give a worse derivative on a computer?
options: Round-off error from subtracting nearly equal numbers grows as h shrinks
Truncation error grows as h shrinks
Computers cannot divide by small numbers
The Taylor series stops working for small h
quiz.explain: f(x+h) and f(x) become almost equal, so the subtraction loses digits, and dividing by a tiny h magnifies that round-off error.

quiz.q: Given central estimates D(0.2) = 2.736440 and D(0.1) = 2.722815, what does Richardson extrapolation give?
Which formula estimates the second derivative f''(x)?
quiz.explain: Adding the Taylor series of f(x+h) and f(x-h) cancels the odd terms and gives the 1, -2, 1 pattern divided by h^2, with error O(h^2).

lessons.title: Numerical Integration I: The Trapezoidal Rule
lessons.content:
Imagine your family owns a small pond with a curvy bank, and your father wants to know its area to buy the right amount of fish feed. There is no neat formula for a wobbly shape. But you can do something clever. Stretch a rope straight across, measure the width of the pond every few metres, and treat each strip as a simple shape whose area you know. Add the strips, and you have a good estimate. That is the heart of numerical integration. Today we learn the most basic and most important version: the trapezoidal rule.

What we are computing: The definite integral of f(x) from a to b is the area under the curve y = f(x) between x = a and x = b, counting area below the x axis as negative. In calculus class you found it with an antiderivative: find F with F' = f, then compute F(b) - F(a). But many functions have no simple antiderivative, for example e^(-x^2). And very often we do not even have a formula, only measured values in a table. In both cases we need a numerical method.

The Newton-Cotes idea: Here is the general plan. Split [a, b] using equally spaced points. Replace f by an interpolating polynomial through those points, the kind we built in lessons 17 and 18. Integrate the polynomial exactly, because polynomials are easy to integrate. The result is a weighted sum of the function values. Using a straight line, degree 1, gives the trapezoidal rule. Using a parabola, degree 2, gives Simpson's 1/3 rule, which is lesson 24. These formulas, which use the end points a and b, are called closed Newton-Cotes formulas.

One trapezoid: Take just the two end points, (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)). Join them with a straight line. The region under that line is a trapezoid, a shape with two parallel vertical sides of heights f(a) and f(b) and width h = b - a. Its area is the average height times the width. So the integral is approximately (h/2)(f(a) + f(b)). That is the single trapezoidal rule. It is exact whenever f itself is a straight line, because then the line we drew is the curve.

Our test integral: We need a case with a known exact answer so we can measure errors. We use the integral of 1/(1 + x^2) from 0 to 1. Its antiderivative is arctan x, so the exact value is arctan 1 - arctan 0 = pi/4, which is 0.785398 to 6 decimals. All numbers in this lesson were computed in Python and rounded to 6 decimals unless we say otherwise. Lesson 24 will use the same integral, so you can compare Simpson's rule with today's results.

Single trapezoid on the test integral: Here f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 1/2 = 0.5, and h = 1. The rule gives (1/2)(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. The exact answer is 0.785398, so the error is about 0.035398, and the estimate is about 4.51 percent too small. Not terrible for a single straight line, but we can do much better by using more points.

Composite trapezoidal rule: Split [a, b] into n equal strips of width h = (b - a)/n. The points are x0 = a, x1, x2 and so on up to xn = b, with values y0, y1, up to yn. Put one trapezoid on each strip and add the areas. Each inside point is shared by two neighbouring trapezoids, so it gets counted twice. The result is: integral approximately (h/2) times (y0 + 2y1 + 2y2 + ... + 2y(n-1) + yn). In words: half the step, times the first plus the last, plus twice everything in the middle.

Worked example with n = 2: Now h = 0.5, and the points are 0, 0.5 and 1. The values are f(0) = 1, f(0.5) = 1/1.25 = 0.8 and f(1) = 0.5. The rule gives (0.5/2)(1 + 2 times 0.8 + 0.5) = 0.25 times 3.1 = 0.775. The error is now about 0.010398. Just one extra point cut the error from 0.035398 to 0.010398.

Worked example with n = 4: Now h = 0.25, and the points are 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1. The values, to 6 decimals, are 1, 0.941176, 0.8, 0.64 and 0.5. The middle ones add to 2.381176, so twice that is 4.762353. Adding the ends gives 1 + 0.5 + 4.762353 = 6.262353. Multiply by h/2 = 0.125 and you get 0.782794. The error is about 0.002604. Notice how neat the table is: list the values, mark the inside ones, double them, add, multiply.

Watching the error shrink: Keep doubling n. With n = 8, the trapezoidal value is 0.784747 and the error is about 0.000651. With n = 16, the value is 0.785235 and the error is about 0.000163. Look at the errors in a row: 0.010398, 0.002604, 0.000651, 0.000163. Each time we halve h, the error is divided by almost exactly 4. Our Python ratios were about 3.99 and 4.00. That is the fingerprint of an O(h^2) method.

The error term: Theory gives a precise formula. For the composite trapezoidal rule, the error, meaning exact value minus estimate, is -(b - a) h^2 f''(c) / 12 for some point c between a and b. Three things to read from it. First, the h^2 explains the factor of 4 when h is halved. Second, if f'' is zero, as for a straight line, the error is zero. Third, the error depends on how curved f is, measured by f''.

Using the error bound: We usually do not know c, but we can bound the error with the biggest value of |f''| on [a, b]. For f(x) = 1/(1 + x^2), the second derivative is (6x^2 - 2)/(1 + x^2)^3, and its largest size on [0, 1] is 2, at x = 0. So with n = 4, the error is at most 1 times 0.25^2 times 2 / 12, which is about 0.010417. The real error, 0.002604, is well inside that bound. Bounds are safe promises, often bigger than the truth.

How many strips do I need? You can turn the bound around. Suppose we want the error below 0.0001 for our test integral. We need (b - a) h^2 max|f''| / 12 below 0.0001, so h^2 times 2 / 12 must be below 0.0001, which means h^2 below 0.0006, so h below about 0.0245. With h = 1/n, that means n of at least 41. Exams love this kind of question: find the number of strips needed for a given accuracy.

Over or under? The sign of f'' tells you more. If the curve bends upward, like x^2, which is called convex, each straight chord lies above the curve, so the trapezoidal rule overestimates. For example, a single trapezoid for the integral of x^2 from 0 to 1 gives 0.5, but the exact answer is 1/3. If the curve bends downward, called concave, the rule underestimates. Our test function bends downward near 0 and upward near 1, and overall the trapezoidal values come out a little too small.

A free error estimate: Since the error drops by about 4 when h is halved, we can estimate the error without knowing the exact answer. The error of T(h/2) is roughly (T(h/2) - T(h)) / 3. With T for n = 4 equal to 0.782794 and T for n = 8 equal to 0.784747, this gives about 0.000651, which matches the real error remarkably well. Using this estimate to correct the answer is the start of Romberg integration, which lesson 24 explains.

The algorithm in code: Writing the rule as a program is short. Set h = (b - a) / n. Set total = (f(a) + f(b)) / 2. Then loop i from 1 to n - 1 and add f(a + i h) to total. At the end, the answer is h times total. Notice we halved the ends instead of doubling the middle, which is the same thing after multiplying by h. The work grows in a straight line with n: doubling n means about twice as many function evaluations. A neat saving: when you go from n to 2n, all the old points are reused, so you only compute the new midpoints.

Sanity checks before you trust an answer: First, the estimate should lie between the smallest and largest value of f times (b - a). For our test integral, f goes from 0.5 to 1 on an interval of length 1, so the answer must lie between 0.5 and 1, and 0.782794 passes. Second, compute with n and with 2n. If the two answers agree to the digits you need, you can usually stop. If they jump around, something is wrong: maybe a typo in a value, or a function with a sharp corner or a spike that needs more strips in that region.

Integrating tabulated data: The trapezoidal rule does not need a formula at all, only values at equally spaced points. That makes it perfect for measurements. And if your points are not equally spaced, you can still add up individual trapezoids, each with its own width, using (width/2)(left value + right value) for each strip. Simpson's rule is pickier: it needs equal spacing and an even number of strips.

Real life example 1, distance from speed: A small electric car in a test drive records its speed every 10 seconds: 0, 3, 5, 6, 6 and 4 metres per second. These are example numbers. Distance is the integral of speed over time. With h = 10, the trapezoidal rule gives (10/2) times (0 + 2 times (3 + 5 + 6 + 6) + 4) = 5 times 44 = 220 metres. No formula for the speed was needed, only the readings. Car trip computers and fitness apps do similar sums with their sensor data.

Real life example 2, the pond: Back to the family pond. Suppose you measure the width across the pond every 2 metres along a straight rope. Each pair of neighbouring widths forms a trapezoid with width 2 metres. Add them with the composite formula, and you have the pond's area. Land surveyors have used strip methods like this for a long time, and engineers use the same idea to estimate the cross section area of a river from depth readings.

Where computers use it: The trapezoidal rule is simple, fast and reliable. It is built into many scientific libraries, for example NumPy in Python has a function called trapezoid (older versions call it trapz). For smooth periodic functions integrated over a full period, the trapezoidal rule is surprisingly accurate, much better than its O(h^2) error suggests. It also appears inside methods for differential equations, which you will see when we study ODEs in lessons 25 and 26.

Common mistakes and exam tips: The most common slip is forgetting to double the inside values, or doubling the end values by mistake. Another is using h = b - a when you meant h = (b - a)/n. Some students count points instead of strips: n strips have n + 1 points. Always write a neat table of x and y first. Typical exam questions: evaluate an integral with the trapezoidal rule for a given n, find the error compared with the exact value, use the error formula to choose n, and compute a distance or area from tabulated data.

Recap: Numerical integration replaces a hard curve with simple shapes. The trapezoidal rule joins neighbouring points with straight lines. The single rule is (h/2)(f(a) + f(b)), and the composite rule is (h/2)(y0 + 2(y1 + ... + y(n-1)) + yn). Its error is -(b - a) h^2 f''(c) / 12, so halving h cuts the error by about 4. For our test integral of 1/(1 + x^2) from 0 to 1, the values 0.75, 0.775, 0.782794 and 0.784747 crept steadily toward pi/4 = 0.785398. Next lesson, Simpson's rule uses parabolas and gets there much faster.
key_points: Numerical integration estimates the area under a curve from function values, useful when there is no antiderivative or only a data table.
Newton-Cotes idea: integrate an interpolating polynomial; a straight line (degree 1) gives the trapezoidal rule.
Single trapezoid: integral about (h/2)(f(a) + f(b)) with h = b - a; exact for straight lines.
Composite rule: (h/2)(y0 + 2(y1 + ... + y(n-1)) + yn) with h = (b - a)/n and n + 1 points.
Error = -(b - a) h^2 f''(c) / 12, so the method is O(h^2): halving h cuts the error by about 4.
Bound the error with max |f''| to choose n; for convex f the rule overestimates, for concave f it underestimates.
lessons.tip: Always draw a small x and y table with three columns: ends, inside points, and their sums. Circle the inside values that get doubled. This one habit removes the most common trapezoidal mistake and makes your working easy for the examiner to follow.
lessons.task: Use the trapezoidal rule with n = 4 to estimate the integral of x^2 from 0 to 2 by hand. Compare it with the exact value 8/3, then repeat with n = 8 and check that the error drops by about 4 times.

quiz.q: What is the composite trapezoidal rule with n strips of width h?
quiz.explain: Each inside point is shared by two trapezoids, so inside values are doubled; the ends are counted once, all times h/2.

quiz.q: For the integral of 1/(1 + x^2) from 0 to 1 with n = 2 (h = 0.5), what does the trapezoidal rule give?
quiz.explain: Values 1, 0.8, 0.5 give 0.25 x (1 + 1.6 + 0.5) = 0.775. The exact value is pi/4, about 0.785398.

quiz.q: If you halve h in the composite trapezoidal rule, the error becomes roughly:
quiz.explain: The error is proportional to h^2, so halving h divides it by about 4, as seen in 0.002604 to 0.000651.

quiz.q: For a convex function such as x^2 (curving upward), the trapezoidal rule:
quiz.explain: Straight chords lie above an upward-curving graph, so the trapezoids contain extra area. For x^2 on [0, 1] one trapezoid gives 0.5 versus the exact 1/3.

quiz.q: Speeds of 0, 3, 5, 6, 6, 4 m/s are recorded every 10 s. What distance does the trapezoidal rule give?

lessons.title: Numerical Integration II: Simpson's Rules, Romberg and Gauss
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to know how much rice is in a big pile on the floor. The trapezoidal rule from the last lesson is like measuring the pile with straight sticks laid from top to top. It works, but a pile of rice is round on top, not made of straight lines. What if you used a bendy ruler that can follow a curve? You would get much closer with the same number of measurements. That bendy ruler is the idea behind Simpson's rules. Instead of joining points with straight lines, we join them with smooth curves called parabolas. In this lesson you will learn Simpson's 1/3 rule, Simpson's 3/8 rule, how big their errors are, a clever trick called Romberg integration, and a sneaky method called Gaussian quadrature that picks its own points.

Quick recap: In lesson 23 we wanted the area under a curve y = f(x) from x = a to x = b, which is the integral of f(x) dx from a to b. We cut the interval into n strips of width h = (b - a)/n, joined the tops with straight lines and added the trapezoids. Our test problem was the integral of 1/(1 + x^2) from 0 to 1. Its exact value is pi/4, which is about 0.785398. With 4 strips the trapezoidal rule gave about 0.782794, an error of about 0.002604. We will use the very same integral today, so you can see the improvement with your own eyes. All numbers in this lesson were computed with a short Python program and rounded to 6 decimal places.

Why a parabola: A straight line needs 2 points. A parabola, y = A + Bx + Cx^2, needs 3 points. Most smooth curves bend, and a parabola can bend too, so it hugs the curve much better than a straight line does. Simpson's idea is simple: take the points in groups of 3, fit a parabola through each group, and find the exact area under each parabola. Finding the area under a parabola is easy, because we can integrate x^2 by hand. When you do that algebra once, a very neat formula pops out, and you never have to fit the parabola again.

Simpson's 1/3 rule for one pair of strips: Take two strips of width h, with points x0, x1 = x0 + h and x2 = x0 + 2h. Call the heights f0, f1 and f2. The area under the parabola through these 3 points is (h/3)(f0 + 4f1 + f2). That is the whole rule. The middle point gets weight 4, the two ends get weight 1, and everything is multiplied by h/3. The name 1/3 comes from that h/3 at the front. Notice the middle point counts four times as much as an end. That makes sense, because the middle height tells us the most about how the curve bends.

Worked example with 2 strips: Let us try it on 1/(1 + x^2) from 0 to 1 with n = 2, so h = 0.5. The heights are f(0) = 1, f(0.5) = 0.8 and f(1) = 0.5. Simpson gives (0.5/3)(1 + 4 x 0.8 + 0.5) = (0.5/3)(4.7) = 0.783333. The exact answer is 0.785398, so the error is about 0.002065. Look at that: with only 3 points, Simpson is already a bit better than the trapezoidal rule was with 5 points (error 0.002604). Same rice pile, fewer measurements, better answer.

Composite Simpson's 1/3 rule: For more accuracy we use more strips, but here is the catch: Simpson works on pairs of strips, so n must be even. With n strips, the formula is (h/3)[f0 + 4(f1 + f3 + f5 + ...) + 2(f2 + f4 + ...) + fn]. The pattern of weights is 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, ..., 4, 1. Odd-numbered points get 4, even-numbered inside points get 2, and the two ends get 1. Why 2 for the even inside points? Because each one is the end of one pair and the start of the next pair, so its weight 1 is counted twice.

Worked example with 4 strips: Now n = 4 and h = 0.25. The heights are f(0) = 1, f(0.25) = 0.941176, f(0.5) = 0.8, f(0.75) = 0.64 and f(1) = 0.5. The bracket is 1 + 4(0.941176 + 0.64) + 2(0.8) + 0.5, which is about 9.424706. Multiply by h/3 = 0.25/3 and you get 0.785392. The error is now only about 0.000006.
