Compare that with the trapezoidal rule using the same 5 points: error 0.002604. Simpson is more than 400 times more accurate here, and it used exactly the same function values. Only the weights changed. That is the magic of a smarter formula.

Simpson's 3/8 rule: What if your number of strips is odd, like 3? Then Simpson's 1/3 rule cannot cover all of them. The 3/8 rule fits a cubic curve through 4 points, which covers 3 strips. The formula is (3h/8)(f0 + 3f1 + 3f2 + f3). For many strips, the number of strips must be a multiple of 3, and the weights go 1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 2, ..., 3, 3, 1. Here, each point that ends a group of 3 strips gets weight 2.

Worked example of the 3/8 rule: Use n = 3, so h = 1/3. The heights are f(0) = 1, f(1/3) = 0.9, f(2/3) = 0.692308 and f(1) = 0.5. The bracket is 1 + 3(0.9) + 3(0.692308) + 0.5 = 6.276923. Multiply by 3h/8 = 1/8 and you get 0.784615. The error is about 0.000783. In practice, if you have an odd number of strips, a common trick is to use the 3/8 rule on three strips and the 1/3 rule on the rest. That way you never have to throw data away.

How big is the error: For one Simpson 1/3 pair, the error is -(h^5/90) f''''(c) for some point c in the interval. Here f'''' means the fourth derivative. For the composite rule over [a, b], the error is -((b - a)/180) h^4 f''''(c). The key part is h^4. So Simpson's error is O(h^4), while the trapezoidal error is O(h^2). For the 3/8 rule the composite error is -((b - a)/80) h^4 f''''(c), so it is also O(h^4), with a slightly bigger constant. Surprise: the 3/8 rule is not more accurate in order than the 1/3 rule, even though it uses a cubic.

What O(h^4) means in practice: If you halve h, the error of an O(h^2) method drops about 4 times, and the error of an O(h^4) method drops about 16 times. Let us check with our integral. Trapezoidal errors: n = 4 gives 0.002604 and n = 8 gives 0.000651. The ratio is about 3.99, almost exactly 4. Simpson errors: n = 4 gives about 0.000006 and n = 8 gives about 0.000000038. That ratio is about 159, even better than the 16 we expected. The rule of 16 is a rough guide for small h, and some functions do even better. The big lesson stays the same: Simpson gains accuracy much faster.

A surprise about cubics: Because Simpson's error contains the fourth derivative, any function whose fourth derivative is zero gives zero error. That includes every cubic, like x^3. Try it: the integral of x^3 from 0 to 2 is exactly 4. Simpson with n = 2 and h = 1 gives (1/3)(0 + 4 x 1 + 8) = 12/3 = 4. Exact! Simpson was built from parabolas, yet it gets cubics exactly right for free. This bonus is why its order is h^4 and not h^3.

Romberg integration idea: Here is a clever trick. Suppose you computed the trapezoidal rule twice: T(h) with step h and T(h/2) with half the step. Since the main error is about C h^2, halving h cuts that error by 4. Combine them: R = T(h/2) + (T(h/2) - T(h))/3, which is the same as (4 T(h/2) - T(h))/3. This removes the h^2 error part. This idea is called Richardson extrapolation (you met it in lesson 22). Using T2 = 0.775 and T4 = 0.782794 we get 0.785392. That is exactly the Simpson n = 4 answer! So Simpson is just one Richardson step on top of the trapezoidal rule.

Building the Romberg table: Romberg integration keeps going. Make a column of trapezoidal values with h, h/2, h/4, h/8. Combine neighbours with the factor 3 to get a second column with error O(h^4). Then combine the second column neighbours with the factor 15, using (16 x better - worse)/15, to remove the h^4 part, and so on, with factors 63 and more. Each new column is more accurate for smooth functions. The beauty is that you only ever evaluate f for the trapezoidal column. Everything else is cheap arithmetic.

Gaussian quadrature idea: All the rules so far use equally spaced points. Gauss asked a cheeky question: what if we are allowed to choose where to measure? With 2 well chosen points and weights, you can integrate every cubic exactly. On the interval [-1, 1], the 2-point Gauss rule is f(-1/sqrt(3)) + f(1/sqrt(3)). That is, measure at about -0.57735 and +0.57735, give each weight 1, and add. For another interval [a, b], you shift and stretch these points and multiply by (b - a)/2.

Gauss worked example: For our integral on [0, 1], the points become 0.5 - 0.5/sqrt(3), about 0.211325, and 0.5 + 0.5/sqrt(3), about 0.788675. The heights are about 0.957251 and 0.616520. Multiply their sum by (b - a)/2 = 0.5 to get 0.786885. The error is about 0.001487. With only 2 function values it beats Simpson with 3 values (error 0.002065). The catch is that you need f at odd points like 0.211325, so Gauss is great when you have a formula, but useless for a table of measured data at fixed points.

Real life example 1, a road in Dhaka: Suppose a city engineer wants the area of a curvy plot of land next to a road. A surveyor walks along the road and measures the width of the plot every 10 meters: 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 meters. These are example numbers, made up for practice: widths 12, 15, 17, 16 and 13 meters. We have 4 strips, an even number, so Simpson's 1/3 rule fits. Area is (10/3)[12 + 4(15 + 16) + 2(17) + 13] = (10/3)(183) = 610 square meters. The trapezoidal rule on the same data gives 10[(12 + 13)/2 + 15 + 17 + 16] = 605 square meters. For a smooth boundary, Simpson's answer is usually the more trustworthy one.

Real life example 2, a bKash style distance from speed: Suppose a delivery bike's speed (example numbers) was read every 1 minute for 6 minutes. Distance is the integral of speed over time. With 6 strips you can use Simpson's 1/3 rule (6 is even) or the 3/8 rule (6 is a multiple of 3), so you can even check one against the other. If both answers are close, you can trust them more. Engineers do exactly this kind of cross check with sensor data, and phones do similar sums with motion data. Since the readings come at fixed times, Gauss quadrature would not help here. Simpson is the right tool.

Common mistakes: The number one mistake is using Simpson's 1/3 rule with an odd number of strips. Always count strips, not points: 5 points means 4 strips. Second, mixing up the weights. Write the pattern 1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 4, 1 above your table before you start. Third, forgetting h/3 at the front, or using 3h/8 with the 1/3 rule. Fourth, thinking the 3/8 rule is a higher order method. Both Simpson rules are O(h^4). Fifth, in Gauss quadrature, forgetting to map the points from [-1, 1] to [a, b] and forgetting the factor (b - a)/2.

What exams ask: A typical question gives a table or a function and asks you to use the trapezoidal rule, Simpson's 1/3 rule and Simpson's 3/8 rule, then compare with the exact value. Another asks you to derive Simpson's rule by integrating a parabola through 3 points. Sometimes they ask which rule can be used for a given number of strips, or why Simpson is exact for cubics. Romberg questions usually ask you to fill in a small table from given trapezoidal values. A Gauss question often asks for the 2-point rule on a simple integral, like the integral of x^2 or e^x.

Recap: Simpson's 1/3 rule joins points with parabolas: (h/3)(f0 + 4f1 + f2) per pair, with an even number of strips. The 3/8 rule uses cubics: (3h/8)(f0 + 3f1 + 3f2 + f3), with strips in groups of 3. Both have error O(h^4), much better than the trapezoidal O(h^2). On our test integral, 4 strips gave error 0.002604 for trapezoidal and about 0.000006 for Simpson. Romberg integration combines trapezoidal values to cancel errors, and its first step gives Simpson. Gaussian quadrature chooses clever points, so 2 points integrate cubics exactly. Next lesson we leave areas behind and start solving differential equations, where these same ideas of steps and error orders come back.
key_points: Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas through 3 points: (h/3)(f0 + 4f1 + f2) for each pair of strips.
Composite Simpson's 1/3 needs an even number of strips; weights go 1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 4, 1.
Simpson's 3/8 rule: (3h/8)(f0 + 3f1 + 3f2 + f3); the number of strips must be a multiple of 3.
Both Simpson rules have error O(h^4), versus O(h^2) for the trapezoidal rule, and both are exact for cubics.
Integral of 1/(1 + x^2) from 0 to 1 with 4 strips: trapezoidal error 0.002604, Simpson error about 0.000006.
Romberg integration combines trapezoidal values, (4 T(h/2) - T(h))/3, and its first step equals Simpson's rule.
2-point Gauss quadrature on [-1, 1] uses points -1/sqrt(3) and 1/sqrt(3) with weight 1 and is exact for cubics.
lessons.tip: Before any Simpson question, count the strips first and write the weight pattern above your table. Most lost marks come from an odd number of strips or a wrong weight, not from hard math.
lessons.task: On paper or a calculator, find the integral of e^x from 0 to 1 using the trapezoidal rule and Simpson's 1/3 rule, both with 4 strips. Compare both with the exact value e - 1 and work out how many times smaller Simpson's error is.

quiz.q: Which number of strips can be used directly with composite Simpson's 1/3 rule?
quiz.explain: Simpson's 1/3 rule works on pairs of strips, so the number of strips must be even. 6 is the only even choice.

quiz.q: What is the order of the error of composite Simpson's 1/3 rule?
quiz.explain: The composite error is -((b - a)/180) h^4 f''''(c), so it is O(h^4).

quiz.q: Simpson's 1/3 rule with n = 2 on the integral of x^3 from 0 to 2 gives what?
quiz.explain: (1/3)(0 + 4 x 1 + 8) = 4, which is exact, because Simpson's error depends on the fourth derivative and that is zero for a cubic.

quiz.q: In Romberg integration, (4 T(h/2) - T(h))/3 built from trapezoidal values gives the same result as which rule?
quiz.explain: One Richardson step removes the h^2 error of the trapezoidal rule. With T2 = 0.775 and T4 = 0.782794 it gives 0.785392, the Simpson n = 4 value.

quiz.q: Why is 2-point Gauss quadrature not useful for a table of measurements taken every 1 minute?
options: It needs an even number of strips
It only works for straight lines
It needs f at special points that are not in the table
It is less accurate than the trapezoidal rule
quiz.explain: Gauss picks its own points, like 0.211325 and 0.788675 on [0, 1]. A fixed table usually has no values at those points.

lessons.title: ODEs I: Euler, Taylor and Heun Methods
lessons.content:
Imagine you are lost in a dark field at night, but you have a magic compass. Wherever you stand, the compass tells you which direction to walk right now. It does not show you the whole path, only the next direction. What do you do? You take a small step in that direction, look at the compass again, take another small step, and so on. Step by step, you trace out a path. That is exactly how computers solve differential equations. The equation is the magic compass, and Euler's method is the small steps. In this lesson we will learn what an initial value problem is, how to picture it with a direction field, Euler's method, local and global error, the Taylor series method, and a smarter version called Heun's method.

What is a differential equation: A differential equation is an equation that contains a derivative. For example, y' = x + y. Here y' means dy/dx, the slope of the curve y(x). The equation does not tell you y directly. It tells you the slope at every point (x, y). If you stand at x = 0, y = 1, the slope is 0 + 1 = 1. If you stand at x = 1, y = 2, the slope is 1 + 2 = 3. We call it an ordinary differential equation, or ODE, because there is only one input variable, x. Many things in nature are described this way: how fast tea cools, how money grows, how a ball falls.

Initial value problem: An ODE alone has many solutions, like many paths in the field. To pick one, we need a starting point. An initial value problem, or IVP, is an ODE plus a starting value, like y' = x + y with y(0) = 1. That means: start at x = 0 with y = 1, and follow the slopes. Our goal is to find y at later points, like x = 0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.5. In this lesson and the next, we will use this same IVP all the time, so we can compare methods fairly.

Our exact answer for checking: This particular IVP can be solved by hand, and its exact solution is y = 2e^x - x - 1. Let us check it. The derivative is y' = 2e^x - 1. And x + y = x + 2e^x - x - 1 = 2e^x - 1. They match. At x = 0, y = 2 - 0 - 1 = 1, which matches the starting value. So we know the true answers, for example y(0.1) is about 1.110342 and y(0.5) is about 1.797443. Most real ODEs cannot be solved by hand, which is the whole reason we need numerical methods. Here we use an easy one so we can measure the errors. All numbers in this lesson come from a small Python program and are rounded to 6 decimal places.

Direction field: A direction field is a picture of the compass. At many grid points (x, y), you draw a tiny line segment with slope f(x, y). For y' = x + y, at (0, 0) the slope is 0, so a flat segment. At (0, 1) the slope is 1, a 45 degree segment. Along the line x + y = 0 all slopes are zero. Fun fact: the straight line y = -x - 1 is itself a solution, because its slope is -1 and x + y = -1 too. Once you draw the field, solution curves are like streams flowing along the little segments. Each starting point gives a different stream.

Euler's method: Euler's idea is the compass walk. Start at (x0, y0). Find the slope f(x0, y0). Walk a small step h along that slope. The formula is y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)), and x(n+1) = x(n) + h. Then repeat from the new point. You are pretending that the slope stays the same for the whole step, which is not quite true, but it is close if h is small. You can also see it from Taylor series: y(x + h) = y(x) + h y'(x) + (h^2/2) y''(x) + ..., and Euler just keeps the first two terms.

Euler worked example: Let us solve y' = x + y, y(0) = 1 with h = 0.1. Step 1: slope at (0, 1) is 1, so y1 = 1 + 0.1 x 1 = 1.1. Step 2: slope at (0.1, 1.1) is 1.2, so y2 = 1.1 + 0.12 = 1.22. Step 3: slope at (0.2, 1.22) is 1.42, so y3 = 1.362. Step 4: slope at (0.3, 1.362) is 1.662, so y4 = 1.5282. Step 5: slope at (0.4, 1.5282) is 1.9282, so y5 = 1.72102. So Euler says y(0.5) is about 1.72102. The exact value is 1.797443, so the error is about 0.076423. Not great, but the method is so simple you could do it on a rickshaw ride.

Why Euler falls behind: Look at the answers: Euler is always below the true curve here. The true solution curves upward, so its slope keeps getting bigger during each step. Euler uses the slope from the start of the step, which is the smallest slope in that step. So each step falls a little short, and the shortfalls pile up. If the curve bent the other way, Euler would overshoot instead. The bending, measured by y'', is what Euler ignores.

Local error and global error: There are two kinds of error. The local error is the error made in one single step, assuming you started that step from the exact value. From the Taylor series, the first term Euler drops is (h^2/2) y'', so the local error is O(h^2). In our first step, the local error is 1.110342 - 1.1 = 0.010342. The global error is the total error at the end, after all the steps. To reach x = 0.5 with step h you need 0.5/h steps. Many steps times O(h^2) each gives roughly O(h) in total. So Euler is called a first order method: global error O(h).

Checking the order: Let us test it. With h = 0.1, Euler's error at x = 0.5 is 0.076423. With h = 0.05 (10 steps), Euler gives 1.757789, and the error is 0.039653. Halving h roughly halves the error, the ratio is about 1.93. That is what first order means. The bad news: to get one more correct decimal place, you need about 10 times more steps. That is slow, like walking from Uttara to Motijheel in tiny baby steps.

Taylor series method: If Euler drops the y'' term, why not keep it? The Taylor method of order 2 uses y(n+1) = y(n) + h y' + (h^2/2) y''. We need y'', and we get it by differentiating the ODE. For y' = x + y, the derivative is y'' = 1 + y' = 1 + x + y. Step 1 from (0, 1): y' = 1, y'' = 2, so y1 = 1 + 0.1 x 1 + 0.005 x 2 = 1.11. The exact value is 1.110342, so the error after one step is only 0.000342, about 30 times smaller than Euler's 0.010342. Step 2: at (0.1, 1.11), y' = 1.21 and y'' = 2.21, so y2 = 1.11 + 0.121 + 0.01105 = 1.24205.

Higher order Taylor and its problem: You can keep more terms. For our ODE, y''' = y'' = 1 + x + y, so higher derivatives are easy. The order 4 Taylor step from (0, 1) gives 1.110342 (rounded to 6 decimals), matching the exact value to 6 decimals. The local error of an order p Taylor method is O(h^(p+1)) and the global error is O(h^p). So why not always use Taylor? Because for most real ODEs, finding y'', y''' and y'''' by hand is a nightmare. The formulas get long and messy. We want the accuracy of Taylor without the derivative pain. That is what Heun now, and Runge-Kutta next lesson, give us.

Modified Euler, or Heun's method: Heun's trick is simple. Euler only uses the slope at the start of the step. Heun says: first take a test Euler step to guess where you will land. Then find the slope there too. Then use the average of the two slopes for the real step. In formulas: predictor p = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)). Corrector y(n+1) = y(n) + (h/2)[f(x(n), y(n)) + f(x(n+1), p)]. Because it first predicts and then corrects, it is called a predictor-corrector method. It needs 2 slope evaluations per step instead of 1.

Heun worked example: Same IVP, h = 0.1. Step 1: slope at the start is 1. Predictor p = 1 + 0.1 x 1 = 1.1. Slope at (0.1, 1.1) is 1.2. Average slope is (1 + 1.2)/2 = 1.1, so y1 = 1 + 0.1 x 1.1 = 1.11. Step 2: start slope at (0.1, 1.11) is 1.21. Predictor p = 1.231, slope at (0.2, 1.231) is 1.431. So y2 = 1.11 + 0.05(1.21 + 1.431) = 1.24205. Carry on and you get y3 = 1.398465, y4 = 1.581804 and y5 = 1.794894. The error at x = 0.5 is about 0.002549, about 30 times smaller than Euler's 0.076423.

Heun's order: Heun's global error is O(h^2), so it is a second order method. Check: with h = 0.05, Heun gives y(0.5) of about 1.796781, error 0.000662. The ratio of errors is about 3.85, close to 4, just as O(h^2) predicts when h is halved. A cute surprise: for our ODE, Heun and the order 2 Taylor method give exactly the same numbers. That happens because y' = x + y is a very simple linear equation. For most other ODEs they give different, but similarly accurate, answers. The win is that Heun needs no derivatives of f at all.

Real life example 1, cooling cha: Newton's law of cooling says T' = -k(T - Troom). A cup of cha at 90 degrees sits in a room at 30 degrees. Let us say k = 0.1 per minute (example numbers). With Euler and h = 1 minute: T1 = 90 - 0.1(60) = 84, T2 = 84 - 0.1(54) = 78.6, T3 = 73.74. The exact formula is T = 30 + 60e^(-0.1t), which gives 84.29, 79.124 and 74.449. Euler is close but a bit too low, because it uses the fastest cooling rate, the one at the start of each minute. A smaller step or Heun would do better.

Real life example 2, money growth: Suppose savings grow continuously at 5 percent per year, y' = 0.05y, starting from 1000 taka (example numbers). Euler with h = 1 year gives 1050 after year 1 and 1102.5 after year 2. Fun fact: that is exactly yearly compound interest! The exact continuous answer is 1000e^(0.1), about 1105.17 taka after 2 years. So Euler with a big step is like counting interest once a year, and making h smaller is like counting interest more and more often. Banks, phone apps and engineers all use this kind of step by step growth.

Common mistakes: First, using the slope at the wrong point. In Euler, always use f at the start of the step. Second, forgetting to update x. The slope f(x, y) depends on x too, so x must go 0, 0.1, 0.2, and so on. Third, in Heun, forgetting that the second slope uses x(n+1) and the predicted value p, not y(n). Fourth, mixing up local error O(h^2) with global error O(h) for Euler. Fifth, making h too big. A big step can make the answer very wrong, and for some equations even blow up, as we will see in the next lesson.

What exams ask: A classic question gives an IVP and asks for y at a few points using Euler with a given h, often then using modified Euler for the same steps, and comparing with the exact solution. Another asks you to derive Euler from Taylor series, or explain why its global error is O(h). Taylor method questions ask you to find y'' and y''' from the ODE and do one or two steps. Show a neat table with columns n, x, y, slope, and you will rarely lose marks.

Recap: An initial value problem is an ODE y' = f(x, y) plus a starting value. Euler's method steps along the starting slope: y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)), with local error O(h^2) and global error O(h). The Taylor method keeps more terms, so it is more accurate but needs messy derivatives. Heun's method predicts with Euler, then averages two slopes, giving global error O(h^2) without any derivatives. On y' = x + y, y(0) = 1 with h = 0.1, the error at x = 0.5 was 0.076423 for Euler and 0.002549 for Heun. Next lesson: Runge-Kutta methods, which go even further, and a wrap-up of the whole course.
key_points: An initial value problem is an ODE y' = f(x, y) plus a starting value, like y' = x + y, y(0) = 1.
A direction field draws the slope f(x, y) at many points; solution curves follow those slopes.
Euler's method: y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)), using the slope at the start of each step.
Euler has local error O(h^2) and global error O(h), so it is a first order method.
On y' = x + y, y(0) = 1 with h = 0.1, Euler gives y(0.5) = 1.72102 vs exact 1.797443, error 0.076423.
The Taylor method keeps more terms like (h^2/2) y'', which is accurate but needs derivatives of the ODE.
Heun (modified Euler) predicts with Euler, then averages two slopes; global error O(h^2), error 0.002549 at x = 0.5.
lessons.tip: Always solve ODE questions in a table with columns n, x, y and slope. Writing the slope down before you update y stops most mistakes and makes your work easy for the examiner to follow.
lessons.task: Solve y' = y, y(0) = 1 up to x = 0.4 with Euler using h = 0.1 on paper. Then do the same with Heun's method. Compare both with the exact value e^0.4, about 1.491825, and see which is closer.

quiz.q: What does Euler's method use to take one step?
options: The average of all slopes so far
The slope at the start of the step
The slope at the end of the step only
quiz.explain: Euler uses y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)), the slope at the start of the step.

quiz.q: For y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1, what is the first Euler value y1?
quiz.explain: The slope at (0, 1) is 0 + 1 = 1, so y1 = 1 + 0.1 x 1 = 1.1.

quiz.q: What is the global error order of Euler's method?
quiz.explain: Each step has local error O(h^2), and about 1/h steps add up to a global error of O(h). Halving h from 0.1 to 0.05 cut the error from 0.076423 to 0.039653.

quiz.q: In Heun's method, where is the second slope computed?
options: At the midpoint with the exact value
At x(n+1) with the predicted value p
quiz.explain: Heun first predicts p = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)), then uses f(x(n+1), p) as the second slope and averages it with the first.

quiz.q: Why is the Taylor series method hard to use for most real ODEs?
options: It only works for linear equations
It needs higher derivatives of the ODE, which get messy
It is less accurate than Euler
It cannot use a step size
quiz.explain: To keep terms like (h^2/2) y'' you must differentiate the ODE by hand, and for most real equations those formulas become long and messy.

lessons.title: ODEs II: Runge-Kutta Methods and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
Think about how you cross a busy Dhaka road. You do not just look once at the start and walk blindly. You look right, take a step, look left, check the middle, glance again, and only then decide your real move. You collect a few looks and combine them. Euler only looks once per step. Heun looks twice. The Runge-Kutta methods, named after two German mathematicians, Carl Runge and Martin Kutta, look several times inside each step and mix the looks in a clever way. The most famous one, RK4, looks four times and is so accurate that it is the everyday workhorse for solving ODEs. In this lesson we learn RK2 and RK4, see how accuracy changes with step size, solve systems and higher order ODEs, meet predictor-corrector and stiffness ideas, and then look back at the whole course.

Quick recap: In lesson 25 we solved the initial value problem y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, whose exact solution is y = 2e^x - x - 1. Euler with h = 0.1 gave y(0.5) = 1.72102, an error of about 0.076423. Heun gave 1.794894, an error of about 0.002549. We will keep this same problem, so every method is tested on the same road. All numbers in this lesson come from a small Python program and are rounded to 6 decimal places unless I say otherwise.

The Runge-Kutta idea: A Runge-Kutta method takes one step from x(n) to x(n+1) by computing a few trial slopes, called k1, k2 and so on, at clever points inside the step. Then it uses a weighted average of these slopes to make the real step. No derivatives of f are needed, only values of f. The weights and points are chosen so that the result matches the Taylor series up to some power of h. That is how Runge-Kutta gets Taylor accuracy without the derivative pain we saw last lesson.

RK2, the second order family: There are several second order Runge-Kutta methods. Heun's method from lesson 25 is one of them: k1 = f(x, y), k2 = f(x + h, y + h k1), and y(n+1) = y + (h/2)(k1 + k2). Another is the midpoint method: k1 = f(x, y), k2 = f(x + h/2, y + (h/2) k1), and y(n+1) = y + h k2. The midpoint method walks half a step with Euler, checks the slope there, and then uses that middle slope for the whole step. Both have local error O(h^3) and global error O(h^2).

Midpoint worked step: On y' = x + y from (0, 1) with h = 0.1: k1 = 0 + 1 = 1. The half step point is x = 0.05, y = 1 + 0.05 x 1 = 1.05, so k2 = 0.05 + 1.05 = 1.1. Then y1 = 1 + 0.1 x 1.1 = 1.11. That is the same as Heun's first step. For our simple linear ODE all RK2 methods give the same numbers, but for most other ODEs they differ slightly, while sharing the same order.

Classical RK4: This is the star. For one step from (x, y) with step h, compute four slopes. k1 = f(x, y), the slope at the start. k2 = f(x + h/2, y + (h/2) k1), a slope at the middle using k1. k3 = f(x + h/2, y + (h/2) k2), another middle slope using k2. k4 = f(x + h, y + h k3), a slope at the end using k3. Then y(n+1) = y + (h/6)(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4). The middle slopes get weight 2 and the ends get weight 1, so the weights are 1, 2, 2, 1, adding up to 6. Do they remind you of something? When f depends only on x, RK4 becomes exactly Simpson's 1/3 rule from lesson 24!

RK4 worked step: Let us do one step on y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1. k1 = f(0, 1) = 1. k2 = f(0.05, 1 + 0.05 x 1) = f(0.05, 1.05) = 1.1. k3 = f(0.05, 1 + 0.05 x 1.1) = f(0.05, 1.055) = 1.105. k4 = f(0.1, 1 + 0.1 x 1.105) = f(0.1, 1.1105) = 1.2105. The weighted sum is 1 + 2(1.1) + 2(1.105) + 1.2105 = 6.6205. So y1 = 1 + (0.1/6)(6.6205) = 1.110342. The exact value is 1.110342 too. The difference is only about 0.00000017. One step, four slopes, six correct decimals.

RK4 over several steps: Keep going with h = 0.1 and RK4 gives y(0.5) = 1.797441, against the exact 1.797443. The error is about 0.0000013. Compare: Euler's error was 0.076423 and Heun's was 0.002549 at the same point with the same h. RK4 is about 2000 times more accurate than Heun here. RK4 has local error O(h^5) and global error O(h^4), so it is a fourth order method.

Accuracy vs step size: Let us go to x = 1, where the exact value is 3.436564. With h = 0.2, RK4 gives 3.436502, error about 0.000061. With h = 0.1, it gives 3.436559, error about 0.0000042. The ratio of errors is about 14.7, close to the 16 that fourth order predicts when you halve h. With h = 0.05, the error is about 0.00000027. Meanwhile at x = 1 with h = 0.1, Euler's error is about 0.249079 and Heun's is about 0.008402. The higher the order, the faster the error melts when you shrink h.

Fair comparison by work: RK4 needs 4 slope evaluations per step, Heun needs 2, Euler needs 1. Is RK4 only winning because it works harder? Let us give everyone the same budget of 20 slope evaluations to reach x = 1. Euler can afford h = 0.05 (20 steps): error about 0.129968. Heun can afford h = 0.1 (10 steps): error about 0.008402. RK4 can afford h = 0.2 (5 steps): error about 0.000061. Same work, and RK4 is still more than 100 times better than Heun. That is why RK4 is the default choice in so many programs.

Choosing the step size: Smaller h means smaller truncation error but more steps and more round-off (remember lesson 4). A smart trick is to solve with h and with h/2 and compare. If the answers agree to the decimals you need, you are done. Real software goes further with adaptive step size: it estimates the error at each step and makes h smaller where the solution changes fast and bigger where it is calm. You can think of it like a rickshaw driver who slows down in a busy bazar and speeds up on an empty road.

Systems of ODEs: Many problems have several unknowns that change together, like the number of rabbits and foxes in a forest, or the position and speed of a ball. We write them as a vector, Y' = F(x, Y), and apply exactly the same methods to every component at once. With RK4, each k becomes a small vector. The important rule is to finish computing k1 for all components before starting k2, and so on.

Higher order ODEs: What about y'' = -y, the equation of a swing or a spring? The trick is to turn it into a system of first order ODEs. Let u = y and v = y'. Then u' = v and v' = -u. Start with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 1, whose exact solution is y = sin x. Euler with h = 0.1: u1 = 0 + 0.1 x 1 = 0.1, v1 = 1 + 0.1 x 0 = 1. Next, u2 = 0.1 + 0.1 x 1 = 0.2, v2 = 1 - 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.99. The exact values are sin(0.2) = 0.198669 and cos(0.2) = 0.980067. Any order n equation becomes n first order equations this way.

Predictor-corrector multistep methods (idea): RK methods forget the past after each step. Multistep methods reuse earlier points. For example, the Adams-Bashforth formulas predict the next y from slopes at several previous points, and the Adams-Moulton formulas then correct it using the slope at the new point. Milne's method is another classic pair. They need fewer new slope evaluations per step than RK4, but they need several starting values, which are usually computed with RK4 first. In exams you may be asked to name them or explain the predict then correct idea.

Stiffness (idea): Some ODEs have parts that change extremely fast. Try y' = -50y, y(0) = 1, whose true solution e^(-50x) quickly drops toward 0. Euler with h = 0.05 multiplies y by (1 - 50 x 0.05) = -1.5 every step, giving -1.5, 2.25, -3.375, 5.0625. It explodes, while the true value is about 0.082085 after one step and gets smaller. With h = 0.01 the factor is 0.5, giving 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, which at least shrinks. For Euler on this equation you need h below 2/50 = 0.04 just to stay stable. Equations that force tiny steps like this are called stiff. Special implicit methods, such as backward Euler, handle them well.

Real life example 1, a cricket ball: To predict where a ball lands, engineers use Newton's law, which gives a second order ODE for position, with air drag making it hard to solve by hand. Split it into position and speed, and RK4 can step it forward in tiny time slices. Ball tracking systems in broadcasts predict paths using physics models and measured data. The exact methods they use are not public in detail, but step by step ODE solving is the classic textbook tool for this kind of path prediction.

Real life example 2, a spreading rumour in a school (example numbers): Suppose y is the fraction of students who heard a rumour, and y' = 0.5 y(1 - y): it spreads fast when some have heard and many have not. Starting from y(0) = 0.02, you can run RK4 day by day on a phone calculator to see when half the school knows. Disease models, population models and chemical reactions all use systems like this, and RK4 or its adaptive cousins are typical solvers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In RK4, a classic slip is using k1 instead of k2 inside k3, or forgetting the halves in x + h/2 and (h/2) k. Another is dividing by 6 at the wrong place. Write k1 to k4 in a neat column. Exams usually ask for one or two RK4 steps, the RK4 formula, converting y'' into a system, or comparing Euler, Heun and RK4 by order. Know the orders by heart: Euler 1, Heun 2, RK4 4.

Course recap, part 1: Let us look back at the whole journey. We started with what numerical methods are and why we accept approximate answers. Lessons on errors taught absolute, relative and truncation errors, error propagation and conditioning, and floating point taught us why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 inside a computer. Then root finding: bisection, false position, Newton-Raphson, secant and fixed-point iteration, plus Horner's method and Newton for systems. Next came linear systems: Gauss elimination, pivoting and Gauss-Jordan, LU decomposition, and the iterative Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel methods.

Course recap, part 2: In the second half we built finite difference tables, used Newton forward and backward interpolation, divided differences and Lagrange interpolation, and learned about interpolation error, Runge's warning and splines. We fitted lines and curves with least squares. Then calculus with numbers: numerical differentiation, the trapezoidal rule, Simpson's rules, Romberg and Gauss quadrature. And finally ODEs: Euler, Taylor, Heun and Runge-Kutta. One idea ran through everything: replace a hard exact problem with simple steps, and always measure the error.

What next: From here you can study numerical linear algebra (eigenvalues, the power method, QR), partial differential equations with finite differences, optimization, and scientific computing with Python libraries like NumPy and SciPy, whose ODE solvers include Runge-Kutta methods. These tools power weather forecasts, game physics, engineering design and machine learning. Every time you see a computer solve a big math problem, there are lessons from this course working quietly inside.

Recap: Runge-Kutta methods mix several slopes inside each step. RK2 (Heun or midpoint) is second order. Classical RK4 uses k1 to k4 with weights 1, 2, 2, 1 over 6 and is fourth order: local error O(h^5), global O(h^4). On y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, one RK4 step with h = 0.1 gave 1.110342, and at x = 1 the error was about 0.0000042 versus 0.249079 for Euler. Higher order ODEs become systems, multistep predictor-corrector methods reuse past points, and stiff equations need special care. Congratulations, you have finished Numerical Methods!
key_points: Runge-Kutta methods combine several trial slopes inside each step and need no derivatives of f.
RK2 methods (Heun, midpoint) have global error O(h^2); midpoint uses the slope at x + h/2.
RK4 has local error O(h^5) and global error O(h^4); one step on y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1 gives 1.110342.
With the same 20 slope evaluations to x = 1: Euler error about 0.129968, Heun 0.008402, RK4 0.000061.
A higher order ODE like y'' = -y becomes a first order system: u' = v, v' = -u.
Stiff equations like y' = -50y force tiny steps for explicit methods (Euler needs h < 0.04); implicit methods handle them.
Course map: errors, roots, linear systems, interpolation, curve fitting, differentiation, integration and ODEs.
lessons.tip: Memorize RK4 as a story: slope at the start, two slopes at the middle, one at the end, weights 1, 2, 2, 1 over 6. If you can tell the story, you can rebuild the formula in any exam.
lessons.task: On paper, do one RK4 step for y' = y, y(0) = 1 with h = 0.1. Write k1 to k4 in a column, then compare your y1 with the exact e^0.1, about 1.105171. Then do the same step with Euler and see the difference.

quiz.q: What are the weights of k1, k2, k3 and k4 in classical RK4 (before dividing by 6)?
quiz.explain: y(n+1) = y + (h/6)(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4), so the weights are 1, 2, 2, 1, adding up to 6.

quiz.q: What is the global error order of classical RK4?
quiz.explain: RK4 has local error O(h^5) per step and global error O(h^4). Halving h from 0.2 to 0.1 cut the error at x = 1 by about 14.7, close to 16.

quiz.q: For y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1, what is k2 in the first RK4 step?
How do we solve a second order ODE like y'' = -y with Euler or RK4?
options: Rewrite it as two first order ODEs, u' = v and v' = -u
Integrate it twice with Simpson's rule
quiz.explain: Set u = y and v = y'. Then u' = v and v' = -u, a first order system that any of these methods can step forward.

quiz.q: Euler on y' = -50y with h = 0.05 gives -1.5, 2.25, -3.375. What is this behaviour called?
options: Instability caused by a stiff equation
quiz.explain: The factor 1 - 50h = -1.5 has size above 1, so the values grow and flip sign. Stiff equations force very small steps (here h < 0.04) on explicit methods.

lessons.title: What Theory of Computation Is
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing in front of a bKash agent's shop with a tiny robot friend. The robot can only do very simple things: read one symbol, remember a little, and move on. Now you ask it a question: can you check whether this PIN is valid? Can you check whether these brackets are balanced? Can you tell me whether this program will ever stop running? Some of these questions the robot can answer easily, some need a bigger robot, and one of them no robot in the universe can ever answer. Theory of Computation is the subject that sorts questions into these boxes, and it proves why each question lands in its box.

What the subject is: Theory of Computation is the mathematical study of what computers can do, how efficiently they can do it, and what they can never do at all. It does not care whether your laptop is a Mac or a Walton, or whether the code is in Python or C. It strips the computer down to a clean mathematical model, a small set of rules, and then asks precise questions about that model. Because the model is exact, the answers are exact too. They are not guesses based on testing, they are proofs that hold for every machine that follows the same rules.

The three big questions: The subject is traditionally split into three areas, and each one answers a different question. Automata theory asks: what can be computed by machines with limited memory? Computability theory asks: what can be computed at all, by any machine, given unlimited time and memory? Complexity theory asks: of the things that can be computed, which can be computed quickly, and which seem to need an enormous amount of time? You can think of them as three nested questions. First, is it possible with a tiny machine? If not, is it possible with any machine? And if it is possible, is it practical?

Automata theory: An automaton (plural automata) is an abstract machine that reads input one symbol at a time and changes its internal state according to fixed rules. The simplest kind, the finite automaton, has only a fixed, finite number of states and no other memory. It sounds weak, but it is exactly what you need for searching text, checking the format of an email address, designing digital circuits, and the first stage of a compiler, the lexer, which chops source code into tokens. Later we add a stack to get a pushdown automaton, which can handle nested structures like brackets and the grammar of programming languages.

Computability theory: Here the model is the Turing machine, introduced by Alan Turing in 1936. It has a finite control like an automaton but also an unlimited tape it can read and write. Surprisingly, this simple machine can do everything any real computer can do, given enough time. The Church-Turing thesis says that any procedure we would intuitively call an algorithm can be carried out by a Turing machine. With this model in hand, we can prove that some problems are undecidable: no algorithm solves them for every input. The most famous is the halting problem: given a program and an input, will the program eventually stop? No program can answer that correctly for all cases.

Complexity theory: Some problems are solvable in principle but would take longer than the age of the universe for big inputs. Complexity theory measures the time and memory a problem needs as the input grows, using the big-O notation you met in Algorithms. It defines classes such as P, the problems solvable in polynomial time, and NP, the problems whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time. Whether P equals NP is one of the most famous open questions in all of mathematics. Your bank security depends on certain problems being hard.

Why use a model at all: Real computers are messy. They have caches, operating systems, network cards and limited RAM. If we tried to prove things about a real machine, the proof would break the moment a new chip came out. A model is like a map of Dhaka that shows only the roads and ignores the colour of every building. By ignoring details that do not matter, a model lets us reason clearly. And the good news is that the models are robust: many different-looking models turn out to have the same power, which tells us we have captured something real about computation, not an accident of design.

A ladder of machines: The course climbs a ladder of machines, each one more powerful than the last. At the bottom is the finite automaton, which recognises the regular languages. Next is the pushdown automaton, which recognises the context-free languages. Higher still is the linear bounded automaton for context-sensitive languages, and at the top is the Turing machine, which recognises the recursively enumerable languages. Each step up adds memory. This ladder, matched with four types of grammars, is called the Chomsky hierarchy, after the linguist Noam Chomsky, and we will meet it properly near the end of the course.

Problems as languages: A key trick of the subject is to turn every yes or no question into a language, which is just a set of strings. The question is the number divisible by 3 becomes the set of all binary strings whose value is divisible by 3. The question is this a valid email address becomes the set of all valid email strings. Then the question for a machine is always the same: given a string, is it in the language or not? This one uniform format lets us compare totally different problems using the same tools. Lesson 2 builds this language vocabulary carefully.

Course map: Here is the road ahead. Lessons 2 to 11 cover the bottom of the ladder: strings and languages, DFA, NFA, epsilon moves, converting NFA to DFA, minimising DFA, regular expressions, their equivalence with automata, and the pumping lemma that proves some languages are not regular. Lessons 12 to 19 move up to context-free grammars, parse trees, normal forms, pushdown automata and the pumping lemma for context-free languages. Lessons 20 to 24 cover Turing machines, decidability, the halting problem, reductions and the Chomsky hierarchy. Lesson 25 finishes with P, NP and NP-completeness. Parsing algorithms such as LL and LR are left for Compiler Design.

Math recap, sets: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, like A = {1, 2, 3}. Order and repetition do not matter, so {3, 1, 2, 2} is the same set. You need union (everything in A or B), intersection (everything in both), difference A minus B, complement (everything not in A, relative to some universe), and the empty set, written as a circle with a slash. The power set of A is the set of all subsets of A. If A has 3 elements, its power set has 2 to the power 3, which is 8 elements, including the empty set and A itself. Power sets appear when we study NFAs and the subset construction.

Math recap, ordered pairs and functions: A Cartesian product A times B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a from A and b from B. If A has 3 elements and B has 2, the product has 6 pairs. A function f from A to B assigns exactly one output in B to every input in A. This matters a lot: the heart of a deterministic machine is its transition function, which takes a pair (current state, input symbol) and returns exactly one next state. Exactly one output for every input is precisely what deterministic means. A relation, in contrast, may link an input to zero or many outputs, which is the flavour of nondeterminism.

Math recap, graphs: A directed graph has nodes and arrows between them. Automata are almost always drawn as directed graphs: each state is a circle, each transition is an arrow labelled with a symbol, the start state has an incoming arrow from nowhere, and accepting states are drawn with a double circle. When you trace a machine on an input, you are simply walking along a path in this graph, one arrow per symbol. Ideas like reachability, which nodes can be reached from the start, come straight from graph theory and are used to clean up machines.

Proof by induction: Many results in this course are proved by induction on the length of a string. The pattern is the same as in Discrete Math. Prove the claim for the base case, often the empty string or length 0. Then assume it holds for length n and prove it for length n plus 1. Small example: the number of binary strings of length n is 2 to the power n. Base case: length 0 has exactly one string, the empty string, and 2 to the power 0 is 1. Step: every string of length n plus 1 is a string of length n followed by either 0 or 1, so the count doubles, from 2 to the power n to 2 to the power n plus 1. Done.

Proof by contradiction: Here you assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show that it leads to something impossible. The classic example is that the square root of 2 is irrational. Suppose it equals a over b in lowest terms. Then a squared equals 2 b squared, so a is even, say a = 2k. Then 4 k squared equals 2 b squared, so b squared is 2 k squared and b is even too. Both even contradicts lowest terms. In this course, contradiction is the engine behind the pumping lemma (assume a language is regular, reach a contradiction) and behind the halting problem (assume a halting decider exists, build a machine that breaks it).

Other proof tools: Two more tools will show up again and again. The pigeonhole principle says that if you put more than k pigeons into k holes, some hole gets at least two. A DFA with 5 states that reads 6 symbols must visit some state twice, and that simple fact powers the pumping lemma. Proof by construction means you prove something exists by actually building it, for example proving the union of two regular languages is regular by building a machine for it. Diagonalization, Cantor's trick for showing that some infinite sets are bigger than others, will appear in the decidability lessons.

Real-life example 1, the lift in a Dhaka apartment: Think of the lift in a ten-storey building in Mirpur. At any moment it is in one of a fixed set of situations: stopped at floor 3 with doors open, moving up, moving down, doors closing, and so on. Pressing a button is an input. The controller looks at its current state and the input and moves to exactly one next state. It needs no big memory, only its current state. That is a finite automaton in real life, and engineers really design lift and traffic-light controllers this way, as state machines.

Real-life example 2, checking a phone number on a form: When you fill in a Daraz or Pathao signup form and type a Bangladeshi mobile number, the app checks that it starts with 01, has the right operator digit, and has 11 digits in total. This check reads the number left to right, one digit at a time, keeping only a little information such as how many digits so far. It is a regular-language check, done with a regular expression that is turned into a finite automaton behind the scenes. On the other hand, checking that a whole Java program has balanced braces needs a stack, which is one step up the ladder.

Common mistakes: Students often think that a more powerful model means faster. It does not; power here means the set of languages a model can recognise, not its speed. Another mistake is to mix up the three areas. Asking can a DFA do it is automata theory; asking can anything do it is computability; asking can it be done quickly is complexity. A third mistake is thinking undecidable means we have not found the algorithm yet. It means a proof shows no algorithm can ever exist.

What exams ask: Typical short questions for this lesson include: name the three branches of the theory of computation and the question each answers; why do we use abstract models; what is the Church-Turing thesis; list the Chomsky hierarchy with machines; prove a simple statement by induction; and compute the size of a power set or a Cartesian product.

Recap: Theory of Computation asks three questions: what can limited machines do (automata), what can any machine do (computability), and what can be done efficiently (complexity). We study clean models instead of real hardware because models give exact, lasting answers. Problems become languages, sets of strings, and machines become recognisers of those languages. You will lean on sets, functions, graphs, induction, contradiction and the pigeonhole principle all term. Next lesson, we build the basic vocabulary of alphabets, strings and languages, the raw material every machine in this course reads.
key_points: Theory of Computation has three branches: automata (limited machines), computability (what any machine can do) and complexity (what can be done efficiently).
A model of computation is a precise mathematical machine; it ignores hardware details so we can prove exact results.
Machines form a ladder: finite automaton, pushdown automaton, linear bounded automaton, Turing machine, each recognising a bigger class of languages.
Every yes/no problem can be written as a language: the set of strings for which the answer is yes.
The Church-Turing thesis says any intuitive algorithm can be carried out by a Turing machine.
Some problems, like the halting problem, are undecidable: no algorithm can solve them for all inputs.
Key math tools: sets, power sets (2^n subsets), functions, directed graphs, induction, contradiction and the pigeonhole principle.
lessons.tip: Keep a small definitions notebook for this course. Every time a new term appears (alphabet, DFA, regular language, decidable), write its exact definition and one tiny example. Theory exams reward precise definitions more than long answers.
lessons.task: Pick three everyday machines (a lift, a traffic light, a ceiling fan regulator). For each, write the list of states it can be in and the inputs that change those states. Then draw one of them as circles and arrows. Finally, prove by induction that a set with n elements has 2^n subsets.

quiz.q: Which branch of Theory of Computation asks whether a problem can be solved by any algorithm at all?
quiz.explain: Computability theory studies what can be computed in principle, with unlimited time and memory.

quiz.q: A set A has 4 elements. How many elements does its power set have?
quiz.explain: The power set has 2^n elements; 2^4 = 16, including the empty set and A itself.

quiz.q: What extra memory does a pushdown automaton have compared with a finite automaton?
quiz.explain: A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton plus a stack.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the halting problem is undecidable?
options: Nobody has found an algorithm yet
It is proved that no algorithm solves it for every input
quiz.explain: Undecidable is a proved impossibility, not an open search.

quiz.q: In a deterministic machine, the transition function gives, for each state and input symbol,
quiz.explain: Deterministic means the transition is a function: exactly one next state for every pair.

lessons.title: Alphabets, Strings and Languages
lessons.content:
Think about the keypad on an old Nokia phone or the PIN pad of a bKash app. It only has a few keys: the digits 0 to 9, maybe a star and a hash. Every PIN, every phone number, every message you can type is just a row of those keys, one after another. Machines in this course work exactly like that. Before we can build any machine, we need a clean vocabulary for the things they read: alphabets, strings and languages. This lesson is that vocabulary. It looks simple, and it is, but every definition here will be used in every later lesson, so learn it carefully.

Alphabet: An alphabet is a finite, non-empty set of symbols. We usually write it with the Greek capital letter Sigma. Examples: Sigma = {0, 1} is the binary alphabet. Sigma = {a, b} is a small alphabet we use a lot for examples. Sigma = {0, 1, 2, ..., 9} is the decimal digits. The set of all letters of the English alphabet, or all Bangla letters, or all ASCII characters, are also alphabets. The two rules are that it must be finite and must contain at least one symbol. The set of all natural numbers is not an alphabet, because it is infinite.

Strings: A string (also called a word) over an alphabet is a finite sequence of symbols from that alphabet, written side by side without commas. Over Sigma = {a, b}, examples are a, ab, bba and abab. Order matters and repetition is allowed, so ab and ba are different strings, and aaa is perfectly fine. A string is like a train: each carriage is one symbol, and the carriages come in a fixed order. Notice the difference from a set: in a set, order and repetition do not matter, but in a string they matter completely.

Length: The length of a string w, written |w|, is the number of symbol positions in it, counting repeats. So |abab| = 4, |bba| = 3 and |a| = 1. We also count occurrences of a particular symbol: the number of a's in w, often written |w| with a subscript a, or n_a(w). For w = abaab, the length is 5, the number of a's is 3 and the number of b's is 2. These counts appear constantly in language definitions, like strings with an even number of 0s.

The empty string: There is exactly one string of length 0, the string with no symbols at all. It is called the empty string and written with the Greek letter epsilon (some books use lambda). Epsilon is not a symbol of the alphabet, it is a string. Its length is 0. It is very important not to confuse three things: epsilon (a string of length 0), the empty set (a set with no elements, a language containing no strings) and the set {epsilon} (a language containing exactly one string, the empty string). The empty set and {epsilon} are different languages, a classic exam trap.

Concatenation: To concatenate two strings x and y is to write y right after x, giving xy. If x = ab and y = ba, then xy = abba and yx = baab. So concatenation is not commutative; order matters. It is associative: (xy)z = x(yz), so we can drop brackets. The empty string is the identity: x epsilon = epsilon x = x, just as adding 0 does nothing to a number. Lengths add: |xy| = |x| + |y|. We also write powers: w to the power n means w concatenated with itself n times, with w to the power 0 defined as epsilon. For example (ab) to the power 3 is ababab, and a to the power 4 is aaaa.

Reversal: The reverse of w, written w with a superscript R, is w written backwards. The reverse of abb is bba, and the reverse of epsilon is epsilon. A useful rule is (xy) reversed equals y reversed followed by x reversed. Check: x = ab, y = ba, xy = abba, and its reverse is abba; y reversed is ab and x reversed is ba, so y reversed then x reversed gives abba too. A string equal to its own reverse is a palindrome, like aba, abba or the English word level. Over {a, b} there are 4 palindromes of length 4 and 8 of length 5, because only the first half (plus the middle symbol for odd length) can be chosen freely.

Prefixes, suffixes and substrings: A prefix of w is any string that can be obtained by chopping symbols off the end. The prefixes of abc are epsilon, a, ab and abc, so 4 prefixes. A string of length n always has n plus 1 prefixes. A suffix is obtained by chopping symbols off the front: the suffixes of abc are epsilon, c, bc and abc. A substring is any contiguous block inside w: for abc these are epsilon, a, b, c, ab, bc and abc, which is 7 distinct substrings. Note that ac is not a substring of abc, because the symbols must be next to each other. A proper prefix or suffix is one that is not equal to w itself.

Sigma to the power k: The set of all strings of length exactly k over Sigma is written Sigma to the power k. For Sigma = {a, b}, Sigma squared is {aa, ab, ba, bb}. Sigma to the power 0 is {epsilon}, for any alphabet. If the alphabet has m symbols, Sigma to the power k has m to the power k strings, because each of the k positions can be filled in m ways. Over {a, b, c}, there are 3 cubed, that is 27, strings of length 3.

Sigma star and Sigma plus: Sigma star (the Kleene star of the alphabet) is the set of all strings over Sigma of every finite length, including epsilon. In symbols, Sigma star is the union of Sigma to the power 0, Sigma to the power 1, Sigma to the power 2, and so on forever. Sigma plus is the same but without the length-0 part, so Sigma plus equals Sigma star minus {epsilon}. Sigma star is infinite, but every single string inside it is finite. That is a subtle but important point: there are infinitely many strings, yet no string is infinitely long.

Counting strings: Counting questions are common in exams. Over {a, b}, the number of strings of length at most 3 is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. In general, over a binary alphabet the number of strings of length at most n is 2 to the power n plus 1, minus 1. The number of binary strings of length 4 with exactly two 1s is 4 choose 2, which is 6. These small counts are a good way to check a machine later: if you claim a DFA accepts all strings of length 3 with an odd number of a's, there should be exactly 4 of them out of 8, and you can list and test them.

Languages: A language over Sigma is any set of strings over Sigma, in other words any subset of Sigma star. It can be finite, like {a, ab, abb}, or infinite, like the set of all strings with an even number of a's. The empty set is a language, {epsilon} is a language, and Sigma star itself is a language. We usually describe infinite languages with set-builder notation, such as L = {w in {0,1}* : w ends with 1}, or L = {a to the n b to the n : n at least 0}, which contains epsilon, ab, aabb, aaabbb and so on. That second language will become very famous later.

Languages as problems: As promised in Lesson 1, every decision problem becomes a language. The problem is this binary number even becomes the language of binary strings ending in 0 (if we ignore leading-zero issues). The problem is this word a palindrome becomes the language of palindromes. A machine solves the problem by accepting exactly the strings that are in the language. So the main question of automata theory becomes: for a given language, what is the weakest machine that can recognise it?

Set operations on languages: Since languages are sets, union, intersection, difference and complement all work as usual. If L1 = {a, ab} and L2 = {ab, b}, then L1 union L2 = {a, ab, b} and L1 intersect L2 = {ab}. The complement of L is Sigma star minus L, everything over the alphabet that is not in L. For example, if L is the set of strings with an even number of a's, its complement is the set of strings with an odd number of a's.

Concatenation of languages: The concatenation L1 L2 is the set of all strings xy where x is in L1 and y is in L2. Take L1 = {a, ab} and L2 = {b, bb}. The combinations are a with b giving ab, a with bb giving abb, ab with b giving abb again, and ab with bb giving abbb. Since abb appears twice but a set keeps it only once, L1 L2 = {ab, abb, abbb}, which has 3 strings, not 4. Two special facts: L concatenated with {epsilon} is L, and L concatenated with the empty set is the empty set, because there is no y to pick.

Powers and Kleene star of a language: L to the power 0 is {epsilon}, L to the power 1 is L, and L to the power n is L concatenated with itself n times. The Kleene star L star is the union of all powers, so it is every string you can build by gluing together zero or more strings from L. If L = {a, ab}, then the strings of L star with length at most 3 are epsilon, a, aa, ab, aaa, aab and aba. Notice abb is not there, because no piece of L ends with bb. L plus is the union of powers from 1 upward. Two surprising facts: the empty set star is {epsilon}, and {epsilon} star is also {epsilon}, because gluing zero pieces always gives epsilon.

Real-life example 1, mobile numbers: Take Sigma = {0, 1, ..., 9}. The language of valid Bangladeshi mobile numbers in local format contains strings of length 11 that start with 01 followed by an operator digit, such as 017 or 019, and then 8 more digits. Each number is a string, its length is 11, and 01 is a prefix of every member. The whole set is a finite language. If we wanted to count how many numbers start with 017, the last 8 positions are free, so there are 10 to the power 8, which is 100 million possible strings with that prefix.

Real-life example 2, cricket ball-by-ball: Imagine writing each ball of an over as a symbol from Sigma = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, W}, where W means wicket. An over with six legal balls is then a string of length 6, such as 1 0 4 W 6 1, written 104W61. The set of all possible six-ball overs is Sigma to the power 6, with 7 to the power 6 strings. The language of overs with no wicket is a subset of it, and the language of maiden overs is just {000000}. Questions like did the bowler concede a boundary become questions about whether the string contains 4 or 6 as a substring.

Common mistakes: The biggest mistake is mixing up epsilon, the empty set and {epsilon}. Remember: epsilon is a string, the empty set is a language with no strings, and {epsilon} is a language with one string. Another mistake is thinking concatenation is commutative; ab followed by ba is not ba followed by ab. Students also forget that epsilon is a prefix, a suffix and a substring of every string, and that Sigma star always contains epsilon while Sigma plus does not. Finally, when counting the strings of L1 L2, do not simply multiply the sizes; duplicates like abb above can make the answer smaller.

What exams ask: Expect questions like: define alphabet, string, language, Sigma star and Sigma plus; list all prefixes, suffixes and substrings of a given string; find L1 L2 or L star up to some length; state whether the empty set and {epsilon} are equal; count strings of a given length over an alphabet; and prove a small identity such as the length of xy equals the length of x plus the length of y, or the reverse rule, by induction on the length of y.

Recap: An alphabet is a finite non-empty set of symbols. A string is a finite sequence of symbols, and epsilon is the unique string of length 0. Concatenation glues strings, is associative, not commutative, and has epsilon as identity. Sigma star is all strings including epsilon; Sigma plus excludes it. A language is any subset of Sigma star, and we can combine languages with union, intersection, complement, concatenation and Kleene star. With this vocabulary ready, the next lesson builds our first real machine: the deterministic finite automaton.
key_points: An alphabet Sigma is a finite, non-empty set of symbols; a string is a finite sequence of those symbols.
Epsilon is the empty string with length 0; it is different from the empty set and from the language {epsilon}.
Concatenation is associative, not commutative, with epsilon as identity, and |xy| = |x| + |y|.
A string of length n has n+1 prefixes and n+1 suffixes (counting epsilon and itself).
If |Sigma| = m, there are m^k strings of length k; Sigma* contains all finite strings, Sigma+ = Sigma* minus {epsilon}.
A language is any subset of Sigma*; decision problems are written as languages.
L1L2 = {xy : x in L1, y in L2}; L* is the union of all powers L^0, L^1, L^2, ... and always contains epsilon.
Empty set star = {epsilon}; L concatenated with the empty set is the empty set.
lessons.tip: Whenever a definition feels abstract, test it on a tiny example with the alphabet {a, b} and strings of length at most 3. Writing out the actual strings catches almost every mistake about epsilon and duplicates.
lessons.task: With Sigma = {a, b}, write all 15 strings of length at most 3. Mark which ones are palindromes. Then let L1 = {a, b} and L2 = {epsilon, a}; compute L1 L2 and L2 L1 and check whether they are equal. Finally list every string of {ab}* of length at most 6.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an alphabet?
options: The set of all natural numbers
quiz.explain: An alphabet must be finite; the natural numbers form an infinite set.

quiz.q: How many prefixes does the string abba have, counting epsilon and the string itself?
quiz.explain: A string of length n has n+1 prefixes: epsilon, a, ab, abb, abba.

quiz.q: If L1 = {a, ab} and L2 = {b, bb}, how many strings are in L1L2?
quiz.explain: ab, abb, abb, abbb: abb appears twice, so the set is {ab, abb, abbb}.

quiz.q: What is the Kleene star of the empty language?
quiz.explain: L^0 = {epsilon} for every L, and all higher powers of the empty set are empty.

quiz.q: How many strings of length 3 are there over the alphabet {a, b, c}?
quiz.explain: Each of the 3 positions has 3 choices: 3^3 = 27.

lessons.title: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
lessons.content:
Picture the ticket gate at a Dhaka metro rail station. It is either locked or unlocked. Tap a valid card and a locked gate becomes unlocked. Walk through and it locks again. Tap while it is already unlocked and it simply stays unlocked. The gate does not remember who came before you or how many people passed today. It only knows its current state and what just happened. That tiny, forgetful but perfectly reliable machine is the idea behind a deterministic finite automaton, or DFA, the first real machine of this course.

What a DFA is: A DFA reads an input string one symbol at a time, from left to right, exactly once. It is always in one of a finite number of states. For each state and each input symbol, there is exactly one next state, decided in advance. When the input runs out, the DFA looks at the state it ended in. If that is an accepting state, it says yes and accepts the string; otherwise it rejects. It cannot go back, cannot write anything, and has no memory besides its current state. Deterministic means there is never a choice: one state, one symbol, one move.

The formal definition: A DFA is a 5-tuple M = (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F). Q is a finite set of states. Sigma is the input alphabet. delta is the transition function from Q times Sigma to Q, so delta(q, a) is the single state the machine moves to from q on symbol a. q0, an element of Q, is the start state. F, a subset of Q, is the set of accepting (final) states. F can be empty, in which case the DFA accepts nothing, or it can be all of Q, in which case it accepts everything. Because delta is a total function, every state must have exactly one outgoing transition for every symbol.

State diagrams: We draw a DFA as a directed graph. Each state is a circle with its name inside. An arrow from p to q labelled a means delta(p, a) = q. If several symbols lead to the same place, we write them on one arrow, like 0,1. The start state has a short arrow coming in from nowhere. Accepting states have a double circle. A good habit is to check every state in your drawing: over {0, 1}, each circle must have exactly one arrow leaving for 0 and exactly one for 1, counting self-loops.

Transition tables: The same information can be written as a table. Rows are states, columns are symbols, and each cell holds the next state. The start state is marked with an arrow and accepting states with a star. For a DFA over {0, 1} with 3 states, the table has 3 rows and 2 columns, so 6 cells, and every cell must be filled with exactly one state. Tables are easier for computer programs and for algorithms like minimization; diagrams are easier for humans to understand.

Example 1, even number of 0s: Let Sigma = {0, 1} and L = strings with an even number of 0s. We need to remember only one thing: is the number of 0s seen so far even or odd? So two states: E (even, start, accepting) and O (odd). Transitions: from E on 0 go to O, from E on 1 stay in E, from O on 0 go to E, from O on 1 stay in O. Reading 1 never changes the parity, reading 0 always flips it. Note that epsilon has zero 0s, which is even, so the start state E is accepting.

Tracing a DFA: A trace lists the states visited, one per symbol. For the input 1001 on the even-zeros DFA: start in E; read 1, stay E; read 0, go to O; read 0, go back to E; read 1, stay E. The final state E is accepting, so 1001 is accepted, which is right, since it has two 0s. For 0100: E, then 0 to O, 1 stays O, 0 back to E, 0 to O. It ends in O, so it is rejected; indeed 0100 has three 0s. A trace of a string of length n always lists n plus 1 states, including the start.

The extended transition function: delta handles one symbol. To talk about a whole string we define the extended transition function, often written delta-hat, from Q times Sigma star to Q, by induction on the string. Base: delta-hat(q, epsilon) = q, because reading nothing moves you nowhere. Step: delta-hat(q, wa) = delta(delta-hat(q, w), a), meaning first process w, then take one more step on a. So delta-hat(q0, w) is just the state where the trace of w ends. This recursive definition is the official version of what you do by hand when tracing, and many proofs use induction on it.

Acceptance and the language of a DFA: M accepts w if delta-hat(q0, w) is in F; otherwise M rejects w. The language of M, written L(M), is the set of all strings M accepts. We say M recognises L(M). Very important: L(M) must contain exactly the strings we want, no more and no less. A DFA that accepts all strings in L plus a few extra ones is wrong, and so is one that misses some. A DFA always halts, after exactly |w| steps, so it always gives an answer.

Example 2, strings over {a, b} that end with ab: What do we need to remember? Only how much of the pattern ab we have just seen at the end. Three states: q0 means the string so far does not end with a or ab in a useful way, q1 means it ends with a, and q2 means it ends with ab (accepting). Transitions: q0 on a goes to q1, q0 on b stays q0. q1 on a stays q1 (still ending with a), q1 on b goes to q2. q2 on a goes to q1 (now ending with a), q2 on b goes back to q0, since abb ends with b and no part of ab is useful any more.

Traces for Example 2: For abab: q0, a to q1, b to q2, a to q1, b to q2. It ends in q2, accepted. For aaba: q0, q1, q1, q2, then a to q1, rejected, which is correct because aaba ends in ba. For abb: q0, q1, q2, then b to q0, rejected. I checked this DFA by computer on every string over {a, b} of length up to 8, and it accepts exactly the ones ending in ab. Doing such a brute-force check, even by hand for lengths up to 3 or 4, is a great habit.

Example 3, binary numbers divisible by 3: Let the input be a binary number read from the most significant bit. The trick is that reading a new bit b turns the value v into 2v plus b. So if we only remember the remainder r = v mod 3, the new remainder is (2r plus b) mod 3. Three states, 0, 1 and 2, with 0 as start and accepting state. The transitions are: from 0, bit 0 goes to 0 and bit 1 goes to 1; from 1, bit 0 goes to 2 and bit 1 goes to 0; from 2, bit 0 goes to 1 and bit 1 goes to 2.

Traces for Example 3: Input 110 is 6. Start 0; read 1, (0 plus 1) mod 3 is 1; read 1, (2 plus 1) mod 3 is 0; read 0, (0 plus 0) mod 3 is 0. Ends in 0, accepted, and 6 is divisible by 3. Input 1001 is 9: states 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, accepted. Input 1011 is 11: states 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, ending in 2, rejected, and indeed 11 leaves remainder 2. The empty string ends in state 0 and is accepted, which matches the convention that it represents 0. The same idea gives a DFA with k states for divisibility by any k.

Dead states: Sometimes, once something bad happens, the string can never be accepted, whatever comes next. Example: strings over {a, b} that start with a. From the start state s, reading a goes to an accepting state A that loops on both a and b. Reading b first goes to a state D that loops on both symbols and is not accepting. D is a dead state, also called a trap or sink state. Many textbooks leave dead states out of drawings to keep them clean, but in a formal DFA they must be there, because delta has to be defined for every state and symbol.

How to design a DFA: A reliable recipe works for most exam questions. First, ask what the machine must remember about the prefix read so far to decide the future, and make one state for each distinct situation. Second, decide the start state, which is the situation for epsilon. Third, mark accepting states. Fourth, fill in every transition, asking for each state and symbol which situation we are in now. Fifth, test: run several strings that should be accepted and several that should be rejected, including epsilon, very short strings and the tricky ones like aab for the ends-with-ab language.

States as memory: The number of states is the only memory a DFA has. With k states it can tell apart at most k different situations. This is why a DFA can count mod 3, or remember the last two symbols, but cannot count without limit. To check a to the n b to the n for every n, it would need to remember the exact number of a's, which can be as large as you like, and no finite number of states is enough. We will prove that properly with the pumping lemma in Lesson 11.

Real-life example 1, a vending machine at a bus terminal: A drinks machine at Sayedabad sells a bottle for 20 taka and accepts 10 and 20 taka notes. Its states are 0 taka, 10 taka and 20 taka inserted. From 0, a 10 note goes to 10, a 20 note goes to 20. From 10, a 10 note goes to 20. When the machine reaches 20, it releases a bottle. Treat a reached-20 situation as accepting. Real machines also handle refunds and overpayment, but the core is a DFA: a finite set of situations and fixed responses.

Real-life example 2, a lexer in a compiler: When a compiler reads your C program, the first stage scans characters and groups them into tokens such as identifiers, numbers and keywords. A DFA for unsigned integers has a start state, a digit takes it to an accepting state that loops on more digits, and anything else is an error. Lexer generators such as lex and flex take patterns written as regular expressions and automatically build one combined DFA, which then runs in time proportional to the length of the input. That is why lexing is so fast.

Common mistakes: Forgetting transitions is the most common error: in a formal DFA every state needs exactly one arrow for every symbol. Another error is giving a state two arrows on the same symbol, which breaks determinism. Students also forget to decide whether epsilon should be accepted; if it should, the start state must be accepting. In the ends-with-ab example many people send q2 on a back to q0, losing the fact that the string now ends with a. Always test with strings like aab and abab, where the pattern overlaps itself.

What exams ask: Typical questions: give the 5-tuple of a DFA; draw the diagram from a table or the table from a diagram; trace a string and say whether it is accepted; write the extended transition function definition; design DFAs for strings with an even number of 0s and odd number of 1s, strings containing or ending with a pattern, strings whose length is divisible by k, or binary numbers divisible by k. Show your states with a short meaning for each, such as q1 means ends with a, because examiners give marks for clear reasoning.

Recap: A DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) with exactly one move for every state and symbol. It reads its input once, left to right, and accepts if it ends in an accepting state. The extended transition function delta-hat follows a whole string. Design means choosing what to remember, one state per situation, then filling every transition and testing. Dead states catch strings that can never be accepted. In the next lesson we use DFAs to define regular languages and learn design patterns such as complement and the product construction.
key_points: A DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) where delta: Q x Sigma -> Q gives exactly one next state.
It reads the input once, left to right, and accepts if the final state is in F.
The extended transition function: delta-hat(q, epsilon) = q and delta-hat(q, wa) = delta(delta-hat(q, w), a).
L(M) is exactly the set of strings M accepts, no more and no less.
Design by deciding what to remember: one state per situation, then fill every transition and test.
Binary divisible by k: track the remainder r; on bit b go to (2r + b) mod k.
A dead (trap) state is non-accepting and loops on every symbol; formal DFAs need it even if diagrams omit it.
lessons.tip: After designing a DFA, test it with at least five strings: epsilon, one short string that should be accepted, one that should be rejected, and two tricky ones where the pattern overlaps, like aab or abab. If you can code, a 10-line simulator lets you test every string up to length 8.
lessons.task: Draw a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts binary numbers divisible by 3, then trace 1100 (12), 111 (7) and 10010 (18). Next, design a DFA over {a, b} for strings that end with ba and test it on a, ba, aba, bba and abab.

quiz.q: In the 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) of a DFA, what is F?
quiz.explain: F is a subset of Q containing the accepting (final) states.

quiz.q: Using the DFA that tracks binary remainders mod 3, which state is reached after reading 1011?
quiz.explain: States go 0, 1, 2, 2, 2; 1011 is 11, and 11 mod 3 = 2.

quiz.q: A DFA over {0, 1} has 4 states. How many entries does its full transition table have?
quiz.explain: One entry per state and symbol: 4 x 2 = 8.

quiz.q: For the DFA accepting strings over {a, b} that end with ab, where should the state meaning ends with ab go on input a?
options: To the state meaning ends with a
It should stay in the same state
quiz.explain: After ab followed by a, the string ends with a, which is the start of the pattern again.

quiz.q: For a DFA to accept the empty string, what must be true?
options: It must have a dead state
Its start state must be accepting
It must have a self-loop on every symbol
It needs at least two accepting states
quiz.explain: delta-hat(q0, epsilon) = q0, so epsilon is accepted exactly when q0 is in F.

lessons.title: Regular Languages and DFA Design Patterns
lessons.content:
Think of a cook at a busy biryani shop in Old Dhaka. He has a few standard tricks: double the recipe, swap the meat, combine two dishes on one plate. With these tricks he can serve hundreds of orders without inventing each one from scratch. DFA design works the same way. Last lesson you built DFAs one at a time. In this lesson you learn the family of languages DFAs recognise, the regular languages, and a small set of design patterns that let you build big DFAs from small ones almost mechanically.

Regular language: A language L over Sigma is called regular if there is some DFA M with L(M) = L. That is the whole definition. The language of strings with an even number of 0s is regular, because we built a DFA for it. So are strings ending with ab, and binary numbers divisible by 3. Every finite language is regular too, because you can build a DFA that walks a tree of all the strings and sends everything else to a dead state. Later we will see that NFAs and regular expressions describe exactly the same family, which is why this family has several equivalent definitions.

Why the definition matters: To show a language is regular, you only need to give one correct DFA, or later an NFA or a regular expression.
