To show a language is not regular, you must show that no DFA at all can recognise it, which needs a proof tool such as the pumping lemma in Lesson 11. So for regular languages, the positive direction is a construction and the negative direction is an impossibility proof. Keep that asymmetry in mind.

Pattern 1, complement by swapping accepting states: Suppose M = (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) recognises L. Build M' with the same states, alphabet, transitions and start state, but with accepting set Q minus F. On any input w, both machines follow exactly the same path and end in the same state, since they have the same delta. That state is in F for M exactly when it is not in Q minus F for M'. So M' accepts exactly the strings M rejects, and L(M') is the complement of L. This proves that the complement of a regular language is regular.

Complement example: Take the DFA for strings over {a, b} ending with ab, with states q0, q1, q2 and accepting state q2. Swap: now q0 and q1 are accepting and q2 is not. The new machine accepts exactly the strings that do not end with ab, including epsilon, a, b, ba and abb. I confirmed by computer that it agrees with the language on every string up to length 8. One warning: the swap only works on a complete DFA. If the dead state was left out of a drawing, you must add it first, because in the complement those trapped strings must become accepted.

Pattern 2, the product construction: Suppose M1 recognises L1 with states Q1 and M2 recognises L2 with states Q2, both over the same alphabet. We build one machine that runs both at the same time, like a student watching two cricket matches on a split screen. Its states are pairs (p, q) with p in Q1 and q in Q2. The start state is (start of M1, start of M2). On symbol a, the pair (p, q) moves to (delta1(p, a), delta2(q, a)), so each half moves exactly as its own machine would. If M1 has m states and M2 has n states, the product has m times n states.

Choosing the accepting states: The product machine tracks both machines, so we can choose what to accept. For intersection, accept (p, q) when p is in F1 and q is in F2. For union, accept when p is in F1 or q is in F2. For difference L1 minus L2, accept when p is in F1 and q is not in F2. For symmetric difference, accept when exactly one is accepting. One construction, four results. This proves that regular languages are closed under union, intersection and difference.

Product example: Let L1 be strings over {0, 1} with an even number of 0s (states E, O for zeros) and L2 be strings with an odd number of 1s (states E, O for ones). The product has 4 states, which we can name EE, EO, OE and OO, where the first letter is the parity of 0s and the second the parity of 1s. Start is EE. Reading 0 flips the first letter, reading 1 flips the second. For the intersection, even 0s and odd 1s, the only accepting state is EO. For the union, even 0s or odd 1s, the accepting states are EE, EO and OO; only OE is rejecting.

Tracing the product: Input 001: EE, then 0 to OE, 0 to EE, 1 to EO. It ends in EO, accepted: two 0s (even) and one 1 (odd). Input 0110: EE, OE, OO, OE, EE, ending in EE, rejected for the intersection since the number of 1s is even. A fun check: any string in the intersection has even plus odd symbols, so its length is odd. Counting by computer, there are 0 such strings of length 4 and 4 of length 3, namely 111, 001, 010 and 100. Small counts like this are a great test of a product DFA.

Pattern 3, counting modulo k: Many languages say something about a count being a multiple of k, or leaving a certain remainder. Use k states arranged in a cycle, 0, 1, ..., k minus 1. For the length of the string divisible by 3, every symbol moves from r to (r plus 1) mod 3, the start is 0 and the accepting state is 0. For the number of a's leaving remainder 1 when divided by 4, an a moves r to (r plus 1) mod 4, a b keeps the state, the start is 0 and the accepting state is 1. Both machines were checked on all strings up to length 8.

Pattern 4, remembering the last few symbols: To check something about the last k symbols, such as ends with 01 or the second-to-last symbol is a, a DFA can store the last k symbols in its state. That needs at most 2 to the power k states over a binary alphabet, plus a few states for the beginning when fewer than k symbols have been read. Often you can do better with the pattern approach of the next paragraph, but this brute-force idea always works and is a good fallback when you are stuck.

Pattern 5, substring check: For strings containing a pattern such as 101, the states record the longest suffix of the input so far that is also a prefix of 101. The possible values are epsilon, 1, 10 and 101, so four states, and once 101 has been seen we stay in an accepting trap state. Transitions: from epsilon, 0 stays at epsilon and 1 goes to 1. From 1, 0 goes to 10 and 1 stays at 1, because the newest 1 could start the pattern. From 10, 1 goes to 101 and 0 goes back to epsilon, since 100 ends with no useful part of 101. From 101, both symbols stay in 101.

Substring traces: For 1101, the states are epsilon, 1, 1, 10, 101, so it is accepted. For 1001, they are epsilon, 1, 10, epsilon, 1, so it is rejected, correctly, because 1001 does not contain 101. The careful part is deciding where to fall back after a mismatch. This is the same idea used by the Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching algorithm you may have seen in Algorithms. If you want strings that do not contain 101, just complement: make epsilon, 1 and 10 accepting and 101 not accepting. As a check, 21 of the 32 binary strings of length 5 avoid 101.

Combining patterns: Real exam questions mix conditions, such as strings that contain 101 and have even length. Build each part separately, the 4-state substring DFA and the 2-state length-parity DFA, then use the product construction to get an 8-state machine with accepting states where both parts accept. You may later reduce its size with minimization, Lesson 8, but a correct big DFA always earns more marks than a small wrong one.

Closure properties preview: A family of languages is closed under an operation if applying it to members always gives a member. We have now proved that regular languages are closed under complement, union, intersection and difference, using swapping and products. They are also closed under concatenation, Kleene star and reversal, but those are much easier to prove with NFAs and epsilon moves, so we will see them in Lessons 5 to 7. Closure is not just theory; it is also a tool for proving that a language is not regular, which we use in Lesson 11.

Why closure helps design: Closure lets you break a hard language into easy pieces. Strings over {a, b} that do not end with ab and have an odd number of b's is the intersection of a complement and a parity language. Instead of guessing one big machine, you build two tiny ones and combine them. This mirrors how good programmers build big programs from small, tested functions.

Real-life example 1, a bKash-style PIN rule: Imagine an app that accepts a 5-digit PIN only if it does not contain the same digit three times in a row and the sum of its digits is not divisible by 5. Each rule alone is a small DFA: one tracks the last digit and how many times it repeated, the other tracks the digit sum mod 5. The full rule is the intersection of the first with the complement of the second, built by the product construction. Real apps use code rather than drawn DFAs, but the logic is the same.

Real-life example 2, a traffic signal monitor: A traffic camera at Farmgate logs each signal change as G, Y or R. A safety rule might say the sequence must never contain G followed immediately by R, and the number of R phases in a shift must be even. The first rule is the complement of a substring language, the second is counting mod 2. A monitor that checks both is a product DFA, and because it is a DFA it can check the log in one fast pass with constant memory.

Common mistakes: Swapping accepting states on an incomplete DFA, without the dead state, gives a wrong complement. Swapping accepting states on an NFA also gives a wrong answer, as we will see in the next lesson. In the product construction, students sometimes add the two state counts instead of multiplying, or forget that both machines need the same alphabet. In the substring pattern, the fallback after a mismatch is the usual source of bugs: always ask what the longest useful suffix is right now.

What exams ask: Define a regular language; show that the complement of a regular language is regular; construct the product DFA for two given DFAs and mark accepting states for union or intersection; design DFAs for languages like even number of a's and odd number of b's, strings not containing aa, or strings where the number of 1s is a multiple of 3; and state closure properties of regular languages. Writing the meaning of each product state, like EO means even 0s and odd 1s, makes your answer easy to mark.

Recap: A language is regular if some DFA recognises it. Swapping accepting and non-accepting states of a complete DFA gives the complement. The product construction runs two DFAs in parallel with m times n paired states, and choosing the accepting pairs gives union, intersection or difference. Counting mod k uses a cycle of k states, and substring checks use states that remember the longest useful suffix. Regular languages are closed under all these operations. Next lesson we relax determinism and meet the NFA, a machine that can guess.
key_points: A language is regular if some DFA recognises it; every finite language is regular.
Complement: keep a complete DFA and swap accepting and non-accepting states.
Product construction: states are pairs (p, q), start (q01, q02), move both halves together; m x n states.
Accept pairs where both accept for intersection, either accepts for union, first but not second for difference.
Counting mod k: k states in a cycle; substring checks: states = longest suffix that is a prefix of the pattern.
Regular languages are closed under complement, union, intersection, difference, concatenation, star and reversal.
Break hard languages into simple pieces and combine with closure operations.
lessons.tip: When a question has the words and, or, not, split it into separate small DFAs first. Draw each one, test it, and only then combine them with the product construction. This is slower to write but almost never wrong.
lessons.task: Build the 4-state product DFA for strings over {0, 1} with an even number of 0s and an odd number of 1s. Trace 001, 0110 and 10111. Then change only the accepting states to get the union and the difference (even 0s but not odd 1s), and list all accepted strings of length 3 for each.

quiz.q: How do you get a DFA for the complement of L(M), where M is a complete DFA?
options: Add a dead state and nothing else
quiz.explain: Same paths, opposite verdicts: Q minus F becomes the accepting set.

quiz.q: A DFA with 3 states and a DFA with 5 states are combined by the product construction. How many states does the product have?
quiz.explain: Product states are pairs, so 3 x 5 = 15.

quiz.q: In the product of the even-0s DFA and the odd-1s DFA, which states accept for the union?
quiz.explain: Union rejects only when 0s are odd and 1s are even, which is OE.

quiz.q: In the DFA for strings containing 101, where does the state 10 go on input 0?
quiz.explain: 100 ends with no prefix of 101 (it ends in 0), so we fall back to epsilon.

quiz.q: Why is every finite language regular?
options: A DFA can follow a tree of the finitely many strings and send everything else to a dead state
Because a DFA may use infinitely many states
Because the pumping lemma says so
quiz.explain: A finite set of strings fits in a finite tree of states plus a dead state.

lessons.title: Nondeterministic Finite Automata (NFA)
lessons.content:
Imagine you are looking for your friend's house in Mohammadpur. At a junction you are not sure whether to turn left or right. A normal person must pick one road and, if it is wrong, walk back. But imagine you had a magic power: at every junction you split into copies, and each copy tries a different road at the same moment. If any one copy reaches the house, the search succeeds. Copies that hit a dead end simply vanish. That magic is nondeterminism, and the machine that uses it is the nondeterministic finite automaton, or NFA.

What changes from a DFA: A DFA has exactly one move for each state and symbol. An NFA relaxes this in two ways. From a state, on a symbol, it may have several possible next states, or it may have none at all. When there are several, the machine follows all of them in parallel. When there are none, that particular branch dies. The NFA accepts a string if at least one way of reading the whole string ends in an accepting state. It rejects only if every possible way fails. Lesson 6 adds a third freedom, moves on the empty string; in this lesson we keep to moves on real symbols.

The formal definition: An NFA is a 5-tuple N = (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F), exactly like a DFA except for delta. Q, Sigma, q0 and F mean the same as before. The transition function now goes from Q times Sigma to the power set of Q. So delta(q, a) is a set of states, possibly empty. In a DFA, delta(q, a) = p; in an NFA, delta(q, a) = {p, r} or {p} or the empty set. Because the power set of a set with n states has 2 to the power n members, this definition hides the famous blow-up that appears when we convert an NFA to a DFA in Lesson 7.

Drawing an NFA: The drawing rules are the same as for DFAs, circles for states, labelled arrows for moves, an incoming arrow for the start and double circles for accepting states. The difference is that one state may have two arrows with the same label, or no arrow for some symbol. Missing arrows do not mean anything is wrong; they mean that branch dies on that symbol. This is why NFA drawings are usually smaller and cleaner than DFA drawings for the same language.

A first example, strings ending with 01: Over {0, 1}, take states p, q and r with p the start and r accepting. From p, on 0 go to p or q; on 1 go to p. From q, on 1 go to r. State q has no move on 0, and r has no moves at all. The idea is simple: p reads freely, and at some 0 the machine guesses this is the second last symbol and jumps to q. If the next symbol is 1 and it is the last one, the branch is in r at the end and the string is accepted. If the guess was wrong, that branch dies or ends in a non-accepting state, which does no harm.

Tracking sets of states: The practical way to run an NFA is to keep the set of all states that some branch could be in. Start with {p}. For input 1001: read 1, from p we go to {p}. Read 0, from p we go to {p, q}. Read 0 again, p gives {p, q} and q has no move on 0, so we have {p, q}. Read 1, p gives {p} and q gives {r}, so {p, r}. The final set contains r, an accepting state, so 1001 is accepted. For 010: {p}, then {p, q}, then {p, r}, then on 0 we get {p, q} because r has no moves. No accepting state, so 010 is rejected.

The extended transition function: Just as for DFAs, we define delta-hat on whole strings, but now it returns a set. Base: delta-hat(q, epsilon) = {q}. Step: delta-hat(q, wa) is the union, over every state p in delta-hat(q, w), of delta(p, a). In words, collect all states you could be in after w, then from each of them take every possible move on a, and gather everything together. The NFA accepts w if delta-hat(q0, w) contains at least one accepting state, that is, if its intersection with F is not empty. The language L(N) is the set of all strings accepted.

Computation trees: Another way to picture an NFA run is a tree. The root is the start state. Each level corresponds to one input symbol, and each node branches into all the states it can move to. A branch with no possible move stops early, a dead branch. A string is accepted if at least one leaf at full depth is an accepting state. The set-tracking method is just the tree with each level squashed into a set, so duplicate states are counted once. Trees are great for understanding; sets are better for calculation, because a tree can grow exponentially.

The star example, third symbol from the end is 1: Let L be strings over {0, 1} whose third symbol from the end is 1, such as 100, 0111 and 0100. An NFA with just 4 states does this. State q0 is the start and loops on both 0 and 1. On 1, q0 can also jump to q1, guessing that this 1 is third from the end. From q1, any symbol leads to q2, and from q2 any symbol leads to q3, which is accepting and has no outgoing moves. A branch is in q3 at the end only if the guessed 1 was followed by exactly two more symbols.

Trace of the star example: For 0100, track sets: {q0}; read 0, {q0}; read 1, {q0, q1}; read 0, {q0, q2}; read 0, {q0, q3}. It contains q3, accepted, and indeed the third last symbol is 1. For 0011: {q0}, {q0}, {q0}, {q0, q1}, {q0, q1, q2}. No q3, rejected, correct since the third last symbol is 0. As a computation tree, 0100 has two branches that survive to the end: one staying in q0 all the way, and one going q0, q0, q1, q2, q3, which accepts. For 1101, the branch that jumped on the first 1 dies, because it reaches q3 after three symbols with one symbol still left to read.

Checking the example: I ran this NFA by computer on all binary strings up to length 8 and compared it with the rule third symbol from the end is 1. They agree everywhere, including strings shorter than 3, which are correctly rejected since no branch can reach q3. As a counting check, there are 16 strings of length 5 in the language, because the third-last position is fixed to 1 and the other four positions are free, and 2 to the power 4 is 16.

Why this example is famous: A DFA for the same language must remember the last three symbols, since any of them might turn out to be the important one when the input ends. That needs 8 states, one for each pattern of the last three bits, and in fact no DFA with fewer than 8 states can do it. In general, for the n-th symbol from the end, the NFA has n plus 1 states while the smallest DFA has 2 to the power n. When I ran the subset construction on our 4-state NFA, exactly 8 reachable sets appeared. Lesson 7 shows this conversion step by step.

NFAs are not more powerful: Even though an NFA can guess, it recognises exactly the same languages as DFAs, the regular languages. This theorem is due to Rabin and Scott, who introduced NFAs in 1959. One direction is easy: every DFA is basically an NFA, with delta(q, a) replaced by the one-element set {delta(q, a)}. The other direction is the subset construction: a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states can simulate the set-tracking method. So nondeterminism buys convenience and smaller machines, not new power. Remember this: for finite automata, guessing does not change what can be recognised.

Is nondeterminism real: No physical machine actually splits into copies. Nondeterminism is a thinking tool. You can read it as lucky guessing: the machine always guesses right if a right guess exists. Or as parallel search: try all branches at once. Or as a certificate: a string is accepted if there is a path that proves it. That last view returns in the definition of the class NP in Lesson 25, where a nondeterministic machine guesses a solution and checks it. For finite automata, simulation costs at most a bigger set of states; for Turing machines and time, whether guessing helps is the P versus NP question.

Designing with NFAs: The NFA style is to guess where something interesting starts. For strings containing 101, loop at the start on 0 and 1, then guess the start of 101 and walk through states for 1, 0, 1 to an accepting state that loops on everything. That is 4 states with no fallback logic, much easier than the DFA from Lesson 4. For strings that end with abb, loop at the start, then guess the last three symbols. For the union of two languages, you can put two NFAs side by side under a new start state; Lesson 6 shows the cleanest way with epsilon moves.

Complement is not easy: For a DFA, swapping accepting states gives the complement. For an NFA, it does not. Take the ends-with-01 NFA and make p and q accepting instead of r. On input 01, the final set is {p, r}, which contains p, so the swapped machine accepts 01, even though 01 does end with 01 and should be rejected by the complement. The reason is that the NFA accepts when some branch accepts, and the swap only flips individual branches. To complement an NFA, first convert it to a DFA, then swap.

Real-life example 1, searching chats: Suppose you want your phone to find every message containing the word bKash. A search engine can think of this as an NFA: stay in the start state while reading any character, and at any position guess that the word begins here, then follow b, K, a, s, h to an accepting state. Tools such as grep work with patterns in this spirit; some implementations simulate the NFA by tracking sets of states, and others convert to a DFA first, trading memory for speed.

Real-life example 2, a delivery rider's route: A Foodpanda rider in Dhanmondi may know several valid routes to a customer. Asking whether some route avoids a blocked road and arrives within the time limit is an exists question, just like NFA acceptance: we accept if at least one path works. Checking every route one by one is the deterministic version; reasoning about all routes at once, as a set of possible positions, is exactly the set-tracking simulation of an NFA.

Common mistakes: Thinking an NFA rejects if one branch rejects is the most common error; it accepts if any branch accepts. Another error is forgetting that an empty set of current states means every branch has died, and the string is rejected no matter what follows. Students also write delta(q, a) = p for an NFA instead of a set. Some believe NFAs recognise more languages than DFAs; they do not. Finally, swapping accepting states of an NFA does not give the complement.

What exams ask: Give the formal definition of an NFA and explain how delta differs from a DFA; trace an NFA on a string using sets of states or a computation tree; design NFAs for strings ending with a pattern, containing a pattern, or with the k-th symbol from the end fixed; explain why an NFA for the n-th symbol from the end needs only n plus 1 states while a DFA needs 2 to the power n; and state that NFAs and DFAs recognise the same class of languages.

Recap: An NFA is like a DFA whose transitions return sets of states, so it may have several moves or none. It accepts if some path through the input ends in an accepting state. We simulate it by tracking the set of possible current states, or picture it as a computation tree. NFAs are often far smaller and easier to design, as the third-symbol-from-the-end example shows, but they recognise exactly the regular languages. Next lesson adds epsilon moves, which make building NFAs for union, concatenation and star almost effortless.
key_points: An NFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) with delta: Q x Sigma -> power set of Q.
From a state on a symbol an NFA may have several next states or none; a branch with no move dies.
An NFA accepts w if at least one path ends in an accepting state: delta-hat(q0, w) intersect F is not empty.
Simulate an NFA by tracking the set of all possible current states, level by level.
Third symbol from the end is 1: NFA with 4 states, but the smallest DFA needs 8; in general n+1 vs 2^n.
NFAs and DFAs recognise exactly the same languages, the regular languages (Rabin and Scott, 1959).
Swapping accepting states of an NFA does not give the complement; convert to a DFA first.
lessons.tip: When tracing an NFA, write the set of current states under each symbol in a single row, like {q0}, {q0, q1}, {q0, q2}. It is faster than drawing the tree and you will never miss a branch.
lessons.task: Draw a 4-state NFA over {a, b} that accepts strings ending with abb. Trace it with sets of states on abb, aabb, abab and babb. Then try to draw a DFA for the same language and count how many states you needed.

quiz.q: What does the transition function of an NFA return?
options: A set of states, possibly empty
quiz.explain: delta: Q x Sigma -> power set of Q, so each move gives a set of states.

quiz.q: When does an NFA accept a string?
options: When every path ends in an accepting state
When at least one path ends in an accepting state
When the start state is accepting
quiz.explain: Acceptance needs just one successful path.

quiz.q: For the NFA accepting strings whose third symbol from the end is 1, what is the set of states after reading 0100?
Which statement about NFAs and DFAs is true?
options: NFAs recognise more languages than DFAs
DFAs recognise more languages than NFAs
An NFA can only have one accepting state
They recognise exactly the same class of languages
quiz.explain: Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA by the subset construction.

quiz.q: The smallest DFA for strings whose 3rd symbol from the end is 1 has how many states?
quiz.explain: It must remember the last three bits: 2^3 = 8 states.

lessons.title: Epsilon-NFA and Epsilon-Closure
lessons.content:
Imagine you are walking through Dhaka on a rainy evening. Some roads ask you to pay a toll, some ask you to show a pass, but a few lanes are just open corridors. You can step into them without giving anything at all. A normal NFA is like a city where every single step costs one symbol of input. Today we add free corridors. A move that uses up no input symbol is called an epsilon move, and a machine that is allowed such moves is called an epsilon-NFA. It sounds like a tiny change, but it makes building machines much easier.

Quick recap: In the last lesson we met the NFA. It has a set of states Q, an alphabet Sigma, a start state q0, a set of accepting states F, and a transition function delta that sends a state and a symbol to a set of states, maybe several, maybe none. The NFA accepts a string if at least one path through the machine reads the whole string and ends in an accepting state. Epsilon-NFAs keep all of that and add one more kind of arrow.

What an epsilon move is: Remember that epsilon is the empty string, the string of length zero. An arrow labelled epsilon from state p to state r means the machine may jump from p to r without reading anything. The input pointer does not move. It is a free jump, and like everything in an NFA it is optional. The machine can take it or not, and if there are several free jumps it can take any of them, and even chain them one after another.

The formal definition: An epsilon-NFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F), exactly like an NFA, except that the transition function now has the type delta : Q x (Sigma union {epsilon}) -> P(Q). Here P(Q) is the power set of Q, the set of all subsets. So delta(p, epsilon) is the set of states you can reach from p by one free jump. Some books write Sigma_epsilon for Sigma union {epsilon}. Nothing else changes: same states, same start, same accepting set.

Our running example: Let the alphabet be {a, b, c}. Take three states q0, q1, q2 with q0 the start and q2 the only accepting state. State q0 has a loop on a. State q1 has a loop on b. State q2 has a loop on c. There is an epsilon arrow from q0 to q1 and another epsilon arrow from q1 to q2. Think of it as three rooms in a row. In room one you may eat as many a's as you like, then you slip for free into room two to eat b's, then slip for free into room three to eat c's. The language is all strings of some a's, then some b's, then some c's, where any of the groups may be empty. In regular expression notation, which you will meet in lesson 09, that is a*b*c*.

Why free moves help: Try to build a plain DFA for a*b*c* and you need to think about every case: what happens when a b arrives while you are still in the a part, what happens if an a arrives after a c, and you need a dead state. With epsilon arrows the design almost writes itself: one room per block, glued together by free corridors. This gluing idea is the real reason epsilon-NFAs exist. They are a building tool. Later we turn them back into ordinary machines.

Epsilon-closure: The most important tool for this lesson is the epsilon-closure of a state, written ECLOSE(q). It is the set of all states you can reach from q using zero or more epsilon arrows and nothing else. Zero is allowed, so q itself is always in ECLOSE(q). For a set of states S, ECLOSE(S) is the union of ECLOSE(q) over all q in S. You can think of it as asking: if I am standing in this room, which rooms can I walk into without paying?

How to compute the closure: It is just graph search, which you know from Algorithms. Put q into a result set and onto a stack. Repeatedly pop a state p, look at every epsilon arrow from p to some r, and if r is not yet in the result, add it and push it. When the stack is empty, the result is ECLOSE(q). In pseudo-code: R = {q}; stack = [q]; while stack not empty: p = pop; for r in delta(p, epsilon): if r not in R: add r to R, push r. Every state is pushed at most once, so it is fast.

Closures in the example: Start from q0. It is in its own closure. The epsilon arrow takes us to q1, and from q1 another epsilon arrow takes us to q2. So ECLOSE(q0) = {q0, q1, q2}. From q1 we reach only q2 for free, so ECLOSE(q1) = {q1, q2}. From q2 there are no epsilon arrows at all, so ECLOSE(q2) = {q2}. Notice that closures follow chains: q0 reaches q2 through q1 even though there is no direct arrow from q0 to q2. Forgetting these chains is the number one mistake students make.

Running the machine: To process a string, keep a set of current states, just like for an NFA, but take closures at the right moments. Begin with ECLOSE({q0}). Then for each input symbol x: first collect every state reachable from the current set by one arrow labelled x, then take the epsilon-closure of that collection. After the last symbol, accept if the current set contains at least one accepting state. Formally, the extended transition function is delta-hat(q, epsilon) = ECLOSE(q), and delta-hat(q, wx) = ECLOSE of the union of delta(p, x) over all p in delta-hat(q, w).

A trace of aabc: Start: ECLOSE(q0) = {q0, q1, q2}. Read a: only q0 has an a arrow, it goes to q0, and the closure gives {q0, q1, q2}. Read a again: same thing, {q0, q1, q2}. Read b: only q1 has a b arrow, it goes to q1, closure {q1, q2}. Read c: only q2 has a c arrow, it goes to q2, closure {q2}. The input is finished and q2 is accepting, so aabc is accepted. Now try ca. Start {q0, q1, q2}, read c and get {q2}, then read a: q2 has no a arrow, so the set becomes empty, and an empty set can never accept. Rejected, as it should be, since an a cannot come after a c.

Acceptance of the empty string: With no input at all, the current set is just ECLOSE(q0) = {q0, q1, q2}, which contains q2. So the empty string is accepted, even though q0 itself is not an accepting state. This surprises many students. In an epsilon-NFA the start state can effectively be accepting through a free path. Always check the closure of the start state when you ask whether epsilon is in the language.

Removing epsilon moves: Epsilon-NFAs are not more powerful than plain NFAs. We can always remove the epsilon arrows and keep the same states. The new transition function is delta'(q, x) = ECLOSE( union of delta(p, x) for p in ECLOSE(q) ). In words: from q, first take any free walks, then pay for one real symbol x, then take any free walks again. The new accepting set F' contains every state q whose closure ECLOSE(q) contains an original accepting state. The start state stays q0.

The removal on our example: Using the closures above we get this table. From q0: on a, {q0, q1, q2}; on b, {q1, q2}; on c, {q2}. From q1: on a, nothing; on b, {q1, q2}; on c, {q2}. From q2: on a and b, nothing; on c, {q2}. All three states contain q2 in their closures, so all three become accepting. The result is an ordinary NFA with no epsilon arrows that still accepts exactly a*b*c*. For example, aabc goes q0, then {q0, q1, q2}, then again, then {q1, q2}, then {q2}, which is accepting. A computer check on every string up to length 8 agrees with the original machine.

Why the accepting set must grow: Suppose we forgot to make q0 and q1 accepting. Then the empty string would end in {q0}, which is not accepting, and we would wrongly reject it. The safe rule is simple: if a state can reach an accepting state for free, it must itself be accepting in the new machine.

Building union with epsilon: Now the fun part. Epsilon arrows let us snap machines together like Lego. Suppose N1 accepts language L1 and N2 accepts L2. Make a brand new start state s, and draw epsilon arrows from s to the start of N1 and to the start of N2. Keep all old accepting states. The new machine guesses, for free, which of the two machines to run. It accepts L1 union L2.

Building concatenation: To accept L1 L2, meaning a string from L1 followed by a string from L2, draw an epsilon arrow from every accepting state of N1 to the start of N2, and make the old accepting states of N1 non-accepting. Only N2's accepting states remain accepting. The machine reads a part of the input in N1 and, when it guesses the first part is complete, jumps for free into N2. The guess is fine because an NFA only needs one lucky path to accept.

Building star: To accept L1*, which means zero or more strings from L1 glued together, add a new start state s that is accepting, put an epsilon arrow from s to the old start, and put an epsilon arrow from every accepting state of N1 back to the old start. The back arrows let the machine run N1 again and again. The new accepting start state handles the empty string. A classic trap: simply making the old start state accepting is wrong in general, because the old start may have incoming arrows, and then strings that should be rejected sneak in. The fresh start state avoids this.

Where this leads: These three constructions prove that regular languages are closed under union, concatenation and star, a fact you met as a preview in lesson 04. They are also the heart of Thompson's construction, which turns any regular expression into an epsilon-NFA, and you will see it properly in lesson 10. And in the very next lesson, the subset construction will turn any epsilon-NFA into a DFA, by starting from ECLOSE(q0) and taking closures after every step.

Real life example 1, the bKash menu: When you dial *247#, you see a menu. Some screens wait for your key press, and some screens move on by themselves, for example a short message that says the request is processing and then shows the next screen without you pressing anything. Those automatic steps are like epsilon moves: the system changes state without reading any input from you. If you wanted to model the menu, the closure of a screen would be all the screens you could end up at before you press the next key.

Real life example 2, a number checker: A form that accepts amounts like 250, -40 or +15 can be built in pieces. One small machine handles an optional sign, one handles one or more digits. Optional means either a sign symbol or nothing at all, and the nothing is exactly an epsilon arrow that skips the sign machine. Then a concatenation epsilon glues the sign part to the digit part. Programmers who write lexers, the first stage of a compiler, think exactly this way, and you will meet that again in Compiler Design.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting that q is in its own closure. Second, stopping the closure after one epsilon step instead of following chains. Third, taking the closure only at the start and forgetting to take it after every symbol. Fourth, in epsilon removal, forgetting to grow the accepting set. Fifth, confusing epsilon the string with the empty set: an epsilon arrow is a free move, while the empty set as a result of delta means there is no move at all.

What exams ask: Typical questions give you a small epsilon-NFA and ask you to compute ECLOSE of every state, to trace a string and write the set after each symbol, to decide whether the empty string is accepted, to convert the machine into an equivalent NFA without epsilon moves, or to build an epsilon-NFA for the union, concatenation or star of two given machines. Write your sets clearly, step by step, and always say which closures you used.

Recap: An epsilon-NFA is an NFA that may also move for free on epsilon. The epsilon-closure of a state is everything reachable by zero or more free moves, found with a simple stack search. To run the machine, take closures at the start and after every symbol. Epsilon moves add convenience, not power: delta'(q, x) = ECLOSE(delta(ECLOSE(q), x)) removes them, with every state whose closure touches F becoming accepting. And epsilon arrows let us build machines for union, concatenation and star. Next up: turning all of this into a DFA.
key_points: An epsilon move changes state without reading any input symbol; it is optional, like every NFA move.
An epsilon-NFA is a 5-tuple whose transition function has type Q x (Sigma union {epsilon}) -> P(Q).
ECLOSE(q) is every state reachable from q by zero or more epsilon arrows, so q is always in it.
Run an epsilon-NFA by starting from ECLOSE(q0) and taking the closure again after every symbol.
Epsilon removal: delta'(q, x) = ECLOSE(delta(ECLOSE(q), x)), and q is accepting if ECLOSE(q) meets F.
Union: new start with epsilon arrows to both machines. Concatenation: epsilon from N1's accepting states to N2's start.
Star: a fresh accepting start state plus epsilon arrows from accepting states back to the old start.
Epsilon-NFAs, NFAs and DFAs all recognise exactly the regular languages.
lessons.tip: When you compute a closure, physically tick states on the diagram with a pencil and keep a small stack written beside it. Do not trust your eye to follow epsilon chains; follow the stack until it is empty.
lessons.task: Draw the epsilon-NFA for a*b*c* from this lesson on paper. Compute ECLOSE of each state, then trace the strings abbc, bca and the empty string, writing the set of states after every symbol. Finally, build an epsilon-NFA for (strings of a's of even length) union (strings of b's of odd length) using a new start state.

quiz.q: In an epsilon-NFA, ECLOSE(q) always contains:
options: Nothing if q has no epsilon arrows
quiz.explain: Zero epsilon moves are allowed, so q is always in its own closure.

quiz.q: States q0, q1, q2 with epsilon arrows q0->q1 and q1->q2 only. What is ECLOSE(q0)?
quiz.explain: Follow the chain: q0 reaches q1 for free, and q1 reaches q2 for free.

quiz.q: When removing epsilon moves, which states become accepting in the new NFA?
options: Every state whose epsilon-closure contains an original accepting state
Every state with an incoming epsilon arrow
quiz.explain: If a state can reach an accepting state for free, it must accept in the new machine.

quiz.q: To build an epsilon-NFA for L1 L2 from N1 and N2, you:
options: Add a new start with epsilon arrows to both machines
Add epsilon arrows from N1's accepting states to N2's start and make N1's accepting states non-accepting
Add epsilon arrows from N2's accepting states back to N1's start
quiz.explain: The machine finishes a piece in N1, then jumps for free into N2; only N2's accepting states remain.

quiz.q: For the a*b*c* epsilon-NFA, what is the set of current states after reading the string ab?
quiz.explain: Start {q0, q1, q2}; after a it is again {q0, q1, q2}; after b only q1 moves, to q1, and the closure is {q1, q2}.

lessons.title: Subset Construction (NFA to DFA)
lessons.content:
Imagine you are trying to find your friend at a crowded Eid fair. You do not know exactly where he is, but you know he is somewhere among a few stalls: maybe the balloon stall, maybe the fuchka stall. Instead of guessing one place, you keep a list of every place he could be. Each time you get a new clue, you update the whole list. You never guess, you just track the set of possibilities. That is exactly how we turn a nondeterministic machine into a deterministic one. The method is called the subset construction, or the powerset construction.

The big question: An NFA can be in many states at once, and an epsilon-NFA can even move for free. A DFA is much stricter: exactly one state at a time and exactly one move per symbol. It feels like NFAs should be stronger. Today we prove they are not. For every NFA there is a DFA that accepts exactly the same language. This result is due to Rabin and Scott, who published it in 1959, and it is one of the cornerstones of the whole course.

Recap: A DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) where delta(q, x) is a single state. An NFA has the same parts, but delta(q, x) is a set of states, possibly empty. An epsilon-NFA also allows arrows labelled epsilon, and ECLOSE(q), from lesson 06, is the set of states reachable from q by zero or more epsilon arrows. Simulating an NFA by hand already meant keeping a set of current states. The subset construction simply turns that habit into a machine.

The power-set idea: Let the NFA be N = (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F). We build a DFA D whose states are sets of N's states. If Q has n states, there are 2^n subsets, so D has at most 2^n states. The DFA state {q0, q2} literally means: right now, the NFA could be in q0 or in q2, and nowhere else. Since the set of possibilities after reading a string is completely determined by the string, each step is deterministic. The nondeterminism has been moved into the bookkeeping.

The rules for a plain NFA: The start state of D is {q0}. For a DFA state S and a symbol x, the move is delta_D(S, x) = the union of delta(p, x) over all p in S. In words, look at every NFA state you might be in, follow all of its x arrows, and collect every place you land. A DFA state S is accepting if S contains at least one accepting state of N, because then at least one path accepts. The empty set is a legal DFA state too. It has no way out, so it behaves like a dead state.

The rules with epsilon moves: If N has epsilon arrows, add closures. The start state of D becomes ECLOSE(q0). The move becomes delta_D(S, x) = ECLOSE( union of delta(p, x) for p in S ). So: follow the real x arrows, then take every free walk. Accepting states are the same as before: any set containing an accepting state of N. If you remember only one formula from today, remember this one, because the plain-NFA version is just the special case where every closure is the state itself.

Only reachable subsets: Writing all 2^n subsets is wasteful. Most of them can never be reached from the start. The smart method is lazy: start with the start set, compute its moves on every symbol, and add a new row to the table only when a new set appears. Keep a to-do list of sets whose rows are not yet filled. When the list is empty, you are done. In pseudo-code: todo = [start]; seen = {start}; while todo not empty: S = take from todo; for each x: T = move(S, x); record S -x-> T; if T not in seen: add T to seen and to todo.

Worked example, the NFA: Alphabet {0, 1}. We want strings that end in 01. The NFA has three states q0, q1, q2, start q0, accepting q2. From q0, on 0 it can go to q0 or q1, and on 1 it goes to q0. From q1, on 1 it goes to q2, and on 0 there is no move. From q2 there are no moves at all. The idea: q0 loops over everything, and at some moment the NFA guesses that the final 01 is starting and jumps to q1.

Worked example, step one: The start set is {q0}. Call it A. On 0, q0 goes to {q0, q1}. That is new, call it B. On 1, q0 goes to {q0}, which is A again. So the first row is: A on 0 goes to B, A on 1 goes to A.

Worked example, step two: Now fill in B = {q0, q1}. On 0: q0 gives {q0, q1}, q1 gives nothing, so the union is {q0, q1}, which is B. On 1: q0 gives {q0}, q1 gives {q2}, so the union is {q0, q2}. That is new, call it C. Second row: B on 0 goes to B, B on 1 goes to C.

Worked example, step three: Fill in C = {q0, q2}. On 0: q0 gives {q0, q1}, q2 gives nothing, so we get B. On 1: q0 gives {q0}, q2 gives nothing, so we get A. Third row: C on 0 goes to B, C on 1 goes to A. No new sets appeared, so the to-do list is empty and we stop. Only C contains q2, so C is the only accepting state.

The finished DFA: Three states instead of the eight possible subsets. A = {q0} means nothing useful has been seen, B = {q0, q1} means the last symbol was 0, and C = {q0, q2} means the last two symbols were 01. Trace 1001: start A, read 1 to A, read 0 to B, read 0 to B, read 1 to C. We end in C, so 1001 is accepted, which is correct since it ends in 01. Trace 0110: A, B, C, A, B, ends in B, rejected. I checked this DFA by computer against the rule ends with 01 on every string up to length 10, and they agree.

Example with epsilon moves: Take the epsilon-NFA for a*b*c* from lesson 06, with states q0, q1, q2, loops on a, b, c respectively, and epsilon arrows q0 to q1 and q1 to q2. The start set is ECLOSE(q0) = {q0, q1, q2}. On a, only q0 moves, to q0, and the closure is {q0, q1, q2} again. On b we get ECLOSE(q1) = {q1, q2}. On c we get {q2}. From {q1, q2}: a gives the empty set, b gives {q1, q2}, c gives {q2}. From {q2}: a and b give the empty set, c gives {q2}. From the empty set, every symbol stays in the empty set.

Reading that result: We got four DFA states, {q0, q1, q2}, {q1, q2}, {q2} and the empty set, out of eight possible subsets. The first three contain q2, so they are accepting. The empty set is the dead state. Read in words, the DFA says: I am still allowed a's, or I am in the b part, or I am in the c part, or something went wrong. This is the same DFA you would design by hand, but here it came out mechanically. A brute-force check on every string up to length 7 confirms it accepts exactly a*b*c*.

Why it is correct: The key claim is that after reading any string w, the DFA is in exactly the set of NFA states reachable on w. Proof by induction on the length of w. For the empty string the DFA is in the start set, which is exactly the states reachable without reading anything. If the claim holds for w, then reading one more symbol x applies the move rule, which collects exactly the states reachable from those by x followed by free moves. So the claim holds for wx. Since the DFA accepts when the set contains an accepting NFA state, and the NFA accepts when some reachable state is accepting, they accept the same strings.

Equivalence of DFA and NFA: Every DFA is already an NFA, one where every set has exactly one element. And now every NFA, with or without epsilon moves, has an equivalent DFA. So the three models recognise exactly the same class of languages: the regular languages. This gives us freedom. When designing, use an NFA, because it is short and easy to think about. When running on a real computer, or when you need to complement a language by swapping accepting states, convert to a DFA first.

The blow-up example: Is 2^n ever really needed? Yes. Let L_n be the strings over {0, 1} whose n-th symbol from the end is 1. An NFA needs only n + 1 states: a start state p0 that loops on 0 and 1, an arrow from p0 to p1 on 1 that guesses this 1 is the important one, then arrows p1 to p2 up to p_(n-1) to p_n on any symbol, with p_n accepting. The subset construction on this NFA reaches all 2^n subsets that contain p0. Running it by computer gives 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 DFA states for n from 1 to 6.

Why no DFA can do better: Take any two different strings u and v of length n. They differ at some position i, say u has 1 there and v has 0. Append i - 1 zeros to both. Now position i has become the n-th symbol from the end, so u followed by those zeros is in L_n and v followed by them is not. If a DFA reached the same state after u and after v, it would give the same answer after the extra zeros, which is impossible. So all 2^n strings of length n need different states. The DFA must have at least 2^n states. This is the price of determinism.

Real life example 1, cricket scoreboards: Suppose a commentator only knows that a ball could have gone for a single, or could have been a wide that also gave a run, until the umpire signals. A careful scorer does not pick one. He writes down every possible scoreboard state, and when the umpire signals, he crosses out the impossible ones. His notebook state at each moment is a set of possibilities, and it changes deterministically with each new signal. That is the subset construction in a scorer's notebook.

Real life example 2, search tools: The command grep and many text editors search for patterns written as regular expressions. A common method is to turn the pattern into an NFA, and then either simulate the set of states on the fly, or build DFA states lazily, only for the subsets that the actual text needs. That way a fast DFA-like scan is possible without paying for all 2^n states up front. Lexers in compilers often build the full DFA ahead of time, because the token patterns are fixed and the speed is worth it.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting the epsilon-closure of the start state, or forgetting the closure after a move. Second, marking only the set that equals F as accepting, instead of every set that contains at least one accepting state. Third, dropping the empty set. It is a real state and must have its own row, looping to itself on every symbol, unless your teacher allows leaving dead states out. Fourth, writing all 2^n subsets when the question asks only for reachable ones. Fifth, treating {q0, q1} and {q1, q0} as different. They are the same set.

What exams ask: Expect a small NFA or epsilon-NFA, three to five states, and a request to convert it into a DFA, showing the transition table, the start state and the accepting states. You may then be asked to trace a string on both machines, to state the maximum number of DFA states, or to explain the 2^n lower bound with the n-th symbol from the end language. Draw your table with columns for each symbol and name each new subset as soon as it appears.

Recap: The subset construction builds a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states. Start with ECLOSE(q0). Move with ECLOSE of the union of all x arrows. Accept any set containing an NFA accepting state. Generate only reachable subsets with a to-do list. The result proves that DFAs, NFAs and epsilon-NFAs are equally powerful. The DFA can need 2^n states, and for the n-th symbol from the end language it really does. Next lesson: the DFA we get is often bigger than necessary, so we learn to minimise it.
key_points: The subset construction builds a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states; it was published by Rabin and Scott in 1959.
Start state: ECLOSE(q0). Move: delta_D(S, x) = ECLOSE(union of delta(p, x) for p in S).
A DFA state is accepting if it contains at least one accepting state of the NFA.
Only build reachable subsets, using a to-do list; the empty set is a legal dead state.
For the ends-with-01 NFA the construction gives just 3 DFA states: {q0}, {q0, q1}, {q0, q2}.
DFAs, NFAs and epsilon-NFAs recognise exactly the same languages: the regular languages.
An n-state NFA can need up to 2^n DFA states; the n-th symbol from the end is 1 language forces 2^n.
lessons.tip: Make a table with one column per symbol and give each new subset a capital letter the moment it appears. Before filling a row, write its subset again beside the letter, so you never confuse which NFA states are inside.
lessons.task: Draw the NFA for strings over {a, b} whose second symbol from the end is a: p0 loops on a and b, p0 goes to p1 on a, p1 goes to p2 on a or b, and p2 accepts. Run the subset construction by hand, list every reachable subset, and check that you get 4 DFA states. Then trace abb and bab on your DFA.

quiz.q: In the subset construction, which DFA states are accepting?
options: Only the set equal to F
Every set containing at least one NFA accepting state
quiz.explain: If the set contains an accepting NFA state, some path accepts, so the DFA accepts.

quiz.q: An NFA has 5 states. What is the maximum number of states of the DFA from the subset construction?
quiz.explain: DFA states are subsets of the 5 NFA states, and there are 2^5 = 32 subsets.

quiz.q: For an epsilon-NFA, the DFA start state is:
options: The set of all accepting states
quiz.explain: The NFA can be in any state reachable from q0 for free before reading input.

quiz.q: For the ends-with-01 NFA (q0 loops on 0,1; q0 -0-> q1; q1 -1-> q2), what is the move of {q0, q1} on 1?
quiz.explain: q0 on 1 gives q0 and q1 on 1 gives q2, so the union is {q0, q2}.

quiz.q: Why does any DFA for the n-th symbol from the end is 1 language need at least 2^n states?
options: Because DFAs cannot have dead states
Because any two different strings of length n can be extended by the same suffix so that one is accepted and the other is not
quiz.explain: Distinguishable strings must reach different states, and all 2^n strings of length n are pairwise distinguishable.

lessons.title: DFA Minimization
lessons.content:
Imagine a school with six classrooms, but two of them teach exactly the same lessons, with the same teacher's notes, at the same speed, and a third one is locked and no student can ever get in. The headmaster would happily merge the two identical rooms and close the locked one. Nobody would notice any difference, and the school would be cheaper to run. DFA minimization does exactly this for machines. It finds states that behave identically, merges them, and throws away states nobody can reach, without changing which strings are accepted.

Why minimise at all: The subset construction from lesson 07 often produces DFAs with more states than needed, and DFAs designed by hand can contain duplicates too. A smaller DFA uses less memory and is easier to read, test and draw. There is also a beautiful theoretical bonus. For every regular language there is one minimal DFA, unique up to renaming the states. That means we can test whether two DFAs accept the same language by minimising both and comparing the results.

Before we start: The algorithms in this lesson assume a complete DFA, one where every state has exactly one arrow for every symbol. If your DFA is missing arrows, first add a dead state that loops to itself on every symbol and send all missing arrows there. Remember from lesson 03 that delta-hat(q, w) means the state reached from q after reading the whole string w.

Unreachable states: A state is unreachable if no string leads to it from the start state. Such states can never affect the answer, so delete them first. Finding them is a simple graph search, breadth-first or depth-first, from the start state along the arrows. Any state not visited is unreachable. This step is cheap and must come first, because unreachable states can confuse the later steps and make the final answer bigger than it should be.

Equivalent states: Two states p and q are equivalent if, for every string w, delta-hat(p, w) is accepting exactly when delta-hat(q, w) is accepting. In plain words: if you drop a robot into p and another into q and feed them the same input, they always agree, yes or yes, no or no, whatever the input. Equivalent states can be merged into one. Note the word every: one string where they disagree is enough to break equivalence.

Distinguishable states: If there is at least one string w for which one of delta-hat(p, w) and delta-hat(q, w) is accepting and the other is not, then p and q are distinguishable, and w is called a distinguishing string. The simplest case is w = epsilon: an accepting state and a non-accepting state are always distinguishable, by the empty string. All minimisation algorithms grow from this one observation, and then push it backwards through the arrows.

The backward rule: Suppose on some symbol x, p goes to p' and q goes to q', and we already know p' and q' are distinguishable by a string w. Then p and q are distinguishable by the string xw, because reading x takes them to p' and q', and then w makes them disagree. So distinguishability spreads backwards along arrows. Keep applying this rule until nothing new appears. Whatever is still not distinguished at the end is equivalent.

Our example DFA: Alphabet {0, 1}. States A, B, C, D, E, F, start A, only C accepting. Transitions: A on 0 goes to B, on 1 to A. B on 0 goes to D, on 1 to C. C on 0 goes to E, on 1 to A. D on 0 goes to D, on 1 to C. E on 0 goes to D, on 1 to C. F on 0 goes to C, on 1 to F. Take a minute to stare at it. You might already suspect that B, D and E do the same job. Let us prove it properly.

Step 1, remove unreachable states: From A we can reach A and B. From B we reach D and C. From C we reach E and A. From D and E we reach only D and C. Nothing ever goes into F, so F is unreachable. Delete it. We now have five states: A, B, C, D, E.

Step 2, the table-filling method: Draw a triangle-shaped table with one cell for each unordered pair of states. With five states there are 5 times 4 divided by 2, which is 10 pairs. Round 0: mark every pair where one state accepts and the other does not. C is the only accepting state, so we mark AC, BC, CD and CE. Four marks.

Step 2 continued, round 1: For each unmarked pair, check both symbols. Pair AB: on 1, A goes to A and B goes to C, and AC is marked, so mark AB. Pair AD: on 1, A goes to A and D goes to C, mark AD. Pair AE: same reason, mark AE. Pair BD: on 0, B goes to D and D goes to D, the same state; on 1, both go to C. Nothing marked, so leave it. Pair BE: on 0 both go to D, on 1 both go to C. Leave it. Pair DE: on 0 both go to D, on 1 both go to C. Leave it.

Step 2 finished, round 2: Go over the unmarked pairs BD, BE and DE again. Their successor pairs are only DD and CC, which are not pairs of different states at all, so nothing new can be marked. Stop. The unmarked pairs BD, BE and DE are equivalent. Since equivalence is an equivalence relation, as you know from Discrete Math, we can group them into one class {B, D, E}. The final classes are {A}, {C} and {B, D, E}.

Step 3, build the minimal DFA: Make one new state per class. Call them A, B for the class {B, D, E}, and C. Copy arrows from any member, since all members agree. A on 0 goes to B, on 1 to A. B on 0 goes to B, on 1 to C. C on 0 goes to B because C went to E, which is in class B, and on 1 to A. Start state A, accepting state C. Three states instead of six. Look closely and you will recognise it: it is the DFA for strings ending in 01 from lesson 07. A computer check on every string up to length 10 confirms the original six-state DFA, the minimal one and the rule ends with 01 all agree.

Partition refinement: A second method, often called Moore's algorithm, works with groups instead of pairs. Start with two groups: accepting states and non-accepting states. Then repeatedly split a group if two of its members go, on some symbol, into different groups. Stop when no group splits. On our example: start with {C} and {A, B, D, E}. On 1, A goes to A, which is in the big group, but B, D and E go to C, in the other group. So split into {A} and {B, D, E}. Now check {B, D, E}: on 0 they all go to D, on 1 they all go to C. No more splits. Same answer, as it must be.

Which method to use: Table filling is easy to draw on paper for up to about eight states, and exam questions love it. Partition refinement is faster to do by hand for bigger machines and is the idea behind real implementations. Hopcroft's algorithm, a clever version of partition refinement, runs in O(n log n) time for a fixed alphabet, where n is the number of states. Simple table filling takes about O(n^2) work per round.

Uniqueness of the minimal DFA: Here is a theorem: if two complete DFAs with no unreachable states are both minimal for the same language, they are identical except for the names of the states. Mathematicians say they are isomorphic. So it does not matter which DFA you start from or which algorithm you use, the minimal one you get is always the same machine. This is what makes equivalence testing possible: minimise both DFAs and check whether they are the same up to renaming.

The Myhill-Nerode idea: There is an even deeper way to see all this, without any machine. For a language L, call two strings x and y equivalent if for every string z, xz is in L exactly when yz is in L. In words, no continuation can tell them apart. This relation splits all strings into classes. The Myhill-Nerode theorem says L is regular if and only if the number of classes is finite, and the number of classes equals the number of states of the minimal DFA.

Myhill-Nerode on our language: For strings ending in 01, there are three classes. Class one: strings ending in 0, like 0 or 110. Class two: strings ending in 01. Class three: everything else, which means the empty string, the string 1, and strings ending in 11. Check that the classes are really different: 0 and 01 are separated by z = epsilon, since 01 is in L but 0 is not. The empty string and 0 are separated by z = 1: the string 1 is not in L, but 01 is. So three classes, three states, exactly our minimal DFA.

A preview of non-regular languages: Take a^n b^n, the strings with some a's followed by the same number of b's. The strings a, aa, aaa and so on are all in different classes, because a^i b^i is in the language but a^j b^i is not when i and j differ. Infinitely many classes means, by Myhill-Nerode, that the language is not regular. Lesson 11 gives another tool for this, the pumping lemma, so here we just mention it and move on.

Real life example 1, the vending machine: A shop near a Dhaka university has a snack machine that takes 5 and 10 taka coins and gives a packet at 20 taka. An engineer designs states like paid 0, paid 5 after a 5, paid 5 after a 10 that was refunded, and so on, and ends up with twelve states. Many of them remember the same thing: the amount paid so far. Minimisation merges them, leaving just one state for each amount paid so far, such as 0, 5, 10 or 15 taka. A smaller machine means simpler wiring and fewer bugs.

Real life example 2, checking two programs: Two students in a lab both submit a DFA for the same assignment, one with nine states and one with five. Did they solve the same problem? Instead of testing a thousand strings, the teacher minimises both. If the minimal DFAs are the same up to renaming, the two answers accept exactly the same language. Tools in hardware design use the same idea to check that an optimised circuit still behaves like the original one.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to delete unreachable states before minimising. Second, minimising an incomplete DFA without first adding a dead state. Third, in table filling, checking only one round; you must repeat until a full round marks nothing new. Fourth, starting partition refinement with one group for every state instead of just the two groups accepting and non-accepting. Fifth, merging states just because they have the same arrows out on one symbol; they must agree on every symbol, and keep agreeing all the way down.

What exams ask: Expect a DFA with five to eight states, maybe with an unreachable state and a pair or two of duplicate states, and a request to minimise it using table filling or partition refinement, showing every round. Other common questions: give a distinguishing string for two states, state the Myhill-Nerode theorem, list the equivalence classes of a simple language, or explain why the minimal DFA is unique.

Recap: Delete unreachable states, then find equivalent states and merge them. Two states are distinguishable if some string makes one accept and the other reject; accepting versus non-accepting is the start, and distinguishability spreads backwards through arrows. Table filling marks pairs, partition refinement splits groups, and both stop when nothing changes. The minimal DFA is unique up to renaming, and its states correspond to the Myhill-Nerode classes. Next lesson, we leave machines for a while and write languages as regular expressions.
key_points: Minimise in two steps: delete unreachable states, then merge equivalent states.
States p and q are equivalent if for every string w, delta-hat(p, w) and delta-hat(q, w) are both accepting or both not.
Accepting and non-accepting states are always distinguishable, by the empty string.
If p -x-> p' and q -x-> q' and p', q' are distinguishable, then p, q are distinguishable too.
Table filling marks pairs round by round; partition refinement starts with {F, Q - F} and splits groups.
The minimal complete DFA of a regular language is unique up to renaming states.
Myhill-Nerode: L is regular iff it has finitely many equivalence classes, and that number equals the minimal DFA's state count.
lessons.tip: For every pair you mark in table filling, write the symbol and the already-marked pair that caused it, like AB: 1 -> AC. It slows you down for a minute but makes mistakes easy to spot and earns method marks in exams.
lessons.task: Copy the six-state DFA A to F from this lesson onto paper. Delete the unreachable state, then minimise it twice, once with table filling and once with partition refinement, and check that both give three states. Finally, for the pair A and B, find a shortest distinguishing string and check it by tracing.

quiz.q: Which pair of states is always distinguishable?
options: An accepting state and a non-accepting state
Two states with the same arrows
quiz.explain: The empty string already separates them: one accepts it, the other does not.

quiz.q: Partition refinement starts with which groups?
options: Each state in its own group
quiz.explain: The first split is by the empty string, which separates F from Q - F.

quiz.q: In the lesson's example, why is the pair AB marked?
options: On 1, A goes to A and B goes to C, and AC is already marked
quiz.explain: A and C are distinguishable, so the backward rule makes A and B distinguishable by the string 1.

quiz.q: The Myhill-Nerode theorem says a language is regular if and only if:
options: It has finitely many equivalence classes of strings
quiz.explain: Finitely many classes means a finite DFA, and the number of classes is the size of the minimal DFA.

quiz.q: How many Myhill-Nerode classes does the language of strings over {0,1} ending in 01 have?
quiz.explain: Strings ending in 0, strings ending in 01, and everything else: three classes, matching the 3-state minimal DFA.

lessons.title: Regular Expressions
lessons.content:
Imagine you lost a phone number. You remember it started with 017 and ended with 45, but nothing in between. You type a search into your contacts: 017, then anything, then 45. Without knowing it, you just described a set of strings with a short pattern. That is what a regular expression is: a compact formula that names a language. DFAs and NFAs describe languages as machines. Regular expressions describe them as algebra, like writing 2x + 3 instead of drawing a graph.

Why learn them: Regular expressions, or regex for short, are everywhere. Programmers use them to search code, to check form inputs like email addresses and phone numbers, to find errors in huge log files, and to split text into tokens in a compiler. In theory, they give us a third way to describe exactly the regular languages, next to DFAs and NFAs. The proof that all three are equally powerful comes in lesson 10. Today we learn to read and write them well.

Quick recap of language operations: From lesson 02, for languages L and M, the union L + M (also written L union M) contains strings in either one. The concatenation LM contains every string xy with x in L and y in M. The Kleene star L* contains every string made by gluing together zero or more strings from L, so the empty string epsilon is always in L*. Regular expressions are just names for languages built with these three operations.

The formal definition: Over an alphabet Sigma, the regular expressions are defined step by step, which is an inductive definition. Base cases: the symbol empty set is a regular expression and means the empty language with no strings. The symbol epsilon is a regular expression and means the language containing only the empty string. Every symbol a in Sigma is a regular expression meaning the language {a}. Inductive cases: if R and S are regular expressions, then so are (R + S), meaning the union, (RS), meaning the concatenation, and (R*), meaning the star. Nothing else is a regular expression. We write L(R) for the language that R describes.

Two shortcuts: R+ means one or more copies of R, so R+ = RR*. And in many books and tools, R? means zero or one copy, so R? = (epsilon + R). These are not new powers, just shorter spellings. Careful: in theory books + between two expressions means union, while + written after an expression as a superscript means one or more. Most textbooks avoid confusion by raising the second one. In this lesson, a plus between two expressions always means union.

Precedence: Just as multiplication binds tighter than addition in arithmetic, star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union. So 01* + 1 means (0(1*)) + 1. Its language is 0, 01, 011, 0111 and so on, plus the single string 1. It does not mean (01)* + 1, and it does not mean 0(1* + 1). When in doubt, add parentheses. They never hurt, and examiners will not punish extra brackets.

Empty set versus epsilon: These two are different and students mix them up all the time. L(empty set) has zero strings. L(epsilon) has exactly one string, the empty one. Some rules follow. R + empty set = R, because adding nothing changes nothing. R empty set = empty set, because you cannot pick a string from an empty language to glue on. R epsilon = R, because gluing the empty string changes nothing. And empty set star = epsilon, because star always includes zero copies, which gives the empty string.

Reading regular expressions, part 1: Let Sigma = {0, 1}. The expression (0 + 1)* means any string at all, since each position can be 0 or 1, any number of times. So (0 + 1)*01 means any string that ends in 01. The expression 0*1(0 + 1)* means some zeros, then a 1, then anything: that is exactly the strings containing at least one 1. The expression 1*01*: some ones, a single zero, some ones, which means strings with exactly one 0.

Reading regular expressions, part 2: The expression ((0 + 1)(0 + 1))* glues together pairs of symbols, so it means all strings of even length, including the empty string. The expression (0 + 1)*1(0 + 1)(0 + 1) means a 1 followed by exactly two more symbols at the end, so the third symbol from the end is 1. You met this language as an NFA in lesson 05. Notice how short the expression is compared to its DFA, which needs eight states.

Writing regular expressions, even number of 0s: Over {0, 1}, describe strings with an even number of 0s. Idea: the zeros come in pairs, and ones can appear anywhere. The answer is 1*(01*01*)*. Read it as: some leading ones, then any number of blocks, where each block is a 0, some ones, another 0, some ones. Each block adds exactly two zeros, and the leading 1* handles strings with no zeros at all.

Writing regular expressions, no two 1s in a row: Think about what a 1 must be followed by: if it is not the last symbol, it must be followed by a 0. So the string is made of pieces 0 and 10, and may end with a single extra 1. The answer is (0 + 10)*(epsilon + 1). Test it: 0101 is 0, 10, then a final 1, accepted. 0110 cannot be split into 0 and 10 pieces, rejected. Good.

How to check your answer: For each expression in this lesson I tested the claim by computer. For every string of 0s and 1s up to length 8, I compared Python's re.fullmatch on the expression, with + written as the | symbol and epsilon as an empty alternative, against a direct check of the property. All of them agreed. You can do the same on paper with a small list: write five strings that should be in, five that should not, and test both lists.

Algebraic identities: Like ordinary algebra, regular expressions have laws. Union is commutative and associative: R + S = S + R. Union is idempotent: R + R = R. Concatenation is associative, but not commutative: 01 is not the same as 10. Concatenation distributes over union from both sides: R(S + T) = RS + RT and (S + T)R = SR + TR. The empty set is the identity for union and epsilon is the identity for concatenation.

Star identities: (R*)* = R*, because starring twice adds nothing new. R*R* = R*. epsilon + RR* = R*, which says a star is either empty or one copy followed by more. (a + b)* = (a*b*)* = (a* + b*)*, all meaning every string over a and b. a(ba)* = (ab)*a, both meaning strings like a, aba, ababa. And a*(a + b)* = (a + b)*. I checked each of these by comparing both sides on every string over {a, b} up to length 8.

A false identity: Students often think (ab)* = a*b*. It is wrong. (ab)* contains abab, but a*b* does not, since in a*b* every a comes before every b. And a*b* contains aab, but (ab)* does not. To disprove an identity, one string that is in one side and not the other is enough. To prove one, you need an argument for every string, or a chain of known identities.

Simplifying with identities: Simplify (epsilon + 0)(0)*. Using distributivity, it is 0* + 00*. Since 00* is already inside 0*, the union is just 0*. Another one: (0 + 1)*(0 + 1)* simplifies to (0 + 1)*, by the rule R*R* = R*. Simplification is a common exam task. Write each step and name the rule you used.

Theory regex versus tool regex: Real tools like grep, Python's re module, JavaScript and Java use a richer syntax. The union is written with a vertical bar |, the dot . means any single character, [0-9] means any digit, a+ means one or more a's, a? means optional, a{3} means exactly three a's, and ^ and $ anchor the start and end of a line. Most of these are just shortcuts and stay within regular languages. A pattern like 01[3-9][0-9]{8} matches a Bangladeshi mobile number: 01, then an operator digit from 3 to 9, then eight more digits, eleven digits in all.

Where tools go beyond theory: Some tool features are not regular at all. A backreference like (.+)\1 in Python matches a string followed by an exact copy of itself, such as abcabc. That is the language of strings ww, which is not regular, and no DFA can recognise it. That is why such patterns can run very slowly: the engine has to backtrack. So in the theory of computation, regex always means the pure version with union, concatenation and star only.

Real life example 1, a bKash-style form: An app asks for your mobile number and a 4 digit PIN. The developer writes two patterns: 01[3-9][0-9]{8} for the number, and [0-9]{4} for the PIN. When you type 0171234567, which has only ten digits, the number pattern fails and the app shows a red warning before sending anything to the server. Behind the scenes the regex library turns each pattern into an automaton, very much like the constructions in lessons 06, 07 and 10.

Real life example 2, reading server logs: A system administrator at a Dhaka data centre has a log file with a million lines. She wants only the lines that mention an error or a timeout. She runs grep -E "ERROR|TIMEOUT" server.log, and in a second she has her answer. The pattern ERROR|TIMEOUT is exactly the theory expression ERROR + TIMEOUT, a union of two strings. With patterns like [0-9]+ ms she can also pull out response times.

Common mistakes: First, confusing the empty set with epsilon. Second, forgetting precedence and reading 01* as (01)*. Third, assuming concatenation is commutative. Fourth, writing a regex that accepts too much, like (0 + 1)*11(0 + 1)* when you wanted no 11 at all; that one is the opposite, the strings that do contain 11. Fifth, forgetting the empty string, for example writing (0 + 10)* for no two 1s in a row and missing strings like 1 and 01 that end in a single 1.

What exams ask: Write a regular expression for a described language. Describe in words the language of a given expression. Decide whether two expressions are equal, proving with identities or disproving with a counterexample string. Simplify an expression. List all strings of length at most 3 in L(R). Explain the difference between empty set and epsilon. Converting between regex and automata comes in the next lesson.

Recap: A regular expression is built from empty set, epsilon and single symbols, using union, concatenation and star. Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union. (0 + 1)* means everything; add pieces before and after to say what you want. Identities like (R*)* = R* and epsilon + RR* = R* let you simplify, while one counterexample string is enough to disprove an identity. Real tools add shortcuts, and backreferences even step outside the regular languages. Next: proving that regex and automata describe exactly the same languages.
key_points: Regular expressions are built from empty set, epsilon and single symbols using union (+), concatenation and star.
Precedence: star first, then concatenation, then union; 01* + 1 means (0(1*)) + 1.
L(empty set) has no strings, L(epsilon) has only the empty string, and empty set star = epsilon.
Concatenation is associative and distributes over union, but it is not commutative.
Useful identities: (R*)* = R*, R*R* = R*, epsilon + RR* = R*, a(ba)* = (ab)*a; but (ab)* is not a*b*.
Example answers: even number of 0s is 1*(01*01*)*; no two 1s in a row is (0 + 10)*(epsilon + 1).
Tool regex adds shortcuts like [0-9], ?, {n}; backreferences go beyond regular languages.
lessons.tip: After writing a regex, always test it with two short lists: three strings that must match, including the shortest one, often epsilon, and three strings that must not match. Most wrong answers fail on the empty string or on a string of length one.
lessons.task: Write regular expressions over {0, 1} for: strings starting with 1 and ending with 0; strings with exactly two 1s; strings whose length is a multiple of 3. Then test each one on your phone or computer with any online regex tester, using | for union and ^...$ around the pattern, on at least six strings.

quiz.q: What does 01* + 1 mean, using standard precedence?
quiz.explain: Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union.

quiz.q: Which language is L(empty set star)?
quiz.explain: Star always includes zero copies, which gives the empty string, and nothing else.

quiz.q: Which expression describes strings over {0,1} with no two 1s in a row?
quiz.explain: Pieces 0 and 10 never create 11, and an optional single 1 can end the string.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a valid identity?
quiz.explain: abab is in (ab)* but not in a*b*, so they are different.

quiz.q: The Python backreference pattern (.+)\1 matches strings of the form ww. What is true?
options: The language ww is not regular, so no DFA recognises it
It can be written with union, concatenation and star
It matches every string of even length
quiz.explain: Backreferences need to remember an unbounded string, which goes beyond the regular languages.

lessons.title: Regex and Finite Automata Equivalence (Kleene's Theorem)
lessons.content:
Imagine two friends describing the route from Mirpur to Motijheel. One draws a map with arrows at every junction. The other writes a sentence: take the main road, keep going straight, turn left after the flyover. Both describe the same journey. In this course, automata are the maps and regular expressions are the sentences. Today we prove that every map can be turned into a sentence and every sentence into a map. This is Kleene's theorem, and it closes the circle of the first part of the course.

Kleene's theorem: A language is regular, meaning some DFA accepts it, if and only if some regular expression describes it. Stephen Kleene proved this in the 1950s. Together with lesson 07, which showed that DFAs, NFAs and epsilon-NFAs are equally powerful, we get a loop of conversions: regular expression to epsilon-NFA, epsilon-NFA to DFA, DFA to regular expression.
