Any description can be turned into any other.

Plan of the lesson: For the direction regex to automaton, we use Thompson's construction, which builds an epsilon-NFA piece by piece. For the direction automaton to regex, we learn two methods: state elimination using a generalised NFA, and Arden's theorem, which solves equations over regular expressions. You already know the glue we need from lesson 06: epsilon arrows for union, concatenation and star.

Thompson's construction, the shape rule: Ken Thompson described this method in 1968, and it was used in early text editors and later in the Unix tool grep. Every machine it builds has exactly one start state and exactly one accepting state, no arrows go into the start state and no arrows leave the accepting state. Keeping this shape makes the pieces easy to snap together, like Lego blocks with one plug on each side.

Thompson's base cases: For the regular expression empty set, make a start state and an accepting state with no arrow between them, so nothing is ever accepted. For epsilon, make a start state and an accepting state joined by one epsilon arrow. For a single symbol a, make a start state and an accepting state joined by one arrow labelled a. Every base machine has exactly two states.

Thompson's inductive cases: Suppose we already have machines N(R) and N(S). Union R + S: add a new start state with epsilon arrows to the starts of N(R) and N(S), and a new accepting state with epsilon arrows from both old accepting states. Concatenation RS: add an epsilon arrow from the accepting state of N(R) to the start of N(S); the start of N(R) is the new start and the accepting state of N(S) is the new accepting state. Star R*: add a new start s and a new accepting state f, with epsilon arrows from s to the old start, from s directly to f, which allows zero copies, from the old accepting state back to the old start, which allows repeats, and from the old accepting state to f.

Counting states: Each base case adds 2 states, and so does each union and each star. With the epsilon-link version of concatenation shown here, concatenation adds no new states. So the machine has at most twice as many states as there are symbols and operators in the expression. That means the size grows linearly with the length of the expression, never exponentially. Some books, like the Dragon Book for compilers, merge the two touching states at each concatenation, which saves one state per concatenation. Both versions are correct.

Worked example, a(b + c)*: Build from the inside out. Machine for a: states 1 and 2 with an a arrow. Machine for b: states 3 and 4. Machine for c: states 5 and 6. Union b + c: new start 7 with epsilon arrows to 3 and 5, new accept 8 with epsilon arrows from 4 and 6. Star: new start 9 and new accept 10, with epsilon arrows 9 to 7, 9 to 10, 8 to 7 and 8 to 10. Finally concatenation: an epsilon arrow from 2 to 9. Start state 1, accepting state 10. That is 10 states and 12 arrows. I built exactly this machine in Python and compared it with re.fullmatch for a(b|c)* on every string over {a, b, c} up to length 8. They agree.

Tracing the Thompson machine: Take the string abc. Start: ECLOSE(1) = {1}. Read a: go to 2, closure {2, 9, 7, 3, 5, 10}. Read b: only 3 moves, to 4, closure {4, 8, 7, 3, 5, 10}. Read c: only 5 moves, to 6, closure {6, 8, 7, 3, 5, 10}. The set contains 10, so abc is accepted. The string ba would die at once, because from {1} nothing moves on b.

A bigger example: For (a + b)*abb, the classic exam expression, Thompson's construction with epsilon-linked concatenation gives 14 states. The merged version from the Dragon Book gives 11. After the subset construction from lesson 07 and minimisation from lesson 08, both end up as the same minimal DFA, because the minimal DFA of a language is unique. A computer check confirms the 14-state machine accepts exactly the strings ending in abb, for every string up to length 9.

From automaton to regex, the GNFA: A generalised NFA, or GNFA, is like an NFA whose arrows are labelled with whole regular expressions instead of single symbols. Reading an arrow labelled R means reading any string in L(R). We first put the automaton into a standard form: add a new start state with an epsilon arrow to the old start, add a new accepting state with epsilon arrows from every old accepting state, and merge parallel arrows between the same two states into one arrow labelled with the union of their labels.

State elimination, the rule: Now remove the old states one by one. To remove a state k, look at every pair of states i and j where i has an arrow into k labelled R1 and k has an arrow to j labelled R3. Let R2 be the label of k's self-loop, or epsilon if there is none, and let R4 be the existing label from i to j, or the empty set if there is none. Replace the arrow from i to j with the label R1 R2* R3 + R4. In words: go from i into k, loop in k as often as you like, then leave to j, or take the old direct road. When only the new start and the new accepting state remain, the label between them is the answer.

State elimination, worked example: Take the DFA for strings over {0, 1} that end in 1. It has states q0, the start, and q1, accepting. q0 on 0 stays at q0, q0 on 1 goes to q1, q1 on 1 stays at q1, q1 on 0 goes back to q0. Add a new start S with S to q0 on epsilon, and a new accept F with q1 to F on epsilon. Eliminate q0 first. Arrows into q0 come from S, labelled epsilon, and from q1, labelled 0. The self-loop of q0 is 0. The arrow out of q0 goes to q1, labelled 1. So S to q1 becomes 0*1, and q1 to q1 becomes 1 + 00*1, combining the old loop 1 with the new path through q0.

Finishing the example: Now eliminate q1. Into q1 comes S with label 0*1. Its self-loop is 1 + 00*1. Out of q1 goes F with label epsilon. So S to F becomes 0*1(1 + 00*1)*. That is our answer. It looks very different from the simple (0 + 1)*1, but both describe strings that end in 1. A computer check with re.fullmatch on every string up to length 10 confirms they are equal. The order of elimination changes how the answer looks, never the language it describes.

Arden's theorem: This is a neat algebra trick. Let P and Q be regular expressions, and suppose epsilon is not in L(P). Then the equation R = Q + RP has exactly one solution, R = QP*. Why does this make sense? R is either Q, or something in R followed by P. Unfold it: Q, then QP, then QPP, and so on, which is QP*. The condition on P matters: if P could be empty, the solution would not be unique.

Setting up equations: For each state q, let q also stand for the set of strings that lead from the start to q. Each state gets one equation: it is the union of p x for every arrow from p to q labelled x, plus epsilon if q is the start state. For the ends-in-1 DFA: q0 = epsilon + q0 0 + q1 0, and q1 = q0 1 + q1 1. The answer is the union of the accepting states, here just q1.

Solving with Arden: The equation q1 = q0 1 + q1 1 has the form R = Q + RP with Q = q0 1 and P = 1. So q1 = q0 1 1*. Substitute into the first equation: q0 = epsilon + q0 0 + q0 1 1* 0 = epsilon + q0 (0 + 11*0). Apply Arden again with Q = epsilon and P = 0 + 11*0, to get q0 = (0 + 11*0)*. Therefore q1 = (0 + 11*0)*11*. Again it looks different, and again a computer check over all strings up to length 10 shows it is exactly the strings ending in 1.

A second Arden example: The DFA for an even number of 0s has states E, the start and accepting, and O. E on 1 stays, E on 0 goes to O, O on 1 stays, O on 0 goes back to E. Equations: E = epsilon + E1 + O0, and O = E0 + O1. Arden on the second gives O = E01*. Substituting: E = epsilon + E(1 + 01*0), so E = (1 + 01*0)*. That is another correct expression for the even-zeros language, different from the 1*(01*01*)* of lesson 09, but checked to be equal on all strings up to length 10.

Real life example 1, building a lexer: In a compiler, the first stage reads your program text and cuts it into tokens: keywords, numbers, names. Tools like lex and flex let programmers write each token as a regular expression, for example [0-9]+ for a number. The tool then does exactly this lesson: it builds an NFA for the patterns, converts it to a DFA, minimises it, and produces fast code. You will build one in Compiler Design.

Real life example 2, safe search engines: Google's RE2 library, used in several Google products, deliberately supports only true regular expressions, with no backreferences. That lets it use automata and guarantee running time linear in the length of the input. Backtracking engines can take exponential time on some patterns, which has crashed real websites. Kleene's theorem is the reason RE2's promise is possible: every pure regex has an automaton.

Common mistakes: In Thompson's construction, forgetting the s to f arrow in star, which loses the empty string, or reusing an old state as the new start instead of adding a fresh one. In state elimination, forgetting the R4 part, which deletes existing direct arrows, or forgetting the self-loop of the eliminated state. With Arden, applying it when P contains epsilon, or writing R = PQ* instead of QP*. And finally, panicking when your answer looks different from the model answer: different expressions can be equal.

What exams ask: Build a Thompson epsilon-NFA for a short expression such as (a + b)*abb or ab* + c. Convert a two or three state DFA to a regular expression by state elimination, showing each step. Write the Arden equations for a DFA and solve them. State and explain Kleene's theorem, and draw the conversion cycle regex to epsilon-NFA to DFA to regex.

Recap: Kleene's theorem says regular expressions and finite automata describe exactly the same languages. Thompson's construction turns a regex into an epsilon-NFA with one start and one accept, at most two states per symbol or operator. State elimination on a GNFA turns an automaton into a regex using the label R1 R2* R3 + R4. Arden's theorem solves R = Q + RP as R = QP* when P does not contain epsilon. Next lesson: the pumping lemma, which proves that some languages are not regular at all.
key_points: Kleene's theorem: a language is regular if and only if some regular expression describes it.
Thompson's machines have one start state with no incoming arrows and one accepting state with no outgoing arrows.
Thompson's star adds new s and f with epsilon arrows s to old start, s to f, old accept to old start, old accept to f.
Thompson's construction uses at most two states per symbol or operator, so the size is linear in the expression.
State elimination: removing k replaces the label from i to j with R1 R2* R3 + R4.
Arden's theorem: if epsilon is not in L(P), then R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP*.
Different-looking expressions such as 0*1(1 + 00*1)* and (0 + 1)*1 can describe the same language.
lessons.tip: In state elimination, before removing a state, list every in-arrow and every out-arrow of it in two columns. Then make one new label for each in-out pair. Writing the pairs first stops you from forgetting a path.
lessons.task: Build the Thompson epsilon-NFA for ab* + c on paper and count its states (you should get 10 with epsilon-linked concatenation). Then take the 2-state DFA for an even number of 1s over {0, 1} and find a regular expression twice: once by state elimination and once with Arden's theorem. Test both answers on six strings.

quiz.q: Kleene's theorem states that:
options: A language is regular if and only if some regular expression describes it
Every NFA has a smaller DFA
Regular expressions cannot describe infinite languages
quiz.explain: Regular expressions and finite automata describe exactly the same class of languages.

quiz.q: In Thompson's construction for R*, which epsilon arrow lets the machine accept the empty string?
options: New start s directly to new accept f
quiz.explain: The arrow from s straight to f skips the inner machine, giving zero copies.

quiz.q: In state elimination, removing state k with in-label R1, self-loop R2, out-label R3 and old direct label R4 gives:
quiz.explain: Enter k, loop any number of times, leave to j, or take the existing direct arrow.

quiz.q: Arden's theorem gives which solution to R = Q + RP, when epsilon is not in L(P)?
quiz.explain: Unfolding gives Q, QP, QPP, and so on, which is QP*.

quiz.q: Which expression does state elimination give for the ends-in-1 DFA when q0 is eliminated first?
quiz.explain: Eliminating q0 gives S to q1 = 0*1 and the loop 1 + 00*1; eliminating q1 then gives 0*1(1 + 00*1)*.

lessons.title: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
lessons.content:
Imagine a rickshaw puller in Dhaka who can remember only five things at once. You ask him to count how many passengers got on today and then tell you exactly the same number of passengers got off. After passenger number six he starts forgetting. His memory is limited, so he cannot keep a count that grows forever. A finite automaton is exactly like this rickshaw puller. It has a fixed number of states, and that fixed number is its whole memory. In this lesson we learn the most famous tool for proving that some languages are too hard for any finite automaton: the pumping lemma for regular languages.

Why we need a proof tool: In the earlier lessons we built DFAs, NFAs and regular expressions, and we saw in lesson 10 that they all describe the same family, the regular languages. Building a machine proves a language is regular. But how do you prove a language is NOT regular? You cannot try every DFA, because there are infinitely many. You need an argument that works for all DFAs at once. The pumping lemma gives such an argument. It describes a property that every regular language must have. If a language fails that property, it cannot be regular.

The pigeonhole idea: Recall the pigeonhole principle from Discrete Mathematics. If you put 6 pigeons into 5 holes, some hole gets at least two pigeons. Now think of a DFA with p states reading a string of length p or more. Before reading anything it is in the start state, and after each symbol it is in some state. Reading p symbols means visiting p + 1 states counting the start. With only p different states, some state must be visited twice. So the path through the machine contains a loop.

Loops can be repeated: Suppose the DFA is in state q after reading the part x, then reads a part y and comes back to the same state q, and then reads the rest z and ends in an accepting state. Because y brings the machine from q back to q, the machine cannot tell whether it went around that loop once, twice, ten times or zero times. So xz, xyz, xyyz, xyyyz and so on all end in the same accepting state. All of them are in the language. Going around the loop again is called pumping, as if you pump extra copies of y into the string, or pump them out.

The formal statement: If L is a regular language, then there is a number p, called the pumping length, such that every string s in L with length at least p can be split into three parts, s = xyz, satisfying three conditions. First, for every i ≥ 0, the string x y^i z is in L. Second, |y| ≥ 1, so y is not empty. Third, |xy| ≤ p, so the loop appears within the first p symbols. Here y^i means i copies of y written one after another, and y^0 is the empty string. One valid choice of p is the number of states of a DFA for L.

Why each condition matters: The condition |y| ≥ 1 makes sure pumping actually changes the string. Without it you could pick y empty and nothing would happen. The condition |xy| ≤ p comes from the pigeonhole argument: the first repeated state appears while reading the first p symbols. This condition is very useful in proofs, because it tells us where y must lie. The condition for all i ≥ 0 includes i = 0, pumping down, which removes y completely. Students often forget that i = 0 is allowed, and sometimes it gives the easiest contradiction.

A regular language that pumps fine: Take L as the strings over {a, b} whose number of a's is divisible by 3. A DFA with 3 states counts a's modulo 3, so p = 3 works. Take s = abaa, which has 3 a's and length 4. Suppose we split x = empty, y = a, z = baa. Then pumping down gives xz = baa, which has only 2 a's, so this particular split fails. That is no problem, because the lemma only promises that SOME split works, not every split. Choose x = a, y = b, z = aa, with |xy| = 2 ≤ 3 and |y| = 1. Pumping y adds or removes only b's, so every string x b^i z still has exactly 3 a's and stays in L. The lemma holds, as it must for a regular language.

The lemma is a one-way street: The pumping lemma says regular implies pumpable. It does not say pumpable implies regular. Some non-regular languages also satisfy the pumping conditions. So you can never use the pumping lemma to prove a language IS regular. You only use it in the other direction: if a language is not pumpable, it is not regular. To prove a language is regular, build a DFA, an NFA or a regular expression, or use closure properties.

The adversary game: Proofs with the pumping lemma are easiest to think of as a game between you and an opponent who claims L is regular. Step 1: the opponent picks p. You do not know its value, so you must treat it as an unknown number. Step 2: you pick one string s in L with |s| ≥ p, cleverly, using p. Step 3: the opponent splits s into xyz any way they like, obeying |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1. You must handle every possible split. Step 4: you pick one i so that x y^i z is not in L. If you can always win, L is not regular.

Example 1, a^n b^n: Let L = { a^n b^n : n ≥ 0 }, equal a's followed by equal b's. Assume L is regular with pumping length p. Choose s = a^p b^p, which is in L and has length 2p ≥ p. Any split with |xy| ≤ p puts x and y entirely inside the first p symbols, which are all a's. So y = a^k for some k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p. Pump with i = 2: x y^2 z = a^(p+k) b^p. This has more a's than b's, so it is not in L. Contradiction, so L is not regular.

Seeing it with numbers: Pretend p = 4. Then s = aaaabbbb. One allowed split is x = a, y = aa, z = abbbb, with |xy| = 3 ≤ 4. Pumping up with i = 2 gives aaaaaabbbb, six a's and four b's, outside L. Pumping down with i = 0 gives aabbbb, two a's and four b's, also outside L. Whatever split the opponent picks, y is made of a's only, so the counts break.

Example 2, palindromes: Let L be the palindromes over {a, b}, strings that read the same forwards and backwards, like aba or abba. Assume L is regular with pumping length p. Choose s = a^p b a^p, a palindrome of length 2p + 1. Since |xy| ≤ p, y lies inside the first block of a's, so y = a^k with k ≥ 1. Pump with i = 2: we get a^(p+k) b a^p. The b is no longer in the middle, the left block is longer than the right, and the reverse a^p b a^(p+k) is a different string. So it is not a palindrome. Contradiction, palindromes are not regular.

Choosing the string well: Notice why we did not choose s = a^p, which is also a palindrome. Every pumped version of a^p is still a string of a's only, which is still a palindrome. The opponent would win. The art of the proof is choosing s so that the condition |xy| ≤ p traps y in a part where changing its length breaks the language. A good habit is to put p copies of one symbol at the very start, so y must be made of that symbol.

Example 3, a^(n^2): Let L = { a^(n^2) : n ≥ 0 }, strings of a's whose length is a perfect square: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 and so on. Assume L is regular with pumping length p. Choose s = a^(p^2). Any split has y = a^k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p, because |y| ≤ |xy| ≤ p. Pump with i = 2: the length becomes p^2 + k. Now p^2 < p^2 + k ≤ p^2 + p, and p^2 + p is smaller than (p + 1)^2 = p^2 + 2p + 1. So the new length lies strictly between two neighbouring squares, p^2 and (p + 1)^2, and cannot be a square. For example with p = 3, the length becomes 9 + k with k from 1 to 3, giving 10, 11 or 12, none of them squares, since 16 is the next square. Contradiction, L is not regular.

Other famous non-regular languages: The same method shows that { a^n b^m : n < m }, { ww }, balanced parentheses and { a^q : q is prime } are not regular. Each needs to remember an amount that grows without limit, and a finite automaton can only count up to a fixed bound.

Using closure properties instead: Sometimes a clever shortcut is easier than pumping. Regular languages are closed under intersection, union, complement and more. Let EQ be the strings over {a, b} with equal numbers of a's and b's. If EQ were regular, then EQ intersected with the regular language a*b* would also be regular. But that intersection is exactly a^n b^n, which we proved is not regular. So EQ is not regular. This avoids choosing a string that EQ would let the opponent wriggle out of.

Myhill-Nerode as another tool (lesson 8): Two strings u and v are distinguishable for L if some suffix w puts exactly one of uw and vw in L. A language is regular exactly when it has finitely many classes of mutually indistinguishable strings. For a^n b^n, the strings a, aa, aaa, and so on are pairwise distinguishable: a^i followed by b^i is in L, but a^j followed by b^i is not when i ≠ j. Infinitely many distinguishable strings means infinitely many classes, so no DFA works. Unlike the pumping lemma, Myhill-Nerode is an if and only if, so it can also prove regularity.

Real life example 1, bKash PIN counting: A bKash app might lock your account after 3 wrong PIN attempts. That rule needs only a counter from 0 to 3, a few states, and is perfectly regular. But suppose a rule said: accept a transaction log only if the number of cash-in entries equals exactly the number of cash-out entries, with no limit on the length. That is like EQ above. No fixed number of states can track an unbounded difference. Real software uses an integer variable, which is more memory than any finite automaton has, and that is fine, because real programs are not finite automata.

Real life example 2, checking brackets in code: When you write a program in C or Python, the compiler must check that every opening bracket has a matching closing one, even nested deeply like ((((x)))). Balanced brackets are not regular, by a pumping argument with s = (^p )^p, just like a^n b^n. This is exactly why a regular expression alone cannot validate source code nesting, and why compilers use context-free grammars, which start in the next lesson.

Common mistakes in exams: First, choosing the split yourself. You choose s and i, but the opponent chooses x, y and z, so your argument must cover all valid splits. Second, choosing a specific number for p, such as p = 5. The proof must work for every p. Third, choosing a string shorter than p, or a string not in L. Fourth, trying to use the lemma to prove that a language is regular, which is impossible. Fifth, forgetting the condition |xy| ≤ p, which is usually what forces y into one block and makes the proof short.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: state the pumping lemma for regular languages; prove that a^n b^n, ww, palindromes, a^(n^2) or a^(2^n) are not regular; explain why the lemma cannot show a language is regular; and decide whether a given language is regular, then either build a DFA or prove it is not. For the last type, first ask yourself whether the language needs unbounded counting. If yes, try pumping; if no, try to build a machine.

Recap: Every DFA has finitely many states, so any long accepted string forces a repeated state and a loop. That loop gives the pumping lemma: s = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and x y^i z in L for all i ≥ 0. To show a language is not regular, play the adversary game: pick s smartly, handle every split, and pick an i that breaks the language. Closure properties and Myhill-Nerode are two more weapons. Next we meet context-free grammars, which can describe a^n b^n and balanced brackets easily.
key_points: A DFA with p states reading p or more symbols must repeat a state (pigeonhole), creating a loop.
Pumping lemma: if L is regular, there is p such that every s in L with |s| ≥ p splits as xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, and x y^i z in L for all i ≥ 0.
The lemma only proves languages NOT regular; it can never prove a language regular.
Proof game: opponent picks p, you pick s, opponent picks the split, you pick i.
a^n b^n, palindromes, a^(n^2), ww and balanced parentheses are not regular.
i = 0 (pumping down) is allowed and sometimes gives the easiest contradiction.
Closure properties (e.g. EQ ∩ a*b* = a^n b^n) and Myhill-Nerode are other ways to prove non-regularity.
lessons.tip: Always write the four game steps as headings in your answer: p unknown, choose s, any split xyz, choose i. Examiners look for exactly these steps, and writing them stops you from accidentally choosing the split yourself.
lessons.task: On paper, prove that { a^n b^(2n) : n ≥ 0 } is not regular using s = a^p b^(2p). Then try p = 3 with a concrete split, write the pumped strings for i = 0 and i = 2, and check by counting that they fall outside the language.

quiz.q: In the pumping lemma for regular languages, which condition is NOT part of the statement?
options: x y^i z is in L for all i ≥ 0
quiz.explain: z may be empty. The conditions are |y| ≥ 1, |xy| ≤ p and x y^i z in L for every i ≥ 0.

quiz.q: In a pumping lemma proof, who chooses the split s = xyz?
options: The opponent, so you must handle every valid split
You, so you pick the easiest split
Nobody, it is always x empty
quiz.explain: You choose s and i, but the split is chosen by the opponent, so the argument must work for all splits with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1.

quiz.q: To prove a^n b^n is not regular we pick s = a^p b^p. Why must y contain only a's?
options: Because z must contain all the b's by definition
Because |xy| ≤ p and the first p symbols are all a's
quiz.explain: The condition |xy| ≤ p puts x and y inside the first p symbols, which are all a's.

quiz.q: A language satisfies the pumping conditions. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing certain; some non-regular languages also pump
quiz.explain: The lemma is one-way: regular implies pumpable, not the other way round.

quiz.q: For L = { a^(n^2) }, pumping s = a^(p^2) with i = 2 gives length p^2 + k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p. Why is that not a square?
options: Because it lies strictly between p^2 and (p + 1)^2
quiz.explain: p^2 < p^2 + k ≤ p^2 + p < p^2 + 2p + 1 = (p + 1)^2, so no square fits.

lessons.title: Context-Free Grammars
lessons.content:
Think about how a child learns to make sentences. Nobody gives them a list of every sentence in the world. Instead they learn rules: a sentence is a subject followed by an action, a subject can be a name like Rahim or a word like the boy, and so on. With a handful of rules they can build millions of sentences, even sentences nobody has said before. A context-free grammar is exactly this idea made precise. It is a small set of replacement rules that can generate a whole infinite language.

Why we need grammars: In the last lesson we proved that a^n b^n, palindromes and balanced parentheses are not regular. No finite automaton and no regular expression can describe them. But these languages are everywhere: every programming language needs matched brackets, matched begin and end, and nested if statements. Context-free grammars, CFGs for short, describe all of these easily. They are the main tool for defining the syntax of programming languages, for building compilers, and for processing structured text such as JSON, XML and HTML.

The four parts: A context-free grammar is a 4-tuple G = (V, Σ, R, S). V is a finite set of variables, also called non-terminals, usually written as capital letters like S, A, B. Σ is a finite set of terminals, the actual symbols of the strings we want, like a, b, ( or +. V and Σ have no symbols in common. R is a finite set of rules, also called productions, each of the form A → w, where A is a single variable and w is any string of variables and terminals, possibly empty. S, a member of V, is the start variable.

How rules are used: You begin with the start variable S. At each step you choose any variable in your current string and replace it with the right side of one of its rules. You keep going until no variables are left. The final string, made only of terminals, is generated by the grammar. One replacement is written with a double arrow, for example aSb ⇒ aaSbb, and a sequence of replacements is called a derivation. We study derivations and their tree pictures in detail in the next lesson. The language of G, written L(G), is the set of all terminal strings that can be derived from S.

Short notation: When a variable has several rules, we write them on one line separated by a vertical bar. So S → aSb | ε means two rules, S → aSb and S → ε. The symbol ε means the empty string, so the rule S → ε lets S simply disappear. A rule like this is called an epsilon-production.

Example 1, a^n b^n: The language { a^n b^n : n ≥ 0 } that defeated finite automata needs just one variable: S → aSb | ε. To derive aaabbb we go S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaaSbbb ⇒ aaabbb, using the first rule three times and then the epsilon rule once. Every use of S → aSb adds one a on the left and one b on the right at the same time, so the counts always stay equal. The strings of length up to 8 that this grammar generates are exactly ε, ab, aabb, aaabbb and aaaabbbb.

Why the grammar is correct: To show L(G) equals a language L you must prove two things. First, every string G generates is in L, usually by induction on the number of derivation steps: each step keeps the form a^k S b^k, and the last step removes S. Second, every string in L can be generated: for a^n b^n, use the first rule n times and then the epsilon rule. Both directions matter. A grammar that generates too much or too little is wrong.

Small changes, new languages: Changing one rule changes the language. S → aSbb | ε adds two b's for every a, so it generates { a^n b^(2n) : n ≥ 0 }, such as abb and aabbbb. S → aSb | aS | ε lets you add extra a's on the left at any time, so it generates a^i b^j with i ≥ j, such as aab or aaabb. Playing with rules like this is the best way to build intuition.

Example 2, palindromes: Palindromes over {a, b} read the same in both directions. Build them from the middle out: S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε. The rules aSa and bSb wrap a matching pair around a smaller palindrome. The middle is a single a, a single b, or nothing, which gives odd and even lengths. To derive ababa: S ⇒ aSa ⇒ abSba ⇒ ababa. A finite automaton could not do this, because it must remember the whole first half, but a grammar handles it with five rules.

Example 3, balanced parentheses: The grammar S → (S) | SS | ε generates all properly nested strings of brackets. The rule (S) wraps a balanced string in one more pair, the rule SS puts two balanced strings side by side, and ε is the empty balanced string. To derive ()(()) we go S ⇒ SS ⇒ (S)S ⇒ ()S ⇒ ()(S) ⇒ ()((S)) ⇒ ()(()). The number of balanced strings with n pairs is the Catalan number: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14 for n = 0 to 4, so this grammar generates 23 strings of length up to 8.

Example 4, equal a's and b's: For EQ, all strings over {a, b} with as many a's as b's, one grammar is S → aSbS | bSaS | ε. The idea: a non-empty string in EQ starts with a or b, and we can match that first symbol with the point where the counts first become equal again. The parts in between and after are again balanced. We checked by computer that this grammar generates exactly the strings of EQ up to length 8, including ones like ba, abba and baab.

Example 5, arithmetic expressions: A grammar for expressions with plus, times, brackets and a single name a is: E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a. Here E stands for expression, T for term and F for factor. It generates a + a * a, (a + a) * a and a * (a + a), but not broken strings like a + * a. The three levels encode that multiplication binds tighter than addition. A simpler grammar E → E + E | E * E | (E) | a describes the same strings but is ambiguous, which is the topic of the next lesson.

Why context-free: The name comes from the shape of the rules. The left side is always a single variable, so a variable can be replaced no matter what symbols stand around it, its context. More powerful grammars, called context-sensitive grammars, allow rules like aAb → aab that only apply when A sits between a and b. They appear later in the Chomsky hierarchy, lesson 24.

Context-free languages: A language is context-free if some context-free grammar generates it. So a^n b^n, palindromes, balanced parentheses, EQ and the arithmetic expressions are all context-free languages, CFLs for short. In lesson 17 we meet the matching machine, the pushdown automaton, which is a finite automaton plus a stack. Not every language is context-free: a^n b^n c^n is the classic example, proved in lesson 19.

Every regular language is context-free: Take any DFA. Make one variable for each state. For each transition from state Q on symbol a to state R, add the rule Q → aR. For each accepting state Q, add Q → ε. The start variable is the start state. For strings over {a, b} with an even number of a's, a DFA with states E (even) and O (odd) gives E → aO | bE | ε and O → aE | bO. Grammars of this shape, with at most one variable at the right end, are called right-linear or regular grammars. So regular languages sit inside the context-free languages, and the inclusion is strict because a^n b^n is context-free but not regular.

Building grammars from pieces: Complicated languages can often be split. For a union L1 ∪ L2, if S1 generates L1 and S2 generates L2, add S → S1 | S2. For a concatenation, add S → S1 S2. For a star, add S → S S1 | ε. For example { a^n b^n c^m : n, m ≥ 0 } is a^n b^n followed by any number of c's: S → XC, X → aXb | ε, C → cC | ε. This gives ε, c, ab, abc, aabbcc and so on. These closure properties are studied properly in lesson 18.

BNF in programming languages: Programmers write grammars in a notation called Backus-Naur Form, BNF, first used to describe the language ALGOL 60. Variables appear in angle brackets and the arrow becomes ::=, for example <expr> ::= <expr> + <term> | <term>. Language specifications for C, Java and Python use BNF or extended variants of it. A compiler's parser reads your code and checks it against such a grammar. The fast parsing methods called LL and LR belong to the Compiler Design course; here we only care about what grammars can describe.

Real life example 1, a tiny English grammar: Take rules SENTENCE → SUBJECT VERB OBJECT, SUBJECT → Rahim | Karim, VERB → eats | buys, OBJECT → rice | fish. This grammar generates 2 times 2 times 2 = 8 sentences, such as Rahim buys fish. Add a rule OBJECT → OBJECT and OBJECT, and suddenly the language is infinite: Rahim buys fish and rice and fish. Linguist Noam Chomsky studied grammars like these in the 1950s, and his work became the foundation of this part of computer science. Real human languages are much messier, but the idea is the same.

Real life example 2, nested JSON from an app: When the Pathao or bKash app talks to its server, the data often travels as JSON, like {"user": {"name": "Rina", "balance": 500}}. Objects can contain objects, which can contain lists, which contain more objects, to any depth. The rules of JSON are given as a context-free grammar. A rule such as value → object | array | string | number and object → { members } lets values nest inside each other, just like S → (S) nests brackets. That is why a JSON parser is built from a grammar, not from one regular expression.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting the base case. S → aSb alone generates nothing, because S never disappears. Second, generating too much. S → aS | Sb | ε does not generate a^n b^n. It generates a*b*, any number of a's followed by any number of b's, because the a's and b's are added independently. Third, writing a terminal on the left side of a rule, which is not allowed in a CFG. Fourth, forgetting to check both directions when proving a grammar correct.

What exams ask: Give the formal 4-tuple of a grammar. Write a CFG for a language such as a^n b^(2n), a^i b^j with i ≠ j, palindromes, or strings with equal numbers of a's and b's. Show a derivation of a given string. Describe in words the language of a given grammar. Prove that a grammar generates a stated language, usually by induction. Explain why every regular language is context-free by turning a DFA into a right-linear grammar.

Recap: A context-free grammar G = (V, Σ, R, S) uses rules A → w that replace a single variable regardless of context. Starting from S and replacing variables until only terminals remain generates the strings of L(G). Grammars easily describe languages that finite automata cannot, like a^n b^n, palindromes and balanced parentheses, and they define the syntax of real programming languages through BNF. Next lesson we look closely at derivations, parse trees, and what happens when one string has two different trees.
key_points: A CFG is a 4-tuple G = (V, Σ, R, S): variables, terminals, rules A → w, and a start variable.
A derivation starts at S and repeatedly replaces one variable by a right side until only terminals remain; L(G) is all such strings.
S → aSb | ε generates a^n b^n, which no finite automaton can recognise.
Palindromes: S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε. Balanced parentheses: S → (S) | SS | ε.
Context-free means the left side is a single variable, replaced regardless of its neighbours.
Every regular language is context-free (DFA to right-linear grammar), but not the other way round.
Programming language syntax is written in BNF, a notation for context-free grammars.
lessons.tip: When you design a grammar, test it on paper with the three shortest strings that should be in the language and one string that should not. Most wrong grammars fail on one of these four checks.
lessons.task: Write a CFG for { a^n b^m : m = n + 1 }, for example b, abb, aabbb. Derive aabbb step by step, then list every string your grammar generates up to length 5 and check that each one has exactly one more b than a's.

quiz.q: Which language does S → aSb | ε generate?
options: All strings with equal a's and b's
quiz.explain: Each use of aSb adds one a and one b, and ε ends the derivation, so the counts are equal and n = 0 is allowed.

quiz.q: In a context-free grammar, what can the left side of a rule be?
options: A terminal followed by a variable
Any string with at least one variable
quiz.explain: Context-free rules have the form A → w with a single variable A on the left.

quiz.q: Which grammar generates exactly the balanced parentheses?
quiz.explain: (S) nests, SS places side by side, and ε is the base case. The others miss strings like (()) or never finish.

quiz.q: What language does S → aS | Sb | ε generate?
options: a*b*, any a's followed by any b's
Strings with more a's than b's
quiz.explain: a's and b's are added independently, so the counts are not tied together.

quiz.q: Why is every regular language context-free?
options: Because a DFA's transitions can be written as right-linear rules Q → aR and Q → ε
quiz.explain: Each state becomes a variable, each transition a rule Q → aR, and each accepting state gets Q → ε.

lessons.title: Derivations, Parse Trees and Ambiguity
lessons.content:
Read this sign aloud: "Fresh fish and rice for 100 taka." Does 100 taka buy both fish and rice, or is only the rice 100 taka? The words are the same, but there are two ways to group them, and the two groupings mean different things. Humans sort this out from context and common sense. A computer cannot. When a compiler reads 2 + 3 * 4, it must know for certain whether to compute (2 + 3) * 4 = 20 or 2 + (3 * 4) = 14. This lesson is about how grammars show the structure of a string, and what goes wrong when one string can have two structures.

Derivations again: In the last lesson we met derivations: start from S and keep replacing variables using rules. A single step is written with ⇒, and when several steps are taken we write ⇒* for zero or more steps. A string made of variables and terminals that appears during a derivation is called a sentential form. When a sentential form has more than one variable, we have a choice about which one to replace first. That choice does not change the final string, but it changes the order of the steps.

Leftmost derivations: In a leftmost derivation we always replace the leftmost variable. Take the expression grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a. The leftmost derivation of a + a * a is: E ⇒ E + T ⇒ T + T ⇒ F + T ⇒ a + T ⇒ a + T * F ⇒ a + F * F ⇒ a + a * F ⇒ a + a * a. That takes 8 steps. At every step, look at the leftmost capital letter: that is the one that gets replaced.

Rightmost derivations: In a rightmost derivation we always replace the rightmost variable. For the same string: E ⇒ E + T ⇒ E + T * F ⇒ E + T * a ⇒ E + F * a ⇒ E + a * a ⇒ T + a * a ⇒ F + a * a ⇒ a + a * a. Again 8 steps, using exactly the same rules, just in a different order. Rightmost derivations matter in compiler design, because bottom-up LR parsers effectively build a rightmost derivation in reverse; that story belongs to the Compiler Design course.

Parse trees: A derivation is a list of steps, but what we really care about is the structure, and a picture shows it better. A parse tree, also called a derivation tree, is built like this. The root is labelled with the start variable. Every internal node is labelled with a variable, and if the node is A and its children, from left to right, are X1, X2, ..., Xk, then A → X1 X2 ... Xk must be a rule. The leaves are terminals, or ε when a rule A → ε was used. Reading the leaves from left to right gives the yield of the tree, which is the derived string.

Drawing a tree in words: For a + a * a in the layered grammar, the root E has three children: E, +, and T. The left E goes down E → T → F → a. The right T has three children: T, *, and F, and each of those goes down to a. Written with brackets, the tree is E( E(T(F(a))) + T( T(F(a)) * F(a) ) ). Notice that the multiplication sits lower in the tree, inside the right subtree of the plus. Lower means computed first. So this tree says a + (a * a), which is exactly the usual school rule.

One tree, many derivations: A single parse tree can be produced by many different derivations, depending on the order of replacements. But each parse tree has exactly one leftmost derivation and exactly one rightmost derivation. That is why leftmost derivations are a handy way to name trees: two different trees for the same string means two different leftmost derivations, and the other way round.

Ambiguity defined: A grammar is ambiguous if some string in its language has two or more different parse trees. Equivalently, some string has two or more different leftmost derivations. Ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not of the string alone. One string with two trees is enough to make the whole grammar ambiguous.

The classic ambiguous grammar: Consider E → E + E | E * E | (E) | a. It generates the same strings as the layered grammar, but now a + a * a has two leftmost derivations. First: E ⇒ E + E ⇒ a + E ⇒ a + E * E ⇒ a + a * E ⇒ a + a * a. Here the top rule is the plus, so the tree means a + (a * a). Second: E ⇒ E * E ⇒ E + E * E ⇒ a + E * E ⇒ a + a * E ⇒ a + a * a. Here the top rule is the times, so the tree means (a + a) * a. With a values 2, 3 and 4 in that order, the first tree gives 14 and the second gives 20.

How bad can it get: Ambiguity grows fast. In the grammar E → E + E | E * E | (E) | a, the string a + a + a has 2 parse trees and a + a + a + a has 5. The string a * a + a * a also has 5. In general, a chain of n operators has a Catalan number of trees: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 for n = 1 to 5. We counted these with a small program to be sure. For addition alone the trees all compute the same sum, but for subtraction they do not: (8 - 3) - 2 = 3 while 8 - (3 - 2) = 7.

Why ambiguity is a problem: A compiler uses the parse tree to decide what the program means: which operation happens first, which else belongs to which if. If the grammar allows two trees, the meaning is not defined by the grammar. Also, most efficient parsing methods require an unambiguous grammar, and conflicts in parser generators are often a sign of ambiguity. So language designers either remove the ambiguity from the grammar or add an explicit rule that says which tree to pick.

Removing ambiguity with precedence levels: The fix for expressions is the layered grammar we started with. Use one variable per precedence level: E for sums, T for products, and F for the smallest units, names and bracketed expressions. A plus can only appear at the E level and a times only at the T level, so a times can never be the parent of a plus unless brackets are used. We checked by computer that this grammar generates exactly the same 60 strings up to length 7 as the ambiguous one, and that each of them has exactly one parse tree.

Associativity: The layered grammar also fixes the direction of grouping. The rule E → E + T has the recursion on the left, so a + a + a is grouped as (a + a) + a. This is called left associativity, which is what we want for minus and divide: 8 - 3 - 2 should be 3. If we wanted right associativity, as for a power operator where 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is usually read as 2 ^ (3 ^ 2), we would write the recursion on the right, like P → F ^ P | F.

The dangling else: Many languages have the rules S → if E then S | if E then S else S | other. Now read: if E then if E then other else other. Does the else belong to the inner if or the outer if? Both are allowed by the grammar, so there are two parse trees. In the first, the outer if has no else and the inner if has one. In the second, the outer if owns the else. If the condition of the outer if is false, the two trees do different things.

Fixing the dangling else: Languages like C and Java use the rule that an else belongs to the nearest unmatched if. You can build this into the grammar by splitting statements into matched ones, M, where every if has its else, and unmatched ones, U: S → M | U, M → if E then M else M | other, U → if E then S | if E then M else U. A then-part that is followed by an else must be matched, so the else can only attach to the nearest if. We checked that this grammar generates the same strings as the original up to length 9 and gives each exactly one tree. Python avoids the problem differently, by using indentation to show which if an else belongs to.

Inherent ambiguity: Sometimes we can find an unambiguous grammar for the same language, as with expressions. But some context-free languages have no unambiguous grammar at all. Such a language is called inherently ambiguous. The standard example is { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k }. Strings like a^n b^n c^n satisfy both conditions, and it can be proved that every grammar for this language gives some of them two parse trees. The proof is long and not usually asked; just remember the example and the definition.

A hard limit: You might hope for a program that reads any grammar and tells you whether it is ambiguous. No such program can exist. Deciding ambiguity of context-free grammars is undecidable, a fact that will make more sense after lessons 22 to 24. In practice, tools like parser generators detect conflicts for restricted grammar classes, and designers fix them by hand.

Real life example 1, the calculator on your phone: Type 2 + 3 × 4 into the basic calculator on most smartphones and you get 14, because it follows precedence: multiplication first. Some very simple calculators instead apply each operation as soon as you press the next key, giving 20. The difference is exactly the two parse trees of the ambiguous grammar. A good calculator app, like a compiler, works with an unambiguous grammar or fixed precedence rules so every user gets the same answer.

Real life example 2, a confusing SMS: Suppose your elder brother texts: "Bring old books and notebooks from Nilkhet." Are the notebooks old too, or only the books? The phrase old books and notebooks has two trees: old (books and notebooks), or (old books) and notebooks. In everyday Bangla or English, you would call him back and ask. A program has nobody to call, which is why programming language grammars are designed so that every valid program has only one tree.

Common mistakes: First, thinking that two different derivations prove ambiguity. They do not; one tree has many derivations. You need two different parse trees, or two different leftmost derivations. Second, calling a language ambiguous when only a particular grammar is. Third, drawing a parse tree whose node and children do not match any rule. Fourth, forgetting that the yield is read left to right from the leaves. Fifth, claiming an unambiguous grammar exists for every context-free language; inherently ambiguous languages exist.

What exams ask: Give leftmost and rightmost derivations of a string and draw its parse tree. Show that a grammar is ambiguous by giving one string with two parse trees. Rewrite the expression grammar to be unambiguous with correct precedence and associativity. Explain the dangling else and how languages resolve it. Define inherent ambiguity and give the standard example.

Recap: Leftmost and rightmost derivations are two fixed orders of replacing variables. A parse tree shows the structure of a derived string, and its yield is the string. Each tree has exactly one leftmost derivation, so a grammar is ambiguous when a string has two trees, or two leftmost derivations. Ambiguity can often be removed with precedence levels and left or right recursion for associativity, as in E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a. Some languages are inherently ambiguous. Next we learn how to clean grammars by removing useless symbols, epsilon rules and unit rules.
key_points: A leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost variable; a rightmost derivation always replaces the rightmost one.
A parse tree has the start variable at the root, a rule at each internal node, and its yield (leaves left to right) is the derived string.
Each parse tree has exactly one leftmost and one rightmost derivation.
A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations).
E → E + E | E * E | (E) | a is ambiguous: a + a * a has two trees, giving 14 or 20 for 2 + 3 * 4.
Precedence levels (E, T, F) and left recursion for left associativity give the unambiguous grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a.
The dangling else is resolved by matching else with the nearest if; some languages, like { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k }, are inherently ambiguous.
lessons.tip: To prove ambiguity, always present two parse trees or two LEFTMOST derivations of the same string. Two derivations in different orders prove nothing, and examiners take marks for that mistake.
lessons.task: Using E → E + E | E * E | (E) | a, draw all parse trees for a + a + a + a on paper; you should find exactly 5. Then draw the single tree for the same string in the layered grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a.

quiz.q: When is a grammar ambiguous?
options: When a string has two different derivations
When some string has two different parse trees
When it generates an infinite language
quiz.explain: Two derivations may build the same tree. Ambiguity needs two distinct parse trees, or two distinct leftmost derivations.

quiz.q: How many leftmost derivations does a single parse tree have?
options: One per variable in the tree
It depends on the string length
quiz.explain: The leftmost order is fixed, so each tree corresponds to exactly one leftmost derivation.

quiz.q: In E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a, why is a + a + a grouped as (a + a) + a?
options: Because F is the start variable
Because of the brackets in F → (E)
Because the recursion in E → E + T is on the left
quiz.explain: Left recursion makes the operator left associative.

quiz.q: Which statement about the dangling else is correct?
options: It shows that if-statements are not context-free
C and Java attach an else to the nearest unmatched if
It is solved by removing else from the language
quiz.explain: C and Java use the nearest-if rule; the grammar can be rewritten with matched and unmatched statements to encode it.

quiz.q: What is an inherently ambiguous language?
options: A language whose grammar has epsilon rules
A regular language with two DFAs
A language that is not context-free
A context-free language for which every grammar is ambiguous
quiz.explain: For such a language no unambiguous grammar exists; { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k } is the standard example.

lessons.title: Simplifying Context-Free Grammars
lessons.content:
Imagine the shelves of an old mudi dokan. Some boxes are empty and can never be sold. Some items are hidden behind other boxes where no customer can ever reach them. Some labels just say "see the other shelf" and point somewhere else. The shop still works, but it is messy and slow. Before the owner can reorganise the shop into a neat new system, he must throw out the empty boxes, clear out the unreachable corner, and replace the pointer labels with the actual goods. Simplifying a context-free grammar is exactly this kind of clean-up.

Why simplify: A grammar can contain rules that do nothing useful, rules that make nothing but empty strings, and rules that just rename one variable as another. These rules do not change the language much, but they make grammars larger, slow down algorithms, and get in the way of normal forms. The Chomsky normal form in the next lesson and the Greibach normal form after it both start from a cleaned grammar. In this lesson we learn three clean-ups: removing useless symbols, removing epsilon-productions, and removing unit productions, and we learn the right order to do them in.

Useful and useless symbols: A symbol X is useful if it takes part in at least one complete derivation of a terminal string, that is, S ⇒* αXβ ⇒* w for some terminal string w. Otherwise X is useless and can be deleted, together with every rule that mentions it, without changing the language. A symbol can be useless for two different reasons, so we split usefulness into two tests: generating and reachable.

Generating symbols: X is generating if X ⇒* w for some string w made only of terminals. Every terminal is generating, since it already is a terminal string. To find the generating variables, repeat: if there is a rule A → α where every symbol of α is already known to be generating, mark A as generating. A rule A → ε also makes A generating, since ε is a terminal string. Stop when nothing new gets marked. Variables that are never marked can never finish their job and must go.

Reachable symbols: X is reachable if S ⇒* αXβ for some α and β, meaning X can appear in some sentential form. Start with S marked as reachable. Then repeat: if A is reachable and A → α is a rule, mark every symbol of α as reachable. Stop when nothing changes. A variable that is never reached can be deleted, because no derivation ever uses it.

A small example: Take S → AB | a, A → a, B → bB. First find generating symbols. a and b are terminals. A → a makes A generating. S → a makes S generating. B has only the rule B → bB, and B needs B to finish, so B is never marked. B is not generating. Delete B and every rule containing B. That removes S → AB and B → bB, leaving S → a and A → a. Now find reachable symbols from S: only S and a. A is unreachable, so delete A → a. The final grammar is S → a, and its language is {a}, exactly as before.

The order matters: In the example we removed non-generating symbols first and unreachable symbols second. Try it the other way round. At the start S → AB mentions both A and B, so all symbols are reachable and nothing is deleted. Then we remove the non-generating B and get S → a and A → a. Now A is useless, but we already did the reachability step, so A stays. So the rule is: first remove non-generating symbols, then remove unreachable ones. Done in that order, the result has no useless symbols at all.

Epsilon-productions: A rule A → ε is an epsilon-production. Grammars with them are convenient to write, as in S → aSb | ε, but some algorithms dislike them, because a variable might quietly vanish. Here is a key fact. If L is generated by a CFG, then L minus {ε} is generated by a CFG with no epsilon-productions at all. If ε itself must stay in the language, we allow one special rule S → ε for the start variable only, and we make sure S never appears on the right side of any rule.

Nullable variables: A variable A is nullable if A ⇒* ε. Find them the same way as generating symbols: if A → ε is a rule, A is nullable. If A → B1 B2 ... Bk and every Bi is already nullable, A is nullable. Repeat until nothing changes. Only variables made of other nullable variables count; a rule like A → aB never makes A nullable, because the terminal a can never vanish.

Removing epsilon-productions: For every rule A → X1 X2 ... Xk, add new versions of it where any subset of the nullable occurrences is left out. If the rule has m nullable occurrences, you get up to 2^m versions. Then delete every rule of the form A → ε, and never add one back. For example, if A is nullable, the rule X → AbA becomes the four rules X → AbA | bA | Ab | b. The b is a terminal, so it is never left out.

Worked epsilon example: Let S → AB, A → aA | ε, B → bB | ε. A is nullable from A → ε, B from B → ε, and S from S → AB because both A and B are nullable. Now rewrite. S → AB becomes S → AB | A | B. We do not add S → ε. A → aA becomes A → aA | a, and B → bB becomes B → bB | b. The epsilon rules are deleted. The old grammar generated a*b*, all a's followed by all b's, including ε. The new one generates a*b* without ε. We checked by computer that the two languages agree on every string up to length 8 except ε.

Unit productions: A rule of the form A → B, where both sides are single variables, is a unit production. It does not produce any terminal; it just renames. The expression grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → (E) | a has two of them: E → T and T → F. Units make derivations longer, and chains or cycles of units, like A → B and B → A, can make algorithms loop.

Unit pairs: To remove units, first find all unit pairs (A, B) such that A ⇒* B using unit productions only. Every (A, A) is a unit pair, with zero steps. If (A, B) is a pair and B → C is a unit rule, then (A, C) is a pair. Then, for every pair (A, B) and every NON-unit rule B → α, add the rule A → α. Finally delete all the unit rules. This handles cycles safely, because we only follow pairs and never chase rules forever.

Worked unit example: In the expression grammar, the unit pairs are (E, E), (E, T), (E, F), (T, T), (T, F) and (F, F). The non-unit rules are E → E + T, T → T * F, F → (E) and F → a. Copying gives: E → E + T | T * F | (E) | a, T → T * F | (E) | a, F → (E) | a. No unit rules remain. We checked by computer that this grammar generates exactly the same expressions as the original up to length 9.

The safe order of steps: To clean a grammar completely, do the three steps in this order. First, remove epsilon-productions. Second, remove unit productions. Third, remove useless symbols, non-generating first and then unreachable. The reason is that each step can create work for later steps but not for earlier ones. Removing epsilon rules can create new unit rules: S → AB with A nullable produces S → B. Removing unit rules can make some variables unreachable, because nothing points to them any more. Removing useless symbols only deletes rules, so it cannot create new epsilon or unit rules.

A full worked example: Start with S → AB | C, A → aAb | ε, B → bB | b, C → cC, D → d. Step 1, epsilon: only A is nullable, since B needs at least one b and C never ends. S → AB becomes S → AB | B, A → aAb becomes A → aAb | ab, and A → ε is deleted. Step 2, units: now S → B and S → C are unit rules. The pairs (S, B) and (S, C) copy B's rules and C's rule into S, giving S → AB | bB | b | cC. Step 3, useless: C → cC never ends, so C is not generating; delete it and S → cC. Then D is not reachable from S; delete D → d.

The clean result: The final grammar is S → AB | bB | b, A → aAb | ab, B → bB | b. It generates a^n b^m with m > n ≥ 0: b, bb, abb, bbb, abbb, aabbb and so on. We compared it with the original grammar by computer for every string up to length 9, and they generate exactly the same strings. Notice that the original had a useless C and D, an epsilon rule and two unit rules, and none of them changed the language.

Real life example 1, cleaning code: When you compile a big program, the compiler or a linter often warns about unused functions and code that can never run. An unused function is like an unreachable variable: nothing calls it. A function that always calls itself and never returns is like a non-generating variable: it can never finish. A wrapper function that only calls another function is like a unit rule. Compilers delete or inline such code to make the program smaller and faster, the same spirit as cleaning a grammar.

Real life example 2, a USSD menu: Think of dialling a mobile banking USSD code. The menu says 1 Send Money, 2 Cash Out, 3 Mobile Recharge, and so on. Suppose a designer left an option that leads to a sub-menu with only a "next page" link pointing back to itself; no transaction can ever finish there, like a non-generating variable. Suppose another sub-menu exists in the system but no option leads to it; that is unreachable. And an option that only says "go to menu 2" is a unit rule. A clean menu removes all three, and users reach the same services faster.

Common mistakes: First, removing unreachable symbols before non-generating ones, which can leave useless symbols behind. Second, forgetting that a variable built only from nullable variables is nullable too, like S → AB above. Third, when removing epsilon rules, dropping a terminal along with the nullable variables, or forgetting some of the 2^m combinations. Fourth, re-adding A → ε for non-start variables. Fifth, removing units by copying unit rules instead of only non-unit rules, which keeps the units alive.

What exams ask: Given a grammar, find its generating, reachable and nullable variables. Remove useless symbols and explain why the order matters. Eliminate epsilon-productions and say what happens to ε in the language. Eliminate unit productions using unit pairs. Simplify a full grammar in the correct order, often as the first part of a question that then asks for Chomsky normal form.

Recap: A useful symbol must be both generating and reachable; remove non-generating symbols first, then unreachable ones. Epsilon-productions are removed by finding nullable variables and adding every version of each rule with nullable occurrences left out; the language loses only ε. Unit productions are removed by finding unit pairs and copying non-unit rules. The safe overall order is: epsilon, then unit, then useless. A clean grammar is the starting point for Chomsky normal form in the next lesson.
key_points: A symbol is useful only if it is both generating (derives a terminal string) and reachable (appears in some sentential form from S).
Remove non-generating symbols first, then unreachable ones; the other order can leave useless symbols.
A variable is nullable if it derives ε; find nullable variables by repeated marking.
To remove epsilon-productions, add every version of each rule with nullable occurrences left out (up to 2^m), then delete A → ε; only ε is lost from the language.
Unit productions A → B are removed by finding unit pairs and copying the non-unit rules of B into A.
Safe overall order: remove epsilon-productions, then unit productions, then useless symbols.
A simplified grammar is the starting point for Chomsky and Greibach normal forms.
lessons.tip: Keep three small lists on the side of your page while simplifying: nullable, unit pairs, generating/reachable. Writing these sets first, before rewriting any rule, prevents almost every mistake in long exam questions.
lessons.task: Simplify this grammar on paper in the safe order: S → aA | B | ε, A → aA | bB | ε, B → bB, C → c. Write the nullable set, the unit pairs and the generating and reachable symbols, then the final grammar, and list its strings up to length 3 to check them against the original.

quiz.q: Which symbols should be removed first when deleting useless symbols?
quiz.explain: Removing non-generating symbols first may make others unreachable; doing reachability second catches them.

quiz.q: In S → AB, A → aA | ε, B → bB | ε, which variables are nullable?
quiz.explain: A and B have epsilon rules, and S → AB has only nullable variables, so S is nullable too.

quiz.q: With A nullable, what does X → AbA become after removing epsilon-productions?
quiz.explain: Each of the two nullable A's may be kept or dropped, giving 4 versions; b is a terminal and stays.

quiz.q: How are unit productions removed?
options: By deleting them and nothing else
By replacing each A → B with B → A
By finding unit pairs (A, B) and adding A → α for each non-unit rule B → α
quiz.explain: Copy the non-unit rules along unit pairs, then delete all unit rules.

quiz.q: What is the safe order for full simplification?
options: Any order gives the same result
quiz.explain: Epsilon removal can create unit rules, and unit removal can create unreachable symbols, so useless symbols go last.

lessons.title: Chomsky Normal Form and the CYK Algorithm
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket tournament played as a knockout. Every match has exactly two teams, and every match produces exactly one winner who moves up. However many teams start, the whole tournament is a neat binary tree, and if 16 teams start you always need exactly 15 matches. Because the shape is so regular, it is easy to plan, easy to draw and easy to reason about. Chomsky normal form does the same thing for grammars: it forces every parse tree into a neat binary shape, and that regular shape makes powerful algorithms and proofs possible.

The definition: A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form, CNF, if every rule has one of two shapes. Either A → BC, where A, B and C are variables and neither B nor C is the start variable, or A → a, where a is a single terminal. One exception is allowed: if the language contains the empty string, the rule S → ε is allowed for the start variable S. The name honours Noam Chomsky, who introduced this form.

What is not allowed: So these rules are not in CNF: A → aB, because a terminal is mixed with a variable; A → BCD, because the right side is too long; A → B, because it is a unit rule; A → ε for a variable other than the start; and any rule with the start variable on its right side. Each of these problems has a matching repair step in the conversion below.

Why CNF is useful: In CNF every internal node of a parse tree has either two variable children or one terminal child. So the tree is binary, apart from the bottom layer. Three big benefits follow. First, every derivation of a string of length n ≥ 1 takes exactly 2n - 1 steps. Second, the CYK algorithm can decide whether any string belongs to the language using dynamic programming. Third, proofs become simpler; for example, the pumping lemma for context-free languages in lesson 19 uses the fact that a CNF parse tree whose longest path has h edges yields a string of length at most 2^(h-1).

Exactly 2n - 1 steps: Why 2n - 1? A string of length n needs n terminals, and each terminal is produced by one rule of the form A → a, so that is n steps. Each rule A → BC turns one variable into two, increasing the number of variables by one. We start with one variable and need n of them, one above each terminal, so we need n - 1 such steps. In total n + (n - 1) = 2n - 1. Like the knockout tournament: 16 teams, 15 matches.

Every CFG can be converted: For every context-free grammar G there is a grammar in CNF that generates the same language. The conversion is mechanical and uses the clean-up steps from the last lesson plus two new steps. Here is the standard order. Step 1: add a new start variable. Step 2: remove epsilon-productions. Step 3: remove unit productions. Step 4: replace terminals inside long rules by new variables. Step 5: break long rules into chains of two-variable rules. Useless symbols can be removed at the end if any appear.

Step 1, a new start variable: Add a new start variable S0 and the rule S0 → S. Now the start variable never appears on any right side, even if the old S did, as in S → SS. This protects the special rule S0 → ε, which is only safe when the start variable cannot show up in the middle of a derivation.

Steps 2 and 3, epsilon and unit rules: Find the nullable variables and remove epsilon-productions as in lesson 14, but if S0 is nullable keep S0 → ε. Then find unit pairs and remove unit productions by copying non-unit rules. A rule like S → S, which can appear after epsilon removal, does nothing and is simply deleted.

Step 4, terminals in long rules: In any rule whose right side has length 2 or more, replace each terminal a by a new variable, say A, and add the rule A → a. For example, S → aSb becomes S → ASB with A → a and B → b. Rules with a single terminal on the right, like S → a, are already fine and stay as they are.

Step 5, breaking long rules: A rule with three or more variables, A → X1 X2 ... Xk, is broken into a chain using new variables: A → X1 Y1, Y1 → X2 Y2, and so on, until Y(k-2) → X(k-1) Xk. A right side of length k becomes k - 1 rules. For example, S → ASB becomes S → AX and X → SB.

Worked conversion, step by step: Let us convert the grammar S → aSb | SS | ε. With a as an opening bracket and b as a closing one, this generates the balanced strings: ε, ab, aabb, abab and so on. Step 1: add S0 → S. Step 2: S and S0 are nullable. S → aSb gives aSb and ab; S → SS gives SS and S; we delete the useless S → S. Since ε is in the language, keep S0 → ε. Now S0 → S | ε and S → aSb | ab | SS.

Finishing the conversion: Step 3: the unit pair (S0, S) copies S's rules into S0, giving S0 → aSb | ab | SS | ε. Step 4: new variables A → a and B → b turn the rules into S → ASB | AB | SS and the same for S0. Step 5: break ASB using X → SB. The final CNF grammar is: S0 → AX | AB | SS | ε, S → AX | AB | SS, X → SB, A → a, B → b. We checked by computer that it generates exactly the same strings as the original grammar for every length up to 10.

Checking 2n - 1: Derive aabb, which has length 4, in the CNF grammar: S0 ⇒ AX ⇒ aX ⇒ aSB ⇒ aABB ⇒ aaBB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aabb. Count the steps: 7, which is 2 × 4 - 1. Three steps used two-variable rules, S0 → AX, X → SB and S → AB, and four steps used terminal rules. Every derivation of aabb in this grammar has the same length, whatever order you choose.

The membership problem: Given a grammar G and a string w, is w in L(G)? For a DFA this is easy: just run it. For a grammar, trying derivations blindly could take forever, since grammars with epsilon or unit rules can loop. CNF fixes the length: a derivation of w has exactly 2n - 1 steps, so trying all derivations of that length always finishes. But there can be exponentially many of them. We want something faster.

The CYK algorithm: The Cocke-Younger-Kasami algorithm, CYK, named after three researchers who found it independently, uses dynamic programming, which you know from Algorithms. For a string w = w1 w2 ... wn, it fills a table where cell (i, j) holds the set of variables that can derive the substring from position i to position j. Short substrings are done first, then longer ones built from them. At the end, w is in the language exactly when the start variable is in the cell for the whole string.

Filling the table: For length 1, cell (i, i) gets every variable A with a rule A → wi. For a longer substring from i to j, try every split point k between them: the left part i to k and the right part k + 1 to j. If B is in cell (i, k), C is in cell (k + 1, j), and A → BC is a rule, put A in cell (i, j). Because both parts are shorter, their cells are already filled. In pseudo-code: for len = 2 to n, for i = 1 to n - len + 1, j = i + len - 1, for k = i to j - 1, for each rule A → BC, if B in T[i][k] and C in T[k+1][j], add A to T[i][j].

CYK on aabb: Use the CNF grammar above. Length 1: positions 1 and 2 are a, so they get {A}; positions 3 and 4 are b, so they get {B}. Length 2: aa needs a rule with right side AA, none exists, so the cell is empty. ab has A then B, and S → AB gives {S, S0}. bb needs BB, none, so it is empty. Length 3: aab splits as a + ab, giving A then S, but no rule has right side AS; or aa + b, where aa is empty, so the cell is empty. abb splits as a + bb, empty, or ab + b, giving S then B, and X → SB puts X in the cell. Length 4: aabb splits as a + abb, giving A then X, and S → AX and S0 → AX put {S, S0} in the top cell. The start variable S0 is there, so aabb is accepted.

CYK rejecting abba: Length 1 gives A, B, B, A. Length 2: ab gets {S, S0}, bb and ba are empty. Length 3: abb gets {X} from ab + b, and bba is empty. Length 4: the splits are a + bba, which is A and empty; ab + ba, which is S and empty; and abb + a, which is X then A, and no rule has right side XA. The top cell is empty, so abba is rejected, as it should be, because abba is not a balanced string. We ran CYK by computer on every string over {a, b} up to length 8, and it agreed with the grammar every time.

How fast is CYK: The table has n(n + 1)/2 cells, and each cell tries up to n - 1 split points, checking the grammar's rules each time. So CYK runs in O(n^3 × |G|) time, where |G| is the size of the grammar. For a fixed grammar that is O(n^3). It works for every context-free grammar once converted to CNF, even ambiguous ones. Compilers prefer the linear-time LL and LR parsers, which work only for restricted grammars; those are covered in Compiler Design.

Real life example 1, language processing: Natural language processing has used CYK, often called the CKY parser there, to find the structure of sentences. A sentence like "Rina saw the man with the telescope" has two parse trees: either Rina used the telescope, or the man had it. A probabilistic version of CKY attaches a probability to each rule and picks the most likely tree, learned from many real sentences. This is how parsing tools could decide that in most texts one reading is more common than the other.

Real life example 2, biology: RNA molecules fold back on themselves, and base pairs can nest inside one another, like matching brackets. Scientists use stochastic context-free grammars and CYK-style dynamic programming to predict how an RNA strand folds. The idea is exactly the table you just filled: work out the best structure for every short stretch first, then combine them into longer stretches.

Common mistakes: First, leaving the start variable on a right side, for example keeping S → SS with S as the start; that is why Step 1 adds S0. Second, forgetting S0 → ε when ε is in the language, or keeping epsilon rules for other variables. Third, leaving a terminal inside a long rule, like A → aB, which is not CNF. Fourth, in CYK, forgetting a split point or writing only one variable when a cell has several. Fifth, concluding the string is rejected because some cell is empty; only the top cell decides.

What exams ask: Define CNF and say which rules violate it. Convert a given grammar to CNF, showing every step. Prove that a derivation of a length-n string takes 2n - 1 steps. Run CYK on a short string, show the full table, and say whether the string is accepted. State the running time of CYK and why CNF is needed for it.

Recap: In Chomsky normal form every rule is A → BC or A → a, plus S0 → ε when needed, and the start variable never appears on the right. Any CFG can be converted by adding a new start, removing epsilon and unit rules, replacing terminals in long rules, and breaking long rules into pairs. Parse trees become binary and every derivation of a length-n string takes 2n - 1 steps. The CYK algorithm fills a triangular table in O(n^3) time to decide membership for any context-free language. Next lesson we meet a second normal form, Greibach normal form.
key_points: CNF: every rule is A → BC (B, C variables, not the start) or A → a; S0 → ε is allowed only for the start variable when ε is in the language.
Every CFG can be converted to CNF: new start, remove epsilon rules, remove unit rules, replace terminals in long rules, break long rules into pairs.
S → aSb | SS | ε becomes S0 → AX | AB | SS | ε, S → AX | AB | SS, X → SB, A → a, B → b.
In CNF every derivation of a string of length n ≥ 1 takes exactly 2n - 1 steps: n terminal steps and n - 1 branching steps.
CYK fills a triangular table: cell (i, j) holds all variables deriving the substring from i to j, built from split points k.
A string is accepted exactly when the start variable is in the top cell for the whole string.
CYK runs in O(n^3 × |G|) time and works for every CFG in CNF, including ambiguous ones.
lessons.tip: When running CYK by hand, draw the table as a triangle with length-1 cells at the bottom, and for each cell write its split points in pencil before filling it. Most CYK mistakes come from a skipped split point.
lessons.task: Using the CNF grammar S0 → AX | AB | SS | ε, S → AX | AB | SS, X → SB, A → a, B → b, run CYK on abab on paper. You should find {S, S0} for both ab cells and in the top cell. Then try aab and confirm the top cell is empty.

quiz.q: Which rule is allowed in Chomsky normal form?
options: A → BC, where B and C are not the start variable
quiz.explain: CNF allows only A → BC and A → a, plus S0 → ε for the start variable.

quiz.q: In a CNF grammar, how many steps does any derivation of a string of length 6 take?
quiz.explain: 2n - 1 = 2 × 6 - 1 = 11: six terminal steps and five branching steps.

quiz.q: Why does the CNF conversion first add a new start variable S0 → S?
options: So the start variable never appears on a right side, which keeps S0 → ε safe
Because CYK needs two start variables
quiz.explain: If the old S appears on right sides, as in S → SS, an S → ε rule would act inside derivations.

quiz.q: In CYK, what does cell (i, j) contain?
options: The rules used at step i
All variables that can derive the substring from position i to j
quiz.explain: Each cell stores the set of variables deriving that substring; the top cell decides acceptance.

quiz.q: What is the running time of CYK for a fixed grammar and a string of length n?
quiz.explain: About n^2/2 cells, each trying up to n - 1 split points, gives O(n^3).

lessons.title: Greibach Normal Form
lessons.content:
Imagine a queue of people at a bKash shop, and the rule of the shop is simple: every time you step up to the counter, you must hand over exactly one real coin before you can do anything else. Nobody is allowed to say "first let me call my friend, and he will pay". In a grammar, that friend-calling is a variable that starts a rule, and it is the thing that can make grammars wander around in circles. Greibach normal form is the shop rule for grammars: every single step of a derivation must put down exactly one real terminal symbol first.

Where we are: In the last lessons you met context-free grammars, parse trees, simplification (removing useless symbols, epsilon-productions and unit productions) and Chomsky normal form (CNF), where every rule looks like A -> BC or A -> a. Today we learn the second famous normal form, named after the American computer scientist Sheila Greibach, who published it in 1965. It is the normal form that connects grammars most directly with pushdown automata, which is the next lesson.

The definition: A context-free grammar is in Greibach normal form (GNF) if every production has the form A -> a alpha, where a is a single terminal and alpha is a string of zero or more variables.
