So A -> a, A -> aB and A -> aBCD are all fine. A -> BC is not allowed because it starts with a variable. A -> abB is not allowed in the strict form because after the first terminal only variables may follow. Many books also allow the one extra rule S -> epsilon when the empty string is in the language and S never appears on a right-hand side, just like in CNF.

The big theorem: Every context-free language that does not contain the empty string can be generated by a grammar in Greibach normal form. If the language does contain epsilon, we build GNF for L minus epsilon and then add S -> epsilon. GNF only changes the shape of the rules, not the power.

Small examples: The language a^n b^n with n at least 1 has the usual grammar S -> aSb | ab. That is not GNF, because the terminal b sits at the end of the rules. Fix it by giving b its own variable: S -> aSB | aB and B -> b. Now every rule starts with one terminal followed only by variables. Derive aabb: S => aSB => aaBB => aabB => aabb. Four letters, four steps. That is not a coincidence.

One terminal per step: In a GNF grammar, every derivation step adds exactly one terminal to the front part of the sentential form. So a string of length n takes exactly n steps to derive, and in a leftmost derivation the terminals appear from left to right, one per step, just like reading the input one symbol at a time. Compare CNF, where a string of length n needs 2n - 1 steps.

No left recursion: A grammar is left recursive if some variable A can derive a string that starts with A again, like A -> Ab, or A -> Bc together with B -> Ad. Top-down methods that always expand the leftmost variable can loop forever on such grammars: to expand A they expand A, which needs A again. In GNF this can never happen, because every step puts a terminal in front. So the main job of converting to GNF is killing left recursion. Two simple tools do the whole job.

Tool 1, substitution: If we have a rule A -> B gamma, and all the B-rules are B -> beta1 | beta2 | ... | betak, then we may delete A -> B gamma and add A -> beta1 gamma | beta2 gamma | ... | betak gamma. The language stays the same, because any derivation that used A -> B gamma would have to expand that B by one of its rules sooner or later anyway. We are only doing that step in advance. Example: A -> Bc with B -> a | Bd becomes A -> ac | Bdc.

Tool 2, removing immediate left recursion: Suppose the A-rules are A -> A alpha1 | ... | A alpham | beta1 | ... | betan, where no beta starts with A. Look at what A can produce: one beta first, followed by any number of alphas. So add a brand-new variable Z and replace all A-rules by A -> betai | betai Z for every i, and Z -> alphaj | alphaj Z for every j. Now A produces a beta, and Z produces one or more alphas, and nobody calls itself from the left anymore.

Tiny left recursion examples: Take S -> Sa | b. Here alpha is a and beta is b, and the language is b followed by any number of a's. The new grammar is S -> b | bZ and Z -> a | aZ. It is already in GNF. A second classic example from expression grammars: E -> E+T | T becomes E -> T | TZ with Z -> +T | +TZ. That one is not GNF yet, because T is a variable at the front, but the left recursion is gone. Compiler Design uses exactly this trick before building top-down parsers. I checked both conversions by generating all strings up to length 8 from the old and the new grammars, and the sets are equal.

The full algorithm, step 0: First simplify the grammar and put it into CNF (lessons 14 and 15). This is not strictly necessary, but it makes the rules short and predictable: every rule is either A -> BC or A -> a. Then give the variables an order, A1, A2, ..., An. The goal of the next phase is that every rule of the form Ai -> Aj gamma has j bigger than i. In words: a variable may only start with a variable that comes later in the order.

Step 1, going up: Process i = 1, 2, ..., n in order. For each rule Ai -> Aj gamma with j smaller than i, substitute the Aj-rules (which are already fixed, so they start with a terminal or a later variable). Repeat until every Ai rule starts with a terminal, with Ak where k is bigger than i, or with Ai itself. Then remove the immediate left recursion Ai -> Ai alpha using tool 2, which creates a new variable Zi. After this phase, the last variable An has only rules that start with a terminal, because there is no variable after it.

Step 2, coming down: Now go backwards, i = n - 1 down to 1. Every Ai rule starts with a terminal or with a later variable, and the later variables are already in GNF. So substitute them, and now Ai is in GNF too. Finally, the new Z variables: their rules start with an original variable (never with a Z), and all originals are now in GNF, so one more round of substitution finishes them. If a terminal still sits in the middle of a rule, replace it by a variable like B -> b. Done.

Worked example, the grammar: Let us convert G with rules S -> AA | a and A -> SS | b. It is already in CNF. Order the variables S first, then A. Rule S -> AA starts with A, which comes later, so S is fine for now. Rule A -> SS starts with S, which comes earlier, so we must substitute.

Worked example, substitution and left recursion: Replace the S at the front of A -> SS by both S-rules. S -> AA gives A -> AAS, and S -> a gives A -> aS. So the A-rules are now A -> AAS | aS | b. Now A is immediately left recursive with alpha = AS, and the betas are aS and b. Tool 2 with a new variable Z gives A -> aS | b | aSZ | bZ and Z -> AS | ASZ. Every A-rule now starts with a terminal.

Worked example, coming back down: S -> AA starts with A, so substitute the four A-rules for the first A: S -> aSA | bA | aSZA | bZA, plus the old S -> a. Z -> AS and Z -> ASZ also start with A, so substitute again: Z -> aSS | bS | aSZS | bZS and Z -> aSSZ | bSZ | aSZSZ | bZSZ. The final GNF grammar has 5 S-rules, 4 A-rules and 8 Z-rules. Every rule is one terminal followed by variables only.

Worked example, checking: Compare derivations of the string aab. Old grammar: S => AA => SSA => aSA => aaA => aab, five steps. New grammar: S => aSA => aaA => aab, three steps, one per letter. The string baa: S => bA => baS => baa. To be sure no mistake crept in, I generated every string of length up to 8 from the original grammar, from both middle stages and from the final GNF grammar with a small Python program. All four sets were identical, 167 strings each. When you convert by hand in an exam, at least test two or three short strings like this.

Size warning: GNF grammars can get large. You saw two rules for A grow into four, and two rules for Z grow into eight, after only one substitution round. With more variables, the number of rules can grow a lot, which is why GNF is mainly a theoretical tool, while CNF is used in algorithms like CYK.

Why GNF matters, link to PDAs: In the next lesson you will meet the pushdown automaton, a finite machine with a stack. From a GNF grammar you can build a PDA in which every move reads exactly one input symbol: for a rule A -> a B1 B2 ... Bk, when A is on top of the stack and the next input is a, pop A and push B1 ... Bk. The stack holds the variables still waiting to be expanded. Because each move eats an input symbol, the machine never runs an infinite chain of moves without reading anything, and it uses exactly n moves on input of length n. Lesson 18 does the general CFG to PDA construction.

Why GNF matters, other uses: Because every variable starts with a terminal, a top-down parser that guesses rules can always check its guess against the next input symbol right away, and it cannot loop on left recursion. The real parsing techniques, LL and LR, are for the Compiler Design course; we only note that left recursion removal from this lesson is exactly the first step taught there for LL parsing.

Real-life example 1, the cricket scoreboard: Think of an umpire signalling each ball. A rule like Over -> ball Over or Over -> ball is GNF style: each step is one real delivery, then the rest of the over is still pending. A left recursive rule like Over -> Over ball says to finish the whole over before the last ball, which makes no sense when you are watching live ball by ball. Live reading wants rules that produce the next real thing immediately, and that is exactly GNF.

Real-life example 2, the rickshaw route: A Dhaka rickshaw puller asked for directions might hear "to reach Farmgate, first reach Farmgate, then turn left". Useless, he goes in a circle. That is left recursion. Good directions say "go straight to the first signal, then the rest of the way is ...", one real move first, then the remaining plan. Removing left recursion is rewriting circular directions into step-first directions.

Common mistakes: Students often forget that the new variable Z also needs substitution at the end, leaving rules like Z -> AS that start with a variable. Another mistake is removing left recursion only for A -> A alpha but missing indirect left recursion such as A -> Bx and B -> Ay; the ordering phase is what catches these. A third mistake is leaving terminals in the middle, like A -> aBc; replace c with a new variable C -> c. Also be careful with epsilon: GNF is built for L without epsilon, and S -> epsilon is added only at the end.

What exams ask: Define GNF and compare it with CNF. Convert a small grammar to GNF, usually with left recursion. Remove left recursion from E -> E+T | T. Prove that a string of length n has a derivation of exactly n steps in GNF. Explain why GNF helps build a PDA.

Recap: GNF rules look like A -> a followed by variables. Every CFL without epsilon has a GNF grammar. Conversion uses two tools, substitution and left recursion removal, in an order-up then substitute-down plan. Derivations take one step per terminal, which makes GNF the natural bridge to pushdown automata, our next lesson.
key_points: GNF: every production is A -> a alpha, with a a terminal and alpha a string of variables (S -> epsilon allowed if epsilon is in L).
Every context-free language without epsilon has a grammar in GNF (Greibach, 1965).
In GNF a string of length n is derived in exactly n steps; CNF needs 2n - 1.
Substitution: replace A -> B gamma by A -> beta gamma for every B -> beta; the language does not change.
Left recursion removal: A -> A alpha | beta becomes A -> beta | beta Z and Z -> alpha | alpha Z.
Algorithm: CNF, order variables, make Ai start only with later variables, remove left recursion, substitute back down, then fix the new Z variables.
GNF grammars can be much larger than the original; GNF is mainly a theoretical bridge to PDAs that read one symbol per move.
lessons.tip: After every conversion, derive two or three short strings in both the old and the new grammar. If a string appears in one but not the other, you dropped or added a rule somewhere, usually in the Z variable.
lessons.task: Remove left recursion from S -> Sab | c, then turn the result into strict GNF (only variables after the first terminal). Write all strings of length up to 7 from both grammars on paper and check they match.

quiz.q: Which production is in Greibach normal form?
quiz.explain: GNF needs one terminal first, then only variables. aBC fits; BC and Ba start with a variable; abB has a terminal after the first position.

quiz.q: In a GNF grammar, how many derivation steps are needed for a string of length 6?
quiz.explain: Each GNF step adds exactly one terminal, so length n needs n steps. 11 = 2n - 1 would be the CNF count.

quiz.q: Removing left recursion from A -> Ab | c with a new variable Z gives:
options: A -> c | cZ, Z -> b | bZ
A -> b | bZ, Z -> c | cZ
quiz.explain: A produces c followed by any number of b's. So A -> c | cZ and Z -> b | bZ.

quiz.q: Why is left recursion a problem for top-down expansion?
options: Expanding the leftmost A can produce A again at the front, so the expansion can loop forever
It adds epsilon to the language
quiz.explain: A -> A alpha puts A back at the front, so a leftmost-first expander can keep expanding A without reading input.

quiz.q: What is the main reason GNF is linked to pushdown automata?
options: From a GNF grammar we can build a PDA where every move reads exactly one input symbol
GNF removes the need for a stack
quiz.explain: For A -> a B1...Bk, the PDA pops A, reads a and pushes B1...Bk, so each move consumes one input symbol.

lessons.title: Pushdown Automata
lessons.content:
Think of a tiffin box stack, the steel carrier with three or four bowls on top of each other. You can only put a new bowl on the top, and you can only take off the top bowl. You cannot pull out the middle one without first taking off the ones above it. That simple rule, last in, first out, is called a stack. Give a finite automaton one such stack, as tall as it likes, and you get a new and stronger machine: the pushdown automaton, or PDA.

Why we need more than a DFA: In lesson 11 we proved with the pumping lemma that a^n b^n is not regular. A DFA has only a fixed number of states, so it cannot remember an unbounded count of a's. But a^n b^n is easily generated by the context-free grammar S -> aSb | epsilon. So we need a machine model that matches context-free grammars, the way DFAs match regular expressions. The PDA is that model: finite control plus one unbounded stack.

The stack: A stack supports three things. Push puts a symbol on top. Pop removes the top symbol. And the machine can look at the top symbol to decide what to do. There is no limit on height, but the machine sees only the top. So the stack is unlimited memory with very restricted access. That restriction is exactly why PDAs are weaker than Turing machines, which we meet in lesson 20.

The formal definition: A PDA is a 7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, Z0, F). Q is a finite set of states. Sigma is the input alphabet. Gamma is the stack alphabet, which may contain symbols that never appear in the input. q0 is the start state. Z0 is the start stack symbol, sitting alone at the bottom when the machine begins, so the machine can tell when the stack is back to empty. F is the set of accepting states. Some books, like Sipser, use a 6-tuple without Z0 and push their own bottom marker with a first move; the idea is the same.

The transition function: delta takes three things: the current state, an input symbol or epsilon, and the symbol on top of the stack. It returns a finite set of choices, each a pair (new state, string to push). Formally delta maps Q x (Sigma with epsilon) x Gamma to finite subsets of Q x Gamma*. The move always pops the top symbol and then pushes the given string, whose leftmost symbol becomes the new top. In diagrams we write a move as a, X / gamma, which reads: on input a with X on top, replace X by gamma.

Three kinds of stack action: Push: a, X / AX keeps X and puts A on top of it. Pop: a, X / epsilon removes X. Leave alone: a, X / X reads the input but keeps the stack as it was. If the input part is epsilon, the move happens without reading anything, which is called an epsilon-move. Because delta returns a set, a PDA is nondeterministic by default: it may have several moves, or none, from the same situation.

Instantaneous descriptions: To trace a PDA we use an instantaneous description, or ID, a triple (q, w, gamma): the current state, the input still unread, and the whole stack written top first. One move from one ID to the next is written with the turnstile sign, which we will write as |-. Several moves in a row are written |-*. An ID is a snapshot of everything the machine needs, like a photo of the scoreboard, the remaining overs and the batting order all at once.

Example 1, a^n b^n: Here is a PDA for a^n b^n with n at least 0, accepting by final state. States q0, q1, q2, start q0, accepting state q2, stack symbols A and Z. Moves: delta(q0, a, Z) = (q0, AZ) and delta(q0, a, A) = (q0, AA): push an A for every a. delta(q0, b, A) = (q1, epsilon): the first b pops one A and switches to q1. delta(q1, b, A) = (q1, epsilon): every later b pops one A. delta(q1, epsilon, Z) = (q2, Z) and delta(q0, epsilon, Z) = (q2, Z): when the bottom Z shows again, jump to the accepting state.

Trace on aabb: (q0, aabb, Z) |- (q0, abb, AZ) |- (q0, bb, AAZ) |- (q1, b, AZ) |- (q1, epsilon, Z) |- (q2, epsilon, Z). The input is finished and the machine is in q2, so aabb is accepted. Each step of this trace was checked move by move with a small simulator program.

Rejection examples: On aab the machine reaches (q1, epsilon, AZ). There is still an A on top, the epsilon-move needs Z on top, so it is stuck outside F and rejects. On abb it reaches (q1, b, Z) after ab. It may jump to q2, but then a b is still unread and q2 has no moves, so this path dies too. On ba the very first move needs an A on top, but the stack has only Z, so it dies at once. Remember, acceptance needs both things: all input read, and an accepting state. I ran this PDA on all 511 strings over a and b up to length 8, and it accepted exactly the strings a^n b^n.

Example 2, balanced brackets: For strings of ( and ) that are properly matched, one state is almost enough. In q0, on ( push an X, on ) with X on top pop the X. When Z is on top, an epsilon-move goes to an accepting state q1, which has no moves of its own. On (()) the stack goes Z, XZ, XXZ, XZ, Z and then the machine jumps to q1 with nothing left to read, so it accepts. On (() an X is still on top at the end, so it rejects. On ()) the last ) finds Z on top and has no move, so that path dies.

Example 3, ww^R and the power of guessing: Let L be the even-length palindromes, w followed by its reverse, like abba or baab. Plan: push every symbol of the first half, then pop and compare during the second half. But where is the middle? The machine cannot know. So it guesses. In q0 it pushes A for a and B for b, and at any moment it may take an epsilon-move to q1 without changing the stack. In q1, input a with A on top pops it, input b with B on top pops it. When Z shows again, an epsilon-move goes to accepting q2.

Trace on abba, the lucky path: (q0, abba, Z) |- (q0, bba, AZ) |- (q0, ba, BAZ) |- (q1, ba, BAZ) |- (q1, a, AZ) |- (q1, epsilon, Z) |- (q2, epsilon, Z). The machine guessed the middle after two symbols. Other guesses, like jumping to q1 after one symbol, end up stuck, but that does not matter. Just like an NFA, a PDA accepts if at least one branch of its computation tree accepts. This PDA was tested on all strings up to length 8 and accepted exactly the even palindromes.

Acceptance by final state: This is what we used so far. The PDA accepts w if from (q0, w, Z0) it can reach (q, epsilon, gamma) with q in F, for any stack contents gamma. The stack may still hold junk; only the state matters.

Acceptance by empty stack: Here the PDA accepts w if it can reach (q, epsilon, epsilon) for any state q: input finished and stack completely empty, even Z0 popped. F is not used. For a^n b^n, change the last moves to delta(q1, epsilon, Z) = (q1, epsilon) and delta(q0, epsilon, Z) = (q0, epsilon), and the machine accepts by emptying its stack. This version was also checked on all strings up to length 8.

The two acceptance modes are equal in power: For nondeterministic PDAs, any language accepted by final state is accepted by empty stack by some other PDA, and the other way round. From final state to empty stack: whenever the machine is in a final state, allow an epsilon-move to a special draining state that pops everything. From empty stack to final state: put a new bottom marker under Z0 at the start; if the machine ever sees that marker on top, its own stack is empty, so jump to a new accepting state. The extra bottom marker also stops the draining machine from accepting by accident when the old machine emptied its stack.

Deterministic PDAs: A PDA is deterministic (a DPDA) if in every situation it has at most one possible move. Precisely: for each state q, input a and top X, delta(q, a, X) has at most one element, and if an epsilon-move delta(q, epsilon, X) exists then no move delta(q, a, X) on real input exists. Our a^n b^n machine above breaks the second rule in q0 with Z on top: it can read a or jump on epsilon. A small fix makes it deterministic: let the start state itself be accepting so the empty string is accepted, move to a pushing state on the first a, and only take the epsilon-move to the final state when Z shows in the popping state. So a^n b^n is a deterministic context-free language, or DCFL.

DPDA versus NPDA: For finite automata, DFAs and NFAs have the same power. For PDAs this is false. The even palindromes ww^R are context-free, but no DPDA accepts them, because a deterministic machine cannot know where the middle is. If we mark the middle with a special symbol, as in wcw^R, a DPDA works: push until c, then pop and compare. So the picture is: regular languages are inside the DCFLs, which are inside all CFLs, and both inclusions are strict. Also, for DPDAs the empty-stack mode is weaker than the final-state mode, because a DPDA that empties its stack cannot continue; it can only accept languages where no accepted string is a prefix of another.

Real-life example 1, code editors: When you type code in an editor and a bracket turns red, the editor is doing PDA work. Every (, [ or { is pushed; every closing bracket must match the top and pops it. If a ] arrives while ( is on top, there is an error. A finite automaton could only check brackets up to some fixed depth, but a stack handles any depth, just like our balanced bracket PDA.

Real-life example 2, a wedding plate stack: At a biye bari the helpers stack clean plates as they wash them and the servers take plates from the top. Suppose the rule is that every washed plate must later be served, and nobody serves from an empty stack. If you write W for washed and S for served, the valid sequences are exactly the balanced bracket strings, with W as ( and S as ). The plate stack is a PDA, and the guests never see more than the top plate.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that every move pops the top, so to keep X you must push it back with X / X or X / AX. Writing the pushed string in the wrong order: in AZ, A is the new top. Forgetting the bottom marker, so the machine cannot tell when the stack is back to empty. Accepting before the whole input is read; in final-state mode, a final state in the middle of the input means nothing. And believing DPDAs and NPDAs are equal, as with DFAs and NFAs; they are not.

What exams ask: Give the 7-tuple and explain each part. Design a PDA for a^n b^n, a^n b^2n, ww^R, wcw^R, balanced parentheses or strings with equal numbers of a's and b's. Show the sequence of IDs on a given string. Explain final state versus empty stack acceptance and why they are equivalent. Define a DPDA and give a language that a PDA accepts but no DPDA does. Converting a grammar to a PDA is in the next lesson.

What comes next: In lesson 18 we prove that PDAs and context-free grammars describe exactly the same languages, and we look at what CFLs are closed under. Lesson 19 shows languages, like a^n b^n c^n, that even a PDA cannot handle. The reason is simple: one stack can match one pair of counts, but checking a, b and c all at once would need the a-count twice, and popping destroys it.

Recap: A PDA is a finite automaton with one unbounded stack. Its moves depend on state, input or epsilon, and the top of the stack, and each move pops the top and pushes a string. We trace it with IDs (state, rest of input, stack). It accepts by final state or by empty stack, which are equivalent for nondeterministic PDAs. Nondeterminism really adds power here: ww^R needs a guessing PDA.
key_points: A PDA is a finite automaton plus one unbounded stack; it sees only the top of the stack.
7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, Z0, F); delta(q, a or epsilon, X) gives a finite set of (state, string to push) pairs.
Every move pops the top symbol and pushes a string; the leftmost symbol of that string becomes the new top.
An instantaneous description (q, w, gamma) records state, unread input and the stack; |- means one move.
Acceptance by final state and by empty stack give the same class of languages for nondeterministic PDAs.
A PDA accepts if at least one computation branch accepts; ww^R needs this guessing of the middle.
DPDAs are strictly weaker than NPDAs: wcw^R is deterministic, ww^R is not. Regular is inside DCFL, which is inside CFL.
lessons.tip: When you design a PDA, first write the plan in one sentence, like push every a, pop one A per b, accept when Z shows. Only then write the moves. Most mistakes come from writing moves without a clear plan.
lessons.task: Design a PDA for a^n b^2n (n at least 0): push two A's for each a, pop one A for each b. Trace your machine on aabbbb and on aabbb with IDs on paper, and check that one is accepted and the other rejected.

quiz.q: In the move a, X / AX, what happens to the stack?
options: X is popped and nothing is pushed
X stays and A is pushed on top of it
quiz.explain: The move pops X and pushes AX; the leftmost symbol A becomes the new top, so X is kept just under A.

quiz.q: What does an instantaneous description (q, w, gamma) record?
options: The state, the unread input and the stack contents
Only the state and the stack
The input already read and the state
quiz.explain: An ID is a snapshot: current state, the rest of the input still to read, and the stack written top first.

quiz.q: Which language is context-free but cannot be accepted by any deterministic PDA?
quiz.explain: A DPDA cannot know where the middle of ww^R is. With a middle marker, wcw^R, a DPDA works.

quiz.q: A PDA accepts by empty stack when, at the end of the input:
options: It is in a final state
quiz.explain: Empty-stack acceptance needs all input read and the stack fully empty, including Z0; the state does not matter.

quiz.q: On input aab, the PDA for a^n b^n from the lesson:
options: Accepts, because it reads all input
Rejects, because an A is still on top and it cannot reach q2
quiz.explain: After aab it is in (q1, epsilon, AZ). The move to q2 needs Z on top, so no accepting ID is reachable.

lessons.title: PDA and CFG Equivalence, and Properties of CFLs
lessons.content:
Imagine two cooks in a Dhaka restaurant. One has a written recipe book: to make biryani, make rice, then make meat, then layer them. The other has no book at all, just a big stack of steel bowls and a habit of working with whatever bowl is on top. Can the second cook make every dish the first one can, and the other way round? For context-free languages the answer is yes. The recipe book is a context-free grammar, the bowl stack is a pushdown automaton, and today we prove they are equally powerful. Then we use both views to learn what CFLs can and cannot be combined with.

The main theorem: A language is context-free, meaning some CFG generates it, if and only if some pushdown automaton accepts it. This is the context-free version of Kleene's theorem from lesson 10, which said regular expressions and finite automata are equal in power. The proof has two directions: build a PDA from any grammar, and build a grammar from any PDA. The first is easy and very useful; the second is more technical, so we will see its main idea.

Direction 1, the idea: A PDA can act out a leftmost derivation. Keep the part of the sentential form that still needs work on the stack. If the top is a variable, replace it with the right-hand side of one of its rules, guessing nondeterministically which rule. If the top is a terminal, it must match the next input symbol, so read the input and pop. If the stack empties all the way down to the bottom marker exactly when the input ends, the guesses formed a correct derivation.

Direction 1, the construction: Take states p, q and f, start state p, accepting state f, bottom symbol Z. First move: delta(p, epsilon, Z) = (q, SZ), which pushes the start variable. For every rule A -> beta, add delta(q, epsilon, A) containing (q, beta). For every terminal a, add delta(q, a, a) = (q, epsilon). Finally delta(q, epsilon, Z) = (f, Z). The stack alphabet is all variables, all terminals and Z. Many books give an even shorter one-state version that accepts by empty stack: the same variable and terminal moves, with S as the start stack symbol.

Trace for S -> aSb | epsilon on aabb: (p, aabb, Z) |- (q, aabb, SZ) |- (q, aabb, aSbZ) |- (q, abb, SbZ) |- (q, abb, aSbbZ) |- (q, bb, SbbZ) |- (q, bb, bbZ) |- (q, b, bZ) |- (q, epsilon, Z) |- (f, epsilon, Z). Look at the stack column: S, aSb, then after matching a, Sb, then aSbb, then Sbb, then bb. Together with the input already read, this is exactly the leftmost derivation S => aSb => aaSbb => aabb. I checked each step of this trace against a simulator, and checked that the built PDA accepts exactly a^n b^n on all strings up to length 8. The same construction for the grammar S -> (S)S | epsilon accepted exactly the balanced bracket strings.

Why the guesses are safe: If a wrong rule is guessed, sooner or later a terminal on top will not match the input, or the input will run out with symbols left on the stack, and that branch simply dies. Only a branch that followed a real derivation of the input can reach f with all input read. And every leftmost derivation of w gives such a branch. So the PDA accepts exactly the language of the grammar.

A GNF bonus: If the grammar is in Greibach normal form (lesson 16), we can merge each expansion with the match that follows it. For a rule A -> a B1 ... Bk use the single move delta(q, a, A) containing (q, B1 ... Bk). Now every move reads one input symbol, there are no epsilon-moves in the middle, and an input of length n is decided in about n moves. This is why GNF is often called the bridge between grammars and PDAs.

Direction 2, the idea: Going from a PDA to a grammar is harder, because a PDA can do anything with its stack. The trick is to first tidy up the PDA so that it has a single accepting state, empties its stack before accepting, and on every move either pushes exactly one symbol or pops exactly one symbol, never both or neither. Any PDA can be changed into this shape without changing its language.

Direction 2, the variables: For every pair of states p and q, make a variable A_pq. It should generate exactly the strings that can take the PDA from state p with an empty stack to state q with an empty stack. Think about such a run. Either the symbol pushed at the first move is the same one popped at the last move, and then the rule is A_pq -> a A_rs b, where a is read at that first push, b at that last pop, and A_rs covers the middle. Or the stack becomes empty somewhere in the middle at a state r, and then the rule is A_pq -> A_pr A_rq. Add A_pp -> epsilon for every p. The start variable is A for the start state and the accepting state. A proof by induction on the length of runs and derivations shows it works. Hopcroft and Ullman use a similar construction with variables written [pXq], meaning go from p to q while popping X.

What the equivalence gives us: Now we can use whichever view is easier. To show a language is context-free, either write a grammar or design a PDA. To show closure properties, sometimes grammars are easier, sometimes machines. Let us do both.

Closure under union: If L1 has a grammar with start S1 and L2 has a grammar with start S2, rename the variables so they do not clash and add a new start S -> S1 | S2. Example: S1 -> aS1b | epsilon for a^n b^n, and S2 -> aS2bb | epsilon for a^n b^2n. Then S -> S1 | S2 generates their union. As a machine: a PDA that guesses at the start which of the two machines to run.

Closure under concatenation and star: For concatenation add S -> S1 S2. For star add S -> S1 S | epsilon. Example: with T -> aTb | ab, the grammar S -> TS | epsilon generates any number of blocks a^n b^n glued together, like ab aabb ab. I generated all strings up to length 8 from this grammar and compared them with a direct checker, and they matched. CFLs are also closed under reversal (reverse every right-hand side) and under homomorphism (replace every terminal by a string), but we will not need those today.

Not closed under intersection: Let L1 be the strings a^n b^n c^m, with the same number of a's and b's and any number of c's. Grammar: S -> XC, X -> aXb | epsilon, C -> cC | epsilon. Let L2 be the strings a^m b^n c^n, with any number of a's and the same number of b's and c's. Grammar: S -> AY, A -> aA | epsilon, Y -> bYc | epsilon. Both are context-free. But a string in both must have as many a's as b's and as many b's as c's, so L1 intersected with L2 is a^n b^n c^n, which lesson 19 proves is not context-free. I checked this intersection by brute force for all strings up to length 9.

Not closed under complement: Suppose CFLs were closed under complement. They are closed under union, and by De Morgan's law, L1 intersect L2 equals the complement of (complement of L1 union complement of L2). Then they would be closed under intersection, which we just showed is false. So some CFL has a complement that is not context-free. Be careful though: this does not mean every complement fails. For example, the complement of a^n b^n c^n is context-free, even though a^n b^n c^n itself is not.

Intersection with a regular language: Here is the good news. If L is context-free and R is regular, then L intersect R is context-free. Proof by product machine: run the PDA for L and the DFA for R side by side. The new states are pairs (PDA state, DFA state). The stack belongs to the PDA alone, because the DFA needs no stack. On an input symbol both machines move; on an epsilon-move only the PDA moves and the DFA stays. Accept when both parts accept. The DFA rides along like a passenger who only needs to remember a finite thing.

Using it in proofs: Let L be all strings over a, b, c with equal numbers of a's, b's and c's, in any order. Is L context-free? Intersect it with the regular language a*b*c*. The result is a^n b^n c^n. If L were context-free, the intersection would be too, which is false. So L is not context-free. This trick, cutting a messy language down with a regular filter, is very common in exams and makes pumping proofs much easier.

Deterministic CFLs: A DCFL is a language accepted by a deterministic PDA by final state (lesson 17). DCFLs behave differently from general CFLs. They are closed under complement: roughly, make the DPDA always read its whole input, then swap accepting and non-accepting states, with some extra care for epsilon-moves. But DCFLs are not closed under union or intersection. Indeed L1 and L2 above are both DCFLs, yet their intersection is not even context-free. And if DCFLs were closed under union, then by complement and De Morgan they would be closed under intersection too.

Why parsers love DCFLs: Every DCFL has an unambiguous grammar, and a deterministic machine never needs to backtrack, so it can parse in time proportional to the input length. Programming languages are designed so their syntax is deterministic. Donald Knuth showed in 1965 that the LR(k) grammars generate exactly the DCFLs. How LL and LR parsers build their tables is the job of the Compiler Design course; here it is enough to know that they are deterministic PDAs in disguise.

Real-life example 1, a compiler front end: A language like C or Python is defined by a grammar, often written in BNF. A parser generator such as Bison or ANTLR reads that grammar and produces parsing code, which is a stack machine. That is direction 1 of today's theorem, done by a program, with the extra rule that the result should be deterministic so the compiler is fast. When the parser says syntax error, it means no branch of the machine could continue with the next token.

Real-life example 2, filtering bKash statements: Suppose a valid statement must have its opening and closing brackets matched, a context-free condition, and must also contain no line longer than some fixed limit, a regular condition. Checking both at once is a CFL intersected with a regular language, so a single stack machine can still do it. But if you add a second independent counting condition, for example cash-in count equals cash-out count equals fee count, you have left the context-free world, like a^n b^n c^n.

Common mistakes: Saying CFLs are closed under intersection or complement because regular languages are. Forgetting to rename variables before combining two grammars, so rules of one grammar leak into the other. Thinking that the CFG to PDA construction needs many states; three states, or even one, are enough because the stack does all the work. Mixing up DCFL closure with CFL closure: DCFLs are closed under complement, CFLs are not.

What exams ask: Convert a given CFG to a PDA and show the moves on a string. State and prove closure under union, concatenation and star with grammars. Show that CFLs are not closed under intersection with the a^n b^n c^m and a^m b^n c^n example, and derive non-closure under complement with De Morgan. Prove that CFL intersect regular is a CFL. Use that fact to show a language is not context-free.

Recap: CFGs and PDAs describe exactly the same languages. Grammar to PDA: put the start variable on the stack, expand variables by guessing rules, match terminals with the input. PDA to grammar: variables A_pq for runs from p to q that start and end with an empty stack. CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star and intersection with regular languages, but not under intersection or complement. DCFLs are closed under complement, and parsers are built on them. Next lesson: the pumping lemma that proves languages like a^n b^n c^n are not context-free.
key_points: A language is context-free if and only if some PDA accepts it.
CFG to PDA: push S; on a variable on top, guess a rule and replace it; on a terminal on top, match the input and pop; accept when the bottom marker returns.
PDA to CFG: tidy the PDA, then variables A_pq generate the strings that take it from p to q starting and ending with an empty stack.
CFLs are closed under union (S -> S1 | S2), concatenation (S -> S1 S2) and star (S -> S1 S | epsilon).
CFLs are not closed under intersection: a^n b^n c^m intersect a^m b^n c^n = a^n b^n c^n; by De Morgan, not under complement either.
CFL intersect regular is always a CFL (product of a PDA and a DFA); this helps prove languages are not context-free.
DCFLs are closed under complement but not under union or intersection; LR(k) grammars generate exactly the DCFLs.
lessons.tip: For any closure question, first ask: is there a simple grammar trick (new start rule) or a product machine? If neither works, look for a counterexample built from a^n b^n c^n.
lessons.task: Write the CFG to PDA construction for the grammar S -> (S)S | epsilon. Then trace your PDA with IDs on the input ()() and on the input ()), and mark where the second one gets stuck.

quiz.q: In the CFG to PDA construction, what does the PDA do when a variable A is on top of the stack?
options: Reads an input symbol and pops A
Replaces A by the right side of some A-rule with an epsilon-move
quiz.explain: Variables are expanded by guessing a rule, without reading input. Terminals on top are matched against the input.

quiz.q: Which operation are context-free languages NOT closed under?
quiz.explain: a^n b^n c^m and a^m b^n c^n are context-free, but their intersection a^n b^n c^n is not.

quiz.q: If L is context-free and R is regular, then L intersect R is:
quiz.explain: Run the PDA and the DFA together; the stack belongs to the PDA. The product is a PDA, so the result is context-free.

quiz.q: Why are CFLs not closed under complement?
options: Because complement of every CFL is regular
Because with union and De Morgan's law, complement would give intersection, which fails
Because PDAs cannot swap accept states
Because a^n b^n has a non-context-free complement
quiz.explain: L1 intersect L2 = complement(complement L1 union complement L2). Closure under complement plus union would force closure under intersection.

quiz.q: Which statement about deterministic CFLs is true?
options: They cannot be parsed in linear time
quiz.explain: DCFLs are closed under complement, but not union or intersection; ww^R is a CFL that is not a DCFL.

lessons.title: Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages
lessons.content:
At the Kamalapur railway station imagine three counters: one sells tickets, one checks them at the gate, and one collects them at the exit. At the end of the day the station master wants all three counts equal. A clerk with one stack of tokens can easily check two of the counts against each other: push a token per ticket sold, pop one per ticket checked. But by then the tokens are gone, and he has nothing left to compare with the third counter. That is the intuition for today: one stack can match one pair of counts, not three. The pumping lemma for context-free languages turns this intuition into a proof.

Quick recap of the regular version: In lesson 11, every long enough string of a regular language could be written xyz, with y nonempty and close to the start, so that repeating y any number of times stayed in the language. The reason was a DFA with p states must repeat a state on any input of length p. For context-free languages the repeating thing is a variable in a parse tree, and because a variable can grow on both sides, we pump two pieces at the same time.

The statement: If L is a context-free language, then there is a number p, the pumping length, such that every string s in L with length at least p can be split into five parts, s = uvxyz, so that three conditions hold. First, |vy| is at least 1, so v and y are not both empty. Second, |vxy| is at most p, so the pumped part is a short window somewhere in the string. Third, for every i at least 0, the string u v^i x y^i z is in L. So v and y are pumped together, the same number of times.

Where the window can be: Notice the difference from the regular lemma. There the pumped part had to be inside the first p symbols. Here the window vxy can be anywhere, at the start, in the middle or at the end, as long as it is short. That makes proofs a little harder, because you must handle every possible position of the window, not only the start.

Why it is true, part 1, trees grow tall: Take a grammar for L in Chomsky normal form with m variables (lesson 15). Every inner node has two children, except the last step A -> a. So a parse tree whose longest root to leaf path has h edges can yield at most 2^(h-1) letters. Set p = 2^m. If s has at least p letters, its parse tree must have a path with at least m + 1 edges. That path has at least m + 1 variable nodes before the terminal leaf.

Why it is true, part 2, pigeonhole: There are only m different variables, but the path has at least m + 1 variable nodes, so some variable, call it A, appears twice. Choose the repeat among the lowest m + 1 variables of the path. Now the upper A derives a piece of the form v A y, and the lower A derives x. So S derives u A z, A derives v A y, and A derives x. We can use the step A => vAy as many times as we like, or skip it and replace the upper A directly by x. That gives u v^i x y^i z for every i.

Why it is true, part 3, the two conditions: Because we chose the repeat near the bottom, the subtree of the upper A has height at most m + 1, so its yield vxy has at most 2^m = p letters. And because CNF has no unit rules and no epsilon rules, the upper A uses a rule A -> BC, and one of B or C sits outside the lower A and yields at least one letter. So vy is not empty.

A tiny picture: In the grammar S -> aSb | ab, the parse tree of aaabbb has S three times on its spine. Take the top two S's: the upper one makes a S b around the lower one. So v = a and y = b, and pumping gives a^n b^n for any n. In fact a^n b^n is context-free and pumps fine: with s = a^p b^p, take u = a^(p-1), v = a, x empty, y = b, z = b^(p-1). Every u v^i x y^i z is a^(p-1+i) b^(p-1+i), still in the language. I checked this for p up to 5 and i up to 5.

How to use it, the game: The lemma is used to prove a language is NOT context-free, by contradiction. Play it as a game against an opponent. The opponent picks p. You pick a string s in L with |s| at least p. The opponent picks any split uvxyz that obeys |vy| at least 1 and |vxy| at most p. You pick an i and show u v^i x y^i z is not in L. If you can win against every possible split, L is not context-free. You choose s and i; you never choose the split.

Example 1, a^n b^n c^n: Suppose L = {a^n b^n c^n : n at least 0} were context-free with pumping length p. Choose s = a^p b^p c^p, length 3p. Look at the window vxy. Its length is at most p, and the block of b's between the a's and the c's has length p, so the window cannot touch both a's and c's. It touches at most two neighbouring kinds of letters.

Example 1, the cases: Case 1, v and y each contain only one kind of letter. Then pumping up with i = 2 adds letters to at most two of the three blocks, and since vy is not empty, at least one block grows. The third block stays at p, so the counts are no longer equal. Case 2, v or y contains two kinds of letters, like ab. Then v^2 or y^2 contains ab twice, so a b appears before an a, and the string is out of order. In both cases u v^2 x y^2 z is not in L. Contradiction, so a^n b^n c^n is not context-free. A brute force program tried every legal split of a^p b^p c^p for p from 1 to 6, and none of them survived i = 2.

Example 2, ww, choosing s badly: Let L = {ww : w in {a, b}*}, strings made of some word written twice, like abab or aabaab. A tempting choice is s = a^p b a^p b. But the opponent wins: when p is at least 3, take v as the last a of the first block, x as the middle b, and y as the first a of the second block. Then u v^i x y^i z = a^(p-1+i) b a^(p-1+i) b, which is ww with w = a^(p-1+i) b, for every i. The string pumps happily, and your proof fails.

Example 2, a better s: Choose s = a^p b^p a^p b^p, which is ww with w = a^p b^p. Pump down with i = 0, so s' = uxz, which has length 4p minus |vy|. If |vy| is odd, s' has odd length and cannot be ww. So suppose |vy| = 2m with m at least 1. Then s' has length 4p - 2m, and each half should have length 2p - m.

Example 2, the window positions: Case A, the window lies inside the first a^p b^p. Then the second half of s' is the last 2p - m letters of s, namely a^(p-m) b^p, which ends with b. But the first half of s' ends with the first m letters of the third block, which are a's. The halves differ. Case B, the window lies inside the last a^p b^p. Then the first half of s' is a^p b^(p-m), starting with a, but the second half starts with the last m b's of the second block. The halves differ. Case C, the window crosses the middle. Since it is short, it only touches b's of the second block and a's of the third block, so s' = a^p b^j a^k b^p with j + k less than 2p. If both j and k are positive, ww would force w = a^p b^j = a^k b^p, so j = k = p, impossible. If j or k is 0, s' has only one block of a's, but ww needs a's in both halves, separated by b's. So s' is never in L, and ww is not context-free. Brute force agreed for p from 1 to 6: no legal split survives i = 0.

Compare with ww^R: The even palindromes ww^R are context-free, as we built a PDA for them in lesson 17. The copy language ww is not. The difference is the stack: to check a mirror image, you pop in reverse order, which is exactly what a stack gives. To check a copy, you would need the first symbol first, and a stack hides it at the bottom.

More non-context-free languages: The same style proves that {a^i b^j c^k : i < j < k}, {a^(n^2) : n at least 0} and the set of strings over a, b, c with equal numbers of each letter are not context-free. For the last one, remember the shortcut from lesson 18: intersect with the regular language a*b*c* to get a^n b^n c^n, and you are done without a new pumping argument.

Only a one-way test: The pumping lemma says every CFL pumps. It does not say every language that pumps is a CFL. So you can never use the lemma to prove a language IS context-free; for that you write a grammar or a PDA. Some non-context-free languages even satisfy the pumping condition, and then the lemma is too weak to catch them.

Ogden's lemma: A stronger version, due to William Ogden, lets you mark at least p positions of s as special. Then the split guarantees that vy contains at least one marked position and vxy contains at most p marked positions. By marking only the positions you care about, you stop the opponent from pumping some harmless part of the string. A textbook example is {a^i b^j c^k d^l : i = 0 or j = k = l}, which the ordinary lemma cannot handle, because the opponent just pumps the a's, but Ogden's lemma shows it is not context-free.

Real-life example 1, declare before use: In C or Java a variable must be declared before it is used. If you model a program as a declaration of a name w followed later by a use of the same name w, it looks like the language w c w, which is close to the copy language and not context-free. This is why compilers do not check declarations in the grammar. The parser checks the context-free shape, and a later phase called semantic analysis checks names with a symbol table. You will see this in Compiler Design.

Real-life example 2, a three-way cricket check: A scorer wants a match log in which the number of balls bowled, the number of balls faced and the number of deliveries recorded on the scoreboard are all equal, written as three separate sections. That log language is a relative of a^n b^n c^n, so no grammar and no PDA can check it. A program with two counters, or any normal code with variables, checks it easily.

Common mistakes: Choosing the split yourself, for example saying let v = a and y = b; the opponent chooses. Forgetting that the window vxy can be anywhere, not just at the start. Choosing s shorter than p, or not in L. Checking only i = 2 when your case needs i = 0, or the other way round. Forgetting the case where v or y contains two kinds of letters. And claiming a language is context-free because you could pump one string.

What exams ask: State the pumping lemma for CFLs with all three conditions. Explain the proof idea from parse tree height and pigeonhole. Prove that a^n b^n c^n, ww, a^(n^2) or a^i b^j c^k with i < j < k is not context-free. Explain why the lemma cannot prove that a language is context-free. Compare the regular and context-free versions: xyz with |xy| at most p, versus uvxyz with |vxy| at most p.

Recap: Every long string of a CFL can be written uvxyz, where v and y pump together inside a short window vxy, because a tall parse tree must repeat a variable on some path. To prove a language is not context-free, play the game: pick a clever s, consider every legal split, and pick an i that breaks it. a^n b^n c^n and ww are the classic victims. Next lesson we meet the machine that can handle them, the Turing machine.
key_points: If L is context-free, there is p so that every s in L with |s| >= p splits as uvxyz with |vy| >= 1, |vxy| <= p and u v^i x y^i z in L for all i >= 0.
Proof idea: a CNF parse tree of a long string has a long path, so some variable repeats (pigeonhole); A => vAy can be repeated or skipped.
With m variables in CNF, p = 2^m works, because a tree with longest path h edges yields at most 2^(h-1) letters.
The window vxy can be anywhere in s, so proofs must consider every position.
a^n b^n c^n is not context-free: the short window touches at most two kinds of letters.
ww is not context-free (use s = a^p b^p a^p b^p), while ww^R is context-free.
The lemma only proves non-context-freeness; Ogden's lemma is a stronger version with marked positions.
lessons.tip: Before writing a pumping proof, draw the string as blocks and slide a box of width p across it. Every position of the box where it touches one block or two blocks is a case. If your cases cover every box position, your proof is complete.
lessons.task: Prove that L = {a^n b^n c^n} is not context-free once more, but this time pump down with i = 0 instead of i = 2. Write each case on paper and check that the shorter string really fails.

quiz.q: In the CFL pumping lemma, which condition is correct?
quiz.explain: The pumped window vxy has length at most p, and |vy| >= 1. x may be empty, and v, y can be different.

quiz.q: Why must some variable repeat in the parse tree of a long string?
options: Because the string is a palindrome
Because a long string forces a long path, which has more variable nodes than there are variables
quiz.explain: A tree with a bounded height has a bounded yield. A long string needs a path with more than m variable nodes, so by pigeonhole a variable repeats.

quiz.q: For L = {a^n b^n c^n}, why can the window vxy of s = a^p b^p c^p not touch both a's and c's?
options: Because |vxy| <= p and the b block between them has length p
Because x must contain all the b's
quiz.explain: To reach from an a to a c, the window would have to cover all p b's plus at least two more letters, which is longer than p.

quiz.q: Which language is context-free?
quiz.explain: Even palindromes ww^R are accepted by a PDA that pushes the first half and pops while matching the second. The others are not context-free.

quiz.q: A language satisfies the pumping condition for some p. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing for sure; the lemma is only a necessary condition
quiz.explain: Every CFL pumps, but some non-context-free languages also pump. To show a language is context-free, give a grammar or a PDA.

lessons.title: Turing Machines
lessons.content:
Picture a very patient clerk in an old government office in Motijheel. He has a long roll of paper divided into boxes, a pencil with an eraser, and a small card of rules. He looks at one box at a time. Depending on his current mood, which is one of a few fixed moods, and the symbol in the box, the card tells him what to write in the box, whether to step one box left or right, and which mood to switch to. That is all. In 1936 the British mathematician Alan Turing argued that this simple clerk can carry out any step-by-step calculation a human can. We call his model the Turing machine, and it is the most important machine in this course.

Why we need it: Finite automata have no memory beyond their states. Pushdown automata add a stack but can only touch its top. In lesson 19 we proved that a^n b^n c^n and ww are not context-free, so no PDA handles them. Yet a tiny program in any language checks them easily. A Turing machine has a tape it can read and write anywhere, by walking to that place. That freedom turns out to be enough for every algorithm we know.

The parts: The tape is divided into cells and is infinite to the right. At the start it holds the input string in the leftmost cells, and every other cell holds the blank symbol, which we write as an underscore. The head sits on the leftmost cell. In each step the machine reads the symbol under the head, writes a symbol (maybe the same one), moves the head one cell left or right, and changes state. If it tries to move left from the leftmost cell, it simply stays there. Unlike a DFA, the machine does not stop when the input ends; it stops only when it enters a halting state.

The formal definition: Following Sipser, a Turing machine is a 7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, q_accept, q_reject). Q is a finite set of states. Sigma is the input alphabet, which does not contain the blank. Gamma is the tape alphabet; it contains Sigma, the blank, and any extra marker symbols we like. delta maps Q x Gamma to Q x Gamma x {L, R}. q0 is the start state, and q_accept and q_reject are the two halting states, which must be different. Hopcroft and Ullman write a slightly different 7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, B, F), with the blank B and a set F of accepting states, and they halt when no move is defined. The two styles have the same power.

Reading a transition: delta(q1, 1) = (q2, Y, L) means: in state q1, if the head reads 1, write Y in that cell, move the head left, and go to state q2. In a state diagram the arrow from q1 to q2 is labelled 1 -> Y, L. The basic machine is deterministic: for each state and symbol there is at most one move. In our examples, if no move is listed for a state and symbol, the machine goes to q_reject. That keeps tables short.

Configurations: A configuration is a snapshot of the whole machine: the tape contents, the state and the head position. We write it as u q v, where u is the tape to the left of the head, q is the state, and the head is on the first symbol of v. For example X0 q1 11 means the tape is X011, the state is q1, and the head reads the first 1. The start configuration on input w is q0 w. A configuration with state q_accept is accepting, one with q_reject is rejecting, and both are halting. We write C1 |- C2 when one move takes C1 to C2.

Example, the plan for 0^n 1^n: We build a TM for {0^n 1^n : n at least 1}. A PDA can do this, but the TM method shows the typical TM style: crossing off. Repeat: change the leftmost 0 into X, run right to the first 1 and change it into Y, run back left to the X, and step right to the next 0. When no 0 is left, check that only Y's remain until the blank. If at any point a needed symbol is missing, reject.

Example, the transitions: States q0, q1, q2, q3 and q_accept. In q0 (find a 0): on 0 write X, move R, go to q1. On Y move R, go to q3. In q1 (run right to a 1): on 0 or Y keep the symbol and move R. On 1 write Y, move L, go to q2. In q2 (run back left): on 0 or Y keep it and move L. On X move R, go to q0. In q3 (final check): on Y move R. On blank move R and go to q_accept. Every other case goes to q_reject. That is ten moves in total.

Example, the full trace on 0011: q0 0011 |- X q1 011 |- X0 q1 11 |- X q2 0Y1 |- q2 X0Y1 |- X q0 0Y1 |- XX q1 Y1 |- XXY q1 1 |- XX q2 YY |- X q2 XYY |- XX q0 YY |- XXY q3 Y |- XXYY q3 _ |- XXYY_ q_accept. Count them: 13 moves, then accept. Read it slowly: the first 0 became X, the first 1 became Y, the head came back, the second pair was crossed off, and the final check walked over YY to the blank.

Example, a rejection: On 001 the machine goes q0 001 |- X q1 01 |- X0 q1 1 |- X q2 0Y |- q2 X0Y |- X q0 0Y |- XX q1 Y |- XXY q1 _. Now q1 is looking for a 1 but reads a blank, and there is no move for that, so the machine rejects. The second 0 has no partner. I wrote a small TM simulator, checked that every line of both traces matches it exactly, and ran the machine on all 511 strings of 0s and 1s up to length 8. It accepted exactly 01, 0011, 000111 and 00001111, and rejected everything else.

How long does it take: For 0^n 1^n the simulator counted 5, 13, 25 and 41 moves for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. These fit the formula 2n^2 + 2n + 1, so the time grows like n squared, because the head walks back and forth across the string once for each pair. A single tape TM pays for walking. Lesson 21 shows that more tapes can speed things up, and lesson 25 turns these counts into complexity classes.

Beyond context-free, a^n b^n c^n: The same crossing off idea handles a^n b^n c^n, which no PDA can do. In each pass, change one a into X, the next b into Y and the next c into Z, then return to the X. When no a is left, check that only Y's and Z's remain. I built this machine with five working states and tested it on every string over a, b and c up to length 8; it accepted exactly abc and aabbcc and halted on every input. The TM can do it because it can revisit and rewrite any cell; nothing is destroyed by reading it, unlike popping a stack.

Turing machines that compute: A TM can also compute a function: the answer is what is left on the tape when it halts. Example, unary addition: the input 111011 means 3 plus 2, written as ones separated by a 0. Plan: skip the 1s, change the 0 into 1, run to the right end, step back left, and erase the last 1. The tape now holds 11111, which is 5. This small machine, three working states plus the accept state, was checked for all m and n from 0 to 5. Functions computed this way are called computable functions.

Three possible outcomes: On a given input a TM can accept, reject, or loop, which means run forever without halting. Looping is new: DFAs and PDAs of the kinds we built always finish when the input is read, but a TM may wander forever. Example: in q0, on 0 accept; on 1 go to q1; in q1, move right forever whatever you read. On 0 or 01 it accepts, on the empty string it rejects, and on 1 or 10 it walks right forever into the blanks and never stops.

Recognizable languages: The language of a TM M is the set of strings it accepts. A language is Turing-recognizable, also called recursively enumerable, if some TM accepts exactly its strings. On strings outside the language that TM may reject or may loop. So a recognizer gives a clear yes, but its no might look like waiting forever. You can never be sure whether it is still thinking or will never answer.

Decidable languages: A TM is a decider if it halts on every input, accepting or rejecting. A language is decidable, also called recursive, if some decider accepts it. Both of our examples are deciders, since they halt on every input, so 0^n 1^n and a^n b^n c^n are decidable. The looping machine above is not a decider, but its language, strings starting with 0, is still decidable, because a different machine that rejects on 1 decides it. Decidability is about the language: is there at least one decider for it?

How they relate: Every decidable language is recognizable, since a decider is also a recognizer. The other way fails: in lesson 23 we will see that the halting problem is recognizable but not decidable. A language is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are recognizable: run the two recognizers side by side, one step each in turn, and whichever accepts gives the answer. Lessons 22 to 24 build on these two words, so learn them well.

How strong is it: Every regular language and every context-free language is decidable by a TM. And a TM can simulate a PDA with its tape, or even two stacks. Variants such as many tapes or nondeterminism, which add no extra power, and the Church-Turing thesis, which says this model captures all algorithms, are the topic of lesson 21.

Real-life example 1, the exam hall attendance sheet: An invigilator in a Dhaka exam hall has two lists, the students present and the answer scripts collected. She ticks one name on the first list, then finds a matching script and ticks it, then returns to the first list for the next name. That is exactly the 0^n 1^n crossing off machine: one mark on each side per round, walking back and forth. If a script has no matching name, or the other way round, something is wrong, which is rejection.

Real-life example 2, your phone as a tape machine: Your phone's memory is like the tape, the processor's current instruction is like the state, and reading or writing one memory address is like a head step. A real phone has finite memory, so strictly it is a huge finite automaton, but its memory is so big that the Turing machine, with its unlimited tape, is the right model. When someone says a problem is unsolvable by computers, they mean no Turing machine decides it, no matter how much memory and time you give.

Common mistakes: Thinking the TM stops when the input ends; it stops only in a halting state. Forgetting that the tape is writable, which is the whole point. Writing configurations with the head in the wrong place; in u q v the head reads the first symbol of v. Mixing up recognizable and decidable: a recognizer may loop on strings outside the language, a decider never loops. And calling a language undecidable because one particular machine loops on it.

What exams ask: Give the 7-tuple and explain each part. Design a TM for 0^n 1^n, a^n b^n c^n, ww, palindromes or unary addition, with a transition table or diagram. Trace your machine on a short input as a sequence of configurations. Define accept, reject and loop. Define Turing-recognizable and decidable languages, and explain why every decidable language is recognizable.

Recap: A Turing machine is a finite control with an infinite read and write tape and a head that moves left or right. Its moves are delta(q, a) = (p, b, L or R), and its configurations are written u q v. It can accept, reject or loop. Recognizable means some TM accepts exactly the language; decidable means some TM also always halts. Next lesson: variants of the TM and the Church-Turing thesis.
key_points: A Turing machine has a finite control, an infinite tape it can read and write, and a head that moves one cell left or right per step.
7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, q_accept, q_reject); delta(q, a) = (p, b, L or R).
A configuration u q v means tape uv, state q, head on the first symbol of v; the start configuration is q0 w.
Crossing off with markers like X and Y is the standard TM technique; it decides 0^n 1^n and even a^n b^n c^n.
On an input a TM can accept, reject, or loop forever.
Turing-recognizable (recursively enumerable): some TM accepts exactly L, possibly looping on strings outside L.
Decidable (recursive): some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly L; a language is decidable iff it and its complement are recognizable.
lessons.tip: Always write the plan of a TM in plain words first, like cross off one 0, find a 1, come back. Then turn each sentence into one state. Tracing a short input like 0011 by hand catches almost every bug.
lessons.task: Using the lesson's transition list, trace the 0^n 1^n machine on the inputs 0101 and 000111 as configurations on paper. Say where 0101 gets rejected, and count the moves for 000111 (the simulator says 25).

quiz.q: What can a Turing machine do that a pushdown automaton cannot?
options: Read and write any cell of its tape by moving left and right
quiz.explain: The TM's tape is writable and the head can move both ways. A PDA can only touch the top of its stack. Both can accept a^n b^n.

quiz.q: In the configuration X0 q1 11, where is the head?
options: On the blank after the input
quiz.explain: In u q v the head reads the first symbol of v. Here v = 11, so the head is on the first 1.

quiz.q: Which three outcomes are possible for a TM on an input?
options: Accept, reject, or crash the tape
quiz.explain: A TM may halt in q_accept, halt in q_reject, or never halt at all.

quiz.q: A language is decidable when:
options: Some TM accepts it, even if it loops on other inputs
Some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly that language
quiz.explain: A decider must halt on every input. A recognizer only needs to accept the strings in the language.

quiz.q: For the lesson's 0^n 1^n machine on input 001, what happens?
options: It reaches q1 reading a blank, has no move, and rejects
It accepts because there are more 0s than 1s
quiz.explain: After crossing off one pair, q1 looks for a 1 but finds a blank. No move exists, so the machine rejects.

lessons.title: Turing Machine Variants and the Church-Turing Thesis
lessons.content:
Imagine two cooks. The first has one small pan and one long notebook. The second has five pans, three notebooks and a magic book that tries many recipes at once. The second cook finishes faster. But is there any dish the second cook can make that the first can never make, even with endless time? For Turing machines, the answer is no. More tapes, more heads, guessing power: each upgrade makes the machine faster or easier to program, but never lets it solve a new problem. That is today's lesson.

Quick recap of the standard machine: In the last lesson we met the Turing machine as a 7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, q_accept, q_reject). Q is a finite set of states, Sigma the input alphabet, Gamma the tape alphabet that includes Sigma and the blank symbol, q0 the start state, and q_accept and q_reject the two halting states. The tape is infinite to the right, the head reads one cell, and the transition function delta maps (state, symbol) to (new state, symbol to write, move L or R). On any input the machine accepts, rejects, or loops forever. A language is Turing-recognizable if some TM accepts exactly its strings, and decidable if some TM accepts them and also halts on every input.

What equivalent means: We call two models equivalent when they recognize exactly the same class of languages. The way to prove it is always the same trick: simulation. We show that machine type A can imitate every step of machine type B, and type B can imitate type A. Simulation may be slow, but here we only ask what can be computed, not how fast.

The stay-put variant: The smallest upgrade lets the head stay where it is, so moves are L, R or S. Is this more powerful? No. A standard machine replaces each S move by two moves: step right into a temporary state, then step straight back left. One step becomes two, the answer stays the same. That is the pattern of the whole lesson: an extra feature is a shortcut the plain machine can fake.

Multitape Turing machines: Now give the machine k tapes, each with its own head. The input starts on tape 1 and the other tapes are blank. The transition function becomes delta: Q x Gamma^k -> Q x Gamma^k x {L, R, S}^k. In one step the machine reads all k symbols under its heads, writes k new symbols and moves each head separately. They are much nicer to program. For example, to check whether a string is a palindrome, a 2-tape machine copies the input to tape 2, moves head 1 back to the left end while head 2 sits on the last symbol, then compares: head 1 walks right while head 2 walks left. On "abba" this takes about 13 moves, roughly 3n for a string of length n.

Simulating many tapes with one tape: Here is the classic construction. A single-tape machine S writes all k tapes one after another on its own tape, separated by a new symbol #, like #abba#abba#. A dotted copy of a symbol, like a-dot, marks the cell under each virtual head. To simulate one step, S sweeps to the last # reading the k dotted symbols into its finite state, then sweeps again to update those cells and move the dots. If a virtual head walks onto the # at the end of its section, S shifts everything to the right by one cell to make room for a blank. So every multitape TM has an equivalent single-tape TM.

How slow is the simulation? If the multitape machine runs t(n) steps, each of its tapes holds at most about t(n) symbols, so one sweep of S costs O(t(n)) moves, and S needs O(t(n)) sweeps. The total is O(t(n) squared). A quick simulation of a simple zigzag palindrome checker on one tape, which crosses off the first symbol, runs to the end, checks the last symbol and runs back, makes about 560 moves for a string of 32 a's, while the 2-tape version makes about 97. Quadratic against linear, but both give the same yes or no. We will use this squared slowdown again in the complexity lesson.

Two-way infinite tape: What if the tape is infinite in both directions? Again no new power. One method folds the tape in half: use a tape with two tracks, where the upper track holds cells 0, 1, 2, ... and the lower track holds cells -1, -2, -3, ... in order. A marker on the first cell tells the machine when it is at the fold, and the state remembers which track it is currently working on, so a left move on the lower track becomes a right move. Another method shifts the tape contents one cell right whenever the head tries to fall off the left end.

Multi-track tapes: A tape with k tracks means each cell holds k symbols stacked like floors of a building. It is really just a bigger alphabet: a cell holding (a, X, blank) is one symbol from Gamma x Gamma x Gamma, which is still finite. Tracks are handy for marks, like a check above every symbol already compared.

Nondeterministic Turing machines: An NTM may have several possible moves in a situation, so delta: Q x Gamma -> P(Q x Gamma x {L, R}), a set of choices. Its computation is a tree: the root is the start configuration, and each node branches into all possible next configurations. The NTM accepts w if at least one branch reaches q_accept. Branches that reject or loop do not matter as long as one branch accepts. It is a guessing superpower: to show a number is composite, an NTM guesses a factor and divides.

Simulating an NTM deterministically: A deterministic TM D explores the computation tree breadth-first, level by level. Depth-first search is a trap, because D could dive into one infinite branch and never come back, missing an accepting branch next door. Sipser's version uses three tapes: the untouched input, a scratch tape for one branch, and an address like 2-1-3 saying which choice to take at each step. D tries addresses in shortlex order, 1, 2, ..., then 11, 12, and so on, restarting the branch each time. If any branch accepts, D finds it. If the branching factor is 2, the tree up to depth 3 has 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes, and in general the number grows exponentially with depth. So every NTM has an equivalent deterministic TM, and if every branch of the NTM halts, D can be made a decider too. Whether this exponential blow-up is ever avoidable in general is exactly the P versus NP question of lesson 25.

Enumerators: An enumerator is a TM with an attached printer. Starting from a blank tape, it prints strings, maybe forever, with repeats, in any order. The language it enumerates is the set of all strings it ever prints. Theorem: a language is Turing-recognizable if and only if some enumerator enumerates it. One direction is easy: given an enumerator E, build M that on input w runs E and accepts whenever E prints w. If w is never printed, M runs forever, which a recognizer may do.

Dovetailing, the other direction: Given a recognizer M, we want an enumerator. List all strings over Sigma in shortlex order: s1, s2, s3, and so on. We cannot run M on s1 until it finishes, because M might loop on s1 and we would never reach s2. Instead, in round i, run M for i steps on each of s1 up to si, and print any that are accepted. The pairs (string, steps) visited are (1,1), then (1,2), (2,2), then (1,3), (2,3), (3,3), and so on. Every accepted string is accepted within some finite number of steps, so it is printed in some round. This trick is called dovetailing. A related fact: a language is decidable exactly when some enumerator prints it in shortlex order.

Other models that are equivalent: Church's lambda calculus, the general recursive functions, Post's rewriting systems, register machines with unbounded counters, a pushdown automaton with two stacks, and any ordinary programming language such as C, Python or Java, assuming unlimited memory, all compute the same things as Turing machines. Some restrictions do lose power, though: a pushdown automaton with one stack only gets context-free languages, and a TM that may move both ways but never write behaves like a finite automaton and recognizes only regular languages.

Encoding machines as strings: A Turing machine is a finite object, so we can write it down as a string, written in angle brackets as the encoding of M. Here is one simple scheme for machines with tape symbols 0, 1 and blank. Number the states q1, q2, q3 and so on, call the symbols X1 = 0, X2 = 1, X3 = blank, and the directions D1 = L, D2 = R. A transition delta(qi, Xj) = (qk, Xl, Dm) is written as 0^i 1 0^j 1 0^k 1 0^l 1 0^m, and transitions are separated by 11. For example, delta(q1, 0) = (q2, 1, R) becomes 010100100100, and delta(q2, 1) = (q1, 0, L) becomes 00100101010. The whole machine is 010100100100 11 00100101010. Because every machine is a finite binary string, the set of all Turing machines is countable, a fact that powers the next two lessons.

The universal Turing machine: Turing's big idea in his 1936 paper was a single machine U that can run any other machine. U takes the input made of the encoding of M together with w, and simulates M on w step by step. A handy design uses three tapes: M's description, M's tape, and M's current state. For each step, U finds the matching transition in the description and updates the simulated tape and state. U accepts if M accepts, rejects if M rejects, and loops if M loops. So U recognizes the language A_TM, the set of pairs where M accepts w. This is the stored-program idea that every modern computer uses: programs are just data in memory.

The Church-Turing thesis: In 1936 Alonzo Church, with his lambda calculus, and Alan Turing, with his machines, independently answered Hilbert's decision problem negatively, and Turing showed the two models compute the same functions. The Church-Turing thesis says: every function that can be computed by an algorithm, in the intuitive sense of a step-by-step mechanical procedure, can be computed by a Turing machine. It is called a thesis, not a theorem, because algorithm is an informal idea, so it cannot be proved mathematically. The evidence: every reasonable model ever invented turned out equivalent. Thanks to the thesis, once we prove no TM solves a problem, we may say no computer can.

What the thesis does not say: The thesis is about what can be computed, not how fast. A quantum computer can be simulated by an ordinary Turing machine, possibly very slowly, so it does not break the thesis. Questions of speed belong to complexity theory, which treats polynomial time as the practical meaning of efficient.

Real life example 1, emulators and interpreters: When a developer in Dhaka tests a bKash-style app on a laptop, she often runs an Android emulator. The laptop's processor and the phone's processor are different, yet the laptop simulates the phone instruction by instruction. That is a simulation proof come alive: slower, same result. Likewise, the Python interpreter is a universal machine: you give it a program's text plus its input, like giving U the pair of M and w, and it runs the program.

Real life example 2, the human computer: Turing modelled his machine on a person doing calculations with pencil and paper, who looks at a few symbols at a time, keeps a finite state of mind, and writes or erases one symbol at a time. Think of a mudi dokan shopkeeper adding a long bill digit by digit, carrying numbers in his head. With unlimited paper and time, the thesis says he can compute exactly what a Turing machine can. A supercomputer is far faster, but not more powerful in this sense.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think more tapes or nondeterminism let a TM decide more languages; they only change speed. Another mistake is simulating an NTM depth-first. Remember that the Church-Turing thesis is not a theorem, and that an enumerator may print strings in any order with repeats. Typical exam tasks: describe the single-tape simulation of a k-tape TM and its O(t squared) cost; prove the enumerator theorem with dovetailing; encode a transition as a binary string; explain the universal TM.

Recap: Stay-put moves, many tapes, tracks, two-way tapes and nondeterminism all have the same power as the plain TM, proved by simulation at constant, quadratic or exponential cost. Enumerators capture exactly the recognizable languages. Machines are strings, so a universal machine runs them all, and there are only countably many. The Church-Turing thesis ties this to the everyday idea of an algorithm. Next lesson: which problems can a TM decide at all?
key_points: Two models are equivalent if they recognize the same languages; equivalence is proved by simulating each with the other.
A k-tape TM can be simulated by a single-tape TM using # separators and dotted head markers, with O(t(n)^2) slowdown.
Stay-put moves, multi-track tapes and two-way infinite tapes add convenience but no power.
An NTM accepts if some branch accepts; a deterministic TM simulates it by breadth-first search, possibly exponentially slower.
A language is Turing-recognizable if and only if some enumerator enumerates it; the proof uses dovetailing.
