Every TM can be encoded as a finite binary string, so there are only countably many TMs.
The universal TM U simulates M on w from the input pair of M and w and recognizes A_TM.
The Church-Turing thesis (Church and Turing, 1936): every algorithm can be carried out by a Turing machine; it is a thesis, not a theorem.
lessons.tip: When an exam asks you to prove that a TM variant is equivalent, always answer with two simulations, one in each direction, and say clearly how one step of the fancy machine becomes several steps of the plain one. Speed is never the point.
lessons.task: On paper, encode the transition delta(q2, 0) = (q3, 1, L) with the scheme from this lesson (X1 = 0, X2 = 1, X3 = blank, D1 = L, D2 = R). Then write the first 10 (string, steps) pairs that a dovetailing enumerator visits, and check that the pattern matches (1,1), (1,2), (2,2), (1,3), ...

quiz.q: Which variant can decide a language that a standard single-tape TM cannot decide?
quiz.explain: All these variants are equivalent to the standard TM. They change speed or convenience, never which languages are decidable.

quiz.q: A k-tape TM runs in t(n) steps. Roughly how many steps does the standard single-tape simulation need?
quiz.explain: Each simulated step needs sweeps over a tape of length O(t(n)), and there are t(n) steps, giving O(t(n)^2).

quiz.q: Why must a deterministic simulation of an NTM use breadth-first search rather than depth-first search?
options: Depth-first search may follow an infinite branch forever and miss an accepting branch
Depth-first search cannot read the input
Breadth-first search is always polynomial time
quiz.explain: A depth-first explorer could dive into a looping branch and never return, so it might miss an accepting branch elsewhere.

quiz.q: What does dovetailing do in the proof that every recognizable language has an enumerator?
options: Runs M on s1 until it halts, then on s2
In round i, runs M for i steps on each of s1 to si
quiz.explain: Interleaving with growing step limits avoids getting stuck on a string where M loops.

quiz.q: Why is the Church-Turing thesis not a theorem?
options: Because it was proved false by quantum computers
Because algorithm is an informal idea that cannot be proved equal to a formal model
Because it only applies to finite automata
quiz.explain: The thesis links an informal notion (algorithm) to a formal one (TM), so it can be supported by evidence but not proved.

lessons.title: Decidability
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket umpire with a perfect rule book. Every time the bowler appeals, the umpire checks the book and gives a decision, out or not out, always within a few seconds. Now imagine a different umpire who sometimes says "let me think" and then keeps thinking forever. The first umpire is a decider. The second is only a recognizer: if the batter is out, he will eventually say so, but if not, he may never answer. Today we ask which questions about machines and languages have a perfect umpire, and we discover, by a clever counting trick, that some questions can never have one.

Quick recap: A language L is decidable if some Turing machine halts on every input and accepts exactly the strings in L. L is Turing-recognizable if some TM accepts exactly the strings in L, but may loop on strings outside L. Every decidable language is recognizable, and by the Church-Turing thesis, decidable means solvable by an algorithm that always finishes.

Problems as languages: To feed a question to a TM, we encode its objects as strings. For a DFA B and a string w, we write the encoding of the pair (B, w) as one string listing B's states, alphabet, transitions, start state and accept states, followed by w. A decision problem then becomes a language: the set of encodings whose answer is yes. A decider for the problem first checks that the input is a valid encoding and rejects garbage, then does the real work. From now on we skip the garbage check, since it is always easy.

A_DFA, does a DFA accept a string: A_DFA is the set of pairs (B, w) where B is a DFA that accepts w. A decider simply simulates B on w: start in q0, read w one symbol at a time, follow the transitions, and when the input ends, accept if the current state is an accept state, otherwise reject. The simulation takes exactly |w| moves, so it always halts. Example: let B track the parity of 0s, with state 0 meaning even and accepting, and w = 1001. The trace is 0, then 0 after reading 1, then 1 after 0, then 0 after 0, then 0 after 1. It ends in state 0, so the pair is in A_DFA.

A_NFA and A_REX: For an NFA we cannot just follow one path, but we can first convert it to a DFA with the subset construction from lesson 7, and then run the A_DFA decider. For a regular expression R, we convert R to an NFA with Thompson's construction from lesson 10, then to a DFA. This shows a powerful habit: once a problem is decidable, its decider can be used as a subroutine to decide other problems.

E_DFA, is the language empty: E_DFA is the set of DFAs A whose language is empty. Testing every string is impossible because there are infinitely many. Instead we use reachability. Mark the start state. Repeat: mark any state that has a transition coming in from an already marked state. Stop when nothing new gets marked. If no accept state is marked, accept, because no string can reach an accept state. This is just graph search from the Algorithms course, and it takes at most |Q| rounds.

E_DFA worked example: Take states 0, 1, 2, 3 over {a, b}, start state 0 and accept state 3. From 0, a goes to 1 and b stays at 0. From 1, a stays at 1 and b goes to 0. From 2, a goes to 3 and b stays at 2. State 3 loops on both letters. Marking from 0 reaches 0 and 1 only. State 3 is never marked, because the only way into it is from 2, which is unreachable. So the language is empty, and the decider accepts. A simple breadth-first search in Python confirms the reachable set is exactly {0, 1}.

EQ_DFA, do two DFAs accept the same language: EQ_DFA is the set of pairs (A, B) of DFAs with L(A) = L(B). The trick is the symmetric difference: build a DFA C for the strings accepted by exactly one of the two, that is (L(A) minus L(B)) union (L(B) minus L(A)). Regular languages are closed under complement, intersection and union, and the product construction from lesson 4 builds C. Then L(A) = L(B) exactly when L(C) is empty, which the E_DFA decider checks. Two deciders glued together give a third.

EQ_DFA worked example: Let A be the 2-state DFA for an even number of 0s, with states 0 (even, accepting) and 1 (odd). Let B have three states p, q, r, with p and r accepting. On 0, p and r go to q and q goes to r. On 1, p goes to r, r stays at r and q stays at q. Running the product from the start pair (0, p), the reachable pairs are (0, p), (1, q) and (0, r). In each pair both states agree, both accepting or both rejecting, so no reachable pair is in C's accept set, and the DFAs are equivalent. A brute force check of all binary strings up to length 8 agrees.

A_CFG, does a grammar generate a string: A_CFG is the set of pairs (G, w) where the context-free grammar G generates w. A naive machine that tries derivations one by one is only a recognizer, since if w is not generated it may search forever. The fix is Chomsky normal form from lesson 15. In CNF, any derivation of a string of length n at least 1 has exactly 2n - 1 steps. So convert G to CNF, list all derivations with 2n - 1 steps, a finite number, and accept if one of them yields w. For w the empty string, just check whether the rule S -> epsilon exists. Faster still, the CYK algorithm decides it in O(n cubed) time.

Every context-free language is decidable: Fix a CFL L with grammar G. A TM that has G built in and runs the A_CFG decider on (G, w) decides L. So the classes nest: regular inside context-free inside decidable inside Turing-recognizable. Note the grammar is fixed inside the machine; we do not need to convert a PDA to a TM directly, because a nondeterministic PDA branch might run forever.

E_CFG, does a grammar generate anything: Mark every terminal symbol. Repeat: mark a variable A if some rule A -> U1 U2 ... Uk has every Ui marked. When nothing changes, accept if the start variable is unmarked. Example: S -> AB, A -> a, B -> bB. First a and b are marked, then A, because A -> a. B is never marked, because its only rule needs B itself. So S is never marked, and the language is empty. You saw this generating-symbols idea in lesson 14.

A surprising gap, EQ_CFG: For DFAs, equivalence was decidable. For context-free grammars, EQ_CFG is not decidable. The symmetric difference trick fails because context-free languages are not closed under complement or intersection. The actual proof needs a reduction, the tool of lesson 24. So the boundary between decidable and undecidable already appears with simple grammars.

Are there undecidable problems at all: To answer, we compare sizes of infinite sets. Two sets have the same size if there is a bijection, a perfect one-to-one pairing, between them. A set is countable if it is finite or has the same size as the natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}. Countable means you can list the elements as first, second, third, and so on, and every element appears at some finite position.

Countable surprises: The even numbers are countable, because n pairs with 2n, even though they look like half of N. The integers are countable: list them as 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3 and so on. Sigma star, all strings over {0, 1}, is countable: list them in shortlex order, the empty string, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, and so on. Even pairs of natural numbers are countable, using the Cantor pairing function f(x, y) = (x + y)(x + y + 1)/2 + y, which gives (0,0) -> 0, (1,0) -> 1, (0,1) -> 2, (2,0) -> 3, (1,1) -> 4, (0,2) -> 5. Walking the grid diagonal by diagonal like this also shows the positive rational numbers are countable.

Diagonalization, the uncountable: Georg Cantor showed in 1891 that the set of all infinite binary sequences is not countable. Suppose someone claims a complete list. Here are its first four rows: row 1 starts 0110, row 2 starts 1010, row 3 starts 1100, row 4 starts 0001. Read the diagonal: the 1st digit of row 1, the 2nd of row 2, and so on, giving 0, 0, 0, 1. Now flip every digit to get 1, 1, 1, 0, and keep flipping forever down the diagonal. The new sequence differs from row i at position i, for every i, so it is nowhere in the list. Any list misses something, so the set is uncountable. The same argument shows the real numbers are uncountable, with care about numbers like 0.0999... = 0.1000... that have two decimal forms.

Languages are uncountable: Every language over {0, 1} is a subset of Sigma star. List Sigma star in shortlex order and write a 1 under each string that belongs to the language and a 0 under each that does not. This characteristic sequence identifies the language uniquely. For the order empty string, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, the language {0, 00, 11, ...} begins 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1. So languages match infinite binary sequences one to one, and there are uncountably many languages.

Machines are countable: In lesson 21 we encoded every Turing machine as a finite binary string. The set of all such strings is countable, so the set of all TMs is countable too. Now compare: countably many machines, uncountably many languages. Each machine recognizes only one language, so most languages are recognized by no machine at all. Conclusion: there exist languages that are not Turing-recognizable, and therefore also not decidable.

A named example: The counting argument proves existence without naming a language. Diagonalization can name one. List all TMs as M1, M2, M3, ... and let L_d contain the encoding of Mi exactly when Mi does not accept its own encoding. If some Mj recognized L_d, ask whether the encoding of Mj is in L_d. If it is, Mj must accept it, but then by definition it is not in L_d. If it is not, Mj does not accept it, so it is in L_d. Either way we get a contradiction, so no TM recognizes L_d. The next lesson uses the same idea on the acceptance problem A_TM.

Real life example 1, checking form rules: Suppose a bKash-style app validates Bangladeshi mobile numbers with the pattern 01 followed by one digit from 3 to 9 and then eight more digits. A teammate writes a different-looking pattern. Are they the same rule? Because both are regular expressions, convert each to a DFA and run the EQ_DFA decider: the answer is guaranteed. Can a filter ever match anything at all? That is E_DFA, again guaranteed. Tools for checking network firewall rules and text filters really do use these automata algorithms.

Real life example 2, rickshaw plates and lucky rules: Every rickshaw licence plate in Dhaka is a finite string, so even if the city printed plates forever, we could list them in one long queue. Now think of all possible rules for calling a plate lucky, such as "ends in 7" or "digits sum to a prime". Each rule is a language, a set of plates, and by the diagonal argument there are uncountably many such rules. Computer programs, like plates, can be listed. So there are far more rules than programs, and most rules can never be checked by any program.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Do not confuse recognizable with decidable; a machine that may loop is not a decider. For A_CFG, trying all derivations without CNF gives only a recognizer. Countable does not mean finite. In a diagonal proof you must change every diagonal entry and show the new item differs from every row. The counting argument shows non-recognizable languages exist, but does not name one. And remember the asymmetry: EQ_DFA is decidable, EQ_CFG is not. Exams often ask you to give deciders for A_DFA, E_DFA, EQ_DFA and E_CFG, to show that N x N or the rationals are countable, and to prove the binary sequences uncountable by diagonalization.

Recap: Decision problems become languages through encodings. A_DFA, A_NFA, A_REX, E_DFA, EQ_DFA, A_CFG and E_CFG are all decidable, mostly by simulation, reachability, closure constructions and CNF. Every context-free language is decidable, but EQ_CFG is not. Using bijections, we saw that N, the integers, Sigma star and N x N are countable, while binary sequences and languages are uncountable by Cantor's diagonalization. Since TMs are countable, some languages are not recognizable at all. Next lesson: the most famous undecidable problem, the halting problem.
key_points: A language is decidable if some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly its strings; recognizers may loop.
A_DFA is decided by simulating the DFA; A_NFA and A_REX by converting to a DFA first.
E_DFA is decided by marking reachable states; EQ_DFA by testing the symmetric difference DFA for emptiness.
A_CFG is decidable using Chomsky normal form (derivations of length 2n - 1) or CYK; every CFL is decidable.
E_CFG is decidable by marking generating variables, but EQ_CFG is undecidable.
Countable means listable; N, Z, Sigma star and N x N are countable via bijections such as Cantor pairing.
Cantor's diagonal argument (1891) shows infinite binary sequences, and so all languages, are uncountable.
TMs are countable but languages are not, so some languages are not Turing-recognizable.
lessons.tip: For any decidability question, first ask: can I turn it into a finite search? Simulation for a bounded number of steps, marking until nothing changes, or a known decider used as a subroutine are the three moves that solve almost every exam question here.
lessons.task: Draw a 4 x 4 table of your own binary digits, read its diagonal, flip it, and check by hand that the new row differs from every row. Then write the shortlex list of all binary strings up to length 3 and mark the characteristic sequence of the language of strings ending in 1.

quiz.q: Which method decides E_DFA?
options: Try all strings up to length 100
Mark states reachable from the start state and check whether any accept state is marked
Convert the DFA to a grammar and run CYK
quiz.explain: Reachability marking finishes in at most |Q| rounds; the language is empty exactly when no accept state is reachable.

quiz.q: Why does converting to Chomsky normal form help decide A_CFG?
options: Every derivation of a length-n string (n at least 1) has exactly 2n - 1 steps, so the search is finite
quiz.explain: Bounding the derivation length to 2n - 1 turns an endless search into a finite one.

quiz.q: Which of these problems is undecidable?
quiz.explain: Equivalence of context-free grammars is undecidable; the other three have deciders.

quiz.q: Which set is uncountable?
options: The set of all infinite binary sequences
The set of all Turing machines
quiz.explain: Cantor's diagonal argument shows the binary sequences cannot be listed; the other three are countable.

quiz.q: Why must some languages be non-recognizable?
options: Because every TM loops on some input
Because DFAs are weaker than TMs
Because there are countably many TMs but uncountably many languages
quiz.explain: Each TM recognizes one language, and countably many machines cannot cover uncountably many languages.

lessons.title: The Halting Problem and Undecidability
lessons.content:
You have surely seen it: an app freezes and your phone asks, "App isn't responding. Wait or close?" Why does the phone ask you? Wouldn't it be nicer if the phone simply knew whether the app is stuck forever or just slow? In this lesson we prove that no program can ever know this for every app. This is the halting problem, the most famous impossible problem in computer science, and the proof fits on one page.

Where we stand: In lesson 21 we built the universal Turing machine U, which takes the encoding of a machine M together with an input w and simulates M on w. U accepts when M accepts, rejects when M rejects, and loops when M loops. So U recognizes the language A_TM, the set of all pairs (M, w) where M accepts w. In lesson 22 we learned by counting that some languages are undecidable. Now we find a specific, important one: A_TM itself.

The theorem: A_TM is undecidable. In other words, no Turing machine can take any machine M and any input w and always halt with the correct answer to "does M accept w?". Turing's 1936 paper on computable numbers already contained this kind of result. The name "halting problem" came into use later, but the idea is his.

Step 1 of the proof, assume a decider: Suppose, hoping for a contradiction, that some TM H decides A_TM. That means for every M and w, H halts, and H accepts if M accepts w, and H rejects if M does not accept w, whether M rejects or loops. Remember, H always halts, even when M itself would loop. That is exactly the superpower we are going to show is impossible.

Step 2, build the troublemaker D: Using H as a subroutine, build a new machine D. On input the encoding of a machine M, D runs H on the pair (M, encoding of M), which asks: does M accept its own description? Then D does the opposite. If H accepts, D rejects. If H rejects, D accepts. Feeding a machine its own code may sound strange, but it is legal: a description is just a string, and a compiler that compiles its own source code does the same thing. Since H always halts, D always halts too.

Step 3, run D on itself: Now give D its own encoding. By its definition, D accepts the encoding of D exactly when H says that D does not accept the encoding of D. And since H is always right, that means D accepts its own encoding exactly when D does not accept its own encoding. That is impossible: a statement cannot be true exactly when it is false. The only assumption we made was that H exists, so H cannot exist, and A_TM is undecidable.

The table picture: Why is this called diagonalization? List all TMs as rows M1, M2, M3, M4, ... and their encodings as columns. Entry (i, j) shows what Mi does on the encoding of Mj. Suppose the first rows read: M1 gives accept, reject, accept, loop; M2 gives loop, accept, reject, accept; M3 gives reject, reject, loop, accept; M4 gives accept, accept, accept, accept. The diagonal is accept, accept, loop, accept. D, which uses H to look at each diagonal entry, outputs the opposite: reject, reject, accept, reject. A check in Python confirms D differs from every row at its diagonal spot. D is a TM, so it must be some row Mk, yet it disagrees with Mk at column k. That is the contradiction, drawn as a picture, exactly Cantor's trick from lesson 22.

The same proof in code: Imagine someone sells you a Python function halts(f, x) that always returns True or False correctly, telling whether f(x) would finish. Now write: def trouble(f): if halts(f, f): loop forever with while True: pass, else: return. Ask what happens with trouble(trouble). If halts says it finishes, it loops forever. If halts says it loops, it returns at once. Either way halts gave the wrong answer, so no such function can be written in any language.

Self-reference, like old puzzles: The trick is the same as in the liar sentence "This sentence is false", or the barber who shaves exactly those who do not shave themselves. In each case an object is asked about itself and told to do the opposite. The difference is that the halting proof is not a word game. It is a precise statement about machines and works because programs can read programs.

HALT_TM is also undecidable: HALT_TM is the set of pairs (M, w) where M halts on w, accepting or rejecting. Suppose a TM R decides HALT_TM. Build S to decide A_TM: on input (M, w), run R on (M, w). If R rejects, M loops on w, so reject. If R accepts, M surely halts, so simulate M on w without fear, and accept if M accepts, reject if M rejects. S always halts and decides A_TM, which is impossible. So R cannot exist. This is our first reduction, a method the next lesson makes formal.

Recognizable but not decidable: A_TM is recognizable, because U accepts exactly its members. HALT_TM is recognizable too: simulate M on w and accept as soon as M halts. So both languages sit strictly between decidable and recognizable. This shows the decidable languages form a strictly smaller class than the recognizable ones.

Co-recognizable languages: A language is co-Turing-recognizable if its complement is Turing-recognizable. Theorem: a language L is decidable if and only if L is both recognizable and co-recognizable. One direction is easy: if L is decidable, its decider also decides the complement, just swap accept and reject. For the other direction, let M1 recognize L and M2 recognize the complement. On input w, run them in parallel, one step of M1, then one step of M2, then one more of M1, and so on. Every w is either in L or in its complement, so exactly one of them eventually accepts. If M1 accepts, accept; if M2 accepts, reject. This machine always halts, so L is decidable.

A language that is not recognizable: Apply the theorem to A_TM. A_TM is recognizable. If its complement were also recognizable, A_TM would be decidable, which we just proved false. So the complement of A_TM, all pairs (M, w) where M does not accept w, is not Turing-recognizable. Here is our first concrete language beyond the reach of every recognizer. There are even languages, such as EQ_TM, the question of whether two TMs recognize the same language, that are neither recognizable nor co-recognizable.

Why "just run it and see" fails: You can run M on w and wait. If it halts, you know the answer. But if after a million steps it is still running, you cannot tell whether it will stop at step one million and one or never. Waiting gives a recognizer, never a decider. Notice, though, that the bounded question, "does M halt on w within 1,000,000 steps?", is decidable: run it for that many steps and look. Timeouts in real systems answer exactly this bounded question, not the real halting question.

Where halting is decidable: Restricted machines can be fully analysed. A DFA always halts after reading its input. A linear bounded automaton, a TM that only uses the cells where the input sits, has a finite number of configurations: with q states, g tape symbols and an input of length n there are at most q times n times g to the power n of them. For example, with 3 states, 2 symbols and n = 4, that is 3 x 4 x 16 = 192. If such a machine runs longer than that, some configuration repeated, so it loops forever. Hence acceptance for linear bounded automata is decidable. Turing machines escape because their tape is unbounded.

Undecidable does not mean hopeless: The theorem says no single algorithm answers correctly for every machine and every input. For a particular program, people often can prove that it halts, for example a loop for i from 1 to 10 clearly stops. Tools that check termination, used by some compilers and verifiers, do succeed on many real programs. They just must sometimes say "I don't know", or else be wrong sometimes.

A mathematical example, Goldbach: The Goldbach conjecture, from a 1742 letter of Christian Goldbach to Leonhard Euler, says every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes, for example 28 = 5 + 23 = 11 + 17. Write a program that checks 4, 6, 8, ... one by one and stops when it finds an even number that is not such a sum. This program halts if and only if the conjecture is false. A quick Python check confirms every even number from 4 to 10,000 works, and computers have checked far beyond that, but nobody has a proof. A halting decider would settle this famous open problem instantly, which shows how strong such a decider would be.

Real life example 1, the perfect antivirus does not exist: Suppose a company claims a perfect detector that, given any program, says whether it will ever do something harmful, like deleting your files. Build a program that asks the detector about itself, and if the answer is "harmless", deletes files, and if "harmful", does nothing. Just like D, it makes the detector wrong. That is why real antivirus tools combine signatures of known malware, behaviour rules and sandboxes, and why they sometimes give false alarms or miss new threats.

Real life example 2, servers and timeouts: A bKash-style payment server in Dhaka handles millions of requests. If one request runs too long, the system cannot know whether it is stuck forever or just slow, for the same reason your phone cannot. So engineers use watchdog timers: after a fixed limit, say a few seconds, the request is cancelled and retried. This is the bounded halting question in action. Engineers accept that a slow but correct request may sometimes be killed, because the perfect answer is impossible.

Common mistakes: Do not forget that H must halt on every input, including when M loops; that is the assumption we break. In the proof, D runs H on M with its own description, not on an arbitrary input. Do not mix A_TM, about accepting, with HALT_TM, about halting; both are undecidable but the definitions differ. Remember that undecidable problems can still be recognizable. And never claim that we cannot check any program at all; we just cannot check all programs with one method.

What exams ask: Prove A_TM undecidable by diagonalization, with the construction of D and the run of D on its own encoding. Show HALT_TM undecidable using a decider for HALT_TM to decide A_TM. Prove that L is decidable if and only if L and its complement are recognizable, and conclude that the complement of A_TM is not recognizable. Explain why the bounded halting problem is decidable, and why acceptance for linear bounded automata is decidable using the configuration count.

Recap: The universal machine recognizes A_TM, but no machine decides it, by the self-referential diagonal proof. HALT_TM is undecidable too. Decidable means recognizable and co-recognizable, so the complement of A_TM is not even recognizable. Bounded halting and restricted machines are decidable, and specific programs can often be proved to halt, but no single method works for all. Next lesson turns the HALT_TM argument into a general tool, reductions, and finds many more undecidable problems.
key_points: A_TM = {(M, w) : M accepts w} is recognizable by the universal TM but undecidable.
Proof: assume a decider H, build D that does the opposite of H on (M, encoding of M), then run D on its own encoding to get a contradiction.
The proof is a diagonalization: D differs from every machine Mi on the encoding of Mi.
HALT_TM is undecidable: a decider for it would give a decider for A_TM.
L is decidable if and only if L is recognizable and co-recognizable (run both recognizers in parallel).
The complement of A_TM is not Turing-recognizable.
Bounded halting (within k steps) and acceptance for linear bounded automata are decidable.
No perfect virus detector or infinite-loop checker can exist; real tools use heuristics and timeouts.
lessons.tip: Practice writing the A_TM proof from memory in exactly three steps: assume H, build D, run D on itself. Then draw the accept/reject/loop table and show where D disagrees with each row. Examiners love seeing both views.
lessons.task: Write the trouble(f) function from this lesson on paper and trace trouble(trouble) for both possible answers of halts. Then, on your phone or computer, check by hand or with a tiny script that every even number from 4 to 50 is a sum of two primes.

quiz.q: In the proof that A_TM is undecidable, what does D do on input the encoding of M?
options: Runs M on the empty string
Runs H on (M, encoding of M) and outputs the opposite answer
Runs U on (M, w) and copies its answer
quiz.explain: D asks H whether M accepts its own description and then does the opposite; running D on itself gives the contradiction.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about A_TM?
options: It is neither recognizable nor co-recognizable
It is recognizable but not decidable
quiz.explain: The universal TM recognizes it, but the diagonal proof shows no decider exists.

quiz.q: Why is the complement of A_TM not Turing-recognizable?
options: If it were, A_TM would be both recognizable and co-recognizable, hence decidable
Because every TM halts on it
quiz.explain: A language is decidable iff it and its complement are recognizable; since A_TM is recognizable but undecidable, its complement cannot be recognizable.

quiz.q: Which of these problems IS decidable?
options: Does M halt on w within 1,000 steps?
quiz.explain: Simulate M for 1,000 steps and look; a bounded question always finishes.

quiz.q: A program searches even numbers 4, 6, 8, ... and stops at the first one that is not a sum of two primes. When does it halt?
options: Exactly when the Goldbach conjecture is false
quiz.explain: It halts only if a counterexample exists, so a halting decider would settle Goldbach's open conjecture.

lessons.title: Reductions and the Chomsky Hierarchy
lessons.content:
Suppose your friend boasts, "I have a gadget that tells you whether any Dhaka bus route will ever reach Gulistan." You know a trick that turns any halting question into a bus-route question, so the gadget would also solve the halting problem. But we proved last lesson that nothing solves the halting problem. So your friend's gadget cannot exist. This style of argument, turning one problem into another, is called a reduction. It is the main tool for proving problems impossible, and today we use it to find a whole family of undecidable problems. Then we step back and see how all our machines fit together in the Chomsky hierarchy.

Computable functions: A function f from strings to strings is computable if some Turing machine, started with w on its tape, always halts with f(w) on its tape. Examples are adding two numbers, reversing a string, or editing the description of a machine, such as adding a few new states to it. The important point is that f must always halt; it may build a machine, but it must not run a machine that could loop.

Mapping reductions: Language A is mapping reducible to language B, written A <=m B, if there is a computable function f such that for every string w, w is in A if and only if f(w) is in B. Think of f as a translator: it turns every question about A into a question about B with the same yes or no answer. Then a solver for B gives a solver for A: on input w, compute f(w) and ask the B solver.

The four rules: If A <=m B and B is decidable, then A is decidable. Flipped around, if A <=m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable. The same works for recognizability: if B is recognizable, so is A, and if A is not recognizable, neither is B. Also, A <=m B exactly when the complement of A reduces to the complement of B with the same f. In words: hardness flows forward along the arrow, easiness flows backward.

Watch the direction: To prove a new problem B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem, such as A_TM, to B. That is, show A_TM <=m B, never B <=m A_TM. Reducing B to A_TM only says B is no harder than A_TM, which tells us nothing. This is the number one mistake in exams, so say it to yourself: from the known hard problem, to the new problem.

A friendly decidable example: You already saw a reduction in lesson 22. EQ_DFA reduces to E_DFA by the function f(A, B) = C, where C is the product DFA for the symmetric difference of L(A) and L(B). L(A) = L(B) exactly when L(C) is empty, and building C always finishes. Since E_DFA is decidable, so is EQ_DFA. Reductions are not only for bad news.

A_TM reduces to HALT_TM: Given a pair (M, w), let f output (M', w), where M' is this machine: on input x, run M on x; if M accepts, accept; if M rejects, enter a loop that never ends. Check all three cases for w. If M accepts w, M' accepts, so M' halts. If M rejects w, M' loops. If M loops on w, M' loops too. So M accepts w exactly when M' halts on w. The function f only rewrites M's description, by sending the reject state into a new looping state, so it always halts. Hence A_TM <=m HALT_TM, and HALT_TM is undecidable. Compare it with lesson 23, where we argued with deciders; this version gives a clean mapping.

E_TM, is a machine's language empty: E_TM is the set of TMs M with L(M) empty. Given (M, w), build M1: on input x, if x is not w, reject; if x = w, run M on w and accept if M accepts. Then L(M1) is {w} if M accepts w, and empty otherwise. So M accepts w exactly when M1 is not in E_TM. This maps A_TM to the complement of E_TM, so the complement of E_TM is undecidable, and so is E_TM, because decidable languages are closed under complement. Even more: the complement of E_TM is recognizable by dovetailing over all strings and step counts, so E_TM is co-recognizable but not recognizable.

EQ_TM and friends: EQ_TM asks whether two TMs recognize the same language. Map M to the pair (M, M_empty), where M_empty rejects everything. Then L(M) is empty exactly when L(M) = L(M_empty), so E_TM <=m EQ_TM and EQ_TM is undecidable. In the same style one proves REGULAR_TM undecidable, the question of whether L(M) is a regular language. Each proof builds a machine whose language changes depending on whether M accepts w.

Rice's theorem: Henry Gordon Rice proved in 1953 a sweeping generalization. Call P a property of TM languages if it depends only on the language: whenever L(M1) = L(M2), either both have P or neither does. Call it nontrivial if some TM has it and some TM does not. Rice's theorem says every nontrivial property of the languages of Turing machines is undecidable. So these are all undecidable: is L(M) empty, finite, infinite, regular, context-free, does it contain the string 0, does it contain the word bKash.

What Rice does not cover: Properties of the machine itself, not of its language, may be decidable. Does M have at most 5 states? Look at the description. Does M move left at least once within its first 100 steps on the empty input? Simulate 100 steps. Rice's theorem only talks about what M accepts, not how M is built or how it behaves within a fixed number of steps.

Proof idea of Rice's theorem: Suppose R decides a nontrivial property P. We may assume the empty language does not have P; otherwise work with the complement of P. Since P is nontrivial, pick a TM T whose language has P. Given (M, w), build M_w: on input x, first simulate M on w; if M accepts, run T on x and answer like T. If M accepts w, L(M_w) = L(T), which has P. If not, L(M_w) is empty, which does not. So R on M_w answers whether M accepts w, deciding A_TM. Contradiction.

Post's correspondence problem: Emil Post introduced this puzzle in 1946. You get a set of dominoes, each with a string on top and a string on the bottom, and unlimited copies of each. Can you line up a sequence of dominoes, repeats allowed, so that the top string equals the bottom string? Example dominoes: 1 is b over ca, 2 is a over ab, 3 is ca over a, 4 is abc over c. Take the order 2, 1, 3, 2, 4. The top reads a, b, ca, a, abc, giving abcaaabc. The bottom reads ab, ca, a, ab, c, giving abcaaabc. A match! A breadth-first search in Python finds exactly this sequence as the shortest match.

When PCP has no match, and why it matters: The dominoes abc over ab, ca over a and acc over ba have no match, because every top is longer than its bottom, so the top string always stays longer. In general, though, PCP is undecidable; the proof encodes a TM's computation history into dominoes. Trying all sequences of length 1, then 2, then 3, gives a recognizer that halts whenever a match exists, so PCP is recognizable but not decidable. PCP is a favourite starting point for reductions to grammar problems, for example proving that it is undecidable whether a context-free grammar is ambiguous.

The Chomsky hierarchy: In 1956 Noam Chomsky classified grammars into four types by the shape of their rules. Each type matches a machine model from this course, and together they summarize everything we have built. Type 3 is the smallest class and Type 0 the largest.

Type 3, regular grammars: Every rule has the form A -> aB or A -> a, one terminal optionally followed by one variable, with S -> epsilon allowed. Machine: finite automaton. Example: S -> aS | bS | b generates all strings over {a, b} that end in b. Regular languages are exactly the Type 3 languages.

Type 2, context-free grammars: Every rule has a single variable on the left, A -> gamma, with any string on the right. Machine: pushdown automaton. Example: S -> aSb | epsilon gives a^n b^n, which is context-free but not regular, as the pumping lemma of lesson 11 showed.

Type 1, context-sensitive grammars: Rules have the form alpha A beta -> alpha gamma beta with gamma nonempty, so a variable may be rewritten only in a given context. An equivalent and simpler definition: every rule is noncontracting, the right side is at least as long as the left side. Machine: linear bounded automaton, a TM confined to the input cells. Example for a^n b^n c^n, which is not context-free: S -> aSBC | aBC, CB -> BC, aB -> ab, bB -> bb, bC -> bc, cC -> cc. Derivation of aabbcc: S, aSBC, aaBCBC, aaBBCC, aabBCC, aabbCC, aabbcC, aabbcc. A search over all sentential forms up to length 9 confirms the grammar produces exactly abc, aabbcc and aaabbbccc in that range.

Type 0, unrestricted grammars: Any rule alpha -> beta with alpha containing a variable. Machine: Turing machine. Type 0 languages are exactly the Turing-recognizable languages, also called recursively enumerable. A_TM is Type 0, and the complement of A_TM is not even Type 0.

How the classes nest: Regular is strictly inside context-free, which is strictly inside context-sensitive, which is strictly inside recursively enumerable. The decidable languages sit between the last two: every context-sensitive language is decidable, because a linear bounded automaton has finitely many configurations, as lesson 23 showed. Separating examples: a^n b^n is context-free but not regular, a^n b^n c^n is context-sensitive but not context-free, and A_TM is recognizable but not decidable. Membership is decidable for Types 1 to 3 but not Type 0, and emptiness is decidable for Types 2 and 3 but not for Types 1 and 0.

Real life example 1, a compiler's layers: A compiler for C or Python uses the hierarchy layer by layer. The lexer that splits code into tokens is a Type 3 machine built from regular expressions. The parser that checks brackets and statement structure uses a Type 2 grammar. Checks like "every variable is declared before it is used" are context-sensitive, so compilers do them with extra code over the parse tree rather than with a grammar.

Real life example 2, app checkers: Imagine an app store tool that checks whether an app will ever send your contact list to a server. Whether a program ever does something is a property of its behaviour on inputs, and by the same reasoning as Rice's theorem no perfect checker can exist. Real analysis tools, like the warnings in Android Studio, approximate: they flag code that might be dangerous and sometimes raise false alarms. Knowing Rice's theorem tells you why perfection is impossible and good approximation is the goal.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Reducing in the wrong direction is the classic error. Another is letting the reduction function run M; it must only build a new description. When applying Rice's theorem, check that the property is about the language and is nontrivial; do not apply it to state counts or step limits. In the hierarchy, remember the decidable class lies between context-sensitive and recursively enumerable. Exams ask: define mapping reduction; show A_TM <=m HALT_TM; prove E_TM undecidable; state and apply Rice's theorem; solve a small PCP instance; give the four Chomsky types with their rule shapes, machines and example languages.

Recap: A mapping reduction A <=m B is a computable translator that preserves yes and no answers; undecidability flows from A to B. From A_TM we derived HALT_TM, E_TM, EQ_TM and REGULAR_TM undecidable, and Rice's theorem covers every nontrivial language property at once. Post's correspondence problem is a simple-looking puzzle that is undecidable. The Chomsky hierarchy ties grammars to machines: Type 3 with finite automata, Type 2 with pushdown automata, Type 1 with linear bounded automata and Type 0 with Turing machines. Next and final lesson: not whether, but how fast.
key_points: A <=m B means a computable f with w in A iff f(w) in B; if B is decidable so is A, and if A is undecidable so is B.
To prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem (like A_TM) TO B, never the other way.
A_TM <=m HALT_TM by turning M's reject into an infinite loop; the reduction edits M, it never runs it.
E_TM is undecidable (and not recognizable); EQ_TM and REGULAR_TM are undecidable too.
Rice's theorem (1953): every nontrivial property of the language of a TM is undecidable.
Post's correspondence problem (Post, 1946) is undecidable but recognizable; example match 2,1,3,2,4 gives abcaaabc.
Chomsky hierarchy (1956): Type 3 regular/FA, Type 2 context-free/PDA, Type 1 context-sensitive/LBA, Type 0 unrestricted/TM.
Regular is inside CFL, inside CSL, inside decidable, inside recursively enumerable; all inclusions are strict.
lessons.tip: Before writing any reduction, draw an arrow on paper: known hard problem -> new problem. Then write the three cases (M accepts, rejects, loops) and check that your new machine gives the right answer in each. That checklist catches almost every mistake.
lessons.task: Find a match for the PCP dominoes a over ab, ba over a, b over bb by hand, or argue why none exists. Then write a Type 3 grammar for binary strings that start with 1, and a context-free grammar for strings with the same number of 0s and 1s.

quiz.q: If A <=m B and A is undecidable, what can we conclude?
quiz.explain: Undecidability flows forward along a reduction: a decider for B would give one for A.

quiz.q: In the reduction A_TM <=m HALT_TM, what does the new machine M' do when M rejects?
options: Runs M again on a different input
quiz.explain: Turning reject into a loop makes 'M' halts' equal to 'M accepts', so the answer is preserved.

quiz.q: Which question is decidable, so Rice's theorem does NOT apply?
options: Does M have at most 5 states?
quiz.explain: The number of states is a property of the machine's description, not of its language.

quiz.q: For dominoes 1 = b/ca, 2 = a/ab, 3 = ca/a, 4 = abc/c, which sequence is a match?
quiz.explain: Top: a+b+ca+a+abc = abcaaabc; bottom: ab+ca+a+ab+c = abcaaabc.

quiz.q: Which machine model matches Type 1 (context-sensitive) grammars?
quiz.explain: Context-sensitive languages are exactly those accepted by linear bounded automata.

lessons.title: Complexity: P, NP and NP-Completeness
lessons.content:
A delivery rider in Dhaka has 60 parcels to drop. A computer could find the best order by checking every possible order, so the problem is decidable. But there are so many orders that every computer on Earth working together would not finish before the Sun burns out. Decidable is not the same as doable. In this final lesson we stop asking whether a problem can be solved and start asking how fast. Your Algorithms course already met P and NP informally; here we build them properly on Turing machines and see why NP-completeness is one of the deepest ideas in computer science.

Measuring time on a Turing machine: Let M be a decider. Its running time is the function f(n) giving the maximum number of steps M takes on any input of length n. We use big-O, so constants and small terms do not matter. TIME(t(n)) is the class of languages decided by some deterministic single-tape TM in O(t(n)) time. For example, a single-tape TM can decide 0^n 1^n by zigzagging, crossing off one 0 and one 1 per pass, in O(n squared) time. A cleverer single-tape machine that crosses off every other 0 and every other 1 and checks parities does it in O(n log n), and a 2-tape machine that copies the 0s to tape 2 and matches them against the 1s does it in O(n).

Does the model matter: Yes, but only a little. In lesson 21 we saw that a multitape TM running in t(n) can be simulated by a single-tape TM in O(t(n) squared). Squaring a polynomial gives another polynomial, so all reasonable deterministic models agree on what runs in polynomial time. Nondeterminism is different: the best known deterministic simulation of an NTM running in t(n) takes 2 to the power O(t(n)), an exponential jump. That gap is the whole story of this lesson.

The class P: P is the union of TIME(n^k) over all k, the languages decided in polynomial time by a deterministic single-tape TM. P is robust, it does not change between reasonable deterministic models, and it roughly captures practically solvable problems. Compare n cubed and 2 to the n at n = 60: n cubed is 216,000 steps, while 2 to the 60 is about 1.15 x 10^18. At a billion steps per second, the second takes about 36 years.

Problems in P: PATH, whether a directed graph has a path from s to t, is in P by breadth-first search. RELPRIME, whether two numbers are relatively prime, is in P by Euclid's algorithm, which runs in time polynomial in the number of digits. Every context-free language is in P, thanks to the O(n cubed) CYK algorithm from lesson 15. Even PRIMES, testing whether a number is prime, was shown to be in P in 2002 by Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena. Careful: for numbers, input size is the number of digits, so trying all divisors up to N is exponential, not polynomial.

NP through verifiers: A verifier for a language A is an algorithm V such that A is the set of strings w for which V accepts the pair (w, c) for some string c. The string c is called a certificate, or proof. A is in NP if it has a verifier that runs in time polynomial in the length of w; that also forces the useful part of c to be polynomially short. Think of NP as the problems where a yes answer is easy to check, if someone hands you the proof. For HAMPATH, whether a graph has a path visiting every vertex once, the certificate is the path itself. For COMPOSITES the certificate is a factor.

NP through nondeterministic machines: Equivalently, NP is the class of languages decided by a nondeterministic TM in polynomial time, the union of NTIME(n^k). Why are the two definitions the same? An NTM can guess a certificate, one symbol per branch, and then run the verifier. In the other direction, a verifier can treat the sequence of choices of an NTM's accepting branch as the certificate. NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not "non-polynomial".

P inside NP, and coNP: Every language in P is in NP, because a verifier can ignore the certificate and just decide. Whether P = NP is the famous open question. The class coNP contains the complements of NP languages, for example the set of unsatisfiable formulas, where a no answer has a short proof. Nobody knows whether NP equals coNP either.

SAT and 3SAT: A Boolean formula uses variables, AND, OR and NOT. It is satisfiable if some assignment of true and false makes it true. SAT is the set of satisfiable formulas. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is an OR of literals, and a formula in conjunctive normal form, CNF, is an AND of clauses. In 3CNF every clause has exactly three literals, and 3SAT is the set of satisfiable 3CNF formulas.

A small 3SAT example: Take phi = (x1 OR x2 OR x3) AND (NOT x1 OR NOT x2 OR x3) AND (NOT x1 OR x2 OR NOT x3). Setting all three variables true works: clause 1 is satisfied by x1, clause 2 by x3 and clause 3 by x2. A brute force check of all 8 assignments in Python finds exactly 5 satisfying ones. Checking one assignment takes time linear in the formula size, which is why SAT is in NP. Finding one by trying everything takes 2 to the n steps for n variables, and that is the hard part.

Polynomial-time reductions: A is polynomial-time reducible to B, written A <=p B, if there is a function f computable in polynomial time with w in A exactly when f(w) is in B. It is the mapping reduction of lesson 24 with a clock attached. If A <=p B and B is in P, then A is in P: compute f(w), which has polynomial size, then run B's polynomial algorithm, and a polynomial of a polynomial is a polynomial.

NP-complete and NP-hard: A language B is NP-complete if B is in NP and every language A in NP satisfies A <=p B. B is NP-hard if only the second condition holds. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP: if any one of them is in P, then every NP problem is in P and P = NP. If any one of them is not in P, then none of them is.

The Cook-Levin theorem: SAT is NP-complete. Stephen Cook proved it in 1971, and Leonid Levin found it independently in the Soviet Union around the same time. Proof idea: take any NTM N deciding A in time n^k. An accepting computation fits in an n^k by n^k table, called a tableau, whose rows are configurations. Make Boolean variables saying which symbol is in each cell. Write a formula that says the first row is the start configuration on w, every 2 by 3 window of cells is consistent with N's transitions, and an accept state appears somewhere. The formula has polynomial size, and it is satisfiable exactly when N has an accepting branch on w. Splitting long clauses with fresh variables shows 3SAT is NP-complete too.

A chain of NP-complete problems: Once one problem is NP-complete, new ones are easier: to show C is NP-complete, show C is in NP and reduce a known NP-complete problem to C. In 1972 Richard Karp used this to prove 21 problems NP-complete, including CLIQUE, vertex cover and Hamiltonian cycle. Today thousands are known, from scheduling to generalized Sudoku.

3SAT reduces to CLIQUE: CLIQUE asks whether a graph has k vertices that are all pairwise connected. Given a 3CNF formula with k clauses, build a graph with 3k nodes, one per literal, grouped in triples by clause. Connect two nodes unless they are in the same triple or are contradictory, like x1 and NOT x1. If phi is satisfiable, pick one true literal from each clause; those k nodes are pairwise connected, a k-clique. Conversely, a k-clique must take one node from each triple and never a contradictory pair, so setting those literals true satisfies every clause. Building the graph takes polynomial time, so 3SAT <=p CLIQUE, and since CLIQUE is in NP, CLIQUE is NP-complete.

The CLIQUE example checked: For our phi with 3 clauses, the graph has 9 nodes. Between different triples there are 27 pairs, of which 6 are contradictory, leaving 21 edges. A brute force search in Python finds 12 triangles, that is 3-cliques. One of them is x1 from clause 1, x3 from clause 2 and x2 from clause 3, which matches the all-true assignment we found earlier.

Independent set and vertex cover: An independent set has no edges inside it; a vertex cover touches every edge. S is a clique in G exactly when S is an independent set in the complement graph, and S is an independent set exactly when V minus S is a vertex cover. So a graph with n vertices has an independent set of size k exactly when it has a vertex cover of size n minus k, and all three problems are NP-complete. Example, the 5-cycle with vertices 0 to 4: the largest independent set has size 2, such as {0, 2}, and the smallest vertex cover has size 3, such as {0, 1, 3}. Indeed 2 + 3 = 5, and a Python check confirms the complement rule for all 32 subsets.

NP-hard but not in NP: Some NP-hard problems are much harder than NP. HALT_TM is NP-hard: map a formula phi to a machine that tries all assignments and halts if one works, otherwise loops forever. But HALT_TM is undecidable, so it is certainly not in NP. Optimization versions, like finding the shortest delivery route, are also called NP-hard.

P versus NP: Is P = NP? Nobody knows. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems, with one million US dollars for a solution. Most researchers believe P is not equal to NP. If P = NP, then every problem whose solutions are easy to check would be easy to solve, and much of today's cryptography would break, because, for example, finding the factors of a large number is in NP, and RSA relies on that being hard.

Living with NP-hardness: Algorithms gave you the practical tools: approximation, like the 2-approximation for vertex cover, heuristics, special cases in P like 2SAT, and SAT solvers that handle huge real formulas despite an exponential worst case. NP-completeness is not a stop sign; it says stop hunting for a perfect fast algorithm and choose a smarter strategy.

Real life example 1, exam routine: A university in Bangladesh must schedule exams so that no student has two exams at the same time. Make each course a vertex and connect two courses if some student takes both. Using k time slots is coloring the graph with k colors so that neighbours differ, and graph k-coloring is NP-complete for k at least 3. Checking a given routine is easy: look at every edge. Finding one with the fewest slots is hard, so offices use heuristics like scheduling the courses with the most clashes first.

Real life example 2, the rider's route: Back to our Dhaka rider. "Is there a route through all 60 stops shorter than 40 km?" is in NP: if someone shows you a route, you add up the distances and check it in seconds. That decision version of the travelling salesman problem is NP-complete. Delivery apps use quick heuristics that give good routes, exactly the right response to NP-hardness.

Common mistakes and exam questions: NP does not mean non-polynomial. NP-hard problems need not be in NP. To prove a new problem C NP-complete, reduce a known NP-complete problem to C, not C to it, and show C is in NP with a certificate. A reduction must run in polynomial time and you must prove both directions of the "if and only if". Exams often ask you to define P and NP both ways, prove a problem is in NP, state Cook-Levin, show 3SAT <=p CLIQUE, and relate clique, independent set and vertex cover.

Course wrap-up: Look how far we travelled. We started with alphabets, strings and languages. Finite automata, DFAs, NFAs and regular expressions, captured the regular languages, and the pumping lemma showed their limits. Context-free grammars and pushdown automata added a stack and gave us the structure of programming languages. Turing machines gave the most general model, and the Church-Turing thesis said it captures every algorithm. Then we found the edge of computation: undecidable problems like the halting problem, reductions and Rice's theorem. Finally, complexity sorted the decidable problems into easy and apparently hard ones.

Where to go next: Compiler Design turns grammars and automata into real parsers. Cryptography builds on the belief that some NP problems are hard. Advanced algorithms and complexity courses go deeper into approximation, randomness and space complexity. Recap of this lesson: P is polynomial deterministic time, NP is polynomial verification, Cook-Levin made SAT the first NP-complete problem, reductions spread hardness to CLIQUE, vertex cover and thousands more, and P versus NP is still open, maybe waiting for you.
key_points: TIME(t(n)) uses deterministic single-tape TMs; multitape gives at most a square slowdown, so polynomial time is model-independent.
P is the union of TIME(n^k); examples: PATH, RELPRIME, every CFL, PRIMES (2002).
NP = languages with polynomial-time verifiers = languages decided by polynomial-time NTMs; NP means nondeterministic polynomial.
A <=p B is a polynomial-time mapping reduction; if B is in P and A <=p B, then A is in P.
NP-complete = in NP and NP-hard; if any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP.
Cook-Levin (Cook 1971, Levin independently): SAT is NP-complete; 3SAT is NP-complete too.
3SAT <=p CLIQUE using one node per literal and edges between non-contradictory literals in different clauses; Karp (1972) listed 21 NP-complete problems.
Clique in G = independent set in the complement; S independent iff V minus S is a vertex cover; P vs NP is open.
lessons.tip: For every NP-completeness proof, write the same four headings: 1. In NP (what is the certificate?), 2. Known problem and arrow direction, 3. The construction and why it is polynomial, 4. Both directions of the iff. Filling in four boxes is much easier than writing a proof from nothing.
lessons.task: Take the formula (x1 OR x2 OR NOT x3) AND (NOT x1 OR x3 OR x2) AND (NOT x2 OR NOT x3 OR x1). Find a satisfying assignment by hand, then draw the 9-node CLIQUE graph from the reduction and circle the triangle that matches your assignment.

quiz.q: Which definition of NP is correct?
options: Languages not solvable in polynomial time
Languages decided in exponential time only
quiz.explain: NP = languages whose yes-instances have certificates checkable in polynomial time, equivalently decided by polynomial-time NTMs.

quiz.q: If A <=p B and B is in P, what follows?
quiz.explain: Compute f(w) in polynomial time, then decide it with B's polynomial algorithm.

quiz.q: Which result first showed a problem to be NP-complete?
quiz.explain: Cook (1971), and independently Levin, proved SAT NP-complete by encoding an NTM's computation as a formula.

quiz.q: In the 3SAT to CLIQUE reduction, a formula with k clauses is satisfiable exactly when the graph has:
options: An independent set of size k
quiz.explain: One true literal from each clause gives k pairwise compatible nodes, a k-clique, and vice versa.

quiz.q: A graph has 10 vertices and its largest independent set has 4 vertices. What is the size of its smallest vertex cover?
quiz.explain: S is independent iff V minus S is a vertex cover, so the minimum cover has 10 - 4 = 6 vertices.

lessons.title: What Data Communication Is
lessons.content:
Imagine you are at home in Dhaka and you send your friend in Rajshahi a message that says Hi. You press send, and less than a second later her phone buzzes. Between your thumb and her screen, your two letters became numbers, the numbers became bits, the bits became radio waves, the waves hit a Grameenphone tower, turned into light inside a glass fibre, travelled hundreds of kilometres, turned back into radio, and finally became letters again. Nobody carried a paper letter on a rickshaw. That whole journey, done correctly and fast, is what data communication is about, and this course is about how every step of it really works.

The definition: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through some form of transmission medium, such as a wire, a glass fibre or the air. The word data means information represented in a form the devices agree on, usually as bits, 0s and 1s. Communication is only useful if it actually works, so the devices must be part of a system made of hardware (the physical equipment) and software (the programs that follow the rules). When we say data communication in this course, we mostly mean the lower part of that system: how bits are turned into signals, how those signals travel, and how two directly connected machines make sure a block of bits arrives correctly.

The five-part model: The classic textbook picture of any communication system has five boxes in a row. First the source, which creates the data; for example, your phone app holding the text Hi. Second the transmitter, which converts the data into a signal that can travel; for example, the phone's radio chip, or a modem. Third the transmission medium (or transmission system), the path the signal travels on: copper wire, fibre, air. Fourth the receiver, which takes the signal from the medium and turns it back into data. Fifth the destination, which uses the data; for example, the messaging app on your friend's phone. Every example in this course, from a keyboard cable to a satellite link, fits these five boxes.

Another way to list the parts: Some books, such as Forouzan's, list five components a little differently: the message (the information itself), the sender, the receiver, the transmission medium, and the protocol. The two lists are not in conflict. The first list looks at the path the signal takes; the second reminds us that there must also be a message worth sending and a protocol, an agreed set of rules. Without the protocol, two devices are like a person speaking Bangla to a person who only knows Japanese: the sound reaches the ear perfectly, but no communication happens. Exams like to ask for either list, so learn both and say which book's version you are using.

Protocols, the rulebook: A protocol is a set of rules that governs data communication. It answers three kinds of questions. Syntax is the structure or format of the data, for example: the first 8 bits are the address of the receiver, the next 8 bits are the address of the sender, and the rest is the message. Semantics is the meaning of each section: does this bit pattern mean data, an acknowledgement, or a request to resend? Timing is about when data should be sent and how fast. If a sender pushes data at 100 Mbps but the receiver can only handle 1 Mbps, the receiver will be overwhelmed and data will be lost. Good protocols handle all three.

Standards, the shared rulebook: A protocol is only useful if everybody follows the same one, so we need standards. Some standards are de facto, meaning they became common just because everybody used them. Others are de jure, meaning an official body approved them. Important bodies you will meet in this course are ISO (the International Organization for Standardization), ITU-T (the telecom part of the International Telecommunication Union, which defines things like telephone and modem standards), IEEE (which defines Ethernet as 802.3 and Wi-Fi as 802.11), ANSI, and for the Internet, the IETF. When you buy a Wi-Fi router in Dhaka and it works with a phone made in another country, you are seeing standards at work.

How data is represented: Before data can travel, it must be turned into bits. Text uses a code that gives each character a number: in ASCII, capital H is 72, which is 01001000 in 8 bits, and small i is 105, which is 01101001. Unicode extends this idea to every script in the world, which is why Bangla letters also work in messages. Numbers are stored directly in binary. An image is a grid of pixels; a black and white picture of 100 by 100 pixels needs 10,000 bits, one per pixel, while a colour picture often uses 24 bits (3 bytes) per pixel for red, green and blue. Audio and video are continuous in nature and are sampled into numbers, a topic we will meet in the lesson on PCM.

The four goals of a good system: The effectiveness of a data communication system depends on four characteristics. Delivery means the data must reach the correct destination, and only the intended device or user. Accuracy means the data must arrive without errors; a bKash amount of 500 taka that arrives as 5000 is a disaster, so data altered in transit and left uncorrected is useless. Timeliness means the data must arrive on time; late video frames in a live cricket stream are as useless as missing ones, and delivering data as it is produced, in order and without big delays, is called real-time transmission. Jitter is the variation in packet arrival time. If video packets are sent every 30 ms but some arrive after 30 ms and others after 40 ms, the picture becomes uneven.

Data flow directions: Communication between two devices can be simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex. In simplex mode, data flows in only one direction, like a one-way street. A keyboard sends to a computer, and a TV station like BTV sends to your TV, but neither ever listens to the other. In half-duplex mode, both sides can send, but not at the same time. A walkie-talkie is the classic example: you press the button, say over, and release so the other person can speak. When one sends, the whole capacity of the channel is used by that one direction. In full-duplex mode, both sides send and receive at the same time, like a normal phone call where you and your nani can talk over each other.

Point-to-point and multipoint: The line configuration describes how devices attach to a link. A point-to-point connection is a dedicated link between exactly two devices, and the entire capacity is reserved for them. A TV remote talking to the TV through infrared is point-to-point, and so is a cable between two routers. A multipoint (or multidrop) connection is one where more than two devices share a single link. The sharing can be spatial, where several devices use the link at the same time, or temporal (time-shared), where they take turns. How devices take turns on a shared link is a big topic called multiple access, which we study in the last lesson of the course.

Mesh topology: Topology is the geometric arrangement of links and nodes; the four basic ones are mesh, star, bus and ring, often mixed into a hybrid. In a fully connected mesh, every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device. For n devices, the number of links is n(n-1)/2, because each of the n devices connects to n-1 others and each link is counted twice. Each device needs n-1 ports. With 5 devices that is 5 times 4 divided by 2, which is 10 links, and every device needs 4 ports. With 6 devices it jumps to 15 links. The advantages are strong: dedicated links mean no traffic sharing, one broken link does not affect the others, privacy is good, and faults are easy to find. The disadvantage is the huge amount of cabling and ports, so full mesh is used only for a few very important nodes, like the core of a telephone network.

Star topology: In a star, every device has a dedicated link only to a central controller, usually a hub or switch. Devices do not talk directly; everything goes through the centre. For n devices you need only n links, and each device needs one port. A star is cheaper than a mesh, easy to install, and if one link fails only that device is cut off. The weakness is the centre: if the hub or switch dies, the whole network stops. Most home and office Ethernet and Wi-Fi networks are stars, with the router or switch in the middle, which is why everybody shouts when the office switch loses power during load-shedding.

Bus and ring topologies: In a bus, one long cable called the backbone links all devices. Each device connects with a drop line and a tap. A bus uses little cable, but a break in the backbone stops everything, signals get weaker as they travel, and adding devices is limited; old coaxial Ethernet used a bus. In a ring, each device has a dedicated link only to its two neighbours, and the signal travels around the ring in one direction, from device to device, each one acting as a repeater. A ring is easy to install and faults are easy to spot, but in a simple ring one break can disable the whole loop, so real rings often use a second ring or a switch. Token Ring and fibre rings are examples.

Example 1, a bKash payment: Let us map a bKash Send Money of 500 taka onto our model. The source is the bKash app on your phone, which builds a small message containing your number, the receiver's number, the amount and a secret check value. The transmitter is your phone's radio, which turns those bits into a radio signal. The medium is first the air up to the nearest tower, then fibre and microwave links inside the operator's network up to bKash's servers. The receiver is the network equipment at the server end, and the destination is bKash's software, which checks the balance. Accuracy is critical here, so every link uses error detection, and if something is wrong, the bits are sent again.

Example 2, live cricket on TV and on a phone: When Bangladesh plays, BTV broadcasts the match. That is simplex and multipoint: one sender, millions of receivers, and no data flows back. Your friend watching the same match on a streaming app on his phone is in a different situation. His phone and the server talk in both directions, so the link is full-duplex; his phone keeps asking for the next pieces of video and reports what it has received. Timeliness and jitter matter more than perfect accuracy here. A slightly blurry frame is acceptable, but a frame that arrives two seconds late, after the wicket has already fallen on your neighbour's TV, ruins the fun.

The course map: This course follows the journey of a bit from the bottom up. First we place our topic inside the layered model of networks. Then we study signals: analog and digital, bandwidth, and the limits that Nyquist and Shannon put on data rate. We look at impairments like attenuation and noise. Next come the conversions: digital data to digital signal (line coding), analog to digital (PCM), digital to analog (ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM), and analog to analog (AM, FM). Then we learn to share links (multiplexing and spread spectrum), the media themselves (cables, fibre, wireless), and switching. Finally we climb to the data link layer: error detection and correction, flow and error control, HDLC and PPP, and multiple access with Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up half-duplex and simplex; remember that in half-duplex both sides can send, just not at the same moment. Another mix-up is between delay and jitter; jitter is the variation in delay, not the delay itself. In topology questions, check whether the question asks for links or for ports: for a mesh of n devices, links are n(n-1)/2 and ports per device are n-1, while the total number of ports in the whole network is n(n-1). Typical exam questions are: name and explain the five components of a data communication system; explain the three elements of a protocol; compare the four topologies with diagrams; and calculate the cable links needed for a mesh of a given size.

Recap: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices over a medium, following agreed protocols. The five-part model is source, transmitter, medium, receiver and destination. A good system delivers to the right place, accurately, on time, and with little jitter. Data can flow simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex, over point-to-point or multipoint links, arranged in a mesh, star, bus, ring or hybrid topology. Keep the five boxes in mind; every lesson that follows zooms into one of them, starting next time with how networks split this big job into neat layers.
key_points: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices over a transmission medium, under agreed rules.
Five-part model: source, transmitter, transmission medium, receiver, destination (Forouzan: message, sender, receiver, medium, protocol).
A protocol defines syntax (format), semantics (meaning) and timing (when and how fast).
Effectiveness depends on delivery, accuracy, timeliness and jitter; jitter is the variation in delay.
Simplex is one way, half-duplex is both ways but taking turns, full-duplex is both ways at once.
Point-to-point links serve two devices; multipoint links are shared spatially or by time.
Mesh of n devices needs n(n-1)/2 links and n-1 ports per device; a star needs n links but has a single point of failure.
Bus uses one backbone; ring passes the signal from neighbour to neighbour, each device acting as a repeater.
lessons.tip: For every new example you meet in this course, from a USB cable to a satellite, draw the five boxes (source, transmitter, medium, receiver, destination) and label them. If you can place the example in the boxes, you understand where the rest of the lesson fits.
lessons.task: Pick three devices around you (for example a TV remote, your phone on a call, and an FM radio). For each one, write down the source, transmitter, medium, receiver and destination, and say whether it is simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex. Then calculate how many links a full mesh of 8 computers needs.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of half-duplex communication?
options: A keyboard sending to a computer
quiz.explain: In half-duplex both sides can send, but only one at a time, exactly like a walkie-talkie.

quiz.q: How many links does a fully connected mesh of 6 devices need?
Which element of a protocol decides what a particular bit pattern means, such as data or acknowledgement?
quiz.explain: Semantics is the meaning of each section of bits; syntax is the format, timing is when and how fast.

quiz.q: Video packets are sent every 30 ms, but some arrive 30 ms apart and some 40 ms apart. This unevenness is called:
quiz.explain: Jitter is the variation in packet arrival time, which makes audio and video uneven.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of a star topology?
options: One broken link stops the whole network
If the central hub or switch fails, the whole network stops
quiz.explain: Each device depends on the centre, so the hub or switch is a single point of failure.

lessons.title: Layered Thinking: OSI and TCP/IP
lessons.content:
Imagine your khala in Chattogram wants to send you a birthday gift in Dhaka. She writes a card, puts it with the gift, wraps it, and hands it to a courier office. The office puts it in a bigger sack with your district written on it. The sack goes on a truck, the truck drives on the highway, and on your side everything happens in reverse: the sack is opened, your parcel is found, the wrapping comes off, and you read the card. Your khala never thinks about trucks, and the truck driver never reads the card. Each step does one job and trusts the others. That is exactly how networks are built: in layers.

Why layers: Sending data across the world involves hundreds of separate problems: turning bits into voltages, catching errors, finding a path, putting pieces back in order, showing a web page. Solving all of them in one giant program would be impossible to build and to fix. So the job is split into layers. Each layer solves one group of problems, uses the services of the layer below it, and offers services to the layer above it. The boundary between two layers is called an interface. The big win is modularity: you can change one layer, for example replace copper with fibre, and the layers above never notice.

Peers and the real path: When two computers communicate, layer n on one machine has a logical conversation with layer n on the other machine. These matching layers are called peers, and the rules of their conversation are that layer's protocol. But the conversation is only logical. Physically, the data goes down through every layer on the sending side, travels as a signal over the medium at the very bottom, and goes up through every layer on the receiving side. Only the physical layer actually touches the wire. It is like your khala's card: it feels like she is talking to you, but it really went through the courier, the sack and the truck.

The OSI model: In the late 1970s and 1980s the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) defined the Open Systems Interconnection model, usually called OSI. It is a reference model, a way to think and talk about networks, not a protocol you can install. It has seven layers. From the bottom: 1 physical, 2 data link, 3 network, 4 transport, 5 session, 6 presentation, 7 application. A popular memory trick from bottom to top is Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. Layers 1 to 3 are often called the network support layers, layers 5 to 7 the user support layers, and layer 4 links the two groups.

Layer 1, physical: The physical layer moves individual bits from one node to the next. It cares about the medium and the interface to it: what voltage or light level means 1 and what means 0, how long each bit lasts (the data rate), how sender and receiver clocks stay in step (bit synchronisation), the line configuration (point-to-point or multipoint), the physical topology, and the transmission mode (simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex). Its unit of data is simply the bit. Cables, connectors, hubs and repeaters live here. Most of the first two thirds of this course, signals, encoding, modulation, multiplexing and media, are physical layer topics.

Layer 2, data link: The data link layer turns the raw, error-prone bit pipe of the physical layer into a reliable link between two neighbouring nodes, called hop-to-hop or node-to-node delivery. Its jobs are framing (dividing the bit stream into blocks called frames), physical addressing (adding the sender and receiver hardware addresses), flow control (so a fast sender does not drown a slow receiver), error control (detecting and retransmitting damaged or lost frames, usually with a trailer of check bits), and access control (deciding who may send when several devices share one link). Switches and network cards work at this layer. Its unit of data is the frame.

Layer 3, network: The network layer is responsible for source-to-destination delivery, possibly across many links and many networks. The data link layer only gets a frame across one hop; the network layer makes sure the packet gets all the way from your laptop to a server in another country. It does this with logical addressing (IP addresses) and routing (choosing paths through routers). Its unit is the packet, also called a datagram. This is the heart of the Computer Networks course, so in this course we only need to know that it exists and sits right on top of the data link layer.

Layer 4, transport: The transport layer delivers a message from one process (one running program) to another, for example from your browser to a web server program. It uses port numbers to tell processes apart, splits a long message into segments and puts them back in order, and can provide connection control, flow control and error control from end to end, not just per hop. TCP and UDP are the famous transport protocols. Its unit is the segment (for UDP, the user datagram). Again, details belong to Computer Networks; here, just remember that layer 4 is end to end while layer 2 is hop to hop.

Layers 5, 6 and 7: The session layer is the dialog controller. It sets up, maintains and ends conversations, and can insert checkpoints, so that if a transfer of a 2000 page file fails at page 1523, it can restart from the last checkpoint instead of page 1.
