The presentation layer cares about the syntax and meaning of the information: translation between different character codes, encryption for privacy, and compression to reduce the number of bits. The application layer gives services to the user: email, file transfer, web access and so on. In everyday speech, all three are often lumped together as the application.

The TCP/IP model: The Internet does not run on OSI protocols. It runs on the TCP/IP protocol suite, which was developed before OSI and whose layers do not match OSI exactly. The original TCP/IP model is often drawn with four layers: network access (or link), internet, transport, and application. Many modern textbooks, including Forouzan's, use a five-layer version: physical, data link, network, transport and application. Either way, the session and presentation jobs of OSI are folded into the application layer in TCP/IP, and the bottom layers are left open for any standard network, such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi.

OSI versus TCP/IP: The two models differ in history and purpose. OSI was designed as a complete model first and protocols were written for it later, which made it neat but slow to catch on. TCP/IP grew from working protocols first and the model was described afterwards, which made it practical and it won in real life. OSI separates services, interfaces and protocols very clearly, which is why teachers love it for explaining ideas. TCP/IP is what runs on your phone today. A good exam answer says: OSI is the reference model we use to talk about layers, and TCP/IP is the protocol suite the Internet actually uses.

Encapsulation: As data travels down the stack on the sender, each layer adds its own control information to the front, called a header. The data link layer usually adds a trailer at the end as well, which carries the error check bits. The data handed down from the layer above is called the payload of the current layer. So a layer treats everything it receives from above as an opaque package, adds its own label, and passes it down. This wrapping is called encapsulation. At the very bottom, the whole frame is turned into a stream of bits and sent as a signal.

A worked encapsulation example: Suppose an application sends a 1000 byte message. TCP adds a 20 byte header, making a 1020 byte segment. IP adds a 20 byte header, making a 1040 byte packet. Ethernet adds a 14 byte header and a 4 byte trailer (the frame check sequence), making a 1058 byte frame, not counting the preamble. The overhead is 58 bytes out of 1058, about 5.5 percent, so about 94.5 percent of the frame is useful data. Now try a tiny 100 byte message: the frame becomes 158 bytes and the overhead is about 36.7 percent. This is why sending lots of tiny messages wastes capacity.

Decapsulation and devices: At the receiver, the process runs backwards. The physical layer turns the signal back into bits, the data link layer checks the trailer, removes its header and trailer, and passes the packet up; the network layer removes its header and passes up the segment; and so on until the application gets the original 1000 bytes. Intermediate devices only go as high as they need to. A repeater or hub works only at layer 1 and just regenerates bits. A switch opens frames up to layer 2 to read hardware addresses. A router opens packets up to layer 3 to read IP addresses and choose a path.

PDU names: The unit of data at each layer has its own name, called the protocol data unit, or PDU. At the application layer it is the message (or data). At the transport layer it is a segment for TCP or a user datagram for UDP. At the network layer it is a packet or datagram. At the data link layer it is a frame. At the physical layer it is bits. Exams love asking which name belongs to which layer, so remember the bottom three of our course: bits at layer 1, frames at layer 2, packets at layer 3.

Where this course lives: Data communication covers the physical layer and the data link layer. IEEE splits the data link layer of a LAN into two sublayers: logical link control (LLC) on top, which handles flow and error control, and media access control (MAC) underneath, which decides who may use a shared medium. In this course, the physical layer lessons cover signals, data rate limits, impairments, encoding, modulation, multiplexing, media and switching. The data link lessons cover error detection and correction, framing, flow and error control, HDLC and PPP, and multiple access with Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Everything above layer 2 we mention and leave for later courses.

Example 1, sending a photo: You send a photo to your cousin through a messaging app over home Wi-Fi. The app (application) prepares the photo, maybe compressed (a presentation job). The transport layer splits it into segments and numbers them. The network layer puts each segment in a packet with your cousin's server IP address. The Wi-Fi card wraps each packet in a Wi-Fi frame with MAC addresses and a check trailer, and the radio turns the bits into a signal in the 2.4 or 5 GHz band. Your router receives the frame, checks it, removes the Wi-Fi wrapping, and sends the packet onward in a new frame suitable for its fibre or cable link to your ISP.

Example 2, hop by hop through Bangladesh: Follow that packet further. From your house in Mirpur it may cross a fibre link to your ISP, then a link to a national exchange, then the international gateway and the SEA-ME-WE submarine cable landing at Cox's Bazar. On every hop, a different data link technology may be used, so the frame is rebuilt every time with new MAC addresses and a new check trailer. The IP packet inside, with its source and destination IP addresses, rides through all of them mostly unchanged, like the courier parcel that changes sacks and trucks but keeps the same address label inside.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say the data link layer delivers from source to destination; it does not, it delivers only across one hop, and source to destination is the network layer's job. Another mistake is thinking OSI is what the Internet uses; it is a reference model, and the Internet uses TCP/IP. Some forget that the data link layer adds a trailer as well as a header. Typical exam questions are: draw the OSI model and give the functions of each layer; compare OSI and TCP/IP; explain encapsulation with a diagram; name the PDU at each layer; and say at which layer a hub, a switch and a router operate.

Recap: Networks split the communication job into layers, each using the layer below and serving the layer above, with peers on two machines talking through a protocol. OSI has seven layers, from physical to application; TCP/IP has four or five, folding session and presentation into application. On the way down, each layer encapsulates the data with a header, and the data link layer adds a trailer; on the way up, each layer removes its own. PDUs are message, segment, packet, frame and bits. This course lives at layers 1 and 2, and next time we start at the very bottom with the signals themselves.
key_points: Layering splits a huge job into modules; each layer uses the one below and serves the one above through an interface.
Peer layers on two machines talk logically through a protocol, but physically data goes down, across the medium, and up.
OSI has 7 layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.
TCP/IP has 4 layers (link, internet, transport, application) or 5 in the textbook version (physical, data link, network, transport, application).
Data link delivers hop to hop with framing, MAC addresses, flow, error and access control; network delivers source to destination.
Encapsulation adds a header at each layer and a trailer at the data link layer; decapsulation removes them in reverse.
PDUs: message, segment (or user datagram), packet (datagram), frame, bits.
Hubs and repeaters work at layer 1, switches at layer 2, routers at layer 3; this course covers layers 1 and 2.
lessons.tip: Make one A4 sheet with the 7 OSI layers on the left, the 5 TCP/IP layers next to them, and for each layer write its job in five words, its PDU, its address type and one device. Stick it on your wall; almost every later lesson points back to one row of that sheet.
lessons.task: Take a 300 byte message and calculate the size of the Ethernet frame after adding a 20 byte TCP header, a 20 byte IP header, a 14 byte Ethernet header and a 4 byte trailer. Then work out the percentage of overhead. Repeat for a 40 byte message and compare.

quiz.q: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for hop-to-hop delivery of frames?
quiz.explain: The data link layer frames the bits and delivers them across one link, from one node to the next.

quiz.q: What is the PDU of the network layer called?
quiz.explain: The network layer works with packets (datagrams); frames belong to layer 2 and segments to layer 4.

quiz.q: Which layer adds a trailer as well as a header during encapsulation?
quiz.explain: The data link layer adds a trailer with error check bits, such as Ethernet's frame check sequence.

quiz.q: A 1000 byte message gets a 20 byte TCP header, a 20 byte IP header and 18 bytes of Ethernet header plus trailer. How big is the frame?
quiz.explain: 1000 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 = 1058 bytes, not counting the preamble.

quiz.q: In the TCP/IP model, where do the OSI session and presentation jobs go?
quiz.explain: TCP/IP has no separate session or presentation layer; those jobs are handled inside the application layer.

lessons.title: Analog and Digital Signals
lessons.content:
Drop a small stone into a village pond and watch. Rings spread out, each one rising and falling in a smooth rhythm. Now flick a light switch on and off: the room is either dark or bright, with nothing in between. These two pictures are the two families of signals in this course. The pond ripple is analog, smooth and continuous. The light switch is digital, jumping between a few fixed levels. Every bit you send, over a cable, a fibre or the air, travels as one of these. To understand how data moves, we first have to understand what a signal is and how to describe it with a few simple numbers.

Data and signals: Data is the information, and a signal is the physical form it takes to travel, such as a changing voltage, light level or radio wave. Both data and signals can be analog or digital. Analog means continuous: it can take infinitely many values in a range, like the sound of your voice or the hands of a wall clock sweeping smoothly. Digital means discrete: it takes only a limited number of values, like the numbers on a digital clock or the 0s and 1s in your computer's memory. On a graph, an analog signal is a smooth curve, while a digital signal jumps suddenly from one level to another and stays flat in between.

Periodic and nonperiodic: A periodic signal completes a pattern within a fixed amount of time and then repeats that pattern again and again. One full pattern is called a cycle. A nonperiodic (aperiodic) signal never repeats exactly. In data communication, we commonly use periodic analog signals, because they are easy to describe and need less bandwidth, and nonperiodic digital signals, because the pattern of 0s and 1s in real data changes all the time. Keep this pairing in mind: the carrier waves of radio are periodic analog, while the voltage on an Ethernet cable carrying your file is nonperiodic digital.

The sine wave: The most basic periodic analog signal is the sine wave. Its formula is s(t) = A sin(2 pi f t + phi). Only three numbers describe it completely: the peak amplitude A, the frequency f, and the phase phi. Every other periodic signal, no matter how strange it looks, can be built by adding sine waves together, which is why the sine wave is the building block of this whole subject. If you can read these three parameters off a graph or a formula, you can describe almost any signal you will meet in this course.

Peak amplitude: The peak amplitude is the absolute value of the signal's highest intensity, which for electrical signals is usually measured in volts. It tells you how strong the signal is. The electricity in a Bangladeshi home is a sine wave usually quoted as 220 volts. That 220 is the rms (effective) value, not the peak; for a sine wave the peak is the rms value times the square root of 2, so about 311 volts. A battery, by contrast, gives a steady 1.5 or 9 volts that does not wave at all. Amplitude is what we lose when a signal travels a long way and gets weaker.

Period and frequency: The period T is the time one cycle takes, measured in seconds. The frequency f is how many cycles happen in one second, measured in hertz (Hz). They are inverses: f = 1/T and T = 1/f. Bangladesh's power grid runs at 50 Hz, so one cycle lasts 1/50 of a second, which is 20 milliseconds. A signal with a period of 100 ms has a frequency of 10 Hz. A signal of 100 kHz has a period of 10 microseconds. Learn the unit ladders: seconds, milliseconds (10^-3), microseconds (10^-6), nanoseconds (10^-9), picoseconds (10^-12), and hertz, kilohertz (10^3), megahertz (10^6), gigahertz (10^9), terahertz (10^12).

What frequency really means: Frequency is the rate of change of a signal with respect to time. A change over a long span of time means low frequency; a change over a short span means high frequency. Two extreme cases are worth remembering. If a signal never changes at all, like a battery's steady voltage, its frequency is zero; we call it a DC signal. If a signal changes instantly, jumping from one level to another in no time, its frequency would be infinite. Real digital signals have very fast but not instant jumps, which, as we will see, means they contain many high frequencies.

Phase: Phase describes the position of the waveform relative to time zero. If you imagine the wave sliding left or right along the time axis, phase tells you how far it has slid. It is measured in degrees or radians, where 360 degrees equals 2 pi radians, one full cycle. A sine wave with phase 0 starts at zero amplitude and rises. With phase 90 degrees, it starts at its peak. With phase 180 degrees, it starts at zero but goes down first. A shift of one sixth of a cycle is 360/6 = 60 degrees, which is pi/3, about 1.047 radians. Phase becomes very important later, when PSK and QAM carry bits by changing it.

Wavelength: Wavelength is the distance a simple signal travels during one period. It depends on both the frequency and the medium: wavelength = propagation speed / frequency, or wavelength = speed times period. In a vacuum, and nearly in air, light and radio travel at about 3 x 10^8 metres per second. So an FM station like Radio Foorti at 88.0 MHz has a wavelength of 3 x 10^8 / 88 x 10^6, about 3.41 metres. Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz has a wavelength of 12.5 centimetres. In a copper cable, signals travel slower, roughly 2 x 10^8 metres per second, so a 1 MHz signal has a wavelength of 200 metres in the cable but 300 metres in air.

Time domain and frequency domain: So far we drew signals in the time domain, with time on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. A time-domain plot shows how the signal changes from moment to moment. There is a second view, the frequency domain, which plots peak amplitude against frequency. It hides the shape over time and shows instead which frequencies the signal contains and how strong each one is. A pure sine wave of 50 Hz and peak 5 V becomes a single vertical spike at 50 Hz with height 5. The two views describe the same signal; engineers switch between them all the time, like looking at a map or a photo of the same place.

Composite signals: A single sine wave is boring for communication: it repeats forever and carries no changing information. Useful signals are composite, made of many sine waves added together. The French mathematician Fourier showed that any composite signal can be written as a combination of simple sine waves with different frequencies, amplitudes and phases. The detailed mathematics belongs to Signals and Systems; here we only need the idea. If the composite signal is periodic, it contains a discrete set of frequencies: a fundamental frequency f and harmonics at whole-number multiples 2f, 3f, and so on. If it is nonperiodic, it contains a continuous range of frequencies.

A tiny worked composite: Take s(t) = 4 sin(2 pi 1000 t) + (4/3) sin(2 pi 3000 t). The first term is the fundamental, a 1 kHz sine with peak 4. The second is the third harmonic, a 3 kHz sine with peak 4/3, about 1.33. Plot the sum in the time domain and you get a wave with flatter tops, starting to look like a square wave. In the frequency domain it is simply two spikes: height 4 at 1 kHz and height 1.33 at 3 kHz. Add a fifth harmonic, a 5 kHz sine with peak 4/5, and it gets even closer to square. The range from the lowest to the highest frequency present is called bandwidth, the star of the next lesson.

Digital signals and levels: A digital signal uses a limited number of levels. With two levels, for example positive voltage for 1 and zero for 0, each level carries one bit. With four levels, each level can carry two bits: 00, 01, 10 or 11. In general, a signal with L levels carries log2 L bits per level. So 8 levels carry 3 bits each and 16 levels carry 4 bits. If L is not a power of 2, the formula still works but gives a fraction, which real systems avoid. Using more levels squeezes more bits into each signal element, but the levels get closer together and noise confuses them more easily, a trade-off we will meet again with Nyquist and Shannon.

A digital signal is secretly analog: Here is a surprising fact. A digital signal, with its sharp jumps, is itself a composite analog signal. A perfect square wave of 0s and 1s alternating is made of a fundamental sine plus an infinite set of odd harmonics, 3f, 5f, 7f and so on, getting weaker as they go up. This means a perfect digital signal needs an infinite range of frequencies. Real channels pass only a limited range, so the jumps get rounded off. How many harmonics we actually need, and how that links bandwidth to bit rate, is exactly what the next lesson works out.

Analog or digital, which is better: Both travel through the same physical world, but they handle noise differently. When an analog signal travels far, it weakens and picks up noise; an amplifier makes it stronger, but it amplifies the noise too, so the noise piles up over long distances. A digital signal can be regenerated: a repeater looks at the weakened signal, decides whether each part was a 0 or a 1, and sends out a fresh clean copy, throwing the noise away, as long as the noise was not big enough to flip a decision. Digital signals are also easy for computers to store, process, compress and protect with error-checking codes. That is why the world has moved from analog to digital almost everywhere.

Example 1, the electricity in your wall: The socket in your room gives a sine wave of about 220 V rms and 50 Hz. Read its parameters: peak amplitude about 311 V, frequency 50 Hz, period 20 ms, and the phase depends on when you start your stopwatch. During load-shedding, when your IPS or generator takes over, cheaper inverters often produce a stepped, square-ish wave instead of a clean sine. That stepped wave is a composite signal with extra harmonics, and some fans and motors buzz or run hot on it, because those extra frequencies are energy the device was not designed for. So the theory of composite signals is literally humming in your fan.

Example 2, FM radio and your voice: Tune an FM radio to 88.0 MHz. The station sends a high-frequency carrier with a wavelength of about 3.41 metres, and a simple antenna works well when its length is a sizable fraction of that, such as a quarter wavelength of about 85 centimetres, which is why FM radios have telescopic antennas of roughly that size. The music riding on that carrier is a composite signal, a mix of thousands of frequencies at once. Your own voice on a phone call is the same: a composite analog signal whose important frequencies sit roughly between 300 and 3400 Hz, which is the band a traditional telephone line was designed to carry.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up phase with frequency; phase is a shift in time, frequency is how fast the cycles repeat. Another common error is computing wavelength with 3 x 10^8 m/s for a cable, when the question gives a slower propagation speed. Watch your units: 1 ms is 10^-3 s and 1 microsecond is 10^-6 s, and when you invert them, kHz pairs with ms and MHz with microseconds. Typical exam questions are: find the frequency from a period, or the reverse; find the phase of a shifted sine in degrees and radians; compute a wavelength; draw the time-domain and frequency-domain plots of a composite signal; and compare analog and digital signals.

Recap: Data and signals can each be analog (continuous) or digital (discrete). Periodic signals repeat in cycles; in data communication we mostly use periodic analog signals and nonperiodic digital signals. A sine wave is fully described by peak amplitude, frequency (f = 1/T) and phase; wavelength equals propagation speed divided by frequency. Any signal can be viewed in the time domain or the frequency domain, and every composite signal is a sum of sine waves, with harmonics for periodic ones. A digital signal with L levels carries log2 L bits per level and is secretly a composite analog signal, which leads straight into bandwidth, our next lesson.
key_points: Analog signals are continuous with infinitely many values; digital signals take a limited number of discrete levels.
Data communication commonly uses periodic analog signals and nonperiodic digital signals.
A sine wave s(t) = A sin(2 pi f t + phi) is fully described by peak amplitude, frequency and phase.
Frequency and period are inverses: f = 1/T; 50 Hz mains has a 20 ms period.
Phase is measured in degrees or radians; 360 degrees = 2 pi radians, so a 1/6 cycle shift is 60 degrees.
Wavelength = propagation speed / frequency; 88 MHz in air is about 3.41 m.
Composite signals are sums of sine waves; periodic ones contain a fundamental plus harmonics, shown as spikes in the frequency domain.
A digital signal with L levels carries log2 L bits per level, and a square wave contains odd harmonics, so it needs many frequencies.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a sine formula, circle its three numbers, A, f and phi, and immediately write T = 1/f next to it. Doing this every time makes exam questions on signals almost automatic.
lessons.task: On graph paper, plot 4 sin(2 pi t) and (4/3) sin(2 pi 3t) for t from 0 to 1 using steps of 0.05, then add them point by point and plot the sum. Notice how the sum starts to look like a square wave. Then find the FM frequency of your favourite radio station and calculate its wavelength.

quiz.q: A signal has a period of 20 ms. What is its frequency?
quiz.explain: f = 1/T = 1/0.020 s = 50 Hz, the same as Bangladesh's power grid.

quiz.q: What is the wavelength of a 100 MHz radio signal in air (speed 3 x 10^8 m/s)?
quiz.explain: Wavelength = 3 x 10^8 / 100 x 10^6 = 3 m.

quiz.q: A sine wave is shifted by one quarter of a cycle. What is its phase shift?
quiz.explain: A full cycle is 360 degrees, so a quarter cycle is 360/4 = 90 degrees, or pi/2 radians.

quiz.q: What does the frequency-domain plot of a pure sine wave look like?
options: A single spike at its frequency
A flat line across all frequencies
Two spikes at 0 Hz and infinity
quiz.explain: A pure sine has only one frequency, so the frequency domain shows one spike whose height is the peak amplitude.

quiz.q: A digital signal has 8 levels. How many bits can each level carry?
quiz.explain: Bits per level = log2 L = log2 8 = 3.

lessons.title: Bandwidth and Digital Signal Properties
lessons.content:
Think of a road in Dhaka. One way to describe it is by its width: a narrow lane in Old Dhaka versus the wide expressway near the airport. Another way is by how many people it moves per minute. These are different numbers, but they are connected: a wider road can usually move more people. Data communication has exactly the same two ideas, and both are confusingly called bandwidth. One is measured in hertz and describes the width of a range of frequencies. The other is measured in bits per second and describes how much data flows. This lesson untangles them and introduces the basic numbers of every digital signal.

Bandwidth in hertz: The bandwidth of a composite signal is the difference between the highest and the lowest frequencies it contains. If a signal is made of sine waves at 100, 300, 500, 700 and 900 Hz, its bandwidth is 900 minus 100, which is 800 Hz. It is a width, not a position: a signal from 1000 to 1800 Hz also has a bandwidth of 800 Hz. You can work backwards too. If a periodic signal has a bandwidth of 20 Hz and its highest frequency is 60 Hz, its lowest frequency is 40 Hz. In a frequency-domain plot, the bandwidth is simply how wide the group of spikes, or the continuous hump, is along the frequency axis.

Bandwidth of a channel: Media and devices also have a bandwidth: the range of frequencies they pass without too much loss. A traditional telephone line passes roughly 300 to 3400 Hz, a bandwidth of 3100 Hz, which is why your voice sounds thinner on an old landline than in real life. A channel that passes frequencies from 0 up to some limit is called a low-pass channel. A channel that passes only a band that does not start at 0, like 88 to 108 MHz for FM radio, is called a band-pass channel. To send a signal through a channel without damage, the channel's band must cover the signal's band.

Bandwidth in bits per second: In networking talk, bandwidth also means the number of bits per second a channel or link can carry. When your ISP sells a 20 Mbps package, or when we say Fast Ethernet has a bandwidth of 100 Mbps, we are using this meaning. The two meanings are related: in general, an increase in bandwidth in hertz means an increase in the possible bandwidth in bits per second. Exactly how they are related depends on the encoding and on noise, which is what the Nyquist and Shannon formulas in the next lesson tell us. In exams, always check the unit to know which bandwidth is meant.

Bit rate and bit interval: Most digital signals are nonperiodic, so period and frequency do not describe them well. Instead we use the bit rate, the number of bits sent in one second, in bps, and the bit interval (or bit duration), the time one bit takes. They are inverses: bit interval = 1 / bit rate. At 1 Mbps, each bit lasts 1 microsecond. At 10 Mbps, each bit lasts 100 nanoseconds. At 20 Mbps, 50 nanoseconds. As links get faster, bits get shorter, and the electronics must decide whether each tiny slice of time is a 0 or a 1, which becomes harder when the signal is noisy or distorted.

How many bits per second do we need: Suppose you want to download a 100-page text document in one second, and each page has 24 lines of 80 characters, with 8 bits per character. The bits needed are 100 x 24 x 80 x 8, which is 1,536,000 bits, so you need a bit rate of about 1.536 Mbps. Now uncompressed HD video: 1920 x 1080 pixels per frame, 30 frames per second, 24 bits per pixel. That is 1920 x 1080 x 30 x 24 = 1,492,992,000 bps, about 1.5 Gbps. No home connection in Bangladesh sends that raw, which is why video is always heavily compressed before it travels.

Bit length: Bit length is the distance one bit occupies on the medium. It equals propagation speed times bit duration. In a copper cable with a propagation speed of about 2 x 10^8 m/s, a 1 Mbps signal has a bit duration of 1 microsecond, so each bit is stretched over 200 metres of cable. At 1 Gbps on the same cable, a bit is just 20 centimetres long. This idea becomes useful later: when we ask how many bits can be in flight on a long link at once, or why Ethernet needs a minimum frame size, we are really asking about bit length.

Data elements and signal elements: A data element is the smallest piece of information, a bit. A signal element is the shortest unit of the signal in time, for example one voltage level held for a moment. They are not always the same. If each signal element carries one bit, the counts match. But with four voltage levels, each signal element can carry two bits; with 16 levels, four bits. We write r for the number of data elements carried per signal element. For L levels, r = log2 L. Think of signal elements as rickshaws and bits as passengers: a rickshaw carrying two passengers moves twice as many people with the same number of trips.

Baud versus bit rate: The data rate (bit rate) N counts bits per second. The signal rate, also called the baud rate or modulation rate, S counts signal elements per second, measured in baud. They are linked by S = N / r, ignoring a small case factor that some books include. Worked example: a signal sends 9600 bps with 4 bits per signal element, so S = 9600 / 4 = 2400 baud. Another: a 16-level signal carries log2 16 = 4 bits per element, so at 1000 baud it delivers 4000 bps. Baud is never larger than bit rate when r is at least 1, and the two are equal only when each element carries exactly one bit.

Why baud matters more than bits: The bandwidth a digital signal needs depends on how fast the signal changes, which is the baud rate, not directly on the bit rate. That gives engineers a clever trick: to send more bits through the same bandwidth, pack more bits into each signal element. Using 4 levels instead of 2 doubles the bit rate without changing the baud, and so without needing more hertz. The price is that the levels are closer together, so noise can confuse them more easily. This trade-off, more levels against more errors, is the heart of the data rate limits in the next lesson.

Square waves and harmonics: In the last lesson we saw that a digital signal is secretly a composite analog signal. Let us make it precise for the worst-case pattern, 0101..., which changes the most. At a bit rate N, one 0 and one 1 together make one cycle, so the pattern is a square wave of fundamental frequency N/2. Fourier analysis says a square wave is the sum of its odd harmonics: the fundamental f, then 3f, 5f, 7f and so on, with peak amplitudes proportional to 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7. For a square wave that swings between +1 and -1, these amplitudes are about 1.27, 0.42, 0.25 and 0.18. They never stop, but they keep getting weaker.

How much bandwidth is enough: A perfect square wave needs infinite bandwidth, but a receiver only has to tell 0 from 1, so a rough copy is enough. Take a 1 kbps signal. Its worst-case fundamental is 500 Hz. Sending only that fundamental needs a bandwidth of about N/2 = 500 Hz and gives a smooth wave that still shows where the 1s and 0s are. Adding the third harmonic needs 3N/2 = 1500 Hz and the edges get sharper. Adding the fifth needs 5N/2 = 2500 Hz and the shape gets close to square. So the required bandwidth is proportional to the bit rate: double the bit rate and you need double the hertz for the same quality.

Baseband transmission: Baseband transmission means sending a digital signal over a channel without changing it into an analog signal. It needs a low-pass channel, one whose bandwidth starts at 0 Hz, because long runs of the same bit act like very low frequencies close to DC. A dedicated cable between two computers is a good example; an Ethernet cable in your office carries baseband signals. In theory a perfect baseband channel would need infinite bandwidth, but as we just saw, a limited low-pass channel of about N/2 or more works in practice. How the bits are drawn as voltages, called line coding, is a whole lesson of its own later.

Broadband or passband transmission: Broadband (passband) transmission means changing the digital signal into an analog signal by modulating a carrier, so that it fits into a band-pass channel. This is necessary when the channel does not pass low frequencies at all, or when many users must share a medium by each using a different band. Radio, mobile networks and Wi-Fi all work this way: they cannot send a raw 0101 voltage through the air, so they shape bits onto a high-frequency carrier. Note the confusing word: in this course broadband means passband, not just fast internet. Modulation (ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM) gets two lessons later.

Choosing between them: Baseband is simple and cheap, and is used where you have a dedicated low-pass medium, like a short copper cable inside a building. Passband is used when the medium is a band-pass channel, when several signals must share the medium side by side, or when the signal has to travel through the air. Many real systems mix both: your phone handles bits in baseband form inside its chips, then its radio converts them to passband for the air, and the tower converts them back to baseband before sending them into fibre or cable as a different kind of signal.

Example 1, a home internet package: Your family buys a 20 Mbps broadband plan. The bit interval is 1 / 20,000,000 seconds, which is 50 nanoseconds per bit. A 500 MB movie, where MB means 10^6 bytes, is 500 x 8 x 10^6 = 4 x 10^9 bits, so at a steady 20 Mbps it would take 4 x 10^9 / 20 x 10^6 = 200 seconds, a little over three minutes. In real life it takes longer because of headers, sharing with your siblings' phones, and the ISP's own limits. Notice also that 20 Mbps is a bandwidth in bps; the hertz bandwidth of the fibre or cable carrying it is a completely different number.

Example 2, the old telephone modem: Before broadband, people in Bangladesh and everywhere else connected to the internet through dial-up modems over a voice telephone line with roughly 3100 Hz of bandwidth. The line could not carry high frequencies, so the modem used passband transmission inside the voice band. Early standard modems sent 2400 signal elements per second, and by packing 4 data bits into each signal element they reached 9600 bps. Same baud, more bits per element, more speed: exactly the trade-off from this lesson, and the reason later modems kept pushing to more complex signal patterns.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The biggest confusion is between bandwidth in Hz and bandwidth in bps; always look at the unit. Students also mix up baud and bit rate: baud counts signal elements, bit rate counts bits, and S = N / r. Some forget that bandwidth is a difference, not the highest frequency. Another mistake is thinking baseband means slow; it only means no carrier modulation. Typical exam questions are: find the bandwidth of a composite signal; compute bit interval and bit length; convert between baud and bit rate for a given number of levels; find the bandwidth needed to send N bps using the first, third or fifth harmonic; and compare baseband and broadband transmission.

Recap: Bandwidth in hertz is the width of a frequency range, highest minus lowest, for a signal or a channel; bandwidth in bps is how many bits a link carries per second, and more hertz generally allows more bps. Digital signals are described by bit rate and bit interval (1 / bit rate), and bit length is propagation speed times bit interval. The baud rate counts signal elements; with r bits per element, baud S = N / r, and the bandwidth needed depends on baud. A worst-case digital signal is a square wave with odd harmonics, needing about N/2, 3N/2 or 5N/2 Hz. Baseband sends digital signals on low-pass channels; broadband modulates a carrier for band-pass channels. Next: the hard limits on data rate.
key_points: Bandwidth in Hz = highest frequency minus lowest frequency of a signal or channel; a phone line is about 300-3400 Hz, 3100 Hz wide.
Bandwidth in bps is the data a link can carry per second; more Hz generally allows more bps.
Bit interval = 1 / bit rate (1 Mbps gives 1 microsecond); bit length = propagation speed x bit interval.
Baud (signal rate) counts signal elements per second; S = N / r, where r = log2 L bits per element.
The bandwidth a digital signal needs depends on its baud rate, so more levels give more bps in the same Hz, at the cost of noise margin.
A worst-case 0101 signal at N bps is a square wave with fundamental N/2 and odd harmonics 3N/2, 5N/2 with amplitudes falling as 1, 1/3, 1/5.
Baseband sends the digital signal directly over a low-pass channel; broadband (passband) modulates a carrier for a band-pass channel.
lessons.tip: Write the unit next to every number you compute in this part of the course: Hz, bps, baud, seconds, metres. Most lost marks in data rate questions come from silently mixing hertz with bits per second or baud with bits.
lessons.task: Check your phone or home internet speed with any speed test app. Write down the download rate, calculate the bit interval in nanoseconds, and calculate how long a 1 GB (10^9 bytes) file would take at that speed. Then work out the baud rate if that speed were sent with 16-level signal elements.

quiz.q: A composite signal contains frequencies from 1000 Hz to 5000 Hz. What is its bandwidth?
quiz.explain: Bandwidth = highest - lowest = 5000 - 1000 = 4000 Hz.

quiz.q: What is the bit interval of a 10 Mbps signal?
quiz.explain: Bit interval = 1 / 10^7 s = 10^-7 s = 100 ns.

quiz.q: A signal carries 4 bits per signal element at 9600 bps. What is its baud rate?
For a worst-case 0101... signal at 1 kbps, what is the fundamental frequency?
quiz.explain: One 0 and one 1 make one cycle, so the fundamental is N/2 = 500 Hz.

quiz.q: Sending a digital signal as it is, without modulating a carrier, over a low-pass channel is called:
quiz.explain: Baseband transmission sends the digital signal directly and needs a channel whose band starts at 0 Hz.

lessons.title: Data Rate Limits: Nyquist and Shannon
lessons.content:
Imagine you are at a busy tea stall near Karwan Bazar, trying to tell your friend a phone number across the table. If the stall is quiet, you can speak fast and he catches every digit. If buses are honking and the kettle is screaming, you must slow down or repeat yourself. And no matter how quiet it is, your mouth can only make sounds so fast. Data communication faces the same two limits. One comes from how fast the channel can change, its bandwidth. The other comes from how much noise drowns the signal. This lesson gives you the two famous formulas that put a hard ceiling on how many bits per second any channel can carry.

Three things decide the data rate: How fast we can send data over a channel depends on three factors: the bandwidth available, the number of signal levels we use, and the quality of the channel, which really means its level of noise. Two theoretical formulas capture this. Nyquist's formula is for an ideal, noiseless channel, and it tells us the bit rate for a given bandwidth and a given number of levels. Shannon's formula is for a real, noisy channel, and it tells us the maximum possible bit rate no matter how clever our levels are. Together they form the backbone of every data rate calculation in this course.

Nyquist bit rate: For a noiseless channel, Nyquist's result is BitRate = 2 x B x log2 L, where B is the bandwidth of the channel in hertz, L is the number of signal levels used to represent data, and BitRate is in bits per second. Where does the 2B come from? Nyquist showed that a channel of bandwidth B can carry at most 2B independent signal elements per second, so 2B is the maximum baud rate. Each signal element with L levels carries log2 L bits, as we saw last lesson. Multiply the two and you get the bit rate. It is the baud rate formula from lesson 4, pushed to its maximum.

Nyquist worked examples: Take a noiseless channel with a bandwidth of 3000 Hz. With two signal levels, BitRate = 2 x 3000 x log2 2 = 6000 bps. With four levels, log2 4 = 2, so BitRate = 2 x 3000 x 2 = 12,000 bps. With eight levels, log2 8 = 3, so BitRate = 18,000 bps. Notice the pattern: doubling the bandwidth doubles the bit rate, but doubling the number of levels only adds one more bit per signal element. Going from 2 to 4 levels doubles the rate, but going from 4 to 8 only raises it by half, and from 8 to 16 by a third. Levels give diminishing returns.

Why not use a million levels: Nyquist's formula seems to promise any bit rate you want: just keep increasing L. The catch is the receiver. With more levels, the voltage steps between them get smaller, and the receiver has to tell apart levels that are very close together. In a perfectly noiseless world that would be fine, but no real channel is noiseless. A tiny bit of noise can push a level up or down into its neighbour, and the receiver decodes the wrong bits. So increasing the number of levels reduces the reliability of the system. Nyquist tells us what levels can do in theory; Shannon tells us where noise stops us.

Nyquist in reverse: Exams often ask how many levels you need. Suppose we must send 265 kbps over a noiseless channel with a bandwidth of 20 kHz. Then 265,000 = 2 x 20,000 x log2 L, so log2 L = 6.625 and L is about 98.7 levels. Since practical systems use a power of 2 so that each level maps to a whole number of bits, we have two choices. We can use 128 levels, giving 2 x 20,000 x 7 = 280 kbps, which is a bit more than needed. Or we can use 64 levels, giving 2 x 20,000 x 6 = 240 kbps, and accept a lower rate. Either way, the answer must be a whole power of 2.

Noise and SNR: Noise is any unwanted signal mixed into the one we want: random electron motion, interference from nearby wires, lightning, a microwave oven near your Wi-Fi. To measure how bad it is, we compare powers. The signal-to-noise ratio is SNR = average signal power / average noise power. It is a plain ratio with no unit. A high SNR means the signal is much stronger than the noise, which is good. A low SNR means the signal is barely above the noise. Because we divide power by power, an SNR of 1 means the noise is just as strong as the signal, and an SNR of 1000 means the signal is a thousand times stronger.

Decibels: SNR values range from tiny fractions to millions, so engineers use a logarithmic unit, the decibel. SNR in dB = 10 log10 SNR. An SNR of 10 is 10 dB, 100 is 20 dB, 1000 is 30 dB, and 1 is 0 dB. Doubling the power adds about 3 dB, since 10 log10 2 is about 3.01. For example, if the signal power is 10 milliwatts and the noise power is 1 microwatt, SNR = 0.01 / 0.000001 = 10,000, which is 40 dB. To go back from decibels to a plain ratio, use SNR = 10^(dB/10); 35 dB is 10^3.5, about 3162. The next lesson uses decibels again for attenuation along a cable.

Shannon capacity: In 1948, Claude Shannon found the highest data rate that any noisy channel can support. It is C = B x log2(1 + SNR), where C is the capacity in bits per second, B is the bandwidth in hertz, and SNR is the plain signal-to-noise ratio, not the decibel value. Notice that the number of levels does not appear. Shannon's capacity is a property of the channel itself. No matter how many levels or how clever an encoding you use, you cannot reliably send more than C bits per second. Below C, Shannon proved that error-free communication is possible in principle, with good enough coding.

Shannon worked examples: First an extreme case. If the SNR is 0, meaning the signal is so weak that it is lost in the noise, then C = B log2(1 + 0) = B log2 1 = 0. No matter how wide the channel, you cannot send anything. Now a classic: a traditional telephone line with a bandwidth of about 3000 Hz and an SNR of about 3162, which is 35 dB. Then C = 3000 x log2(3163). Since log2 3163 is about 11.63, C is about 34,881 bps, roughly 34.9 kbps. So no matter what modem you put on a pure analog phone line like that, it cannot reliably exceed about 35 kbps.

A handy shortcut: When the SNR is large, 1 + SNR is almost the same as SNR, and log2 SNR = SNR_dB / (10 log10 2), which is about SNR_dB / 3.01. So C is approximately B x SNR_dB / 3. For example, a channel with a bandwidth of 2 MHz and an SNR of 36 dB has an approximate capacity of 2 x 10^6 x 36 / 3 = 24 Mbps. The exact calculation, using SNR = 10^3.6, about 3981, gives 2 x 10^6 x log2 3982, which is about 23.9 Mbps. The shortcut is excellent for quick estimates and checking your exam answers, but it should not be used when the SNR is small, say below 10 dB.

Bandwidth versus SNR: Look at Shannon's formula again. Bandwidth sits outside the logarithm, and SNR sits inside it. That makes a huge practical difference. Doubling the bandwidth doubles the capacity. Doubling the SNR, at a high SNR, only adds about B bits per second, because log2 2 is just 1. For a 1 MHz channel, raising the SNR from 1000 to 2000 adds only about 1 Mbps. So extra bandwidth is the most powerful way to raise capacity, which is why mobile operators pay huge sums when the regulator, BTRC in Bangladesh, auctions new spectrum. Extra transmit power helps, but only slowly.

Using both together: In practice, the two formulas work as a team. Shannon gives the upper limit, the ceiling you can never break. Nyquist tells you how many signal levels you need to reach a chosen rate below that ceiling. The usual procedure has three steps. First, use Shannon to find the capacity C. Second, pick a target bit rate somewhat below C, to leave a safety margin, because real equipment is never perfect. Third, use Nyquist with that target rate to find L, and round to a sensible power of 2. This is exactly how textbook problems on channel design are solved.

A full worked design: We have a channel with a bandwidth of 1 MHz and an SNR of 63. Step one, Shannon: C = 10^6 x log2(1 + 63) = 10^6 x log2 64 = 10^6 x 6 = 6 Mbps. That is the upper limit. Step two, for better performance we choose something lower, say 4 Mbps. Step three, Nyquist: 4,000,000 = 2 x 1,000,000 x log2 L, so log2 L = 2 and L = 4. So we design a system using four signal levels at 2 million signal elements per second, giving 4 Mbps, safely below the 6 Mbps ceiling. That margin leaves room for real noise spikes and imperfect hardware.

What Shannon does not tell you: Shannon's theorem tells you the limit exists, but not how to reach it. Getting close requires clever error-correcting codes and modulation. For decades, real systems ran far below the Shannon limit. Modern codes such as turbo codes and LDPC codes, used in 4G, 5G and Wi-Fi, come remarkably close. Also note that C is a limit on reliable information, not on raw signalling: a sloppy system can blast bits faster than C, but many of them will arrive wrong. And Shannon assumes a particular kind of random noise; real channels with interference or fading need extra care, which later lessons and later courses discuss.

Example 1, a 4G channel: Imagine a Grameenphone or Robi 4G carrier using 20 MHz of bandwidth, and your phone sees an SNR of 20 dB, which is a ratio of 100. Shannon gives C = 20 x 10^6 x log2 101, about 133 Mbps, for one antenna-to-antenna path. Real phones use multiple antennas (MIMO) to open several parallel paths, but every path still obeys Shannon. And that capacity is shared by everyone connected to the same cell, so in a crowded place like a stadium during a cricket match, each person gets only a slice. Move behind thick concrete walls and the SNR drops, and so does your share.

Example 2, Wi-Fi in your home: Your home Wi-Fi uses a 20 MHz channel. In the same room as the router, the SNR might be 30 dB, a ratio of 1000, so the Shannon ceiling is about 20 x 10^6 x log2 1001, roughly 199 Mbps. In a far bedroom behind two walls, the SNR might fall to 10 dB, a ratio of 10, and the ceiling falls to about 20 x 10^6 x log2 11, roughly 69 Mbps. The router notices this and switches to a scheme with fewer levels per symbol, so that noise does not cause errors, which is the Nyquist trade-off in action. We will see exactly how in the QAM lesson.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The number one error is plugging the decibel value straight into Shannon's formula; always convert to a plain ratio first, SNR = 10^(dB/10). Second, using log10 instead of log2; on a calculator without log2, use log2 x = log10 x / log10 2, about log10 x / 0.301. Third, using Nyquist for a noisy channel; Nyquist assumes no noise. Fourth, giving a fractional number of levels; round to a power of 2 and say what rate you get. Typical exam questions are: compute Nyquist bit rate; convert between SNR and dB; compute Shannon capacity; find the number of levels for a target rate; and combine both to design a channel.

Recap: Data rate depends on bandwidth, signal levels and noise. Nyquist, for a noiseless channel: BitRate = 2B log2 L, with at most 2B signal elements per second; more levels add bits but reduce reliability. Noise is measured by SNR = signal power / noise power, often in decibels: SNR_dB = 10 log10 SNR. Shannon, for a noisy channel: C = B log2(1 + SNR), a hard ceiling that does not depend on levels; for high SNR, C is about B x SNR_dB / 3. Bandwidth raises capacity linearly, SNR only logarithmically. Use Shannon for the ceiling and Nyquist for the levels. Next we look at what makes signals weak and noisy in the first place.
key_points: Data rate depends on bandwidth, number of signal levels, and channel noise.
Nyquist (noiseless): BitRate = 2B log2 L; a channel of bandwidth B carries at most 2B signal elements per second.
More levels add bits per element but bring levels closer, so noise causes more errors; practical L is a power of 2.
SNR = average signal power / average noise power; SNR_dB = 10 log10 SNR (1000 = 30 dB, doubling = about +3 dB).
Shannon (noisy): C = B log2(1 + SNR), using the plain ratio; it is the ceiling for any encoding.
For high SNR, C is approximately B x SNR_dB / 3; capacity grows linearly with bandwidth but only logarithmically with SNR.
Design method: Shannon for the upper limit, choose a lower target rate, then Nyquist for the number of levels (1 MHz, SNR 63 gives C = 6 Mbps; 4 Mbps needs L = 4).
lessons.tip: Before every Shannon calculation, write a separate line converting decibels to a plain ratio. Then sanity-check your answer with the B x SNR_dB / 3 shortcut. If the two numbers are far apart, you probably used log10 or forgot the conversion.
lessons.task: Using a phone calculator, find the Shannon capacity of a 4 kHz channel with an SNR of 20 dB. Then find how many levels Nyquist would need to send 20 kbps over the same 4 kHz if it were noiseless, rounded to a power of 2. Finally, check how much the capacity grows if you double the bandwidth versus if you double the SNR.

quiz.q: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 3000 Hz and uses 4 signal levels. What is the Nyquist bit rate?
quiz.explain: BitRate = 2 x 3000 x log2 4 = 2 x 3000 x 2 = 12,000 bps.

quiz.q: An SNR of 1000 equals how many decibels?
What is the Shannon capacity of a 1 MHz channel with an SNR of 63?
What is the Shannon capacity of any channel when the SNR is 0?
quiz.explain: C = B log2(1 + 0) = B log2 1 = 0; the signal is lost in the noise.

quiz.q: A 1 MHz channel has a Shannon capacity of 6 Mbps. We choose to send 4 Mbps. How many levels does Nyquist require?
quiz.explain: 4 x 10^6 = 2 x 10^6 x log2 L, so log2 L = 2 and L = 4.

lessons.title: Transmission Impairments and Performance
lessons.content:
Imagine you shout a message to your friend across a busy Dhaka road. Your voice gets weaker the farther it travels. The horns of buses and the ringing of rickshaw bells mix into it. If your friend stands far away, your words arrive a little late, and some of them come out blurred. Every real communication link has the same three troubles: the signal gets weaker, it changes shape, and unwanted noise gets added. On top of that, everything takes time. This lesson is about those troubles, called transmission impairments, and about how we measure how good a link really is.

Why impairments matter: A transmission medium is never perfect. What the receiver gets is not exactly what the transmitter sent. For analog signals, this means lower quality, like a crackly radio. For digital signals, it means bit errors: a 1 is read as a 0, or the other way around. Engineers must know how much damage to expect so they can add amplifiers, repeaters, better cables or error control. The three main impairments are attenuation, distortion and noise. After that we look at performance: bandwidth, throughput, latency, the bandwidth-delay product and jitter.

Attenuation: Attenuation means loss of energy. As a signal travels through a wire, part of its energy turns into heat because of the resistance of the conductor. In wireless links, the energy spreads out in space, so each square metre gets less of it. A signal that starts strong at the transmitter arrives weak at the receiver. To fight this, analog systems use amplifiers that boost the signal, and digital systems use repeaters that read the bits and send a fresh, clean copy. Attenuation usually grows with distance and also with frequency, so high-frequency parts of a signal fade faster.

The decibel: Engineers measure gain and loss in decibels, written dB. The formula is dB = 10 log10(P2 / P1), where P1 is the power at the start and P2 is the power at the end. If the power drops from 10 mW to 5 mW, the change is 10 log10(5/10) = about -3.01 dB, which we usually call -3 dB. So -3 dB means the power was cut in half, and +3 dB means it was doubled. A negative dB value is a loss, and a positive one is a gain. If you measure voltage instead of power, you use 20 log10(V2 / V1), because power is proportional to the square of voltage.

Why decibels are handy: Decibels turn multiplication into addition. Suppose a signal passes through a cable that loses 3 dB, then an amplifier that gains 7 dB, then another cable that loses 3 dB. The total is -3 + 7 - 3 = +1 dB. Another example: an optical fibre that loses 0.2 dB per kilometre will lose 0.2 x 50 = 10 dB over 50 km. A 10 dB loss means the power is multiplied by 10 to the power -1, so only one tenth of the power arrives. A 30 dB loss means only one thousandth arrives.

dBm, an absolute unit: Sometimes we want to state an actual power level, not just a ratio. The unit dBm compares power to 1 milliwatt: dBm = 10 log10(P / 1 mW). So 1 mW is 0 dBm, 10 mW is 10 dBm, and 0.5 mW is about -3 dBm. Your phone often shows Wi-Fi or mobile signal strength in dBm, with numbers like -60 or -90. The more negative, the weaker the signal. A phone near a Grameenphone tower might show around -70 dBm, and deep inside a building it might show -100 dBm or worse.

Distortion: Distortion means the signal changes its shape. A composite signal is made of many sine waves of different frequencies, as we saw in lesson 3. Each frequency travels through the medium at a slightly different speed and gets a slightly different delay. At the receiver, the parts no longer line up the way they did at the sender, so the shape is bent. In digital links, distortion makes pulses spread into their neighbours, which can confuse the receiver about which bit it is reading.

Noise: Noise is any unwanted energy that adds itself to the signal. If noise is small compared with the signal, everything is fine. If noise is large, bits flip. This is why the signal-to-noise ratio, SNR, from lesson 5 is so important: SNR = signal power / noise power, often written in dB as 10 log10(SNR). There are four classic types of noise, and each comes from a different place.

Thermal noise: Electrons inside every conductor jiggle randomly because of heat. This random motion creates a small noise voltage, also called white noise because it is spread evenly over all frequencies. It cannot be removed, only kept small. Its power is N = kTB, where k is the Boltzmann constant 1.38 x 10 to the power -23 joules per kelvin, T is temperature in kelvin and B is bandwidth in hertz. At room temperature, 290 K, with B = 1 MHz, N = 1.38e-23 x 290 x 1,000,000 = about 4.0 x 10 to the power -15 watts, roughly -144 dBW or -114 dBm. Tiny, but a very weak signal from a far satellite can be close to that.

Induced noise and crosstalk: Induced noise comes from outside sources such as motors, fans, fluorescent lights and power lines. The wire acts like a receiving antenna and picks them up. Crosstalk is when one wire picks up the signal of a neighbouring wire. Twisting the pairs and shielding cables reduce both effects, as we will see in the lesson on guided media.

Impulse noise: Impulse noise is a sudden, short spike of high energy. It comes from lightning, a switch turning on, or a faulty power line. During a storm in the monsoon, you might hear clicks on a radio. For analog voice, a click is annoying but harmless. For digital data, one spike lasting 10 milliseconds at 10 Mbps can wipe out 100,000 bits in a row. That is why impulse noise is the main cause of burst errors, which we will learn to detect later with CRC.

Performance, bandwidth: Now we switch from troubles to measurements. The word bandwidth has two meanings. In hertz, it is the range of frequencies a channel can pass, like 4 kHz for a voice channel. In bits per second, it is the maximum number of bits the link can carry, like a 100 Mbps Ethernet port. The two are connected through Nyquist and Shannon from lesson 5, but in everyday speech, people say bandwidth and mean the bit rate.

Throughput: Throughput is how many bits actually get through per second. It is often less than the bandwidth, just like a road built for 60 km per hour carries traffic at 20 km per hour during a jam. Worked example: a link has a bandwidth of 10 Mbps, but on average only 12,000 frames per minute pass, each with 10,000 bits. Throughput = 12,000 x 10,000 / 60 = 2,000,000 bits per second = 2 Mbps. So the link is being used at only one fifth of its capacity. The slowest link on a path limits the whole path, like the narrowest part of a pipe.

Latency: Latency, or delay, is how long it takes for an entire message to arrive, from the moment the first bit leaves the source. It has four parts: Latency = propagation time + transmission time + queuing time + processing delay.

Propagation time: Propagation time is how long one bit takes to travel from one end to the other. Propagation time = distance / propagation speed. In copper or fibre, signals travel at about 2 x 10 to the power 8 metres per second, about two thirds the speed of light in vacuum. For a 250 km fibre between Dhaka and Chattogram, propagation time = 250,000 / 200,000,000 = 1.25 ms. For a 12,000 km cable at 2.4 x 10 to the power 8 m/s, it is 12,000,000 / 240,000,000 = 0.05 s = 50 ms. A geostationary satellite is about 35,786 km up, so one hop up and down is about 71,572 km, which at light speed takes about 0.24 s. That is why live TV through satellite has a noticeable pause.

Transmission time: Transmission time is how long it takes to push all the bits of a message onto the line. Transmission time = message size / bandwidth. A 2,500 byte email is 20,000 bits; at 1 Gbps it takes 20,000 / 1,000,000,000 = 20 microseconds. A 5 MB photo (40,000,000 bits) at 1 Mbps takes 40 seconds. Notice the difference: propagation depends on distance, transmission depends on size and bandwidth. For short messages over long distance, propagation dominates. For large files on slow links, transmission dominates.

Queuing and processing: Queuing time is the waiting time inside a device, like a switch or router, when packets arrive faster than they can be sent out. It changes with traffic: almost zero at midnight, large at peak hours, just like the queue at a bKash agent shop on Eid. Processing delay is the small time a device needs to read headers, check for errors and decide where to send the frame.

Bandwidth-delay product: The bandwidth-delay product tells how many bits can be in the pipe at one moment. Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth x delay. A 1 Mbps link with 20 ms delay holds 1,000,000 x 0.02 = 20,000 bits in flight. A 100 Mbps link with 10 ms delay holds 1,000,000 bits. Picture the link as a long pipe: bandwidth is how wide it is, delay is how long it is, and the product is its volume. This number matters a lot for flow control in lesson 23: a sender that waits for an answer after every frame leaves most of this pipe empty.

Jitter: Jitter is variation in delay. If packets of a video call arrive 30 ms, 31 ms, 80 ms and 29 ms after being sent, the average may look fine, but the 80 ms one arrives late. For a voice or video call, this causes choppy sound or a frozen face. Receivers fight jitter with a small playout buffer: they hold packets for a short time and then play them at a steady pace. Watching a cricket match online, the few seconds of buffering at the start partly exists for this reason.

Real-life example 1, a phone call to Rajshahi: You call your grandmother in Rajshahi on a mobile network. Your voice is converted to bits, sent by radio to a tower, then over fibre to a switch, and on to a tower near her house. Attenuation weakens the radio signal inside thick brick walls, so her phone might show -95 dBm. Thermal and induced noise add errors, and the network corrects many of them. Propagation over a few hundred kilometres of fibre is only a couple of milliseconds, but processing and queuing in many devices add more. If the network is busy at night, jitter grows and your voice may sound broken for a moment.

Real-life example 2, a satellite TV link: Suppose a TV channel sends a live cricket match from a stadium to its studio using the Bangabandhu-1 satellite. The signal travels about 36,000 km up and the same down, and loses a huge amount of power over that distance, so large dish antennas with high gain are needed. Rain in the monsoon adds more attenuation at high frequencies. The total up-and-down delay of about a quarter of a second is why the studio presenter and the reporter at the ground sometimes talk over each other.

Common mistakes: Students often mix up propagation and transmission time. Remember: propagation is distance divided by speed and does not care about message size; transmission is size divided by bandwidth and does not care about distance. Another mistake is adding decibel values as if they were watts, or forgetting the minus sign for loss. Using 10 log for voltage instead of 20 log is a classic error too. Finally, many students think more bandwidth always means less delay; for a tiny message across a continent, propagation time stays the same no matter how fast the link is.

What exams ask: Typical questions: define attenuation, distortion and noise with causes; compute dB gain or loss through a chain of amplifiers and cables; find power after a given loss; calculate thermal noise kTB; compute throughput from frames per minute; find latency for a given distance, speed, message size and bandwidth; compute the bandwidth-delay product and explain it with the pipe picture; explain jitter and how buffering helps.

Recap: Signals get weaker (attenuation), change shape (distortion) and pick up noise (thermal, induced, crosstalk, impulse). Decibels, dB = 10 log10(P2/P1), make gains and losses easy to add. Performance is measured by bandwidth, throughput, latency and jitter. Latency is propagation plus transmission plus queuing plus processing. The bandwidth-delay product is the number of bits that fill the link. Next lesson, we start turning bits into actual voltage patterns with line coding.
key_points: The three impairments are attenuation (energy loss), distortion (change of shape) and noise (unwanted added energy).
dB = 10 log10(P2/P1) for power and 20 log10(V2/V1) for voltage; -3 dB means half the power, and dB values along a path simply add.
dBm is power relative to 1 mW: 1 mW = 0 dBm, 10 mW = 10 dBm.
Noise types: thermal (N = kTB), induced, crosstalk and impulse; impulse noise causes burst errors.
Throughput is the bits actually delivered per second, often less than the bandwidth.
Latency = propagation time (distance / speed) + transmission time (size / bandwidth) + queuing time + processing delay.
Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth x delay = number of bits that fill the link.
Jitter is variation in delay; playout buffers smooth it for voice and video.
lessons.tip: For every delay problem, first write the four parts of latency as a line, then fill in only the parts the question gives. Keep units consistent: convert bytes to bits and km to metres before dividing.
lessons.task: Open your phone settings (Android: About phone, Status, or a free signal app) and note the mobile signal strength in dBm in three places: near a window, in the middle of your home and in a bathroom or stairwell. Work out how many dB weaker each place is than the window and what fraction of power that means.

quiz.q: A signal power falls from 20 mW to 10 mW. What is the loss in decibels?
quiz.explain: 10 log10(10/20) = 10 log10(0.5) = about -3 dB: half the power.

quiz.q: Which type of noise comes from random motion of electrons and is given by N = kTB?
quiz.explain: Thermal (white) noise comes from heat-driven electron motion and its power is kTB.

quiz.q: A 2,500 byte message is sent at 1 Gbps. What is its transmission time?
A link has a bandwidth of 100 Mbps and a delay of 10 ms. What is its bandwidth-delay product?
quiz.explain: 100 x 10^6 x 0.01 = 10^6 = 1,000,000 bits can be in the link at once.

quiz.q: Packets of a voice call arrive with delays of 30, 31, 80 and 29 ms. What problem does this show?
quiz.explain: Jitter is variation in delay; one late packet among steady ones is exactly that.

lessons.title: Line Coding I: NRZ, RZ and Manchester
lessons.content:
Imagine you and your best friend live in neighbouring buildings in Mirpur. At night, you want to send each other secret messages with a torch from the rooftop. You agree: torch on means 1, torch off means 0, and each bit lasts one second. It works fine for 1010. But then you send 1000000001. Your friend sees a long stretch of darkness and starts to wonder: was that seven seconds of dark or eight? Did the torch battery die? This little game already shows every problem that line coding has to solve.

What line coding is: Inside a computer, data is a sequence of bits. To send those bits over a wire, we must turn them into a digital signal: voltage levels that change over time. Line coding is the rule that maps bits to signal levels. The sender has a line encoder, and the receiver has a decoder that turns the signal back into bits. Line coding happens at the physical layer, and it is the very last step before bits leave the network card as electricity or light.

Data elements and signal elements: A data element is the smallest piece of information, one bit. A signal element is the shortest unit of the signal, one constant piece of voltage in time. The ratio r is the number of data elements carried by one signal element. If one bit is sent as one voltage level, r = 1. If one bit needs two half-bit levels, as in Manchester, r = 1/2. If two bits are packed into one level, as in some schemes of the next lesson, r = 2.

Data rate and signal rate: The data rate N is the number of bits per second (bps). The signal rate S, also called the baud rate or pulse rate, is the number of signal elements per second (baud). They are linked by S = c x N x (1/r), where c is a case factor that depends on the data pattern: worst case, best case or average case, and we usually take c = 1/2 for the average. Example: an NRZ signal with N = 100 kbps and r = 1 has an average signal rate S = 1/2 x 100,000 x 1 = 50 kbaud. Manchester with the same data rate and r = 1/2 gives S = 1/2 x 100,000 x 2 = 100 kbaud. A higher signal rate needs more bandwidth, so engineers want S small.

Baseline wander: A receiver decides whether a level means 0 or 1 by comparing it with a running average of the received power, called the baseline. If the signal stays at the same level for a long time, for example during a long run of 1s, the average drifts towards that level. The receiver then gets confused about where the middle is. This drift is called baseline wander. A good line code keeps flipping often enough that the average stays in the middle.

DC component: If the voltage stays constant for a long time, the signal contains very low frequencies, close to zero hertz. That zero-frequency part is called the DC component. Many links cannot pass DC: telephone lines and links that use transformers for electrical isolation block very low frequencies. A signal with a DC part also wastes energy, because that part carries no information. So a good line code tries to have an average voltage of zero, which we call DC balanced.

Self-synchronisation: The receiver must know exactly where each bit starts and ends, so its clock must match the sender's clock. If the receiver's clock is only a tiny bit off, errors pile up. Example: if the receiver clock is 0.1 percent faster than the sender, at 1 kbps it thinks it received 1,001 bits in one second instead of 1,000, so 1 extra bit per second. At 1 Mbps that becomes 1,001,000 instead of 1,000,000, so 1,000 extra bits every second. A self-synchronising code has enough transitions in the signal itself, so the receiver can keep correcting its clock, just like your torch friend would be happy if you blinked at the start of every second.

Other wishes for a line code: Some codes have built-in error detection, because certain level patterns are illegal and reveal an error. A code should be immune to noise, so that a small disturbance does not change a 0 into a 1. And it should be simple, because complex codes need costly circuits. No single code wins on every point, which is why so many line codes exist.

The families: Line codes are grouped into five families. Unipolar codes use one polarity: a positive voltage and zero. Polar codes use two polarities: positive and negative. Bipolar codes use three levels: positive, zero and negative, with alternating pulses. Multilevel codes pack several bits into one level, and multitransition codes cycle through levels. This lesson covers unipolar and polar codes, including Manchester. The next lesson covers bipolar, multilevel and multitransition codes, block coding and scrambling.

Unipolar NRZ: NRZ stands for non-return-to-zero: the signal does not return to zero in the middle of the bit. In unipolar NRZ, bit 1 is +V and bit 0 is 0 V. It is the simplest idea, just like our torch. Its problems are big. It has a strong DC component, it has no self-synchronisation for long runs of 0s or 1s, and it is costly in power: for the same distance between the two levels, its normalised power is twice that of polar NRZ. That is why unipolar NRZ is rarely used in data communication today.

Polar NRZ-L: In polar NRZ, the two levels are +V and -V. In NRZ-L, L stands for level: the level itself tells the bit. We use the convention of the popular Forouzan textbook: bit 0 is +V and bit 1 is -V. Some books use the opposite, so always read the convention given in the question. NRZ-L still suffers from baseline wander and loses synchronisation during long runs of either 0s or 1s.

Polar NRZ-I: In NRZ-I, I stands for invert. Here the level is not the bit; a change is the bit. If the next bit is 1, the signal inverts (flips from +V to -V or back). If the next bit is 0, there is no change. Long runs of 1s now give plenty of transitions, so the clock stays in step. Long runs of 0s still give a flat line, so the problem is only half solved. Both NRZ-L and NRZ-I have an average signal rate of N/2, so for 1 Mbps they need roughly 500 kHz of bandwidth. USB uses a variant of NRZ-I where a 0 causes the flip, plus extra bits inserted to break long runs.

Worked example, NRZ: Let us encode the data 01001110. Unipolar NRZ: 0, +V, 0, 0, +V, +V, +V, 0. NRZ-L with 0 = +V and 1 = -V: +, -, +, +, -, -, -, +. NRZ-I, assuming the line was at +V before the first bit: bit 0 keeps +, bit 1 flips to -, bit 0 keeps -, bit 0 keeps -, bit 1 flips to +, bit 1 flips to -, bit 1 flips to +, bit 0 keeps +. So NRZ-I gives +, -, -, -, +, -, +, +.

Polar RZ: RZ means return-to-zero. It uses three levels: +V, 0 and -V. In each bit, the signal goes to a level for the first half and returns to zero for the second half. We take bit 1 as +V then 0, and bit 0 as -V then 0. For 01001110 that gives: (-,0), (+,0), (-,0), (-,0), (+,0), (+,0), (+,0), (-,0). Every single bit has a change in the middle, so the receiver always finds the clock. The price: two signal changes per bit, so more bandwidth, and three levels are harder to build and detect.

Manchester: Manchester coding combines the ideas of RZ and NRZ-L. Each bit is split into two halves, and there is always a transition in the middle of the bit. The direction of that middle transition tells the bit. In the IEEE 802.3 convention used by Ethernet, 0 is a high-to-low transition and 1 is a low-to-high transition. Since every bit has a middle transition, the code is fully self-synchronising, and since each bit spends half its time at +V and half at -V, it has no DC component. Classic 10 Mbps Ethernet (for example 10BASE-T) uses Manchester.

Worked example, Manchester: For 01001110, writing the two halves of each bit: 0 = (+,-), 1 = (-,+), 0 = (+,-), 0 = (+,-), 1 = (-,+), 1 = (-,+), 1 = (-,+), 0 = (+,-). Notice that between two equal bits, such as the two 0s in positions 3 and 4, the signal also has to flip at the bit boundary to get back to the right starting level. That extra flip is fine; the receiver only reads the middle transition. Some older books use the opposite convention, where 0 is low-to-high, so check which one the question uses.

Differential Manchester: Differential Manchester combines the ideas of RZ and NRZ-I. There is always a transition in the middle of each bit, used only for the clock. The bit value is shown at the start of the bit: if the next bit is 0, there is a transition at the start; if the next bit is 1, there is no transition at the start. Because it looks at changes, not levels, swapping the two wires does not corrupt the data. It was used in IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks.

Worked example, differential Manchester: Take 01001110 again, and assume the line was at +V at the end of the previous bit. Bit 0: transition at start, so (-,+). Bit 1: no transition at start, so it starts where it was, at +, giving (+,-). Bit 0: transition, the line was at -, so (+,-). Bit 0: (+,-). Bit 1: no transition, starts at -, so (-,+). Bit 1: (+,-). Bit 1: (-,+). Bit 0: transition from +, so (-,+). Result: (-,+), (+,-), (+,-), (+,-), (-,+), (+,-), (-,+), (-,+).

Bandwidth cost of Manchester: Manchester and differential Manchester have r = 1/2, because one bit needs two signal elements. With c = 1/2, the average signal rate is S = N, twice that of NRZ. In the worst case, a long run of all 0s or all 1s, the line changes twice per bit, so 10 Mbps Ethernet produces up to 20 million changes per second. In short: Manchester buys perfect synchronisation and zero DC by paying double bandwidth. Faster Ethernet versions moved to other codes for exactly this reason, as the next lesson shows.

Real-life example 1, the old Ethernet lab: Many university and office computer labs in Dhaka once ran 10 Mbps Ethernet over twisted pair. Each network card turned every bit into a Manchester pair of half-bit levels. Because every bit had a middle transition, two cards from different makers with slightly different clocks could still talk all day without losing track. The cost was that the cable had to carry about twice the signal rate of the data rate, which was fine at 10 Mbps.

Real-life example 2, the torch on the rooftop: Go back to our torch game. With plain on-off (unipolar NRZ), a long 0000000 looked like a dead battery. Now try Manchester: for 1, keep the torch off for the first half second and on for the second half; for 0, on then off. Your friend always sees a change in the middle of every second, so counting is easy, even for 1000000001. You have just rebuilt Ethernet's trick with a torch.

Common mistakes: Mixing up conventions is the top error: NRZ-L and Manchester conventions differ between textbooks, so always state yours. In NRZ-I, students wrongly flip on 0; in Forouzan's NRZ-I, a 1 causes the flip. In differential Manchester, students forget that the middle transition is always present and that only the start of the bit carries the value. Another mistake is thinking that NRZ-I fully solves synchronisation; it fails on long runs of 0s. Finally, many forget that Manchester doubles the signal rate.

What exams ask: Typical questions: define data rate, signal rate and r; compute S = c x N x (1/r) for a given scheme; explain baseline wander, DC component and self-synchronisation; draw the signal for a given bit pattern in unipolar NRZ, NRZ-L, NRZ-I, RZ, Manchester and differential Manchester; compare the schemes in a table of DC, synchronisation and bandwidth; and compute extra bits caused by clock drift.

Recap: Line coding maps bits to signal levels. A good code avoids baseline wander and DC, and gives self-synchronisation without wasting bandwidth. Unipolar NRZ is the simplest but worst. NRZ-L uses levels, NRZ-I uses inversions on 1. RZ returns to zero mid-bit. Manchester puts a transition in the middle of each bit (0 high-to-low, 1 low-to-high in IEEE 802.3), and differential Manchester signals the bit with a transition or no transition at the start. Manchester buys synchronisation with double bandwidth.
key_points: Line coding converts bits into a digital signal; r = data elements per signal element.
Signal rate S = c x N x (1/r) baud, with c = 1/2 for the average case; higher S needs more bandwidth.
A good line code avoids baseline wander and DC components and is self-synchronising.
Unipolar NRZ: 1 = +V, 0 = 0; high DC and twice the power of polar NRZ.
NRZ-L: level gives the bit; NRZ-I: a 1 inverts the level, a 0 keeps it; both fail on long runs of 0s.
RZ uses three levels and returns to zero in mid-bit, costing extra bandwidth.
Manchester: always a mid-bit transition (IEEE 802.3: 0 high-to-low, 1 low-to-high), no DC, used by 10 Mbps Ethernet.
Differential Manchester: always a mid-bit transition; 0 = transition at start, 1 = no transition at start.
lessons.tip: When drawing line codes, first draw dotted lines for every bit boundary and mid-bit point, then write the rule of the scheme at the top of the page. Most marks are lost on conventions, not on drawing.
lessons.task: Take the bit pattern of the first letter of your name in 8-bit ASCII (for example A = 01000001). On squared paper, draw it in unipolar NRZ, NRZ-L, NRZ-I, Manchester and differential Manchester. Count the number of level changes in each and see which one changes the most.

quiz.q: Which problem happens when a long run of the same level makes the receiver lose track of the average signal power?
quiz.explain: Baseline wander is drift of the running average (baseline) during long constant stretches.

quiz.q: An NRZ signal has a data rate of 100 kbps. With c = 1/2, what is the average signal rate?
In NRZ-I (Forouzan convention), what causes the signal level to change?
options: Only the middle of each bit
quiz.explain: In NRZ-I a 1 inverts the level, a 0 keeps it.

quiz.q: Which line code always has a transition in the middle of every bit, with the direction telling the bit?
quiz.explain: Manchester has a mid-bit transition whose direction gives the bit value.

quiz.q: In differential Manchester, how is a bit 0 shown?
options: By a transition at the start of the bit
quiz.explain: Differential Manchester always has a mid-bit transition; a 0 adds a transition at the start, a 1 does not.

lessons.title: Line Coding II, Block Coding and Scrambling
lessons.content:
Think about the queue at a Dhaka metro rail ticket gate. If everyone walks through in the same rhythm, the guard can count people easily. If a long gap appears, he loses count. Last lesson we met codes like NRZ and Manchester, which either lose the rhythm during long runs or pay double bandwidth to keep it.
