Today we learn smarter tricks: three-level bipolar codes, codes that pack several bits into one level, block codes that add a few extra bits, and scrambling that quietly breaks up long runs of zeros.

Where we are: In lesson 7 we covered unipolar and polar codes. Remember the three wishes: no DC component, no baseline wander, and self-synchronisation, all with as little bandwidth as possible. Manchester gets the first three but uses a signal rate of about N, double NRZ. The codes in this lesson try to keep the signal rate low while still giving the receiver enough transitions.

Bipolar AMI: Bipolar codes use three levels: positive, zero and negative. In AMI, which stands for alternate mark inversion, a 0 is sent as zero voltage, and each 1 is sent as a pulse whose polarity alternates: the first 1 is +V, the next 1 is -V, the next +V, and so on. The word mark comes from old telegraph language, where a 1 was called a mark. Because positive and negative pulses alternate, they cancel out on average, so AMI has no DC component, even for a long run of 1s.

Worked example, AMI: Encode 01001110, assuming the last pulse before it was negative. The bits give: 0 is 0, 1 is +, 0 is 0, 0 is 0, 1 is -, 1 is +, 1 is -, 0 is 0. So the signal is 0, +, 0, 0, -, +, -, 0. Check that the nonzero pulses alternate: +, -, +, -. They do.

Pseudoternary: Pseudoternary is the mirror image of AMI. A 1 is sent as zero voltage, and each 0 is sent as an alternating pulse. For 01001110, again assuming the last pulse was negative: 0 is +, 1 is 0, 0 is -, 0 is +, 1 is 0, 1 is 0, 1 is 0, 0 is -. So the signal is +, 0, -, +, 0, 0, 0, -. Pseudoternary and AMI have the same properties; they only swap the roles of 0 and 1.

Strengths and weaknesses of bipolar: Bipolar codes have no DC component and a signal rate similar to NRZ, so they save bandwidth compared with Manchester. They also give free error detection: if two pulses in a row have the same polarity, something went wrong. This is called a bipolar violation. Their weakness: in AMI, a long run of 0s is a flat zero line with no transitions, so synchronisation is lost. In pseudoternary, a long run of 1s has the same problem. We fix this with scrambling later in this lesson. AMI was used in the early North American T1 digital telephone lines.

Multilevel coding, the idea: So far each signal element carried at most one bit. If we use more levels, each level can carry more bits. With L levels, one signal element can carry log2(L) bits. So four levels carry 2 bits per element, and the signal rate halves. Codes are named mBnL: m binary bits are sent as n signal elements, each using one of L levels. For a code to work, we need 2 to the power m to be at most L to the power n, so that each bit pattern gets its own signal pattern.

2B1Q: 2B1Q means two binary, one quaternary: two bits become one signal element with four levels. Here r = 2, so the average signal rate is S = 1/2 x N x 1/2 = N/4. A common mapping, used in the ANSI standard for ISDN lines, is: 10 is +3, 11 is +1, 01 is -1, 00 is -3. The first bit gives the sign and the second the size. Some textbooks use a variant where the level also depends on the previous one, so always check your table. With this mapping, 01001110 splits into 01, 00, 11, 10 and becomes -1, -3, +1, +3. Four bits per pair of signal elements means a 2 Mbps link needs only about 500 kbaud on average. The price is that four levels are closer together, so noise causes errors more easily.

8B6T, a quick mention: 8B6T sends 8 bits as 6 signal elements with three levels each. Since 3 to the power 6 = 729 is more than 2 to the power 8 = 256, there are spare patterns, which are chosen to keep DC balance. It was used in the older 100BASE-T4 Ethernet over four pairs. You only need to know the name and the idea.

MLT-3: MLT-3 stands for multiline transmission, three levels. It uses +V, 0 and -V and moves through them in a cycle: 0, +V, 0, -V, 0, +V, and so on. The rule: a 0 bit means no change, and a 1 bit means move one step forward in the cycle. For 01001110, starting at 0 and going towards +V first: 0 stays 0, 1 moves to +, 0 stays +, 0 stays +, 1 moves to 0, 1 moves to -, 1 moves to 0, 0 stays 0. So the signal is 0, +, +, +, 0, -, 0, 0. In the worst case, all 1s, it takes four bits to complete one full cycle, so the highest fundamental frequency is only one quarter of the bit rate.

Why MLT-3 matters: Fast Ethernet over copper, 100BASE-TX, sends 125 Mbaud on the cable after block coding. With MLT-3, the worst-case fundamental frequency is only 125 / 4 = 31.25 MHz, which an ordinary Category 5 twisted pair can carry. However, MLT-3 alone does not give synchronisation for long runs of 0s, since a 0 means no change. That is why it is combined with the next idea: block coding.

Block coding: Block coding changes the bits before line coding. It replaces each group of m bits with a group of n bits, where n is larger than m. The extra bits are not used for data. They let the code choose only nice patterns, for example patterns with enough 1s, so that a long run of 0s never happens. Block coding has three steps: divide the data into m-bit groups, substitute each group with an n-bit code word, and combine the code words into a new stream that then goes to a line coder.

4B/5B: In 4B/5B, every 4 data bits are replaced by a 5-bit code word. There are 16 possible 4-bit groups but 32 possible 5-bit words, so we can pick only the 16 friendliest ones. The table is designed so that no code word has more than one leading 0 and no more than two trailing 0s. As a result, the output never has more than three 0s in a row. For example, 0000 becomes 11110, 0100 becomes 01010, 1110 becomes 11100 and 1111 becomes 11101. So 0100 1110 becomes 01010 11100. Several of the unused 5-bit words act as control symbols such as idle, and the rest are illegal, so receiving one reveals an error.

4B/5B with NRZ-I: NRZ-I loses synchronisation only on long runs of 0s, and 4B/5B guarantees at most three 0s in a row, so the pair works well together. The cost is 25 percent extra bits: to carry 100 Mbps of data, the line must carry 100 x 5/4 = 125 Mbps. Fast Ethernet over fibre (100BASE-FX) uses 4B/5B with NRZ-I, and 100BASE-TX uses 4B/5B with MLT-3. That is still much better than Manchester, which would need a signal rate of about 200 Mbaud in the worst case for 100 Mbps.

8B/10B: 8B/10B replaces each byte with a 10-bit word. Inside, it is built from a 5B/6B part and a 3B/4B part. It has 1,024 possible 10-bit words for 256 bytes, so it can choose words with nearly equal numbers of 0s and 1s. It also tracks running disparity, the running difference between 1s and 0s sent so far. If too many 1s have gone out, it sends the version of the next word with more 0s, which keeps the DC near zero. The overhead is again 25 percent: 1 Gbps Gigabit Ethernet over fibre sends 1.25 Gbaud. 8B/10B is also used in SATA, PCI Express 1.0 and 2.0, and USB 3.0. Newer links such as 10 Gigabit Ethernet use 64B/66B, which has only 2/64 = 3.125 percent overhead.

Scrambling: Block coding adds bits and needs a higher signal rate. For long-distance telephone links, engineers wanted to keep AMI's bandwidth but fix its long-zero problem. Scrambling does this: it looks for a run of zeros and replaces it with a special pattern of pulses that deliberately breaks the AMI rule. The receiver spots the rule-breaking pattern and turns it back into zeros. No extra bits are added, so the bandwidth stays the same.

B8ZS: B8ZS, bipolar with 8-zero substitution, is used in North American T1 lines. Every run of eight 0s is replaced by 000VB0VB. V is a violation: a pulse with the same polarity as the previous pulse, breaking the AMI rule. B is a normal bipolar pulse that follows the AMI rule. Worked example: send 1 00000000 1, and suppose the first 1 is +. B8ZS gives +, 0, 0, 0, +, -, 0, -, +, and then the last 1 is - because it alternates with the final +. Note the two violations: + after + and - after -. They come as a pair with opposite polarity, so the DC balance is kept.

HDB3: HDB3, high-density bipolar 3-zero, is used in E1 lines, the European standard used in most of the world. It replaces every run of four 0s with either 000V or B00V. The choice depends on the number of nonzero pulses since the last substitution: if it is odd, use 000V; if it is even, use B00V. This rule makes consecutive violations alternate in polarity, so the line stays DC balanced. Worked example: send 1 0000 0000 1 with the first 1 as +. One pulse since the start, odd, so the first four 0s become 000V with V = +. Now zero pulses since that substitution, even, so the next four 0s become B00V with B = - and V = -. The final 1 is +. Result: +, 0, 0, 0, +, -, 0, 0, -, +.

Real-life example 1, Fast Ethernet at home: The Ethernet cable from your Wi-Fi router to your desktop computer probably runs at 100 Mbps or 1 Gbps. At 100 Mbps, every 4 bits from your computer are first turned into a 5-bit 4B/5B code word, then the stream of 125 Mbaud is sent with MLT-3 on the copper. That combination keeps the clock in step and keeps the frequency low enough for a cheap Category 5 cable. When you watch a cricket highlight on YouTube, every frame of it passes through this little chain.

Real-life example 2, E1 trunks: Older telephone networks, like those of BTCL, joined exchanges with E1 lines carrying 2.048 Mbps, and mobile operators also used E1 links to connect towers before fibre and IP links took over. A quiet phone call can produce long runs of zero bits. Without HDB3, the receiving equipment would lose its clock during these silent parts. With HDB3, every run of four zeros is replaced by a recognisable pattern, so the clock never drifts. You will see how E1 frames are built in lesson 15.

Common mistakes: Students often forget the starting polarity: always state the polarity of the last pulse before your bit pattern. In B8ZS, the V pulses copy the previous pulse; B pulses alternate as normal. In HDB3, count only the nonzero pulses since the last substitution, not all bits. Mixing up 4B/5B with 8B/10B overhead is common; both are 25 percent. And many think block coding is error correction. It is not: it only shapes the bit stream, though illegal code words can reveal an error.

What exams ask: Typical questions: draw AMI and pseudoternary signals for a bit pattern; encode with 2B1Q or MLT-3; compute the signal rate for 2B1Q or MLT-3 for a given data rate; explain why 4B/5B is combined with NRZ-I and compute the line rate for 100 Mbps; encode a stream with B8ZS or HDB3 given the starting polarity; and compare block coding with scrambling. Remember the formula S = c x N x (1/r) from the last lesson and write r for each scheme.

Recap: Bipolar AMI and pseudoternary use three levels with alternating pulses: no DC and free violation checking, but long runs of 0s or 1s lose sync. 2B1Q packs 2 bits per level and quarters the average signal rate; MLT-3 cycles through three levels to lower the frequency. Block coding (4B/5B, 8B/10B) adds 25 percent extra bits to avoid long zero runs and balance DC. Scrambling (B8ZS for T1, HDB3 for E1) replaces zero runs with patterns containing deliberate violations, adding no extra bits.
key_points: AMI: 0 is zero voltage, each 1 is an alternating +/- pulse; pseudoternary swaps the roles of 0 and 1.
Bipolar codes have no DC and detect errors as bipolar violations, but lose sync on long runs of 0s (AMI).
mBnL multilevel codes need 2^m <= L^n; 2B1Q sends 2 bits per four-level element, average signal rate N/4.
MLT-3 cycles 0, +V, 0, -V on each 1 and stays on 0; 100BASE-TX uses it to keep 125 Mbaud within 31.25 MHz.
Block coding replaces m bits with n bits: 4B/5B gives at most three 0s in a row, with 25 percent overhead (100 Mbps -> 125 Mbps).
8B/10B uses running disparity for DC balance (Gigabit Ethernet, SATA, PCIe 1/2, USB 3.0); 64B/66B has 3.125 percent overhead.
B8ZS (T1) replaces eight 0s with 000VB0VB.
HDB3 (E1) replaces four 0s with 000V if an odd number of pulses since last substitution, else B00V.
lessons.tip: For every scrambling problem, write the polarity of the last pulse on top, then mark each pulse as B or V as you go. Checking that V pulses copy the previous pulse catches almost every mistake.
lessons.task: Write down the bit pattern 1 0000 0000 0000 1 1. Encode it by hand with AMI, then with B8ZS (first 1 is +), then with HDB3 (first 1 is +). Check that in HDB3 the violations alternate in polarity and that the total of all + and - pulses stays close to zero.

quiz.q: In bipolar AMI, how is a binary 1 sent?
options: As a pulse whose polarity alternates with each 1
quiz.explain: AMI sends 0 as zero and every 1 as an alternating positive or negative pulse.

quiz.q: Using the mapping 10 = +3, 11 = +1, 01 = -1, 00 = -3, what is 2B1Q for 1100?
quiz.explain: 11 is +1 and 00 is -3.

quiz.q: 100 Mbps of data is sent with 4B/5B. What is the bit rate on the line?
quiz.explain: Each 4 bits become 5, so 100 x 5/4 = 125 Mbps.

quiz.q: What does B8ZS replace a run of eight 0s with?
quiz.explain: B8ZS substitutes 000VB0VB, where V is a violation and B a normal bipolar pulse.

quiz.q: In HDB3, an even number of nonzero pulses have been sent since the last substitution. Four 0s arrive. What replaces them?
quiz.explain: Even count means B00V; odd count means 000V. This keeps violations alternating.

lessons.title: Analog-to-Digital Conversion: PCM
lessons.content:
Imagine your little cousin is drawing the path of a kite flying over a field in Rajshahi. She cannot draw it continuously, so every second she puts a dot on paper at the kite's height. Then she rounds each height to the nearest metre and writes the numbers in her notebook. Later, anyone can read those numbers and redraw a good copy of the flight. That is exactly how your voice becomes bits on a phone call. The method is called pulse code modulation, or PCM, and it is the classic way to turn an analog signal into digital data.

Why convert analog to digital: Voices, music and sensor readings are analog: they vary smoothly in time. But digital signals are easier to protect. A repeater can regenerate clean bits, while an amplifier boosts noise along with the signal. Digital data can be compressed, encrypted, error-checked and mixed with other data on the same link. That is why telephone networks went digital decades ago and why your phone records voice notes as files of bits.

The three steps of PCM: A PCM encoder does three things in order. First, sampling: measure the analog signal at regular moments in time. Second, quantization: round each measured value to one of a fixed set of levels. Third, encoding: write the level number of each sample as a group of bits. At the receiver, a decoder turns the bits back into levels and smooths them into an analog signal with a low-pass filter.

Sampling: Sampling takes the value of the signal every Ts seconds. Ts is the sampling interval, and its inverse fs = 1/Ts is the sampling rate in samples per second. Three methods exist. Ideal sampling takes instant pulses, which is a mathematical idea only. Natural sampling switches the signal on for a short time and keeps its natural shape during that moment. Flat-top sampling, also called sample-and-hold, measures the value and holds it constant for a short time; this is what real converter circuits do.

The sampling theorem: How fast must we sample? The Nyquist sampling theorem gives the answer: to reproduce a signal whose highest frequency is fmax, the sampling rate must be at least twice that: fs >= 2 fmax. The rate 2 fmax is called the Nyquist rate. Example: a signal with frequencies up to 4 kHz needs at least 8,000 samples per second. The full proof uses the Fourier transform, which you will meet in Signals and Systems; here we only need the rule. Do not confuse this with the Nyquist bit-rate formula from lesson 5; same person, different question.

Why twice: Think of a sine wave. To capture it, you need at least one sample on each hill and one in each valley, so at least two samples per cycle. With fewer, different sine waves can pass through exactly the same dots, and the receiver cannot tell them apart. In practice, engineers sample a little faster than the minimum to leave room for imperfect filters. Telephone voice is limited to about 300 to 3,400 Hz, so the Nyquist rate would be 6,800 samples per second, but the standard uses 8,000 samples per second.

Aliasing: If we sample too slowly, high frequencies disguise themselves as low ones. This false frequency is called an alias. For a single tone of frequency f, sampled at fs, with f between fs/2 and fs, the alias appears at fs - f. Example: a 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz looks exactly like a 3 kHz tone, because 10 - 7 = 3. Once aliased, the error cannot be undone. So every PCM system puts an anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the sampler, removing anything above fs/2.

Aliasing you can see: Have you watched a video where a car wheel or a fan seems to spin slowly backwards? The camera takes a fixed number of frames per second, which is sampling in time. When the wheel turns almost a full circle between two frames, the eye sees it moving a little backwards. That is aliasing with your own eyes. In audio, aliasing turns into strange whistling tones that were never in the original sound.

Quantization: After sampling, each sample can still have any value, like 1.3172 volts. Bits can only describe a finite number of values, so we round. We divide the range from Vmin to Vmax into L equal zones. The height of each zone is the step size, delta = (Vmax - Vmin) / L. Each sample is replaced by the middle value of its zone. With n bits per sample, we can have L = 2 to the power n levels. So 8 bits give 256 levels and 16 bits give 65,536 levels.

Worked example, quantization: Let the signal range be -4 V to +4 V and let L = 8, so n = 3 bits and delta = 8 / 8 = 1 V. The zones are -4 to -3, -3 to -2, and so on up to 3 to 4, numbered 0 to 7, with middle values -3.5, -2.5, up to 3.5. Five samples arrive: 1.3, 2.9, -0.4, -3.6 and 3.95 V. Sample 1.3 falls in zone 5 (1 to 2), quantized to 1.5, error -0.2. Sample 2.9 is in zone 6, quantized to 2.5, error +0.4. Sample -0.4 is in zone 3, quantized to -0.5, error +0.1. Sample -3.6 is in zone 0, quantized to -3.5, error -0.1. Sample 3.95 is in zone 7, quantized to 3.5, error +0.45. Every error is at most delta / 2 = 0.5 V.

Quantization error: The difference between the real value and the quantized value is the quantization error. It is never more than delta / 2 in size. Since the error behaves like a small random noise, it is called quantization noise. It is not caused by the channel; it is created by the converter itself, and it is the price we pay for using a finite number of bits. A 10-bit converter reading a 0 to 5 V sensor has delta = 5 / 1,024, about 4.88 mV, so its error is at most about 2.44 mV.

SQNR: The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio measures how good the quantization is. For a full-scale sine wave and uniform quantization with n bits, SQNR = 6.02 n + 1.76 dB. So each extra bit adds about 6 dB, which means the noise power drops to about a quarter. With 8 bits, SQNR = 6.02 x 8 + 1.76 = 49.92 dB, about 50 dB. With 12 bits it is about 74 dB, and with 16 bits, like a music CD, it is about 98 dB. Exam tip: if a question asks how many bits are needed for at least a given SQNR, solve 6.02 n + 1.76 >= target and round n up.

Encoding: After quantization, each sample is a zone number from 0 to L - 1. Encoding simply writes that number in binary with n bits. In our worked example, the zones 5, 6, 3, 0 and 7 become 101, 110, 011, 000 and 111. Put together, the digital stream is 101110011000111. These bits then go to a line coder, like the ones in lessons 7 and 8, to become a real signal on the wire.

PCM bit rate: The bit rate is simply samples per second times bits per sample: N = fs x n. The classic telephone voice channel uses fs = 8,000 samples per second and n = 8 bits, so N = 8,000 x 8 = 64,000 bps = 64 kbps. This 64 kbps channel is the basic building block of the digital telephone network, and it reappears in T1 and E1 in lesson 15. A music CD samples at 44,100 per second with 16 bits and 2 stereo channels: 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bps, about 1.41 Mbps. One minute of CD audio is about 10.6 MB.

Bandwidth of PCM: Turning a signal into bits costs bandwidth. With a simple two-level line code, the minimum bandwidth is about half the bit rate, which gives B_min = n x B_analog. For voice with B_analog = 4 kHz and n = 8, the digital signal needs about 32 kHz, eight times the 4 kHz of the original analog voice. We accept this because digital signals survive noise and can be regenerated perfectly.

Companding: Quiet sounds are small, and uniform steps make their relative error large. Our voices have many quiet moments, so uniform quantization wastes levels on loud values that rarely happen. Companding (compressing plus expanding) fixes this: before uniform quantization, the signal passes through a curve that boosts small values and squeezes large ones; the receiver applies the opposite curve. Two standards exist: mu-law with mu = 255, used in North America and Japan, and A-law with A = 87.6, used in Europe and most of the rest of the world. With mu-law, an input at 1 percent of full scale moves up to about 23 percent of the output range, and 10 percent moves to about 59 percent, so quiet sounds get many more levels. With companding, 8 bits give a dynamic range similar to about 13 or 14 uniform bits.

Real-life example 1, a phone call home: When you call your mother on Grameenphone, the microphone in your phone produces an analog voltage. A filter removes frequencies too high for the sampling rate, then the converter samples your voice thousands of times per second and turns each sample into bits. On classic digital telephone lines, this is exactly the 8,000 samples per second and 8 bits of the 64 kbps channel, with A-law companding. Mobile phones then compress the bits further with special voice codecs, but sampling and quantization always come first.

Real-life example 2, recording a song: Suppose you record your friend singing a Rabindra Sangeet with your phone's voice recorder at 48,000 samples per second and 16 bits, in stereo. The raw bit rate is 48,000 x 16 x 2 = 1,536,000 bps. One minute without compression is 1,536,000 x 60 / 8 = 11.52 million bytes, about 11.5 MB. That is why the recorder saves the song as a compressed file instead. A radio station like Radio Foorti works the same way when it streams online: PCM in the studio, compressed audio over the internet.

Common mistakes: Students often use fmax as the sampling rate instead of 2 fmax. Another mistake is using L instead of n: the bit rate is fs times n, not fs times L. Remember L = 2 to the power n. In quantization, people forget to use the middle of the zone or compute delta as range / (L - 1); in this standard textbook method it is range / L. Many also believe sampling faster always improves quality forever; above the Nyquist rate it helps filters, but quantization bits decide the noise floor. Finally, aliasing cannot be fixed after sampling; it must be prevented with a filter before.

What exams ask: Typical questions: state the sampling theorem; find the Nyquist rate of a signal; find the alias of a tone sampled too slowly; quantize a set of samples given the range and L, listing zone, quantized value, error and code; compute SQNR for n bits or the bits needed for a target SQNR; compute PCM bit rate and minimum bandwidth; explain companding with mu-law and A-law. Draw a small table for quantization questions, one row per sample.

Recap: PCM turns analog into digital in three steps: sample, quantize, encode. Sample at fs >= 2 fmax, or aliasing appears; filter before sampling. Quantize with step delta = (Vmax - Vmin) / L; error is at most delta / 2, and SQNR = 6.02 n + 1.76 dB. Encode each level with n = log2 L bits. Bit rate = fs x n, so telephone voice is 8,000 x 8 = 64 kbps. Companding (mu-law, A-law) gives quiet sounds more levels. Next lesson: delta modulation, a one-bit cousin of PCM, and how bits travel in parallel or serial.
key_points: PCM has three steps: sampling, quantization and encoding.
Sampling theorem: fs >= 2 fmax; 2 fmax is the Nyquist rate. Telephone voice uses 8,000 samples per second.
Sampling too slowly causes aliasing: a 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz appears as 3 kHz. An anti-aliasing filter must come before the sampler.
Quantization: L = 2^n levels, step delta = (Vmax - Vmin) / L, error at most delta / 2.
SQNR = 6.02 n + 1.76 dB; each extra bit adds about 6 dB (8 bits: about 50 dB).
PCM bit rate N = fs x n: voice 8,000 x 8 = 64 kbps; CD 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bps.
Minimum PCM bandwidth is about n x B_analog (32 kHz for 8-bit voice).
Companding (mu-law 255 in North America and Japan, A-law 87.6 elsewhere) gives quiet signals more levels.
lessons.tip: Build every quantization answer as a table with columns: sample, zone number, quantized value, error, code. Examiners love tables, and the error column lets you check yourself: no value can be bigger than delta / 2.
lessons.task: Draw one cycle of a sine wave with amplitude 4 on graph paper. Take 12 equally spaced samples, quantize each with L = 8 levels between -4 and +4, and write the 3-bit codes. Then compute the bit rate if this sine had a frequency of 1 kHz and you sampled 12 times per cycle.

quiz.q: A signal has a highest frequency of 5 kHz. What is its Nyquist sampling rate?
quiz.explain: The Nyquist rate is 2 fmax = 2 x 5 kHz = 10,000 samples per second.

quiz.q: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz without filtering. At what frequency does its alias appear?
quiz.explain: Sampled below its Nyquist rate, the tone appears at fs - f = 10 - 7 = 3 kHz.

quiz.q: What is the approximate SQNR of 8-bit uniform PCM for a full-scale sine wave?
Telephone PCM samples 8,000 times per second with 8 bits per sample. What is the bit rate?
What is the main purpose of companding (mu-law or A-law)?
options: To give quiet signals more quantization levels
quiz.explain: Companding boosts small values before uniform quantization, so quiet sounds get finer steps.

lessons.title: Delta Modulation and Transmission Modes
lessons.content:
Imagine you are guiding a friend who is blindfolded, walking up and down the stairs of an old building in Puran Dhaka. You cannot tell him the exact floor every moment. Instead, every second you shout only one word: up or down. He takes one step each time. As long as you shout often enough, he follows you closely. This one-word-at-a-time trick is the heart of delta modulation. In this lesson we meet delta modulation and its cousins, and then we look at how bits actually travel on wires: side by side in parallel, or one after another in serial.

From PCM to delta modulation: In lesson 9, PCM sent n bits for every sample, for example 8 bits, describing the full value. But neighbouring samples of a voice signal are usually very close to each other. So why send the whole value again and again? Delta modulation, DM, sends only the change, and it uses just one bit per sample. A 1 means the signal went up, a 0 means it went down. It is the simplest possible analog-to-digital method.

How DM works: Both sender and receiver keep a staircase signal, a running guess of the analog value. At each sampling moment, the sender compares the real input with the staircase. If the input is higher, it sends 1 and the staircase climbs by a fixed step size delta. If the input is lower or equal, it sends 0 and the staircase drops by delta. The receiver starts from the same value and moves its own staircase up or down by delta for each bit it receives, then smooths it with a low-pass filter. The bit rate of DM is simply the sampling rate: N = fs x 1.

Worked example, DM: Let delta = 1 V, the staircase start at 0, and the samples be 0.4, 1.7, 2.9, 3.2, 2.6, 1.1 and 0.8 V. Sample 0.4 is above 0, so send 1, staircase becomes 1. Sample 1.7 is above 1: send 1, staircase 2. Sample 2.9 is above 2: send 1, staircase 3. Sample 3.2 is above 3: send 1, staircase 4. Sample 2.6 is below 4: send 0, staircase 3. Sample 1.1 is below 3: send 0, staircase 2. Sample 0.8 is below 2: send 0, staircase 1. The transmitted bits are 1111000, and the receiver's staircase 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1 roughly follows the hill shape of the input.

Slope overload: What if the input climbs faster than the staircase can? The staircase can rise at most delta per sample, so its fastest slope is delta x fs volts per second. If the signal rises faster than that, the staircase falls behind, sending 1, 1, 1, 1 while still lagging. This error is called slope overload distortion. For example, if the input climbs 2.5 V per sample and delta = 1 V, after four samples the input is at 10 V but the staircase is only at 4 V.

Avoiding slope overload: For a sine wave A sin(2 pi f t), the steepest slope is 2 pi f A. To avoid slope overload we need delta x fs >= 2 pi f A. Worked example: a 1 kHz tone with amplitude 1 V, sampled at 64,000 samples per second, needs delta >= 2 pi x 1,000 x 1 / 64,000, which is about 0.098 V. So a step of about 0.1 V is just enough. If we only sampled at 32,000 per second with a 2 V amplitude, we would need delta of about 0.39 V. Faster sampling or bigger steps both help.

Granular noise: Big steps fix slope overload but create another problem. When the input is flat or changes slowly, the staircase cannot stay still; it must move every sample. So it keeps hunting around the true value: up, down, up, down. If the input stays at 2.0 V and the staircase is at 2, it goes 1, 2, 1, 2 and so on. This back-and-forth error is called granular noise, and it gets worse with a larger delta. So DM is caught in a tug of war: small delta means slope overload on steep parts, large delta means granular noise on flat parts.

Adaptive delta modulation: Adaptive DM, ADM, solves the tug of war by changing the step size on the fly. If the sender keeps sending the same bit several times in a row, like 1, 1, 1, the signal must be climbing fast, so the step grows. If the bits alternate, like 1, 0, 1, 0, the signal must be nearly flat, so the step shrinks. The receiver sees the same bits, so it can apply exactly the same rule and stay in step without any extra information. ADM gives much better quality at the same bit rate.

DPCM, the middle path: Differential PCM sits between PCM and DM. Like DM, it sends differences instead of full values. Like PCM, it uses several bits for each difference, not just one. The sender predicts the next sample from previous ones, often just using the last one, then quantizes and sends the prediction error. Since the errors are usually small, fewer bits are needed than in plain PCM. Many voice and image compression schemes build on this idea. We only need the idea here; compression in depth belongs to other courses.

Comparing PCM and DM: PCM uses n bits per sample at a rate just above the Nyquist rate. DM uses 1 bit per sample but usually needs a much higher sampling rate, often several times the Nyquist rate, to follow the signal. DM circuits are very simple and cheap, which made them attractive in early systems. PCM gives better quality for the same bit rate in most cases, which is why it became the standard for the telephone network.

Transmission modes, the question: Now we have bits, from a file, from PCM or from DM. How do they travel on the link? There are two big choices. Parallel transmission sends several bits at the same time over several wires. Serial transmission sends the bits one after another over a single path. Serial transmission itself comes in three flavours: asynchronous, synchronous and isochronous.

Parallel transmission: In parallel transmission, we use n wires to send n bits at once, usually 8 bits, one byte per clock tick. If each wire carries 1 Mbps, eight wires carry 8 Mbps. The advantage is speed for a given clock. The disadvantages are cost and distance: n wires plus ground are expensive, and over a long cable the bits on different wires arrive at slightly different times, a problem called skew. Old printer ports used parallel cables, and very short paths inside a computer, such as memory buses, still do.

Serial transmission: In serial transmission, bits go one at a time over a single wire pair or fibre. Inside each device, data usually lives in parallel form, so the sender needs a parallel-to-serial converter and the receiver a serial-to-parallel converter. These are simple shift registers. Because serial links have no skew between wires, they can run at very high speeds over long distances. That is why modern links like USB, SATA, Ethernet and PCI Express are serial; PCI Express even gangs several separate serial lanes instead of using a parallel bus.

Asynchronous transmission: In asynchronous serial transmission, the timing of each byte does not matter, but bits inside one byte must keep a known rhythm. Each byte is wrapped with a start bit, which is 0, and one or more stop bits, which are 1. Between bytes, the line rests at 1, and the gap can be any length. The receiver waits for the 1-to-0 change of the start bit, then samples the next bits using its own clock. Because it resynchronises on every start bit, small clock differences never grow big. Asynchronous here means not synchronised at the byte level; inside the byte, timing is still strict.

Efficiency of asynchronous: The extra start and stop bits cost capacity. The most common format, 8N1, has 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit, so each byte uses 10 bits and the efficiency is 8 / 10 = 80 percent. At 9,600 bps, that gives 9,600 / 10 = 960 characters per second, even with no gaps. With a parity bit and 2 stop bits, one byte uses 12 bits and the efficiency drops to 8 / 12, about 66.7 percent. Asynchronous transmission is cheap and simple, perfect for slow devices like a keyboard, a GPS module or a microcontroller's serial port.

Synchronous transmission: In synchronous transmission, bits are sent as a continuous stream without start and stop bits or gaps between bytes. The receiver must count bits to find byte boundaries, so bytes are grouped into frames that begin with a special pattern or flag. Sender and receiver stay in step using the transitions of the line code, like Manchester or 4B/5B from earlier lessons. The overhead is small: a frame of 1,000 data bytes with 8 bytes of header, flag and check has an efficiency of 1,000 / 1,008, about 99.2 percent. That is why fast links like Ethernet are synchronous. Framing is the topic of lessons 23 and 24.

Isochronous transmission: Some data needs not only correct bits but a steady arrival rate. For live audio and video, a frame that arrives late is as bad as a lost one. Isochronous transmission guarantees that data arrives at a fixed, regular rate, like one video frame every 40 ms. It is synchronous transmission with a timing promise for the whole stream. USB, for example, has an isochronous transfer type used by webcams and audio devices, which reserves bandwidth in every time slot.

Real-life example 1, a GPS and a microcontroller: When a student at a Dhaka university robotics club connects an Arduino board to a GPS module, they talk over a serial port, often at 9,600 bps in 8N1 format. Every character from the GPS, like the letters of a position message, travels as a start bit, eight data bits and a stop bit. If the GPS sends 500 characters per second, the link is used at 500 x 10 = 5,000 bps, about half its capacity. Since a byte can come at any time, asynchronous transmission is perfect here.

Real-life example 2, watching cricket live: When you watch a cricket match on BTV through a set-top box or stream it on your phone, the video and sound must arrive smoothly. The camera at the stadium converts sound with PCM-style sampling, then compresses it. The bits travel over synchronous links, like fibre and Ethernet, packed into large frames with tiny overhead. And at the receiving end, the player behaves isochronously: it plays frames at a fixed rate, using a buffer to hide jitter, so the batsman's shot looks smooth.

Common mistakes: In DM, students forget that the step moves on every sample, even when the input is flat; that is the source of granular noise. Mixing up slope overload, a big error on steep parts, with granular noise, a small error on flat parts, is common. In asynchronous transmission, the start bit is 0 and the stop bit is 1, not the other way round. And asynchronous does not mean no clock at all: each byte is timed by the receiver's own clock after the start bit. Remember too that the DM bit rate equals the sampling rate.

What exams ask: Typical questions: explain DM with a staircase diagram; encode a list of samples with DM given delta; state and use the slope overload condition delta x fs >= 2 pi f A; explain granular noise and how ADM fixes both problems; compare PCM, DM and DPCM; compare parallel and serial transmission; explain asynchronous framing and compute efficiency or characters per second; and compare synchronous with isochronous.

Recap: DM sends 1 bit per sample, moving a staircase up or down by delta. Too small a step causes slope overload; too big a step causes granular noise; ADM adapts the step. DPCM sends multi-bit differences. Parallel transmission sends many bits at once but suffers skew; serial sends one bit at a time and rules modern links. Asynchronous serial frames each byte with a start bit 0 and stop bit 1 (8N1 is 80 percent efficient), synchronous sends continuous frames, and isochronous adds a guaranteed steady rate.
key_points: Delta modulation sends 1 bit per sample: 1 moves the staircase up by delta, 0 moves it down; bit rate = fs.
Slope overload happens when the input rises faster than delta x fs; for a sine, avoid it with delta x fs >= 2 pi f A.
Granular noise is the up-down hunting of the staircase on flat parts; a larger delta makes it worse.
Adaptive DM grows the step during runs of equal bits and shrinks it when bits alternate.
DPCM sends multi-bit differences between a sample and its prediction.
Parallel transmission sends n bits at once over n wires but suffers skew; serial sends one bit at a time and needs shift registers.
Asynchronous: start bit 0, data, stop bit 1, gaps allowed; 8N1 efficiency is 8/10 = 80 percent.
Synchronous transmission sends continuous frames with tiny overhead; isochronous also guarantees a steady rate for real-time media.
lessons.tip: For DM questions, make a three-column table: sample, bit sent, staircase after. Fill it row by row, and only compare the new sample with the staircase value from the row above.
lessons.task: Draw a small hill-shaped curve on graph paper. Choose delta = 1 square and take a sample every square along the time axis. Encode it with DM, write the bit sequence, then redraw the staircase from the bits alone. Repeat with delta = 2 squares and compare where slope overload and granular noise appear.

quiz.q: How many bits does basic delta modulation send per sample?
quiz.explain: DM sends a single bit per sample: up or down.

quiz.q: What is the name of the error when the input rises faster than the DM staircase can follow?
quiz.explain: Slope overload happens when the signal slope exceeds delta x fs.

quiz.q: In asynchronous transmission with 8N1 format, what is the efficiency?
quiz.explain: Each byte uses 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10 bits, so 8/10 = 80 percent.

quiz.q: Why are long-distance high-speed links serial rather than parallel?
options: Parallel wires suffer skew and cost more
quiz.explain: Bits on parallel wires arrive at slightly different times (skew), and many wires are expensive.

quiz.q: Which transmission mode guarantees a fixed, steady arrival rate for live audio and video?
quiz.explain: Isochronous transmission adds a guaranteed regular timing to synchronous transmission.

lessons.title: Digital-to-Analog Conversion I: ASK, FSK and PSK
lessons.content:
Imagine you and your friend live on opposite rooftops in Old Dhaka at night. You want to send her a secret message in binary, but you only have a torch. You could switch the torch on for 1 and off for 0. You could use a red torch for 1 and a green torch for 0. Or you could wave the torch in one direction for 1 and flip the direction for 0. Three different tricks, one idea: take a steady signal that can travel far, and change one of its features to carry your bits. This lesson covers those three tricks: ASK, FSK and PSK.

Why convert digital to analog at all: In lesson 07 and 08 we sent bits straight onto a wire as voltage levels (line coding). That works on a short copper cable, which is a low-pass channel: it carries frequencies from almost 0 Hz upward. But many channels are band-pass. A telephone line passes roughly 300 to 3400 Hz. A radio channel is a narrow slice far up the spectrum, for example around 2.4 GHz for Wi-Fi. A low-pass digital signal simply does not fit in such a slice. So we take a sine wave that already sits in the allowed band and modulate it with our data. This is digital-to-analog conversion, also called digital modulation or passband transmission.

The carrier signal: The steady sine wave is called the carrier. Before any data arrives, the transmitter produces a pure sine wave s(t) = A sin(2 pi f t + phase) at the carrier frequency fc. The receiver is tuned to that frequency. Data is then carried by changing, or modulating, the carrier. A sine wave has exactly three knobs: amplitude A, frequency f and phase. Turn the amplitude knob and you get Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK). Turn the frequency knob and you get Frequency Shift Keying (FSK). Turn the phase knob and you get Phase Shift Keying (PSK). Turn amplitude and phase together and you get QAM, which is lesson 12.

Data element versus signal element: A data element is one bit. A signal element is one piece of the modulated signal that the receiver can tell apart, for example one burst of carrier with a certain amplitude. Let r be the number of data elements carried by one signal element. If the signal has L distinguishable levels or states, then r = log2 L. The bit rate N (bits per second) and the baud or signal rate S (signal elements per second) are linked by S = N / r. With two states, r = 1 and baud equals bit rate. With four states, r = 2 and the baud is half the bit rate.

The d factor: Real transmitters do not send perfect rectangular bursts. They shape and filter the signal, and the amount of filtering is described by a factor d, which lies between 0 and 1. A value of 0 is the ideal, tightest case; a value near 1 means more extra bandwidth. Most textbook bandwidth formulas for digital modulation look like B = (1 + d) x S. Read it like this: the minimum bandwidth equals the baud rate, and real filtering adds a fraction d on top.

Amplitude Shift Keying: In ASK the carrier frequency and phase stay fixed and the amplitude changes with the data. In binary ASK (BASK) there are two amplitudes, one for bit 1 and one for bit 0. The receiver measures how strong the carrier is during each bit time and decides. ASK is easy to build: an oscillator plus a switch or a multiplier is enough. Its bandwidth is B = (1 + d) x S, centred on fc. So the spectrum sits from fc - B/2 to fc + B/2.

On-Off Keying: The most common kind of binary ASK sets one of the amplitudes to zero. Bit 1 sends the carrier, bit 0 sends nothing. This is On-Off Keying (OOK), the rooftop torch from our opening. OOK saves power because the transmitter is silent for every 0. It is used in cheap remote controls for car alarms and garage doors, in simple RFID tags, and, in light form, in many fibre optic links where a laser is switched on and off. The old Morse code telegraph radio was also OOK: carrier on for dots and dashes, carrier off for the gaps.

The weakness of ASK: Noise mostly adds to amplitude. Lightning, a motor starting, or a neighbour's microwave oven add random spikes to the received signal. Because ASK hides the data in the amplitude, noise attacks it directly. Attenuation also changes the amplitude, so the receiver needs a good threshold that adapts as the signal fades. That is why ASK alone is rarely used for fast radio links, while it remains popular where cost matters more than speed.

Worked example, ASK: We have a band of 100 kHz, from 200 kHz to 300 kHz, and we choose d = 1. What carrier frequency and bit rate can binary ASK use? The carrier sits in the middle: fc = (200 + 300) / 2 = 250 kHz. From B = (1 + d) S we get S = B / (1 + d) = 100 / 2 = 50 kbaud. Binary ASK has r = 1, so the bit rate is also 50 kbps. A second quick one: an ASK signal at 2000 baud with d = 0.5 needs B = 1.5 x 2000 = 3000 Hz.

Frequency Shift Keying: In FSK the amplitude and phase stay fixed and the frequency changes. Binary FSK (BFSK) uses two carrier frequencies, f1 for bit 1 and f2 for bit 0. You can think of it as two ASK signals side by side: when one is on, the other is off. The receiver uses two filters, one tuned to f1 and one to f2, and checks which filter has more energy in each bit time. Because the data lives in frequency, not in amplitude, FSK resists amplitude noise much better than ASK, and the receiver does not need to know the exact signal strength.

BFSK bandwidth: Each of the two carriers needs (1 + d) S of bandwidth, like ASK. If the two carrier frequencies are separated by 2 delta f (so f1 = fc + delta f and f2 = fc - delta f), the total bandwidth is B = (1 + d) x S + 2 delta f. The extra 2 delta f is the price of FSK: the two frequencies must be far enough apart for the receiver filters to tell them apart. A common design rule is that 2 delta f should be at least S, so that the two spectra do not overlap much.

Worked example, BFSK: Take the same band of 100 kHz from 200 to 300 kHz, d = 1, and put the two carriers 50 kHz apart, at f1 = 275 kHz and f2 = 225 kHz. Then 2 delta f = 50 kHz and the middle is still fc = 250 kHz. From 100 = (1 + 1) S + 50 we get 2S = 50, so S = 25 kbaud, and with r = 1 the bit rate is 25 kbps. Compare with ASK in the same band: 50 kbps. FSK gave us half the speed in exchange for better noise immunity. That trade between speed, bandwidth and robustness is the heart of this whole topic.

Multilevel FSK and where FSK lives: MFSK uses more than two frequencies, for example 4 or 8, so each signal element carries 2 or 3 bits. The bandwidth grows because you need more separated tones, roughly L x S for L tones when they are spaced S apart and d = 0. Old dial-up modems (the Bell 103 standard at 300 bps) used FSK. Caller ID on landline phones uses FSK bursts between rings. Classic Bluetooth uses a smooth form of FSK called GFSK.

Phase Shift Keying: In PSK the amplitude and frequency stay fixed and the phase changes. In binary PSK (BPSK) bit 1 is sent as the carrier with phase 0 degrees and bit 0 as the carrier with phase 180 degrees, which is the same wave turned upside down. Mathematically bit 1 is +A sin(2 pi fc t) and bit 0 is -A sin(2 pi fc t). The receiver multiplies the incoming wave by its own copy of the carrier and looks at the sign of the result: positive means 1, negative means 0. The two signal states are as far apart as they can possibly be for a given power, which makes BPSK the most noise-robust of the three basic schemes.

BPSK bandwidth and cost: Each BPSK signal element is a carrier burst with amplitude +A or -A, so its spectrum looks like binary ASK: B = (1 + d) x S, the same as ASK and less than FSK. Example: a 1 Mbps BPSK link with ideal filtering (d = 0) needs 1 MHz of bandwidth. The cost is a more complex receiver. It must recover the exact phase of the carrier, which needs a phase locked loop or similar circuit. Satellites, deep space probes and GPS use BPSK or close relatives for exactly this reason: the signal arrives incredibly weak and every bit of noise immunity counts.

Differential PSK: Recovering the absolute phase is hard, and if the receiver locks 180 degrees wrong, every bit is inverted. Differential PSK (DPSK) avoids this by encoding data in the change of phase, not the phase itself. For example, bit 0 means keep the same phase as the previous element and bit 1 means flip by 180 degrees. The receiver only compares each element with the one before. This is the same idea as NRZ-I and differential Manchester from lesson 07: information in transitions, not in absolute levels.

Comparing ASK, FSK and PSK: For the same bit rate and d, ASK and BPSK need the same bandwidth, (1 + d) S, while BFSK needs an extra 2 delta f. For noise resistance, PSK is best, FSK is good and ASK is weakest. For cost and simplicity, ASK is cheapest, FSK is simple, and PSK needs careful carrier recovery. For power, OOK saves energy on zeros, while FSK and PSK have constant amplitude, which lets the transmitter run its amplifier efficiently near full power.

Real-life example 1, a car remote in Dhaka: When your uncle presses the lock button on his car key in a Gulshan parking lot, the key fob sends a short code using OOK on a carrier around 315 or 433 MHz, depending on the model. A tiny circuit switches the carrier on and off following the bits of the code. The receiver in the car only needs to detect carrier present or absent. It is cheap, uses almost no battery, and range is a few tens of metres, which is all you need.

Real-life example 2, from GPS to your phone: The GPS satellites above Bangladesh send their navigation data with BPSK, combined with spreading codes we will meet in lesson 16. The signal reaching your phone in a rickshaw on Mirpur Road is far weaker than the background noise, yet the phone can still decode it, because BPSK places its two states as far apart as possible and the receiver patiently tracks the phase. The same kind of choice shows up in the Bangabandhu-1 satellite links: when the signal is weak, simple robust schemes like BPSK and QPSK are preferred over dense ones.

Common mistakes: First, mixing up bit rate and baud. In binary ASK, FSK and BPSK they are equal, but only because r = 1. Second, forgetting the 2 delta f term in BFSK bandwidth, or using delta f instead of 2 delta f. Third, saying FSK changes amplitude: in FSK amplitude is constant. Fourth, thinking BPSK needs twice the bandwidth of ASK: it needs the same. Fifth, putting the ASK carrier at the band edge instead of the middle. Draw the band, mark both edges, and put fc in the centre.

What exams ask: Typical questions give a band (start and end frequency) plus d and ask for fc, baud and bit rate for ASK or BFSK. Others give a bit stream like 1011 and ask you to sketch ASK, OOK, BFSK and BPSK waveforms, one under the other. For the sketch, keep the bit times equal, keep the amplitude constant for FSK and PSK, draw tighter waves for the higher frequency in FSK, and flip the wave at every change between 0 and 1 in BPSK.

Recap: Digital-to-analog conversion puts bits onto a sine carrier so they fit band-pass channels. A sine wave has three knobs, and changing each gives ASK, FSK or PSK. S = N / r and B = (1 + d) S for ASK and PSK, with an extra 2 delta f for BFSK. In the next lesson we combine phase and amplitude to send many bits per symbol with QPSK and QAM, the tricks behind fast Wi-Fi and 4G.
key_points: Digital-to-analog conversion modulates a sine carrier so digital data fits a band-pass channel like a phone line or a radio band.
A carrier has three knobs: amplitude (ASK), frequency (FSK) and phase (PSK).
Baud S = N / r, where r = log2 L bits per signal element; in binary ASK, FSK and BPSK, r = 1 so baud equals bit rate.
ASK and BPSK bandwidth: B = (1 + d) S, with 0 <= d <= 1 set by filtering.
BFSK bandwidth: B = (1 + d) S + 2 delta f, where 2 delta f is the gap between the two carriers.
OOK is ASK with one amplitude zero: cheap and power saving, used in remotes and fibre.
Noise robustness: PSK best, FSK good, ASK weakest; PSK needs carrier phase recovery, DPSK avoids absolute phase.
lessons.tip: Learn the three schemes as one picture: draw the same bit stream four times (ASK, OOK, BFSK, BPSK) under each other on one page. If you can draw that page from memory and write B = (1 + d) S beside it, half the exam questions on this topic are already solved.
lessons.task: On paper, take the bits 1 0 1 1 0 and draw ASK, OOK, BFSK and BPSK waveforms with two cycles per bit. Then solve: a band runs from 400 kHz to 500 kHz, d = 0.25. Find fc and the bit rate for binary ASK, and for BFSK with carriers 40 kHz apart. (Answers: fc = 450 kHz, 80 kbps for ASK; 48 kbps for BFSK.)

quiz.q: Which property of the carrier does FSK change to carry data?
quiz.explain: FSK keeps amplitude and phase fixed and switches between carrier frequencies.

quiz.q: A band of 100 kHz runs from 200 to 300 kHz and d = 1. What is the bit rate of binary ASK?
quiz.explain: S = B / (1 + d) = 100 / 2 = 50 kbaud, and binary ASK has r = 1, so 50 kbps.

quiz.q: Why is ASK the most sensitive to noise of the three basic schemes?
options: Its data is in the amplitude, which noise directly changes
It needs a phase locked loop
quiz.explain: Noise mostly adds to amplitude, and ASK stores the bits in amplitude.

quiz.q: For BFSK with d = 1, baud 20 kbaud and carriers 30 kHz apart, what bandwidth is needed?
quiz.explain: B = (1 + d) S + 2 delta f = 2 x 20 + 30 = 70 kHz.

quiz.q: In BPSK, bits 1 and 0 are sent as carriers that differ in phase by
quiz.explain: BPSK uses 0 and 180 degrees, the same wave and its upside-down copy, which are as far apart as possible.

lessons.title: Digital-to-Analog Conversion II: QPSK, Constellations and QAM
lessons.content:
Think of a rickshaw that is allowed to make only a fixed number of trips per hour on a busy Dhaka road. If each trip carries one passenger, you move very few people. The road will not give you more trips, so the only way to move more people is to fit more passengers into each trip. A radio channel works the same way. Its bandwidth fixes how many symbols per second (the baud) you can send. To send more bits per second, you must pack more bits into every symbol. That packing trick is what this lesson is about: QPSK, constellation diagrams and QAM.

The problem from lesson 11: In binary ASK, FSK and BPSK, every signal element carries exactly one bit, so the bit rate equals the baud. We also saw that the bandwidth is about B = (1 + d) S. So with a fixed band, the baud S is fixed, and so is the bit rate. The way out is to give each symbol more possible states. With M distinguishable states, each symbol carries r = log2 M bits, and the bit rate becomes N = S x log2 M. Four states give 2 bits per symbol, 16 states give 4 bits, 64 states give 6 bits, 256 states give 8 bits.

Two carriers in one band: Here is the clever part. A sine wave and a cosine wave at the same frequency are 90 degrees apart. They are called orthogonal, which means a receiver can separate them perfectly even though they occupy the same band at the same time. The cosine part is called the in-phase or I carrier, and the sine part is called the quadrature or Q carrier. So one band can carry two independent streams of symbols, one on I and one on Q, without needing more bandwidth. Almost every modern digital radio is built around this I and Q idea.

QPSK: Quadrature PSK puts one BPSK signal on the I carrier and another on the Q carrier. Each one carries one bit, so together a symbol carries 2 bits. When you add the two waves, the result is a single carrier with constant amplitude and one of four phases, usually 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees. For example, with a common mapping, 11 gives 45 degrees, 01 gives 135, 00 gives 225 and 10 gives 315. The amplitude never changes, only the phase, so QPSK is still a PSK scheme, just with four phases instead of two.

QPSK bandwidth: Because each half (I or Q) is just a BPSK signal at half the bit rate, QPSK sends twice the bits of BPSK in the same bandwidth. The formula stays B = (1 + d) x S, but now S = N / 2. Worked example: a link must carry 12 Mbps using QPSK with ideal filtering, d = 0. Then S = 12 / 2 = 6 Mbaud and B = (1 + 0) x 6 = 6 MHz. BPSK would need 12 MHz for the same bit rate. That doubling of efficiency for almost no cost in robustness is why QPSK is a favourite for satellite links and for the weak edge of a mobile cell.

Constellation diagrams: Drawing waveforms for four or sixteen states quickly becomes messy. Engineers use a much neater picture called a constellation diagram. Draw two axes: the horizontal axis is the I component and the vertical axis is the Q component. Each possible symbol becomes a single dot. The distance of the dot from the centre is the amplitude of the signal element, and the angle from the positive I axis is its phase. So one dot tells you everything about one signal element, and the whole set of dots is the alphabet of the modulation scheme.

Reading simple constellations: Binary ASK with OOK has two dots on the I axis: one at the centre (amplitude 0) and one at A. BPSK has two dots at +A and -A on the I axis, as far apart as possible for that power. QPSK has four dots on a circle, one in each quadrant at 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees. 8-PSK has eight dots equally spaced around the same circle, 45 degrees apart, carrying 3 bits each. If you can draw these four pictures, you can read any constellation in an exam.

Why not keep adding phases: You could try 16-PSK, with 16 dots around one circle. The trouble is crowding. With the average energy fixed at 1, the distance between neighbouring dots is 1.41 for QPSK, 0.77 for 8-PSK and only 0.39 for 16-PSK. The receiver decides which dot was sent by picking the nearest one, so when dots are close, a little noise pushes the received point into the wrong neighbour. On a circle, all dots compete for the same thin ring. We can use the inside of the circle too, and that leads to QAM.

QAM: Quadrature Amplitude Modulation changes both amplitude and phase. In constellation terms, the dots are no longer limited to one circle; they are spread over a grid in the I-Q plane. Technically, QAM puts a multilevel ASK signal on the I carrier and another multilevel ASK signal on the Q carrier, then adds them. Each dot is one combination of an I level and a Q level. QPSK is actually the simplest QAM, called 4-QAM: two levels on I, two levels on Q, four dots.

16-QAM: Use four levels, -3, -1, +1 and +3, on each axis. That gives 4 x 4 = 16 dots in a square grid, so each symbol carries log2 16 = 4 bits. Look at the dots carefully: the four inner ones, such as (1, 1), have amplitude square root of 2, about 1.41. The four corners, such as (3, 3), have amplitude square root of 18, about 4.24. The eight edge dots, such as (1, 3), have amplitude square root of 10, about 3.16. So 16-QAM uses 3 different amplitudes and 12 different phases. With the same average energy, its closest dots are about 0.63 apart, much better than the 0.39 of 16-PSK. That is why real systems use 16-QAM and not 16-PSK.

Bigger QAM: 64-QAM uses 8 levels per axis, 8 x 8 = 64 dots, 6 bits per symbol. 256-QAM uses 16 levels per axis, 256 dots, 8 bits per symbol. 1024-QAM uses 32 levels per axis, 10 bits per symbol, and newer Wi-Fi goes even higher. Each step packs more bits into a symbol, but the dots get closer together for the same power, so each step needs a cleaner signal. A useful rule: for square QAM, every extra 2 bits per symbol (multiplying M by 4) needs roughly 6 dB more signal-to-noise ratio for the same error rate.

Bit rate versus baud, worked examples: The key formula is N = S x log2 M. Example 1: a 16-QAM signal at 1000 baud carries 1000 x 4 = 4000 bps. Example 2: a 64-QAM signal must carry 24 kbps; the baud is 24000 / 6 = 4000 baud. Example 3: a modem sends 20 Mbaud with 256-QAM; the bit rate is 20 x 8 = 160 Mbps. Notice the pattern: the baud is the slow, physical rate; the bit rate is the baud multiplied by how many bits each symbol holds. When a question gives you the bit rate and asks for bandwidth, always convert to baud first.

Bandwidth worked example: A channel is 1 MHz wide and the filter factor is d = 0.25. The maximum baud is S = B / (1 + d) = 1,000,000 / 1.25 = 800 kbaud. With QPSK the bit rate is 800 k x 2 = 1.6 Mbps. With 16-QAM it is 800 k x 4 = 3.2 Mbps. With 64-QAM it is 800 k x 6 = 4.8 Mbps. Same bandwidth, three times the speed of QPSK, but only if the signal is clean enough. Shannon from lesson 05 still sets the ceiling: no constellation can beat B log2(1 + SNR), so dense QAM is how we climb closer to that ceiling, not how we break it.

Gray coding: Which bit pattern goes to which dot? A smart choice is Gray coding: neighbouring dots differ in exactly one bit. Then the most common error, noise pushing the point into a neighbouring dot, damages only one bit out of four in 16-QAM, instead of possibly two or three. For QPSK, the order 11, 01, 00, 10 around the circle is Gray coded: each step changes one bit. In 16-QAM, Gray coding is done separately on each axis, with the levels -3, -1, +1, +3 labelled 00, 01, 11, 10.

Noise on the constellation: If you capture a real received signal and plot every symbol as a dot, you do not see perfect points. You see little fuzzy clouds around each ideal dot. The receiver draws decision regions, boxes or slices around each ideal dot, and decides that whatever lands in a region was that symbol. When noise grows, the clouds swell, start crossing region borders, and errors begin. Engineers measure how far the received points sit from their ideal spots with a number called error vector magnitude (EVM). A tight constellation means a healthy link.

Adaptive modulation: Because dense QAM needs a clean signal and simple QPSK survives a noisy one, modern systems change the scheme on the fly. Wi-Fi, 4G LTE and 5G measure the channel quality many times a second and pick a modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to match. Close to the transmitter, with a strong clean signal, they use 64-QAM, 256-QAM or higher. Far away or behind thick walls, they fall back to 16-QAM or QPSK. The link never stops working; it just gets slower. Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) tops out at 256-QAM, Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) adds 1024-QAM, and Wi-Fi 7 adds 4096-QAM.

Real-life example 1, 4G in Dhaka: Suppose you are watching a cricket match on your phone using Grameenphone or Robi 4G. On the rooftop near the tower, the signal-to-noise ratio is high, so the network uses 64-QAM or 256-QAM and the video plays in HD. Then you walk down to a basement shop in a New Market building. The signal weakens and noise wins more often, so the network shifts down to 16-QAM and then QPSK. The bars may still show a signal, but the speed drops and the video falls to a lower quality. Nothing is broken: the phone simply has fewer bits per symbol.

Real-life example 2, home Wi-Fi: Put your laptop right next to your home Wi-Fi router and check the link rate; it may show several hundred Mbps because the router is using 256-QAM or 1024-QAM. Now go two rooms away, behind a concrete wall. The link rate drops, often by half or more. The channel width and baud are the same; the router has simply chosen a lower QAM order and stronger error coding so the data still arrives. Cable broadband uses the same idea: DOCSIS cable modems typically use 64-QAM or 256-QAM on their downstream channels.

Common mistakes: First, thinking QPSK changes amplitude: it does not, all four dots lie on one circle. Second, forgetting to divide by log2 M when converting bit rate to baud, especially for 64-QAM (6 bits) and 256-QAM (8 bits). Third, assuming a 16-point constellation means 16 bits per symbol; it means 4 bits. Fourth, saying higher QAM needs more bandwidth: for the same baud it needs the same bandwidth, it needs more SNR. Fifth, mixing up the axes: distance from the centre is amplitude, angle is phase.

What exams ask: Expect questions like: draw the constellation of BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK and 16-QAM; find the bit rate of a 16-QAM signal at a given baud; find the baud and bandwidth for a given bit rate and d; count how many amplitudes and phases a given constellation uses; explain why QAM beats PSK at high orders; or explain why a phone gets slower far from the tower. For the counting questions, list the dots in one quadrant, find their distances and angles, then multiply angles by four.

Recap: To send more bits through a fixed band, put more bits into each symbol: N = S x log2 M and B = (1 + d) S. QPSK uses the I and Q carriers to send 2 bits per symbol at the bandwidth of BPSK. Constellation diagrams show each symbol as a dot: distance is amplitude, angle is phase. QAM spreads dots over a grid, which keeps them further apart than PSK, so 16-, 64-, 256- and 1024-QAM power modern Wi-Fi and 4G. Denser constellations need cleaner signals, so systems adapt the order to the channel. Next we turn to analog-to-analog modulation: AM, FM and PM radio.
key_points: With M states per symbol, each symbol carries log2 M bits, and bit rate N = S x log2 M.
I (cosine) and Q (sine) carriers are orthogonal, so two streams share one band.
QPSK = BPSK on I + BPSK on Q: 4 phases, constant amplitude, 2 bits per symbol, B = (1 + d) N/2.
A constellation diagram plots each symbol as a dot: distance from centre = amplitude, angle = phase.
16-QAM uses a 4 x 4 grid: 4 bits per symbol, 3 amplitudes and 12 phases; 64-QAM 6 bits, 256-QAM 8 bits.
QAM keeps dots further apart than PSK at the same power, so it is preferred above 8 states.
Denser QAM needs higher SNR (about 6 dB more per extra 2 bits); Wi-Fi and 4G adapt the order to signal quality.
Gray coding makes neighbouring dots differ by one bit, so a typical symbol error causes one bit error.
lessons.tip: Always do these questions in two steps: first turn everything into baud with S = N / log2 M, then use B = (1 + d) S. Most wrong answers come from skipping the first step.
lessons.task: On graph paper, draw the 16-QAM constellation with levels -3, -1, 1, 3 on both axes. Label each axis with the Gray code 00, 01, 11, 10 and write the 4-bit label on every dot. Then measure: how many different distances from the centre and how many different angles do you get? (You should find 3 and 12.) Bonus: open your phone's Wi-Fi details next to the router and two rooms away and compare the link speeds.

quiz.q: How many bits does each symbol carry in 64-QAM?
quiz.explain: log2 64 = 6 bits per symbol.

quiz.q: A 16-QAM signal runs at 1000 baud. What is its bit rate?
quiz.explain: N = S x log2 M = 1000 x 4 = 4000 bps.

quiz.q: On a constellation diagram, what does the distance of a dot from the centre show?
quiz.explain: Distance from the origin is amplitude; the angle from the I axis is phase.

quiz.q: A 12 Mbps QPSK link uses d = 0. What bandwidth does it need?
quiz.explain: S = 12 / 2 = 6 Mbaud and B = (1 + 0) x 6 = 6 MHz.

quiz.q: Why does a phone switch from 256-QAM to QPSK when the signal gets weak?
options: Dense constellations need a high SNR, so with noise QPSK keeps errors low
QPSK sends more bits per symbol
quiz.explain: Closer dots are easily confused under noise; QPSK's widely spaced dots survive, at a lower bit rate.

lessons.title: Analog-to-Analog Conversion: AM, FM and PM
lessons.content:
Turn on the radio in a CNG auto-rickshaw stuck in Dhaka traffic and the driver flicks between stations: Radio Foorti on 88.0, Radio Today on 89.6, a news bulletin, a cricket commentary. Every one of those stations is sending a human voice or a song, which is an analog signal with frequencies from a few tens of hertz to about 15 kHz. Yet each one arrives on a different number near 90 MHz, and they do not mix into noise. How does a low-frequency voice ride up to 89.6 MHz and come back down again inside a small radio? The answer is analog-to-analog conversion, better known as analog modulation: AM, FM and PM.

What it is: In analog-to-analog conversion, both the message and the carrier are analog. The message m(t) is a voice, music or any other continuous signal. The carrier is a high-frequency sine wave, Ac cos(2 pi fc t). We change one of the carrier's three knobs in proportion to the message: amplitude gives AM, frequency gives FM, phase gives PM. It is the same knob idea as ASK, FSK and PSK in lesson 11, except the knob now moves smoothly with the message instead of jumping between a few fixed values.

Why modulate at all, reason 1, antenna size: An antenna works well when it is around a quarter or half of the wavelength of the signal. Wavelength is c / f. For a 1 kHz audio tone, the wavelength is 300,000,000 / 1,000 = 300 km, so a quarter-wave antenna would be 75 km long. Impossible. At 89.6 MHz the wavelength is about 3.35 m, so a quarter-wave antenna is about 84 cm, the size of the telescopic antenna on a pocket radio. Moving the message up in frequency makes antennas practical.

Reason 2, sharing the air: All voices and songs use roughly the same low frequencies. If every station sent its audio directly, they would all pile on top of each other and nobody could separate them. Modulation moves each station to its own carrier frequency, so the stations sit side by side in the spectrum. The receiver tunes to one carrier and ignores the rest. This is frequency division multiplexing, which we study properly in lesson 14. Reason 3: the government regulator (BTRC in Bangladesh) assigns specific bands for specific services, and modulation is how you place your signal inside the band you were given.

Amplitude Modulation: In AM the amplitude of the carrier follows the message, while the frequency and phase stay fixed. For a single-tone message the AM signal is s(t) = Ac [1 + m cos(2 pi fm t)] cos(2 pi fc t). The outline of the peaks, called the envelope, has exactly the shape of the message. The receiver can recover the message with a very simple circuit, an envelope detector, which is basically a diode, a capacitor and a resistor. That simplicity is why AM was the first broadcast radio technology and why cheap AM sets have existed for a hundred years.

The modulation index: The number m is the modulation index, m = Am / Ac, the ratio of the message amplitude to the carrier amplitude. It must stay between 0 and 1. If m goes above 1, the envelope crosses zero and gets folded, called overmodulation, and the envelope detector produces badly distorted sound. You can measure m on an oscilloscope: m = (Vmax - Vmin) / (Vmax + Vmin), where Vmax and Vmin are the largest and smallest envelope heights. Example: Vmax = 15 V and Vmin = 5 V gives m = 10 / 20 = 0.5.

AM bandwidth: When you multiply out the AM formula, you find three frequencies: the carrier fc, the upper side frequency fc + fm and the lower side frequency fc - fm. For a real message with bandwidth B (all frequencies from near 0 to B), these become an upper sideband from fc to fc + B and a lower sideband from fc - B to fc. So the AM bandwidth is B_AM = 2B. Example: a carrier at 1000 kHz modulated by a 5 kHz tone has components at 995, 1000 and 1005 kHz, and the whole signal needs 10 kHz. Voice limited to 4 kHz needs 8 kHz of AM bandwidth.

AM power: The carrier itself carries no information; all the information is in the sidebands. The total power is Pt = Pc (1 + m^2 / 2), where Pc is the carrier power. Worked example: Pc = 100 W and m = 0.5 give Pt = 100 x (1 + 0.125) = 112.5 W, and only 12.5 W, about 11 percent, is in the sidebands. Even at the best case m = 1, Pt = 150 W and just one third of the power carries the message. AM is simple but wasteful with power.

Variants of AM: Because the carrier wastes power and the two sidebands carry the same information, engineers made thinner versions. Double sideband suppressed carrier (DSB-SC) removes the carrier and keeps both sidebands, bandwidth still 2B. Single sideband (SSB) keeps only one sideband, so its bandwidth is just B, half of AM, and it is popular with amateur and marine radio for long-distance voice. Vestigial sideband (VSB) keeps one sideband plus a small slice of the other; analog television used VSB for its picture signal because a clean SSB filter for video was too hard to build.

The AM broadcast band: Medium wave AM radio uses roughly 530 to 1700 kHz. Audio on AM is limited to about 5 kHz, so each station needs about 10 kHz. In the Americas stations are spaced 10 kHz apart, while in Asia, including Bangladesh, the spacing is 9 kHz. Bangladesh Betar still broadcasts on medium wave AM, and at night medium wave signals can bend around the earth via the ionosphere, so you can sometimes hear stations from far away. The weak point of AM is noise: lightning and electrical sparks add directly to the amplitude, which is why AM crackles during a storm.

Frequency Modulation: In FM the amplitude stays constant and the instantaneous frequency of the carrier moves up and down with the message. When the message voltage is high, the frequency goes above fc; when it is low, the frequency goes below fc. The largest swing away from fc is the peak frequency deviation, delta f, and it is proportional to the peak message amplitude. The loudness of the sound sets how far the frequency swings; the pitch of the sound sets how fast it swings. The modulation index for FM is beta = delta f / fm, which, unlike AM's m, can be larger than 1.

FM bandwidth and Carson's rule: Mathematically an FM signal has infinitely many sidebands, but most of the power lives within a practical band given by Carson's rule: B_FM = 2 (delta f + B), where B is the message bandwidth. The same rule is often written B_FM = 2 (1 + beta) B. Worked example: broadcast FM uses delta f = 75 kHz and audio up to 15 kHz, so B_FM = 2 x (75 + 15) = 180 kHz, with beta = 75 / 15 = 5. Stations are given 200 kHz each, which leaves a small guard space. A second example: delta f = 50 kHz and B = 10 kHz give 2 x 60 = 120 kHz.

Why FM sounds better: Since the information is in the frequency, the receiver can clip the amplitude flat with a limiter, throwing away most amplitude noise. FM also carries audio up to 15 kHz instead of AM's 5 kHz, so music sounds fuller. FM has a capture effect too: if two stations share a frequency, the receiver locks onto the stronger one instead of mixing them. The price is bandwidth: 200 kHz per FM station versus about 10 kHz per AM station, which is why FM lives much higher in the spectrum where there is room.

The FM broadcast band: FM radio uses 88 to 108 MHz. With 200 kHz per station, 20 MHz divided by 0.2 MHz gives room for 100 channels, though nearby cities avoid using neighbouring channels so they do not interfere. These frequencies travel mainly by line of sight, so an FM station covers a city and its surroundings, around 50 to 100 km depending on tower height and power, not a whole country. That is why a Dhaka station that wants listeners in Chattogram or Sylhet needs separate transmitters in those cities.

Phase Modulation: In PM the amplitude stays constant and the phase of the carrier shifts in proportion to the message. PM and FM are close cousins. Frequency is the rate of change of phase, so FM with message m(t) is the same as PM with the integral of m(t), and PM with m(t) is FM with the derivative of m(t). On an oscilloscope FM and PM look almost the same. PM bandwidth is also B_PM = 2 (1 + beta) B, where beta is now the PM index. PM is less common as a broadcast method, but some FM transmitters are built using phase modulators, and digital PSK from lesson 11 is the switched form of PM.

Comparing AM, FM and PM: AM needs the least bandwidth (2B, or B for SSB) and the simplest receiver, but it is noisy and wastes power in the carrier. FM and PM use much more bandwidth but have constant amplitude, resist noise, and let the transmitter amplifier run efficiently. A useful summary: AM trades quality for cheapness and narrow bandwidth; FM trades bandwidth for quality. The same trade between bandwidth, power and noise appeared with ASK, FSK and PSK; analog and digital modulation obey the same physics.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka FM station: Radio Today broadcasts on 89.6 MHz. In the studio, a presenter's voice and the music are mixed into an audio signal up to 15 kHz. The transmitter makes a carrier at 89.6 MHz and swings its frequency up to 75 kHz either side in step with the audio. By Carson's rule the signal occupies about 180 kHz, inside the 200 kHz slot from 89.5 to 89.7 MHz. Your phone's FM radio (which uses the headphone wire as its antenna) tunes to 89.6, removes amplitude noise with a limiter, converts frequency swings back to voltage, and you hear the song.

Real-life example 2, AM and FM on old analog TV: When BTV and other channels were analog, each TV channel used both kinds of modulation at once. The picture was sent with amplitude modulation in vestigial sideband form, so brightness changes became changes of carrier amplitude. The sound was sent on a separate carrier using FM, which is why the sound stayed clear even when the picture got snowy in a weak-signal village. Today's digital TV and satellite TV use the digital schemes of lessons 11 and 12 instead, but the idea of placing each service on its own carrier is the same.

Common mistakes: First, writing AM bandwidth as B instead of 2B; only SSB has bandwidth B. Second, forgetting that Carson's rule uses delta f plus B, then doubles the sum: 2 (75 + 15), not 2 x 75 + 15. Third, letting the AM index m exceed 1 without noticing it causes distortion. Fourth, thinking FM changes loudness through amplitude: loudness changes how far the frequency swings, the amplitude stays the same. Fifth, confusing the modulation index of AM (m, between 0 and 1) with the modulation index of FM (beta, often larger than 1).

What exams ask: Typical questions: find the bandwidth of an AM station with a 5 kHz audio signal (10 kHz); find total and sideband power for given Pc and m; find m from Vmax and Vmin; use Carson's rule for an FM signal with given delta f and B; compute how many stations fit in the FM band; sketch AM, FM and PM waveforms for a sine message; explain why FM is less noisy than AM; and explain why modulation is needed using antenna length. Keep the three formulas on one line: AM 2B, FM 2(delta f + B), PM 2(1 + beta)B.

Recap: Analog modulation puts an analog message onto a high-frequency carrier so antennas become practical and many stations can share the air. AM varies amplitude: B = 2B, Pt = Pc (1 + m^2 / 2), simple but noisy and power hungry; DSB-SC, SSB and VSB trim the waste. FM varies frequency: Carson's rule B = 2 (delta f + B), about 200 kHz per broadcast station in 88 to 108 MHz, with better sound. PM varies phase and is FM's twin. Next we look at multiplexing: FDM, WDM and TDM, the ways many signals share one link.
key_points: Analog modulation varies a carrier's amplitude (AM), frequency (FM) or phase (PM) smoothly with an analog message.
We modulate to make antennas practical (length about lambda/4), to share the spectrum, and to fit assigned bands.
AM: s(t) = Ac[1 + m cos(2 pi fm t)] cos(2 pi fc t), m = Am / Ac must stay at or below 1; bandwidth 2B.
AM power: Pt = Pc (1 + m^2 / 2); at m = 1 only one third of the power is in the sidebands.
SSB needs only B, DSB-SC drops the carrier, VSB was used for analog TV pictures.
FM: Carson's rule B = 2 (delta f + B) = 2 (1 + beta) B; broadcast FM uses delta f = 75 kHz, 15 kHz audio, 200 kHz slots in 88 to 108 MHz.
FM resists amplitude noise and sounds better; AM is narrow and simple; PM is FM's twin with B = 2 (1 + beta) B.
lessons.tip: Make a three-row table (AM, FM, PM) with columns: what changes, bandwidth formula, index, one real use. Revise from that table the night before the exam; almost every question is one row of it.
lessons.task: Scan the FM band on your phone or a radio and write down five station frequencies you hear. Check that they all lie between 88 and 108 MHz and that the gaps are multiples of 0.2 MHz or more.
