Packets of the same message may take different routes, arrive out of order or get lost, and the end systems must sort that out. The Internet's IP layer works this way; the details of routing and IP belong to the Computer Networks course.

The virtual-circuit approach: A virtual-circuit network is a middle path. Like circuit switching, it has setup, data transfer and teardown phases, and all packets of a connection follow the same path, so they arrive in order. Like packet switching, packets are stored and forwarded and bandwidth is shared rather than strictly reserved. Each packet carries a short label called a virtual circuit identifier, VCI, instead of the full address. The VCI only has meaning on one link; each switch swaps it for a new one.

VCI table example: Suppose a switch has this entry in its table: incoming port 1, VCI 14 goes to outgoing port 3, VCI 22. A packet arrives on port 1 labelled 14. The switch looks up the pair, rewrites the label to 22 and sends the packet out of port 3. The next switch has its own table entry for port-and-VCI 22. During setup, every switch along the path adds such an entry; during teardown, the entries are deleted. Frame Relay and ATM networks worked like this, and label switching in today's carrier networks uses the same idea.

Message switching: Before packets, there was message switching. A whole message, however long, was stored at each node and forwarded when the next link was free, as in the old telegraph and telex systems. No circuit was set up, but each node needed lots of storage, a long message tied up a link for a long time, and the delay was large because the whole message had to arrive before any of it moved on. Packet switching fixed this by cutting messages into pieces so that several links can work in parallel.

Delay ingredients: Before comparing, recall two delays from the lesson on performance. Transmission delay is the time to push all bits onto a link: L / R, the number of bits divided by the rate. Propagation delay is the time for a bit to travel the length of the link: distance divided by signal speed. Queuing and processing delays come on top in packet networks; we will ignore them in the example below to keep the arithmetic clean.

Worked comparison, the setup: Send a message of L = 8,000 bits from A to B through two switches, so the path has N = 3 links. Each link runs at R = 1 Mbps and has a propagation delay of 1 ms. Transmitting 8,000 bits on one link takes 8,000 / 1,000,000 = 8 ms. Ignore headers, queuing and processing.

Message switching result: The whole message must cross link 1 before switch 1 can forward it. Each link costs 8 ms of transmission plus 1 ms of propagation, so 9 ms per link, and the links are used one after another. Total: 3 x 9 = 27 ms.

Packet switching result: Now cut the message into P = 8 packets of 1,000 bits, so each takes 1 ms to transmit. The first packet reaches B after 3 x (1 + 1) = 6 ms. Behind it the other packets arrive in a pipeline, one every 1 ms, so the last arrives 7 ms later, at 13 ms. A general formula is (N + P - 1) x (L/P)/R + N x propagation = (3 + 8 - 1) x 1 + 3 x 1 = 13 ms. Smaller packets let all three links work at once. In real life each packet also has a header, so making packets too small wastes capacity on headers; there is a sweet spot.

Circuit switching result: Suppose setting up the circuit takes 10 ms of signalling. Then the 8,000 bits flow straight through the reserved path with no store-and-forward: 8 ms to transmit plus 3 ms of propagation, so 11 ms. Total: 10 + 11 = 21 ms, plus a short teardown. Here packet switching wins at 13 ms. But if we were sending a long stream, say a whole hour of voice, the setup cost is paid once and the circuit's steady, queue-free delay is a big plus. That is the classic trade-off: circuits for long, steady flows; packets for short, bursty data.

The telephone network: The traditional telephone network is the best-known circuit-switched system. Your home phone connects over the local loop, a twisted pair, to an end office, also called a local exchange. End offices connect through trunks to tandem and toll offices, which connect to regional offices, forming a hierarchy. Voice on the local loop is analog, limited to about 4 kHz; trunks are digital and carry many 64 kbps calls in TDM. Signalling between exchanges uses a separate packet network called SS7. BTCL's landline exchanges in Bangladesh were built on this model, and 2G and 3G mobile voice calls are also circuit switched.

Real-life example 1, a normal call versus a WhatsApp call: When your grandmother in Rajshahi calls you on a 2G or 3G voice line, the network builds a circuit, and your voice gets its own reserved channel the whole time, so the delay is steady. When you call her back on WhatsApp over mobile data, your voice is chopped into packets that share the network with everyone's videos and downloads. Usually it works fine, but on a busy evening queues grow, packets arrive late or out of order, and the voice breaks up. Voice over 4G, VoLTE, is also packet based, but the operator gives voice packets priority so it feels like a circuit.

Real-life example 2, roads in Dhaka: Circuit switching is like a VIP motorcade: police clear and hold the whole route before the cars leave, and nobody else may use those lanes until it passes. Virtual circuit is like a fixed bus route: the path is decided at the start and every bus on that route follows it in order, but buses share the road with others. Datagram packet switching is like rickshaws: each one picks its own lanes and turns at every junction based on where it is going, so two rickshaws leaving together may arrive in a different order.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say circuit switching is always slower; it is slower to start, but faster and steadier once running. Do not confuse virtual circuits with circuit switching: a virtual circuit does not necessarily reserve bandwidth, it fixes the path and uses labels. Remember that a VCI is local to one link. Exams love: list the three phases of circuit switching, compare datagram and virtual circuit in a table, fill in a VCI table, compute crossbar and multistage crosspoints, and compute total delay for message, packet and circuit switching like our 27, 13 and 21 ms example.

Recap: Switching lets many users share links instead of wiring everyone to everyone. Circuit switching reserves a path through setup, transfer and teardown, giving steady delay but wasting idle capacity; crossbars need N^2 crosspoints, and multistage and time-slot switches reduce the cost. Packet switching shares links on demand by store-and-forward: datagrams travel independently, while virtual circuits fix the path with per-link VCI labels. Message switching forwards whole messages and is mostly history. Pipelining is why packets beat whole messages. Next we start the data link layer by asking how a receiver knows a bit has gone wrong: error detection.
key_points: A full mesh of n users needs n(n-1)/2 links; switches let many users share fewer links.
Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path (FDM channel or TDM slot) through setup, data transfer and teardown phases.
A crossbar needs N^2 crosspoints; a three-stage switch needs 2kN + k(N/n)^2 and is non-blocking (Clos) when k is at least 2n - 1.
Packet switching uses store-and-forward and statistical multiplexing: efficient for bursty data but delay varies.
Datagram networks are connectionless, each packet routed independently; virtual-circuit networks set up a path and use per-link VCI labels.
Message switching stores and forwards whole messages; it is slow and needs large storage.
Packet pipelining delay: (N + P - 1) x (packet size / R) + N x propagation.
Example: 8,000 bits over 3 links at 1 Mbps with 1 ms propagation: message 27 ms, packets (8) 13 ms, circuit 21 ms with 10 ms setup.
lessons.tip: For delay questions, draw a time-line diagram: one vertical line per node, time going down, and slanted bands for each packet. Packet pipelining becomes obvious on paper, and you will not forget to count the propagation on every link.
lessons.task: Redo the worked comparison with 4 packets instead of 8, and then with 16. Write the three total delays next to each other and notice the trend. Then, with a friend, call each other once on a normal voice call and once on a data-based app while walking around, and note which one breaks up more and why.

quiz.q: How many links does a full mesh of 10 stations need?
In a virtual-circuit network, what does the VCI in a packet identify?
options: The connection on that particular link, rewritten at each switch
quiz.explain: A VCI is local to one link; each switch looks it up and swaps it for the next link's VCI.

quiz.q: A message of 4,000 bits crosses 2 links of 1 Mbps, each with 1 ms propagation, using message switching. What is the total delay?
quiz.explain: Each link: 4 ms transmission + 1 ms propagation = 5 ms; two links one after the other = 10 ms.

quiz.q: Which statement about circuit switching is true?
options: Every packet carries a full destination address
Resources are reserved for the whole call, even during silence
Packets may arrive out of order
quiz.explain: A circuit reserves its channel or slot for the call's whole life, which gives steady delay but wastes idle capacity.

quiz.q: A three-stage switch has N = 200, n = 20, k = 4. How many crosspoints does it need?

lessons.title: Error Detection: Parity, Hamming Distance and Checksum
lessons.content:
Your aunt reads her bKash number to you over a bad phone line during load-shedding, with a generator roaring in the background. You write it down, and then you read it back to her to check. If one digit was misheard, she catches it. That reading back is a kind of error control. Digital links have the same problem: noise flips bits, and the receiver must at least notice when something went wrong. This lesson is about how a receiver can detect errors using a few extra bits, from simple parity to the Internet checksum.

Why errors happen: Every physical link has noise: thermal noise, interference from motors and lightning, crosstalk from neighbouring wires, fading on wireless links. When noise pushes a signal across the decision threshold, a 0 is read as 1 or a 1 as 0. We can reduce errors with better cables and stronger signals, but never to zero. So the data link layer adds error control: detect errors and then either correct them or ask for the frame again.

Single-bit errors: A single-bit error means only one bit in a data unit, such as a byte or a frame, changed. For example, the byte 00000010, which is 2, arrives as 00001010, which is 10. Single-bit errors are actually rare in serial transmission, because a noise spike usually lasts longer than one bit time. At 1 Mbps a bit lasts only 1 microsecond, and most noise is much longer than that.

Burst errors: A burst error means two or more bits changed. The length of the burst is counted from the first corrupted bit to the last corrupted bit, even if some bits in between are fine. If 0100010001000011 is sent and 0101110101100011 is received, the bits at positions 3, 4, 7 and 10, counting from 0 on the left, are wrong, so the burst length is 10 - 3 + 1 = 8. The faster the data rate, the more bits one noise event can hit: noise lasting 1/100 of a second hits 10 bits at 1 kbps but 10,000 bits at 1 Mbps.

Redundancy: To detect or correct errors, we must send some extra bits, called redundant bits, along with the data. They are computed from the data by a rule both sides know. The receiver recomputes them and compares. Detection only asks a yes-or-no question: is there an error? Correction must also work out how many bits are wrong and where, which needs more redundancy. This lesson is about detection; correction with Hamming codes comes two lessons later.

Block coding: In block coding the message is split into datawords of k bits, and each is turned into a codeword of n = k + r bits by adding r redundant bits. There are 2^k datawords, so only 2^k of the 2^n possible n-bit patterns are valid codewords. If the receiver gets a pattern that is not on the list, it knows an error happened. The code rate k / n tells how much of the line carries real data.

A tiny block code: Take k = 2 and n = 3, with this table: 00 becomes 000, 01 becomes 011, 10 becomes 101, and 11 becomes 110. Only 4 of the 8 three-bit patterns are valid. If 011 arrives, it is valid, so the receiver accepts 01. If 111 arrives, it is not in the table, so an error is detected and the frame is discarded. But if 000 was sent and two bits flip to give 011, the receiver sees a valid codeword and wrongly accepts 01. Every code has limits, and the next idea measures them.

Hamming distance: The Hamming distance d(x, y) between two words of the same length is the number of positions where they differ. The quick way to find it is to XOR the two words and count the 1s. For example, d(000, 011) = 2, because 000 XOR 011 = 011, which has two 1s. And d(10101, 11110): the XOR is 01011, which has three 1s, so the distance is 3. Each bit error moves a word a distance of 1 away from where it started.

Minimum distance: The minimum Hamming distance d_min of a code is the smallest distance between any two different codewords. In our 2-bit table every pair of codewords differs in exactly 2 places, so d_min = 2. Another classic code maps 00 to 00000, 01 to 01011, 10 to 10101 and 11 to 11110. Checking all six pairs gives distances 3, 3, 4, 4, 3 and 3, so d_min = 3. The bigger d_min is, the more errors a code can handle.

The detection rule: To be sure of detecting up to s errors in any codeword, we need d_min of at least s + 1. The reason: s bit flips can move a codeword at most distance s, and if every other codeword is at least s + 1 away, the corrupted word cannot land exactly on another valid codeword. Our d_min = 2 code detects any single-bit error. The d_min = 3 code detects up to 2 errors. Some larger errors may also be caught, but they are not guaranteed.

The correction rule: To be sure of correcting up to t errors, we need d_min of at least 2t + 1. Then the corrupted word is still closer to the true codeword than to any other, so the receiver picks the nearest one. With the d_min = 3 code, suppose 01001 arrives. Its distances to 00000, 01011, 10101 and 11110 are 2, 1, 3 and 4. The nearest is 01011, so the receiver corrects it and outputs dataword 01. The same code could either correct 1 error or detect 2, but not both promises at once.

Linear block codes: Most practical codes are linear: the XOR of any two codewords is also a codeword. For linear codes, finding d_min is easy: it equals the smallest number of 1s in any non-zero codeword. In the 5-bit code, 01011 XOR 10101 = 11110, which is in the table, and the non-zero codewords have weights 3, 3 and 4, so d_min = 3, matching what we found by checking every pair. Parity, CRC and Hamming codes are all linear.

Simple parity check: The simplest detection code adds one parity bit. With even parity, the bit is chosen so that the total number of 1s, including the parity bit, is even. The data 1101101 has five 1s, so the parity bit is 1 and we send 11011011. The receiver XORs all eight bits; this result, called the syndrome, is 0 if the count is even, so it accepts. This is a code with k = 7, n = 8 and d_min = 2. Odd parity works the same way but makes the count odd.

What parity catches and misses: Suppose the fourth bit flips and 11001011 arrives. It has five 1s, which is odd, so the syndrome is 1 and the error is detected. Now suppose two bits flip. The count of 1s changes by 0 or 2, so it stays even and the error slips through. Simple parity detects any odd number of bit errors, but misses any even number. Because burst errors often flip several bits, simple parity is weak on real links; it was used in old serial ports and some memory chips.

Two-dimensional parity: A stronger trick arranges data in a table and adds parity to every row and every column. Take four 7-bit rows: 1100111, 1011101, 0111001 and 0101001. Their even-parity bits are 1, 1, 0 and 1, so the rows become 11001111, 10111011, 01110010 and 01010011. Then a final row holds the parity of each column: 01010101. All five 8-bit rows are sent. The receiver recomputes every row and column parity.

What 2D parity can do: If one bit flips, exactly one row parity and one column parity fail, and their crossing point shows which bit is wrong, so it can even be corrected. Two-dimensional parity detects all errors of 1, 2 or 3 bits. It misses some 4-bit errors: if four flipped bits sit at the corners of a rectangle, every row and every column still has an even count, and nothing looks wrong. It also costs many extra bits: here 12 parity bits for 28 data bits.

The Internet checksum idea: Another family of detection codes adds numbers instead of counting bits. The sender splits the data into 16-bit words and adds them using one's complement arithmetic: any carry out of the top bit is wrapped around and added back to the bottom. Then it complements the sum, flipping every bit, and sends this as the checksum. The receiver adds all words including the checksum the same way. If nothing went wrong, the sum is all 1s, so its complement is 0 and the data is accepted.

Checksum worked example in 4 bits: To see the idea with small numbers, use 4-bit words: 7, 11, 12, 0 and 6. Their ordinary sum is 36. In 4 bits, 36 is 2 x 16 + 4, so we wrap the 2 around: 4 + 2 = 6. The checksum is the complement of 6 in 4 bits: 15 - 6 = 9. The sender sends 7, 11, 12, 0, 6 and 9. The receiver adds them: 45, which is 2 x 16 + 13, so wrapped it is 13 + 2 = 15, all 1s in binary 1111. Its complement is 0, so no error is detected.

Checksum worked example in 16 bits: Now the real size. Take three 16-bit words in hex: 4F6B, A3C2 and 9D10. Their sum is 1903D, which needs 17 bits. Wrap the carry: 903D + 1 = 903E. Complement it: FFFF - 903E = 6FC1, which is the checksum. The receiver adds 4F6B + A3C2 + 9D10 + 6FC1, wraps the carries and gets FFFF; its complement is 0000, so the data is accepted. This checksum is used in the IPv4 header and in UDP and TCP; how those protocols work belongs to the Computer Networks course.

Checksum weaknesses: Because addition does not care about order, if two 16-bit words swap places, the sum does not change and the error is missed. If one word goes up by 1 and another goes down by 1, the errors cancel. The checksum is very cheap to compute in software, which is why higher layers use it, but at the data link layer, where bursts are common, a stronger check is used: the cyclic redundancy check, CRC, the topic of the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, the supermarket barcode: Pick up a packet of biscuits in a Shwapno or Agora outlet and look at the 13-digit barcode. Codes starting with 941 are issued through GS1 Bangladesh. The last digit is a check digit, computed like a checksum: multiply the first 12 digits alternately by 1 and 3, add, and choose the last digit to make the total a multiple of 10. For 941234567890 the weighted sum is 106, so the check digit is 4. If the cashier types 941234567809 by mistake, swapping the last two digits, the check digit would need to be 6, not 4, so the till rejects it. That is error detection at the checkout.

Real-life example 2, Wi-Fi in a crowded flat: In a Dhaka apartment block, dozens of Wi-Fi routers fight for the same channels. Many frames arrive damaged. Every Wi-Fi and Ethernet frame carries a check value, a CRC, at its end. The receiver recomputes it; if it does not match, the frame is silently thrown away, and in Wi-Fi the missing acknowledgement makes the sender try again. You never see the broken frames; you only notice the video loading a bit slower. Detection plus retransmission, which we study in data link control, keeps your data clean.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse the two rules: detecting s errors needs d_min of at least s + 1, correcting t errors needs d_min of at least 2t + 1. Another mistake is forgetting that burst length is counted from the first to the last bad bit, including good bits in between. In checksums, do not forget the wrap-around carry or the final complement. Exams love: compute a Hamming distance with XOR, find d_min of a code table, apply the two rules, add an even or odd parity bit, build a 2D parity table, and compute a checksum and verify it at the receiver.

Recap: Noise causes single-bit and, more often, burst errors. Detection adds redundant bits: block codes turn k-bit datawords into n-bit codewords, and an invalid codeword reveals an error. Hamming distance counts differing bits, and the minimum distance of a code decides its power: d_min of s + 1 to detect s errors, 2t + 1 to correct t. Simple parity catches odd numbers of errors, 2D parity catches all 1-, 2- and 3-bit errors, and the one's complement checksum adds 16-bit words and complements the sum. Next lesson: CRC, the stronger detector used in Ethernet and Wi-Fi.
key_points: A single-bit error changes one bit; a burst error's length runs from the first to the last corrupted bit, and faster links suffer longer bursts.
Block coding maps k-bit datawords to n-bit codewords (n = k + r); receiving an invalid codeword means an error.
Hamming distance = number of 1s in x XOR y; d_min is the smallest distance between any two codewords (for linear codes, the smallest non-zero weight).
Detect up to s errors: d_min of at least s + 1. Correct up to t errors: d_min of at least 2t + 1.
Even parity makes the number of 1s even; simple parity detects any odd number of errors but misses even numbers.
2D parity detects all 1-, 2- and 3-bit errors and can locate and correct a single-bit error; some 4-bit rectangle errors slip through.
Internet checksum: add 16-bit words in one's complement (wrap carries), complement the sum; the receiver's total must be all 1s.
Checksums miss swapped words and errors that cancel; CRC (next lesson) is stronger for burst errors.
lessons.tip: Do every checksum twice: once as the sender to get the checksum, and once as the receiver, adding everything including the checksum. If the receiver side does not come out to all 1s, you have made an arithmetic slip, and you have caught it before the examiner did.
lessons.task: Take any product with a 13-digit barcode at home and check its last digit using the 1-3-1-3 rule. Then write your own 4 x 4 bit table, add even parity to rows and columns, flip one bit, and find it using the failing row and column. Finally compute the 4-bit checksum of 5, 9, 14 and 3.

quiz.q: What is the Hamming distance between 110010 and 011011?
quiz.explain: 110010 XOR 011011 = 101001, which has three 1s.

quiz.q: A code has d_min = 5. How many errors can it always correct?
quiz.explain: Correction needs d_min of at least 2t + 1, so 5 = 2t + 1 gives t = 2.

quiz.q: With even parity, what parity bit is added to the data 1011010?
options: It depends on the next byte
quiz.explain: 1011010 has four 1s, already even, so the even parity bit is 0.

quiz.q: Which error pattern can two-dimensional parity fail to detect?
options: Four bits flipped at the corners of a rectangle
quiz.explain: Four flips at rectangle corners leave every row and column with an even count, so no parity check fails.

quiz.q: Using 4-bit one's complement words 9, 5 and 6, what is the checksum?
quiz.explain: 9 + 5 + 6 = 20 = 16 + 4; wrapping the carry gives 4 + 1 = 5, and the complement is 15 - 5 = 10.

lessons.title: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC)
lessons.content:
Imagine you send a long bKash transaction message to a friend, and on the way a lightning flash near a Grameenphone tower flips three bits in a row. A simple parity bit might miss it, because three flips can cancel out in odd-even counting. The internet checksum from the last lesson is better, but it still misses some patterns. Engineers wanted something cheap enough to build with a few logic gates, yet strong enough to catch almost every burst of noise. Their answer is the cyclic redundancy check, or CRC, and it is quietly checking nearly every Ethernet frame, Wi-Fi frame and ZIP file you have ever used.

The big idea in one sentence: Treat the message bits as one giant binary number, divide it by an agreed fixed number called the generator, and send the remainder along with the message. The receiver divides again. If the remainder comes out as zero, the data is very probably clean. If it is anything else, something got damaged on the way. The trick is that the division is not normal division. It uses modulo-2 arithmetic, where adding and subtracting are both just XOR, so there are no carries or borrows at all.

Modulo-2 arithmetic: In modulo-2, 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 0 with no carry. Subtraction gives exactly the same table, so 1 - 1 = 0 and 0 - 1 = 1. That is the XOR you already know from Digital Logic Design. So 1011 XOR 1001 = 0010, and that is both their sum and their difference. Because there are no carries, each bit column lives on its own. This is why CRC hardware is so small: a row of flip-flops for a shift register and a few XOR gates, nothing more.

The polynomial view: Engineers like to write a bit string as a polynomial in x, where each bit is the coefficient of a power of x. The leftmost bit gets the highest power. So 1011 has bits for x^3, x^2, x^1 and x^0, and becomes x^3 + x + 1, because the x^2 bit is 0. Likewise 10011 becomes x^4 + x + 1, and 1001 becomes x^3 + 1. The degree of the polynomial is its highest power, which is one less than the number of bits. Writing things as polynomials lets mathematicians use algebra over the field with just two elements, 0 and 1, to prove what errors a CRC will catch.

The names you must know: The data word d(x) is the message, k bits long. The generator g(x) is the divisor, agreed in advance by sender and receiver, with degree r, so it has r + 1 bits. The CRC, also called the remainder or the frame check sequence (FCS), is r bits long. The codeword is the data followed by the CRC, so n = k + r bits are sent. The receiver computes a syndrome, which is just the remainder it gets when it divides the received codeword by g(x). Syndrome zero means accept; non-zero means an error was detected.

Encoding step by step: First, append r zeros to the end of the data. In polynomial language this is multiplying d(x) by x^r, which shifts it left to make room. Second, divide this longer string by the generator using modulo-2 division. Third, throw away the quotient; you only need the remainder, which has exactly r bits. Fourth, replace the r appended zeros with this remainder. The result is the codeword. Mathematically, the codeword is x^r d(x) minus the remainder, and since minus is XOR, that makes the codeword an exact multiple of g(x). That exact-multiple property is the whole secret.

Modulo-2 long division: Write the dividend. Put the divisor under the leftmost 1. XOR them. The bits under the divisor change, and the rest come down unchanged. Now find the new leftmost 1 and put the divisor under it again. Keep going until the leftmost 1 is inside the last r positions, where the divisor no longer fits. Whatever is left in the last r bits is the remainder. If at some step the leading bit is 0, you simply move one position right. Unlike school division, you never ask whether the divisor is bigger or smaller. Only the leading 1 matters.

Worked example, the encoder: Data = 1001, generator = 1011 (x^3 + x + 1), so r = 3. Append three zeros: 1001000. Put 1011 under the first four bits: 1001 XOR 1011 = 0010. The string is now 0010000. The next leftmost 1 is at the third position, so put 1011 under bits three to six, which are 1000. 1000 XOR 1011 = 0011. Now the string is 0000110. The leading 1 now sits inside the last three bits, so we stop. The remainder is 110. Replace the three zeros with it, and the codeword sent on the wire is 1001110.

Worked example, the decoder: The receiver gets 1001110 and divides by 1011. 1001 XOR 1011 = 0010, giving 0010110. Next, put 1011 under 1011 (bits three to six): 1011 XOR 1011 = 0000, and the string becomes 0000000. The remainder is 000, so the syndrome is zero and the frame is accepted. The receiver then strips the last three bits and keeps 1001 as data. Now suppose noise flips the third bit, so 1011110 arrives. Dividing it by 1011 leaves a remainder of 110, not zero. The receiver knows the frame is damaged and throws it away. Note that CRC detects; it does not tell you which bit to fix.

A bigger textbook example: A classic example uses data 1101011011 and generator 10011, which is x^4 + x + 1. Append four zeros to get 11010110110000, divide by 10011 using the same slide-and-XOR process, and the remainder comes out as 1110. So the transmitted frame is 11010110111110. If you get a different remainder, the most common reasons are forgetting to append the zeros, or appending r + 1 zeros instead of r. Remember, the number of zeros equals the degree of the generator, which is one less than its length in bits.

Why the error shows up: Think of what noise does in polynomial form. The received word is c(x) + e(x), where e(x) is the error pattern, with a 1 wherever a bit was flipped. Since c(x) is an exact multiple of g(x), dividing the received word by g(x) leaves the same remainder as e(x) divided by g(x). So an error is missed only when e(x) itself is an exact multiple of g(x). The whole art of choosing a generator is choosing g(x) so that the common error patterns, like single flips, pairs, odd counts and short bursts, are never multiples of it.

What a good generator catches, part one: Single-bit errors have e(x) = x^i. If g(x) has at least two terms and the x^0 coefficient is 1, it can never divide x^i, so every single-bit error is caught. Two isolated bit errors give e(x) = x^j (x^t + 1). These are all caught if g(x) does not divide x^t + 1 for any t up to the frame length; good standard generators are picked to satisfy this for long frames. Odd numbers of errors are all caught if g(x) has x + 1 as a factor, because any polynomial with an odd number of terms gives 1 when you put x = 1, while every multiple of x + 1 gives 0.

What a good generator catches, part two, bursts: A burst error of length L means the first and last flipped bits are L positions apart, inclusive, with anything in between. With r check bits and a generator whose x^0 term is 1, every burst of length L at most r is caught, all of them, guaranteed. A burst of length exactly r + 1 slips through with probability (1/2)^(r-1). Longer bursts slip through with probability (1/2)^r. For CRC-32, r = 32, so a long random burst sneaks past only about once in four billion frames.

Standard generators: You do not invent your own generator; you use a tested standard. CRC-8 is used, for example, for the header error check in ATM cells. CRC-16-CCITT, x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1, is used in HDLC and many serial links, and we will meet HDLC in lesson 24. CRC-32, the one in Ethernet, is x^32 + x^26 + x^23 + x^22 + x^16 + x^12 + x^11 + x^10 + x^8 + x^7 + x^5 + x^4 + x^2 + x + 1. It is often written in hex as 04C11DB7, dropping the top x^32 term.

CRC-32 in Ethernet: Every Ethernet frame ends with a 4-byte field called the FCS, and it is a CRC-32 computed over the destination address, source address, type or length field and the data. The network card computes it in hardware as the bits stream out, and the card at the other end computes it again as the bits stream in. If the result does not match, the frame is silently dropped. Ethernet does not ask for a resend; recovery is left to higher layers like TCP, which belong to the Computer Networks course. So CRC at the data link layer is a goalkeeper that blocks bad frames, not a doctor that heals them.

Hardware: the shift register: A CRC circuit is a chain of r flip-flops, one per remainder bit, with an XOR gate placed in front of each flip-flop whose position matches a 1 in the generator. Bits enter one per clock tick. The bit falling off the left end is fed back into those XOR gates. After the last data bit and r zeros have been clocked in, the flip-flops hold the remainder. For our generator x^3 + x + 1 you need just three flip-flops and two XOR gates. This is called a linear feedback shift register, or LFSR. It runs at line speed, even at gigabits per second, which is why CRC beats software checksums in network cards.

Real-life example 1, mobile data in Dhaka: When you watch a cricket highlight on your phone over Robi 4G, the radio link between your phone and the tower is noisy, especially in a crowded area like Gulistan. Each small radio block carries its own CRC. Your phone checks it; if the remainder is not zero, the block is thrown away and the network quickly sends that block again using a link-level retransmission scheme. Without CRC, damaged blocks would reach the video decoder and you would see green squares and frozen faces on the screen.

Real-life example 2, downloading a file: Suppose your cousin downloads a big ZIP of class notes from a BUET friend's shared folder. Inside the ZIP, each file stores a CRC-32 of its original content. When you unzip, the program recalculates CRC-32 and compares. If even one byte got corrupted on a weak pen drive, unzip says CRC error, and you know to download again instead of studying from a broken PDF. Same math, different place: in Ethernet it guards one frame on one wire, in ZIP it guards a whole file sitting on a disk for years.

CRC compared with checksum and parity: Parity catches any odd number of flipped bits but misses every even number. The 16-bit internet checksum is simple to compute in software and catches many errors, but it misses cases such as two 16-bit words being swapped, because addition does not care about order. CRC cares about position, because each bit is multiplied by a different power of x. That is why the data link layer, which faces raw physical noise, uses CRC, while the higher layers use the lighter checksum as a second line of defence. Neither CRC nor checksum can correct errors; for correction we need the Hamming code of the next lesson.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget to append r zeros, or append as many zeros as the generator has bits. Others do normal subtraction with borrows instead of XOR. Some forget that the remainder must have exactly r bits and drop leading zeros, writing 10 instead of 010. Exams typically ask you to compute the CRC for given data and generator, to check a received codeword, to convert a bit string to a polynomial, to state which errors a generator with x + 1 as a factor detects, or to calculate the probability of missing a burst of a given length.

Recap: CRC treats data as a polynomial, appends r zeros, divides by a generator of degree r using XOR, and sends the r-bit remainder as the frame check sequence. The codeword is an exact multiple of the generator, so the receiver expects a zero remainder. A good generator catches all single-bit errors, all odd error counts if it has x + 1 as a factor, and all bursts up to length r. CRC-32 protects every Ethernet frame and is built in hardware with a shift register and XOR gates. Next lesson we go one step further: not just detecting the damaged bit, but finding and fixing it.
key_points: CRC divides the data, padded with r zeros, by a generator g(x) of degree r using modulo-2 (XOR) division and sends the r-bit remainder.
A bit string maps to a polynomial: 1011 = x^3 + x + 1; r equals the generator's length in bits minus one.
The codeword is an exact multiple of g(x), so the receiver accepts only when the syndrome (remainder) is zero.
Worked example: data 1001, g = 1011 gives remainder 110 and codeword 1001110.
An error e(x) is missed only if g(x) divides e(x); a factor of x + 1 catches all odd numbers of errors.
With r check bits, all bursts of length r or less are caught; longer bursts slip by with probability about (1/2)^r.
CRC-32 (04C11DB7) is the 4-byte FCS of every Ethernet frame, computed in hardware with a shift register (LFSR).
lessons.tip: When you do a CRC by hand, write each XOR step on its own line and keep the bits vertically aligned like a school long division. Then always verify by dividing your final codeword again: if you do not get zero, you have made a slip somewhere.
lessons.task: On paper, compute the CRC for data 101101 with generator 1101 (x^3 + x^2 + 1). Then flip one bit of your codeword and divide again to see a non-zero syndrome. If you have a computer, write a 10-line function that does modulo-2 division and check your answer.

quiz.q: In CRC, how many zeros are appended to the data before dividing by a generator of 1011?
quiz.explain: 1011 is x^3 + x + 1, degree 3, so r = 3 zeros are appended.

quiz.q: What is 1011 XOR 1001 in modulo-2 arithmetic?
Data 1001 is encoded with generator 1011. Which codeword is sent?
quiz.explain: Dividing 1001000 by 1011 gives remainder 110, so the codeword is 1001110.

quiz.q: A generator that contains x + 1 as a factor is guaranteed to detect which errors?
options: All burst errors of any length
All errors with an odd number of flipped bits
All errors with an even number of flipped bits
Only single-bit errors in the CRC field
quiz.explain: Any error polynomial with an odd number of terms is not divisible by x + 1, so all odd-count errors are caught.

quiz.q: Which CRC is used as the frame check sequence in Ethernet?
quiz.explain: Ethernet frames end with a 4-byte FCS computed with CRC-32.

lessons.title: Error Correction and Hamming Code
lessons.content:
Imagine BTV is showing a cricket final through the Bangabandhu-1 satellite to millions of homes. Some noise hits the signal over Sylhet and a few bits get flipped. With CRC alone, every damaged frame would have to be thrown away and asked for again. But a satellite cannot listen to millions of TVs shouting send that again. The only way out is to send the data in a clever form so that the receiver can find the wrong bit and fix it by itself. This is error correction, and the simplest beautiful example is the Hamming code, invented by Richard Hamming at Bell Labs around 1950.

Detection versus correction: In the last two lessons we learned to detect errors: parity, checksum and CRC only say something is wrong. Correction needs more. The receiver must know which bit is wrong, and in binary, knowing which bit is enough, because a wrong bit can only be fixed by flipping it. Recall the Hamming distance rule from lesson 20: to detect up to s errors you need a minimum distance d_min of at least s + 1, and to correct up to t errors you need d_min of at least 2t + 1. So correcting one error needs d_min = 3.

How many check bits: Suppose we have m data bits and add r check bits, so n = m + r bits are sent. With r check bits the receiver can compute a pattern of r bits, giving 2^r different answers. It must be able to say no error, or name any one of the n positions as the wrong one. That is n + 1 situations. So we need 2^r to be at least m + r + 1. For m = 4, r = 3 works, because 8 is at least 8. For m = 7 or m = 8 you need r = 4. For m = 16 you need r = 5, for m = 32 you need r = 6, and for m = 64 you need r = 7.

The Hamming (7,4) code: The famous small case has 4 data bits and 3 check bits, 7 bits in total, written (7,4). Number the positions 1 to 7 from the left. The trick is placement: the check bits sit at the positions that are powers of two, so positions 1, 2 and 4. The data bits fill the rest: positions 3, 5, 6 and 7. We call the parity bits p1, p2 and p4, and the data bits d3, d5, d6 and d7 after their positions.

Who checks whom: Write each position in binary with three bits. Position 3 is 011, 5 is 101, 6 is 110, 7 is 111. Parity bit p1 looks after every position whose binary form has a 1 in the ones place: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Parity bit p2 looks after every position with a 1 in the twos place: 2, 3, 6 and 7. Parity bit p4 looks after positions with a 1 in the fours place: 4, 5, 6 and 7. Each check bit is set to make even parity over its group, meaning the XOR of the whole group is 0. So p1 = d3 XOR d5 XOR d7, p2 = d3 XOR d6 XOR d7, and p4 = d5 XOR d6 XOR d7.

Worked example, encoding: Let the data be 1011. Put it into the data positions in order: d3 = 1, d5 = 0, d6 = 1, d7 = 1. Now p1 = d3 XOR d5 XOR d7 = 1 XOR 0 XOR 1 = 0. Then p2 = d3 XOR d6 XOR d7 = 1 XOR 1 XOR 1 = 1. Then p4 = d5 XOR d6 XOR d7 = 0 XOR 1 XOR 1 = 0. Lay out positions 1 to 7: p1 p2 d3 p4 d5 d6 d7 = 0 1 1 0 0 1 1. So the codeword sent is 0110011.

Decoding with a syndrome: The receiver gets seven bits r1 to r7. It recomputes each group: s1 = r1 XOR r3 XOR r5 XOR r7, s2 = r2 XOR r3 XOR r6 XOR r7, s4 = r4 XOR r5 XOR r6 XOR r7. If nothing went wrong, all three are 0, because the sender made each group even. Now write them as a binary number in the order s4 s2 s1. This three-bit number is called the syndrome. If it is 000, accept the word. If it is anything else, read it as a number from 1 to 7. That number is the position of the flipped bit.

Worked example, a single error: The sender transmits 0110011, but noise flips position 5, so 0110111 arrives. Compute s1 over positions 1, 3, 5, 7: 0, 1, 1, 1, whose XOR is 1. Compute s2 over 2, 3, 6, 7: 1, 1, 1, 1, giving 0. Compute s4 over 4, 5, 6, 7: 0, 1, 1, 1, giving 1. The syndrome s4 s2 s1 is 101, which is 5 in decimal. The receiver flips bit 5 back from 1 to 0, gets 0110011 again, and reads the data from positions 3, 5, 6 and 7: 1, 0, 1, 1. The original 1011 is recovered without asking for anything again.

Why the syndrome points at the bit: A flip at position k changes exactly those groups whose parity bit appears in k's binary form. Position 5 is 101, so it belongs to the p4 group and the p1 group but not the p2 group, and so exactly s4 and s1 become 1. Every position from 1 to 7 has a different non-zero binary pattern, so every single error produces a different, non-zero syndrome. If the flipped bit is a check bit itself, say position 2, the syndrome is 010 = 2, and the receiver corrects the check bit while the data was never harmed.

The matrix view: Textbooks also describe this with a parity-check matrix H, which has 3 rows and 7 columns. Column k of H is simply the binary form of k, written top to bottom as the fours, twos and ones bits. The syndrome is H times the received word, using modulo-2 arithmetic. A valid codeword gives the zero vector. A single error at position k adds column k to the result, so the syndrome equals column k, which is the binary for k.

The limit: two errors: The (7,4) code has d_min = 3, so it can correct one error or detect two, but not both at once. Watch what happens if bits 1 and 2 both flip in 0110011. The received word is 1010011. s1 becomes 1 and s2 becomes 1 while s4 stays 0, so the syndrome is 011 = 3. The receiver happily flips bit 3, and now three bits are wrong instead of two. This is called miscorrection. If two-bit errors are common on your channel, you need a stronger code.

SEC-DED, the extended Hamming code: Add one more parity bit over all seven bits, giving an (8,4) code with d_min = 4. Now the receiver can do single error correction and double error detection, called SEC-DED. If the syndrome is non-zero and the overall parity is wrong, there was one error: fix it. If the syndrome is non-zero but the overall parity is right, there were two errors: do not fix, just report. This is exactly what ECC memory in servers does: 64 data bits are stored with 8 check bits, 72 bits per word, so a single flipped memory cell is fixed on the fly.

The Hamming family and code rate: Hamming codes exist for every r of at least 2, with n = 2^r - 1 and m = n - r. So r = 3 gives (7,4), r = 4 gives (15,11), and r = 5 gives (31,26). The code rate m/n tells you what fraction of the sent bits is real data. For (7,4) it is 4/7, about 0.57, so 43 percent of the line is spent on protection. For (15,11) the rate is about 0.73, and for (31,26) about 0.84. Longer codes are more efficient, but they still fix only one bit per codeword, so one error in 31 bits is tolerated, not one in 7.

Interleaving against bursts: Real noise often comes in bursts, like a spark that ruins 6 bits in a row. A burst that lands inside one Hamming codeword is hopeless. The fix is interleaving. Take 7 codewords and write them as the 7 rows of a table. Send the table column by column: bit 1 of every word, then bit 2 of every word, and so on. A burst of up to 7 consecutive bits on the wire now damages at most one bit in each codeword, and each one is fixed separately.

FEC versus retransmission: There are two ways to deal with errors. Backward error correction, also called ARQ (automatic repeat request), detects the error and asks for the frame again; we study it in the next lesson. Forward error correction, FEC, adds enough redundancy to fix errors at the receiver with no return message. ARQ is cheap in bits when errors are rare, but it needs a return channel and costs a round trip each time. FEC costs bits all the time, but it has no waiting. FEC wins for one-way broadcast, for long-delay links like geostationary satellites, and for live voice and video. Modern 4G and 5G mix both, called hybrid ARQ.

A peek at Reed-Solomon: Hamming codes fix single bits. Reed-Solomon codes work on symbols, usually whole bytes, and can fix several of them. An RS(n, k) code takes k data symbols and adds n - k check symbols, and it can correct up to (n - k)/2 wrong symbols. The well-known RS(255, 223) adds 32 check bytes and corrects up to 16 bad bytes in each block of 255. Because a symbol is a byte, a burst that ruins all 8 bits of one byte counts as just one symbol error. That makes Reed-Solomon excellent against bursts.

Reed-Solomon around you: Every QR code has Reed-Solomon built in. QR codes offer four correction levels, L, M, Q and H, which can recover roughly 7, 15, 25 and 30 percent of damaged codewords. That is why the bKash or Nagad QR sticker on a tea stall in Mirpur still scans after it gets wet, torn at the corner or covered with a little logo in the middle. Audio CDs use a scheme called cross-interleaved Reed-Solomon coding, two Reed-Solomon codes plus interleaving, so a scratch a couple of millimetres long is fully corrected and the music plays on.

Real-life example 1, satellite TV: Bangabandhu-1 carries TV channels to homes across Bangladesh, and the dish on the roof receives a weak signal after a journey of about 36,000 kilometres. Satellite TV standards add strong FEC codes before transmission, and your set-top box corrects errors on the fly. The box cannot ask the satellite to repeat a frame, and even if it could, the round trip of about half a second would wreck live cricket. So the broadcaster pays with extra bits to save the viewers from frozen screens.

Real-life example 2, bank servers: A bank like the ones behind bKash runs servers that hold balances in RAM for millions of users. Cosmic rays and electrical noise can flip a memory bit now and then. In a balance, one flipped bit could change 1,000 taka into a very different number. So servers use ECC RAM with SEC-DED Hamming-style codes: 8 check bits per 64 data bits. A single flipped bit is corrected silently, and a double flip is detected and reported, so the server can stop before using a wrong number.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often put parity bits at the wrong positions, or number positions from the right instead of the left. Another classic mistake is computing the syndrome in the wrong order and reading 101 as s1 s2 s4. Some forget that a syndrome pointing to positions 1, 2 or 4 means a check bit failed, so the data is fine. Typical exam questions: find r for m data bits using 2^r of at least m + r + 1; encode 4 or 7 data bits with Hamming code; locate and correct a single-bit error; explain why two errors cause miscorrection; and compare FEC with ARQ.

Recap: To correct t errors a code needs d_min of at least 2t + 1. The number of check bits obeys 2^r of at least m + r + 1. In Hamming (7,4), parity bits sit at positions 1, 2 and 4, each covering the positions whose binary form has that bit set. The receiver computes the syndrome s4 s2 s1, and its value is the error position. Data 1011 encodes to 0110011, and a flip at position 5 gives syndrome 101. Adding an overall parity bit gives SEC-DED, used in ECC memory. FEC fixes without asking; ARQ asks again. Reed-Solomon protects QR codes and CDs. Next lesson: how ARQ actually works.
key_points: Correcting t errors needs d_min of at least 2t + 1; Hamming codes have d_min = 3, so they fix one error.
Check bits needed: the smallest r with 2^r of at least m + r + 1 (m = 4 gives r = 3, m = 8 gives r = 4).
In Hamming (7,4), parity bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4; p1 covers 1,3,5,7, p2 covers 2,3,6,7, p4 covers 4,5,6,7.
Data 1011 encodes to 0110011; if bit 5 flips, the syndrome s4 s2 s1 = 101 points straight at position 5.
Two errors cause miscorrection in (7,4); an extra overall parity bit gives SEC-DED (used in ECC RAM, 72 bits per 64 data bits).
Interleaving spreads a burst over many codewords so each sees at most one error.
FEC fixes errors without a return channel (broadcast, satellite, live media); ARQ detects and resends.
Reed-Solomon corrects whole symbols (bytes): RS(255,223) fixes 16 bad bytes; it protects QR codes and CDs.
lessons.tip: Memorise just one picture: positions 1 to 7 in binary. Once you can write 001 to 111, you can rebuild every parity group, every syndrome and the H matrix in an exam without memorising anything else.
lessons.task: Encode the data 0110 with Hamming (7,4) on paper. Then ask a friend to secretly flip one bit of your codeword. Compute the syndrome, find the flipped bit and fix it. Finally, scan a QR code on any product after covering a small corner with your thumb and see that it still works.

quiz.q: For m = 8 data bits, what is the minimum number of Hamming check bits r?
quiz.explain: 2^r must be at least m + r + 1. r = 3 gives 8, less than 12; r = 4 gives 16, at least 13. So r = 4.

quiz.q: In Hamming (7,4), which positions does parity bit p2 cover?
quiz.explain: p2 covers every position whose binary form has a 1 in the twos place: 2, 3, 6 and 7.

quiz.q: Using Hamming (7,4) with parity at positions 1, 2, 4, what codeword encodes data 1011?
A received (7,4) word gives s4 = 1, s2 = 0, s1 = 1. What should the receiver do?
options: Ask for retransmission because two bits are wrong
quiz.explain: The syndrome s4 s2 s1 = 101 = 5, so bit 5 is flipped back.

quiz.q: Why is forward error correction preferred for satellite TV broadcasting?
options: It uses fewer bits than ARQ in all cases
There is no practical return channel and the round-trip delay is long
It can correct any number of errors
quiz.explain: A broadcast to millions cannot collect resend requests, and a geostationary round trip takes about half a second, so FEC fixes errors at the receiver.

lessons.title: Data Link Control: Framing, Flow and Error Control
lessons.content:
Think of a teacher dictating notes to a class in a Dhaka school. If she talks too fast, students fall behind, so she pauses and asks, done? If a student misses a sentence because a bus honked outside, he raises his hand and says, sir, again please. And she must make clear where one sentence ends and the next begins, or the notes become one long mess. These three habits, marking boundaries, pacing the speed and repeating what was lost, are exactly the three jobs of data link control: framing, flow control and error control.

Where we are: The physical layer only moves raw bits. The data link layer turns that bit pipe into a reliable link between two neighbouring nodes, such as your laptop and a Wi-Fi access point. It works hop by hop; routing and TCP belong to Computer Networks. Last lessons gave us tools to detect errors (CRC) and correct a few (Hamming). Now we build the rules, called protocols, that decide what to do when a frame is late, lost or broken.

Framing: The bits on a wire are one long stream. Framing chops it into units called frames, each with a header (addresses, control information), the data, and a trailer (usually a CRC). The receiver must be able to tell where each frame starts and ends. Frames can be fixed size, like the 53-byte cells of ATM, where no boundary marker is needed because you just count. Most links use variable-size frames, so they need a delimiter, a special pattern that marks the edges. Two classic answers exist, byte stuffing and bit stuffing.

Character-oriented framing and byte stuffing: Older protocols carried text, so they used a special flag byte at each end of a frame. To protect data that happens to contain the flag byte, the sender inserts an escape byte, ESC, in front of it. The receiver sees ESC and knows the next byte is data, not a boundary. But what if the data contains ESC itself? Then the sender adds another ESC before it, so ESC ESC means one real ESC. Example: data A FLAG B ESC C is sent as FLAG A ESC FLAG B ESC ESC C FLAG. The receiver removes one ESC from each pair and gets the original back.

Bit-oriented framing and bit stuffing: Modern protocols treat data as plain bits, not characters. They use the flag 01111110, six 1s in a row with a 0 on each side. To make sure the data can never imitate the flag, the sender follows one rule: after any five consecutive 1s in the data, insert a 0, whatever the next bit is. The receiver does the opposite: after five 1s, if the next bit is 0, delete it. If the next bit is 1, it is a real flag (or an abort).

Worked example, bit stuffing: Suppose the data is 01111110, which looks exactly like a flag. Read it bit by bit and count the 1s. After 0 and five 1s, insert 0. Then the remaining bits 1 and 0 follow. The stuffed result is 011111010, nine bits, and it no longer contains six 1s in a row. Another example: 11111111 becomes 111110111. A longer one: 0111111111110 has eleven 1s in a row; after the first five insert 0, after the next five insert another 0, giving 011111011111010. The receiver removes each 0 that follows five 1s and recovers the data exactly.

Flow control versus error control: Flow control is about speed. A fast sender, like a server, can flood a slow receiver, like a cheap sensor, whose buffer will overflow and drop frames. Flow control is a set of rules that makes the sender wait for permission before sending more. Error control is about damage and loss. It means detecting bad frames, usually with CRC, and getting them sent again. At the data link layer, the two are combined in protocols called ARQ, automatic repeat request: the receiver's acknowledgements both say I got it and say you may send more. Three ARQ protocols are standard: Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat.

Stop-and-Wait ARQ: The sender sends one frame, keeps a copy, and starts a timer. Then it stops and waits. If the receiver gets a good frame, it sends an acknowledgement, ACK. When the ACK arrives, the sender discards its copy and sends the next frame. If the frame is damaged, the receiver silently drops it; if it is lost, nothing arrives. Either way, no ACK comes, the timer expires, and the sender resends its copy.

Why sequence numbers are needed: Suppose the frame arrives fine but the ACK gets lost. The sender's timer expires and it resends the same frame. Without some label, the receiver would think this is a new frame and deliver the data twice, like a bKash transfer happening twice. So each frame carries a sequence number. In Stop-and-Wait, one bit is enough: frames are numbered 0, 1, 0, 1 and so on. The ACK carries the number of the next frame expected. If the receiver is waiting for frame 1 and frame 0 arrives again, it knows it is a duplicate, discards it and sends ACK 1 once more.

Timing terms: Transmission time Tt is how long it takes to push all the bits of a frame onto the line: Tt = L / R, frame length divided by data rate. Propagation time Tp is how long one bit takes to travel the distance: Tp = d / v, where v is about 2 x 10^8 metres per second in cable or fibre. Define a = Tp / Tt. In Stop-and-Wait, one cycle takes Tt for the frame, plus Tp for it to arrive, plus another Tp for the ACK to come back (ignoring the tiny ACK transmission and processing time). The link is useful only for Tt of that time, so efficiency U = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp) = 1 / (1 + 2a).

Worked example, a long link: A 1 Mbps link sends 1,000-bit frames, so Tt = 1,000 / 1,000,000 = 1 ms. The link is 4,000 km of fibre, so Tp = 4,000,000 / (2 x 10^8) = 20 ms. Then a = 20 / 1 = 20, and U = 1 / (1 + 40) = 1/41, about 2.4 percent. Now take a 100 m LAN cable with the same frames: Tp = 0.5 microseconds, a = 0.0005, and U is about 99.9 percent. Lesson: Stop-and-Wait is fine when a is small, terrible when a is large. The bandwidth-delay product, here 1 Mbps times 40 ms = 40,000 bits, shows how much the pipe could hold.

Sliding window, the fix: Instead of one frame at a time, let the sender keep up to W frames in flight before it must stop for an ACK. If W is at least 1 + 2a, the sender never runs out of permission before the first ACK returns, and efficiency is close to 100 percent; otherwise U = W / (1 + 2a). In our 4,000 km example, 1 + 2a = 41, so a window of 41 frames fills the pipe. Sequence numbers now use m bits and count modulo 2^m, from 0 to 2^m - 1.

Go-Back-N ARQ: The sender may have up to 2^m - 1 frames outstanding. The receiver is strict: it has a window of size 1 and accepts frames only in order. If frame 2 is lost, frames 3, 4 and 5 that arrive after it are discarded, even though they are fine. ACKs are cumulative: ACK 2 means everything before 2 has arrived, send 2 next. When the timer for frame 2 expires, the sender goes back and resends 2, 3, 4 and 5, all frames sent after the lost one.

Why Go-Back-N's window is at most 2^m - 1: Take m = 2, so the numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3. Suppose the window were 4. The sender sends frames 0, 1, 2, 3. All four arrive, and the receiver now expects the next frame 0. But all four ACKs are lost. The sender times out and resends the old frame 0. The receiver, expecting a new frame numbered 0, accepts the old one as new: a duplicate slips in. With a window of 3, the sender sends 0, 1, 2, and the receiver then expects 3. A resent old 0 does not match and is correctly rejected. So the rule is W of at most 2^m - 1; for m = 3, W is at most 7.

Selective Repeat ARQ: Here the receiver also has a window and buffers frames that arrive out of order. If frame 2 is lost but 3, 4 and 5 arrive, the receiver keeps them and sends a NAK (negative acknowledgement) for 2, or the sender's timer for 2 expires. Only frame 2 is resent. When it arrives, the receiver delivers 2, 3, 4 and 5 in order to the layer above. This saves bandwidth on noisy or long links, but needs more memory and logic at both ends. The window rule is stricter: both sender and receiver windows can be at most 2^(m-1). For m = 3 that is 4.

Why Selective Repeat needs 2^(m-1): With m = 2, numbers 0 to 3, imagine windows of size 3. The sender sends 0, 1, 2. All arrive, and the receiver's window slides to 3, 0, 1. All ACKs are lost, so the sender resends old frame 0. Frame number 0 is inside the receiver's new window, so the old frame is accepted as if it were the new frame 0. With window size 2, the receiver's window after receiving 0 and 1 is 2, 3, which does not overlap the sender's old numbers 0 and 1. The two windows together must never be larger than the number space, so W at most 2^m / 2 = 2^(m-1).

Choosing m, a worked example: Back to the 4,000 km link with 1 + 2a = 41. With m = 3, Go-Back-N allows W = 7, so U = 7/41, about 17 percent; Selective Repeat allows only 4, about 9.8 percent. To fill the pipe, Go-Back-N needs 2^m - 1 to be at least 41, so m = 6, giving 63. Selective Repeat needs 2^(m-1) of at least 41, so m = 7, giving 64. One extra sequence bit is the price of Selective Repeat's smarter receiver.

Piggybacking: Real links usually carry data both ways, like a video call between Dhaka and Chattogram. Sending a separate small ACK frame for every data frame wastes capacity. With piggybacking, the receiver waits a short moment and puts the acknowledgement number inside the header of its own outgoing data frame. Each frame header then carries two numbers: its own sequence number and the acknowledgement of the other direction. If no data is ready within a set time, a plain ACK is sent anyway so the other side's timer does not expire. HDLC, in the next lesson, uses exactly this.

Real-life example 1, Wi-Fi in a cafe: At a coffee shop in Dhanmondi, your phone and the Wi-Fi access point share a noisy radio channel with many other phones and the microwave oven behind the counter. Each unicast Wi-Fi data frame must be answered by a short ACK from the receiver, right after it arrives. If no ACK comes back, the sender retries that frame, up to a retry limit. It is close to Stop-and-Wait at the frame level, and it works well because the distance is only a few metres, so a is tiny.

Real-life example 2, a satellite link: Imagine a bank branch on Hatiya island connected by a VSAT dish through a geostationary satellite, with a round trip of roughly half a second. Even at a modest 2 Mbps with 1,000-bit frames, about 1,000 frames could be in flight during one round trip. Stop-and-Wait would leave the link idle nearly all the time. Such links need large windows and usually Selective Repeat, so that one lost frame does not force hundreds of good frames to be resent.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up transmission time and propagation time; remember Tt depends on frame size and data rate, while Tp depends only on distance and speed. Others forget the factor 2 in 1 + 2a, because the ACK must also travel back. Many write Go-Back-N's limit as 2^m, or Selective Repeat's as 2^m - 1. Typical questions: stuff or unstuff a bit string; compute efficiency of Stop-and-Wait; find the window needed to fill a link; find m for Go-Back-N or Selective Repeat; and trace which frames are resent after a loss.

Recap: Data link control does framing, flow control and error control on one link. Byte stuffing escapes flag and ESC bytes; bit stuffing inserts a 0 after five 1s, so the flag 01111110 never appears in data. Stop-and-Wait sends one frame and waits, uses 1-bit sequence numbers, and has efficiency 1/(1 + 2a). Sliding windows keep many frames in flight. Go-Back-N resends everything after a loss and allows up to 2^m - 1 frames; Selective Repeat resends only what was lost and allows 2^(m-1). Piggybacking puts ACKs inside data frames.
key_points: Data link control has three jobs on one link: framing, flow control and error control.
Byte stuffing puts ESC before any flag or ESC byte in the data; bit stuffing inserts 0 after every five consecutive 1s (01111110 becomes 011111010).
Stop-and-Wait ARQ uses a timer and 1-bit sequence numbers; its efficiency is 1/(1 + 2a) with a = Tp/Tt.
Example: 1 Mbps, 1,000-bit frames, 4,000 km gives a = 20 and efficiency 1/41, about 2.4 percent.
Sliding window efficiency is W/(1 + 2a) when W is less than 1 + 2a; a window of 1 + 2a fills the pipe.
Go-Back-N: receiver window 1, cumulative ACKs, resend all frames after a loss, window at most 2^m - 1.
Selective Repeat: receiver buffers out-of-order frames, resends only lost ones, windows at most 2^(m-1).
Piggybacking carries ACK numbers inside data frames going the other way.
lessons.tip: For every ARQ question, first compute Tt, Tp and a on one line. Almost every efficiency, window size or sequence-number question becomes simple once you know 1 + 2a.
lessons.task: Take the string 0111111011111100 and bit-stuff it by hand, then unstuff it to check. Next, compute the Stop-and-Wait efficiency for a 10 Mbps link, 2,000-bit frames and a 2,000 km cable, and find the smallest m for Go-Back-N and for Selective Repeat that keeps the link fully busy.

quiz.q: After bit stuffing, what does the data 01111110 become?
quiz.explain: After five consecutive 1s a 0 is inserted: 011111 + 0 + 10 = 011111010.

quiz.q: A link has a = Tp/Tt = 20. What is the Stop-and-Wait efficiency?
With 3-bit sequence numbers, what is the maximum send window for Go-Back-N?
quiz.explain: Go-Back-N allows at most 2^m - 1 = 7 outstanding frames.

quiz.q: In Selective Repeat ARQ with m = 3, what is the maximum window size?
quiz.explain: Selective Repeat windows can be at most 2^(m-1) = 4.

quiz.q: In Go-Back-N, frame 2 is lost while frames 3, 4 and 5 arrive correctly. What happens?
options: The receiver discards 3, 4, 5 and the sender resends 2, 3, 4, 5
The receiver buffers 3, 4, 5 and only 2 is resent
quiz.explain: The Go-Back-N receiver accepts only in-order frames, so everything after the lost frame is resent.

lessons.title: HDLC and PPP
lessons.content:
In the last lesson we built ideas: framing, bit stuffing, sliding windows, Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat and piggybacking. Today we meet two real protocols built from them. HDLC, High-level Data Link Control, is the classic bit-oriented protocol that many later protocols copied. PPP, the Point-to-Point Protocol, is its simpler cousin that carried dial-up internet for years and still lives inside many home broadband connections in Bangladesh, every time your router logs in to your ISP with a username and password.

HDLC in one paragraph: HDLC was standardised by ISO and works on point-to-point and multipoint links. It is bit-oriented, so it uses the flag 01111110 and bit stuffing. It supports the sliding window ARQ of the last lesson, with 3-bit sequence numbers normally and 7-bit numbers in an extended mode. Many famous protocols are children of HDLC: LAPB used in X.25 networks, LAPD used in ISDN telephone signalling, and the frame style of PPP. Cisco routers even use their own variant of HDLC as the default on serial links.

Station types: HDLC names three kinds of station. A primary station is the boss: it sends commands. A secondary station only obeys: it sends responses. A combined station can do both. These stations can be arranged in two configurations. In an unbalanced configuration, one primary controls one or more secondaries, like a teacher with a class. In a balanced configuration, two combined stations are equal partners, like two friends on a phone call.

Transfer modes: HDLC defines how stations take turns. In Normal Response Mode, NRM, the link is unbalanced: a secondary may transmit only when the primary polls it, that is, asks it to talk. This suits one computer controlling many terminals or sensors on a shared line. In Asynchronous Balanced Mode, ABM, the link is balanced: either combined station may start sending whenever it likes, without waiting to be asked. ABM is the common mode for point-to-point links between routers. A third mode, Asynchronous Response Mode, ARM, lets a secondary speak without being polled while a primary still controls the link, but it is rarely used.

The HDLC frame format: Every HDLC frame has six fields. First, a flag, 01111110, eight bits. Second, an address field, usually eight bits, which can be extended. Third, a control field of eight bits, or sixteen in extended mode, that says what kind of frame this is and carries sequence numbers. Fourth, the information field with the user's data, of variable length; some frames have none. Fifth, the frame check sequence, a CRC of 16 or 32 bits, which we computed in lesson 21. Sixth, a closing flag, 01111110.

Flags and bit stuffing in HDLC: Because the flag is 01111110, the sender stuffs a 0 after every five consecutive 1s between the flags, in the address, control, information and FCS fields. For example, ten 1s in a row, 1111111111, are sent as 111110111110. And 0011111100 becomes 00111110100. The receiver removes those zeros. If the receiver sees seven or more 1s in a row, that cannot be data or a flag, so it is treated as an abort signal, meaning the sender gave up on this frame. Because stuffing works on bits, the information field can be any number of bits, not just whole bytes.

Three types of frame: The first bits of the control field say which type a frame is. Information frames, I-frames, carry user data and also carry acknowledgements by piggybacking. Supervisory frames, S-frames, carry only control information for flow and error control, like ACK and NAK, when there is no data to piggyback on. Unnumbered frames, U-frames, manage the link itself: setting it up, choosing a mode, disconnecting and reporting problems.

The I-frame control field: In the basic 8-bit control field, an I-frame starts with a 0. Then come three bits of N(S), the send sequence number of this frame. Then one P/F bit. Then three bits of N(R), the receive sequence number, which is the piggybacked acknowledgement: it means I have received everything before N(R), send N(R) next. With three bits, numbers run from 0 to 7. Example: an I-frame with N(S) = 3, P/F = 1 and N(R) = 5 has the control bits 0, 011, 1, 101, written together as 00111101 in the order textbooks draw it.

The P/F bit: This single bit has two names. When a primary sends a command with the bit set, it is called the Poll bit, P, and it means please respond now. When a secondary sends a response with the bit set, it is called the Final bit, F, and it means this is my final frame, your turn. In NRM this bit is the talking stick passed back and forth. In ABM it is used to force an immediate reply, for example to check that a quiet partner is still alive.

S-frames: A supervisory frame starts with the bits 10, then two code bits, then P/F, then N(R). The two code bits give four types. RR, Receive Ready, is a normal acknowledgement: I got everything before N(R) and I am ready for more. RNR, Receive Not Ready, acknowledges but says stop for now, my buffer is full; this is flow control. REJ, Reject, says frame N(R) was bad, resend it and everything after it; this is Go-Back-N. SREJ, Selective Reject, says resend only frame N(R); this is Selective Repeat. So HDLC can run either ARQ style from the last lesson.

U-frames: An unnumbered frame starts with the bits 11 and uses five code bits spread over the rest of the field, enough for up to 32 commands and responses. Important ones: SNRM, set normal response mode; SABM, set asynchronous balanced mode; SNRME and SABME for the extended versions with 7-bit sequence numbers; UA, unnumbered acknowledgement, the reply that says OK, accepted; DISC, disconnect; DM, disconnected mode; and FRMR, frame reject, meaning I got a frame that makes no sense, such as an unknown control field. U-frames carry no N(S) or N(R), which is why they are called unnumbered.

A sample HDLC conversation: Station A wants to talk to station B in balanced mode. A sends a U-frame SABM. B answers with UA. The link is now up. A sends I-frames with N(S) = 0, 1 and 2, each with N(R) = 0 because B has sent nothing yet. B has data too, so it sends its own I-frame with N(S) = 0 and N(R) = 3, piggybacking: I have your 0, 1, 2, send 3 next. Later B's buffer fills, so it sends an S-frame RNR. When it is ready again it sends RR. Finally A sends DISC and B replies UA.

Why PPP was needed: In the 1990s, millions of homes connected to the internet through a modem over a telephone line, one point-to-point link from your computer to the ISP. HDLC was heavier than needed for that, and its windows and modes were overkill for a link where TCP already handled reliability end to end. People wanted something simpler that could carry different network-layer protocols, negotiate options like maximum frame size, check a username and password, and hand out an IP address. PPP did all of that. It is byte-oriented, so it works over the asynchronous serial links of modems as well as synchronous ones.

The PPP frame: A PPP frame looks like HDLC on purpose. Flag 0x7E, which is 01111110. Address 0xFF, which means all stations, because on a point-to-point link there is only one other side anyway. Control 0x03, which in HDLC terms means an unnumbered information frame, so no sequence numbers. Then a 2-byte protocol field that says what the payload is. Then the payload, with a default maximum of 1,500 bytes, called the MRU. Then an FCS of 2 bytes by default, or 4 if both sides agree. Then the closing flag.

What PPP does not do: PPP checks the FCS and silently drops bad frames, but it has no sequence numbers, no acknowledgements and no flow control. It is not an ARQ protocol. If a frame is lost, PPP does not notice; TCP at a higher layer will notice and resend, which belongs to the Computer Networks course. This is a design choice: on a reasonably clean line, end-to-end recovery is enough, and keeping the link layer simple makes it fast and cheap.

Byte stuffing in PPP: PPP is byte-oriented, so it uses byte stuffing instead of bit stuffing. The escape byte is 0x7D. When a 0x7E or a 0x7D appears in the data, the sender writes 0x7D and then the original byte XOR 0x20. So 0x7E becomes 7D 5E, and 0x7D becomes 7D 5D. Worked example: the payload bytes 41 7E 42 7D 43 are sent as 41 7D 5E 42 7D 5D 43. The receiver, on seeing 7D, deletes it and XORs the next byte with 0x20 to get the original back. On asynchronous links, some control characters below 0x20 can also be escaped, by agreement.

The protocol field: Because the protocol field names the payload, one PPP link can carry many kinds of traffic. Some well-known values: 0xC021 is LCP, the Link Control Protocol. 0xC023 is PAP and 0xC223 is CHAP, the two authentication protocols. 0x8021 is IPCP, the network control protocol for IPv4, and 0x0021 is an actual IPv4 packet. IPv6 has its own pair, 0x8057 for IPv6CP and 0x0057 for IPv6 data. You do not need to memorise every number, but notice the pattern: values starting with C are link-level control, 8 is network control, and 0 is real network-layer data.

PPP phases: A PPP link moves through phases like a state machine. Dead: no carrier, nothing happening. Establish: the two sides exchange LCP packets to agree on options like MRU, FCS size and which authentication to use. Authenticate: optional, using PAP or CHAP. Network: NCP packets, such as IPCP for IPv4, configure the network layer, for example giving your computer an IP address and DNS server. Open: data flows. Terminate: LCP terminate packets close the link politely. Then back to Dead. If authentication fails, the link goes straight to Terminate.

PAP and CHAP: PAP, the Password Authentication Protocol, is a two-way handshake. The user sends an Authenticate-Request with username and password, and the server replies Ack or Nak. The password travels in plain text, so anyone sniffing the line can read it. CHAP, the Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol, is a three-way handshake. The server sends a random challenge. The user replies with a hash, usually MD5, of an identifier, the shared secret password and the challenge. The server computes the same hash and compares, then sends Success or Failure. The password itself never crosses the line, and the server can rechallenge at any time during the session.

PPPoE, PPP for home broadband: Today most homes do not dial up; they use fibre or Ethernet to the ISP's equipment, and Ethernet is a shared, multi-access network, not point-to-point. But ISPs liked PPP's login and address assignment, so they invented PPP over Ethernet, PPPoE. First comes a discovery stage: your router broadcasts PADI, looking for a server; the access concentrator answers PADO, an offer; your router sends PADR, a request; and the server confirms with PADS, giving a session ID. Then the normal PPP phases run inside Ethernet frames. PADT ends the session. Many Bangladeshi ISPs give customers a PPPoE username and password to type into the router.

Real-life example, why your router says MTU 1492: An Ethernet frame can carry 1,500 bytes of payload. PPPoE adds a 6-byte PPPoE header and the 2-byte PPP protocol field inside it, 8 bytes in total. So only 1,500 - 8 = 1,492 bytes are left for the IP packet. That is why router settings for a PPPoE connection often show MTU 1492. If someone sets 1500 by mistake, large packets may have to be split or dropped, and some websites load strangely, a classic help-desk puzzle at ISPs from Dhaka to Rajshahi. A second example: the serial links between some older routers in bank and telecom networks still run HDLC or PPP framing today.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse HDLC's bit stuffing with PPP's byte stuffing; HDLC is bit-oriented, PPP is byte-oriented. Others think PPP does retransmission; it does not. Some mix up REJ and SREJ: REJ is Go-Back-N, SREJ is Selective Repeat. Remember that U-frames have no sequence numbers and I-frames have both N(S) and N(R). Typical questions: draw the HDLC frame and name its fields; explain NRM versus ABM; list the S-frame types; draw PPP's phase diagram; compare PAP and CHAP; and byte-stuff a PPP payload or bit-stuff an HDLC field.

Recap: HDLC is the bit-oriented parent protocol: primary, secondary and combined stations; NRM and ABM modes; a frame of flag, address, control, information, FCS and flag; bit stuffing after five 1s; I-frames with N(S) and N(R), S-frames RR, RNR, REJ and SREJ, and U-frames like SABM, UA and DISC. PPP is the byte-oriented, simpler child for point-to-point links: flag 7E, address FF, control 03, a protocol field, byte stuffing with 7D and XOR 20, error detection only, and phases Dead, Establish, Authenticate, Network, Open, Terminate, with PAP or CHAP login and PPPoE at home.
key_points: HDLC is bit-oriented: flag 01111110, bit stuffing, frame = flag, address, control, information, FCS (16 or 32 bits), flag.
Stations are primary, secondary or combined; NRM needs polling by the primary, ABM lets either combined station send.
I-frames carry N(S), P/F and N(R); S-frames are RR, RNR, REJ (Go-Back-N) and SREJ (Selective Repeat); U-frames manage the link (SABM, UA, DISC).
PPP frame: 7E, FF, 03, 2-byte protocol, payload (default MRU 1,500), FCS, 7E; error detection only, no ARQ.
PPP byte stuffing: 7E becomes 7D 5E and 7D becomes 7D 5D (escape 7D, then XOR 0x20).
PPP phases: Dead, Establish (LCP), Authenticate (PAP or CHAP), Network (NCP such as IPCP), Open, Terminate.
PAP sends the password in plain text (two-way); CHAP uses a challenge and a hash (three-way), so the password never crosses the line.
PPPoE runs PPP inside Ethernet with PADI, PADO, PADR, PADS discovery; its 8-byte overhead gives MTU 1,492.
lessons.tip: Draw the HDLC frame and the PPP frame one under the other. Once you see that PPP is HDLC with fixed address FF and control 03 plus a protocol field, half the exam answers write themselves.
lessons.task: Open your home Wi-Fi router's settings page (or ask the family member who set it up) and check the WAN connection type. If it says PPPoE, look for the MTU value. Then byte-stuff the PPP payload 7D 7E 00 7E by hand and check that unstuffing gives it back.

quiz.q: Which HDLC transfer mode lets either of two combined stations start sending without being polled?
quiz.explain: In ABM both combined stations are equal and may transmit at any time.

quiz.q: Which HDLC S-frame asks the sender to resend only the one frame named in N(R)?
quiz.explain: SREJ, Selective Reject, asks for a single frame, like Selective Repeat ARQ.

quiz.q: In PPP byte stuffing, how is a data byte 0x7E sent?
quiz.explain: PPP sends the escape byte 0x7D followed by 0x7E XOR 0x20 = 0x5E.

quiz.q: Which statement about PPP is correct?
options: PPP uses Go-Back-N with 3-bit sequence numbers
PPP is bit-oriented and uses bit stuffing
PPP detects errors with the FCS but does not retransmit
PPP needs a primary station to poll the other side
quiz.explain: PPP drops frames with a bad FCS and leaves recovery to higher layers; it has no ARQ.

quiz.q: Why does CHAP keep the password safer than PAP?
options: CHAP encrypts the whole PPP frame
