CHAP sends a hash of a random challenge and the secret, not the password itself
quiz.explain: With CHAP, the server sends a challenge and checks a hash; the secret is never sent over the line.

lessons.title: Multiple Access, Ethernet and Wireless LANs
lessons.content:
Picture a class of forty students and one teacher who says, ask anything you like. If two students shout questions at the same moment, nobody understands either. Computers sharing one cable or one radio channel face exactly this problem. The rules they use are called multiple access protocols, and they live in the lower part of the data link layer, the MAC (medium access control) sublayer.

Three families: Multiple access methods fall into three groups. Random access: nobody is in charge, any station may send when it wants, and collisions are handled when they happen. ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA belong here. Controlled access: stations take turns by reservation, polling or passing a token, so there are no collisions. Channelization: the channel is divided in frequency, time or code, as FDMA, TDMA and CDMA, which we met in the multiplexing and spread spectrum lessons.

Pure ALOHA: The first random access protocol was ALOHA, built at the University of Hawaii around 1970 to link islands by radio. The rule is almost childish: send whenever you have a frame. Then wait for an acknowledgement. If none comes back within a timeout, assume a collision, wait a random time, and send again. Let Tfr be the time to send one frame. A frame is safe only if no other frame starts within Tfr before it or Tfr after it, so its vulnerable time is 2 x Tfr.

Pure ALOHA throughput: Let G be the average number of frames that stations try to send per frame time Tfr, counting retries. Using the Poisson model of random arrivals, the throughput, meaning the average number of successful frames per Tfr, is S = G x e^(-2G). This is largest when G = 0.5, giving S = 1/(2e), about 0.184. So at best only 18.4 percent of the channel carries useful frames. Worked example: 200-bit frames on a 200 kbps channel give Tfr = 1 ms. If the system offers 1,000 frames per second, G = 1 and S = e^(-2), about 0.135, so about 135 frames per second succeed.

More of the same example: If the stations offer 500 frames per second, G = 0.5 and S is about 0.184, so about 184 frames per second get through, the best case. If they offer 250 frames per second, G = 0.25 and S = 0.25 x e^(-0.5), about 0.152, so about 152 frames per second succeed, roughly 60 percent of the attempts.

Slotted ALOHA: Divide time into slots of length Tfr, and allow a station to start sending only at the beginning of a slot. Now two frames either collide completely in the same slot or not at all, so the vulnerable time is cut to Tfr. The throughput becomes S = G x e^(-G), with a maximum at G = 1 of S = 1/e, about 0.368, or 36.8 percent, double pure ALOHA. In the same 200 kbps example, 1,000 frames per second gives about 368 successes, 500 gives about 303, and 250 gives about 195. The price is that all stations need synchronised clocks.

CSMA, listen before you talk: Carrier Sense Multiple Access adds manners: before sending, listen to the medium, and send only if it is idle. A signal needs propagation time Tp to travel along the cable. Station A may start sending, and station B, far away, still hears silence for up to Tp and starts too. So the vulnerable time of CSMA is Tp, the propagation delay. On a short LAN Tp is tiny compared with Tfr, which is why CSMA works so much better than ALOHA there, and why it would work poorly on a satellite link with a huge Tp.

Persistence methods: What should a station do if the channel is busy? 1-persistent: keep listening and send immediately, with probability 1, the moment it becomes idle. Nonpersistent: if busy, wait a random time and then sense again. Fewer collisions, but the channel may sit idle while everyone is waiting. p-persistent, used with slotted channels: when the channel is idle, send with probability p; with probability 1 - p, wait for the next slot and repeat. Classic Ethernet uses 1-persistent with collision detection on top.

CSMA/CD: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection lets a sending station keep listening while it transmits. If the signal on the wire differs from what it is sending, there is a collision. The station stops at once, sends a short jam signal so that everyone notices the collision, and then backs off for a random time before trying again. But there is a catch: the sender can only detect a collision while it is still transmitting. If it finishes too early, it might think a frame was delivered when it actually collided far away.

Minimum frame size, worked example: The worst case is a collision at the far end of the cable. The first bit takes Tp to reach the far end, and the collision signal takes another Tp to come back. So the sender must still be transmitting after 2Tp, which means Tfr must be at least 2Tp. Classic 10 Mbps Ethernet allowed a worst-case round trip, including repeaters, of 51.2 microseconds. The minimum frame length is then 10,000,000 x 51.2 x 10^-6 = 512 bits, which is 64 bytes. That is exactly why every Ethernet frame is at least 64 bytes, and short data is padded to reach it. The 51.2 microsecond period is called the slot time.

Binary exponential backoff: After a collision, how long should a station wait? Ethernet uses binary exponential backoff. After the nth collision of the same frame, the station picks a random integer K from 0 to 2^n - 1 and waits K slot times. After the first collision K is 0 or 1; after the second, 0 to 3; after the third, 0 to 7, so the wait is at most 7 x 51.2 = 358.4 microseconds at 10 Mbps. The range stops growing after n = 10, at 0 to 1,023, and after 16 failed attempts the station gives up and reports an error.

The Ethernet frame: An Ethernet frame starts with a 7-byte preamble of alternating 1s and 0s that lets the receiver's clock lock on, followed by a 1-byte start frame delimiter, SFD. Then come the 6-byte destination address, the 6-byte source address, a 2-byte type or length field, the data of 46 to 1,500 bytes, and a 4-byte CRC-32, the FCS from lesson 21. Counting from destination address to CRC, the minimum is 6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes, matching our collision math, and the maximum is 6 + 6 + 2 + 1,500 + 4 = 1,518 bytes.

MAC addresses: Every Ethernet and Wi-Fi interface has a 48-bit MAC address, usually written as six hex bytes like 4A:30:10:21:10:1A. The first 24 bits are normally the OUI, a number the IEEE assigns to the manufacturer. The least significant bit of the first byte says unicast (0) or multicast (1). In 4A, binary 01001010, that bit is 0, so it is a unicast address. In 47, binary 01000111, it is 1, so multicast. The address of all 1s, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, is broadcast, meaning every station on the LAN.

Ethernet grows up: Standard Ethernet ran at 10 Mbps with Manchester coding, first on thick and thin coaxial cable as a shared bus, then on twisted pair with hubs, called 10Base-T. Fast Ethernet, 100 Mbps, uses 4B/5B block coding with MLT-3 on twisted pair in 100Base-TX, both from lesson 8. Gigabit Ethernet runs over fibre with 8B/10B, or over all four pairs of Cat 5e copper in 1000Base-T. The big change was the switch. With a switch and full-duplex links, each cable has only two stations sending in separate directions, so there are no collisions and CSMA/CD is simply not used.

Why Wi-Fi cannot use collision detection: A radio cannot easily hear others while it is sending, because its own signal is millions of times stronger at its antenna. Also, in a wireless network not every station can hear every other. Imagine your phone and your friend's laptop on opposite sides of a Wi-Fi router in a hall; both reach the router but cannot hear each other. This is the hidden terminal problem. Both sense an idle channel, both send, and they collide at the router without knowing it. So Wi-Fi tries to avoid collisions instead: CSMA/CA, Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance.

How CSMA/CA works: A station with a frame first senses the channel. When the channel has been idle for a gap called DIFS, it does not send at once. It picks a random backoff count of slots from a contention window and counts down only while the channel stays idle, pausing if someone else starts. When the count reaches zero, it sends. The receiver, after a shorter gap called SIFS, replies with an ACK. No ACK means a probable collision, so the contention window is doubled and the station tries again.

RTS, CTS and NAV: To beat hidden terminals, a station can first send a short Request To Send, RTS, to the access point. The access point answers with Clear To Send, CTS, which every station near the AP hears, including the hidden one. Every station that hears either sets its NAV, network allocation vector, a timer saying the channel is reserved, keep quiet. Then the data frame and ACK go through safely. RTS/CTS costs extra time, so it is usually turned on only for large frames or crowded networks.

802.11 basics: The IEEE 802.11 family is Wi-Fi. A basic service set, BSS, is one access point with its stations; several BSSs joined through a wired network form an extended service set, ESS, like the many APs across a university campus with the same network name. Wi-Fi frames can carry up to four addresses, because a frame may pass through an AP between wired and wireless parts. Generations include 802.11b and g at 2.4 GHz, 802.11a at 5 GHz, 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4), 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) and 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6), each faster, using higher-order QAM from lesson 12 and more antennas.

Controlled access and channelization recap: In reservation, each station books a slot in a short reservation period before data is sent. In polling, a primary station asks each secondary in turn whether it has data, as in HDLC's NRM from lesson 24. In token passing, a special frame called the token travels around a logical ring, and only the holder may send, as in Token Ring and FDDI. Channelization splits the channel itself: FDMA by frequency, TDMA by time slot and CDMA by code. GSM 2G, still used by Grameenphone, Robi and Banglalink for voice, combines FDMA carriers of 200 kHz with 8 TDMA time slots each.

Real-life example 1, an office LAN: In a small office in Motijheel, ten computers and a printer connect by Cat 6 cables to one Ethernet switch. Each link is full duplex at 1 Gbps, so no collisions happen and nobody runs CSMA/CD. The switch learns which MAC address lives on which port by reading source addresses, and sends each frame only where it needs to go; a frame to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF goes to every port.

Real-life example 2, Wi-Fi in a student hall: In a crowded university hall at night, a hundred phones and laptops share a few access points. CSMA/CA means each device must wait for idle air and count down random backoffs, and every collision doubles the contention window. Throughput per person falls far below the router's advertised speed. That is why such Wi-Fi feels fast at 6 a.m. and slow at 11 p.m., and why network engineers add more access points on non-overlapping channels and use the 5 GHz band, giving each smaller group its own air to share.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students swap the ALOHA formulas; pure is G e^(-2G) with a maximum of 18.4 percent at G = 0.5, slotted is G e^(-G) with a maximum of 36.8 percent at G = 1. Others forget the factor of 2 in Tfr at least 2Tp, or think modern switched Ethernet still uses CSMA/CD. Typical questions: compute ALOHA throughput for a given load; find the minimum Ethernet frame size for a given rate and distance; give the backoff range after the nth collision; draw the Ethernet frame; decide if a MAC address is unicast or multicast; and explain the hidden terminal problem with RTS/CTS.

Course wrap-up: Look how far we have come. We started with the five-part communication model and the layer map, learned what signals are, measured bandwidth and capacity with Nyquist and Shannon, and saw how noise and attenuation hurt them. We turned bits into line codes, analog into PCM, bits into ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM, and shared channels with FDM, TDM, spread spectrum and multiplexing hierarchies. We met cables, fibre and radio, and circuit and packet switching. Then we protected bits with parity, checksums, CRC and Hamming, built ARQ, HDLC and PPP, and today shared the medium with ALOHA, Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Next stop: Computer Networks, where IP, routing and TCP build the internet on top of all this.
key_points: Multiple access families: random access (ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), controlled access (reservation, polling, token passing) and channelization (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA).
Pure ALOHA: vulnerable time 2Tfr, S = G e^(-2G), maximum 18.4 percent at G = 0.5.
Slotted ALOHA: vulnerable time Tfr, S = G e^(-G), maximum 36.8 percent at G = 1.
CSMA/CD needs Tfr at least 2Tp; at 10 Mbps with a 51.2 microsecond slot time, the minimum frame is 512 bits = 64 bytes.
Binary exponential backoff: after the nth collision wait K slots, K random from 0 to 2^n - 1 (capped at n = 10, give up after 16 attempts).
Ethernet frame: preamble 7, SFD 1, destination 6, source 6, type 2, data 46 to 1,500, CRC 4 bytes; 64 to 1,518 bytes.
A 48-bit MAC address is unicast if the lowest bit of the first byte is 0, multicast if 1; FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is broadcast.
Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA with DIFS, SIFS, random backoff, ACKs and optional RTS/CTS with NAV to handle hidden terminals.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page table with three columns, pure ALOHA, slotted ALOHA and CSMA/CD, and rows for vulnerable time, throughput formula, best G and maximum efficiency. Most exam questions on this topic can be answered straight from that table.
lessons.task: On your phone or laptop, find your Wi-Fi MAC address (in the Wi-Fi or About settings). Write the first byte in binary and decide whether it is unicast and whether it looks randomised (many phones set the second-lowest bit, the locally administered bit, for privacy). Then compute pure and slotted ALOHA throughput for 200-bit frames on a 200 kbps channel at 800 frames per second.

quiz.q: What is the maximum throughput of pure ALOHA, and at what load?
quiz.explain: S = G e^(-2G) is largest at G = 0.5, giving 1/(2e), about 0.184.

quiz.q: For 10 Mbps Ethernet with a slot time of 51.2 microseconds, what is the minimum frame size?
quiz.explain: 10,000,000 x 51.2 x 10^-6 = 512 bits = 64 bytes, so a sender is still transmitting when a far-end collision returns.

quiz.q: After the 3rd collision of a frame, binary exponential backoff chooses K from which range?
quiz.explain: After the nth collision K is chosen from 0 to 2^n - 1, so 0 to 7 for n = 3.

quiz.q: Why does Wi-Fi use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?
options: A radio cannot reliably hear collisions while sending, and hidden terminals cannot hear each other
quiz.explain: A station's own signal drowns others and hidden stations cannot sense each other, so Wi-Fi avoids collisions instead of detecting them.

quiz.q: A MAC address starts with the byte 47 (binary 01000111). What kind of address is it?
quiz.explain: The lowest bit of the first byte is 1, which marks a multicast address.

lessons.title: What Signals and Systems Are
lessons.content:
Close your eyes during a monsoon evening in Dhaka and listen to rain on a tin roof. At first it is a soft tap, tap. Then it becomes a loud roar, and later it fades again. That changing sound is carrying information to you: how hard it is raining, right now, second by second. Now imagine your little cousin calls you on the phone and says "it is raining here too". Her voice travels into the phone, gets changed into numbers, flies through the air as radio waves and comes out of your phone's speaker. The rain sound and her voice are signals. The phone, the tower and the speaker are systems. This whole course is about these two words and how they talk to each other.

What a signal is: A signal is any quantity that changes with something else, usually time, and carries information. In maths we write it as a function, x(t), where t is time and x(t) is the value at that moment. The value could be air pressure in a sound wave, voltage in a wire, temperature in a room, or the price of a share at the Dhaka Stock Exchange. If nothing ever changes, there is no news in it, so a perfectly flat line is a very boring signal. The interesting part of a signal is always how it moves.

Everyday signals: Your voice is a signal: tiny changes in air pressure, thousands of times per second. An ECG in a hospital is a signal: the small voltage, about one millivolt, that your heart makes as it beats, measured on the skin. A stock price is a signal: one number per day, or per minute, going up and down. The temperature shown on a weather app every hour is a signal. Even a cricket score on TV is a signal: runs as a function of the ball number. Once you start looking, signals are everywhere.

Signals of space, not time: A photo is also a signal, but its value depends on position, not time. A grey picture is a function x(m, n) that gives the brightness of the pixel at row m and column n. A Full HD screen has 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, so one frame is a signal with about two million values. A video adds time on top, so it depends on three variables. In this course we mostly use one variable, time, but every idea you learn also works for images later in image processing.

Notation you will see all course: For a signal that exists at every instant of time we write x(t) with round brackets, and t can be any real number, like 0.5 or 2.718. For a signal that exists only at whole-number steps we write x[n] with square brackets, and n is an integer: ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, .... The square brackets are a promise: x[1.5] simply does not exist. Remember this rule from day one, because teachers do cut marks for mixing the brackets up.

What a system is: A system is anything that takes a signal in and gives a signal out. We draw it as a box. The input x(t) goes in on the left, the output y(t) comes out on the right, and we write y(t) = T{x(t)}, where T is the rule of the box. The rule can be simple, like "double everything", or very complicated, like "recognise the words being spoken". In this course we care about what the box does to the signal, not about which wires or chips are inside it.

Examples of systems: A microphone turns air pressure into voltage. An amplifier makes the voltage bigger, for example y(t) = 5 x(t). A loudspeaker turns voltage back into sound. A camera turns light into numbers. Your bKash account is a system too: deposits and withdrawals go in each day, and the balance comes out. Even your ear and brain together form a system that takes sound and gives understanding. A system does not have to be electronic. Anything with an input signal and an output signal counts.

A tiny worked system: Let us build a simple smoothing system that averages each value with the one before it: y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1]) / 2. Take the input x[0] = 2, x[1] = 4, x[2] = 6, x[3] = 8, and assume x[-1] = 0. Then y[0] = (2 + 0) / 2 = 1, y[1] = (4 + 2) / 2 = 3, y[2] = (6 + 4) / 2 = 5, and y[3] = (8 + 6) / 2 = 7. The output is 1, 3, 5, 7. This little box is called a moving average, and you will meet it again and again, because it removes quick jitter from data like stock prices or sensor readings.

Continuous time signals: A continuous-time (CT) signal has a value at every instant. Between t = 1 and t = 2 there are infinitely many times, and the signal has a value at each one. The sound in the room, the voltage on a power line, and the height of a swinging pendulum are continuous-time signals. Nature mostly gives us continuous-time signals, because the real world does not jump from one tick to the next.

Discrete time signals: A discrete-time (DT) signal has values only at separate moments, usually equally spaced. The daily closing price of a share, the number of rickshaws passing a gate each minute, or the hourly temperature are discrete-time signals. Very often we get a discrete-time signal by measuring a continuous one every T seconds: x[n] = x(nT). This is called sampling. A phone call uses 8000 samples per second, so a three-second hello becomes 3 x 8000 = 24,000 numbers. We study sampling properly in lessons 17 and 18.

Analog versus digital: Continuous and discrete talk about the time axis. Analog and digital talk about the value axis. An analog signal can take any value in a range, like 1.2347 volts. A digital signal can take only a fixed list of values, for example the 256 levels of an 8-bit number, or just 0 and 1. A music CD stores 44,100 samples per second, each one rounded to a 16-bit number, so its sound is both discrete in time and digital in value. Rounding values to levels is called quantization.

The four boxes: Put the two ideas together and you get four kinds. Continuous time and analog: the voltage from a microphone. Discrete time and analog: samples taken by a circuit but not yet rounded. Continuous time and digital: the voltage on a computer wire that is either 0 V or 3.3 V but can switch at any instant. Discrete time and digital: the numbers inside your laptop. Computers can only store the last kind, which is why so much of engineering is about moving between these boxes.

Block diagrams: Engineers draw systems as block diagrams. A box with a rule written inside is a system. An arrow is a signal. A circle with a plus sign adds two signals. A triangle, or a box with a number like 0.5, multiplies a signal by a constant, called a gain. A box with the letter D, or z^(-1), holds a discrete signal for one step, called a delay. The moving average above is drawn as: x[n] goes into a delay box to give x[n-1], then x[n] and x[n-1] meet at an adder, and the sum passes through a gain of 0.5 to give y[n].

Connecting systems: Boxes can be joined in three main ways. In series, or cascade, the output of one is the input of the next, like microphone, then amplifier, then speaker. In parallel, the same input goes into two boxes and their outputs are added. In feedback, part of the output is sent back to the input. You have heard feedback at a waz mahfil or a mosque loudspeaker when the microphone hears its own speaker and makes a loud howl. That howl is a feedback system becoming unstable, a word we study in lesson 7.

Why this course matters: Every phone call, every YouTube video, every Wi-Fi packet, every X-ray image and every self-driving robot uses the ideas of this course. Data Communication uses them to send bits through cables and air. Digital Signal Processing uses them to build filters and the FFT. Control engineering uses them to keep drones steady and fans at the right speed. Machine learning on sound and images starts with signal processing too. If you understand signals and systems well, a lot of later courses feel much easier.

Real life example 1, a mobile call: When you call your nani on Grameenphone, your voice is a continuous-time analog signal. The microphone, a system, turns it into a voltage. A converter samples it 8000 times per second and rounds each sample to a number, giving a discrete-time digital signal. A speech coder squeezes those numbers, the radio sends them to the tower, and the network carries them to her phone. Her phone runs all of it backwards and the speaker makes air pressure again. That is a long chain of systems in series, and each box changes the signal in a known way.

Real life example 2, an ECG: In a hospital, small metal pads on your chest pick up the heart's voltage. It is a continuous-time signal of about one millivolt. The wires also pick up hum from the 50 Hz mains supply used in Bangladesh, so the machine has a system, a filter, that removes that hum. Then it finds the time between two big peaks. If the peaks come every 0.833 seconds, the heart rate is 60 / 0.833, about 72 beats per minute. The doctor sees a clean line and a number, but under the hood it is pure signals and systems.

What you already know: This course builds on Math III. There you learned complex numbers, Euler's formula e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, Fourier series and the Fourier transform, the Laplace transform and partial fractions. We will not teach that maths again. When we need it, we will recap it in a few lines and move on. One small change: in maths you wrote i for the square root of -1, but engineers use j, because i is already used for electric current. The new thing here is the systems view: what does a box do to a signal, and how can we predict it?

Course map, part one: Lessons 2 to 5 are about signals themselves. We classify them, meet the basic building block signals like the step and the impulse, both in continuous and discrete time, and learn operations like shifting, flipping and stretching. Lessons 6 and 7 are about properties of systems: memory, causality, invertibility, linearity, time invariance and stability. Lessons 8 to 12 are the heart of the course: linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, the impulse response, convolution in discrete and continuous time, and systems described by differential and difference equations.

Course map, part two: Lessons 13 to 16 look at signals through frequency: Fourier series, the Fourier transform, its properties, and the frequency response of a system. Lessons 17 and 18 cover sampling, aliasing and reconstruction. Lesson 19 is the discrete-time Fourier transform. Lessons 20 to 24 bring in the Laplace transform and the Z-transform, poles and zeros, transfer functions and stability. Lesson 25 is an introduction to filters and a full recap. Detailed filter design and the FFT wait for Digital Signal Processing, and modulation waits for Data Communication.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mix-up is thinking discrete means digital. Discrete is about time, digital is about values, and a signal can be one without the other. Another mistake is writing x[2.5] or treating n as a real number. Students also forget that a system's output is a whole signal, not just one number. Exams love short questions like: define signal and system with two examples each, classify given signals as CT or DT and analog or digital, compute a few output values of a given difference equation, or draw the block diagram of y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 x[n-1].

Recap: A signal is a function that carries information, written x(t) for continuous time and x[n] for discrete time. A system is a box that turns an input signal into an output signal, y = T{x}. Continuous versus discrete is about time; analog versus digital is about values. Block diagrams use boxes, arrows, adders, gains and delays, joined in series, parallel or feedback. Math III gave us the tools; this course teaches us to use them to predict what systems do. Next lesson, we start sorting signals into families.
key_points: A signal is a function that carries information, usually of time: x(t) in continuous time, x[n] in discrete time with n an integer.
A system is a box that maps an input signal to an output signal: y = T{x}.
Continuous vs discrete describes the time axis; analog vs digital describes the value axis.
Sampling makes a discrete-time signal from a continuous one: x[n] = x(nT).
Block diagrams use boxes, arrows, adders, gains and delays; systems connect in series, parallel and feedback.
Example: the moving average y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1]) / 2 turns 2, 4, 6, 8 into 1, 3, 5, 7 (with x[-1] = 0).
Math III (complex numbers, Fourier, Laplace) is assumed; this course adds the systems view.
lessons.tip: For every gadget you use this week, say out loud: what is the input signal, what is the output signal, and is each one continuous or discrete? Doing this with real things makes the words stick much faster than memorising definitions.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the block diagram of y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1]) / 2 using a delay box, an adder and a gain of 0.5. Then feed it the last seven days of temperatures from your phone's weather app (take x[-1] = 0) and compute all seven outputs by hand. Do the smoothed values wiggle less than the originals?

quiz.q: Which notation correctly shows a discrete-time signal?
options: x[n], where n is an integer
x(t), where t is any real number
x(n) with n allowed to be 0.5
quiz.explain: Square brackets with an integer index n mark a discrete-time signal. x[2.5] does not exist.

quiz.q: A signal is discrete in time but can still take any value in a range. It is:
quiz.explain: Discrete is about the time axis and analog is about the value axis, so such samples (not yet rounded) are discrete-time analog.

quiz.q: A microphone near a loudspeaker makes a loud howl. Which kind of connection causes this?
quiz.explain: The speaker's output gets back into the microphone, which is the input, so it is a feedback loop that has become unstable.

quiz.q: A phone samples voice at 8000 samples per second. How many samples are in 3 seconds?

lessons.title: Classifying Signals
lessons.content:
Walk into Karwan Bazar early in the morning. Fish go to one side, vegetables to another, rice and dal to a third. Nobody sells hilsa next to green chillies by accident. Sorting things into groups is how we know how to handle them: fish need ice, rice needs a dry sack. Signals work the same way. Once you know which family a signal belongs to, you instantly know which tools and formulas to use on it. In this lesson we sort signals in four ways: deterministic or random, periodic or aperiodic, even or odd, and energy or power.

Why sorting helps: Each family comes with its own shortcuts. A periodic signal can be broken into a Fourier series. An energy signal has a Fourier transform that behaves nicely. An even signal has a purely real cosine-type spectrum. A random signal needs probability instead of a single formula. So these labels are not just names to memorise for the exam. They tell you, before you do any heavy maths, what kind of answer you should expect.

Deterministic versus random: A deterministic signal is one you can predict exactly, because there is a formula or a rule for it, like x(t) = 3 cos(2t). If I ask you its value at t = 1, you can compute it. A random signal is one you cannot predict exactly in advance. The hiss of a radio between stations, the exact pattern of raindrops on a tin roof, and tomorrow's share price are random. We describe random signals by averages and probabilities, like "on average the noise is this strong". This course works almost entirely with deterministic signals. Random signals return in later courses on communication and statistics.

Periodic signals: A continuous-time signal is periodic if it repeats itself exactly: x(t + T) = x(t) for every t, for some positive number T. If T works, then 2T, 3T and so on also work. The smallest positive T that works is called the fundamental period, T0. From it we get the fundamental frequency f0 = 1 / T0 in hertz, and the angular frequency ω0 = 2π / T0 in radians per second. For example cos(2t) repeats when 2t grows by 2π, so T0 = π seconds.

Aperiodic signals and a small warning: A signal that never repeats is aperiodic. A single clap, a decaying exponential like e^(-t) u(t), and one rectangular pulse are aperiodic. Strictly speaking, a periodic signal must go on forever, from minus infinity to plus infinity. Real signals start and stop, so in practice we call a signal periodic when it repeats for a long time, like the 50 Hz mains voltage. One odd case: a constant x(t) = 5 is periodic for every T, but it has no smallest positive period, so it has no fundamental period.

Sum of two periodic signals: Suppose x(t) = x1(t) + x2(t), with periods T1 and T2. The sum is periodic only if we can find whole numbers k and m with k T1 = m T2, which means T1 / T2 must be a rational number, a fraction of two integers. Then the period of the sum is the least common multiple. Worked example: x(t) = cos(2t) + sin(3t). The periods are T1 = 2π / 2 = π and T2 = 2π / 3. The ratio T1 / T2 = 3 / 2 is rational. Since 2 x π = 3 x (2π / 3) = 2π, the fundamental period is T0 = 2π.

When the sum is not periodic: Now try x(t) = cos(t) + cos(πt). The periods are T1 = 2π and T2 = 2π / π = 2. The ratio T1 / T2 = π, which is irrational. No matter how long you wait, the two waves never line up again at the same time. So this sum is aperiodic, even though each part on its own is perfectly periodic. Exams love this trick question, so always check the ratio of the periods, not just whether each piece repeats.

Discrete-time periodicity: A discrete signal is periodic if x[n + N] = x[n] for all n, where N must be a positive integer. This extra rule changes everything. Take x[n] = cos(Ω0 n). For it to repeat after N steps, Ω0 N must be a whole multiple of 2π: Ω0 N = 2πm. So x[n] is periodic only if Ω0 / (2π) = m / N is a rational number, and the fundamental period N is the denominator after reducing the fraction. For cos(πn/4), Ω0 / 2π = 1/8, so N = 8. For cos(3πn/5), Ω0 / 2π = 3/10, so N = 10.

The big surprise: Consider x[n] = cos(n), so Ω0 = 1. Then Ω0 / 2π = 1 / (2π), which is irrational. That means cos(n) is not periodic at all! The continuous cos(t) repeats every 2π seconds, but the samples land at whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ... and 2π is not a whole number, so they never land on exactly the same pattern again. Sampling a periodic signal does not automatically give a periodic sequence. For sums in discrete time, if each part is periodic the sum is too: cos(πn/4) + cos(πn/3) has N1 = 8 and N2 = 6, so N = LCM(8, 6) = 24.

Even and odd signals: A signal is even if it is a mirror image around t = 0: x(-t) = x(t). Fold the graph along the vertical axis and the two halves match. cos(t) and t² are even. A signal is odd if x(-t) = -x(t): the left half is the right half flipped upside down. sin(t) and t are odd. Every odd signal must be zero at t = 0, because x(0) = -x(0) forces x(0) = 0. The same definitions work in discrete time with n in place of t.

Splitting any signal into even and odd parts: Most signals are neither even nor odd, but every signal can be written as an even part plus an odd part. The formulas are xe(t) = [x(t) + x(-t)] / 2 and xo(t) = [x(t) - x(-t)] / 2. Add them and the x(-t) terms cancel, giving back x(t). Example: for x(t) = e^t, the even part is (e^t + e^(-t)) / 2 = cosh t, and the odd part is (e^t - e^(-t)) / 2 = sinh t. For the unit step u(t), the even part is 1/2 everywhere (except t = 0) and the odd part is +1/2 for t > 0 and -1/2 for t < 0.

A discrete worked example: Let x[0] = 1, x[1] = 2, x[2] = 3, and zero elsewhere. To get xe[n] we average x[n] with x[-n]. At n = 0: (1 + 1) / 2 = 1. At n = 1 and n = -1: (2 + 0) / 2 = 1. At n = 2 and n = -2: (3 + 0) / 2 = 1.5. So xe is 1.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.5 for n = -2 to 2. For xo[n] we take half the difference: at n = 0 it is 0, at n = 1 it is 1, at n = 2 it is 1.5, and the negative side is the negative of that: -1.5, -1. Check n = 2: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3. Check n = -2: 1.5 - 1.5 = 0. It works.

Handy symmetry facts: Even times even is even, odd times odd is even, and even times odd is odd, just like multiplying plus and minus signs. The integral of an odd signal over a symmetric range like -a to a is zero, because the areas cancel. The integral of an even signal over -a to a is twice the integral over 0 to a. These facts save you lots of time in Fourier series problems, where you can predict that some coefficients are zero before computing anything.

Energy and power, the definitions: Think of x(t) as a voltage across a 1 ohm resistor. The power at each instant is |x(t)|², so the total energy is E = ∫ |x(t)|² dt from minus infinity to infinity. The average power is P = lim as T goes to infinity of (1 / 2T) ∫ |x(t)|² dt from -T to T. In discrete time we use sums: E = Σ |x[n]|² over all n, and P = lim as N goes to infinity of (1 / (2N + 1)) Σ |x[n]|² from n = -N to N.

Energy signals, power signals, and neither: If 0 < E < ∞, the signal is an energy signal, and then its average power is automatically 0, because a finite energy spread over infinite time averages to nothing. If 0 < P < ∞, it is a power signal, and its energy must be infinite. A signal cannot be both. Some signals are neither: the ramp t u(t) and the growing exponential e^t have infinite energy and infinite power. A quick rule: short, bounded pulses are energy signals, periodic signals are power signals, and signals that grow without limit are neither.

Worked energy calculations: A rectangular pulse of height 3 and width 2 has E = 3² x 2 = 18. For x(t) = e^(-2t) u(t), E = ∫ e^(-4t) dt from 0 to ∞ = 1/4. Notice we squared first: (e^(-2t))² = e^(-4t). In discrete time, x[n] = (1/2)^n u[n] gives E = Σ (1/4)^n from n = 0 to ∞, which is a geometric series equal to 1 / (1 - 1/4) = 4/3. All three are finite, so all three are energy signals with zero average power.

Worked power calculations: For a periodic signal, the power is just the average of |x|² over one period. For x(t) = 5 cos(ωt), cos² averages to 1/2, so P = 25 / 2 = 12.5. In general A cos(ωt + φ) has power A² / 2. A complex exponential A e^(jω0 t) has |x|² = |A|² at every instant, so P = |A|². For a sum of sinusoids with different frequencies, the powers simply add: 3 cos(t) + 4 sin(2t) has P = 9/2 + 16/2 = 12.5. The unit step u(t) is 1 for half of all time and 0 for the other half, so P = 1/2. The same is true for u[n].

Real life example 1, the mains and the IPS: The electricity in a Bangladeshi home is a 50 Hz sinusoid with an RMS value of 220 V. Its peak is about 220 x √2 ≈ 311 V. Over a 1 ohm load, its average power is 311² / 2 ≈ 220² = 48,400, which is exactly why RMS is defined the way it is. It is periodic with T0 = 1/50 = 20 ms, and it is a power signal. During load shedding the IPS takes over and tries to produce the same kind of periodic power signal from a battery. A lightning spark, on the other hand, is a short burst, an energy signal.

Real life example 2, a cricket match on TV: When the batsman hits the ball, the microphone near the stumps picks up a short sharp "tok". It lasts a fraction of a second and then dies away, so it is an energy signal and aperiodic. The ceiling fan humming in your room is almost periodic, a power signal. The roar of the crowd at Mirpur stadium is random: no formula can tell you its exact value at the next millisecond, only its average loudness. One broadcast, three families of signals.

Common mistakes: Students often forget to square the signal before integrating for energy, or square only the amplitude and forget the exponent. Another mistake is claiming cos(n) is periodic with N = 2π, but N must be an integer. Some also say that the sum of two periodic signals is always periodic in continuous time, which is false when the period ratio is irrational. Finally, remember that an energy signal has zero power and a power signal has infinite energy. Saying a signal is both is always wrong.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: find the fundamental period of a sum like cos(2t) + sin(3t), decide if cos(3πn/5) or cos(n) is periodic, find the even and odd parts of a short sequence or of e^(-at) u(t), and compute the energy or power of signals like A e^(-at) u(t), A cos(ωt), u(t) or a^n u[n], then state whether each is an energy signal, a power signal or neither. Show the formula, the integral or sum, and the final classification, and you will collect full marks.

Recap: Deterministic signals have a formula, random ones only averages. A periodic signal satisfies x(t + T0) = x(t); sums are periodic only when period ratios are rational, and discrete sinusoids are periodic only when Ω0 / 2π is rational. Every signal splits into even and odd parts with xe = [x(t) + x(-t)] / 2 and xo = [x(t) - x(-t)] / 2. Energy E = ∫ |x|² dt and power P is the long-run average of |x|². Pulses are energy signals, periodic signals are power signals, and growing signals are neither. Next, we meet the basic building block signals.
key_points: Deterministic signals follow a formula; random signals are described by averages and probabilities.
Periodic: x(t + T0) = x(t), with T0 the smallest positive period; f0 = 1/T0 and ω0 = 2π/T0.
A sum of periodic signals is periodic only if T1/T2 is rational; e.g. cos(2t) + sin(3t) has T0 = 2π.
cos(Ω0 n) is periodic only if Ω0/2π is rational; cos(πn/4) has N = 8 but cos(n) is not periodic.
Even part xe = [x(t) + x(-t)]/2, odd part xo = [x(t) - x(-t)]/2; e.g. e^t = cosh t + sinh t.
Energy E = ∫|x|² dt; power P = long-run average of |x|². Energy signals have P = 0, power signals have E = ∞.
Examples: e^(-2t)u(t) has E = 1/4; A cos(ωt) has P = A²/2; u(t) has P = 1/2; t u(t) is neither.
lessons.tip: Make a tiny table with three columns, signal, E and P, and fill it for ten common signals. Seeing that exactly one of E or P is finite (or neither) for each row trains your eye faster than reading the definitions again.
lessons.task: On paper, decide whether each is periodic and find its period: cos(πn/6), cos(2n), sin(4t) + cos(6t), and cos(t) + sin(√2 t). Then use your phone calculator to check the energy of x[n] = (0.9)^n u[n] by adding the first 30 terms of (0.81)^n and comparing with 1 / (1 - 0.81).

quiz.q: What is the fundamental period of x(t) = cos(2t) + sin(3t)?
quiz.explain: The periods are π and 2π/3. Their ratio 3/2 is rational, and 2 x π = 3 x 2π/3 = 2π.

quiz.q: Is x[n] = cos(n) periodic?
quiz.explain: A discrete period must be an integer, and 2πm/1 is never an integer, so cos(n) never repeats exactly.

quiz.q: What is the energy of x(t) = e^(-2t) u(t)?
quiz.explain: E = ∫ e^(-4t) dt from 0 to ∞ = 1/4. Remember to square the signal first.

quiz.q: How is the unit step u(t) classified?
quiz.explain: Its energy is infinite, and its average power is lim (1/2T) x T = 1/2, so it is a power signal.

quiz.q: What is the even part of x(t) = e^t?
quiz.explain: xe(t) = (e^t + e^(-t)) / 2, which is cosh t.

lessons.title: Basic Continuous-Time Signals
lessons.content:
With just 26 letters you can write every English story ever told. With a few LEGO bricks you can build a house, a car or a spaceship. Signals have their own small alphabet too. A handful of simple signals, the step, the ramp, the pulse, the impulse, the exponential, the sinusoid and the sinc, can be shifted, scaled and added to build almost any signal you will ever meet. Learn them well; every big formula later is built from them.

Unit step: The unit step u(t) is 0 for t < 0 and 1 for t > 0. It is the maths of a switch being turned on at t = 0. Think of the moment load shedding ends and the lights come back: before, nothing; after, full power. At exactly t = 0 the value is a matter of convention. Some books leave it undefined, some use 1, some use 1/2. It almost never matters in calculations. A shifted step u(t - 3) switches on at t = 3 instead, and u(-t) is 1 for t < 0, a switch that turns off at t = 0.

Why the step is so useful: Multiplying any signal by u(t) chops off everything before t = 0. So sin(t) u(t) is a sine wave that starts at t = 0 and is zero before. Signals that are zero for t < 0 are called causal or right-sided signals, and we will use u(t) all the time to write them. The step is also the test input engineers love: switch on the input and watch how the system settles. That output is called the step response, and you will meet it in lesson 11.

Unit ramp: The unit ramp r(t) = t u(t) is 0 for t < 0 and grows with slope 1 after that, like water filling a bucket at a steady rate. The ramp and step are linked: the slope of r(t) is 0 before zero and 1 after, so dr/dt = u(t), and the other way round r(t) = ∫ u(τ) dτ from -∞ to t. A scaled and shifted ramp like 2 r(t - 1) starts at t = 1 and climbs with slope 2, so at t = 3 its value is 2 x (3 - 1) = 4.

Rectangular pulse: A rectangular pulse is a signal that is a constant for a while and zero elsewhere. The standard one, rect(t), has height 1 and width 1, centred on t = 0, so it is 1 for |t| < 1/2. Any pulse can be built from two steps: switch on, then switch off. For example u(t) - u(t - 2) is 1 from t = 0 to t = 2 and 0 elsewhere. And 3 [u(t - 1) - u(t - 4)] is a pulse of height 3 from t = 1 to t = 4. Its area is 3 x 3 = 9.

Building shapes from ramps and steps: Ramps let us make slopes. A triangle that rises from 0 at t = 0 to 1 at t = 1 and falls back to 0 at t = 2 is r(t) - 2 r(t - 1) + r(t - 2). Read it like instructions: start climbing with slope 1, at t = 1 change the slope by -2 so it becomes -1, at t = 2 change it by +1 so it becomes 0. Check: at t = 0.5 we get 0.5, at t = 1 we get 1, at t = 1.5 we get 1 - 2 x 0.5 = 0.5, and at t = 3 we get 3 - 4 + 1 = 0. Exams often give you a graph and ask for exactly this kind of formula.

The unit impulse, the idea: Imagine a rectangular pulse of width ε and height 1 / ε. Its area is always ε x 1/ε = 1. Now squeeze it: make ε smaller and smaller. The pulse gets thinner and taller, but the area stays 1. In the limit we get the unit impulse δ(t), also called the Dirac delta. It is a model of something very strong that happens in a very short time, like a cricket bat hitting the ball, a hammer tap or a lightning spark. What matters is not its height, but its total area, its strength.

The unit impulse, the rules: δ(t) = 0 for every t ≠ 0, and ∫ δ(t) dt = 1 over any range that includes t = 0. It is not an ordinary function, because no normal function is zero everywhere except one point and still has area 1. Mathematicians call it a generalized function. We draw it as an upward arrow at t = 0 with its area written next to it. So 5 δ(t - 2) is an arrow at t = 2 labelled 5. The number on the arrow is the area, not the height.

Sampling and sifting: Because δ(t - t0) lives only at t = t0, multiplying it with a signal keeps only the value there: x(t) δ(t - t0) = x(t0) δ(t - t0). Integrate both sides and we get the sifting property: ∫ x(t) δ(t - t0) dt = x(t0). The impulse "sifts out" one value, like a sieve catching one grain. Worked: ∫ (t² + 1) δ(t - 2) dt over all t = 2² + 1 = 5. And ∫ cos(t) δ(t - π) dt = cos(π) = -1. But be careful: ∫ (t² + 1) δ(t - 2) dt from 0 to 1 is 0, because the impulse at t = 2 lies outside the limits.

Impulse and step are partners: The step u(t) jumps from 0 to 1 at t = 0. Its slope is zero everywhere except at the jump, where it is "infinitely steep" for an instant, with a total rise of 1. That is exactly an impulse of area 1, so δ(t) = du/dt, and u(t) = ∫ δ(τ) dτ from -∞ to t. In general, a jump of size A in a signal shows up as A δ(t - t0) in its derivative. One more rule worth knowing: δ(at) = δ(t) / |a|, so δ(2t) = (1/2) δ(t), because squeezing the time axis also squeezes the area.

Real exponentials: x(t) = C e^(at), where C and a are real numbers. If a < 0 the signal decays, like a capacitor discharging or hot tea cooling towards room temperature. If a > 0 it grows, like an uncontrolled chain reaction or money in a bank with interest. If a = 0 it is a constant. For decay, the time constant τ = 1 / |a| tells you how fast. After one time constant the signal has dropped to e^(-1), about 36.8 percent. For e^(-2t), τ = 0.5 s, and after 5τ = 2.5 s only e^(-5), about 0.7 percent, is left, which engineers treat as "basically finished".

Sinusoids: The most important signal of all is x(t) = A cos(ω0 t + φ). A is the amplitude, the peak value. ω0 is the angular frequency in radians per second. The ordinary frequency is f0 = ω0 / 2π in hertz, cycles per second, and the period is T0 = 1 / f0. φ is the phase, which tells you where in its cycle the wave is at t = 0. Worked: 5 cos(100πt + π/3) has A = 5, ω0 = 100π rad/s, f0 = 50 Hz, T0 = 20 ms, and phase π/3, which is 60 degrees. That is the shape of the mains voltage in Bangladesh, just with a different amplitude.

Phase as a time shift: We can write cos(ω0 t + φ) = cos(ω0 (t + φ / ω0)), so a phase φ is the same as shifting the wave left in time by φ / ω0. In the example above, (π/3) / (100π) = 1/300 s, about 3.33 ms. We say the wave leads by 60 degrees. Also sin(ω0 t) = cos(ω0 t - π/2), so a sine is just a cosine that lags by 90 degrees. A plus sign on the phase means the wave arrives earlier, so it leads.

Complex exponentials: From Math III you know Euler's formula, e^(jω0 t) = cos(ω0 t) + j sin(ω0 t), with j the square root of -1. Picture it as an arrow of length 1 spinning around the origin of the complex plane, ω0 radians every second, anticlockwise if ω0 > 0. Its real part is a cosine and its imaginary part is a sine. Going the other way, cos(ω0 t) = (e^(jω0 t) + e^(-jω0 t)) / 2, so every real sinusoid is two spinning arrows going opposite ways. It is periodic with T0 = 2π / |ω0|. This signal is the star of the Fourier half of the course.

General complex exponentials: Let s = σ + jω be a complex number and look at e^(st) = e^(σt) e^(jωt). The first factor is a real exponential that grows or shrinks the size; the second spins. So e^(st) is a spiral. Its real part, e^(σt) cos(ωt), is a sinusoid inside an exponential envelope. If σ < 0 the oscillation dies away, if σ > 0 it blows up, and if σ = 0 it is a pure sinusoid. This one family covers constants, real exponentials, sinusoids and damped sinusoids, and the same s becomes the Laplace variable in lesson 20.

Damped sinusoids: Take x(t) = e^(-t) cos(10t) u(t). It wiggles with angular frequency 10 rad/s, so one wiggle takes 2π / 10, about 0.63 s, while the envelope e^(-t) shrinks it, dropping to about 37 percent after 1 second. A plucked guitar string, a bell, a car bouncing after a speed breaker and the ringing of a mosque loudspeaker after a loud word all look like this. Whenever you see a system that "rings and then settles", think damped sinusoid.

Sinc: The sinc function is sinc(x) = sin(πx) / (πx). At x = 0 the formula is 0 / 0, but the limit is 1, so sinc(0) = 1. It crosses zero at x = ±1, ±2, ±3 and so on, wiggling with smaller and smaller ripples that shrink like 1 / x. For example sinc(0.5) = 2 / π, about 0.64. Its total area is 1. Warning: some books define sinc(x) = sin(x) / x instead, with zeros at multiples of π, sometimes called Sa(x). Check which one your teacher uses. Sinc appears as the spectrum of a rectangular pulse in lesson 14 and in ideal reconstruction in lesson 18.

Real life example 1, power coming back: Load shedding ends at time t0. The voltage at your socket is roughly 311 cos(100πt + φ) u(t - t0): a sinusoid multiplied by a shifted step. Before t0 it is zero, after t0 it is the full 50 Hz wave. The IPS sees this step, notices the mains is back and switches over. Two of our bricks, step and sinusoid, describe the whole event in one line.

Real life example 2, a cricket shot and a charger: When the bat hits the ball, a huge force acts for about a millisecond. For the ball's motion, only the area under the force curve matters, the change in momentum, so physicists and engineers model the hit as an impulse with that area. Meanwhile, the capacitor in your phone charger, after you plug it in, charges like V (1 - e^(-t/RC)) u(t): a step minus a decaying exponential. After one time constant RC it reaches about 63.2 percent of V. Impulses and exponentials are not just textbook toys.

Common mistakes: Writing the height of δ(t) as 1 instead of remembering that 1 is its area. Using the sifting property without checking that t0 lies inside the integration limits. Mixing up rad/s and Hz, so saying cos(100πt) is 100π Hz instead of 50 Hz. Forgetting the 1/|a| when an impulse is scaled, as in δ(2t). And sketching u(t - 3) at t = -3 instead of t = 3: the step turns on when the bracket becomes zero.

What exams ask: Sketch signals like u(t) - u(t - 2), 2 r(t - 1) or e^(-t) u(t). Write a given staircase or triangle graph using steps and ramps. Evaluate integrals with δ like ∫ e^(-t) δ(t - 1) dt. Find amplitude, frequency, period and phase of a given sinusoid. Prove du/dt = δ(t) or r'(t) = u(t). Write a damped sinusoid as the real part of a complex exponential. These are quick marks if you have practised the rules here.

Recap: u(t) switches on, r(t) = t u(t) climbs with slope 1 and dr/dt = u. Pulses are differences of steps. δ(t) has area 1, lives only at 0, sifts out values with ∫ x(t) δ(t - t0) dt = x(t0), and equals du/dt. Real exponentials decay or grow with time constant 1/|a|. A cos(ω0 t + φ) has f0 = ω0 / 2π and phase φ. e^(jω0 t) is a spinning arrow, and e^(st) covers sinusoids, exponentials and damped sinusoids together. sinc(x) = sin(πx) / (πx). Next lesson, we build the discrete-time versions of these bricks.
key_points: u(t) = 0 for t < 0 and 1 for t > 0; multiplying by u(t) makes a signal start at t = 0.
r(t) = t u(t), and dr/dt = u(t); pulses are differences of steps, e.g. u(t) - u(t - 2).
δ(t) has zero width and area 1; sifting: ∫ x(t) δ(t - t0) dt = x(t0); and δ(t) = du/dt.
Scaling: δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|; an impulse outside the integration limits contributes 0.
C e^(at) decays for a < 0 with time constant 1/|a|; after one time constant about 36.8% remains.
A cos(ω0 t + φ): amplitude A, f0 = ω0/2π Hz, T0 = 1/f0, phase φ (a time shift of φ/ω0).
e^(st) with s = σ + jω gives sinusoids, exponentials and damped sinusoids; sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx), zeros at nonzero integers.
lessons.tip: Keep a one-page "brick sheet" with a small sketch and the key formula of each basic signal. Before every later lesson, glance at it for one minute; most big formulas in this course are just these bricks in disguise.
lessons.task: On graph paper, sketch x(t) = r(t) - r(t - 2) - 2u(t - 3) for t from -1 to 5, then write its value at t = 1, 2.5 and 4. Next, on a free online graphing calculator such as Desmos, plot e^(-0.5t) cos(4t) for t ≥ 0 and mark where the envelope falls to 37 percent.

quiz.q: What is ∫ (t² + 1) δ(t - 2) dt over all t?
quiz.explain: By the sifting property the impulse picks out the value at t = 2: 2² + 1 = 5.

quiz.q: The derivative of the unit ramp r(t) is:
quiz.explain: r(t) has slope 0 for t < 0 and slope 1 for t > 0, which is exactly u(t).

quiz.q: What is the frequency in hertz of 5 cos(100πt + π/3)?
With sinc(x) = sin(πx) / (πx), where is the first positive zero?
quiz.explain: sin(πx) is zero at whole numbers, and sinc(0) = 1, so the first positive zero is at x = 1.

quiz.q: The signal 3 [u(t - 1) - u(t - 4)] is:
options: A pulse of height 3 from t = 1 to t = 4
A pulse of height 1 from t = 3 to t = 4
A ramp that starts at t = 1
A pulse of height 3 from t = -4 to t = -1
quiz.explain: u(t - 1) switches on at t = 1 and u(t - 4) switches it off at t = 4; the factor 3 sets the height.

lessons.title: Basic Discrete-Time Signals
lessons.content:
Watch a cricket match on TV and look at the corner of the screen. The score does not change smoothly like water flowing. It jumps once per ball: 0, 4, 4, 5, 11. Between two balls there is nothing to update. That list of numbers, one per ball, is a discrete-time signal. Your bKash balance at the end of each day, the number of passengers on each trip of a bus, and every sample stored in a music file are the same kind of thing. In this lesson we build the basic bricks of the discrete-time world, the cousins of the step, impulse, exponential and sinusoid from the last lesson.

What a discrete-time signal is: A discrete-time signal x[n] is just a list of numbers, one for each integer n. It is also called a sequence. Often it comes from sampling a continuous signal every T seconds, x[n] = x(nT), but it can also be naturally discrete, like daily prices. On paper we often write a short sequence as a list with a small arrow under the n = 0 value. For example x[n] = {2, -1, 3} with the arrow under 2 means x[0] = 2, x[1] = -1, x[2] = 3, and zero everywhere else.

The unit sample: The simplest discrete signal is the unit sample, or discrete impulse, δ[n]. It equals 1 at n = 0 and 0 at every other n. That is all. Unlike the continuous impulse δ(t), which is an infinitely tall, infinitely thin idea, δ[n] is a perfectly ordinary sequence with height 1. No limits, no generalized functions. The shifted version δ[n - 3] is 1 at n = 3 and 0 elsewhere. Remember the rule: the spike sits where the bracket becomes zero.

Sampling and sifting in discrete time: Multiplying a sequence by δ[n - k] keeps only the value at n = k: x[n] δ[n - k] = x[k] δ[n - k]. Adding up over all n gives the discrete sifting property: Σ x[n] δ[n - k] = x[k]. For example, Σ n² δ[n - 3] over all n is 3² = 9. It is the same idea as in continuous time, but with sums instead of integrals, and it is much easier because there is no infinity hiding inside δ[n].

The unit step: The discrete unit step u[n] is 1 for n ≥ 0 and 0 for n < 0. Notice that u[0] = 1, clearly defined, with none of the arguments we had about u(0) in continuous time. The shifted step u[n - 2] is 0 for n < 2 and 1 from n = 2 onwards. As before, multiplying any sequence by u[n] makes it start at n = 0, which gives us causal sequences.

Impulse and step are partners again: In continuous time, δ was the derivative of u. In discrete time we cannot take derivatives, but we can take differences. The first difference of the step is u[n] - u[n - 1]. Check: at n = -1 it is 0 - 0 = 0, at n = 0 it is 1 - 0 = 1, and at n = 1 it is 1 - 1 = 0. So δ[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1]. Going the other way, a running sum plays the role of an integral: u[n] = Σ δ[k] for k from -∞ to n, which can also be written u[n] = Σ δ[n - k] for k from 0 to ∞. The step is a pile of impulses, one at every n ≥ 0.

Pulses and ramps: A discrete pulse is a difference of steps. u[n] - u[n - 4] is 1 for n = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 0 elsewhere. Careful: that is four samples, not three. It switches on at 0 and off at 4, so the last 1 is at n = 3. The discrete ramp is r[n] = n u[n], giving 0, 1, 2, 3, ... for n ≥ 0. Its first difference r[n] - r[n - 1] is u[n - 1], a step that starts at n = 1, which is a small trap many students fall into.

Real exponentials: The sequence x[n] = a^n u[n] is the discrete version of e^(at). It behaves in four different ways depending on a. If 0 < a < 1 it decays: 0.5^n gives 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125. If a > 1 it grows: 2^n gives 1, 2, 4, 8. If -1 < a < 0 it decays while flipping sign every step: (-0.5)^n gives 1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125. If a < -1 it flips and grows: (-2)^n gives 1, -2, 4, -8. So |a| decides whether the size shrinks or grows, and the sign of a decides whether it alternates. Also a = 1 gives the step, and a = -1 gives 1, -1, 1, -1 forever.

A discrete exponential you know: Put 1000 taka in a savings account with 5 percent interest per year. After n years the balance is 1000 x 1.05^n, a growing exponential with a = 1.05. After 10 years it is about 1628.89 taka. This is a natural discrete-time signal: the bank only adds interest once per year, so there is no meaning to the balance at year 2.5 in this model. Decaying exponentials like 0.9^n appear as the echo of a moving average filter or the response of many digital systems, as you will see in the convolution lessons.

Discrete sinusoids and complex exponentials: The discrete sinusoid is x[n] = A cos(Ω0 n + φ), and the discrete complex exponential is e^(jΩ0 n) = cos(Ω0 n) + j sin(Ω0 n). Here Ω0 is the discrete frequency, measured in radians per sample, not radians per second. When x[n] comes from sampling cos(ω0 t) every T seconds, Ω0 = ω0 T = 2π f0 / fs, where fs = 1/T is the sampling rate. We use a capital Ω for discrete frequency and a small ω for continuous frequency so we never mix them up.

Worked sampling example: A 1 kHz tone sampled at 8 kHz, like in a phone call, gives Ω0 = 2π x 1000 / 8000 = π/4. So x[n] = cos(πn/4). From lesson 2, Ω0 / 2π = 1/8, so its period is N = 8 samples. That makes sense: 8000 samples per second divided by 1000 cycles per second is 8 samples in every cycle. The samples are 1, 0.707, 0, -0.707, -1, -0.707, 0, 0.707, and then it repeats.

Why discrete frequency repeats every 2π: Here is the most important new idea of this lesson. Add 2π to the frequency: e^(j(Ω0 + 2π)n) = e^(jΩ0 n) e^(j2πn). Since n is an integer, e^(j2πn) = 1, so the two sequences are identical. In continuous time, e^(jω t) and e^(j(ω + 2π)t) are different signals because t can be 0.5 or 0.1. In discrete time we only look at whole n, so the extra full turn is invisible. Example: cos(0.25πn) and cos(2.25πn) give exactly the same samples. This means we only need frequencies in one range of width 2π, usually -π < Ω ≤ π or 0 ≤ Ω < 2π.

Low and high frequency in discrete time: Ω = 0 gives a constant, the slowest possible sequence. As Ω increases towards π the sequence wiggles faster and faster. At Ω = π we get cos(πn) = (-1)^n: 1, -1, 1, -1, which is the fastest a sequence can possibly change, flipping every sample. Then, surprisingly, from π to 2π it gets slower again. cos(1.9πn) is exactly the same as cos(0.1πn), a slow wave. So in discrete time, frequencies near 0 or 2π are "low", and frequencies near π are "high". This is the seed of aliasing, which we study properly in lesson 18.

A quick reminder on periodicity: From lesson 2, cos(Ω0 n) is periodic only if Ω0 / 2π is a rational number m/N, and then the period is N after reducing the fraction. So cos(πn/4) repeats every 8 samples, but cos(n) never repeats. Combined with the 2π rule, discrete sinusoids are a bit strange compared to continuous ones: some never repeat, and many different-looking frequencies give exactly the same sequence. Keep both facts together in your head.

Any sequence as a sum of shifted impulses: Here is a simple idea with huge consequences. Any sequence can be written as a sum of shifted, scaled unit samples: x[n] = Σ x[k] δ[n - k], summing over all k. Each term places the value x[k] at position k and zero elsewhere. Example: x = {2, -1, 3} starting at n = 0 is 2δ[n] - δ[n - 1] + 3δ[n - 2]. Check at n = 1: the first and last terms are 0, the middle one gives -1. Correct.

Why the impulse sum matters: More examples: u[n] - u[n - 3] = δ[n] + δ[n - 1] + δ[n - 2], and 0.5^n for n = 0 to 3 is δ[n] + 0.5δ[n - 1] + 0.25δ[n - 2] + 0.125δ[n - 3]. This looks like simple bookkeeping now, but in lesson 8 it becomes the key that unlocks everything. If we know how a linear time-invariant system responds to one δ[n], then by writing any input as a sum of impulses, we can find the response to any input. That idea is called convolution.

Continuous versus discrete, side by side: δ(t) is an infinitely tall idea with area 1; δ[n] is an ordinary spike of height 1. u(0) is unclear; u[0] = 1. δ(t) = du/dt; δ[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1]. Integrals become sums. Sampling e^(-bt) gives (e^(-bT))^n, an a^n with a = e^(-bT), so decaying in continuous time (b > 0) means |a| < 1 in discrete time. Every frequency ω is different in continuous time; discrete frequencies repeat every 2π. Making this little comparison table yourself is one of the best ways to prepare for the exam.

Real life example 1, a phone call and a sneaky tone: In a call, sound is sampled at 8 kHz. A 1 kHz tone becomes cos(πn/4). Now imagine a 9 kHz whistle reaching the microphone with no filter in front. Its discrete frequency is 2π x 9000 / 8000 = 2.25π, and we just learned that cos(2.25πn) is the same as cos(0.25πn). So the phone records the 9 kHz whistle as a 1 kHz tone! The numbers cannot tell them apart. That is why phones filter out high frequencies before sampling. Lesson 18 explains this fully.

Real life example 2, money and medicine: A Grameenphone package that renews every month, a weekly bazar budget, and a savings account are all naturally discrete. If you save 500 taka each month starting at month 0, the deposit signal is 500 u[n], and the total saved is a ramp: 500 (n + 1) after month n. If instead a loan grows by 2 percent each month, it is an exponential C x 1.02^n. Even medicine levels are sometimes modelled this way: if the body removes half the drug each day, the amount left is a decaying exponential, D x 0.5^n.

Common mistakes: Writing u[n] - u[n - 4] as three samples instead of four. Writing the spike of δ[n - 3] at n = -3. Thinking δ[n] has infinite height like δ(t). Forgetting that n must be an integer and drawing a smooth curve through the dots as if it were the signal. Treating cos(2.25πn) as a faster signal than cos(0.25πn). And mixing Ω in radians per sample with ω in radians per second, or with f in hertz. Always draw discrete signals as lollipops: a vertical line with a dot on top at each integer.

What exams ask: Sketch sequences like δ[n + 1], u[n - 2], u[n] - u[n - 5] or 0.8^n u[n]. Show that δ[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1] and u[n] = Σ δ[n - k]. Write a given finite sequence as a sum of shifted impulses. Classify a^n u[n] as growing, decaying or alternating for given a. Find Ω0 when a tone of f0 hertz is sampled at fs hertz. Show that discrete frequencies Ω and Ω + 2π give the same sequence, or that cos(πn) = (-1)^n is the fastest discrete oscillation.

Recap: A discrete-time signal x[n] is a list of numbers at integer n. δ[n] is 1 only at n = 0 and sifts values with Σ x[n] δ[n - k] = x[k]. u[n] is 1 for n ≥ 0, and δ[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1]. a^n u[n] decays if |a| < 1, grows if |a| > 1, and alternates if a < 0. Discrete frequency Ω is in radians per sample, Ω = 2π f0 / fs, and it repeats every 2π, with Ω = π the fastest. Every sequence is Σ x[k] δ[n - k], which leads to convolution. Next lesson: shifting, flipping and stretching signals.
key_points: A discrete-time signal x[n] is a sequence defined only at integer n; drawn as lollipops.
δ[n] is 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere (an ordinary sequence); Σ x[n] δ[n - k] = x[k].
u[n] is 1 for n ≥ 0 (u[0] = 1); δ[n] = u[n] - u[n - 1] and u[n] = Σ δ[n - k] for k ≥ 0.
a^n u[n] decays if |a| < 1, grows if |a| > 1, alternates in sign if a < 0; e.g. (-0.5)^n: 1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125.
Discrete frequency Ω is in radians per sample: Ω = 2π f0 / fs; a 1 kHz tone at 8 kHz gives cos(πn/4).
e^(j(Ω + 2π)n) = e^(jΩn): discrete frequencies repeat every 2π; Ω = π gives (-1)^n, the fastest oscillation.
Any sequence is x[n] = Σ x[k] δ[n - k], e.g. {2, -1, 3} = 2δ[n] - δ[n - 1] + 3δ[n - 2].
lessons.tip: Always draw discrete signals as lollipops on integer ticks, never as smooth curves. The habit alone prevents half of the classic mistakes, like off-by-one pulse lengths and wrong spike positions.
lessons.task: With a phone calculator, write the first 8 samples of cos(πn/4) and of cos(2.25πn) for n = 0 to 7 and check they match. Then draw lollipop plots of 0.8^n u[n] and (-0.8)^n u[n] for n = 0 to 6, and write {1, 3, -2, 4} (starting at n = 0) as a sum of shifted impulses.

quiz.q: Which relation is correct?
quiz.explain: The first difference of the step is 1 only at n = 0, which is exactly δ[n].

quiz.q: What are the first four values of (-0.5)^n u[n] for n = 0, 1, 2, 3?
quiz.explain: (-0.5)^0 = 1, then each step multiplies by -0.5, so the sign alternates and the size halves.

quiz.q: The sequence cos(2.25πn) is identical to:
quiz.explain: 2.25π = 0.25π + 2π, and adding 2π to a discrete frequency does not change the samples.

quiz.q: Which discrete frequency gives the fastest possible oscillation?
quiz.explain: cos(πn) = (-1)^n flips every sample. Ω = 0 and 2π give a constant, and 3π/2 behaves like π/2.

quiz.q: How is x = {2, -1, 3} (for n = 0, 1, 2) written as shifted impulses?
quiz.explain: Each value x[k] sits at position k, so we need x[k] δ[n - k] for k = 0, 1, 2.

lessons.title: Operations on Signals
lessons.content:
Open any video editing app on your phone. You can turn the volume up, mix in background music, cut out a part, play it at double speed, play it backwards, or start it two seconds later. Every one of those buttons is an operation on a signal. In this lesson we learn the maths behind them: how to scale, add and multiply signals, and how to shift, flip and stretch them in time. These operations look easy, but combining them in the right order is one of the most common exam questions, so we will go slowly and check every step.

Two families of operations: Some operations change the values of the signal, the vertical axis: amplitude scaling, addition and multiplication. Others change the time axis, the horizontal axis: shifting, reversal and scaling. Value operations are easy because they work point by point. Time operations need more care, because they move the whole shape around, and our brains often move it the wrong way. Keep these two families separate in your head.

Amplitude scaling: y(t) = c x(t) multiplies every value by the same constant c. If c = 3 the signal becomes three times taller, like turning up the volume knob or an amplifier with gain 3. If 0 < c < 1 it shrinks. If c is negative the signal is also flipped upside down, so -x(t) is a mirror image across the time axis. The shape in time does not change at all: where x(t) is zero, y(t) is still zero. The same works for discrete signals: y[n] = c x[n].

Addition: y(t) = x1(t) + x2(t) adds the two values at each instant. A singer's voice plus the tabla gives the song you hear. A clean signal plus noise gives what the microphone actually records. Worked: u(t) + (-u(t - 2)) is 1 between 0 and 2 and 0 elsewhere, so adding a step and a negative shifted step makes a pulse. In discrete time, {1, 2, 3} + {4, 0, -1} (both starting at n = 0) is {5, 2, 2}, value by value.

Multiplication: y(t) = x1(t) x2(t) multiplies the two values at each instant. Multiplying by a pulse acts like a gate or a window: x(t) [u(t) - u(t - 3)] keeps x only between 0 and 3 and makes it zero elsewhere. Multiplying by u(t) chops off everything before zero. Multiplying a sound by a fast sinusoid is the idea behind AM radio, called modulation, which you will study in Data Communication. In discrete time, {1, 2, 3} times {4, 0, -1} is {4, 0, -3}.

Our test signal: To see what time operations do, we need a signal that is not symmetric, so we can tell left from right. Let x(t) = t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2, and x(t) = 0 elsewhere. It is a ramp piece: it starts at 0 at t = 0, climbs to 2 at t = 2, and then drops straight back to 0. So we know the low end is at t = 0 and the high end is at t = 2. We will track these two key points through every operation.

Time shifting: y(t) = x(t - t0). If t0 > 0 the signal moves right, which means it happens later: a delay. If t0 < 0 it moves left: an advance. Take y(t) = x(t - 3). The low end was where the bracket is 0, so now t - 3 = 0, t = 3. The high end needs t - 3 = 2, so t = 5. The ramp now lives between 3 and 5. Check one point: y(4) = x(1) = 1. Similarly x(t + 1) lives between -1 and 1. Many students think "minus means left", but it is the other way round: minus means delay, which is right.

Time reversal: y(t) = x(-t) mirrors the signal across the vertical axis at t = 0, like playing a recording backwards. For our ramp, -t must be between 0 and 2, so t is between -2 and 0. The high end, x(2), now appears at t = -2, and the low end at t = 0. So x(-t) is a ramp that falls from 2 at t = -2 to 0 at t = 0. An even signal does not change under reversal, and an odd signal just flips sign, which connects back to lesson 2.

Time scaling: y(t) = x(at) with a > 0. If a > 1 the signal is squeezed, it happens faster. If 0 < a < 1 it is stretched, it happens slower. For x(2t), we need 2t between 0 and 2, so t is between 0 and 1. The ramp now climbs from 0 to 2 in just 1 second. Check: y(1) = x(2) = 2. For x(t/2), t/2 between 0 and 2 means t between 0 and 4, so the ramp takes 4 seconds. Notice that the heights never change, only the widths. The point at t = 0 stays put, because a x 0 = 0.

Combined operations, the rule: Most exam questions mix operations, like y(t) = x(at - b). There are two safe orders. Method one: shift first, then scale. Let v(t) = x(t - b), then y(t) = v(at). Method two: scale first, then shift, but by b/a, not by b, because x(at - b) = x(a(t - b/a)). The classic mistake is to scale first and then shift by b. If a is negative, the scaling step also includes a reversal.

Combined worked example, method one: Find y(t) = x(-2t + 4) for our ramp. Step 1, shift: v(t) = x(t + 4). The ramp moves left by 4 and lives between -4 and -2, with the low end at -4 and the high end at -2. Step 2, scale by -2: y(t) = v(-2t). This reverses and squeezes by 2. Points of v at -4 and -2 come from t = 2 and t = 1. So y lives between t = 1 and t = 2. Its value at t = 1 is x(-2 + 4) = x(2) = 2, at t = 1.5 it is x(1) = 1, and at t = 2 it is x(0) = 0. It is a falling ramp from 2 down to 0.

The key-point shortcut: Here is the fastest exam method. Take each key point of x, set the inside of the bracket equal to it, and solve for t. For x(-2t + 4): the low end needs -2t + 4 = 0, so t = 2. The high end needs -2t + 4 = 2, so t = 1. So the value 0 lands at t = 2 and the value 2 lands at t = 1, and the shape between them is still a straight line. This method never gets the order wrong, because you are not moving anything, you are just solving tiny equations.

The wrong way, to see the trap: Suppose you scale first: x(-2t) lives between -1 and 0. Then you shift right by 4, the b, and get something between 3 and 4. That is wrong; we know the answer is between 1 and 2. The correct shift after scaling is b/a = 4/2 = 2 to the right: x(-2(t - 2)), which moves the interval from [-1, 0] to [1, 2]. Correct. Always double-check one point by plugging in a value of t.

Discrete shifting and reversal: Let x[n] = {1, 2, 3} for n = 0, 1, 2. Then x[n - 2] is the same list moved right to n = 2, 3, 4. And x[-n] lives at n = -2, -1, 0, with x[-n] at n = -2 equal to x[2] = 3, so reading left to right we get 3, 2, 1. Combined: y[n] = x[2 - n]. At n = 0 it is x[2] = 3, at n = 1 it is x[1] = 2, at n = 2 it is x[0] = 1, so y = {3, 2, 1} for n = 0, 1, 2. In discrete time, shifts must be by whole numbers of samples.

Decimation, discrete compression: In discrete time, y[n] = x[2n] keeps every second sample and throws the rest away. Let x = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} for n = 0 to 5. Then y[0] = x[0] = 1, y[1] = x[2] = 3, y[2] = x[4] = 5, so y = {1, 3, 5}. The samples 2, 4 and 6 are gone forever. This is called decimation or downsampling by 2. Unlike continuous time scaling, which you can always undo, decimation can lose information.

Expansion, discrete stretching: The opposite is y[n] = x[n/2] when n is even, and 0 when n is odd, because x[1.5] does not exist. For x = {1, 2, 3}, the result is {1, 0, 2, 0, 3} for n = 0 to 4. This is called expansion or upsampling by 2. The zeros are placeholders; in practice a smoothing filter later fills them with sensible in-between values, which is called interpolation and belongs to Digital Signal Processing. Decimation after expansion gives back the original, but expansion after decimation does not.

Order of operations in short: Value operations, scaling the amplitude and adding a constant, can be done before or after time operations, they do not interfere. Among time operations, order matters. Safe recipe: write the bracket as a(t - t0), shift by t0, then scale by a, and if a is negative also reverse. Or simply use the key-point shortcut. In discrete time, always double-check with a small table of n and the bracket value, because non-integer brackets give no sample.

Real life example 1, the mosque loudspeaker echo: You stand 686 metres from a second loudspeaker that plays the same azan as the one right beside you. Sound travels at about 343 metres per second, so the far copy arrives 686 / 343 = 2 seconds later, and it is weaker. What you hear is roughly y(t) = x(t) + 0.5 x(t - 2): an addition, an amplitude scaling by 0.5 and a time shift by 2 seconds, all in one formula. Echo cancellers in phones and conference systems are built on exactly this model.

Real life example 2, a WhatsApp voice message: When you play a voice message at 2x speed, a 60-second message finishes in 30 seconds. The new signal is x(2t): time is squeezed by 2, and since every vibration happens twice as fast, the pitch also goes up unless the app corrects it. Playing at 1.5x is x(1.5t). Reversing a TikTok clip is x(-t). Trimming the first 3 seconds and starting the rest immediately is x(t + 3) u(t). Your phone does signal operations every day.

Common mistakes: Shifting the wrong way, thinking x(t - 3) moves left. Scaling first and then shifting by b instead of b/a. Changing the height when time scaling, which never happens. Forgetting that x[2n] throws samples away, or putting non-zero values at the odd positions of an expansion. Mixing up -x(t), which flips upside down, with x(-t), which flips left to right. And not checking a single point at the end, which would have caught every one of these errors in ten seconds.

What exams ask: Given a sketch of x(t), sketch x(t - 2), x(-t), x(2t), x(-t + 1), x(2t + 3) or x(-2t + 4). Given a short sequence x[n], list x[n - 3], x[-n], x[2 - n], x[2n] and x[n/2]. Sometimes they ask you to write a combined signal like 2x(t - 1) - x(t + 1) as a single sketch. Show the intermediate step or the key-point equations, label the time axis clearly, and check one point. Neat working wins full marks even when the sketch is a little rough.

Recap: Amplitude scaling c x(t), addition and multiplication act point by point. Time shift x(t - t0) delays to the right when t0 > 0. Reversal x(-t) mirrors around t = 0. Scaling x(at) squeezes for a > 1 and stretches for a < 1, without changing heights. For x(at - b), shift by b then scale by a, or scale then shift by b/a, or just solve the bracket for key points. In discrete time, x[2n] decimates and loses samples, and x[n/2] expands by inserting zeros. Next lesson: properties of systems.
key_points: Amplitude scaling, addition and multiplication act value by value; -x(t) flips upside down.
Time shift: x(t - t0) is delayed (moves right) for t0 > 0; x(t + t0) is advanced (moves left).
Time reversal x(-t) mirrors the signal about t = 0; time scaling x(at) squeezes for a > 1 and stretches for 0 < a < 1, heights unchanged.
For x(at - b): shift by b first then scale by a, or scale first then shift by b/a.
Key-point method: set the bracket equal to each key point of x and solve for t; e.g. x(-2t + 4) of a ramp on [0, 2] lives on [1, 2].
Decimation x[2n] keeps every second sample ({1,2,3,4,5,6} gives {1,3,5}) and can lose information.
Expansion x[n/2] inserts zeros at odd n ({1,2,3} gives {1,0,2,0,3}).
lessons.tip: For every combined time operation, write the two little key-point equations (bracket = start, bracket = end) before drawing anything. It takes fifteen seconds and almost never gets the order wrong.
lessons.task: Draw x(t) = t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 (zero elsewhere) on graph paper. Then sketch x(t + 1), x(-t + 1), x(t/2) and x(-2t + 4), using the key-point equations for each, and check one point of each by plugging in t. Finally, take {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and write x[2n], x[n/2] and x[3 - n].

quiz.q: x(t) is nonzero only for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Where is x(t - 3) nonzero?
quiz.explain: Solve t - 3 = 0 and t - 3 = 2 to get t = 3 and t = 5; a minus shift is a delay to the right.

quiz.q: x(t) is nonzero only for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Where is x(-2t + 4) nonzero?
quiz.explain: -2t + 4 = 0 gives t = 2, and -2t + 4 = 2 gives t = 1.
x[2n] picks x[0], x[2], x[4], which are 1, 3, 5.

quiz.q: To get x(at - b) by shifting first, the correct order is:
options: Shift by b, then scale by a
Scale by a, then shift by b
Shift by a, then scale by b
Reverse, then shift by b, with no scaling
quiz.explain: Let v(t) = x(t - b), then v(at) = x(at - b). If you scale first, the shift must be b/a.

quiz.q: Playing a voice message at 2x speed turns x(t) into:
quiz.explain: Twice as fast means everything happens in half the time, so time is squeezed: x(2t). 2x(t) would only make it louder.

lessons.title: System Properties I: Memory, Causality and Invertibility
lessons.content:
Think about two machines in a Dhaka shop. The first is a simple weighing scale. You put 2 kg of potatoes on it and it shows 2 kg, right now, nothing else.
