It does not care what was on it five minutes ago. The second is the shopkeeper's notebook of dues, the famous "baki khata". Every time you buy on credit, he adds the amount to your total. The number he tells you today depends on everything you bought last week and last month too. Both are systems: something goes in, something comes out. But they behave very differently. In this lesson we learn how to describe those differences with exact words that every engineer uses.

Why properties matter: In lessons 1 to 5 we met signals and learned to shift, flip and scale them. Now we turn to the box in the middle, the system. A system is any rule that takes an input signal x(t) or x[n] and gives an output signal y(t) or y[n]. There are millions of possible systems, so instead of studying each one alone, we sort them by a few yes-or-no properties. If you know a system's properties, you already know what tools you may use on it, and what you are not allowed to do. This is like knowing a cricketer is a left-arm spinner before he even bowls.

The six big properties: The classic list has six properties: memory, causality, invertibility, linearity, time invariance and stability. This lesson covers the first three. Lesson 7 covers linearity, time invariance and stability. For each property we will learn three things: the definition in plain words, a test you can do with pen and paper, and at least one counter-example. A single counter-example is enough to prove a system does NOT have a property. To prove it DOES have a property, you must show it works for every possible input, not just one you picked.

Memoryless systems: A system is memoryless (also called static) if the output at any time depends only on the input at that same time. In symbols, y(t) depends only on x(t), and y[n] depends only on x[n]. Examples: y(t) = 2x(t), y(t) = x(t)², y[n] = 3x[n] - 1, y(t) = cos(x(t)). The weighing scale is memoryless. A resistor is memoryless too: Ohm's law says v(t) = R i(t), so the voltage right now depends only on the current right now. The simplest memoryless system of all is the identity system y(t) = x(t), which just passes the signal through.

Systems with memory: A system has memory (also called dynamic) if the output at some time needs input values from other times, past or future. Examples: the delay y(t) = x(t - 2), which needs the input from 2 seconds ago; y[n] = x[n] + x[n-1], which needs the previous sample; and the accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] for k from minus infinity to n, which adds up the whole past. In circuits, a capacitor has memory: v(t) = (1/C) ∫ i(τ) dτ from minus infinity to t, so its voltage today depends on all the current that ever flowed into it. The baki khata is an accumulator, a system with memory.

The memory test: To test a system, look at the formula and ask, "to compute y at time t, which times of x do I need?" If the answer is only t itself, the system is memoryless. If any other time appears, even t + 1 or t - 0.001, it has memory. Be careful with hidden time. y(t) = x(2t) looks simple, but at t = 1 it needs x(2), a different time, so it has memory. At t = 0 it needs x(0), which is fine, but one bad time is enough. Similarly y[n] = x[-n] has memory, because at n = 3 it needs x[-3].

A tricky case: What about y(t) = t x(t)? The factor t is not an input value, it is just the clock time multiplying the input. To get y(5) you need only x(5), multiplied by 5. So this system is memoryless. Time-varying and memoryless can go together, as we will see in lesson 7. On the other hand, y(t) = x(t) + x(t - 0) is just 2x(t), memoryless, because t - 0 is the same time. Always simplify the formula before deciding.

Causality: A system is causal if the output at any time depends only on the input at the present time and the past, never on the future. A causal system cannot "see" what is coming. All real-time physical systems are causal: a microphone cannot react to a sound before it arrives, and a mobile call cannot send your words before you say them. Examples of causal systems: y(t) = x(t - 1), y[n] = x[n] + x[n-1], the accumulator, and every memoryless system. If a system is memoryless it is automatically causal, because it uses only the present. The reverse is not true: a delay is causal but has memory.

Non-causal systems: A system is non-causal if, for at least one time, the output needs a future input. Examples: y(t) = x(t + 1), which needs the input 1 second ahead; the centered moving average y[n] = (x[n-1] + x[n] + x[n+1]) / 3, which needs the next sample; and y[n] = x[-n]. For y[n] = x[-n], at n = -2 the output needs x[2], which is in the future compared to n = -2. So it is non-causal, even though for n = 3 it needs x[-3], which is in the past. One bad time is enough to break causality.

The causality test, worked: Take y(t) = x(t/2). At t = 4 it needs x(2), the past, fine. At t = -4 it needs x(-2), and -2 is later than -4, so that is the future. Non-causal. Now take y(t) = x(t) cos(t + 1). The cos(t + 1) part is just a known function of clock time, not a future input. y(t) needs only x(t), so the system is causal and memoryless. Rule: only look at the arguments inside x. Compare each argument with t for every possible t, including negative t, which is where students usually forget to check.

Why non-causal is still useful: Non-causal does not mean useless. If the whole signal is already recorded, the "future" samples are sitting in memory, so you can use them. Smoothing a recorded song, cleaning a photo, or fixing yesterday's stock price chart can all use non-causal systems. In images the variable is space, not time, so "left" and "right" pixels are both available and causality hardly matters. Only systems that must work live, like a hearing aid, a mobile call or the TV broadcast of a cricket match, must be causal. A small delay can turn some non-causal systems into causal ones: y[n] = x[n+1] delayed by one sample becomes y[n] = x[n].

Invertibility: A system is invertible if different inputs always give different outputs. Then, by looking at the output, you can always find out exactly which input caused it. If a system is invertible, there exists an inverse system which, connected after it, gives back the original input: x goes into the system, y comes out, y goes into the inverse, and x comes out again. The two together act like the identity system y = x. Encryption is the everyday version: bKash scrambles your PIN for sending, and the server must be able to unscramble it exactly.

Invertible examples: y(t) = 2x(t) + 3 is invertible, the inverse is x(t) = (y(t) - 3) / 2. The delay y(t) = x(t - 2) is invertible, the inverse is an advance, x(t) = y(t + 2). The accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] up to n is invertible, and its inverse is the first difference w[n] = y[n] - y[n-1]. Check: y[n] - y[n-1] removes everything except the newest term, which is x[n]. In continuous time, the running integral y(t) = ∫ x(τ) dτ from minus infinity to t is undone by a differentiator, x(t) = dy/dt.

Non-invertible examples: To show a system is NOT invertible, find two different inputs that give the same output. For y(t) = x(t)², the inputs x(t) = 2 and x(t) = -2 both give y(t) = 4, so the sign is lost forever. For y(t) = 0 for every input, all information is destroyed. For y[n] = x[2n], the output keeps only the even samples, so x[1], x[3] and all odd samples are thrown away: two inputs that differ only at odd n give the same output. For y(t) = cos(x(t)), the inputs 0 and 2π both give 1. Any system that squeezes many inputs into one output cannot be undone.

Worked mini-table: Let us test five systems on all three properties at once. y(t) = 5x(t): memoryless, causal, invertible. y[n] = x[n-3]: memory, causal, invertible. y[n] = x[n] + x[n+1]: memory, non-causal; it is also not invertible, because x[n] = (-1)^n gives x[n] + x[n+1] = 0 for every n, the same output as the zero input. y(t) = x(t)²: memoryless, causal, not invertible. y[n] = Σ x[k] up to n: memory, causal, invertible. Notice how the properties are independent: a system can be causal but not invertible, or have memory but still be invertible. Exams love such tables.

Real-life example 1, the IPS during load shedding: An IPS charges its battery while the grid is on and gives power when load shedding starts. Think of the battery charge as the output and the charging current as the input. The charge at 9 pm depends on all the current that flowed in since morning, so the system has memory, like the accumulator. It is causal, because the battery cannot charge from electricity that has not arrived yet. Is it invertible? If you record the charge level every second, you can find the charging current by looking at how fast the charge changes, which is the differentiator idea. In practice a full battery stops charging, which breaks this neat picture.

Real-life example 2, cricket on TV: When you watch a live match on TV, the picture reaches you a few seconds after the real ball, because of encoding and satellite delay. So the TV chain behaves like a delay system, y(t) = x(t - d) with d a few seconds: it has memory, it is causal, and it is invertible in principle. But the slow-motion replay with a smooth "ball tracking" line is made after the ball is bowled, using frames before and after each moment. That processing is non-causal, which is fine, because it runs on recorded footage. The same match, two systems, two different properties.

Common mistakes: First, students say "y(t) = x(2t) is memoryless because there is no delay." Wrong, check t = 1. Second, they forget negative times in the causality test; y(t) = x(t/2) looks causal for positive t but fails at negative t. Third, they think the time factor in y(t) = t x(t) is memory. It is not; only arguments inside x matter. Fourth, they try to prove invertibility with one example. One example can only disprove a property. Fifth, they mix up "has an inverse formula on some inputs" with "invertible on all inputs"; y = x² is invertible only if you promise the input is never negative.

What exams ask: A typical question gives four to six systems and asks you to mark each as memoryless or not, causal or not, invertible or not, with a reason. Write the reason in one line: "at t = 1, y(1) needs x(2), so it has memory and is non-causal." For invertibility, either give the inverse system or give two inputs with the same output. Some exams ask, "Is every memoryless system causal?" (yes) or "Is every causal system memoryless?" (no, a delay is a counter-example). Another favourite asks for the inverse of the accumulator, which is the first difference.

Looking ahead: These three properties come back again and again. In lesson 8 we will see that for LTI systems, all of them can be read straight from the impulse response h. A memoryless LTI system has h(t) = k δ(t). A causal LTI system has h(t) = 0 for t < 0. Invertibility becomes "can we find another impulse response that undoes this one", which is the idea behind echo cancellers in mobile phones. Keep the pen-and-paper tests in your head; they work for every system, linear or not.

Recap: A memoryless system uses only the present input; anything else means memory. A causal system uses only present and past input; one future value anywhere makes it non-causal, and you must check negative times too. Memoryless always implies causal, but not the other way round. An invertible system never maps two different inputs to the same output, so an inverse system can recover the input; to disprove invertibility, find two inputs that collide. Remember the weighing scale, the baki khata, and the live cricket feed, and these definitions will stay with you.
key_points: A system is memoryless if y at time t depends only on x at the same time t; otherwise it has memory.
Resistor (v = R i) is memoryless; capacitor (v = (1/C) ∫ i dτ) and the accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] have memory.
A system is causal if the output never depends on future inputs; check every t, including negative t.
Every memoryless system is causal, but a causal system (like a delay) can have memory.
Non-causal systems are fine for recorded data and images, but live systems must be causal.
A system is invertible if different inputs always give different outputs; then an inverse system recovers x.
Inverse pairs: delay and advance, accumulator and first difference y[n] - y[n-1], integrator and differentiator.
One counter-example disproves a property; to prove a property you must argue for all inputs.
lessons.tip: Make a habit of checking each system at three times: t = 1, t = 0 and t = -1. Most memory and causality mistakes appear at one of these three points, especially the negative one.
lessons.task: On paper, test these five systems for memory, causality and invertibility, with a one-line reason each: y(t) = 3x(t) - 1, y[n] = x[n-2], y(t) = x(-t), y[n] = x[n]² , y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1]. For each non-invertible one, write two different inputs that give the same output.

quiz.q: Which system is memoryless?
quiz.explain: y(t) = t x(t) needs only x at the same time t; the factor t is clock time, not another input value.

quiz.q: Why is y(t) = x(t/2) non-causal?
options: At t = -4 it needs x(-2), which is a future value
quiz.explain: For negative t, t/2 is later than t, so the output needs future input.

quiz.q: What is the inverse of the accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] for k up to n?
options: The first difference w[n] = y[n] - y[n-1]
quiz.explain: Subtracting consecutive outputs leaves only the newest input term x[n].

quiz.q: Which statement is always true?
options: A system with memory is non-causal
quiz.explain: Memoryless uses only the present, so it never needs the future; a delay shows the reverse is false.

quiz.q: How do you prove y(t) = x(t)² is NOT invertible?
options: Show inputs 2 and -2 give the same output 4
quiz.explain: Two different inputs with the same output means the input cannot be recovered.

lessons.title: System Properties II: Linearity, Time Invariance and Stability
lessons.content:
At a wedding in a community centre, the sound system man taps the microphone and says "hello, hello". If he speaks twice as loud, the speakers become twice as loud. If he speaks now or in ten minutes, the speakers behave the same way. And as long as he keeps his voice normal, the speakers stay calm. But then someone points the microphone at the speaker, and a terrible screech grows louder and louder until somebody pulls the plug. In one evening you have just met the three properties of this lesson: linearity, time invariance and stability. The screech is what an unstable system sounds like.

Where we are: In lesson 6 we learned memory, causality and invertibility. Now we finish the list of six with linearity, time invariance and BIBO stability. These three are the most important in the whole course. Systems that are both linear and time invariant are called LTI systems, and almost every tool you will meet later, convolution, Fourier, Laplace, Z-transform and frequency response, works only for LTI systems. So learning to test for these properties correctly is like learning to check the ticket before boarding a train: get it wrong and every later step goes to the wrong place.

Linearity, the idea: A system is linear if it obeys the superposition principle. In simple words: the response to a sum is the sum of the responses, and if you scale the input, the output scales by the same amount. Superposition has two parts. Additivity: if x1 gives y1 and x2 gives y2, then x1 + x2 must give y1 + y2. Homogeneity, also called scaling: if x gives y, then a x must give a y, for any constant a, even negative or complex. Combined into one line: a x1 + b x2 must give a y1 + b y2.

How to test linearity: Take two general inputs x1 and x2 with outputs y1 and y2 written from the formula. Then feed x3 = a x1 + b x2 into the system, compute y3 from the formula, and check whether y3 equals a y1 + b y2. Example, y(t) = 3x(t - 1). Then y3(t) = 3[a x1(t - 1) + b x2(t - 1)] = a·3x1(t - 1) + b·3x2(t - 1) = a y1(t) + b y2(t). Equal, so the system is linear. Do not test with numbers only like x = 1 and x = 2; one numerical check can disprove linearity but cannot prove it.

Zero-in, zero-out: There is a fast first check. Put a = 0 in the homogeneity rule: zero input must give zero output. If a system gives something non-zero when the input is zero everywhere, it cannot be linear. Example: y(t) = x(t) + 1. With x = 0 the output is 1, so it fails immediately. Be careful: passing this check does not prove linearity. y(t) = x(t)² gives 0 for zero input, yet it is not linear, as we will see. Zero-in zero-out is a quick filter for catching failures, not a proof.

Worked test, y = x²: Let x1 give x1² and x2 give x2². Feed x1 + x2: the output is (x1 + x2)² = x1² + 2x1x2 + x2². The extra 2x1x2 term spoils additivity. With numbers: x = 1 gives 1, x = 2 gives 4, but 2 times the input should give 2 times the output, which would be 2. So y = x² is non-linear. Any system with powers, products of inputs, absolute values, square roots, sin(x) or a constant added is usually non-linear. Multiplying x by something that does not depend on x, like t or cos(t), is still linear.

Worked test, y = x(t) + 1: Additivity: x1 + x2 gives x1 + x2 + 1, but y1 + y2 = x1 + x2 + 2. Not equal, so non-linear. This system is called incrementally linear: the difference between two outputs, y1 - y2 = x1 - x2, does follow a linear rule. Such a system is a linear system plus a fixed offset. Exam answers must still say "non-linear", because strict linearity fails. In the same family: y = 2x + 3, which looks like a straight line in school maths but is not linear in the systems sense.

Time invariance, the idea: A system is time invariant if its behaviour does not change with time. If you delay the input by t0, the output is delayed by exactly t0 and otherwise unchanged. A rickshaw puller's speed does not depend on whether you start at 8 am or 8 pm (ignoring traffic, of course). In symbols: if x(t) gives y(t), then x(t - t0) must give y(t - t0) for every t0. For discrete time, if x[n] gives y[n], then x[n - n0] must give y[n - n0] for every integer n0.

The shift test, step by step: Step 1, feed a shifted input x1(t) = x(t - t0) into the system and write its output y1(t) using the formula, replacing every x(something) with x1(something). Step 2, take the original output y(t) and shift it, writing y(t - t0), which means replacing every t with t - t0. Step 3, compare. If y1(t) = y(t - t0) for every input and every t0, the system is time invariant. The most common error is in step 1: you must only change x, not the t that appears outside x.

Worked test, y = t x(t): Step 1: x1(t) = x(t - t0) gives y1(t) = t x1(t) = t x(t - t0). Step 2: y(t - t0) = (t - t0) x(t - t0). Step 3: t x(t - t0) is not equal to (t - t0) x(t - t0). So the system is time-varying. Makes sense: the gain t keeps growing with clock time, so the same input at a later time gets a bigger gain. Is it linear? a x1 + b x2 gives t(a x1 + b x2) = a t x1 + b t x2. Yes, linear. Linear and time-varying, a very common exam pair.

Worked test, y[n] = x[2n]: This downsampler keeps every second sample. Step 1: x1[n] = x[n - n0] gives y1[n] = x1[2n] = x[2n - n0]. Step 2: y[n - n0] = x[2(n - n0)] = x[2n - 2n0]. Step 3: x[2n - n0] is not x[2n - 2n0]. Time-varying. Try n0 = 1: shifting the input by one sample changes which samples are kept, odd instead of even, so the output is a completely different set of numbers, not a shifted copy. It is linear though, because picking samples treats sums and scaling fairly. Time scaling of any kind, x(2t) or x(t/2), and time reversal x(-t) are time-varying.

Worked tests, y = x² and y = x + 1 for time invariance: For y = x², step 1 gives y1(t) = x1(t)² = x(t - t0)², step 2 gives y(t - t0) = x(t - t0)², equal, so time invariant. For y = x(t) + 1, step 1 gives x(t - t0) + 1, step 2 gives x(t - t0) + 1, equal, time invariant. So these two systems are non-linear but time invariant. Notice the pattern: if t appears only inside x, as x(t - something constant), and nowhere else, the system is usually time invariant. If t appears outside x, or multiplied inside x, be suspicious.

BIBO stability: BIBO means bounded input, bounded output. A system is BIBO stable if every bounded input gives a bounded output. A signal is bounded if there is a finite number B with |x(t)| ≤ B for all t. So the test is: assume |x| ≤ B, and try to find a finite number that |y| can never exceed. If you succeed for every bounded input, the system is stable. If you can find even one bounded input that makes the output grow without limit, the system is unstable. The microphone screech at the wedding is the classic unstable case.

Stability worked tests: y = x²: if |x| ≤ B then |y| ≤ B², finite, so stable. y = x(t) + 1: |y| ≤ B + 1, stable. y[n] = x[2n]: it only picks values of x, so |y| ≤ B, stable. y = e^(x(t)): |y| ≤ e^B, stable. Now y = t x(t): take the bounded input x(t) = 1. The output is y(t) = t, which grows forever. Unstable. The accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] up to n: feed u[n], which is bounded by 1. The output is (n + 1) for n ≥ 0, which grows without limit. Unstable, even though it is linear and time invariant.

Summary table of the four test systems: y = x²: non-linear, time invariant, stable. y = t x(t): linear, time-varying, unstable. y[n] = x[2n]: linear, time-varying, stable. y = x(t) + 1: non-linear, time invariant, stable. Look how every combination appears. None of these four is LTI. A simple LTI example to compare: y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1]) / 2, the two-point average. It is linear, time invariant, and stable, because |y| ≤ (B + B)/2 = B. That is the kind of system we will love for the rest of the course.

Real-life example 1, the mosque loudspeaker: The loudspeaker system at a mosque is designed to be close to linear: the imam's voice, twice as loud, comes out twice as loud. But if the amplifier is pushed too hard, the output clips at the maximum voltage, and the system becomes non-linear, which you hear as a harsh, broken sound. The system is also roughly time invariant: Fajr and Maghrib azan go through the same chain. If the microphone is too close to a loudspeaker, sound loops round and round, getting louder each trip. That feedback loop is unstable, and the howl is the output running away.

Real-life example 2, savings with interest: Suppose a bank adds 1% interest every month and you deposit x[n] taka in month n. The balance follows y[n] = 1.01 y[n-1] + x[n]. This is linear and time invariant, because the rule is the same every month. But it is unstable in the BIBO sense: deposit just 100 taka once, and with no more deposits the balance keeps growing as 100 × 1.01^n, without any limit. For your savings this is happy news; for an electronic circuit the same behaviour would mean an output that blows up. Mathematically they are the same kind of system.

Common mistakes: First, applying the shift to t outside x in step 1 of the shift test. In y = t x(t), the shifted input gives t x(t - t0), not (t - t0) x(t - t0). Second, thinking y = 2x + 3 is linear because its graph is a straight line. Third, testing stability with only one nice input like x = 0 and declaring "stable". You must think about all bounded inputs. Fourth, thinking LTI means stable. The accumulator is LTI and unstable. Fifth, thinking time scaling like x(2t) is time invariant because there is "no t outside". The 2 inside makes it time-varying.

What exams ask: The classic question lists four to eight systems and asks you to check each for memory, causality, linearity, time invariance and stability, sometimes invertibility too, in a table. Show the superposition line for linearity, the three-step shift test for time invariance, and either a bound like |y| ≤ B² or a bounded input that breaks it. Short theory questions: "Define BIBO stability", "Is the accumulator stable?" (no), "Is y = x + 1 linear?" (no, it is incrementally linear). Write the counter-example clearly, because that is where the marks are.

Looking ahead: Once a system is known to be LTI, a single test signal tells us everything about it. That signal is the impulse, and its output is the impulse response h. Lesson 8 shows why, and lessons 9 and 10 turn this idea into convolution. In lesson 11 we will get a neat stability rule for LTI systems: stable if and only if ∫ |h(t)| dt is finite, or Σ |h[n]| is finite in discrete time. You will see the accumulator fail that test, since its h[n] = u[n] adds up to infinity.

Recap: Linear means superposition, additivity plus homogeneity; zero input must give zero output, so adding a constant breaks linearity, and squaring breaks it too. Time invariant means a delayed input gives an equally delayed output; use the three-step shift test, and watch for t outside x and for time scaling. BIBO stable means every bounded input gives a bounded output; prove it with a bound, disprove it with one bounded input that runs away. Linear and time invariant together make LTI, the star of this course. Remember the wedding microphone: loud is fine, howling is not.
key_points: Linear = additivity + homogeneity: a x1 + b x2 must give a y1 + b y2.
Zero-in zero-out is a quick check: y = x + 1 fails it, so it is non-linear (incrementally linear).
y = x² is non-linear because (x1 + x2)² has the extra 2x1x2 term.
Time invariant: x(t - t0) must give y(t - t0); in step 1 shift only the argument of x, never the t outside.
y = t x(t) and y[n] = x[2n] are linear but time-varying; y = x² and y = x + 1 are non-linear but time invariant.
BIBO stable: every bounded input (|x| ≤ B) gives a bounded output.
y = t x(t) and the accumulator are unstable: x = 1 or u[n] gives an output that grows forever.
LTI = linear + time invariant; LTI does not automatically mean stable.
lessons.tip: Keep a small card with the four test systems (x², t x(t), x[2n], x + 1) and their answers. Before an exam, redo all four from memory; if you can, almost any system in the question paper will fall into place.
lessons.task: Test these on paper for linearity, time invariance and BIBO stability: y(t) = x(t) cos(5t), y[n] = x[n] - x[n-1], y(t) = |x(t)|, y(t) = x(-t). For one of them, also check with numbers: pick x = [1, 2, 3] and x = [0, 1, 0], compute outputs, and see if adding the inputs adds the outputs.

quiz.q: Why is y(t) = x(t) + 1 not linear?
quiz.explain: A linear system must give zero output for zero input; the added constant breaks this.

quiz.q: y(t) = t x(t) is:
quiz.explain: Superposition holds, but a shifted input gives t x(t - t0), which is not (t - t0) x(t - t0).

quiz.q: In the shift test for y[n] = x[2n], the shifted input x[n - n0] gives:
quiz.explain: Replace x by x1[n] = x[n - n0], so x1[2n] = x[2n - n0], which differs from y[n - n0] = x[2n - 2n0].

quiz.q: Which system is BIBO unstable?
options: The accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] for k up to n
quiz.explain: Input u[n] is bounded, but the output n + 1 grows without limit.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: A system can be linear and time-varying
Time scaling x(2t) is time invariant
quiz.explain: y = t x(t) and y[n] = x[2n] are both linear yet time-varying; the other statements are false.

lessons.title: LTI Systems and the Impulse Response
lessons.content:
Walk into a big empty hall, like a community centre before the wedding guests arrive, and clap your hands once. You hear the clap, then a few quick echoes from the walls, then a soft ringing that fades away. That tiny sound pattern is like the hall's fingerprint. Record that one clap carefully and you can predict how any song, speech or azan will sound in that hall, without ever playing it there. In signals and systems that clap is called an impulse, and the hall's reply is called the impulse response. This lesson explains why one reply is enough.

Why LTI is special: In lessons 6 and 7 we learned six properties. Two of them, linearity and time invariance, team up to give a superpower. A linear system lets us break an input into pieces, push each piece through separately, and add the results. A time invariant system reacts the same way to a piece whether it comes now or later, just shifted. Put them together and we only need to know the response to one simple piece. Every input can be built from that piece, so every output can be built from its response. For non-LTI systems this trick fails, as we will see.

The building block, the impulse: Recall from lessons 3 and 4. In discrete time, the unit impulse δ[n] is 1 at n = 0 and 0 everywhere else. A shifted impulse δ[n - k] is 1 only at n = k. In continuous time, δ(t) is a pulse that is infinitely narrow and infinitely tall with area 1, and it has the sifting property: ∫ x(τ) δ(t - τ) dτ = x(t). The impulse is the simplest possible "tap" on a system: a single instant of input and nothing else, like one clap or one raindrop.

Impulse response, definition: The impulse response of a system is its output when the input is the unit impulse and the system starts at rest, meaning all its stored energy or memory is zero before the impulse arrives. We write h[n] in discrete time and h(t) in continuous time. In words, h is "what the system does when you tap it once". For an LTI system, h is a complete description. Two LTI systems with the same h are the same system, even if their circuits look totally different inside.

Any input as a sum of impulses: Take a short sequence x[n] with x[0] = 2, x[1] = 1, x[2] = 3, and zero elsewhere. We can write it as x[n] = 2δ[n] + 1δ[n - 1] + 3δ[n - 2]. Each term is one impulse placed at one time and scaled by the value there. In general, x[n] = Σ x[k] δ[n - k], summing over all k. Any sequence at all can be written this way. It is like writing a number in place value: 213 = 2×100 + 1×10 + 3×1. The impulses are the place values of a signal.

From input pieces to output pieces: Now push each piece through an LTI system with impulse response h. By definition, δ[n] gives h[n]. By time invariance, δ[n - k] gives h[n - k], the same reply just shifted to start at time k. By homogeneity, x[k] δ[n - k] gives x[k] h[n - k], the shifted reply scaled by the input value. By additivity, the sum of all pieces gives the sum of all replies. So y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k], summing over all k. This formula is the convolution sum, written y[n] = x[n] * h[n]. The star here means convolution, not multiplication.

Worked example, a simple echo: Let a system add a half-strength echo one step later, so h[n] = δ[n] + 0.5δ[n - 1], that is h = [1, 0.5]. Input x[n] = 2δ[n] + δ[n - 1], that is x = [2, 1]. The impulse at n = 0 with weight 2 gives 2h[n] = [2, 1, 0]. The impulse at n = 1 with weight 1 gives h[n - 1] = [0, 1, 0.5]. Add them: y = [2, 2, 0.5] at n = 0, 1, 2. Check by thinking: at n = 1 we hear the new sample 1 plus the echo of the old sample, 0.5 × 2 = 1, total 2. Correct.

Worked example, a three-tap system: Let h = [1, 1, 1] at n = 0, 1, 2, and x = [1, 2, 3] at n = 0, 1, 2. Piece one: 1 × h[n] = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]. Piece two: 2 × h[n - 1] = [0, 2, 2, 2, 0]. Piece three: 3 × h[n - 2] = [0, 0, 3, 3, 3]. Add column by column: y = [1, 3, 6, 5, 3] for n = 0 to 4. Notice the output has 5 samples, which is 3 + 3 - 1. Also the sum of y is 18, which is the sum of x (6) times the sum of h (3). Both are handy checks that lesson 9 will use a lot.

Two ways to read the sum: The method above is the input side view: each input sample sends out its own scaled copy of h, and we add all the copies. The output side view picks one output time and asks which inputs reach it. For n = 2 in the last example, y[2] = x[0]h[2] + x[1]h[1] + x[2]h[0] = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Notice h is used backwards: the newest input meets h[0] and older inputs meet later parts of h. This backwards use is why convolution is often explained as "flip and slide", which is the main topic of lesson 9.

The continuous-time version: The same story works for continuous signals. Imagine slicing x(t) into very thin rectangles, each of width Δ. Each thin rectangle is almost an impulse of area x(kΔ)Δ located at time kΔ. As Δ shrinks to zero, the staircase becomes the signal, and the sum becomes an integral: x(t) = ∫ x(τ) δ(t - τ) dτ, which is just the sifting property. Each piece produces x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ, and adding all pieces gives y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ. This is the convolution integral, y(t) = x(t) * h(t), the topic of lesson 10.

A gallery of impulse responses: The identity system has h[n] = δ[n]. A pure gain k has h = k δ. A delay by T has h(t) = δ(t - T). The accumulator y[n] = Σ x[k] up to n has h[n] = u[n], since a single tap is remembered forever. The first difference y[n] = x[n] - x[n - 1] has h[n] = δ[n] - δ[n - 1]. The three-point moving average y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2]) / 3 has h = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]. The integrator has h(t) = u(t). And the RC low-pass circuit, which lesson 12 derives, has h(t) = (1/RC) e^(-t/RC) u(t), a decaying exponential.

Reading properties from h: For LTI systems, the properties of lessons 6 and 7 can be read straight off h. Memoryless if and only if h is k δ, a single spike at zero, because any other value of h mixes in other times. Causal if and only if h[n] = 0 for n < 0, or h(t) = 0 for t < 0, because a non-zero value at negative time would mean the system replies before it is tapped. BIBO stable if and only if Σ |h[n]| is finite, or ∫ |h(t)| dt is finite. The accumulator's h = u[n] sums to infinity, which matches what we found in lesson 7: unstable. Lesson 11 proves these rules.

The step response: Sometimes it is easier to feed a step u[n] than an impulse, for example switching on a supply. The output is called the step response s[n]. For LTI systems the two are tightly linked. Since u[n] = Σ δ[n - k] for k ≥ 0, the step response is a running sum of h: s[n] = Σ h[k] for k from minus infinity to n. Going back, h[n] = s[n] - s[n - 1]. In continuous time, s(t) = ∫ h(τ) dτ up to t, and h(t) = ds/dt. For the echo h = [1, 0.5], the step response is s = [1, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5, ...]. For the RC circuit, s(t) = (1 - e^(-t/RC)) u(t).

Why the trick needs LTI: Take the squarer y[n] = x[n]². Feed δ[n]: the output is δ[n]² = δ[n], so its "impulse response" is δ[n], the same as the identity system! But feed 2δ[n] and you get 4δ[n], not 2δ[n]. So h does not describe it. Now take y[n] = n x[n], which is linear but time-varying. Feed δ[n]: output 0 × δ[n] = 0. Feed δ[n - 1]: output δ[n - 1], not zero. One impulse response cannot capture a system whose reply depends on when you tap it. So h is the complete story only when the system is both linear and time invariant.

Measuring h in practice: Real impulses do not exist, since nothing is infinitely narrow. But a pulse that is much shorter than the fastest change the system can make looks like an impulse to that system. Acoustic engineers pop a balloon in a concert hall. Electronics engineers send a very short voltage spike, or measure the step response and differentiate it, using h = ds/dt. In digital systems it is easiest of all: send the sequence 1, 0, 0, 0, ... and record what comes out. That record is h[n], exactly.

Real-life example 1, the hall and the azan: Suppose the loudspeaker of a mosque sits inside a large room, and the walls give echoes at about 0.05 s and 0.12 s, each weaker than the sound before. Record one balloon pop and you have h(t) of that room, roughly a spike, then two smaller spikes, then a fading tail. Now any voice x(t) going through that room comes out as x(t) * h(t): the voice, plus a weaker copy 0.05 s later, plus another 0.12 s later, plus the tail. Music apps use this idea, called convolution reverb, to make a bedroom recording sound like a big hall.

Real-life example 2, rain on a tin roof: During monsoon, each raindrop that hits a tin roof is like a tiny impulse. The roof "rings" for a moment after each hit, and that ringing pattern is the roof's impulse response h(t). A drop hitting at time τ with strength x(τ) creates x(τ) h(t - τ). Thousands of drops at random times give thousands of shifted, scaled copies of the same ring, all added up. That rumbling sound is a live convolution sum. A light drizzle and a heavy storm use the same h; only the inputs differ, which is exactly the LTI idea, at least as long as the roof itself is not damaged.

Common mistakes: First, thinking "impulse response" exists and works for every system. It always exists, but it fully describes only LTI systems. Second, forgetting the "starts at rest" condition. If a capacitor already holds charge, the output includes that stored part too. Third, writing y[n] = x[n] h[n], plain multiplication, instead of convolution. Fourth, mixing up shifted h: the piece from input time k is h[n - k], which starts at n = k, not at n = -k. Fifth, saying the length of the output equals the length of the input; for finite sequences of lengths N and M it is N + M - 1.

What exams ask: "Define impulse response." "Show that for an LTI system y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k]," which means writing the four-step argument: sifting, time invariance, homogeneity, additivity. "Find h[n] for the system y[n] = x[n] + 2x[n - 1]," answer h = δ[n] + 2δ[n - 1]. "Given h and a short x, find y by adding shifted copies." "Is the system with h[n] = 0.5^n u[n] causal and stable?" Yes and yes, since it is zero for n < 0 and Σ 0.5^n = 2. "Find the step response from h" or "find h from the step response."

Looking ahead: Lesson 9 turns the convolution sum into a fast pen-and-paper method, lesson 10 does the same for the integral, and lesson 11 proves the causality and stability rules. Later, the Fourier transform turns convolution into plain multiplication, Y = H X, which is why h and its transform H sit at the centre of filters, communication and control.

Recap: An LTI system is completely described by its impulse response h, its reply to a single tap δ while starting at rest. Any input is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses, x[n] = Σ x[k] δ[n - k]. Time invariance shifts the reply, linearity scales and adds the replies, giving y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k] and y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ. Memory, causality and stability can be read from h, and the step response is the running sum or integral of h. For non-LTI systems, one impulse response is not enough. One clap, and you know the hall.
key_points: Impulse response h = output of the system for input δ, with the system starting at rest.
Any sequence is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses: x[n] = Σ x[k] δ[n - k].
Time invariance turns δ[n - k] into h[n - k]; linearity scales by x[k] and adds them up.
Convolution sum y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k]; convolution integral y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ.
LTI properties from h: memoryless iff h = kδ, causal iff h = 0 for negative time, stable iff Σ|h| (or ∫|h|) is finite.
Step response is the running sum or integral of h; h[n] = s[n] - s[n - 1], h(t) = ds/dt.
h fully describes only LTI systems; y = x² and y = n x[n] are counter-examples.
lessons.tip: Learn the four-word chain behind convolution: sift, shift, scale, sum. If you can explain each word with one line, you can derive the convolution sum in any exam without memorising it.
lessons.task: On paper, let h = [1, 2, 1] at n = 0, 1, 2 and x = [3, 0, 1] at n = 0, 1, 2. Write x as a sum of impulses, draw each scaled shifted copy of h on its own row, add the rows to get y, and check that the sum of y equals sum(x) × sum(h). If you have a computer, confirm with numpy.convolve.

quiz.q: What is the impulse response of a system?
options: Its output for a step input
Its output for input δ when it starts at rest
quiz.explain: h is defined as the reply to a single unit impulse with no stored energy beforehand.

quiz.q: For an LTI system, what does the input δ[n - 3] produce?
quiz.explain: Time invariance: a delayed impulse gives the same impulse response delayed by the same amount.

quiz.q: h = [1, 0.5] and x = [2, 1] (both starting at n = 0). What is y?
An LTI system is causal exactly when:
options: h is a single spike at zero
quiz.explain: A non-zero h before time zero would mean the system replies before it is tapped.

quiz.q: Why does h not fully describe y[n] = x[n]²?
options: Because it is non-linear: input 2δ gives 4δ, not 2δ
quiz.explain: The squarer gives δ for input δ, like the identity, yet it does not scale inputs linearly.

lessons.title: Discrete Convolution: Flip, Slide and Add
lessons.content:
Commentators on TV love to say "they have scored 18 runs in the last three overs." Every over, they drop the oldest over and add the newest one, a running window that slides along the innings. Without knowing it, they are doing a convolution. In lesson 8 we found that any LTI system's output is y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k]. In this lesson we learn three reliable ways to compute a discrete convolution, how to know where the answer starts and how long it is, and how to check your work in ten seconds.

The formula again: y[n] = x[n] * h[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k], summing over all integers k. For one fixed output time n, we walk along k, multiply the input value x[k] by the value h[n - k], and add everything up. A change of variable, m = n - k, gives the same thing written the other way: y[n] = Σ h[m] x[n - m]. So x * h = h * x. This means you may flip whichever sequence is easier, usually the shorter one. The variable k is just a counter used inside the sum; it disappears in the answer.

Flip and slide, the steps: Step 1, draw x[k] and h[k] on a k axis. Step 2, flip h to get h[-k], the mirror image around k = 0. Step 3, slide the flipped copy by n to get h[n - k]; positive n moves it to the right. Step 4, multiply x[k] by h[n - k] at every k where both are non-zero, and add those products. That sum is y[n]. Step 5, repeat for every n where the two sequences overlap. When they stop overlapping, the output is zero.

Worked example, flip and slide: Let x = [1, 2, 3] at k = 0, 1, 2 and h = [1, 1] at k = 0, 1. Flip h: h[-k] has 1 at k = 0 and 1 at k = -1. For n = 0, the flipped h sits at k = -1 and 0; only k = 0 overlaps x, so y[0] = 1 × 1 = 1. For n = 1, it sits at k = 0 and 1: y[1] = 1 + 2 = 3. For n = 2, at k = 1 and 2: y[2] = 2 + 3 = 5. For n = 3, at k = 2 and 3: y[3] = 3. For n = 4 and beyond, no overlap. So y = [1, 3, 5, 3] for n = 0 to 3. This h adds each sample to the previous one.

Where the answer starts and how long it is: If x is non-zero from n = N1 to N2, and h is non-zero from n = M1 to M2, then y can be non-zero only from n = N1 + M1 to N2 + M2. Start plus start, end plus end. If x has N samples and h has M samples, y has N + M - 1 samples. In the last example, x had 3 samples and h had 2, so y has 4, running from 0 + 0 = 0 to 2 + 1 = 3. Always write down the start index before you begin. It is the most common place to lose marks, because the numbers can be right but sitting at the wrong n.

The table method: For short sequences there is a faster way that looks like a multiplication grid. Write the values of x along the top and the values of h down the left side. Fill each cell with the product of its row and column. Then add along the diagonals that go from top right to bottom left: each such diagonal collects all pairs with the same k + (n - k) = n. Try x = [1, 2, 3] and h = [2, 1, -1]. Row 2 is [2, 4, 6], row 1 is [1, 2, 3], row -1 is [-1, -2, -3]. Diagonal sums give y = [2, 5, 7, 1, -3]. Check y[2] = 6 + 2 - 1 = 7.

The long multiplication method: You can also arrange it like long multiplication from primary school, but without carrying. Write x = 1 2 3 on top and h = 2 1 -1 below. Multiply x by each value of h, and shift each new row one place to the right: 2 times x gives 2 4 6, 1 times x gives 1 2 3 shifted once, -1 times x gives -1 -2 -3 shifted twice. Add the columns: 2, 5, 7, 1, -3. Same answer. This is no accident. Convolution of coefficient lists is exactly polynomial multiplication: (1 + 2z + 3z²)(2 + z - z²) = 2 + 5z + 7z² + z³ - 3z⁴. That link returns in the Z-transform lesson.

Two ten-second checks: Check 1, length: N + M - 1 samples, starting at N1 + M1. Check 2, the sum rule: the sum of all output samples equals the sum of the input samples times the sum of the impulse response samples, Σy = (Σx)(Σh). For the last example Σx = 6 and Σh = 2, so Σy should be 12, and indeed 2 + 5 + 7 + 1 - 3 = 12. It catches most addition slips, though not two errors that cancel.

Worked example with a negative start: Let x[-1] = 2, x[0] = -1, x[1] = 3, so x starts at n = -1, and h = [1, 2, 1] at n = 0, 1, 2. The values come from the table: [2, 3, 3, 5, 3]. The start is -1 + 0 = -1 and the end is 1 + 2 = 3. So y[-1] = 2, y[0] = 3, y[1] = 3, y[2] = 5, y[3] = 3. Sum check: Σx = 4, Σh = 4, Σy = 16, and 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16. Notice the table method did not care about the start index at all; you only attach it at the end.

Convolution with an impulse: Convolving with δ[n] changes nothing: x[n] * δ[n] = x[n]. That is why δ is the impulse response of the identity system. Convolving with a shifted impulse just shifts: x[n] * δ[n - n0] = x[n - n0]. And because convolution is linear, combinations work piece by piece. For example, x[n] * (δ[n] + 0.5δ[n - 2]) = x[n] + 0.5x[n - 2], the signal plus a half-strength echo two steps later. Whenever h is a handful of spikes, you can skip flip and slide and simply add shifted, scaled copies of x.

The moving average: A three-point moving average has h = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]. It smooths a signal by replacing each sample with the average of itself and the two before it. Take temperatures over five days, x = [30, 33, 36, 33, 30] °C. Convolving gives y = [10, 21, 33, 34, 33, 21, 10]. The middle three values, 33, 34, 33, come from full overlap, where all three taps sit on real data; they are the true three-day averages. The first two and last two values are edge effects, where part of the window hangs over zeros. When you read a smoothed chart, remember that its ends are less trustworthy than its middle.

Infinite sequences: Convolution also works when sequences go on forever, but then you need a formula, not a table. Let x[n] = u[n] (a step) and h[n] = a^n u[n] with |a| < 1. For n ≥ 0, y[n] = Σ a^k for k = 0 to n, because both sequences are non-zero only when 0 ≤ k ≤ n. This is a geometric series, so y[n] = (1 - a^(n+1)) / (1 - a) for n ≥ 0, and zero for n < 0. With a = 0.5: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 1.5, y[2] = 1.75, y[3] = 1.875, and y[n] climbs towards 1 / (1 - 0.5) = 2. This is the step response of that system.

Setting the limits of the sum: The hard part with infinite sequences is the limits. Write each step function as a condition: u[k] means k ≥ 0, and u[n - k] means k ≤ n. Together they say 0 ≤ k ≤ n, which also tells you that y[n] = 0 when n < 0, because no k satisfies both. Another example: u[n] * u[n] = Σ 1 for k = 0 to n = (n + 1) u[n], a ramp: 1, 2, 3, 4, ... That is the accumulator fed with a step, which is why lesson 7 called it unstable. Always draw the two conditions on a number line before writing the sum.

Which one to flip: Because x * h = h * x, flip the shorter or simpler sequence. If one sequence is a few spikes, use the "add shifted copies" view instead. If both are long but finite, use the table. If one or both are infinite with a formula, write the sum with conditions and use a series formula. Lesson 11 covers the other properties of convolution.

On a computer: In Python, numpy.convolve([1, 2, 3], [1, 1]) returns [1, 3, 5, 3]. In MATLAB or Octave the command is conv. These functions only see lists of numbers; they do not know where your sequences start. So you must still work out the start index N1 + M1 yourself. Direct convolution needs about N × M multiplications, so long signals are often convolved with the FFT, a DSP course topic.

Real-life example 1, runs in the last three overs: Suppose a batting side scores 6, 10, 2, 8 and 12 runs in five overs. "Runs in the last three overs" is the convolution with h = [1, 1, 1]. The result is [6, 16, 18, 20, 22, 20, 12]. The full-window values are 18 (overs 1 to 3), 20 (overs 2 to 4) and 22 (overs 3 to 5). Divide by three and you get the three-over run rate: 6, 6.67 and 7.33. The rising numbers show the batting side speeding up, even though one over in the middle gave only 2 runs. Smoothing hides one bad over and shows the trend.

Real-life example 2, echo on a mobile call: On some long distance calls you hear your own voice come back faintly. Model it simply: the line returns a 30 percent copy three samples later, so h = [1, 0, 0, 0.3]. If you say two quick sounds, x = [4, 2], the other side hears y = [4, 2, 0, 1.2, 0.6]. The 1.2 and 0.6 are the echo of 4 and 2. An echo canceller in the network estimates this h, convolves your voice with the echo part, and subtracts it. Grameenphone, Robi and every other network rely on this kind of convolution millions of times a second.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to flip, which gives a correlation, not a convolution. Second, sliding in the wrong direction; h[n - k] moves to the right as n increases. Third, losing the start index, especially when one sequence starts at a negative n. Fourth, wrong length; always N + M - 1. Fifth, multiplying sample by sample, x[n]h[n], instead of convolving. Sixth, with infinite sequences, forgetting that the answer must include u[n] or a condition like "for n ≥ 0", since the output is zero before the overlap begins.

What exams ask: "Find y[n] = x[n] * h[n] for x[n] = {1, 2, 3} and h[n] = {1, -1}" with an arrow marking n = 0. Show the start index, the method, and the final sequence with its own arrow. "Find the response of h[n] = a^n u[n] to u[n]," using the geometric series. "Find u[n] * u[n]." "What is the length of the output?" "Show that x[n] * δ[n - n0] = x[n - n0]." Some papers want a sketch of each slide position; draw small and neat.

Looking ahead: The same flip and slide picture works for continuous signals, where the sum becomes an integral and the overlap becomes an area. That is lesson 10, with examples like a step entering an RC circuit and two rectangles making a triangle. Lesson 11 then uses convolution to explain series and parallel systems, and to prove the causality and stability rules for h.

Recap: Discrete convolution y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k] can be computed by flip and slide, by the table of products with diagonal sums, or by long multiplication without carry, which is polynomial multiplication. The output starts at N1 + M1 and has N + M - 1 samples, and Σy = (Σx)(Σh) is a quick check. Convolving with δ[n - n0] shifts the signal. A moving average is convolution with equal weights, and its edge values are partial. For infinite sequences, turn step functions into limits and use a series formula, like a^n u[n] * u[n] = (1 - a^(n+1)) / (1 - a) for n ≥ 0.
key_points: y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k]; convolution is commutative, so flip the shorter sequence.
Flip and slide: flip h to h[-k], shift to h[n - k], multiply the overlap, add, repeat for each n.
Output starts at N1 + M1, ends at N2 + M2, and has N + M - 1 samples.
Table method: grid of products, add along diagonals; long multiplication without carry gives the same, like polynomial multiplication.
x[n] * δ[n - n0] = x[n - n0]; spikes in h mean adding shifted, scaled copies of x.
Moving average h = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]; only full-overlap outputs are true averages, edges are partial.
lessons.tip: Before computing any convolution, write two things in the margin: the start index N1 + M1 and the length N + M - 1. After computing, check Σy = (Σx)(Σh). These three numbers catch most mistakes in under a minute.
lessons.task: Compute [1, 2, 1] * [1, 0, -1] and [3, 1, 2] * [1, 1] by hand, once with flip and slide and once with the table method. Check both with the sum rule. If you have a computer or phone with Python, confirm with numpy.convolve, then try a 3-point moving average on the last seven days of temperatures from your weather app.

quiz.q: x has 4 samples and h has 3 samples. How many samples can y = x * h have?
quiz.explain: The length rule is N + M - 1 = 4 + 3 - 1 = 6.

quiz.q: What is [1, 1] * [1, 1] (both starting at n = 0)?
quiz.explain: Flip and slide gives 1, then 1 + 1 = 2, then 1.

quiz.q: x starts at n = -2 and h starts at n = 3. Where does y start?
quiz.explain: The start of y is the sum of the starts: -2 + 3 = 1.

quiz.q: What is x[n] * δ[n - 2]?
quiz.explain: Convolving with a shifted impulse shifts the signal by the same amount.

quiz.q: Σx = 5 and Σh = 3. What must Σy be for y = x * h?
quiz.explain: The sum of a convolution equals the product of the sums: 5 × 3 = 15.

lessons.title: Continuous Convolution: The Convolution Integral
lessons.content:
Take a photo of a busy road at night with your phone, and keep your hand a little shaky. Every rickshaw lamp becomes a short bright streak instead of a dot. Each point of light has been smeared over the time the shutter was open, and the streaks of all the lamps add up to make the blurry picture. That smearing is a convolution, but in continuous time, where nothing comes in neat samples. In lesson 9 we convolved lists of numbers. Now we do the same for smooth signals, where the sum becomes an integral and "add the products" becomes "find the area under the product".

The convolution integral: For a continuous-time LTI system with impulse response h(t), the output for input x(t) is y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ, integrated over all τ from minus infinity to infinity. Here τ is a dummy variable, like k in the sum; it disappears once you integrate. As in the discrete case, the order does not matter: ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ = ∫ h(τ) x(t - τ) dτ, so x * h = h * x. Flip whichever function is simpler, usually the one with the simpler shape or formula.

Flip and slide in continuous time: Step 1, draw x(τ) and h(τ) on a τ axis. Step 2, flip h to get h(-τ). Step 3, slide it to get h(t - τ); for positive t the flipped copy moves to the right. Step 4, multiply x(τ) by h(t - τ) and find the area of the product; that area is y(t). Step 5, repeat for every t. In discrete time we could list every n. In continuous time we cannot list every t, so we split the time axis into cases, and in each case we write one integral with the right limits.

Finding the cases: The cases change whenever an edge of the sliding function passes an edge of the fixed one. So list the edges. If x is non-zero from a1 to a2 and h from b1 to b2, the output can be non-zero only from a1 + b1 to a2 + b2, and the duration of y is the sum of the two durations. Inside that range, the break points are the values of t where the edges meet. Usually you get: no overlap, partial overlap entering, full overlap, partial overlap leaving, and no overlap again. Draw a small sketch for each case; it makes the limits obvious.

Example 1, rectangle with rectangle: Let x(t) = h(t) = 1 for 0 ≤ t < 1 and 0 otherwise, a pulse of width 1 and height 1. The output can live only from 0 + 0 = 0 to 1 + 1 = 2. Flip h: h(-τ) is 1 for -1 < τ ≤ 0. Slide: h(t - τ) is 1 for t - 1 < τ ≤ t. So the product is 1 exactly where both windows overlap, and y(t) is simply the length of that overlap. This is a nice case because no exponentials appear; you only measure lengths.

Example 1, the cases: For t < 0, the sliding window is completely to the left of x: y = 0. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, it overlaps from τ = 0 to τ = t: y(t) = t. For 1 ≤ t ≤ 2, it overlaps from τ = t - 1 to τ = 1: y(t) = 2 - t. For t > 2, no overlap: y = 0. So y rises in a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 1 at t = 1 and falls back to 0 at t = 2. Two rectangles make a triangle. If you use rectangles centred at zero, from -1/2 to 1/2, the answer is the centred triangle y(t) = 1 - |t| for |t| ≤ 1.

Unequal rectangles give a trapezoid: Now let x be 1 from 0 to 2 and h be 1 from 0 to 1. The output lives from 0 to 3. It rises as y = t from 0 to 1, stays flat at y = 1 from t = 1 to 2, because the short window is fully inside the long one, then falls as y = 3 - t from 2 to 3. A trapezoid. The flat top lasts for the difference of the widths, 2 - 1 = 1, and the ramps last for the width of the shorter pulse. Equal widths make the flat top vanish, which is why we got a triangle before.

Example 2, step into an exponential: Let x(t) = u(t) and h(t) = e^(-at) u(t) with a > 0. The steps become conditions: u(τ) means τ ≥ 0, and u(t - τ) means τ ≤ t. Together, 0 ≤ τ ≤ t, which is possible only if t ≥ 0. So for t ≥ 0, y(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of e^(-a(t - τ)) dτ = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)), and y(t) = 0 for t < 0. Final answer: y(t) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)) u(t). With a = 2, at t = 1 we get 0.5 × (1 - e^(-2)) ≈ 0.432, and as t grows the output settles at 1/a = 0.5.

The RC circuit: Lesson 12 shows that a series RC low-pass circuit, output taken across the capacitor, has h(t) = (1/RC) e^(-t/RC) u(t). That is our example 2 with a = 1/RC and an extra factor 1/RC. So its step response is s(t) = (1 - e^(-t/RC)) u(t). The product RC is called the time constant. After one time constant the output reaches 1 - e^(-1) ≈ 63.2 percent of the final value, after two about 86.5 percent, and after five about 99.3 percent. With R = 1 kΩ and C = 1000 µF, RC = 1 second, so the capacitor is practically full after about 5 seconds.

Example 3, two exponentials: Let x(t) = e^(-t) u(t) and h(t) = e^(-2t) u(t). Again the conditions give 0 ≤ τ ≤ t. y(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of e^(-τ) e^(-2(t - τ)) dτ = e^(-2t) ∫ from 0 to t of e^(τ) dτ = e^(-2t)(e^t - 1) = (e^(-t) - e^(-2t)) u(t). The output starts at 0, rises to a peak of 0.25 at t = ln 2 ≈ 0.693, then decays. The general rule for a ≠ b is e^(-at) u(t) * e^(-bt) u(t) = (e^(-at) - e^(-bt)) / (b - a) u(t). Two decaying systems in a row give a "rise then fall" bump.

Example 4, a pulse into the RC circuit: Let x(t) = 1 for 0 ≤ t < 2 (a 2 second pulse) and h(t) = e^(-t) u(t), an RC circuit with RC = 1 s. For t < 0, y = 0. For 0 ≤ t < 2, the window covers τ from 0 to t, so y(t) = 1 - e^(-t), charging: y(1) ≈ 0.632, y(2) ≈ 0.865. For t ≥ 2, the window covers the whole pulse, τ from 0 to 2, so y(t) = ∫ from 0 to 2 of e^(-(t - τ)) dτ = (e^2 - 1) e^(-t), discharging: y(3) ≈ 0.318. The two pieces join smoothly at t = 2, where both give about 0.865.

Convolution with an impulse: Because of the sifting property, x(t) * δ(t) = x(t), and x(t) * δ(t - T) = x(t - T). So a system with h(t) = δ(t - T) is a pure delay. Two shifted impulses combine by adding their shifts: δ(t - a) * δ(t - b) = δ(t - a - b). An echo system h(t) = δ(t) + 0.5δ(t - 0.1) gives y(t) = x(t) + 0.5x(t - 0.1), the sound plus a half-strength copy 0.1 seconds later. As in lesson 9, when h is made of spikes, skip the integral and add shifted copies.

Convolution with a step: x(t) * u(t) = ∫ x(τ) u(t - τ) dτ = ∫ from minus infinity to t of x(τ) dτ. So convolving with u(t) is the same as running integration; the integrator's impulse response is u(t). A neat special case is u(t) * u(t) = t u(t), the unit ramp. In general, the step response of any LTI system is h(t) * u(t), which is the running integral of h, matching lesson 8. This also gives a check: differentiate your step response and you should get back h.

Two quick checks: The area rule: the area under y equals the area under x times the area under h. In example 1 both rectangles have area 1 and the triangle has area 1. In example 4 the pulse has area 2, e^(-t) u(t) has area 1, and the area under y works out to 2. The support rule: y starts at the sum of the starts and ends at the sum of the ends. A pulse from 0 to 2 with a pulse from 0 to 1 gives an output from 0 to 3. If your answer fails either check, look for a wrong limit.

Convolution smooths: Look at the shapes we made. Two rectangles with sharp jumps gave a triangle with no jumps, only corners. Convolve that triangle with another rectangle and even the corners become rounded curves. In general, convolving with a wide, positive h spreads each point of the input over a time interval and blurs sharp changes. This is why low-pass filters soften noise and also why a slow system cannot follow fast changes in its input. The wider the impulse response, the stronger the smoothing.

Real-life example 1, camera blur: Suppose a phone camera's shutter stays open for 0.1 s while your hand moves steadily. A single bright point, like a far-away rickshaw lamp, gets smeared evenly over the path it moves across during that 0.1 s. The blur is a rectangle-shaped h, and the photo is the sharp scene convolved with that rectangle. A line of lamps becomes a set of overlapping streaks, and the brightness at any place is the sum of all the streaks covering it. Photo editing apps that "remove motion blur" try to undo this convolution, which is the invertibility question of lesson 6, and noise makes it hard.

Real-life example 2, power returning after load shedding: Many chargers and adaptors have an RC smoothing stage. When the power comes back after load shedding, the input jumps like a step, and the output rises as 1 - e^(-t/RC), not instantly. If the supply flickers on for just 2 seconds and then drops again, the input is a pulse, and the output is exactly example 4: it charges up during the pulse and then decays smoothly. Engineers choose RC so that brief flickers and spikes are smoothed out while the device still responds fast enough to normal changes.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to turn u(τ) and u(t - τ) into limits, and integrating from minus infinity to infinity. Second, forgetting the final u(t) or the condition "for t ≥ 0", which leaves a formula that seems to give non-zero output before the input arrives. Third, missing a case, especially the "full overlap" or "after the pulse" case. Fourth, flipping in the wrong variable: you flip and slide in τ, while t is the fixed shift for each case. Fifth, a sign slip in e^(-a(t - τ)); expand it as e^(-at) e^(aτ) before integrating.

What exams ask: "Find and sketch y(t) = x(t) * h(t) for x(t) = u(t) - u(t - 2) and h(t) = e^(-t) u(t)," which is example 4. "Show that u(t) * e^(-at) u(t) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)) u(t)." "Convolve two rectangular pulses and sketch the result." "Find the step response of h(t) = e^(-3t) u(t)." "What is x(t) * δ(t - 2)?" Always show the cases with sketches, write each integral with its limits, and give the final answer as one piecewise formula covering all t.

Looking ahead: Lesson 11 collects the properties of convolution, commutative, associative and distributive, and uses them for systems in series and in parallel, along with the causality and stability tests on h. Later, the Fourier and Laplace transforms will turn every one of these integrals into a simple product, Y = H X. But the time-domain picture of flip and slide stays important, because it shows you what the system actually does, moment by moment.

Recap: The convolution integral y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ is the continuous version of the convolution sum. Flip h, slide it by t, multiply, and take the area. Split the t axis into cases where edges meet, and turn step functions into limits. Key results: two equal rectangles give a triangle, unequal ones a trapezoid; u(t) * e^(-at) u(t) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)) u(t); e^(-t) u(t) * e^(-2t) u(t) = (e^(-t) - e^(-2t)) u(t); x * δ(t - T) = x(t - T); x * u = running integral of x. Check with the area rule and the support rule.
key_points: y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ; flip h, slide by t, multiply, take the area; x * h = h * x.
Split t into cases where edges meet; output lives from (start of x + start of h) to (end of x + end of h).
Turn u(τ) and u(t - τ) into limits 0 ≤ τ ≤ t; give the answer with u(t) or 'for t ≥ 0'.
Two width-1 rectangles from 0 to 1 give a triangle from 0 to 2 with peak 1 at t = 1; unequal widths give a trapezoid.
u(t) * e^(-at) u(t) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)) u(t); RC step response 1 - e^(-t/RC) reaches 63.2% at t = RC.
x * δ(t - T) = x(t - T); x * u(t) = running integral of x; u * u = t u(t).
Checks: area of y = area of x × area of h; durations add. Convolution with a wide positive h smooths.
lessons.tip: For every continuous convolution, draw a row of small sketches, one per case, with the fixed function and the sliding window. Write the limits under each sketch before you integrate. The sketches turn a scary integral into simple bookkeeping.
lessons.task: On paper, convolve x(t) = u(t) - u(t - 1) with h(t) = e^(-t) u(t). Find the cases, the formula in each case, and compute y(0.5), y(1) and y(2). Check that the area under y equals 1. If you have Python, check your values with scipy.integrate.quad.

quiz.q: What is x(t) * δ(t - 3)?
quiz.explain: By the sifting property, convolving with a shifted impulse shifts the signal by 3.

quiz.q: Two rectangles, each 1 from t = 0 to t = 1, are convolved. The result is:
options: A triangle from 0 to 2 with peak 1 at t = 1
quiz.explain: The overlap length grows as t for 0 to 1 and shrinks as 2 - t for 1 to 2.

quiz.q: u(t) * e^(-at) u(t) for a > 0 equals:
quiz.explain: With limits 0 ≤ τ ≤ t, the integral of e^(-a(t - τ)) is (1/a)(1 - e^(-at)).

quiz.q: x(t) is non-zero on [0, 2] and h(t) on [1, 4]. Where can y = x * h be non-zero?
quiz.explain: Start = 0 + 1 = 1 and end = 2 + 4 = 6.

quiz.q: The area under x is 2 and the area under h is 3. What is the area under x * h?
quiz.explain: The area of a convolution is the product of the areas: 2 × 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Properties of Convolution and LTI Systems
lessons.content:
Imagine you fill a jug from the tap at home in Dhaka. First the water goes through a filter, then you boil it in the kettle. Your friend does it the other way round: boil first, then filter. Is the water at the end the same? For many real gadgets the answer would be "not exactly". But for one very special family of systems, the LTI systems, the answer is always yes. The order does not matter. In this lesson we find out why, and we learn the small set of rules that make convolution behave a lot like ordinary multiplication.

Where we are: In lesson 8 we met the impulse response h, the output of an LTI system when the input is a single impulse. In lessons 9 and 10 we learned to compute the output with convolution, y = x * h, in discrete time as y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n-k] and in continuous time as y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t-τ) dτ. Here the star * means convolution, not multiplication. Now we step back and ask: what rules does this star obey, and what can the single function h tell us about the whole system without testing it on every possible input?

The big idea: For an LTI system, h is the full identity card of the system. Memory, causality, stability, invertibility, the step response, what happens when you connect two systems together: all of it can be read straight from h. That is a huge saving. Instead of asking questions about a box with infinitely many possible inputs, you ask questions about one function. Exam questions in this topic almost always look like "given h, is the system causal, stable, memoryless?" or "two systems in series, find the overall h".

Commutative property: The first rule is x * h = h * x. In discrete time, put m = n - k inside the sum and Σ x[k] h[n-k] turns into Σ h[m] x[n-m]. Same answer, roles swapped. What does it mean in plain words? The input and the impulse response are interchangeable. Feeding signal x into a system with impulse response h gives exactly the same output as feeding h into a system whose impulse response is x. It also gives you a free choice when you compute by hand: flip whichever of the two signals is simpler. Flipping a short pulse is usually easier than flipping a long, messy signal.

Associative property: The second rule is (x * h1) * h2 = x * (h1 * h2). Think of two LTI systems in a row, a cascade. The signal first goes through h1, the result goes through h2. The rule says you could first combine the two systems into one system with impulse response h1 * h2 and then send x through that once. Together with the commutative rule it also says h1 * h2 = h2 * h1, so the order of LTI blocks in a chain does not matter. That is exactly the filter-and-kettle story from the start, as long as both boxes are linear and time invariant.

A discrete check of series connection: Take h1[n] = {1, 1}, which adds the present sample to the previous one, and h2[n] = {1, -1}, which takes a difference. Their convolution is h1 * h2 = {1, 0, -1}. So the cascade is the single system y[n] = x[n] - x[n-2]. Now test it with x[n] = {1, 2, 3}. Going step by step, x * h1 = {1, 3, 5, 3}, and then {1, 3, 5, 3} * h2 = {1, 2, 2, -2, -3}. Going in one jump, {1, 2, 3} * {1, 0, -1} also gives {1, 2, 2, -2, -3}. Same answer, and you can verify it with a few lines of multiplication on paper.

A continuous check of series connection: Let h1(t) = e^(-t) u(t) and h2(t) = e^(-2t) u(t), two simple decaying systems, like two RC circuits with buffers between them. The overall impulse response is h(t) = h1 * h2 = ∫ from 0 to t of e^(-τ) e^(-2(t-τ)) dτ = (e^(-t) - e^(-2t)) u(t). Notice the shape: it starts at 0, rises, then dies away. One decaying box gives a sudden jump then decay, but two in a row smooth the start. We will get this same answer again in lesson 15 with the Fourier transform, in a much shorter way.

Distributive property: The third rule is x * (h1 + h2) = x * h1 + x * h2. This is the rule for a parallel connection. The input is copied into two systems side by side, and their outputs are added. The whole thing is one LTI system with impulse response h1 + h2. Example: h1[n] = {1, 1} and h2[n] = {1, -1} in parallel give h[n] = {2, 0}, which is just y[n] = 2x[n]. The average part and the difference part add together, the old sample cancels, and only a gain of 2 survives. So the rule to remember is simple: series means convolve, parallel means add.

The identity and the shift: Two special impulse responses act like the numbers 1 and "move". First, x * δ = x, so δ is the identity of convolution, the system that does nothing. Second, x * δ(t - t0) = x(t - t0) in continuous time, and x[n] * δ[n - n0] = x[n - n0] in discrete time. So an impulse response that is a shifted impulse is a pure delay. A pure delay of 3 seconds followed by any system h is the same as h followed by the delay. That is again the commutative rule at work.

Memory from h: A system is memoryless when the output at time n depends only on the input at the same time n. In the sum y[n] = Σ h[k] x[n-k], the only way to avoid past and future samples is h[k] = 0 for every k except k = 0. So an LTI system is memoryless only if h[n] = K δ[n], and then y[n] = K x[n], a plain amplifier. In continuous time it is h(t) = K δ(t). Anything else, even h[n] = {1, 1}, has memory, because it remembers the previous sample.

Causality from h: A causal system never uses future inputs. In y[n] = Σ h[k] x[n-k], a term with negative k uses x[n-k] with n - k bigger than n, which is the future. So an LTI system is causal exactly when h[n] = 0 for n < 0, and in continuous time when h(t) = 0 for t < 0. Quick tests: h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] is causal. h[n] = δ[n + 1] is not causal, because it gives y[n] = x[n + 1], the next sample. A centered moving average with h[n] = 1/3 for n = -1, 0, 1 is also not causal, since it peeks one step into the future.

Stability from h: BIBO stability means every bounded input gives a bounded output. For an LTI system the test is neat: the system is stable exactly when h is absolutely summable, Σ |h[n]| < ∞, or absolutely integrable, ∫ |h(t)| dt < ∞. The reason: if |x| is never bigger than B, then |y[n]| is at most B times Σ |h[k]|. If that sum is finite, the output stays bounded. If the sum is infinite, one can build a bounded input, using the signs of h, that drives the output as large as you like.

Stability examples: For h(t) = e^(-2t) u(t), ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-2t) dt = 1/2, finite, so the system is stable. For h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n], Σ (0.5)^n = 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + ... = 2, finite, stable. For h(t) = u(t), the integrator, ∫ |u(t)| dt is infinite, so it is not stable: feed it the bounded input x(t) = u(t) and the output is the ramp t u(t), which grows forever. The discrete twin, the accumulator h[n] = u[n], is unstable in the same way. And h[n] = (1.2)^n u[n] obviously blows up.

Invertibility from h: An LTI system h is invertible if there is another LTI system g with h * g = δ. Then putting g after h gives back the original input. A beautiful pair: the accumulator h[n] = u[n] and the first difference g[n] = δ[n] - δ[n-1]. Their convolution is u[n] - u[n-1] = δ[n]. So summing up and then taking differences undoes itself, just like adding up your daily bKash spending and then subtracting yesterday's total from today's gives back today's spending. In continuous time the integrator and the differentiator form a similar pair.

Step response: The step response s is the output when the input is the unit step. Since u = Σ of shifted impulses, s[n] = Σ for k from -∞ to n of h[k], and in continuous time s(t) = ∫ from -∞ to t of h(τ) dτ. Going back, h[n] = s[n] - s[n-1] and h(t) = ds/dt. In labs, the step response is easier to measure than the impulse response, because a step is just switching something on, while a perfect impulse is impossible to make. Measure s, take its slope, and you have h.

Worked step responses: For h(t) = e^(-2t) u(t), s(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of e^(-2τ) dτ = (1/2)(1 - e^(-2t)) u(t). It starts at 0 and settles at 1/2, which equals ∫ h, the DC gain of the system. For h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n], s[n] = 1 + 0.5 + ... + (0.5)^n = 2 - (0.5)^n for n ≥ 0. The values are 1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875 and they creep up to 2, again the total sum of h. So the final value of the step response tells you how much the system amplifies a constant input.

Real life example 1, a phone call: When you call your nani in Sylhet on Grameenphone, your voice passes through the phone microphone, a digital filter in your handset, the network, a filter in her handset and her speaker. Engineers model each block that is close to LTI by its own impulse response. Because series means convolve, the whole chain behaves like one system with h = h1 * h2 * h3 * ... Because the order of LTI blocks can be swapped, designers can move a filter from one place to another, for example to where it is cheaper to compute, without changing the final sound.

Real life example 2, a building in an earthquake: Civil engineers think of a tall building in Dhaka as a system whose input is ground shaking and whose output is how much the top floor sways. If they treat it as LTI, the stability test says the response to a bounded shake stays bounded only if h dies out fast enough. Dampers added to tall buildings make h decay faster, which makes ∫ |h| smaller and the sway smaller. A structure whose h does not decay keeps swinging, the way a playground swing keeps going when pushed in rhythm.

Common mistakes: First, the rules only hold for LTI systems. Squaring then delaying equals delaying then squaring, but squaring then adding a constant is not the same as adding then squaring, so do not swap nonlinear boxes. Second, students write "series means add". No: series means convolve h's, parallel means add h's. Third, for stability it is the sum of |h|, with absolute value, not the sum of h. The system h[n] = (-1)^n u[n] has a partial sum that never grows but Σ |h| is infinite, so it is unstable. Fourth, causal means h = 0 for negative time, it says nothing about stability.

What exams ask: Typical questions give you h and ask for causality, stability and memory, with one line of reason for each. Others give two systems in series or parallel and ask for the overall impulse response, often with exponentials like e^(-t) u(t) and e^(-2t) u(t). Some ask you to prove the commutative property by a change of variable, or to find the step response from h, or h from a given step response by differentiating. Some ask you to show that two systems are inverses by showing h * g = δ. Practice each type once and you will feel at home.

Recap: Convolution is commutative, associative and distributive, so LTI blocks in series combine by convolving their impulse responses, in any order, and blocks in parallel combine by adding them. δ is the do-nothing system and a shifted δ is a pure delay. From h alone you can read memory (only K δ is memoryless), causality (h = 0 for negative time), stability (Σ |h| or ∫ |h| finite), invertibility (h * g = δ) and the step response (a running sum or integral of h). Next lesson we see where h comes from in real circuits: differential and difference equations.
key_points: Convolution is commutative (x * h = h * x), associative and distributive, just like multiplication.
LTI systems in series: the overall impulse response is h1 * h2, and the order of the blocks does not matter.
LTI systems in parallel: the overall impulse response is h1 + h2.
x * δ = x, and convolving with δ(t - t0) delays the signal by t0.
An LTI system is memoryless only if h = K δ, and causal exactly when h = 0 for negative time.
An LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when Σ |h[n]| or ∫ |h(t)| dt is finite.
Step response is the running sum or integral of h; h is the difference or derivative of the step response.
Example: e^(-t) u(t) in series with e^(-2t) u(t) gives (e^(-t) - e^(-2t)) u(t).
lessons.tip: Make a tiny cheat card with three columns: property, test on h in discrete time, test on h in continuous time. Memoryless, causal, stable, invertible. Before an exam, cover the last two columns and recite them. These four tests come up again and again.
lessons.task: On paper, convolve h1 = {1, 1} with h2 = {1, -1}, then send x = {1, 2, 3} through h1 then h2, and also through h2 then h1. Check that all three routes give {1, 2, 2, -2, -3}. Then add up the first six terms of (0.5)^n and see how close you get to 2.

quiz.q: Two LTI systems are connected in series with impulse responses h1 and h2. What is the overall impulse response?
options: h1 times h2 sample by sample
quiz.explain: In a cascade the signal is convolved with h1 and then with h2, and by associativity that equals convolving once with h1 * h2.

quiz.q: Which impulse response describes a causal system?
quiz.explain: A causal LTI system has h[n] = 0 for n < 0. Only (0.5)^n u[n] satisfies that; the others have values at negative n.

quiz.q: Which LTI system is NOT BIBO stable?
quiz.explain: ∫ |u(t)| dt is infinite. A bounded step input gives the ramp t u(t), which grows without limit.

quiz.q: What is the step response of h(t) = e^(-2t) u(t)?
quiz.explain: The step response is the running integral of h: ∫ from 0 to t of e^(-2τ) dτ = (1/2)(1 - e^(-2t)) for t ≥ 0.

quiz.q: Which pair of systems are inverses of each other?
options: Accumulator h[n] = u[n] and first difference g[n] = δ[n] - δ[n-1]
A delay δ[n-1] and another delay δ[n-1]
quiz.explain: u[n] * (δ[n] - δ[n-1]) = u[n] - u[n-1] = δ[n], so the difference undoes the running sum.

lessons.title: Differential and Difference Equations
lessons.content:
Put a hot cup of cha on the table and watch it. In the first minute it cools quickly. Later it cools more and more slowly, creeping towards room temperature. Nobody has to tell the cup what to do. A simple rule decides it: the speed of cooling depends on how much hotter the tea is than the room. That rule is an equation that links a quantity with its own rate of change, a differential equation. Most real physical systems, circuits, motors, speakers, even a cup of tea, are described this way. In this lesson we see how such equations become LTI systems.

Where h comes from: In the last few lessons we were simply handed an impulse response h and we convolved. But in real life nobody hands you h. You have a circuit with resistors and capacitors, or a computer program that updates a value every second. These are described by equations. Continuous-time systems are described by differential equations, and discrete-time systems by difference equations. Solving these equations is how we find h, the step response and every other response. Math III already taught you how to solve such equations, including with Laplace. Here we focus on what each part of the solution means for the system.
