quiz.explain: The highest frequency is 300 Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 2 × 300 = 600 Hz.

quiz.q: What does the spectrum of an ideally sampled signal look like?
options: Copies of X repeated every fs, scaled by 1/Ts
X squeezed by a factor fs
Only the DC value of X
quiz.explain: Multiplying by an impulse train convolves X with a comb, giving Xs(jω) = (1/Ts) Σ X(j(ω - kωs)).

quiz.q: CD audio covers hearing up to about 20 kHz. Why is the sampling rate 44.1 kHz and not exactly 40 kHz?
options: It matches the TV frame rate
It leaves room above 20 kHz for a real anti-aliasing filter's transition band
quiz.explain: Real filters cannot cut instantly, so a gap between 20 kHz and the Nyquist frequency 22.05 kHz lets the filter roll off.

quiz.q: What is the sampling period Ts for fs = 8 kHz?
x(t) is band-limited to 2 kHz. What is the Nyquist rate of x²(t)?
quiz.explain: Squaring convolves the spectrum with itself, doubling the band to 4 kHz, so the Nyquist rate is 8 kHz.

lessons.title: Aliasing and Reconstruction: Fake Frequencies and Getting the Signal Back
lessons.content:
Record a video of a spinning ceiling fan with your phone, and play it back. Strange things happen. Sometimes the blades seem to turn slowly, sometimes they stand still, and sometimes they even turn backwards, although the real fan is racing forward. Nothing is wrong with the fan or the phone. The camera takes pictures at a fixed rate, which is sampling, and the fan is turning too fast for that rate. A fast motion has put on the costume of a slow one. This trick of sampling is called aliasing, and in this lesson we learn to predict it, prevent it, and then rebuild a signal correctly from its samples.

What aliasing is: The word alias means a false name. After sampling, a high frequency can show up under the false name of a lower frequency. In lesson 17 we saw that the sampled spectrum is made of copies of X spaced fs apart. If the signal has frequencies above fs/2, the copies overlap, and some high-frequency content lands on top of the low-frequency region. Once that happens, the samples are identical to the samples of a different, lower-frequency signal, and nobody can tell which one was real.

The maths in time: Look at a cosine of frequency f sampled at fs. The samples are cos(2π f n / fs). Now replace f by f + fs. The samples become cos(2π f n/fs + 2πn), and since 2πn is a whole number of turns, they are exactly the same. Now try fs - f. The samples are cos(2πn - 2π f n/fs) = cos(2π f n/fs), again the same, because cosine is even. So the frequencies f, f + fs, fs - f, 2fs - f and so on all give the very same list of numbers. This is the discrete periodicity rule from lesson 4, seen from the sampling side.

Worked example 1: Sample a 700 Hz cosine at fs = 1000 Hz. The Nyquist frequency is 500 Hz, and 700 Hz is above it. Using fs - f, the alias is 1000 - 700 = 300 Hz. If you check with a calculator, cos(2π·700n/1000) and cos(2π·300n/1000) give the same value for every n. A sine behaves almost the same way, but it flips sign: the samples of sin(2π·700n/1000) equal minus the samples of sin(2π·300n/1000). So the frequency is aliased to 300 Hz and the phase is turned upside down.

Worked example 2: Sample a 1200 Hz cosine at fs = 1000 Hz. Now subtract fs once: 1200 - 1000 = 200 Hz. That is already below 500 Hz, so the alias is 200 Hz. The general recipe is: subtract (or add) whole multiples of fs until the result lands between -fs/2 and fs/2, then take the absolute value. In short, f_alias = |f - k fs|, choosing the whole number k that makes the answer as small as possible.

The folding picture: Imagine the frequency axis drawn on a long strip of paper, folded like a fan at every multiple of fs/2. Any frequency, after folding, lands somewhere between 0 and fs/2. That is why fs/2 is also called the folding frequency. Frequencies just above fs/2 fold back to just below it. With fs = 1000 Hz, 510 Hz becomes 490 Hz, 700 Hz becomes 300 Hz, 990 Hz becomes 10 Hz, and 1000 Hz becomes 0 Hz, a constant. A tone sampled exactly once per cycle looks like it is not changing at all.

Worked example 3, a phone line: A phone line samples at 8 kHz, so the folding frequency is 4 kHz. Suppose a 5 kHz whistle reaches the sampler unfiltered. Its alias is 8 - 5 = 3 kHz, right in the middle of the speech band. A 6 kHz tone would appear at 2 kHz. These fake tones are not just noise added on top; they sit at frequencies where real speech lives, so they cannot be removed later without also damaging the voice.

The wagon-wheel effect: Back to our fan. Put a sticker on one blade so you can follow it. Suppose the fan turns 25 times per second and the camera shoots 24 frames per second. Between two frames the blade turns 25/24 of a turn, that is one full turn plus 1/24 of a turn. The full turn is invisible, so the blade seems to creep forward 1/24 turn per frame, which is 1 turn per second. If the fan turns 23 times per second, it moves 1 - 1/24 turns per frame, and it seems to creep backwards at 1 turn per second. At exactly 24 turns per second it seems frozen. A fan with three identical blades makes things even trickier, because the camera cannot tell the blades apart.

The anti-aliasing filter: The cure is to stop high frequencies before they reach the sampler. An analog low-pass filter placed in front of the ADC, called the anti-aliasing filter, removes everything above fs/2. Since real filters cannot cut instantly (lesson 16), we choose fs above twice the highest frequency we care about, to leave a transition band. The filter must be analog and must come before sampling. After sampling, the alias is already sitting on top of the real signal, with exactly the same samples, and no digital processing can separate them.

Two filter examples: In a telephone, the anti-aliasing filter passes roughly 300 to 3400 Hz and strongly attenuates everything above 4 kHz, before the 8 kHz sampler. In CD recording, the filter passes up to 20 kHz and must be well down by 22.05 kHz, the Nyquist frequency of a 44.1 kHz sampler. That narrow gap is why early CD players needed steep, expensive analog filters, and why many modern converters oversample instead: a higher fs gives a wider gap and an easier filter.

Reconstruction idea: Now the happy direction. We have clean samples of a band-limited signal, taken with fs > 2fmax, and we want x(t) back. In frequency, the sampled spectrum has the original copy in the middle and extra copies around every multiple of fs. So we pass the samples through an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff fs/2 and gain Ts. It keeps the middle copy, removes all others, and the gain Ts cancels the 1/Ts scale from sampling. What comes out is exactly X(jω), so exactly x(t).

Sinc interpolation: What does that ideal filter do in time? Its impulse response is a sinc. Each sample sends out its own sinc pulse, scaled by the sample value and centred at its own time. The rebuilt signal is x(t) = Σ x[n] sinc((t - nTs)/Ts), where sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu). At a sample time t = mTs, the m-th sinc equals 1 and every other sinc passes through zero, so the curve goes exactly through every sample. Between samples, all the sincs add up to fill the gap perfectly. Like the ideal filter of lesson 16, this is non-causal and infinitely long, so it is a target to approach, not something built exactly.

Zero-order hold: Real digital-to-analog converters, DACs, usually do something simpler. They hold each sample value steady for Ts seconds, then jump to the next one. The output is a staircase. This is called a zero-order hold, ZOH, because it uses a polynomial of degree zero, a flat line, between samples. In time, its impulse response is a rectangle of width Ts. So in frequency it behaves like a filter with magnitude Ts |sinc(f/fs)|.

The cost of the staircase: That sinc shape causes two problems. First, it does not fully remove the copies around fs, 2fs and so on; the sharp corners of the staircase are exactly those leftover high frequencies. A small analog smoothing filter, often called the reconstruction filter, cleans them up. Second, the sinc droops inside the band. At f = fs/2 its gain is sinc(0.5) = 2/π ≈ 0.637 compared with DC, which is about -3.9 dB. Designers sometimes boost high frequencies slightly to correct for this droop. A first-order hold, which joins the dots with straight lines, is smoother but needs one more sample of delay.

Quantization in one paragraph: Sampling fixes time; the ADC must also fix amplitude. A B-bit quantizer has 2^B levels. If the input range is 3.3 V and B = 12, there are 4096 levels and the step size is Δ = 3.3/4096 ≈ 0.806 mV. Each sample is rounded to the nearest level, so the error is at most Δ/2. This rounding error acts like a small noise added to the signal.

The 6 dB per bit rule: For a full-scale sine wave, the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is about SQNR ≈ 6.02B + 1.76 dB. So 8 bits give about 49.9 dB, and 16 bits, the CD standard, give about 98.1 dB. Every extra bit adds about 6 dB, because it halves the step size. Details of quantizers, coding and noise belong to the DSP and Data Communication courses, so we stop at this pointer.

The whole chain: Put it all together. Analog signal, then anti-aliasing low-pass filter, then sample-and-hold, then quantizer, which together form the ADC. Then digital processing on numbers: filtering, compression, storage, sending. Then the DAC with its zero-order hold, then the reconstruction low-pass filter, then the analog output to a speaker. Every voice call, every song on your phone and every video call follows this path, sample after sample, thousands or even millions of times per second.

Real-life example 1, rickshaw wheels on video: Film a moving rickshaw on a Dhaka street and look at the wheel spokes. Often the spokes seem to stand still, turn slowly, or even turn backwards. Since all spokes look alike, the camera only needs the wheel to turn by one spoke gap per frame for the picture to look frozen. The real rotation is fast, but the frame rate is too slow to see it honestly, so it is aliased to a slow fake motion. Change your walking speed beside it and you can watch the fake motion change direction.

Real-life example 2, moiré in photos: Take a phone photo of a TV screen, or of a friend wearing a shirt with fine stripes. Sometimes strange wavy rainbow patterns appear that were not really there. That is aliasing in space, not time. The camera sensor samples the picture with a grid of pixels. Stripes finer than the pixel grid can handle fold down into big slow waves, called moiré patterns. Many cameras use a slight optical blur in front of the sensor, which is an anti-aliasing filter for images.

Common mistakes: Subtracting fs once when the frequency is more than 1.5 fs, and stopping with an answer above fs/2. Forgetting that the alias of a sine can flip its sign. Thinking a digital filter after the ADC can remove aliasing; it cannot, because the alias is already inside the band. Putting the anti-aliasing filter after the sampler in a block diagram. Forgetting the gain Ts of the ideal reconstruction filter. And calling the zero-order hold an ideal reconstruction; it is only an approximation with droop and leftover images.

What exams ask: Find the alias of a given frequency at a given fs, or list which input frequencies would all alias to the same one. Explain the wagon-wheel effect with numbers. Draw the full ADC and DAC chain and label the anti-aliasing and reconstruction filters. Write the sinc interpolation formula and explain why the curve passes through every sample. Find the ZOH droop at fs/2. Find the step size and SQNR of a B-bit quantizer.

Recap: Aliasing happens when a signal has frequencies above fs/2: after sampling, frequency f looks exactly like |f - k fs|, folded into 0 to fs/2. You cannot undo it after sampling, so an analog anti-aliasing low-pass filter must come first. With clean samples, an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff fs/2 and gain Ts rebuilds x(t) exactly through sinc interpolation. Real DACs use a zero-order hold, which droops to about -3.9 dB at fs/2 and needs a smoothing filter. Quantization adds about 6 dB of quality per bit. Wagon wheels, rickshaw spokes and moiré photos are aliasing you can see with your own eyes.
key_points: Aliasing: after sampling at fs, a frequency f gives the same samples as |f - k fs|; everything folds into the range 0 to fs/2.
Example: 700 Hz sampled at 1000 Hz looks like 300 Hz; 1200 Hz looks like 200 Hz; at 8 kHz, a 5 kHz tone looks like 3 kHz.
Wagon-wheel effect: a fan at 25 rev/s filmed at 24 fps appears to turn forward at 1 rev/s; at 23 rev/s it appears to turn backward at 1 rev/s.
The anti-aliasing filter is an analog low-pass placed before the sampler; aliasing cannot be removed after sampling.
Ideal reconstruction: low-pass with cutoff fs/2 and gain Ts, i.e. x(t) = Σ x[n] sinc((t - nTs)/Ts).
Zero-order hold makes a staircase; its response Ts|sinc(f/fs)| droops to 2/π (about -3.9 dB) at fs/2 and needs a smoothing filter.
Quantization: 2^B levels, step Δ = range/2^B, SQNR about 6.02B + 1.76 dB, so about 6 dB per extra bit.
lessons.tip: For alias questions, draw a short number line from 0 to fs with a mirror at fs/2. Fold the frequency onto it by hand once or twice, and the formula |f - k fs| will start to feel obvious instead of magic.
lessons.task: Record a 5 second slow-motion or normal video of a ceiling fan as it speeds up from off to full speed. Play it back frame by frame and note the moments when the blades look frozen or turn backwards. Try to explain each moment with the 'turns per frame' idea from this lesson.

quiz.q: A 700 Hz cosine is sampled at 1000 Hz. At what frequency does it appear?
quiz.explain: 700 Hz is above the folding frequency 500 Hz, so it folds to 1000 - 700 = 300 Hz.

quiz.q: Where must the anti-aliasing filter be placed?
options: Inside the digital processor, after sampling
Before the sampler, as an analog filter
quiz.explain: Once sampled, the alias has the same samples as a real low frequency, so it must be removed in analog form before sampling.

quiz.q: Which method gives ideal, exact reconstruction of a band-limited signal from its samples?
options: Rounding each sample to the nearest level
An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff fs/2, i.e. sinc interpolation
quiz.explain: The ideal low-pass keeps only the central copy; in time it adds one sinc per sample, passing exactly through all samples.

quiz.q: A fan turns at 23 rev/s and is filmed at 24 frames per second. What does the video show?
quiz.explain: Per frame it turns 23/24 = 1 - 1/24 of a turn, so it seems to slip back 1/24 turn per frame, which is 1 rev/s backwards.

quiz.q: For a full-scale sine, each extra bit of ADC resolution improves SQNR by about
quiz.explain: SQNR ≈ 6.02B + 1.76 dB. One more bit halves the step size, which adds about 6 dB.

lessons.title: The Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT)
lessons.content:
Imagine you write down the price of potatoes at Karwan Bazar every single day for a year. You get a long list of numbers, x[n], one per day. Some changes are slow, like the price creeping up over the months. Some are fast, like a jump on one day and a drop the next. Is the list mostly slow change or mostly fast jitter? The continuous Fourier transform answers this kind of question for smooth signals. For a list of numbers we need its discrete cousin, the discrete-time Fourier transform, or DTFT. It is the frequency-domain view for every sequence you will meet in the digital world.

The definition: For a discrete-time signal x[n], the DTFT is X(e^(jω)) = Σ x[n] e^(-jωn), with the sum over all integers n from minus infinity to plus infinity. It is the same idea as the continuous transform, except the integral over t becomes a sum over n. To go back we use the inverse DTFT, x[n] = (1/2π) ∫ X(e^(jω)) e^(jωn) dω, where the integral runs over just one interval of length 2π, usually from -π to π. Here ω is measured in radians per sample, not radians per second.

Why the strange notation: Why write X(e^(jω)) instead of X(ω)? Because ω only ever appears inside e^(jω). Writing it this way reminds us of two things. First, the transform is periodic, which we see next. Second, it links neatly to the z-transform of lesson 23, where z = e^(jω) is a point on the unit circle. Many books simply write X(ω) too. Both mean the same thing; just be consistent in one answer.

Periodic in 2π: Here is the biggest difference from the continuous transform. Since e^(-j(ω + 2π)n) = e^(-jωn) e^(-j2πn) = e^(-jωn) for every integer n, we get X(e^(j(ω + 2π))) = X(e^(jω)). The DTFT always repeats every 2π. This is the same fact as in lesson 4: a discrete sinusoid at frequency ω and one at ω + 2π give the exact same samples. So we only ever need to look at one period, -π < ω ≤ π. Around ω = 0 live the slow changes. At ω = π lives the fastest possible change, the sequence 1, -1, 1, -1, which flips every sample.

The link to real frequency: If x[n] came from sampling at rate fs, then ω = 2π f / fs, or ω = Ω Ts if Ω is the analog frequency in rad/s. So ω = π matches f = fs/2, the Nyquist frequency of lesson 17, and ω = 2π matches fs itself. For example, with fs = 8 kHz, ω = π/2 corresponds to 2 kHz, and ω = π to 4 kHz. The 2π periodicity of the DTFT is exactly the repeating copies of the sampled spectrum, just measured in radians per sample.

Example 1, the unit sample: Let x[n] = δ[n], which is 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere. Only one term survives in the sum, so X(e^(jω)) = 1 for every ω. A single click contains all frequencies equally, just like δ(t) in continuous time. Now shift it, x[n] = δ[n - n0]. The sum gives e^(-jωn0). The magnitude is still 1 everywhere, and the phase is -ωn0, a straight line. So a delay of n0 samples only adds a linear phase, which is the time shift property in action.

Example 2, the decaying exponential: Let x[n] = a^n u[n] with |a| < 1. Then X(e^(jω)) = Σ (a e^(-jω))^n for n from 0 to infinity. That is a geometric series with ratio a e^(-jω), whose size is |a| < 1, so it converges to X(e^(jω)) = 1 / (1 - a e^(-jω)). If |a| ≥ 1 the series does not converge and the ordinary DTFT does not exist. In particular the unit step u[n], which is a = 1, has no ordinary DTFT; it needs impulses or the z-transform.

Numbers for a = 0.5: At ω = 0, e^(-jω) = 1, so X = 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2. At ω = π/2, |X| = 1/|1 + 0.5j| ≈ 0.894. At ω = π, e^(-jπ) = -1, so X = 1/(1 + 0.5) ≈ 0.667. The magnitude is biggest at low frequency and smallest at high frequency: a low-pass shape, which makes sense, because 1, 0.5, 0.25, ... changes smoothly. Now flip the sign, a = -0.5. The sequence becomes 1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125, a jumpy alternating signal, and indeed |X| becomes 0.667 at ω = 0 and 2 at ω = π. A high-pass shape.

Example 3, the rectangular pulse: Let x[n] = 1 for n = 0, 1, ..., N - 1, and 0 otherwise. The finite geometric series gives X(e^(jω)) = e^(-jω(N-1)/2) · sin(ωN/2) / sin(ω/2). At ω = 0 the value is N, the sum of the samples. The magnitude falls to zero at ω = 2πk/N for every k that is not a multiple of N. For N = 4, X(e^(j0)) = 4 and the zeros are at π/2, π and 3π/2. This shape is the discrete cousin of the sinc, sometimes called the Dirichlet kernel, and the phase term e^(-jω(N-1)/2) just says the pulse is centred at (N-1)/2.

Properties: The DTFT has the same toolbox you learned in lesson 15, with small changes. Linearity: a x1 + b x2 transforms to a X1 + b X2. Time shift: x[n - n0] gives e^(-jωn0) X. Frequency shift: e^(jω0 n) x[n] gives X(e^(j(ω - ω0))). Time reversal: x[-n] gives X(e^(-jω)). Convolution: x[n] * h[n] gives X H, a plain product. Multiplication in time gives a periodic convolution in frequency. And Parseval: Σ |x[n]|² = (1/2π) ∫ |X(e^(jω))|² dω over one period.

Parseval check: Take x[n] = 0.5^n u[n] again. In time, the energy is Σ 0.25^n = 1/(1 - 0.25) = 4/3. In frequency, the integral of |1/(1 - 0.5e^(-jω))|² over -π to π, divided by 2π, also gives 4/3. Same energy counted two ways. Checking Parseval like this is a great way to catch a mistake in a transform you have just computed.

What changes from the CTFT: The continuous transform uses an integral over t and lives on the whole ω axis. The DTFT uses a sum over n and repeats every 2π, so all the action fits in -π to π. The inverse DTFT integrates over one period only. And the DTFT is continuous in ω even though x[n] is discrete. Discrete in time gives periodic in frequency; that pairing, which we met in sampling, is worth remembering.

Frequency response of a discrete LTI system: For a discrete LTI system with impulse response h[n], the frequency response is H(e^(jω)), the DTFT of h[n]. Just like lesson 16, an input e^(jωn) comes out as H(e^(jω)) e^(jωn), and in general Y(e^(jω)) = H(e^(jω)) X(e^(jω)). For example, the recursive system y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 y[n - 1] has h[n] = 0.5^n u[n], so its frequency response is exactly our Example 2: a gentle low-pass with gain 2 at DC and about 0.667 at ω = π.

Two-point moving average: The simplest smoother is y[n] = (x[n] + x[n - 1]) / 2, with h = {1/2, 1/2}. Its DTFT is H(e^(jω)) = (1 + e^(-jω))/2 = e^(-jω/2) cos(ω/2). The magnitude is |cos(ω/2)|: gain 1 at ω = 0, about 0.707 at ω = π/2, and exactly 0 at ω = π. The phase -ω/2 is linear, which means a constant delay of half a sample. So the 2-point average keeps slow trends and completely removes the fastest flip-flop.

Three-point moving average: Now y[n] = (x[n] + x[n - 1] + x[n - 2]) / 3. Its frequency response is H(e^(jω)) = (1/3) e^(-jω) (1 + 2 cos ω). The magnitude |1 + 2cos ω| / 3 equals 1 at ω = 0, 2/3 at ω = π/3, exactly 0 at ω = 2π/3, and 1/3 at ω = π. So it is a low-pass filter, but not a perfect one: it lets a bit of the highest frequency back through. Because h is symmetric, the phase is linear, a delay of one sample, apart from a sign flip where 1 + 2cos ω turns negative.

Worked outputs: Feed x[n] = 1 + (-1)^n, which is 2, 0, 2, 0, ..., into the 2-point average. The DC part has gain 1, the (-1)^n part sits at ω = π where the gain is 0, so y[n] = 1 for every n. You can check directly: (2 + 0)/2 = 1 and (0 + 2)/2 = 1. Now feed x[n] = cos(2πn/3) into the 3-point average. Its frequency 2π/3 is a zero of H, so the output is 0 for every n. Indeed, any three consecutive samples of that cosine add up to zero.

The bridge to DFT and FFT: The DTFT is a continuous function of ω, but a computer cannot store infinitely many values. So for a sequence of length N we compute the DTFT only at N equally spaced points, ω_k = 2πk/N for k = 0, 1, ..., N - 1. Those N numbers are the discrete Fourier transform, the DFT. The FFT is simply a very fast algorithm for computing the DFT, needing about N log N operations instead of N². For example, the 4-point DFT of {1, 1, 1, 1} is {4, 0, 0, 0}: exactly the DTFT of our N = 4 pulse sampled at 0, π/2, π, 3π/2. The DFT, FFT and windowing are covered in depth in the DSP course.

Real-life example 1, the 7-day average: News charts of daily cases, or a shop's daily bKash sales, often wiggle with the week: busy on some days, quiet on Friday. People smooth them with a 7-day moving average. In DTFT terms, a 7-point average has zeros at ω = 2πk/7 for k = 1 to 6. A pattern that repeats every 7 days lives at exactly those frequencies, plus DC. So the 7-day average wipes out the weekly pattern completely and keeps the slow trend. That is not luck; it is the rectangular-pulse DTFT at work.

Real-life example 2, the step counter: Your phone's step counter reads the accelerometer many times per second, giving a sequence of numbers. Walking makes a rhythm of roughly one to three steps per second, while hand shaking and sensor noise are faster and messier. A simple low-pass digital filter, such as a moving average, keeps the walking rhythm and reduces the fast jitter, and its DTFT tells the designer exactly which frequencies survive. The same thinking smooths the price list from Karwan Bazar in our hook.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that the DTFT is periodic and drawing it only once, or drawing it over 0 to π and calling that the whole thing. Mixing ω in radians per sample with Ω in radians per second. Writing 1/(1 - a e^(-jω)) for |a| ≥ 1, where it does not converge. Saying the DTFT and DFT are the same; the DFT is samples of the DTFT for a finite sequence. And ignoring the linear phase factor of a moving average, which is a real delay.

What exams ask: Find the DTFT of δ[n - n0], a^n u[n], or a rectangular pulse, and sketch the magnitude. Prove the 2π periodicity. Use properties to find the DTFT of a shifted or modulated sequence. Find H(e^(jω)) of a moving average or a first-order recursive system and evaluate it at ω = 0, π/2 and π. Find the output for a sinusoidal input. Verify Parseval for a simple sequence. Explain how the DFT relates to the DTFT.

Recap: The DTFT, X(e^(jω)) = Σ x[n] e^(-jωn), is the frequency view of a sequence. It is continuous in ω and periodic with period 2π, so we study -π to π, with ω = π being the fastest change, matching fs/2. δ[n] gives 1, a^n u[n] gives 1/(1 - a e^(-jω)) when |a| < 1, and a length-N pulse gives a discrete sinc with zeros at 2πk/N. Convolution becomes multiplication, so H(e^(jω)) is the frequency response of a discrete LTI system. Moving averages are simple low-pass filters with linear phase. The DFT samples the DTFT at N points, and the FFT computes it fast.
key_points: DTFT: X(e^(jω)) = Σ x[n] e^(-jωn); inverse x[n] = (1/2π) ∫ over one 2π period of X(e^(jω)) e^(jωn) dω.
The DTFT is always periodic with period 2π; only -π < ω ≤ π matters, and ω = π is the fastest change (1, -1, 1, -1).
For sampled signals ω = 2πf/fs, so ω = π matches the Nyquist frequency fs/2.
Pairs: δ[n] → 1; δ[n - n0] → e^(-jωn0); a^n u[n] → 1/(1 - a e^(-jω)) for |a| < 1; length-N pulse → e^(-jω(N-1)/2) sin(ωN/2)/sin(ω/2).
Convolution in n becomes multiplication in ω, so H(e^(jω)), the DTFT of h[n], is the discrete frequency response.
2-point moving average: |H| = |cos(ω/2)|, zero at ω = π; 3-point: |1 + 2cos ω|/3, zero at ω = 2π/3.
The DFT is N equally spaced samples ω_k = 2πk/N of the DTFT of a length-N sequence; the FFT is a fast way to compute it.
lessons.tip: Always check a DTFT answer at ω = 0: it must equal Σ x[n], the plain sum of the samples. This one-second test catches most algebra slips before the examiner does.
lessons.task: Write down the daily maximum temperature (from your phone's weather app history, or make up 21 realistic numbers). Compute a 3-day and a 7-day moving average by hand or in a spreadsheet, and plot all three. Note how much faster wiggles each average removes, and connect that to where the zeros of H(e^(jω)) are.

quiz.q: The DTFT X(e^(jω)) of any sequence is periodic with what period?
quiz.explain: e^(-j(ω+2π)n) = e^(-jωn) for every integer n, so X repeats every 2π.

quiz.q: What is the DTFT of x[n] = 0.5^n u[n] at ω = 0?
quiz.explain: X = 1/(1 - 0.5e^(-jω)); at ω = 0 this is 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2, which also equals Σ 0.5^n.

quiz.q: For the 2-point moving average y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1])/2, what is |H(e^(jω))| at ω = π?
quiz.explain: H = e^(-jω/2) cos(ω/2), and cos(π/2) = 0. The alternating sequence is fully removed.

quiz.q: A signal was sampled at fs = 8 kHz. Which analog frequency does ω = π correspond to?
quiz.explain: ω = 2πf/fs, so ω = π gives f = fs/2 = 4 kHz, the Nyquist frequency.

quiz.q: How is the DFT related to the DTFT?
options: The DFT is the inverse of the DTFT
The DFT only works for infinitely long sequences
The DFT gives N equally spaced samples of the DTFT of a length-N sequence
quiz.explain: For a length-N sequence, the DFT values are X(e^(jω)) at ω_k = 2πk/N, k = 0..N-1; the FFT computes them quickly.

lessons.title: The Laplace Transform for Systems and the Region of Convergence
lessons.content:
Try to look straight at a powerful torch and your eyes just hurt. Put on dark sunglasses and suddenly you can see the bulb clearly. The Fourier transform has the same problem with some signals. A growing signal like e^t u(t) is far too bright: its Fourier integral blows up and gives nothing. Even the humble unit step needs special tricks. The Laplace transform is the pair of sunglasses. It multiplies the signal by a fading factor e^(-σt) before taking the Fourier transform, so even wild signals become something we can look at. In this lesson we use it from the systems view, and meet its most important companion, the region of convergence.

Quick recap from Math III: In Math III you met the Laplace transform as a tool for solving differential equations, with tables and partial fractions. Here we write the complex variable as s = σ + jω, where σ is the real part and ω the imaginary part. The bilateral, or two-sided, Laplace transform is X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(-st) dt, with the integral over all t from minus infinity to plus infinity. Since e^(-st) = e^(-σt) e^(-jωt), X(s) is just the Fourier transform of x(t) e^(-σt). The sunglasses are e^(-σt), and σ decides how dark they are.

Unilateral versus bilateral: The unilateral, or one-sided, transform integrates only from t = 0- to infinity. It ignores everything before t = 0, which is perfect for causal signals and for problems that start at a switch-on moment with initial conditions. That is the version Math III used most. The bilateral transform keeps the whole time axis, which we need to talk about non-causal signals and the full theory of systems. For a signal that is zero for t < 0, both transforms give the same formula.

The region of convergence: The integral ∫ x(t) e^(-st) dt does not converge for every s. The set of s values where it does converge is called the region of convergence, or ROC. Because convergence depends only on how big e^(-σt) is, the ROC depends only on σ = Re{s}, not on ω. So the ROC is always a vertical strip, a half-plane, the whole plane, or nothing, drawn in the s-plane with σ across and jω up.

A right-sided example: Take x(t) = e^(-at) u(t). Then X(s) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-(s + a)t) dt. This converges only when the exponent decays, meaning Re{s + a} > 0, so Re{s} > -a. Then the integral equals 1/(s + a). So e^(-at) u(t) has X(s) = 1/(s + a), with ROC Re{s} > -a. The point s = -a, where X blows up, is a pole. For a right-sided signal, the ROC is everything to the right of a vertical line.

A left-sided example: Now take x(t) = -e^(-at) u(-t), which lives only for t < 0. Then X(s) = -∫ from -∞ to 0 of e^(-(s + a)t) dt. As t goes to minus infinity, this integral converges only when Re{s + a} < 0, so Re{s} < -a. Working it out gives X(s) = 1/(s + a), with ROC Re{s} < -a. For a left-sided signal, the ROC is everything to the left of a vertical line.

Same formula, two signals: Look at what just happened. e^(-at) u(t) and -e^(-at) u(-t) are totally different signals. One starts at t = 0 and lives in the future; the other lives only in the past. Yet both have X(s) = 1/(s + a). The only difference is the ROC: to the right of -a, or to the left of -a. So the formula alone is not enough to know the signal. A Laplace transform answer without its ROC is half an answer, and that is exactly why the ROC matters.

A two-sided example: Let x(t) = e^(-t) u(t) + e^(2t) u(-t). The first part gives 1/(s + 1) with ROC Re{s} > -1. The second part, e^(2t) u(-t), gives -1/(s - 2) with ROC Re{s} < 2. The sum exists only where both converge, so the ROC is the strip -1 < Re{s} < 2. Combined, X(s) = 1/(s + 1) - 1/(s - 2) = -3 / ((s + 1)(s - 2)). Quick check at s = 0: the integral is ∫ e^(-t) dt from 0 to ∞ plus ∫ e^(2t) dt from -∞ to 0, which is 1 + 0.5 = 1.5, and the formula gives -3/((1)(-2)) = 1.5. It matches.

When there is no ROC: Take x(t) = 1 for all t, which is u(t) + u(-t). The right-sided part u(t) needs Re{s} > 0. The left-sided part u(-t) needs Re{s} < 0. No s can do both, so the ROC is empty and this signal has no bilateral Laplace transform at all. Sunglasses that dim the future brighten the past, and a signal that lasts forever in both directions cannot be tamed by one single σ.

ROC rules: First, the ROC is a strip parallel to the jω axis. Second, it never contains a pole, since X is infinite there. Third, for a right-sided signal, the ROC lies to the right of the rightmost pole. Fourth, for a left-sided signal, it lies to the left of the leftmost pole. Fifth, for a two-sided signal it is a strip between two poles, or empty. Sixth, a finite-length signal, like a short pulse, has the whole s-plane as its ROC. For example, δ(t) gives X(s) = 1 for every s.

A small table: These pairs, all with ROC Re{s} > 0 unless noted, cover most exam work. δ(t) gives 1, ROC the whole plane. u(t) gives 1/s. t u(t) gives 1/s². e^(-at) u(t) gives 1/(s + a), ROC Re{s} > -a. cos(ω0 t) u(t) gives s/(s² + ω0²). sin(ω0 t) u(t) gives ω0/(s² + ω0²). For example, sin(3t) u(t) gives 3/(s² + 9). You derived these in Math III, so here just remember each one with its ROC.

Link to the Fourier transform: Setting σ = 0 gives s = jω, and the Laplace integral becomes exactly the Fourier integral. So if the ROC includes the jω axis, then X(jω) = X(s) evaluated at s = jω. For example, e^(-2t) u(t) has X(s) = 1/(s + 2) with ROC Re{s} > -2, which contains σ = 0, so its Fourier transform is 1/(jω + 2), matching lesson 14. But u(t) has ROC Re{s} > 0, which does not include the axis. Plugging s = jω into 1/s misses the impulse term πδ(ω) in its Fourier transform. You may substitute s = jω only when the axis is inside the ROC.

Stability from the ROC: An LTI system is BIBO stable when ∫ |h(t)| dt is finite (lesson 11). That is exactly the condition for the Fourier transform of h to converge, so it means the jω axis is in the ROC of H(s). The rule is: an LTI system is stable if and only if the ROC of H(s) includes the jω axis. Causality has its own rule: a causal system has a right-sided h(t), so its ROC is a right half-plane to the right of the rightmost pole.

Example with one pole: Let H(s) = 1/(s - 1), a pole at s = 1. If we choose ROC Re{s} > 1, then h(t) = e^t u(t). It is causal, but it grows forever, and the ROC misses the jω axis, so it is unstable. If we choose ROC Re{s} < 1, then h(t) = -e^t u(-t). This one includes the jω axis, so it is stable, since ∫ |h| dt = 1, but it lives before t = 0, so it is non-causal. With a pole in the right half-plane you can have causal or stable, but never both.

Example with two poles: Take H(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s - 2)), with poles at -1 and 2. There are three possible ROCs. Re{s} > 2 gives a causal but unstable system. -1 < Re{s} < 2 gives a two-sided, stable, non-causal system, because the strip contains the jω axis. Re{s} < -1 gives an anti-causal, unstable system. One formula, three different systems. This leads to the famous rule we will use in lessons 21 and 24: a causal system is stable exactly when all its poles lie in the left half-plane.

The unilateral transform and initial conditions: The unilateral transform has a special derivative rule: the transform of dx/dt is sX(s) - x(0-). That x(0-) term carries the initial condition straight into the algebra. For example, solve dy/dt + 2y = 0 with y(0-) = 3. Transform: sY(s) - 3 + 2Y(s) = 0, so Y(s) = 3/(s + 2), and y(t) = 3e^(-2t) for t ≥ 0. The charge on a capacitor or the speed of a motor at switch-on enters the answer naturally. Full system analysis with H(s), partial fractions and step responses comes in lesson 22.

Key properties in the systems view: Linearity works as always. A time shift x(t - t0) multiplies by e^(-st0). Differentiation multiplies by s, and integration divides by s. And the star again: convolution becomes multiplication, so for an LTI system Y(s) = H(s) X(s), where H(s), the Laplace transform of h(t), is called the transfer function. It is the same story as Fourier, with s in place of jω, and it works even for unstable systems.

Real-life example 1, the IPS during load shedding: When the grid power goes during load shedding, an IPS switches its inverter on, and the voltage across the load must settle quickly to a steady value. An engineer models the circuit, with its inductors and capacitors, as a system with a transfer function H(s). The poles and the ROC tell, before any part is soldered, whether the switch-on transient dies out, oscillates for a while, or grows dangerously. That is the Laplace transform deciding whether your fan keeps spinning smoothly.

Real-life example 2, a bumpy Dhaka road: A rickshaw or a bus hitting a pothole is a spring and a shock absorber pushed by a sudden input, almost a step. Its motion is a second-order differential equation, so its Laplace transform gives a transfer function with two poles. If the poles are well inside the left half-plane, the bounce dies out quickly. If they are close to the jω axis, the seat keeps bouncing for a long time. Car and bus designers tune the springs and dampers by moving those poles.

Common mistakes: Writing X(s) without its ROC. Saying the ROC depends on ω; it depends only on σ = Re{s}. Substituting s = jω when the ROC does not include the jω axis. Forgetting the minus sign in the left-sided pair -e^(-at) u(-t). Mixing up the unilateral derivative rule sX(s) - x(0-) with the bilateral one, which is simply sX(s). And claiming that every signal has a Laplace transform; a constant over all time does not.

What exams ask: Find X(s) and the ROC of a right-sided, left-sided or two-sided exponential, and sketch the ROC in the s-plane. Given X(s) and several possible ROCs, find the matching time signals and say which is causal and which is stable. State the ROC properties. Decide whether you may get the Fourier transform by setting s = jω. Solve a first-order differential equation with an initial condition using the unilateral transform.

Recap: The Laplace transform X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(-st) dt, with s = σ + jω, is the Fourier transform of x(t) e^(-σt), so it handles signals Fourier cannot. The region of convergence is a vertical strip depending only on Re{s}. Right-sided signals have ROCs to the right of the rightmost pole, left-sided to the left, two-sided in a strip, and some signals have none. The same formula with different ROCs gives different signals, so always give the ROC. If the ROC includes the jω axis, X(jω) = X(s) at s = jω and the system is stable. The unilateral transform brings initial conditions in through sX(s) - x(0-).
key_points: Bilateral Laplace: X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(-st) dt over all t, s = σ + jω; it is the Fourier transform of x(t) e^(-σt).
Unilateral Laplace integrates from 0- to ∞ and brings initial conditions in: L{dx/dt} = sX(s) - x(0-).
The ROC is the set of s where the integral converges; it depends only on Re{s}, so it is a vertical strip or half-plane, and never contains a pole.
e^(-at) u(t) → 1/(s + a), ROC Re{s} > -a; -e^(-at) u(-t) → 1/(s + a), ROC Re{s} < -a: same formula, different signals.
Right-sided: ROC right of the rightmost pole; left-sided: left of the leftmost pole; two-sided: a strip; x(t) = 1 for all t has no ROC.
If the ROC includes the jω axis, the Fourier transform is X(s) at s = jω, and an LTI system is BIBO stable exactly then.
Causal and stable together means all poles of H(s) are in the left half-plane; convolution gives Y(s) = H(s) X(s).
lessons.tip: Never write a Laplace transform without drawing its ROC next to it, even a tiny sketch: a vertical line through each pole and shading on the correct side. Examiners give marks for the ROC, and the sketch makes stability and causality questions almost automatic.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the s-plane and mark the poles of H(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s - 2)). Shade each of the three possible ROCs in a different colour, write the matching h(t) under each, and label each one causal or not, stable or not.

quiz.q: What is the ROC of the Laplace transform of e^(-3t) u(t)?
quiz.explain: ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-(s+3)t) dt converges when Re{s + 3} > 0, i.e. Re{s} > -3.

quiz.q: Which signal has X(s) = 1/(s + 2) with ROC Re{s} < -2?
quiz.explain: The left-sided signal -e^(-at) u(-t) has transform 1/(s + a) with ROC Re{s} < -a; here a = 2.

quiz.q: An LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when the ROC of H(s)
options: lies to the right of all poles
lies to the left of all poles
quiz.explain: Stability means ∫|h| dt is finite, which is the condition for the Fourier transform, i.e. σ = 0, to be inside the ROC.

quiz.q: What is the bilateral Laplace transform of x(t) = 1 for all t?
options: It does not exist, because the two halves have no common ROC
quiz.explain: u(t) needs Re{s} > 0 and u(-t) needs Re{s} < 0; no s satisfies both, so the ROC is empty.

quiz.q: In the unilateral Laplace transform, dy/dt transforms to
quiz.explain: The one-sided transform keeps the initial value: L{dy/dt} = sY(s) - y(0-).

lessons.title: Poles and Zeros: Reading a System from a Few Dots
lessons.content:
Imagine a doctor looking at an X-ray. She does not need to see every cell of your body. A few bright and dark spots tell her almost everything. A transfer function is a long formula, and it can look scary. But hidden inside it are a few special points called poles and zeros. Put them as dots on a map, and you can tell at one glance whether a system will settle down calmly, ring like a bell, or blow up. In this lesson we learn to read that map.

Quick recap from lesson 20: The Laplace transform turns a signal x(t) into X(s), where s = σ + jω is a complex number. For an LTI system that starts at rest, the output transform is Y(s) = H(s) X(s). This H(s) is called the transfer function, and it is simply the Laplace transform of the impulse response h(t). So H(s) is the whole system packed into one function of s. Math III already showed you how to find Laplace transforms and how to do partial fractions, so we will use those tools freely.

Transfer function as a ratio of polynomials: In lesson 12 we described systems with linear differential equations with constant coefficients. Take the Laplace transform of such an equation with zero initial conditions, and every derivative d/dt becomes a multiplication by s. For example, y'' + 5y' + 6y = x' + x becomes (s^2 + 5s + 6) Y(s) = (s + 1) X(s). So H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = (s + 1)/(s^2 + 5s + 6). In general H(s) = N(s)/D(s), a numerator polynomial over a denominator polynomial. Such a function is called rational.

What poles and zeros are: A zero is a value of s where the numerator N(s) is zero, so H(s) = 0 there. A pole is a value of s where the denominator D(s) is zero, so H(s) shoots up to infinity there. Picture |H(s)| as a big rubber sheet stretched over the s-plane. At every pole, a tent pole pushes the sheet up to the sky. At every zero, a nail pins the sheet down to the ground. The shape of the whole sheet, and so the whole behaviour of the system, comes from where those poles and nails are.

Finding them by factoring: For our example, N(s) = s + 1 is zero at s = -1, so there is one zero at -1. The denominator factors as s^2 + 5s + 6 = (s + 2)(s + 3), so the poles are at s = -2 and s = -3. Be careful with the signs. The factor (s + 2) means a pole at minus 2, not plus 2. We can now write H(s) in factored form: H(s) = K (s - z1)(s - z2).../((s - p1)(s - p2)...), where the z's are zeros, the p's are poles and K is a gain constant. Here K = 1.

When it does not factor nicely: Use the quadratic formula. Take H(s) = 1/(s^2 + 2s + 5). The poles are s = (-2 ± √(4 - 20))/2 = (-2 ± √(-16))/2 = -1 ± j2. So this system has a pair of complex poles. Because the coefficients of real systems are real numbers, complex poles and zeros always come in conjugate pairs, like -1 + j2 and -1 - j2. If you ever find a complex pole without its twin, you made a mistake somewhere. Check it right away.

A few useful words: The order of a system is the number of poles, which is the degree of D(s). Our example is second order. If the numerator degree M is not bigger than the denominator degree N, H(s) is called proper, and if M < N it is strictly proper. Almost all real physical systems are proper. Poles, zeros and the constant K together describe H(s) completely.

The pole-zero plot: Draw the s-plane. The horizontal axis is σ, the real part. The vertical axis is jω, the imaginary part. Mark every pole with a small cross (×) and every zero with a small circle (o). For H(s) = (s + 1)/(s^2 + 5s + 6) you draw a circle at -1 and crosses at -2 and -3, all on the real axis. A repeated pole is shown with two crosses on top of each other, or a small number 2 beside it. The vertical axis splits the plane into the left half-plane and the right half-plane, and that split will matter a lot.

Why poles shape the time response: Do partial fractions on H(s). For our example, (s + 1)/((s + 2)(s + 3)) = -1/(s + 2) + 2/(s + 3). Each simple term A/(s - p) is the transform of A e^(pt) u(t). So h(t) = (2e^(-3t) - e^(-2t)) u(t). See the pattern? Every pole p gives one term e^(pt) in the impulse response. These terms are called the natural modes of the system. The zeros do not create new terms. They only decide the weights, here the 2 and the -1. Poles choose the shapes, zeros mix them.

Real poles on the negative axis: A pole at s = -a, with a > 0, gives e^(-at), a decaying exponential. The farther left the pole, the faster it dies. Its time constant is τ = 1/a. A pole at -2 has τ = 0.5 s, while a pole at -10 has τ = 0.1 s and is gone almost at once. When a system has several poles, the one closest to the jω axis dies slowest and controls the long-term shape. We call it the dominant pole. In our example, the e^(-2t) term from the pole at -2 lasts longer than the e^(-3t) term.

Poles at the origin and on the right: A pole exactly at s = 0 gives 1/s, whose inverse is u(t). That term never decays. It just stays. A system with H(s) = 1/s is an integrator: it keeps adding up its input forever. A pole on the positive real axis, say s = +1, gives e^(t), which grows without limit. Such a system is unstable. You have heard this in real life: when the microphone of a mosque loudspeaker picks up its own sound, the howl grows louder and louder until the amplifier hits its limit. That is a pole in the right half-plane in action.

Complex pole pairs: A pair p = -σ ± jωd gives a term like e^(-σt) cos(ωd t + φ). That is a wave that wiggles at ωd radians per second while its size shrinks like e^(-σt). So the real part of the pole tells the decay speed, and the imaginary part tells the wiggle speed. For H(s) = 1/(s^2 + 2s + 5) with poles -1 ± j2, partial fractions with completing the square give h(t) = 0.5 e^(-t) sin(2t) u(t). It shakes at 2 rad/s and fades like e^(-t). A plucked guitar string or a bell behaves exactly like this.

Poles on the jω axis and the full map: Put the pair exactly on the axis, say s = ±j3, as in H(s) = 3/(s^2 + 9). Then h(t) = sin(3t) u(t), a pure wave that never fades. This is called marginal, neither dying nor growing. Push the pair into the right half-plane and you get a wave whose size grows. So here is the whole map in one breath. Left half-plane: the mode dies. Right half-plane: the mode grows. On the axis: it stays. Height above the real axis: how fast it wiggles. Distance to the left of the axis: how fast it fades.

What zeros do to frequency response: Recall from lesson 16 that the frequency response is H(jω), which means walking up the jω axis. There is a lovely picture for it. |H(jω)| = |K| times the product of distances from the point jω to every zero, divided by the product of distances to every pole. Walk close to a pole, and you divide by a small number, so the gain is big. Walk over a zero sitting on the axis, and the gain becomes exactly zero. That is how engineers kill one unwanted frequency on purpose.

A small worked check: Take H(s) = (s + 1)/(s + 2). At ω = 0, the distance to the zero is 1 and to the pole is 2, so |H| = 0.5. At ω = 1, the distances are √2 and √5, so |H| = √(2/5) ≈ 0.632. At ω = 2 they are √5 and √8, so |H| ≈ 0.791. At very large ω both distances are almost equal, so |H| goes towards 1. Now look at H(s) = s/(s + 1), which has a zero at the origin. H(0) = 0, so it blocks DC completely, just like a capacitor in series blocks a steady battery voltage.

Worked RLC example, the transfer function: Take a series RLC circuit driven by a voltage x(t), and call the capacitor voltage y(t). In the s-domain the resistor is R, the inductor is sL and the capacitor is 1/(sC). It is a voltage divider: H(s) = (1/(sC))/(R + sL + 1/(sC)). Multiply top and bottom by sC to get H(s) = 1/(LC s^2 + RC s + 1). Divide by LC: H(s) = (1/(LC))/(s^2 + (R/L)s + 1/(LC)). There are no finite zeros and there are two poles. It is a second-order system.

Worked RLC example, the numbers: Let L = 1 H, C = 0.2 F and R = 2 Ω. Then 1/(LC) = 5 and R/L = 2, so H(s) = 5/(s^2 + 2s + 5). The poles are -1 ± j2. The impulse response is h(t) = 2.5 e^(-t) sin(2t) u(t). For a step input the output is y(t) = 1 - e^(-t)(cos 2t + 0.5 sin 2t). It overshoots to about 1.21 at t = π/2 ≈ 1.57 s and then settles at 1. The DC gain H(0) = 5/5 = 1 makes sense: in the end the capacitor charges to the full source voltage.

Moving the poles with R: Now change only R. With R = 6 Ω the denominator is s^2 + 6s + 5 = (s + 1)(s + 5), so the poles are -1 and -5, both real. No overshoot, just a slow creep up. With R = 2√5 ≈ 4.47 Ω you get a double pole at -√5 ≈ -2.24. This is the fastest response without overshoot. With R = 0 the poles are ±j√5 ≈ ±j2.24, and the circuit rings forever at 2.24 rad/s. As R grows from 0, the pair slides left along a circle of radius √5, because their product is always 1/(LC) = 5. They meet on the real axis and then split apart.

Real-life example 1, the rickshaw on a bumpy road: A rickshaw seat or a car body on its springs is a mass-spring-damper. Its equation, m y'' + b y' + k y = force, has exactly the same shape as the RLC circuit. The damper b plays the role of R. When the shock absorber is worn out, b is small, the poles sit near the jω axis, and the seat keeps bouncing after every pothole on a Dhaka road. A very stiff damper gives real poles and a slow, hard ride. Good design places the poles at a comfortable spot in between.

Real-life example 2, tuning the radio: When you turn the knob to Radio Today or another FM station, an LC circuit inside the radio is being adjusted. This tuning circuit has a pair of lightly damped poles sitting very close to the jω axis at the station's frequency. Walk up the jω axis and you pass very close to that pole, so the gain at the station's frequency becomes huge, while other stations far away on the axis get much less gain. Turning the knob changes C, which moves the poles up or down the axis.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often swap poles and zeros, so say it out loud: poles come from the denominator. They read (s + 2) as a pole at +2. They forget the conjugate twin of a complex pole. Another trap is cancellation. In (s + 1)/((s + 1)(s + 2)) the factor cancels and the input-output view is 1/(s + 2), but inside the real hardware that hidden mode can still exist. Typical exam questions are: find the poles and zeros and draw the plot, find h(t) by partial fractions, say whether the response decays, oscillates or grows, and show how changing R moves the poles.

Recap: H(s) = N(s)/D(s). Zeros are the roots of N, poles are the roots of D. Mark them with circles and crosses on the s-plane. Each pole gives one natural mode e^(pt): left means decay, right means growth, on the axis means it stays, and the imaginary part sets the oscillation. Zeros set the weights and pull the frequency response down near them. For a series RLC, H(s) = (1/(LC))/(s^2 + (R/L)s + 1/(LC)), and R moves the poles. In the next lesson we use these ideas to solve whole systems with Laplace.
key_points: For an LTI system from a differential equation, H(s) = N(s)/D(s) is a ratio of polynomials; each d/dt becomes a factor s.
Zeros are roots of N(s) (H = 0); poles are roots of D(s) (H goes to infinity). Plot poles as × and zeros as o.
Complex poles and zeros of real systems always come in conjugate pairs; order = number of poles.
Each pole p gives a natural mode e^(pt) in h(t); zeros only set the weights of these modes.
Left half-plane poles decay, right half-plane poles grow, jω-axis poles neither decay nor grow; the imaginary part sets the oscillation frequency.
The pole closest to the jω axis dies slowest and dominates the long-term response.
|H(jω)| = |K| × (distances to zeros)/(distances to poles): near a pole the gain is high, a zero on the axis gives zero gain.
Series RLC, output on C: H(s) = (1/LC)/(s^2 + (R/L)s + 1/LC); with L = 1, C = 0.2, R = 2 the poles are -1 ± j2.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a new H(s), make it a habit to sketch the pole-zero plot first, before any heavy algebra. Ten seconds of dots on paper tell you what the answer should look like, so you can catch your own mistakes later.
lessons.task: Take the series RLC with L = 1 H and C = 0.2 F. On paper, find the poles for R = 0, 1, 2, 4.47 and 6 ohms using the quadratic formula, and mark them all on one s-plane. Join the dots and see the circle of radius √5 and the split on the real axis. If you have a computer, check with numpy.roots([1, R, 5]).

quiz.q: What are the poles of H(s) = (s + 4)/(s^2 + 3s + 2)?
quiz.explain: The denominator s^2 + 3s + 2 = (s + 1)(s + 2) is zero at s = -1 and s = -2. The -4 is a zero, from the numerator.

quiz.q: A system has a pole pair at -1 ± j5. What does its impulse response look like?
options: A decaying oscillation at about 5 rad/s
quiz.explain: The real part -1 gives decay like e^(-t) and the imaginary part 5 gives oscillation at 5 rad/s, so it is a fading wave.

quiz.q: What does a zero at s = 0 do to a system?
options: It gives infinite gain at DC
It makes the system oscillate forever
quiz.explain: At s = 0 the numerator is zero, so the gain at zero frequency (DC) is zero, like a series capacitor blocking a steady voltage.

quiz.q: In the series RLC circuit, what happens to the poles when R = 0?
options: They sit on the jω axis, so the circuit oscillates forever
They move into the right half-plane
They both move to the origin
They become two different negative real numbers
quiz.explain: With R = 0 the denominator is s^2 + 1/(LC), so the poles are ±j/√(LC) on the jω axis: undamped, sustained oscillation.

quiz.q: A system has poles at -1 and -10. Which one dominates the long-term response?
options: -10, because it is bigger in size
-1, because its term e^(-t) decays slowest
quiz.explain: e^(-10t) dies very quickly, while e^(-t) lasts much longer, so the pole closest to the jω axis dominates.

lessons.title: Transfer Functions: Solving and Connecting Systems with Laplace
lessons.content:
Imagine you have to cook biryani every day. The first time, you follow every step slowly. After a while, you have a recipe card, and you just follow it. Solving differential equations by hand in time is the slow way. The Laplace transform is the recipe card. It turns calculus into ordinary algebra: multiply, divide, factor. In this lesson we use H(s) and the poles from lesson 21 to find impulse responses, step responses, the effect of initial conditions, and the behaviour of whole systems built from boxes.

The four-step recipe: Step 1, write the differential equation of the system. Step 2, take the Laplace transform of both sides, so every derivative becomes a power of s. Step 3, solve for Y(s) with plain algebra. Step 4, break Y(s) into partial fractions and read the answer y(t) from a table. Math III already drilled step 4. Our job here is to see what each piece means for the system: which part comes from the input, which part comes from the system, and which part comes from the initial energy stored inside.

From the equation to H(s): Suppose a system obeys a2 y'' + a1 y' + a0 y = b1 x' + b0 x, and starts at rest. Transform it: (a2 s^2 + a1 s + a0) Y(s) = (b1 s + b0) X(s). So H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = (b1 s + b0)/(a2 s^2 + a1 s + a0). You can almost read it straight from the equation. The input side gives the numerator, the output side gives the denominator. Our running example for this lesson is y'' + 3y' + 2y = x(t). Then H(s) = 1/(s^2 + 3s + 2) = 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)), with poles at -1 and -2.

Impulse response: For an impulse input, X(s) = 1, so Y(s) = H(s). Partial fractions give 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) = 1/(s + 1) - 1/(s + 2). So h(t) = (e^(-t) - e^(-2t)) u(t). Quick checks are always worth it. At t = 0, h = 1 - 1 = 0, which is right, because the denominator is two powers of s higher than the numerator, so h starts from zero. As t grows, both terms die, because both poles are in the left half-plane. The slower e^(-t) term from the pole at -1 lives longer.

Step response: For a unit step, X(s) = 1/s, so Y(s) = 1/(s(s + 1)(s + 2)). The extra pole at s = 0 comes from the input. Partial fractions give Y(s) = (1/2)/s - 1/(s + 1) + (1/2)/(s + 2). So y(t) = 1/2 - e^(-t) + (1/2) e^(-2t), for t ≥ 0. Check: at t = 0, y = 1/2 - 1 + 1/2 = 0, good. As t goes to infinity, y goes to 1/2. Notice the two kinds of terms. The constant 1/2 comes from the input's pole, and it is the forced response. The exponentials come from the system's poles, and they are the natural response.

Handy shortcuts: The step response is the integral of the impulse response, because u(t) is the integral of δ(t) and the system is LTI. The final value of the step response of a stable system equals H(0), called the DC gain. Here H(0) = 1/2, matching what we found. That is just the final value theorem from Math III: y(∞) = lim s Y(s) as s goes to 0, which gives H(0) for a step. Warning: this only works when all poles of s Y(s) are in the left half-plane. For an unstable system the theorem gives nonsense.

Initial conditions, zero-input and zero-state: Real systems may not start at rest. A capacitor may already be charged. The unilateral Laplace transform handles this, because L{y'} = sY(s) - y(0). Take y' + 2y = x with y(0) = 1 and x = u(t). Then sY - 1 + 2Y = 1/s, so Y(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)) + 1/(s + 2). The first part is the zero-state response, (1/2)(1 - e^(-2t)), caused by the input. The second part is the zero-input response, e^(-2t), caused by the stored energy. The total is y(t) = 1/2 + (1/2) e^(-2t). Remember, H(s) alone only gives the zero-state part.

Block diagrams: Engineers draw systems as boxes joined by arrows, and each box holds its own transfer function. The magic is that in the s-domain, boxes combine with simple algebra instead of convolution integrals. There are three basic ways to connect boxes: in series, in parallel and in feedback. Once you know these three rules, you can shrink a big diagram, step by step, into one single H(s). This is exactly how control and communication engineers think about large systems.

Series connection: When the output of box H1 feeds box H2, the overall transfer function is H1(s) H2(s). In time this is h1 * h2, a convolution, as we saw in lesson 11, but in s it is just a product. Example: 1/(s + 1) followed by 1/(s + 3) gives 1/((s + 1)(s + 3)). Partial fractions give (1/2)/(s + 1) - (1/2)/(s + 3), so the overall impulse response is (1/2)(e^(-t) - e^(-3t)) u(t). The poles of the series combination are simply all the poles of both boxes.

Parallel connection: When the same input goes into H1 and H2 and their outputs are added, the overall transfer function is H1(s) + H2(s). Example: 1/(s + 1) + 1/(s + 3) = (2s + 4)/((s + 1)(s + 3)) = 2(s + 2)/((s + 1)(s + 3)). Look closely. The poles are again -1 and -3, but now a zero has appeared at -2, even though neither box had a zero. Adding paths creates zeros. That is a nice reminder that zeros come from how signals combine, while poles come from each box's own natural modes.

Feedback connection: Now the output is sent back and compared with the input. Let the forward box be G(s) and the feedback box be H(s). The error is E = X - H Y, and the output is Y = G E. Substitute: Y = G X - G H Y, so Y (1 + G H) = G X, and the closed-loop transfer function is Y/X = G/(1 + G H). This one formula is the heart of control engineering. With unity feedback, H = 1, it becomes G/(1 + G). The minus sign at the comparison is why it is called negative feedback.

Feedback example 1: Take G(s) = K/(s + 1) with unity feedback. The closed loop is K/(s + 1 + K). The pole has moved from -1 to -(1 + K). With K = 1 the pole goes to -2, so the system becomes twice as fast. But the DC gain falls from 1 to 1/2. Bigger K makes the system faster and brings the DC gain closer to 1, which is why feedback is so useful. So feedback moves poles. That is its superpower and also its danger, because a badly designed loop can move poles into the right half-plane.

First-order systems: The simplest system has one pole: H(s) = 1/(τ s + 1), pole at -1/τ. Its step response is y(t) = 1 - e^(-t/τ). At t = τ it reaches about 63.2 percent of the final value, at 2τ about 86.5 percent, at 3τ about 95.0 percent, at 4τ about 98.2 percent and at 5τ about 99.3 percent. So engineers say a first-order system has settled after about 4 to 5 time constants. An RC circuit is the classic example, with τ = RC. With R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 μF, τ = 0.1 s, so it settles in about half a second.

Second-order systems, the standard form: Many systems are written as H(s) = ωn^2/(s^2 + 2ζωn s + ωn^2). Here ωn is the natural frequency and ζ (zeta) is the damping ratio. The DC gain is H(0) = 1. The poles are s = -ζωn ± ωn√(ζ^2 - 1). When the poles are complex, they sit at distance ωn from the origin, and the angle θ they make with the negative real axis satisfies cos θ = ζ. So on the pole-zero plot, ωn is the radius and ζ sets the angle.

The four cases of damping: If ζ > 1, the system is overdamped: two different real poles, no overshoot, slow. If ζ = 1, it is critically damped: a double real pole, the fastest response without overshoot. If 0 < ζ < 1, it is underdamped: complex poles -ζωn ± jωd, where ωd = ωn√(1 - ζ^2) is the damped frequency, and the step response overshoots and rings before settling. If ζ = 0, it is undamped: poles on the jω axis and an oscillation that never ends. These match the R = 6, 4.47, 2 and 0 cases of the RLC circuit in lesson 21.

Measuring an underdamped step response: For 0 < ζ < 1 there are three standard numbers. Percent overshoot is 100 × e^(-πζ/√(1 - ζ^2)). Peak time is tp = π/ωd. Settling time to within 2 percent is roughly ts ≈ 4/(ζωn). Worked example: ζ = 0.5 and ωn = 2 rad/s. Then ωd = 2√0.75 = √3 ≈ 1.732 rad/s, tp = π/1.732 ≈ 1.81 s, overshoot = e^(-1.814) ≈ 16.3 percent, and ts ≈ 4/(0.5 × 2) = 4 s. A computer simulation confirms the peak of about 1.163 at about 1.81 s.

Checking the RLC from lesson 21: There we had H(s) = 5/(s^2 + 2s + 5). Matching the standard form, ωn^2 = 5, so ωn = √5 ≈ 2.236 rad/s, and 2ζωn = 2, so ζ = 1/√5 ≈ 0.447. Then ωd = ωn√(1 - 0.2) = 2, tp = π/2 ≈ 1.57 s, and the overshoot is e^(-π × 0.447/0.894) ≈ 20.8 percent. That matches the peak of about 1.21 at t ≈ 1.57 s we found by partial fractions. Two different roads, same answer. That is how you know the method works.

Feedback example 2, the classic trade-off: Take G(s) = K/(s(s + 2)) with unity feedback. The closed loop is K/(s^2 + 2s + K). Matching the standard form, ωn = √K and 2ζωn = 2, so ζ = 1/√K. With K = 1, ζ = 1, critically damped. With K = 4, ωn = 2 and ζ = 0.5, which is exactly our 16.3 percent overshoot example. Push K higher and the system gets faster but overshoots more. Choosing K to balance speed and overshoot is the daily bread of a control engineer, and you will meet it again in a control systems course.

Real-life example 1, the ceiling fan: Switch on a ceiling fan in summer. It does not jump to full speed. It speeds up quickly at first and then more slowly as it gets close to its final speed. That shape is roughly a first-order step response, 1 - e^(-t/τ), with a time constant of a few seconds set by the blades' inertia and the motor. After about four or five time constants it is at full speed. The same shape shows up when an IPS battery charges at a fixed voltage through a resistance, or when a cup of tea cools down on the table.

Real-life example 2, the camera that follows the ball: In a cricket broadcast, a motorised camera mount may turn to follow the ball. A motor with a feedback loop is a second-order system just like G = K/(s(s + 2)) above. If the gain is too high, the camera overshoots and wobbles past the ball. If it is too low, the camera lags behind. Designers often aim for a damping ratio around 0.7, which gives a small overshoot of about 5 percent with a fast response. The same idea is used in drone gimbals and phone camera stabilisers.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students forget the 1/s of the step input, or they forget the initial condition terms like -y(0) when using the unilateral transform. They use the final value theorem on an unstable system. They write G/(1 - GH) for negative feedback; with negative feedback it is G/(1 + GH). They mix up ωn and ωd. Typical questions: find H(s) from a differential equation, find impulse and step responses by partial fractions, reduce a block diagram, find ωn and ζ from a second-order H(s), and compute overshoot, peak time and settling time.

Recap: Laplace turns differential equations into algebra. H(s) comes straight from the equation, h(t) is the inverse of H(s), and the step response is the inverse of H(s)/s, with final value H(0) if stable. Initial conditions add a zero-input part. Series boxes multiply, parallel boxes add, and negative feedback gives G/(1 + GH). First-order systems settle in about 4 to 5 τ. Second-order systems are described by ωn and ζ, with overshoot, peak time and settling time formulas. Next, we bring all of this into discrete time with the Z-transform.
key_points: Recipe: write the ODE, take Laplace, solve for Y(s) algebraically, invert with partial fractions.
The final value of a stable system's step response is the DC gain H(0) (final value theorem).
Initial conditions add a zero-input response; H(s) alone gives only the zero-state response.
Series: H1·H2. Parallel: H1 + H2 (can create new zeros). Negative feedback: G/(1 + GH).
First order 1/(τs + 1): step reaches 63.2% at τ and is settled after about 4-5τ.
Second order ωn^2/(s^2 + 2ζωn s + ωn^2): ζ > 1 overdamped, ζ = 1 critical, 0 < ζ < 1 underdamped, ζ = 0 undamped.
Underdamped: overshoot e^(-πζ/√(1-ζ^2)), tp = π/ωd with ωd = ωn√(1-ζ^2), 2% settling ≈ 4/(ζωn).
lessons.tip: After every partial-fraction answer, do two 5-second checks: put t = 0 and see if the starting value makes sense, and let t go to infinity and compare with H(0). Most algebra slips get caught right there.
lessons.task: On paper, find the closed-loop transfer function of G(s) = K/(s(s + 2)) with unity feedback for K = 1, 4 and 16. For each, write ωn, ζ and the predicted overshoot. If you have a computer, plot the step responses with scipy.signal.step([K], [1, 2, K]) and check that the overshoot grows with K.

quiz.q: What is the transfer function of y'' + 4y' + 3y = x(t), starting at rest?
quiz.explain: Transforming gives (s^2 + 4s + 3)Y(s) = X(s), so H(s) = Y/X = 1/(s^2 + 4s + 3), with poles at -1 and -3.

quiz.q: What is the closed-loop transfer function of a negative feedback loop with forward path G and feedback path H?
quiz.explain: From Y = G(X - HY) we get Y(1 + GH) = GX, so Y/X = G/(1 + GH).

quiz.q: A first-order system 1/(τs + 1) gets a unit step. About how far up is it at t = τ?
quiz.explain: y(τ) = 1 - e^(-1) ≈ 0.632, so about 63.2 percent of the final value.

quiz.q: A second-order system has damping ratio ζ = 0.3. What kind of step response does it have?
quiz.explain: 0 < ζ < 1 means complex poles in the left half-plane, so the step response overshoots and rings before settling.

quiz.q: Two boxes 2/(s + 1) and 3/(s + 4) are connected in series. What is the overall transfer function?
quiz.explain: In series the transfer functions multiply: (2/(s + 1)) × (3/(s + 4)) = 6/((s + 1)(s + 4)).

lessons.title: The Z-Transform and Its Region of Convergence
lessons.content:
Imagine your bKash app shows your balance at the end of each day: day 0, day 1, day 2, and so on. That list of numbers is a discrete-time signal. The Laplace transform was the perfect tool for continuous signals, but sequences like this need their own tool. Meet the Z-transform, the younger sibling of Laplace, made for sequences x[n]. It turns difference equations into algebra, just like Laplace did for differential equations, and it will give us transfer functions, poles and stability for digital systems in the next lesson.

Definition: The Z-transform of a sequence x[n] is X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(-n), where the sum runs over all integers n from minus infinity to plus infinity, and z is a complex number. This is the bilateral Z-transform. If we sum only from n = 0 upward, we get the unilateral version, which is handy for causal signals and initial conditions. A friendly way to see it: z^(-n) is just a label that says "this sample sits at position n". The Z-transform packs a whole sequence into one function, and each coefficient remembers its place.

A first example, a short sequence: Let x[n] = 1, 2, 3 at n = 0, 1, 2, and zero everywhere else. Then X(z) = 1 + 2z^(-1) + 3z^(-2). You can read the sequence straight back from the coefficients: the number in front of z^(-n) is x[n]. For which z does this make sense? Every z except z = 0, because z^(-1) = 1/z blows up at zero. So the region of convergence, or ROC, is the whole z-plane except the origin. If the sequence had a sample at n = -1, we would get a z term, and then z = infinity would be excluded too.

The unit sample: For δ[n], only n = 0 is non-zero, so X(z) = 1 · z^0 = 1. The ROC is the whole z-plane. A shifted impulse δ[n - k] gives z^(-k). So δ[n - 3] becomes z^(-3). This already shows you a key idea. Multiplying by z^(-1) means "move one step later". We will use that again and again, because a digital system is mostly made of delays, multipliers and adders.

The unit step: For u[n], X(z) = Σ z^(-n) for n = 0 to infinity = 1 + z^(-1) + z^(-2) + ... This is a geometric series with ratio z^(-1). From school we know 1 + r + r^2 + ... = 1/(1 - r) only when |r| < 1. So X(z) = 1/(1 - z^(-1)) = z/(z - 1), and it converges only when |z^(-1)| < 1, meaning |z| > 1. The ROC is everything outside the circle of radius 1. There is a pole at z = 1 and a zero at z = 0.

The right-sided exponential: For x[n] = a^n u[n], X(z) = Σ (a z^(-1))^n for n ≥ 0 = 1/(1 - a z^(-1)) = z/(z - a). It converges when |a z^(-1)| < 1, which means |z| > |a|. So the ROC is the outside of a circle of radius |a|. Example: (0.5)^n u[n], the sequence 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and so on, has X(z) = z/(z - 0.5) with ROC |z| > 0.5. Its pole is at z = 0.5 and its zero is at z = 0. The unit step is just the special case a = 1.

The left-sided exponential: Now take x[n] = -a^n u[-n-1], which lives only at n = -1, -2, -3 and so on. Its sum is -Σ a^n z^(-n) for n from minus infinity to -1. Put m = -n and it becomes -Σ (z/a)^m for m = 1 to infinity = -(z/a)/(1 - z/a) = z/(z - a). Exactly the same formula! But this sum converges only when |z/a| < 1, meaning |z| < |a|. So the ROC is the inside of the circle. Same formula, two different signals. Just like with Laplace in lesson 20, the formula alone is not enough. You must give the ROC.

Rules for the ROC: The ROC is always a ring centred at the origin, an annulus, because convergence depends only on |z|. The ROC never contains a pole. A right-sided sequence has an ROC outside its outermost pole. A left-sided sequence has an ROC inside its innermost pole. A two-sided sequence has a ring between two poles. A finite-length sequence has an ROC of the whole plane, maybe without z = 0 or z = infinity. Learn these four lines well, because in the next lesson they decide causality and stability.

A two-sided example: Let x[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] - 2^n u[-n-1]. The first part gives z/(z - 0.5) with |z| > 0.5. The second part gives z/(z - 2) with |z| < 2. The total X(z) = z/(z - 0.5) + z/(z - 2) needs both to converge, so the ROC is the ring 0.5 < |z| < 2. Now flip it: x[n] = 2^n u[n] - (0.5)^n u[-n-1]. The first part needs |z| > 2 and the second needs |z| < 0.5. No z can do both, so this sequence has no Z-transform at all.

Link to the DTFT: Put z = e^(jω), the unit circle. Then z^(-n) = e^(-jωn), and X(z) becomes the DTFT from lesson 19. So the DTFT is the Z-transform walked around the unit circle, just as the Fourier transform is the Laplace transform walked up the jω axis. This works only when the ROC includes the unit circle. (0.5)^n u[n] has ROC |z| > 0.5, which includes the circle, so its DTFT is 1/(1 - 0.5e^(-jω)). The unit step has ROC |z| > 1, which does not include the circle, so it has no ordinary DTFT.

Property 1, linearity: The Z-transform of a x1[n] + b x2[n] is a X1(z) + b X2(z), and the ROC contains at least the overlap of the two ROCs. Example: 3δ[n] + (0.5)^n u[n] has X(z) = 3 + z/(z - 0.5) with ROC |z| > 0.5. Linearity is what lets us break a hard X(z) into simple pieces, invert each piece from the table, and add the answers back. That is exactly the partial-fraction method we will use below.

Property 2, time shift: x[n - k] has transform z^(-k) X(z). So a delay of one sample is multiplication by z^(-1). This is why in digital block diagrams you see a little box marked z^(-1). It is a one-sample memory, like a register in a microprocessor that holds the previous value. A difference equation y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 y[n-1] becomes Y(z) = X(z) + 0.5 z^(-1) Y(z) in one line. The ROC stays the same, except that z = 0 or z = infinity may be added or removed.

Property 3, convolution: If y[n] = x[n] * h[n], then Y(z) = X(z) H(z). Convolution in time becomes multiplication in z. Check it with lesson 9: x = {1, 2} and h = {1, 1, 1}. X(z) = 1 + 2z^(-1) and H(z) = 1 + z^(-1) + z^(-2). Multiply like ordinary polynomials: 1 + z^(-1) + z^(-2) + 2z^(-1) + 2z^(-2) + 2z^(-3) = 1 + 3z^(-1) + 3z^(-2) + 2z^(-3). So y = {1, 3, 3, 2}, the same answer as the table method, and the length is 2 + 3 - 1 = 4.

A few more properties in one breath: Multiplying by a^n scales z: a^n x[n] gives X(z/a). Multiplying by n gives -z dX/dz. For example, from u[n] ↔ z/(z - 1), we get n u[n] ↔ -z d/dz [z/(z - 1)] = z/(z - 1)^2. Time reversal x[-n] gives X(1/z). And the initial value theorem says that for a causal sequence x[0] equals the limit of X(z) as z goes to infinity. For z/(z - 0.5), that limit is 1, and indeed x[0] = 1.

Going back, the inverse Z-transform: There are three practical ways. First, inspection: spot a form you know from the table. Second, partial fractions: break X(z) into simple pieces like 1/(1 - a z^(-1)) and invert each using the ROC. Third, long division: divide to get a power series in z^(-1) and read the samples one by one. There is also a contour-integral formula, but in this course the first three are what you need.

Partial fractions, worked: Let X(z) = 1/((1 - 0.5z^(-1))(1 - 0.25z^(-1))) with ROC |z| > 0.5. Write it as A/(1 - 0.5z^(-1)) + B/(1 - 0.25z^(-1)). Cover-up: A = 1/(1 - 0.25/0.5) = 1/0.5 = 2, and B = 1/(1 - 0.5/0.25) = 1/(1 - 2) = -1. The ROC is outside both poles, so both pieces are right-sided: x[n] = (2(0.5)^n - (0.25)^n) u[n]. The first few values are 1, 0.75, 0.4375, 0.234375. A useful trick: keep everything in powers of z^(-1), or divide X(z) by z first, so you never get mixed up.

Same X(z), different ROC: Keep the same X(z) but choose the ROC |z| < 0.25. Now both pieces are left-sided, so x[n] = (-2(0.5)^n + (0.25)^n) u[-n-1]. Choose the ring 0.25 < |z| < 0.5, and the 0.25 pole piece is right-sided while the 0.5 pole piece is left-sided: x[n] = -(0.25)^n u[n] - 2(0.5)^n u[-n-1]. Three ROCs, three different signals from one formula. The rule is simple: poles inside the ROC's inner edge give right-sided terms, poles outside its outer edge give left-sided terms.

Long division, worked: Write the same X(z) as 1/(1 - 0.75z^(-1) + 0.125z^(-2)), since (1 - 0.5z^(-1))(1 - 0.25z^(-1)) = 1 - 0.75z^(-1) + 0.125z^(-2). Divide 1 by it. The first quotient term is 1, which leaves 0.75z^(-1) - 0.125z^(-2). The next term is 0.75z^(-1), which leaves 0.4375z^(-2) - 0.09375z^(-3). The next is 0.4375z^(-2). So X(z) = 1 + 0.75z^(-1) + 0.4375z^(-2) + ..., giving x[0] = 1, x[1] = 0.75, x[2] = 0.4375, matching the partial fractions. Long division is great for the first few samples, but it does not give a closed formula.

Real-life example 1, savings with interest: Suppose a savings account adds 1 percent interest every month and you deposit x[n] taka in month n. The balance follows b[n] = 1.01 b[n-1] + x[n]. In z: B(z) = X(z)/(1 - 1.01z^(-1)). A single deposit of 1000 taka in month 0 gives b[n] = 1000 (1.01)^n u[n]. The pole sits at z = 1.01, just outside the unit circle, so the balance grows forever. Great for your savings, but in the next lesson you will see that the same pole means the system is unstable.

Real-life example 2, echo in a karaoke app: A simple echo effect is y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 x[n - D], the voice plus a quieter copy D samples later. Its transfer function is H(z) = 1 + 0.5z^(-D). If the phone samples at 8000 samples per second and you want a 0.25 second echo, D = 0.25 × 8000 = 2000. So the whole effect is a single delay box z^(-2000), a gain of 0.5 and an adder. That is the power of the time-shift property: long delays become one tidy term.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students give X(z) without the ROC, which is half an answer. They mix up z^(-1) and z, for example writing z/(z - a) and then reading the pole as -a. They forget that a^n u[n] and -a^n u[-n-1] share a formula. They pick the wrong side when inverting. Typical questions: find X(z) and the ROC of a given sequence and sketch it, show that a two-sided sequence has a ring or no ROC at all, find a convolution with z, and find x[n] by partial fractions and by long division for a given ROC.

Recap: X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(-n). δ[n] ↔ 1 for all z. u[n] ↔ z/(z - 1) with |z| > 1. a^n u[n] ↔ z/(z - a) with |z| > |a|, while -a^n u[-n-1] has the same formula with |z| < |a|. The ROC is a ring without poles; right-sided means outside, left-sided means inside. On the unit circle, X(z) becomes the DTFT. z^(-1) is a one-sample delay, and convolution becomes multiplication. Invert with tables, partial fractions or long division, always guided by the ROC. Next we use this to build discrete transfer functions and test stability.
key_points: X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(-n); z^(-n) marks the position of sample n. Always state the ROC with X(z).
-a^n u[-n-1] has the same formula z/(z - a) but ROC |z| < |a|: same formula, different signal.
The ROC is a ring centred at the origin with no poles inside it: right-sided → outside outermost pole, left-sided → inside innermost pole, two-sided → a ring, or no ROC at all.
On the unit circle z = e^(jω), X(z) becomes the DTFT, if the ROC includes the unit circle.
Time shift: x[n - k] ↔ z^(-k) X(z), so z^(-1) is a one-sample delay; convolution ↔ product X(z)H(z).
Inverse by inspection, partial fractions (e.g. 1/((1-0.5z^(-1))(1-0.25z^(-1))) → (2(0.5)^n - (0.25)^n)u[n] for |z| > 0.5) or long division.
lessons.tip: Make a tiny four-line card: δ, u, a^n u[n], -a^n u[-n-1], each with its formula and ROC drawn as a shaded circle. Most Z-transform questions are just these four plus linearity and the shift property.
lessons.task: Take x = {1, 2, 1} and h = {1, -1}. Write X(z) and H(z), multiply them like polynomials, and read off y = x * h. Then check by doing the convolution with the flip-and-slide table from lesson 9. Finally, use long division on 1/(1 - 0.5z^(-1)) for four terms and compare with (0.5)^n.

quiz.q: What is the Z-transform of the unit sample δ[n]?
quiz.explain: Only n = 0 is non-zero, so X(z) = 1 · z^0 = 1, and the ROC is the whole z-plane.

quiz.q: What is the ROC of x[n] = (0.8)^n u[n]?
