quiz.explain: The geometric series Σ (0.8 z^(-1))^n converges when |0.8 z^(-1)| < 1, which means |z| > 0.8. Right-sided means outside the pole.

quiz.q: In a digital block diagram, what does a box labelled z^(-1) do?
options: Delays the signal by one sample
Multiplies the signal by the number z
Moves the signal one sample earlier
quiz.explain: By the time-shift property, x[n - 1] ↔ z^(-1) X(z), so z^(-1) is a one-sample delay, like a memory register.

quiz.q: Using Z-transforms, what is the convolution of x = {1, 1} and h = {1, 2}?
The formula X(z) = z/(z - a) with ROC |z| < |a| belongs to which signal?
quiz.explain: The left-sided sequence -a^n u[-n-1] has the same formula as a^n u[n], but its ROC is inside the circle, |z| < |a|.

lessons.title: Discrete Transfer Functions and Stability in the s- and z-Planes
lessons.content:
Put a marble inside a bowl and give it a push. It rolls up, rolls back, and soon settles at the bottom. Now balance the same marble on top of an upside-down bowl. The tiniest touch and it rolls away, never to come back. The first is stable, the second is unstable. Every engineer's first question about a system is: which one is this? In this lesson we answer it for both continuous and digital systems, just by looking where the poles sit, and we connect the s-plane to the z-plane with one beautiful formula.

H(z) from a difference equation: A general LTI difference equation is y[n] + a1 y[n-1] + a2 y[n-2] + ... = b0 x[n] + b1 x[n-1] + .... Take the Z-transform with the time-shift rule from lesson 23, where each one-sample delay becomes z^(-1). You get H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) = (b0 + b1 z^(-1) + b2 z^(-2) + ...)/(1 + a1 z^(-1) + a2 z^(-2) + ...). Example: y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 y[n-1], which we rewrite as y[n] - 0.5 y[n-1] = x[n]. Then H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.5z^(-1)), and from the table h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n].

Poles and zeros in the z-plane: To find them, multiply the top and bottom by the highest power of z so that you get ordinary polynomials in z. For 1/(1 - 0.5z^(-1)), multiply by z: H(z) = z/(z - 0.5). So there is a zero at z = 0 and a pole at z = 0.5. Plot them with the same circles and crosses as in lesson 21, but now always draw the unit circle |z| = 1 as well. In the z-plane, the unit circle plays the role that the jω axis played in the s-plane. It is the border between safe and unsafe.

An FIR example: Take y[n] = x[n] + x[n-1]. There is no feedback, so H(z) = 1 + z^(-1) = (z + 1)/z. There is a zero at z = -1 and a pole at z = 0. Every FIR system has all its poles at the origin, so FIR systems are always stable. The zero at z = -1 means something nice. The point z = -1 is e^(jπ), the fastest possible discrete frequency, the sequence 1, -1, 1, -1. Feed that in and each output is 1 + (-1) = 0. The system completely blocks that alternating signal.

A second-order IIR example: Take y[n] = x[n] + y[n-1] - 0.5 y[n-2]. Then H(z) = 1/(1 - z^(-1) + 0.5z^(-2)) = z^2/(z^2 - z + 0.5). The poles are z = 0.5 ± j0.5, which have radius √0.5 ≈ 0.707 and angles ±45 degrees, that is ±π/4. There is a double zero at the origin. Running the equation with an impulse gives h = 1, 1, 0.5, 0, -0.25, -0.25, -0.125, 0, 0.0625, and so on. It swings up and down and shrinks. One full swing takes 2π/(π/4) = 8 samples, and the size shrinks by 0.707 each step.

Reading a pole in the z-plane: A pole p = r e^(jθ) gives terms like r^n cos(θn + φ). The radius r controls size. If r < 1, the term shrinks like r^n. If r = 1, it stays the same size. If r > 1, it grows. The angle θ controls oscillation, measured in radians per sample. A pole on the positive real axis, θ = 0, gives a smooth decay, like (0.5)^n = 1, 0.5, 0.25. A pole on the negative real axis, θ = π, flips the sign every sample, like (-0.5)^n = 1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125, 0.0625.

Stability recap: In lessons 7 and 11 we defined BIBO stability: every bounded input gives a bounded output. For an LTI system, that happens exactly when the impulse response is absolutely summable, Σ |h[n]| < ∞, or absolutely integrable in continuous time, ∫ |h(t)| dt < ∞. Checking that sum directly can be hard. Poles make it easy, because h is just a mix of terms coming from the poles, and we already know which terms die and which do not.

Stability rule in the s-plane: A causal continuous LTI system with a rational H(s) is BIBO stable if and only if every pole has a negative real part, meaning all poles lie strictly in the left half-plane. The reason is simple. Each pole p gives a term like e^(pt), and |e^(pt)| = e^(Re(p) t), which dies only when Re(p) < 0. Examples: 1/(s + 2) is stable. 1/(s - 1) is unstable. 1/(s^2 + 2s + 5) with poles -1 ± j2 is stable. Zeros do not matter for stability. You can put zeros anywhere.

Stability rule in the z-plane: A causal discrete LTI system with a rational H(z) is BIBO stable if and only if every pole is strictly inside the unit circle, |p| < 1. The reason is the same: each pole gives p^n, and |p^n| = |p|^n dies only when |p| < 1. Check our examples. The pole at 0.5 is stable. The pair 0.5 ± j0.5 with radius 0.707 is stable. A pole at 2, as in y[n] = x[n] + 2y[n-1], gives h = 2^n and is unstable. The savings account from lesson 23 with its pole at 1.01 is also unstable as a system, even though you would love that balance.

The general rule with the ROC: Without assuming causality, the rule is: an LTI system is stable exactly when its ROC includes the jω axis (for s) or the unit circle (for z). And a system is causal when its ROC is the right-sided kind: to the right of the rightmost pole in s, or outside the outermost pole in z, including infinity. Put the two together and you get the easy rules above. Causal plus stable means all poles in the left half-plane, or all poles inside the unit circle.

One H(z), three systems: Let H(z) = 1/((1 - 0.5z^(-1))(1 - 2z^(-1))), with poles 0.5 and 2. ROC |z| > 2: causal, but the unit circle is not in the ROC, so it is unstable. ROC 0.5 < |z| < 2: the unit circle is inside, so it is stable, but the impulse response is two-sided, so it is not causal. ROC |z| < 0.5: anticausal and unstable. So with a pole outside the circle you can choose causal or stable, but never both. Real-time systems must be causal, so we need every pole inside.

Marginal stability: When there are simple, non-repeated poles exactly on the border, on the jω axis or on the unit circle, and none outside, the impulse response neither dies nor explodes. This is called marginally stable. But careful, it is not BIBO stable. The accumulator y[n] = x[n] + y[n-1] has H(z) = 1/(1 - z^(-1)), a pole at z = 1, and h[n] = u[n]. Feed it a bounded step and the output is 1, 2, 3, 4, ..., growing without limit. In continuous time, the integrator 1/s behaves the same way, and 3/(s^2 + 9) driven by sin(3t) gives an output that grows with time, called resonance.

A digital oscillator: Take y[n] = x[n] + √2 y[n-1] - y[n-2]. The poles are the roots of z^2 - √2 z + 1, which are e^(±jπ/4), right on the unit circle. The impulse response is h[n] = sin((n + 1)π/4)/sin(π/4), which is 1, 1.414, 1, 0, -1, -1.414, -1, 0, 1, ... and repeats every 8 samples forever. One kick, and it sings a sine wave without stopping. This is a real trick for generating tones in cheap digital circuits. If a pole sits on the border twice, a repeated pole, things get worse: terms like n or t times the mode appear, and the system is truly unstable.

Quick tests without finding roots: For second-order systems there are neat shortcuts. In s, the polynomial s^2 + a s + b has both roots in the left half-plane exactly when a > 0 and b > 0. For bigger polynomials, the Routh-Hurwitz table does the job, and you will meet it in control systems. In z, the polynomial z^2 + a1 z + a2 has both roots inside the unit circle exactly when |a2| < 1 and |a1| < 1 + a2. This is the second-order case of the Jury test. Check: z^2 - z + 0.5 has a2 = 0.5 and |a1| = 1 < 1.5, so it is stable. z^2 - 2.5z + 1 has a2 = 1, which fails, and indeed its poles are 2 and 0.5.

The s-to-z map: Sample a continuous mode e^(pt) every T seconds. You get e^(p n T) = (e^(pT))^n. That is exactly a discrete mode with pole z = e^(pT). So sampling maps every s-plane pole to the z-plane by z = e^(sT). Write s = σ + jω. Then z = e^(σT) e^(jωT), so |z| = e^(σT) and the angle of z is ωT. The real part of s sets the radius, and the imaginary part sets the angle. This one formula ties together everything we did in continuous time with everything in discrete time.

Where things land: If σ < 0, then |z| = e^(σT) < 1, so the left half-plane maps inside the unit circle. If σ = 0, |z| = 1, so the jω axis maps onto the unit circle. The right half-plane maps outside. The origin s = 0 maps to z = 1, and very fast-decaying poles with very negative σ land near z = 0. So stable stays stable. Worked numbers with T = 0.1 s: a pole at s = -2 maps to z = e^(-0.2) ≈ 0.819. A pole at s = -1 + j10 maps to |z| = e^(-0.1) ≈ 0.905 with angle 10 × 0.1 = 1 radian ≈ 57.3 degrees.

Aliasing hides in the map: Since e^(j2π) = 1, the points s and s + j2π/T land on the same z. So the map is many-to-one. Only the horizontal strip -π/T < ω < π/T maps one-to-one onto the whole z-plane, and anything above it folds back in. That is aliasing from lesson 18 again, seen through poles. With T = 0.1 s, the strip edge is π/T ≈ 31.4 rad/s. Digital signal processing uses this map and related ones to turn analog filter designs into digital ones. The design methods themselves belong to the DSP course.

Real-life example 1, the echo that runs away: A simple reverb effect in a music app feeds the output back: y[n] = x[n] + g y[n - D]. Its H(z) = 1/(1 - g z^(-D)) has D poles, all of radius |g|^(1/D). With g = 0.5 and D = 10, the radius is about 0.933, inside the circle, so the echoes fade away nicely. Set g = 1 and the poles land on the unit circle: the echoes never fade. Set g above 1 and they grow louder each round, just like the howl of a mosque microphone placed too close to its own loudspeaker.

Real-life example 2, a drone's flight controller: A drone's flight controller is a digital system. It reads sensors, say a few hundred times per second, and computes motor commands with a difference equation. The whole loop, drone plus code, has poles in the z-plane. If a programmer sets a gain too high, a pair of poles can drift outside the unit circle, and the drone starts shaking harder and harder until it crashes. Tuning a controller is really about keeping every pole safely inside the circle, with some margin.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students apply the z rule in s or the s rule in z, for example calling a z-pole at -0.5 unstable because it is negative. In z, only the size matters, not the sign. They forget that zeros do not affect stability. They call marginally stable systems BIBO stable. They forget causality when using the simple rules. Typical questions: find H(z) from a difference equation, plot its poles and zeros, decide stability, list the possible ROCs and say which is causal or stable, and map given s-poles to the z-plane with z = e^(sT).

Recap: H(z) comes from a difference equation by turning each delay into z^(-1). Plot poles and zeros together with the unit circle. A pole r e^(jθ) gives r^n with oscillation θ per sample. Causal and stable means all s-poles in the left half-plane, or all z-poles inside the unit circle. In general, stable means the ROC holds the jω axis or the unit circle. Simple poles on the border give marginal stability, which is not BIBO stable. And z = e^(sT) maps the left half-plane inside the unit circle. Next, we use all this to understand filters.
key_points: In the z-plane the unit circle is the border, like the jω axis in the s-plane. FIR systems have all poles at z = 0 and are always stable.
A z-pole r e^(jθ) gives r^n cos(θn + φ): r < 1 decays, r = 1 stays, r > 1 grows; θ is the oscillation in radians per sample.
Causal + stable: all s-poles have Re(s) < 0; all z-poles have |z| < 1. Zeros do not affect stability.
In general: stable ⇔ the ROC contains the jω axis (s) or unit circle (z); causal ⇔ ROC right of the rightmost pole / outside the outermost pole.
Simple poles on the border are marginally stable, which is not BIBO stable (accumulator: step in, ramp out).
Second-order tests: s^2 + as + b stable iff a > 0, b > 0; z^2 + a1 z + a2 stable iff |a2| < 1 and |a1| < 1 + a2.
Sampling maps poles by z = e^(sT): |z| = e^(σT), angle ωT; the left half-plane goes inside the unit circle.
lessons.tip: Say the rule as a picture, not a sentence: in s, look left of the wall; in z, look inside the ring. When you see a pole, first ask "which plane am I in?", then check the wall or the ring.
lessons.task: Write three difference equations: y[n] = x[n] + 0.8 y[n-1], y[n] = x[n] - 0.8 y[n-1] and y[n] = x[n] + 1.2 y[n-1]. Find each H(z) and its pole, predict whether h[n] decays, flips sign or grows, then check by computing the first eight values of h[n] by hand or with a short loop on your phone or computer.

quiz.q: A causal discrete-time LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when its poles are where?
options: All strictly inside the unit circle
quiz.explain: Each pole p gives p^n in h[n], which dies only if |p| < 1, so all poles must be strictly inside the unit circle.

quiz.q: What is H(z) for y[n] = x[n] + 0.9 y[n-1]?
A continuous pole at s = -3 is sampled every T seconds. Where does it land in the z-plane?
quiz.explain: Sampling maps poles by z = e^(sT), so s = -3 goes to z = e^(-3T), which is inside the unit circle as expected for a stable pole.

quiz.q: What is true about the accumulator y[n] = x[n] + y[n-1]?
options: Pole at z = 1, marginally stable, and not BIBO stable
Pole at z = 0, so it is always stable
Pole at z = -1, so its output grows
It has no poles at all
quiz.explain: H(z) = 1/(1 - z^(-1)) has a pole at z = 1 on the unit circle. A bounded step input gives the output 1, 2, 3, ..., which is unbounded.

quiz.q: H(z) has poles at 0.5 and 2, and the ROC is 0.5 < |z| < 2. What kind of system is it?
quiz.explain: The ring contains the unit circle, so the system is stable, but a ring ROC means a two-sided impulse response, so it is not causal.

lessons.title: Introduction to Filters and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Think of the small strainer you use when pouring tea. The tea flows through, and the leaves stay behind. A filter in signals and systems does the same job with frequencies. It lets the frequencies you want pass through and holds back the ones you do not want. Every tool from this course, frequency response, poles and zeros, convolution, the Z-transform, comes together when we build filters. So this last lesson is both a meeting with filters and a look back over the whole road we walked.

What a filter is: A filter is simply an LTI system chosen for the shape of its frequency response. Since Y(jω) = H(jω) X(jω), the output spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by H. Where |H| is close to 1, the signal passes. That range is the passband. Where |H| is close to 0, the signal is blocked. That range is the stopband. The region in between is the transition band, and the frequency where the passband ends is called the cutoff frequency. The same ideas work for digital filters with H(e^(jω)).

The five basic types: A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones, like smoothing out hiss. A high-pass filter does the opposite, passing high frequencies and blocking slow changes and DC. A band-pass filter passes only a band in the middle, like a radio picking one station. A band-stop filter blocks one band and passes the rest; a very narrow band-stop is called a notch. An all-pass filter passes every frequency with the same gain of 1 but changes the phase, so it shifts timing without changing loudness.

Ideal filters: The dream low-pass filter has H(jω) = 1 for |ω| < ωc and 0 everywhere else, a perfect brick wall. From lesson 14 we know the inverse Fourier transform of a rectangle is a sinc. So its impulse response is h(t) = sin(ωc t)/(πt). This sinc is non-zero for negative t, so the filter would have to react before the input arrives. It is non-causal. It also goes on forever in both directions. So an ideal filter cannot be built in real time. Ideal filters are a target to aim at, not a thing to buy.

Practical filters and their specs: Real filters accept small compromises. The passband gain may ripple a little around 1. The stopband gain is not zero but small enough, for example 40 dB down. The transition band has some width instead of a sharp wall. And the phase response should not distort the signal too much. A sharper wall needs a higher-order filter, which means more poles and zeros, more components or more computation. Classic design families like Butterworth and Chebyshev, and FIR design by windowing, trade these things off. Those design methods are for the DSP course.

First-order RC low-pass: Put a resistor in series and take the output across a capacitor. Then H(s) = 1/(1 + sRC), with a single pole at s = -1/RC, and H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC). The magnitude is |H| = 1/√(1 + (ωRC)^2). At ω = 0 it is 1. As ω grows, it falls. The cutoff is ωc = 1/RC, or fc = 1/(2πRC) in hertz. At the cutoff |H| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, which is -3 dB, meaning half the power. With R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 μF, fc = 1/(2π × 0.001) ≈ 159 Hz.

Roll-off and phase: Above the cutoff, the first-order low-pass falls by about 20 dB for every factor of 10 in frequency. At 10 fc the gain is 1/√101 ≈ 0.0995, which is about -20 dB. This slope, -20 dB per decade, is the mark of a single pole. A second-order filter falls at -40 dB per decade. The phase is also worth knowing. It starts at 0 degrees, is -45 degrees exactly at the cutoff, and heads towards -90 degrees at high frequency.

First-order RC high-pass: Swap the parts, and take the output across the resistor. Now H(s) = sRC/(1 + sRC). The pole is still at -1/RC, and there is a new zero at s = 0. That zero makes H(0) = 0, so DC is blocked completely, just as we saw in lesson 21. The cutoff is again fc = 1/(2πRC), and at high frequency the gain approaches 1. This is the coupling capacitor you find between stages of an audio amplifier. It passes the music but blocks any steady DC voltage from one stage leaking into the next.

Two-point moving average: In discrete time, the simplest low-pass is y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1])/2. Its H(z) = (1 + z^(-1))/2, with a zero at z = -1. On the unit circle, H(e^(jω)) = (1 + e^(-jω))/2 = e^(-jω/2) cos(ω/2). So |H| = |cos(ω/2)|. It is 1 at ω = 0, about 0.707 at ω = π/2, and 0 at ω = π. Slow signals pass, and the fastest alternating signal is killed. The phase factor e^(-jω/2) is a pure delay of half a sample, so this filter has linear phase and does not distort the shape of a waveform.

Two-point difference, a high-pass: Change the plus to a minus: y[n] = (x[n] - x[n-1])/2. Now H(z) = (1 - z^(-1))/2, with a zero at z = 1, and |H(e^(jω))| = |sin(ω/2)|. It is 0 at DC and 1 at ω = π. Any constant part of the signal disappears, and only changes survive. That is why a difference is used for edge detection in images: a flat area of the picture gives zero, and a sudden jump from dark to bright gives a big output. Same structure as the moving average, just one sign flipped, and the filter type flips too.

Three-point moving average and the 50 Hz hum: Take y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])/3. Its zeros are the roots of z^2 + z + 1, which are e^(±j2π/3), on the unit circle at angles ±120 degrees. So the frequency ω = 2π/3 is blocked completely. Now pick the sampling rate fs = 150 Hz. The digital frequency for f hertz is ω = 2πf/fs, so 50 Hz becomes 2π/3. The 50 Hz mains hum from Bangladesh's power lines is wiped out! The gains at 0, 25, 50 and 75 Hz are 1, 0.667, 0 and 0.333.

Pole-zero intuition for filters: Remember lesson 21's distance picture, now on the unit circle. Walking around the circle from z = 1 (DC) to z = -1 (half the sampling rate) is walking up in frequency, with angle ω = 2πf/fs. A zero sitting on the circle kills the frequency at its angle. A pole sitting just inside the circle boosts the frequency at its angle. So for a low-pass, put poles near z = 1 and zeros near z = -1. For a high-pass, do the opposite. For a band-pass, put a pole pair near the circle at angle ±ω0.

Building a notch: For a notch, put a zero pair right on the circle at ±ω0, and a pole pair just inside at the same angle. The zeros dig a deep hole at ω0. The poles, being so close, fill the area around it back up, so the hole stays narrow and the rest of the spectrum is hardly touched. For example, to remove 50 Hz with fs = 1000 Hz, the angle is ω0 = 2π × 50/1000 = 0.1π, which is 18 degrees. This is how ECG machines in hospitals often clean out mains hum while keeping the heartbeat signal.

A first-order IIR smoother: The filter y[n] = (1 - a) x[n] + a y[n-1], with 0 < a < 1, is called exponential smoothing. Its H(z) = (1 - a)/(1 - a z^(-1)) has a pole at z = a, close to z = 1 when a is near 1. Its DC gain is (1 - a)/(1 - a) = 1. At ω = π the gain is (1 - a)/(1 + a). With a = 0.9 that is 0.1/1.9 ≈ 0.053, so fast jitter is cut to about 5 percent. Phones use simple smoothers like this to steady jumpy sensor readings, such as a battery percentage that would otherwise jump up and down.

All-pass filters: Put a zero exactly mirrored across the jω axis from a pole: H(s) = (s - a)/(s + a) with a > 0. For any ω, the distances from jω to the zero and to the pole are equal, so |H(jω)| = 1 everywhere. Only the phase changes. In discrete time, H(z) = (z^(-1) - a)/(1 - a z^(-1)) with |a| < 1 does the same. All-pass filters are used to correct phase, for example to equalise delays so that all frequencies of a signal arrive lined up together.

Real-life example 1, a mobile phone call: When you call your friend on Grameenphone, the old-style voice path keeps roughly the 300 to 3400 Hz band. That is a band-pass filter. The upper limit also acts as the anti-aliasing filter from lesson 18, so that sampling at 8 kHz is safe, since 3.4 kHz is below 4 kHz. Your voice is still easy to understand, because most of the information in speech sits inside that band.

Real-life example 2, sound systems and medical monitors: The bass and treble knobs on a speaker or a car stereo are simple low-shelf and high-shelf filters, boosting or cutting low or high frequencies. In a hospital, an ECG monitor uses a high-pass to remove slow drift from breathing, a low-pass to remove muscle noise, and often a 50 Hz notch for mains hum. Even a phone camera uses filters: blurring a photo is a two-dimensional low-pass, and sharpening it boosts the high frequencies.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students think -3 dB means half the amplitude. It means half the power, so the amplitude is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. They mix ω in rad/s with f in Hz and forget the 2π. They forget that ideal filters are non-causal. They forget to convert hertz to a digital angle with ω = 2πf/fs. Typical questions: name the filter type from H or from a pole-zero plot, find the cutoff of an RC circuit, compute gains in dB, find the frequency response of a moving average, and find which frequency a zero on the unit circle removes.

Course recap, part 1, the time domain: We started with signals as functions of time and systems as boxes. We classified signals as periodic or not, even or odd, energy or power. We met the building blocks u(t), δ(t), exponentials and sinusoids, and their discrete cousins. We shifted, flipped and scaled signals. We tested systems for memory, causality, invertibility, linearity, time invariance and stability. Then the big idea: an LTI system is completely described by its impulse response h, and the output is the convolution y = x * h. Differential and difference equations gave us real LTI systems.

Course recap, part 2, the frequency domain: Complex exponentials pass through LTI systems changed only by a gain, so we broke signals into sinusoids with Fourier series and the Fourier transform. Convolution became multiplication, Y = H X. The frequency response H(jω) told us gain and phase at every frequency, in decibels and Bode-style plots. Sampling showed us that a sampled spectrum repeats every fs, so we need fs > 2 fmax to avoid aliasing. The DTFT gave discrete signals their own spectrum, periodic in 2π.

Course recap, part 3, the s and z worlds: The Laplace transform extended Fourier with s = σ + jω and brought the ROC. Poles and zeros became a map of the system: left half-plane poles decay, right ones grow. Transfer functions let us solve circuits, join blocks in series, parallel and feedback, and describe first and second order systems with τ, ωn and ζ. The Z-transform did the same for sequences, with z^(-1) as a delay. Stability became one picture: poles left of the jω axis, or inside the unit circle, joined by z = e^(sT). And today, all of it built filters.

Where this goes next: Digital Signal Processing (cse-5-7) takes these tools further: the DFT and FFT for computing spectra fast, windowing, and the real design of FIR and IIR filters, including Butterworth and Chebyshev designs. Data Communication (cse-3-6) uses them for modulation, bandwidth, noisy channels and line coding, where a channel is just a filter that the signal must pass through. Control systems build on transfer functions, feedback, poles and stability margins. Image processing uses two-dimensional convolution, where blur is a low-pass and edge detection is a high-pass. Even the convolutional neural networks of machine learning are built on convolution.

Final recap: A filter is an LTI system shaped in frequency: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop or notch, and all-pass. Ideal brick walls are non-causal, so real filters trade sharpness for order. An RC low-pass has fc = 1/(2πRC), -3 dB at cutoff and -20 dB per decade. Moving averages and differences are the simplest digital low-pass and high-pass filters, and zeros on the unit circle remove exact frequencies, like 50 Hz hum. Keep the big picture: h, H(jω), H(s) and H(z) are four views of the same system. Well done for finishing Signals and Systems!
key_points: A filter is an LTI system chosen for its frequency response: passband, stopband, transition band and cutoff frequency.
Types: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop (notch), and all-pass (gain 1 at all frequencies, only phase changes).
The ideal brick-wall low-pass has a sinc impulse response, which is non-causal and infinitely long, so it cannot be built in real time.
RC low-pass H = 1/(1 + jωRC): fc = 1/(2πRC), |H| = 0.707 (-3 dB, half power) at cutoff, -20 dB per decade, -45° phase at cutoff.
RC high-pass H(s) = sRC/(1 + sRC) has a zero at s = 0, so it blocks DC.
Two-point moving average: |H| = |cos(ω/2)| (low-pass, zero at z = -1); two-point difference: |H| = |sin(ω/2)| (high-pass, zero at z = 1).
Zeros on the unit circle remove the frequency at their angle ω = 2πf/fs; poles just inside the circle boost it. A 3-point average at fs = 150 Hz removes 50 Hz.
Next courses: DSP (DFT/FFT, FIR/IIR design), Data Communication (modulation, channels), control systems (feedback, stability), image processing (2D convolution).
lessons.tip: Make a one-page course map: four boxes labelled h(t) or h[n], H(jω), H(s) and H(z), with arrows showing how to go between them (convolution, Fourier, Laplace, Z, s = jω, z = e^(jω), z = e^(sT)). If you can redraw that page from memory, you understand this course.
lessons.task: Write a short loop (in Python, a spreadsheet, or by hand) that applies the 3-point moving average to x[n] = sin(2π × 50 × n/150) and to x[n] = sin(2π × 10 × n/150), for n = 0 to 20. Compare the outputs after the first few samples: the 50 Hz signal should vanish completely, and the 10 Hz signal should pass through with only a small loss.

quiz.q: What is the cutoff frequency of an RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 μF?
At the -3 dB point of a filter, what is the amplitude gain?
quiz.explain: -3 dB means the power is halved, so the amplitude is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, not 0.5.

quiz.q: What kind of filter is y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1])/2?
options: A low-pass filter with a zero at z = -1
A band-stop filter that blocks DC
quiz.explain: |H(e^(jω))| = |cos(ω/2)| is 1 at DC and 0 at ω = π, because of the zero at z = -1, so it is a low-pass.

quiz.q: Why can an ideal brick-wall low-pass filter not be built for real-time use?
options: Its sinc impulse response starts before t = 0 and lasts forever, so it is non-causal
Its poles are in the right half-plane
quiz.explain: The inverse transform of a rectangle is sin(ωc t)/(πt), which is non-zero for t < 0 and infinitely long, so the filter would need future input.

quiz.q: Which filter passes all frequencies with gain 1 but changes the phase?
quiz.explain: An all-pass filter, like (s - a)/(s + a), has |H(jω)| = 1 for every ω and only shifts the phase.
